provisions.heading: Admit the System Identity on Every System-Run Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `system-access-missing` for a reaction or job that runs, commands, or queries a use case whose access admits no system identity, and `record-invalid` for `runsAs` beside a `system` or `anonymous` grant.
provisions.statement: A use case that a reaction or a job runs, commands, or queries MUST admit the system identity: its grant is `system` or `anonymous`, or it states `runsAs: system` beside its grant for person callers.
provisions.rationale: A reaction or a job runs with no person behind it, so the call it sends carries the system identity. The guard authorizes every call from the use case's access, and a permission, self, or signed-in grant admits only people, so every system run of such a use case is refused at runtime. Stating `runsAs: system` beside the person grant admits the system identity too, and a use case that only system triggers run takes the `system` grant with no `runsAs`.
provisions.example: Claimwick's erase-personal-data use case grants `permission/remove-personal-data` to finance staff and states `runsAs: system`, so the nightly erase job runs it beside them. Without `runsAs`, every nightly run is refused.

provisions.heading: Authenticate Every Caller Through a Declared Authentication Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an `authentication` kind outside session, token, device, link, app, and none.
provisions.statement: Each entry point MUST name its authentication kinds from session, token, device, link, app, and none.
provisions.rationale: The authentication kind says how the caller proves identity before the grant is checked: a session for a signed-in person, a device for a managed scanner, a link for a single-purpose link, an app for a calling application, a token for a bearer token, and none for open calls. Without a declared kind, open calls and authenticated calls look alike, and a reviewer cannot tell which identity the grant was checked against.
provisions.example: An expense submission names `session`, a library self-checkout kiosk names `device`, and a public catalog names `none`.

provisions.heading: Authorize Every Use Case Through a Declared Grant
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a grant outside permission, self, signed-in, anonymous, and system, and `reference-unknown` for a permission no record defines.
provisions.statement: Each access declaration MUST name its grant as a permission, a self grant, signed-in, anonymous, or system.
provisions.rationale: The grant is the check the call passes: a permission for role-held action, a self grant for action on records the caller owns, signed-in for an authenticated caller with no permission, anonymous for open calls, and system for work an internal trigger runs with no outside caller. A grant outside these five forms gives the checker no stated check to enforce, so each caller invents its own test. System never authorizes an outside request, and a call with no authentication where one is needed ends in the derived unauthenticated result. Settled by [decision/0079-cover-the-behavior-reviewers-found-missing](decision/0079-cover-the-behavior-reviewers-found-missing) and [decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order](decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order).
provisions.example: `permission/manage-copies` guards staff work, `self(permission/read-loans)` lets a reader read their own loans, `signed-in` opens a workspace to any signed-in person with no permission, `anonymous` opens a public catalog, and `system` covers an archive use case only its retention job runs.

provisions.heading: Cite the Setting or Plan Behind Every Entitlement
provisions.evidence: Does every entitlement grant cite its setting or plan? Check each grant beside the settings its use case cites.
provisions.statement: A grant that depends on a setting or a plan MUST cite that setting or plan.
provisions.rationale: An entitlement allows one tenant what another is refused, so the grant alone reads as unequal treatment. Citing the setting or plan shows the commercial or configured reason behind the difference, and gives the reviewer the range and setter to judge it against.
provisions.example: An export command cites the caller's plan, so a tenant past its plan limit is refused by the plan rather than by role.

provisions.heading: Declare Access on Every Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a use case without `access`, `grant`, or `tenant`.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST declare its grant and its tenant scope in `access`.
provisions.rationale: The grant and the tenant scope answer the two access questions together: what check the call passes, and which tenant data it may touch. A use case missing one part leaves that question to code, and two implementations of the same record enforce different boundaries. The entry point the call arrives through declares how the caller proved identity.

provisions.heading: Declare Erasure for Every External System
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an external system without `erasure` and `reference-unknown` for an unsupported, manual or not-applicable erasure without an Intent decision.
provisions.statement: An external system MUST declare how personal data it holds is erased in `erasure`.
provisions.rationale: Personal data sent outside stays outside unless some operation or event removes it. The erasure declaration states the call, the integration event, or why removal does not run. An unsupported, manual, or not-applicable erasure cites the Intent decision that accepts the limit, so the gap reads as an accepted decision rather than a missed edge.
provisions.example: A payout archive declares `{"mode": "unsupported", "reason": "settled payouts belong to the bank"}` with the decision that accepts the limit, plus the sentence employees see.

provisions.heading: Define Each Scope Level in the Glossary
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `scope-term-missing` for a role scope with no glossary term titled with the level and Scope.
provisions.statement: Each scope level a role names MUST have a glossary term titled with the level and Scope, stating what the level covers in this product.
provisions.rationale: A bare level such as `platform` or `tenant` reads the same in every product, and each product means a different reach by it. The glossary term states that reach once, so a reviewer reads what `platform` covers in this product rather than guessing it from the word. Proposed by [decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once](decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once).
provisions.example: Claimwick's `platform` scope has a glossary term, Platform Scope, that states it covers every expense in the Claimwick installation.

provisions.heading: Describe Every Served Content Entry with Its Serving Fields
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a served content entry without path, contentType, cacheControl, versioning, or fulfills.
provisions.statement: Each served content entry on a browser entry point MUST carry path, contentType, cacheControl, versioning, and fulfills.
provisions.rationale: Served content is a file the product hands out, not behavior it runs, so the serving fields are the whole contract: where it lives, what it is, how long it caches, how it versions, and which requirement it carries. Without them, a legal text or a static script ships as an unreviewed file with no stated requirement or freshness.
provisions.example: A terms text carries its path, `text/html`, its cache window, its version rule, and the requirement it fulfills.

provisions.heading: Evaluate Access in One Order
provisions.evidence: Does every call evaluate principal, assignments, permission, tenant scope, ownership, and delegation in that order? Walk one allowed and one refused call through the steps.
provisions.statement: Access MUST be evaluated in one order: the authenticated principal, then the role assignments whose bound scope instance matches the target, then the permission, then the use case tenant scope, then the self-ownership restriction, then delegation validity, with several assignments combining as a union.
provisions.rationale: Each step narrows what the next step checks: identity before assignments, assignments before the permission they carry, the permission before the reach it is used at, and ownership and delegation last as restrictions on an otherwise allowed call. One order means two implementations allow and refuse the same calls. A role assignment binds a scope instance as well as a level: the tenant the hold reaches, or the person for a self grant. Several assignments combine as a union: any assignment that allows the call allows it. Settled by [decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order](decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order).
provisions.example: A Claimwick approver holds the approver role for one cost center. A call to approve an expense evaluates as the session principal, then the approver assignment whose cost center matches the expense, then the approve-expense permission, then the own tenant scope, then ownership and delegation. An assignment for another cost center does not match, so the call ends in the derived forbidden result.

provisions.heading: Grant Across Tenants Only Through Declared Delegation
provisions.evidence: Does every cross-tenant delegation grant declare its grant on both sides? Check the delegation grants the tenancy extension declares.
provisions.statement: A grant that acts across tenants through delegation MUST declare its delegation grant on both sides.
provisions.rationale: Delegation lets one actor act for another, so a grant on one side alone leaves the other side unreviewed. Declaring the grant on both sides shows who may delegate and who may be acted for, and the tenancy extension states the fields each side carries.
provisions.example: An assistant acts for a manager only where the manager delegation grant and the assistant acting grant both name the pairing.

provisions.heading: Grant Permissions Through Roles
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a permission with no `grantedTo` entry or a role with no `excludes`, `permission-unused` for a permission no role grants, and `role-unused` for a role no permission names.
provisions.statement: Each permission MUST name the roles that grant it in `grantedTo`, with each role's `excludes` stating what the grant does not cover.
provisions.rationale: The grant is the middle of the chain: it joins the actors that hold the role to the use cases that cite its permissions in their grants. Every link points from the lower or later record to the higher or earlier one, so the permission in Behavior names its Intent roles in `grantedTo` instead of the role naming the permission. A role that no permission names grants nothing, so every use case its holders run breaks the chain at the middle link. The `excludes` state the acts inside the role's scope that the grant does not cover, so a reader sees the edge of the grant on the role itself.
provisions.example: `permission/request-expense` names `role/employee` in `grantedTo`, and the submit use case cites that permission in its grant.

provisions.heading: Keep Permission Sets to Entries
provisions.evidence: Does the explanation beside each permissions file state only risks and boundaries, without restating a meaning, adding a grant, or naming a future role? Check the Risk and Boundaries sections beside each permissions file.
provisions.statement: A module permissions file MUST hold permission entries only, and its explanation states only the risks and boundaries of those entries in `excludes`, without restating a permission's meaning or adding a grant.
provisions.rationale: Each permission is defined once, in its entry: its `meaning` is the one statement of what it allows, and prose that repeats it drifts from the entry. A boundary is what a reader might assume a permission allows but it does not, which the meaning does not say, so `excludes` states what the set does not allow and the explanation holds what the entries cannot. A permission that guards a query or use case disclosing personal or financial data carries the `personal-data` or `access` risk, like a permission for a write. Proposed by [decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once](decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once). Settled by [decision/0079-cover-the-behavior-reviewers-found-missing](decision/0079-cover-the-behavior-reviewers-found-missing).

provisions.heading: Limit the Age of a Sign-In
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a `recentSignIn` that is neither an ISO 8601 duration nor a `setting/` identifier, or that names a setting of another value type, and `reference-unknown` for a setting no record defines.
provisions.statement: A use case that requires a recent sign-in MUST state the window in `recentSignIn` as an ISO 8601 duration or a `setting/` identifier.
provisions.rationale: Some operations need a fresh sign-in: changing a sign-in method or approving a large payout on a week-old session is not the same as doing it just after signing in. A window one use case needs is stated beside it as a duration. A window several use cases share lives in a setting that states its range and setter, and every use case that needs it names the same setting instead of typing its own duration. A call whose sign-in is older than the window ends in the derived sign-in-too-old result. Settled by [decision/0074-declare-access-settings-and-deadlines](decision/0074-declare-access-settings-and-deadlines).
provisions.example: Claimwick reimbursement states `recentSignIn: PT15M`; a session older than fifteen minutes ends in the derived sign-in-too-old result. A payout approval sharing the product window names `setting/spending.sign-in-window` instead and names the setting in `reads`, as `litespec/core/use-cases#name-the-settings-each-use-case-reads` states.

provisions.heading: Model a Hosted Sign-In as Use Cases
provisions.evidence: Does every hosted sign-in run as start and complete use cases against the provider external system, with anonymous grants and declared provider calls? Check the sign-in use cases beside the provider system.
provisions.statement: A sign-in through a hosted identity provider MUST be modeled as use cases that start and complete the sign-in, with the provider as an external system.
provisions.rationale: A product that signs people in through a hosted identity provider runs OpenID Connect with PKCE through its backend for frontend: the browser never holds provider tokens. The start use case builds the provider redirect with its PKCE challenge, and the complete use case exchanges the returned code, validates the tokens, finds or creates the person, and starts the session. The provider is an external system declaring its authorize, token, and logout operations, and the two use cases declare `calls` edges to the operations they use, under `litespec/core/backend-application#dispatch-only-declared-effect-edges`. Both use cases carry the `anonymous` grant, since the caller is not signed in yet, and arrive through the browser entry point whose `authentication` declares the session. Settled by [decision/0103-dotnet-stack-binding](decision/0103-dotnet-stack-binding).
provisions.example: Claimwick signs employees through its hosted provider: `use-case/identity.start-sign-in` builds the redirect, `use-case/identity.complete-sign-in` exchanges the code and starts the session, and `external-system/identity-provider` declares the authorize, token, and logout operations the two use cases call.

provisions.heading: Name Each Permission by a Use-Case Verb
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `permission-verb-unknown` (level G) for a permission name whose opening verb is neither in the table, nor a glossary verb of kind command or either, nor `manage`.
provisions.statement: Each permission name SHOULD open with a verb from the use-case verb table, a glossary verb of kind command or either, or with `manage`.
provisions.rationale: The first word of a permission name tells a reader whether the grant reads or changes, and which kind of use case it covers. A name such as `handle-documents` says nothing about what it includes, so a reader cannot tell whether it reads, writes, or removes. The verb table gives each opening word one meaning across the product, and a project verb carries its kind in its glossary verb term, so a permission opens with a command or either verb from either list. The opening verb is a naming convention only: no permission implies another by its name, and `manage-` grants nothing beyond the use cases that cite the permission. Proposed by [decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once](decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once), and glossary verbs by [decision/0062-declare-project-verbs-in-the-glossary](decision/0062-declare-project-verbs-in-the-glossary). Settled by [decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order](decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order) and [decision/0087-keep-prose-checks-advisory-and-names-per-type](decision/0087-keep-prose-checks-advisory-and-names-per-type).
provisions.example: `permission/approve-expense` opens with `approve` and `permission/manage-policy` opens with `manage`, so both pass. `permission/submit-expense` opens with the glossary verb `submit` and passes. `permission/handle-documents` opens with a word neither list states, so it is reported.

provisions.heading: Name Every Actor with Its Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an actor without `kind` and `record-invalid` for a kind outside person, organization, and system.
provisions.statement: An actor MUST name its kind in `kind`.
provisions.rationale: The kind says whether a human, an organization, or an outside system stands behind the actor, and that decides who answers for what the actor does. Without it, a reviewer assigns responsibility without knowing who stands behind the actor. A `system` actor stands for one outside system in flow steps, and that system's record names the actor in `represents`.
provisions.example: An employee actor carries `person`, the library as a lending party carries `organization`, and the text gateway standing in a flow step carries `system`.

provisions.heading: Name Every Authorization Precondition
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a precondition of another rule kind or one the use case cites nowhere in its steps, inputs, or results, and `reference-unknown` for a precondition no rule holds.
provisions.statement: Each `preconditions` entry MUST name a rule of kind `precondition` that the use case also cites.
provisions.rationale: An authorization condition the behavior does not state lives in prose beside the definition: each definition restates it, and the copies drift from the behavior they guard. Naming a precondition rule the use case already cites keeps one rule with one refusal, evaluated by authorization before the behavior runs and by the behavior itself.
provisions.example: Claimwick approve-expense names `rule/expense.approver-is-not-submitter` in `preconditions`. The rule is kind `precondition`, the use case cites it in its steps, and a call the rule refuses ends in the rule's refusal.

provisions.heading: Name the Caller Identity of a Self Scope
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for `scope` without `identityInput` or `identityInput` without `scope`, for an identity input naming no input or carrying another origin, and for an identity input identifying no actor, and `reference-unknown` for an identity input whose `identifies` names no record.
provisions.statement: A use case declaring `scope: self` MUST name its caller-identity input in `identityInput`, with `origin: verified-claim` identifying an actor.
provisions.rationale: A scope without its identity input leaves the guard guessing which value is the caller: each handler compares its own field with the verified identity, and each comparison is authorization logic sitting in a handler. Naming the verified input beside the scope gives the guard the one value to compare the target with.
provisions.example: Claimwick list-expenses declares `scope: self` with `identityInput: employee`, and its employee input carries `origin: verified-claim` identifying `actor/employee`. A call lists only that employee's own expenses.

provisions.heading: Prove Hierarchies Derived Trust and Delegation with Scenarios
provisions.evidence: Does every hierarchy, trust, or delegation pattern carry an allowed and a refused scenario? Check the scenarios on the use cases that carry the pattern.
provisions.statement: A hierarchy, derived trust, or delegation pattern MUST prove its allowed and refused calls with scenarios.
provisions.rationale: These patterns compose the same access parts into wider reach, so prose alone cannot show where the wider grant stops. Scenarios that walk an allowed call and a refused call pin the boundary as checked facts, and the checker confirms each one through the public boundary.
provisions.example: A delegation story shows an assistant acting for a manager succeeding, and the same assistant acting without delegation ending in the derived forbidden result.

provisions.heading: Record a Delegated Grant Inside One Tenant as a Role Assignment
provisions.evidence: Does every delegated or temporary grant inside one tenant sit on a role assignment with `validFrom`, `validUntil`, and the bound scope instance on an aggregate the access model reads, with its own granting and revoking use cases? Check the assignments beside the actor holds and the use cases that act under them.
provisions.statement: A delegated or temporary grant inside one tenant MUST be recorded as a role assignment with a validity window in `validFrom` and `validUntil` and the bound scope instance, held on an aggregate the access model reads and granted and revoked by its own use cases.
provisions.rationale: Inside one tenant, delegation changes who holds a role for a time, not which grant forms exist. Recording the assignment with its window on an aggregate the access model reads gives the guard one stated source for the deputy, the role, and the dates, and the granting and revoking use cases make the start and the end reviewable acts. A use case acting under the assignment declares its permission as usual, so no new access form appears. The assignment binds the scope instance the deputy reaches, the tenant or team, beside the dates. The tenancy extension adds only the cross-tenant form of delegation; it adds no form inside one tenant. Settled by [decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order](decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order).
provisions.example: In Claimwick, a manager delegating team management to a deputy for 2026-12-20 to 2027-01-05 is recorded as an assignment of the manager role to the deputy, bound to the manager's team, with `validFrom` of 2026-12-20 and `validUntil` of 2027-01-05, granted by its own grant use case and ended by its own revoke use case. The manage use case acting under it still declares `permission/manage-team`.

provisions.heading: Record Every Role an Actor Holds
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `role-unused` for a role held by no actor, and `record-invalid` for a hold that is not a role identifier, such as a hold carrying a scope.
provisions.statement: An actor that acts through a role MUST list the role's identifier in `holds`.
provisions.rationale: The hold is what connects an actor to its grant. Without it, the actor and the role sit on separate pages with no stated connection, and no reviewer can tell what the actor may do. The hold names only the role, because the role holds the scope of its grant, and one actor's hold cannot widen or narrow the reach the role states. Proposed by [decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once](decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once).
provisions.example:
```json
"holds": ["role/employee"]
```

provisions.heading: Remove a Target That Must Be the Caller
provisions.evidence: Which use cases name a caller-owned target in their inputs without a self grant the guard enforces, or compare the caller with a target in a handler? Check their inputs and handlers beside the self grants.
provisions.statement: A message whose target must be the caller MUST carry no target and act on the caller, or declare a self grant that the authorization guard enforces.
provisions.rationale: A target that must equal the caller is a value the caller could forge. Each handler would compare it with the verified identity, and each comparison is authorization logic sitting in a handler. Carrying no target leaves nothing to forge: the call acts on the caller from verified claims. Where the target must stay on the message, a self grant states the scope beside the use case, and the guard enforces it.
provisions.example: "My loans" lists the signed-in reader's loans and takes no reader id.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Grant to Its Tenant Reach
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a tenant scope outside own, cross, public, and none.
provisions.statement: Each access declaration MUST name its tenant scope as own, cross, public, or none.
provisions.rationale: The tenant scope bounds which tenant data the call may touch: `own` stays inside the caller tenant, `cross` reaches across tenants, `public` works beyond tenant boundaries, and `none` touches no tenant data. Without the scope, a read inside one tenant and a read across all tenants look the same, and the widest reach hides inside the narrowest grant.
provisions.example: An expense report names `own`, a staff search across tenants names `cross`, a public catalog names `public`, and a health check names `none`.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Role to Its One Reach
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a role without `scope` and `record-invalid` for a scope outside kebab-case form. A `scope` on a permission entry or on a hold fails the schema as an unknown property.
provisions.statement: A role MUST name its one scope in `scope`.
provisions.rationale: The role is the only home of a grant's reach. The same permission allows platform-wide action in one grant and own-record action in another, so the scope decides what each grant actually reaches. Stating the reach on each hold or each permission as well would keep three copies of one value, and the copies would drift apart, so the role states it once and every permission reads its reach from the roles that grant it. Without a named scope, every grant reads as product-wide, and the narrowest grant gets the widest reach. Proposed by [decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once](decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once).
provisions.example: A scope of `team` bounds the role to one team, while `platform` bounds it to the whole product.

provisions.heading: State Every Permission with Its Meaning
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a permission without `meaning`.
provisions.statement: A permission MUST state what it allows in `meaning`.
provisions.rationale: The `meaning` is the one sentence a reviewer reads to decide whether the grant fits the role. A name alone carries no boundary: two permissions with the same name pattern and no meanings drift into overlapping grants that no audit can separate.
provisions.example: `permission/request-expense` carries "Submit an expense for reimbursement."

provisions.heading: Use Three Conventional Scope Levels
provisions.evidence: Does every role scope use `platform`, `tenant`, or `self`, or a recorded project convention? Check `scope` on each role page.
provisions.statement: Use `platform`, `tenant`, and `self` as role scopes.
provisions.rationale: Three levels cover the grants most products need: product-wide administration, tenant-wide operation, and action on one's own records. A project with different boundaries names its own levels, and every role still carries exactly one scope.

provisions.heading: Advise Without Gating
provisions.evidence: Does the agent output record findings as advice with evidence, with decisions left to the owner? Check the output beside the changed records.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST report its findings as advice with evidence, never as a decision.
provisions.rationale: Decisions belong to the owner: the pull request that changes a record is its review. An agent that records a decision spends authority it was never given. Advice with evidence lets the owner decide faster without moving the decision to the agent.

provisions.heading: Apply Guidance Precedence
provisions.evidence: Does the design apply the project waiver, the extension, the deeper page, and the shallower page in that order? Check the design beside the overlapping guidance.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST apply the project waiver, the extension, the deeper page, and the shallower page in that order.
provisions.rationale: Overlapping guidance is normal: a project waiver narrows a shared provision, an extension replaces a baseline default, and a stack page refines its area page. Without a fixed order, two agents resolve the same overlap differently and the workspace drifts. The order puts the most local decision first, so the broader baseline fills only the gaps it leaves.

provisions.heading: Check Your Own Change Before Handing It Back
provisions.evidence: Does the completion report name the build, model check and analyzers run for the changed paths, each result, and the behavior the agent exercised? Check the report beside the changed paths and the commands it names.
provisions.statement: Before reporting done, an agent, including a worker under another agent, MUST run the narrowest build and model check for the paths it changed, let the configured analyzers run in that build, exercise each behavior change once as `litespec/core/agent#exercise-changed-use-cases-through-the-running-stack` states, and report each command with its result.
provisions.rationale: A worker that hands back code without running its own narrow gates returns compile errors and failing checks for the caller to find. The caller then spends its review on mechanical failures instead of the change. Running the gates on the changed paths catches those failures where the context is freshest, and naming each command and result lets the caller see what actually ran.
provisions.example: After changing one Claimwick command handler, an agent builds the backend project, runs `litespec model check`, submits an expense through the seeded stack, and lists each command with its result in the completion report.

provisions.heading: Exercise Changed Use Cases Through the Running Stack
provisions.evidence: Does the completion report name the seed, walker or direct call for each changed use case and what it showed, and does it call a build-only change unexercised? Look at the report beside the changed use cases.
provisions.statement: Before reporting done, an agent MUST exercise each use case the change affects through the running stack, by the seed, the API walker or a direct call, and state in the completion report what it ran and what it saw, reporting a change verified only by build as unexercised.
provisions.rationale: A build and a passing test show that code compiles and a chosen case passes, not that the endpoint, the handler and the screen agree at runtime. A change can leave an event with no handler, a command needing an id no read returns, or a screen reading less than it shows, and none of those fails a build. Running the changed use case on the seeded stack puts the whole path under the report's evidence, and saying what ran and what was seen lets the owner tell an exercised change from a build-only one.
provisions.example: After changing Claimwick's submit-expense use case, an agent seeds the client-visit scenario, calls the endpoint with Ava's 48.90 EUR fare and reads the approval list back, then reports the request and the returned expense in its completion report. An agent that only ran `dotnet build` reports the change as unexercised.

provisions.heading: Follow the Record, Not the Neighbour
provisions.evidence: Does each new code shape trace to a record and its provisions, with the neighbour used only for style and each contradiction reported? Check the change beside the cited records and the neighbours it read.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST shape new code from the record and the provisions, use a neighbouring file only for style, and follow the record and report the neighbour when the two contradict.
provisions.rationale: A neighbouring file shows the names and idioms this project chose, but it can hold an older or local rule. Copying it spreads one rule into several homes, and the copies drift from the record. The neighbour is not authority: the record is decided Intent, and a contradiction is a defect for the owner to see.
provisions.example: A Claimwick handler's neighbour reads a rate from configuration while the rule record cites dated reference data. The agent reads the rate from the cited reference data and reports the neighbour as out of date.

provisions.heading: Inspect Existing Work Before Editing
provisions.evidence: Does `git status` output precede the edits, with user changes, untracked files, and unrelated generated output untouched? Check the session log beside the working tree.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST read `git status` before editing and preserve user changes, untracked files, and unrelated generated output.
provisions.rationale: A working tree can hold the user's own uncommitted edits, untracked files, and generated output from an unrelated task. An agent that edits without looking overwrites or deletes work outside its scope. Reading `git status` first marks that work as untouchable.

provisions.heading: Inspect Local Examples After Standards
provisions.evidence: Does the change name the neighboring files that shaped it after the standards? Check the change beside its neighbors.
provisions.statement: Inspect neighboring consumer files after loading applicable standards.
provisions.rationale: Standards state the required shape, while neighboring files show the names, folders, and idioms this project chose for it. An agent that skips them writes compliant but foreign-looking code that the next edit rewrites.

provisions.heading: Keep Agent Working Files Under Agents
provisions.evidence: Does every agent working file sit under `.agents/` or the path the working-files convention names? Check the working files beside the convention.
provisions.statement: Keep agent working files under `.agents/`, with tracked `skills/` and `records/` folders and ignored `scratch/` and `delegate/` folders.
provisions.rationale: Agent work with no agreed home lands beside authored records, where it pollutes review, or vanishes with the session, where nobody can audit it. The split keeps durable work in `skills/` and `records/` and machine-local work in the ignored `scratch/` and `delegate/` folders.
provisions.example:
```text
.agents/
  skills/
  records/
  delegate/
  scratch/
```

provisions.heading: Keep the Agent Protocol Current
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `agent-protocol-drift` (level S) when the region differs from what `render` would write, `agent-protocol-missing` (level S) when `AGENTS.md` holds no region, and `skill-drift` (level S) when a project-scope skill copy differs from what the carried release generates.
provisions.statement: A project MUST keep its agent protocol region and its project-scope skill copies equal to what its LiteSpec release generates.
provisions.rationale: The region carries the commands and rules every session loads first. A stale region points agents at an old release, an old selection, or commands that changed, while the tool output stays current. The project-scope skill copies carry the same procedure to tools that load skills on demand, and a stale copy points at the same old release. The release template plus the project file regenerate the region and the project-scope skill copies in one command, so drift is always fixable. Global copies live outside the project and stay outside the check. Settled by [decision/0037-generate-the-agent-protocol](decision/0037-generate-the-agent-protocol) and [decision/0039-ship-a-litespec-skill](decision/0039-ship-a-litespec-skill).
provisions.example: Claimwick upgrades its LiteSpec release and runs `litespec model render`; the region in its `AGENTS.md` and its project-scope skill copies match what the new release generates.

provisions.heading: Load Applicable Extensions
provisions.evidence: Does the change name each extension loaded before editing inside its boundary? Check the change record beside the extensions the project selects.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST load selected project extensions and selected applicable local extensions before editing code or prose inside the extension's boundary.
provisions.rationale: An extension replaces baseline guidance inside its boundary. An agent that edits there without loading the extension follows the baseline the extension replaced, and the change contradicts the project's own selection.
provisions.example: A change to the cached catalog reads the selected caching extension before touching the code its boundary covers.

provisions.heading: Load Applicable Provisions Before Editing
provisions.evidence: Does the completion report answer every judgment provision `litespec rules --since <base>` listed? Compare the rules output with the report.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST run `litespec rules <path>` before editing a file and answer each judgment provision `litespec rules --since <base>` lists before reporting done.
provisions.rationale: Provisions are only usable when retrieved by situation: the query prints the record's contract card first, then what governs the change, grouped by strength, with project conventions and waivers merged in. Checked provisions collapse into one summary line that `litespec rules <...> --all` expands, and `litespec rules <...> --full` adds rationale and example when a statement is not enough. Settled by [decision/0038-narrow-rules-output-per-file-and-change-set](decision/0038-narrow-rules-output-per-file-and-change-set).
provisions.example: `litespec rules use-case/spending.submit-expense` prints the use case's contract card first, then the provisions that govern the change, grouped by strength.

provisions.heading: Make Coherent Scoped Changes
provisions.evidence: Does every changed artifact trace to the authorized request? Check the changed files beside the task text.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST make the smallest coherent change that satisfies the authorized request.
provisions.rationale: A change that stops at code and skips its records, tests, or operating evidence leaves the workspace claiming behavior nothing proves. A change that sprawls past the request drags unrelated files into review. The smallest coherent change keeps the records, code, tests, and evidence that belong together in one reviewable unit.

provisions.heading: Name Judged Provisions in the Completion Report
provisions.evidence: Does the completion report name every judged provision with its judgment? Check the report beside the provisions the query returned.
provisions.statement: A completion report MUST name each provision the agent judged and how it judged it.
provisions.rationale: The report shows which required provisions, defaults, and advisory provisions the change met and the judgment for each, so the owner checks the reasoning without re-reading the change. A provision the query returned but the report skips is a judgment nobody can check.
provisions.example: The report names each returned provision with its judgment: followed, replaced by a named convention, or parked by a waiver.

provisions.heading: Protect Proofs from Implementation Edits
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check --since <ref>` reports `proof-hash-drift` (level S) for each scenario whose proving test method changed since the base while the scenario did not.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST NOT delete, skip, or weaken a test that proves a scenario, or change its expected values, unless the scenario changed in the same change; it reports a test it believes is wrong instead of editing it.
provisions.rationale: A proof that changes with the implementation stops proving the decided behavior and starts restating the code. The proof ledger records each scenario's hash and the hash of each test that proves it, so `model check --since` can report, as a blocking finding, each scenario whose proving test changed while the scenario did not. Hashing the proving test method rather than its file keeps an unrelated edit in the same file from reporting a change. Settled by [decision/0033-agents-never-weaken-proving-tests](decision/0033-agents-never-weaken-proving-tests).
provisions.example: A handler change makes a proving test fail; the agent reports the failing test and the mismatch instead of changing the expected value to fit the new result.

provisions.heading: Raise a Spec Gap Instead of Bending the Code
provisions.evidence: Does each forced shape the agent met have a named concept and an owner question with a recommendation or a backlog item, with no code written around it? Check the completion report beside the gap and the code.
provisions.statement: When a check, a record type, or a provision forces a shape the domain does not have, an agent MUST stop, name the missing concept, and raise it as an owner question with a recommendation or a backlog item instead of writing code around it.
provisions.rationale: A check that accepts a rate table only as an external system, or a refusal with no record to hold it, pushes the agent to a substitute shape. The substitute compiles and passes the check while the real concept stays unmodelled, so the next agent copies it and the gap spreads. A missing concept is an open need: it travels up as a question to the owner with a recommendation or as a backlog item, as `litespec/core/layers#raise-open-needs-as-owner-questions-or-backlog-items` states, and the agent writes no code around it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's checks accept the per-diem rate table only as an external system, but the rates are figures the business changes while the system runs. The agent stops, names the missing concept of dated reference data, and raises a question to the owner with a recommendation instead of adding an external port the domain does not have.

provisions.heading: Read the Full Record Before Changing a Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does each file generation or boundary change cite the full record it matched? Check the change beside the cited records.
provisions.statement: Read the full record, the record file with its explanation file, before generating a file, changing a public boundary, or choosing between patterns.
provisions.rationale: Generating a file or changing a public boundary from a summary risks baking a paraphrase into a contract. The full record carries the exact fields, links, and wording the new surface matches. A small edit that follows an existing local pattern can rely on neighboring code instead.

provisions.heading: Replace Only Declared Conventions
provisions.evidence: Does each convention replacement resolve to a recorded local convention? Check the replacements beside the project documentation.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST apply a replacement for a convention only when the project documentation records that replacement.
provisions.rationale: Conventions exist to be replaced, but only through a recorded decision. An undocumented local preference that silently replaces a baseline default looks identical to a mistake, so the next agent fixes it back. The recorded convention keeps the replacement visible and reviewable.

provisions.heading: Restrict Unapproved Side Effects
provisions.evidence: Does an explicit task instruction naming the action and its bounds cover each consequential action beyond the task, or does the project's `AGENTS.md` grant the wider authority? Check the task text beside the actions taken.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST stay inside its authorized task and take no consequential action beyond it without an explicit task instruction that names the action and its bounds.
provisions.rationale: Inside the task, the agent applies an approved standard or decision, drafts records and proposed decisions, implements the change, and reports findings, including a failed check or a conflict between provisions. It approves no product-policy proposal of its own, widens no scope, invents no business value, and takes no consequential outside action beyond the task. Packages, migrations, authentication, a public API, production data, releases, spending, and outside calls that change state each need an explicit task instruction that names the action and its bounds, because none of them can be judged from the task text alone. A project may grant wider authority in its `AGENTS.md`. Settled by [decision/0086-set-one-agent-authority-boundary](decision/0086-set-one-agent-authority-boundary).
provisions.example: A task that names the migration and its scope approves it; a task silent on releases leaves a release unmade.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Convention to Files It Governs
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `convention-unreached` (level G) for a project convention whose Applies to matches no file in the project tree and no record.
provisions.statement: A project convention MUST state an Applies to that matches at least one file in the project tree or one record the project writes.
provisions.rationale: `rules` returns a convention only when its Applies to meets the queried path or record. A convention that meets nothing reaches no agent, so its rule stays unread while the project believes it is stated. One match keeps every stated convention live.
provisions.example: Claimwick records that every command handler logs its outcome, with `stack: dotnet; artifact: command-handler`; the convention meets each handler file, so `rules` returns it before an agent edits one.

provisions.heading: Search the Provisions Before Recording a Decision
provisions.evidence: Does any technical decision restate a choice a provision already makes? Compare each decision with the `rules` output for its subject.
provisions.statement: Query `litespec rules` for the decision's subject, and where a provision makes the choice, follow that provision instead of recording a decision.
provisions.rationale: Many technical choices are already decided: a provision names the shape, the baseline, or the boundary the code follows. A decision that restates such a choice splits authority between the provision and the record, and the two drift. Searching first keeps one home for each decided choice.
provisions.example: An agent about to record how Claimwick declares integration edges queries `litespec rules` for the subject; the provision declares every edge in a record, so the code follows it and no decision is recorded.

provisions.heading: Select Task Context
provisions.evidence: Does the completion report name the model query that selected the cited records, or the prose-only correction and the record it read? Check the report beside the cited records.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST query the project model for the records that cover the request, and read the query output, before changing behavior, access, a contract, or a trace link; a prose-only correction of an existing record needs only the record and its explanation file.
provisions.rationale: Without the query, an agent reads either too little and invents the missing rules, or half the repository and buries the task in unrelated guidance. The query returns the smallest record set that covers the request, with the links the builder joined between records, so the agent starts from decided Intent. A change that touches behavior, access, a contract, or a trace link always needs that set. A prose-only correction of an existing record needs no joined links: the record and its explanation file show the decided shape, and a query would slow ordinary work without adding information.
provisions.example: `litespec model query use-case/spending.submit-expense` returns the use case with its rules, results, and scenarios. A spelling fix in a setting record reads the record and its explanation file, then edits without querying the model.

provisions.heading: Stop on Unresolved Conflict
provisions.evidence: Does the stopped work quote the conflict with both provision IDs and paths? Check the handoff beside the disagreeing provisions.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST stop when applicable provisions disagree without declared precedence and quote both provision IDs and paths.
provisions.rationale: When two provisions disagree and no precedence decides, any continuation invents a compromise neither provision states. Stopping with both provision identifiers and paths hands the decision to a person with exactly the evidence the decision needs.

provisions.heading: Take Expected Values from the Scenario
provisions.evidence: Do each test's expected values match the scenario's Then, with none taken from a code run? Check the assertions beside the scenario Thens.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST take a test's expected values only from the scenario's Then, never from running the code.
provisions.rationale: Expected values read from a passing run restate what the code already does, so the test stays green while behavior drifts. The scenario's Then states the decided Intent, which makes the test check the behavior rather than copy it.
provisions.example: A scenario whose Then names a total of `42.50` keeps `42.50` as the asserted value even when the code returns `42.51`: the mismatch fails the test instead of updating the expectation.

provisions.heading: Verify Money Calculations and Refusals Against Held-Back Examples
provisions.evidence: Does the check log show money-risk refusal and calculation rows written by a different author, withheld during implementation, and run after? Check the log beside the withheld rows.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST verify a refusal or calculation implementation that carries the money risk against example rows held back from the agent that wrote it.
provisions.rationale: Money rules decide amounts a customer pays or receives, so fitting the code to the examples instead of the rule moves money. A different author than the implementing agent writes the held-back rows. They sit under `proof/withheld/`, which the implementing agent's instructions exclude. Their expected values cite the scenario's rule, and they run in CI. Teams apply the same ceremony to other refusals and calculations as good practice. The money risk is the risk on the permission guarding the use case. Settled by [decision/0085-bind-proof-to-code-and-outcomes](decision/0085-bind-proof-to-code-and-outcomes).
provisions.example: The implementing agent writes a discount calculation from its rule and scenario; a CI check runs the withheld rows from `proof/withheld/` against the result.

provisions.heading: Write Only Rules You Have Seen Hold
provisions.evidence: Does every rule the agent added to the agent file name the run or observation that showed it hold, with none written from assumption? Look at the added lines beside the session log.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST write a rule into the project's agent file only after seeing that rule hold, and a rule about a library's behavior only after running the library.
provisions.rationale: A rule in the agent file reads as decided guidance on every later task, so a guess about how a library behaves becomes an instruction every later agent follows. Running the behavior first gives the rule evidence the agent can name, and leaving an unverified rule out keeps the file to what the project knows.
provisions.example: Before adding a line to Claimwick's `AGENTS.md` about how its orchestrator starts the stack, an agent runs the start command and sees the hosts come up. It leaves out a line about a library's behavior until it has run that library and seen the result.

provisions.heading: Anchor the Audit Chain Outside Its Own Store
provisions.evidence: Does the store publish a checkpoint of head and count for each live segment where its own operators cannot rewrite it? Check the checkpoint destination and the threat model.
provisions.statement: An audit store SHOULD publish a periodic checkpoint of each live segment's chain head and record count to a destination that the store's own operators cannot rewrite.
provisions.rationale: A checkpoint fixes the chain as it stood when published: a reader who kept that checkpoint detects any later change to the records it covers. Records written after the checkpoint stay uncovered until the next checkpoint, so the interval between checkpoints bounds the window in which a rewrite goes unseen. A checkpoint the store's own operators can rewrite proves nothing against those operators. Only a checkpoint held where they cannot rewrite it, published or held by a third party, gives tamper evidence against them, and the adoption decision states whether the store publishes one.
provisions.example: The checkpoint is the chain head and its record count, published per segment at a stated interval. A separate append-only destination, a timestamping authority, and a transparency log each qualify.

provisions.heading: Audit Async Work at Request Time
provisions.evidence: Does every deferred run write its audit record when requested rather than when it runs? Check the audit rows beside the requesting calls.
provisions.statement: Work that runs after its request MUST write its audit record at request time.
provisions.rationale: The actor, the origin, and the grant exist when the request arrives; the later run carries worker identity under system auth, which says nothing about who asked. Writing the record at request time ties the attempt to the caller who made it. A record written when the background run starts would attribute every scheduled and deferred act to the worker instead of the requester.

provisions.heading: Audit Bulk Reads Inside One Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does every above-threshold query produce a record with the subject count? Check the bulk query paths.
provisions.statement: A query returning personal data for more subjects than its declared threshold MUST produce an audit record, inside one tenant or account boundary as well.
provisions.rationale: The cross-boundary rule catches a disclosure to the wrong party, but it misses an export of every record a party may read one at a time, which is the shape a copied dataset has. A query above the declared threshold therefore writes a record even inside one boundary. [Article 30 of the GDPR](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-30-gdpr/) asks what categories of data were processed and by whom, and an unrecorded bulk read answers neither.
provisions.example: Claimwick records the threshold in its adoption decision. A list endpoint whose page size can exceed it audits the read with the subject count rather than naming each subject.

provisions.heading: Audit Every Bulk Export
provisions.evidence: Does every export produce a record naming the requested scope? Check the export paths.
provisions.statement: An export that returns a set of records to a caller MUST produce an audit record naming the requested scope.
provisions.rationale: Bulk extraction is the highest-consequence read in most products: one call moves a dataset across the boundary. Naming the requested scope states what left the system. Without it, the project learns the shape of a leak from the party that received it.

provisions.heading: Audit Every Required Category
provisions.evidence: Does the declared selection cover all eight required categories? Check it against the eight categories this provision names.
provisions.statement: An audit selection MUST include authentication, authorization denial, grant change, monetary action, tenant configuration, personal-data read, bulk export, and background-process change.
provisions.rationale: Each listed category answers a question a security review, a customer, or a supervisory authority asks after an incident: who signed in, who was refused, who changed a grant, who moved money, and the rest. A trail that omits a category has no answer when that question arrives. The list sets the minimum so no project discovers the gap during its first review.

provisions.heading: Audit Only Selected Commands
provisions.evidence: Does every audited category carry a recorded selection reason? Check the declared selection.
provisions.statement: A project MUST NOT audit every Command without a recorded selection.
provisions.rationale: A trail that records every Command hides the sensitive action among routine traffic, and the reviewer who has to read it stops reading. Volume then defeats the review the trail exists to support. A recorded selection keeps the trail small enough to read.

provisions.heading: Audit Reads of the Trail
provisions.evidence: Does every completed trail read produce an audit record? Check the trail read path.
provisions.statement: A read of the audit trail MUST itself produce an audit record.
provisions.rationale: Reading the evidence is itself a sensitive action: the trail shows who did what across the whole product. A read that writes no record leaves the reviewer outside the trail. Recording each read puts the reviewer inside the same accountability as everyone else.

provisions.heading: Chain Records to Expose Tampering
provisions.evidence: Does every stored record carry the chained SHA-256 hash over the canonical serialization? Check the stored chain values.
provisions.statement: An audit store MUST chain each record to its predecessor in its segment with a SHA-256 hash over a canonical serialization of both.
provisions.rationale: The hash chain detects an edit and a removal, because a changed or missing record breaks every value after it. Detection is the obligation: it lets a reviewer prove the trail is intact. Prevention at a higher cost is not required. Each segment verifies from its own genesis record, so deleting a whole closed segment breaks no live link. The algorithm is named because two implementations that each choose their own cannot verify each other. A verifier written later cannot recompute a chain whose algorithm no one recorded. Canonical serialization is named for the same reason. A hash over a serialization that reorders fields verifies nothing.
provisions.example: The chain value is `SHA-256(previousHash || canonical(record))`, where `canonical` sorts object members and encodes every timestamp and number one fixed way.

provisions.heading: Commit a Success Record with Its Business Change
provisions.evidence: Does every succeeded record commit inside its business transaction? Check the success write path.
provisions.statement: An audit record with a `succeeded` outcome MUST commit in the same database transaction as the change it describes.
provisions.rationale: One transaction makes the action and its evidence inseparable: the change commits with its record or neither commits. Separate writes admit both an unrecorded action and a record of a rolled-back action. Either one leaves the trail disagreeing with the data it describes.

provisions.heading: Correct Mistakes with a New Record
provisions.evidence: Is every correction a new record that points at the earlier one? Check the correction records.
provisions.statement: A correction to the trail MUST be a new record that references the earlier one.
provisions.rationale: An edited history carries no evidential value, because the reviewer cannot tell a correction from a cover-up. A new record that references the earlier one keeps both visible: the mistake and its fix. The trail then shows its own repairs instead of hiding them.

provisions.heading: Declare Audit Details on the Command Type
provisions.evidence: Does every Command carry the declaration attribute with its action, target kind, category, and reason selector, or a recorded local convention? Check the Command types.
provisions.statement: Declare the action, target kind, category, and reason selector as an attribute on the Command type, beside the use-case `audit` field.
provisions.rationale: The declaration sits with the code it describes, so a review reads both at once. The use-case page carries the audit position or exemption, while the attribute carries the action, target kind, and category the producer writes. The reason selector names the message field holding the reason value, so the pipeline reads the declared reason without handler help. A selection kept in a separate file drifts from the Commands it names.

provisions.heading: Declare Which Commands Are Audited
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `audit-missing` for a command with neither an audit position nor an exemption, `record-invalid` for an audited command without its category, `audit-target-missing` for an audited command changing a record with no target, `audit-target-unknown` for a target naming no input, an input with no `identifies`, or no output field, and `audit-target-kind-drift` for a target kind differing from what a single target input identifies.
provisions.statement: Every command use case MUST declare its audit position in its `audit` field, or declare an exemption with its justification.
provisions.rationale: An audit selection that lives only in code is invisible: a reader cannot tell an unaudited command from an audited one whose call is missing. The `audit` field states a level of `required`, `optional`, or `none` with its target kind, its category from the fixed vocabulary when audited, and, when the command changes a record, the audited record in `target`: one input, a list of inputs forming a composite target, or the output field carrying it when the handler determines it, or an exemption with its justification, so each omission becomes a visible statement. A level of `none` means the command is not audited. `litespec/core/use-cases#state-the-audit-position-of-every-command` states the field, and review reads the declared positions instead of searching for missing calls. Every command writes the `audit` field.
provisions.example: A Claimwick command that lists public help pages declares an exemption, because reading public text is not a sensitive action.

provisions.heading: Delete Expired Records Through a Separate Operator Account
provisions.evidence: Does all retention deletion and tenant data erasure run through the operator process under its own account? Check the deletion job and the granted store privileges.
provisions.statement: An audit deployment MUST run retention deletion and tenant data erasure through a separate audited operator process under its own account.
provisions.rationale: The application account holds only `INSERT` and `SELECT`, so it cannot delete what retention ends. The operator process holds `DELETE` under its own account, deletes closed segments on schedule, and writes one deletion record per deleted segment. Tenant data erasure runs through the same process, so no application path deletes or removes audit data. Settled by [decision/0097-one-audit-chain-segment-per-category-and-year](decision/0097-one-audit-chain-segment-per-category-and-year).
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps sign-in denials for two years and expense records for seven. A nightly operator job deletes the closed segments whose retention ended and writes one deletion record per deleted segment, while the application account keeps only `INSERT` and `SELECT`.

provisions.heading: Delete Records When Their Retention Ends
provisions.evidence: Does any stored segment outlive its category's declared retention? Check the stored segments against the adoption decision.
provisions.statement: An audit deployment MUST delete a chain segment as a whole after the retention period declared for its category.
provisions.rationale: Each category declares its retention in the adoption decision, and the deployment deletes the category's closed segments when that period ends. A segment is closed with a final checkpoint before it is deleted as a whole, so the remaining segments still verify from their own anchors. Deleting on schedule keeps retention defensible: everything kept has a declared reason, and nothing kept lacks one. An indefinite period is the hardest retention to defend, and the easiest to fix while the design is still open.

provisions.heading: Enforce Append-Only Through Storage Privilege
provisions.evidence: Does any account except the operator deletion account hold update or delete on the audit store? Check the granted store privileges.
provisions.statement: An audit store MUST refuse update and delete through the privileges granted to every account except the operator account that deletes expired records.
provisions.rationale: An audit store that relies on absent code paths stays append-only until someone writes the missing path. Revoked privileges refuse update and delete no matter what the code tries. Retention deletion still needs a delete path, so the operator account that `litespec/core/audit#delete-expired-records-through-a-separate-operator-account` requires holds `DELETE`, and every other account holds neither update nor delete. A reviewer verifies a privilege in the database instead of auditing every line for a write that should not exist.
provisions.example: The application account holds `INSERT` and `SELECT` on the audit table, and it holds neither `UPDATE` nor `DELETE`. The operator account holds `INSERT` and `DELETE` on the same table and writes only through the deletion job.

provisions.heading: Exclude Derived Audit Trails
provisions.evidence: Does any trail write derive from events, triggers, or change capture? Check the producer source.
provisions.statement: An audit trail MUST NOT be derived from domain events, database triggers, or change data capture.
provisions.rationale: Domain events, triggers, and change data capture describe committed state change. They carry no refused attempt, no use-case identity, and no request origin, which are the fields a reviewer reads. A trail derived from them answers what changed and never who attempted it.

provisions.heading: Fail the Build for Commands Without an Audit Declaration
provisions.evidence: Does any Command build or start without an audit position or exemption? Check the build or startup gate.
provisions.statement: An automated check MUST fail when a Command declares neither an audit position nor an exemption, with a composition refusal at startup satisfying this rule.
provisions.rationale: The next Command is written by someone who did not read this page. Only an automated gate catches it: the build or startup fails while the declaration is missing. A selection that depends on every author remembering has gaps.

provisions.heading: Keep Audit Infrastructure in One Location
provisions.evidence: Does every audit part live in the documented location or the recorded local convention? Check under `Infrastructure/Auditing/`.
provisions.statement: Keep the audit record, its store, the producer, and the integrity job under `Infrastructure/Auditing/`.
provisions.rationale: The record, the store, the producer, and the integrity job form one evidence mechanism. One Infrastructure location keeps that mechanism reviewable as a whole instead of scattered across the codebase.

provisions.heading: Keep Secrets and Payment Data from the Trail
provisions.evidence: Does any stored record contain a secret or a payment instrument value? Check the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST NOT contain a secret, as `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data` states, or a payment instrument value.
provisions.rationale: The trail is retained, widely readable, and append-only, which is the worst combination for a secret: retention extends the exposure and append-only removes the repair. A credential or payment value written once stays readable for the whole retention period. Secrets and payment values therefore travel in the systems built to hold them, never in the trail.

provisions.heading: Keep State Copies from Audit Records
provisions.evidence: Does any stored record contain a before or after state copy? Check the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST NOT contain a copy of the state before or after the audited change.
provisions.rationale: The domain event stream already holds each change under its own retention. Copying before and after state into the trail duplicates that storage and widens every record with data the reviewer did not ask for. The trail adds the actor and the reason value, which nothing else holds, and leaves the change itself to the stream.

provisions.heading: Limit Personal Data to Actor and Target Identifiers
provisions.evidence: Does any stored record hold personal data beyond the pseudonymous actor and target identifiers? Check the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST NOT contain personal data other than the pseudonymous identifier of the actor and the target.
provisions.rationale: A record holding a name, an address, or a message body turns retention into an erasure conflict: the law asks for deletion and the trail asks for keeping. Pseudonymous identifiers keep the record meaningful while the mapping lives, and erasable once the mapping goes. The record then survives erasure instead of conflicting with it. A pseudonymous identifier is still personal data where the holder can reverse it, as [the EDPB states](https://edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-012020-processing-personal-data-context-art-6-1). The identifier is therefore safe inside the tenant that owns the mapping, and it becomes a disclosure when it leaves that tenant.
provisions.example: An audit export crossing a tenant boundary replaces each identifier with one derived for that export, so the receiving party cannot join the records back to a subject.

provisions.heading: Link Each Record to Its Operation Trace
provisions.evidence: Does every stored record carry the trace identifier of its operation? Check the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST carry the trace identifier of the operation that produced it.
provisions.rationale: The audit record states what was attempted, and the diagnostic log states what the software did while attempting it. The trace identifier joins the two, so an investigation moves from evidence to detail in one step. Without it, the investigation stops at the audit record and reconstructs the rest by time.

provisions.heading: Mark Actions Taken Under a Support Grant
provisions.evidence: Does every action taken under an administrative or support grant record that the grant was used? Check those records.
provisions.statement: An action that an actor takes under an administrative or support grant MUST record that the grant was used.
provisions.rationale: Support staff act inside customer data under a grant, and without a marker their actions read exactly like customer actions. The marker makes a no-silent-access commitment demonstrable: every supplier-side action says so on its own record. A reviewer who cannot separate the two cannot verify the commitment.

provisions.heading: Name Each Action After Its Use Case
provisions.evidence: Does every action value name the use case the actor invoked? Check the action column against the use case pages.
provisions.statement: An audit `action` MUST use the identity of the use case that the actor invoked.
provisions.rationale: A reviewer who reads an action value opens the specification of that use case to learn the intended behavior. A separate action vocabulary needs a mapping to those specifications, and the mapping drifts as both sides change. Reusing the use-case identity keeps record and specification joined with no mapping to maintain.
provisions.example: `catalog.add-product` is both the use case the actor ran and the value stored in the audit `action` field.

provisions.heading: Provide a Use Case That Reads the Trail
provisions.evidence: Does the trail read carry its access grant and its declared filters? Check the trail read use case.
provisions.statement: An audited system MUST provide a trail read as a use case with its access grant, filtered by tenant, actor, action, target, and outcome.
provisions.rationale: A trail no use case reads is storage, not a control. The read path is a use case with its own access grant: the actor holds a role whose scope reaches the records, the permission names the role in `grantedTo`, and the grant permits the read. Filters on tenant, actor, action, target, and outcome keep each reader inside the records they may see.

provisions.heading: Publish a Copy to the Security Platform
provisions.evidence: Does the local store stay authoritative, with each copy leaving through the recorded convention? Check the delivery path.
provisions.statement: Publish a copy of each record to an external security platform through the outbox, and keep the local store authoritative.
provisions.rationale: Delivery is at-least-once, while evidence needs one durable source. The local store stays authoritative for accountability and the published copy serves detection, so a lost copy never corrupts the evidence.

provisions.heading: Publish Unsuccessful Write Failures
provisions.evidence: Does the deployment publish a write failure count for the unsuccessful path? Check the published metrics.
provisions.statement: An audit deployment MUST publish the write failure count of its unsuccessful-outcome path.
provisions.rationale: The separate connection for unsuccessful records can lose a record when the process dies between the refusal and the write. Steady loss is a defect, and only a published count distinguishes it from a rare loss. The deployment publishes that count so monitoring can tell the two apart.

provisions.heading: Record Each Segment Deletion in the Following Segment
provisions.evidence: Does every deleted segment have its deletion record in the following segment? Check the deletion records against the retention schedule.
provisions.statement: An audit deployment MUST record each deleted chain segment as an audit record in the following segment of the same category.
provisions.rationale: A deleted segment leaves no rows, so without a record the trail cannot show what it removed. The deletion record states which segment was deleted with its record count and final checkpoint. The following year segment is still live, because it expires a year later, so it holds the record. Settled by [decision/0097-one-audit-chain-segment-per-category-and-year](decision/0097-one-audit-chain-segment-per-category-and-year).
provisions.example: Deleting the 2026 sign-in denial segment writes one record into the 2027 denial segment, naming the deleted segment with its count and final checkpoint.

provisions.heading: Record Every Attempt Outcome
provisions.evidence: Does every record carry a `succeeded`, `denied`, or `failed` outcome? Check the outcome column.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST carry an outcome of `succeeded`, `denied`, or `failed`.
provisions.rationale: A trail of successes is a change history, not evidence. The refused attempt carries the security signal, and the failed attempt carries the operating signal. Three outcomes keep both signals in the same trail as the successes they qualify. A validation refusal records `failed` with its refusal code; `denied` stays for a refused authorization, so recording a validation refusal as denied would accuse the actor of an access refusal they did not meet.
provisions.example: `succeeded` names a committed change, `denied` names a refused authorization, and `failed` names a permitted attempt that did not complete. In Claimwick, an expense refused for a missing receipt records `failed` with the receipt refusal code, while an approval by an actor without the permission records `denied` with the forbidden code.

provisions.heading: Record Failed Audited Attempts
provisions.evidence: Does every permitted attempt that threw produce a failed record? Check the error paths beside the trail.
provisions.statement: An audited action that the actor was permitted to take and that did not complete MUST produce an audit record.
provisions.rationale: A permitted attempt that throws is neither a success nor a refusal, and without a record it vanishes entirely. Writing it separates an operating defect from an access problem: failures cluster around broken behavior, denials cluster around missing permission. Support reads that split before opening the logs.

provisions.heading: Record Personal-Data Reads
provisions.evidence: Does every cross-boundary personal-data query produce a record? Check the query paths beside the trail.
provisions.statement: A query returning personal data across a boundary MUST produce an audit record, defining the account boundary in the adoption decision where tenancy is absent.
provisions.rationale: A read changes no state and therefore leaves no other trace, so a disclosure without a record cannot be investigated. The audit record on a cross-boundary personal-data query states who read whose data and when. Where tenancy is absent, the adoption decision defines the account boundary this rule watches.

provisions.heading: Record Refused Authorization
provisions.evidence: Does every refused authorization produce a denied record? Check the refusal paths beside the trail.
provisions.statement: An authorization decision that refuses an audited action MUST produce an audit record.
provisions.rationale: Repeated refusal is the first indicator of a compromised or probing account, and no other record holds it: nothing changed, so nothing else was written. Each refusal therefore writes its own record. A trail without refusals shows an attacker who never failed.

provisions.heading: Record the Audit Adoption Decision
provisions.evidence: Does the adoption decision behind the audited Commands name its categories, threshold, access model, integrity method, and records entry? Check that decision record.
provisions.statement: An audit adoption decision MUST record its audited categories, threshold, access model, integrity method, and records entry.
provisions.rationale: Which actions to audit, how long to keep them, and how to protect them are policy choices, so the project declares them once in the adoption decision. A reviewer reads the declared policy before reading the implementation instead of reconstructing it from the code, which would give two reviewers two different policies. The records entry declares where audit records live: the store that holds them and, where tenants exist, that authentication events live in the global trail apart from tenant activity.

provisions.heading: Record the Refusal Code on an Unsuccessful Attempt
provisions.evidence: Does every denied or failed record carry its refusal code? Check the unsuccessful audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record with a `denied` or `failed` outcome MUST carry the refusal `code` that the attempt produced.
provisions.rationale: A refused permission and an exhausted precondition need different responses, but both look like failure without a code.
