The refusal `code` tells the reviewer which one the attempt produced. It also lets trend queries count one kind of refusal across the whole trail. The operation, the outcome, and the refusal code stay separate fields, so a reviewer reads a validation refusal as a failed attempt, not as a denied access.

provisions.heading: Record the Request Origin
provisions.evidence: Does every record produced from an inbound request carry origin, client, and request identifier? Check the inbound-request audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record produced from an inbound request MUST carry the request origin address, the client description, and the request identifier.
provisions.rationale: Two records naming one account state nothing about location. The same account acting from two countries within one minute states that the account is compromised, but only when each record carries origin, client, and request identifier. The request identifier also joins the record to its exact request in the diagnostic log.

provisions.heading: Record the Required Audit Fields
provisions.evidence: Does every stored record carry actor, action, target, outcome, business time, record time, and tenant? Check the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST contain actor, action, target, outcome, business time, record time, and tenant, fixed where the tenancy extension is absent.
provisions.rationale: Actor, action, target, outcome, the two times, and the tenant together answer who attempted what, against whose data, with what result, and when. Business time states when the action happened and record time states when the evidence was written, so a delayed write stays visible as a delay. The actor carries its kind beside its identifier, and the target carries its own identity apart from the actor, keeping who acted and what was acted on in separate fields. A record missing any of them leaves the accountability question half answered.

provisions.heading: Remove the Identity Mapping on Erasure
provisions.evidence: Does every erasure remove the actor mapping while keeping each audit record? Check the erasure handling and the retained rows.
provisions.statement: An erasure request MUST remove the mapping from actor identifier to person and retain every audit record.
provisions.rationale: Erasure asks that the person stop being identifiable, while accountability asks that the record stay. Removing the mapping from identifier to person satisfies both: the record keeps its evidential value and no longer points at anyone. This works only because the record carries no other personal data.

provisions.heading: Restrict Handler Contribution to Determined Values
provisions.evidence: Does any handler contribution repeat the declared target, the reason value, the actor, the action code, or the timestamp? Check the handler audit calls.
provisions.statement: A handler MUST contribute only the audit values that the handler alone determines.
provisions.rationale: The declaration beside the message already fixes the audit target and the reason value the message carries, as `litespec/core/backend-application#declare-the-audit-target-and-reason-beside-the-message` requires, so the pipeline records both on every outcome, including a denial. Only the handler knows the values it learns while running, such as a generated target identity or a reason value composed from loaded state. Letting the handler write the rest invites a second copy of each field that drifts from the first.
provisions.example: A Claimwick handler that creates an expense contributes the expense identity it generated, and nothing else: no actor, action code, timestamp, or value the message already carries.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Record to Its Tenant
provisions.evidence: Is every record scoped to the right trail, with tenant data carrying its tenant identity and authentication events in the global trail? Check the tenant column and the global trail.
provisions.statement: Every audit record MUST carry the scope it belongs to: an action inside tenant-owned data carries the identity of that tenant, and an authentication event that belongs to no tenant lives in the global trail apart from tenant activity.
provisions.rationale: The tenant is the filter for every read of the trail: each customer reads its own records and no one else's. A record without a tenant identity serves an internal reviewer and no customer. Scoping every record at write time keeps that filter exact. Authentication events belong to no tenant: a sign-in attempt names an account, not a tenant, so those events live in the global trail apart from tenant activity, where a reviewer reads sign-in evidence without opening any tenant's data.

provisions.heading: Segment the Audit Chain by Category and Calendar Year
provisions.evidence: Does every audit record sit in the segment of its category and year, with its own genesis and checkpoints? Check the stored chain values.
provisions.statement: An audit store MUST hold one hash chain segment per audited category and calendar year, each with its own genesis record and checkpoints.
provisions.rationale: Deleting one category's expired records from a shared chain breaks every later link, so verification fails from the first expiry on. One segment per category and year lets the deployment delete a whole closed segment while the remaining segments still verify from their own anchors. The segment is closed with a final checkpoint before it is deleted as a whole. Settled by [decision/0097-one-audit-chain-segment-per-category-and-year](decision/0097-one-audit-chain-segment-per-category-and-year).
provisions.example: Claimwick holds its 2026 sign-in denials in one segment. When their two years end, the deployment deletes that segment whole, and the expense segments keep verifying from their own genesis records.

provisions.heading: Stage the Audit Write Before the Business Commit
provisions.evidence: Does any audit stage run after the business commit stage? Check the pipeline stage order.
provisions.statement: An audit producer that stages a success record MUST run before the pipeline stage that commits the business transaction.
provisions.rationale: A success record staged after the commit reaches a transaction that is already closed, so the write cannot commit. The producer therefore runs before the pipeline stage that commits. Pipeline priority states that order outright instead of leaving it to registration order.

provisions.heading: State the Checkpoint Interval as the Detection Window
provisions.evidence: Does the adoption decision state the checkpoint interval as the window in which records are not yet covered by a checkpoint? Check that decision record.
provisions.statement: An audit adoption decision SHOULD state its checkpoint interval as the window in which a rewrite goes unseen.
provisions.rationale: Records written after the latest checkpoint stay uncovered until the next one, so the interval is the bound on unseen rewrites. Stating it in the adoption decision tells each reviewer and user what the checkpoints do not cover. Without it, a reader mistakes scheduled verification for cover of the newest records.

provisions.heading: Store the Trail Beside the Business Data
provisions.evidence: Does the trail live in the business database or the recorded local convention? Check the audit store and its privileges.
provisions.statement: Store audit records in the business database, with the application account holding `INSERT` and `SELECT` and a separate operator account holding `DELETE`.
provisions.rationale: One database provides the atomic success write the transaction rules depend on. The application account holding only `INSERT` and `SELECT` provides the append-only guarantee, while the operator account holds `DELETE` for retention deletion.

provisions.heading: Use a Closed Actor Set
provisions.evidence: Does every actor value use one of the five kinds, with devices and processes mapped? Check the actor column.
provisions.statement: An audit actor MUST be one of `person`, `company`, `provider`, `system`, or `guest`.
provisions.rationale: An absent actor collapses three answers into one: a scheduled process acted, a device acted, or no one recorded the actor, and only the third is a defect. The five kinds separate them: a device maps to the person whose account authorized it, with the device as the client description, and a named process maps to `system`. A free-text actor would let each writer spell the same actor differently and break every actor filter.
provisions.example: A library self-checkout records the person actor whose account authorized it, while the origin record names the kiosk.

provisions.heading: Use a Fixed Category Vocabulary
provisions.evidence: Does every category value use the eight-value vocabulary or the recorded local convention? Check the declared selection.
provisions.statement: Classify each audited action as `authentication`, `authorization-denial`, `grant-change`, `monetary-action`, `tenant-configuration`, `personal-data-read`, `bulk-export`, or `background-process-change`.
provisions.rationale: The category drives retention and the review query. A free-text value defeats both, because each writer spells the same category differently.

provisions.heading: Verify the Integrity Chain on a Schedule
provisions.evidence: Does the deployment verify each live segment on a schedule and alert on a break? Check the integrity job and its alerts.
provisions.statement: An audit deployment MUST verify each live chain segment on a recurring schedule and raise an alert on a break.
provisions.rationale: Tamper evidence that no one checks proves nothing: a break sits in the store until someone looks. Scheduled verification turns each live segment into a standing claim the deployment re-proves on each run. Verification recomputes each live segment and checks its head and record count against the latest checkpoint that covers it, so it detects any change to the records that checkpoint covers. Records written after it are covered from the next checkpoint, so the checkpoint interval bounds the window in which a rewrite goes unseen. The alert carries the break to an operator instead of waiting for the next review.

provisions.heading: Version the Audit Record Shape
provisions.evidence: Does every stored record carry an explicit schema version? Check the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST carry an explicit schema version.
provisions.rationale: A retained record outlives several shapes of the application that wrote it. An explicit version lets a later reader parse each record in the shape it was written in. Without it, every shape change forces a rewrite of retained evidence.

provisions.heading: Write an Unsuccessful Record Outside the Failed Transaction
provisions.evidence: Does any denied or failed record roll back with its transaction? Check the unsuccessful write path.
provisions.statement: An audit record with a `denied` or `failed` outcome MUST be written on a connection that the failing transaction does not roll back.
provisions.rationale: A denied or failed attempt ends with its transaction rolling back. A record written inside that transaction would roll back with it and vanish. The record therefore travels on a connection the rollback does not touch, so the evidence of a refusal survives the rollback.

provisions.heading: Write Audit Records in the Mediation Pipeline
provisions.evidence: Does every audit write run in the mediation pipeline rather than inside a handler? Check the producer stages and the handler code.
provisions.statement: An audit producer MUST run in the mediation pipeline stages that dispatch the Command.
provisions.rationale: Only the pipeline stages that dispatch the Command observe the whole attempt, including attempts the handler never reaches. An audit call inside the handler misses every attempt that throws before it and every refusal the pipeline makes. The pipeline is therefore the one place that records all three outcomes.
provisions.example: A pre-handler opens the audit scope, a post-handler closes it as `succeeded`, and an error handler closes it as `denied` or `failed`.

provisions.heading: Attach Examples to Their Provisions
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `STANDARD_EXAMPLE_LABEL`, `PAGE_UNKNOWN_SECTION`, or `REFERENCE_EXAMPLE_DECLARATION` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: An informative example MUST belong to its provision or to a Reference Example that names every provision it demonstrates.
provisions.rationale: An example outside its provision looks like a second rule, and readers follow the illustration instead of the obligation. Sitting inside its provision, or inside a Reference Example that names every provision it demonstrates, marks it as illustration.

provisions.heading: Cite Owned Content Instead of Copying It
provisions.evidence: Does any passage restate content another page owns? Compare repeated passages with the owning page.
provisions.statement: A page MUST link to content another page owns instead of restating it.
provisions.rationale: The next unrelated edit updates the source and misses the copy, and readers follow the stale text. One home for each fact keeps every reader on the current text. A link to a record names its identifier, not its file.

provisions.heading: Define Each Glossary Term Under Its Heading
provisions.evidence: Does every glossary entry open with its definition and carry no Term line? Check `docs/reference/glossary.md`.
provisions.statement: A glossary entry MUST hold its definition in the paragraph under its term heading.
provisions.rationale: The heading anchor already carries the term identifier, so a `Term` line would repeat it. The paragraph under the heading holds the definition, and the lines after it name the record layer, established aliases, the source, and rejected synonyms where they exist.

provisions.heading: End Each Provision with One Verification Line
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `VERIFY_MISSING_ID`, `VERIFY_DUPLICATE_ID`, `VERIFY_ORDER`, or `VERIFY_HEADER` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Every provision MUST end its fields with exactly one verification line.
provisions.rationale: A provision with no verification line is a rule nobody checks. Each team assumes a tool covers it, while no tool does. One line per provision, beside the rule it checks, makes each rule reviewable by a person or a tool.

provisions.heading: Exclude a Sequence Number from the Identifier
provisions.evidence: Does any new identifier carry a sequence number? Check the provision IDs the change adds.
provisions.statement: A provision ID MUST NOT contain a sequence number.
provisions.rationale: A counter says where a provision sits among its siblings and nothing about what it requires; words name the obligation. Numbers would renumber every sibling on each insertion and break citations for no gain.

provisions.heading: Exclude Cross-Release Compatibility Work
provisions.evidence: Does any page promise migration, mapping, or alias between releases? Check the release material the change adds.
provisions.statement: The LiteSpec repository MUST NOT publish a compatibility guarantee, migration path, deprecation period, or identifier alias between its own releases.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec is a pinned contract, not a running service: consumers adopt a release whole, on their own schedule. Compatibility guarantees, migration paths, deprecation periods, and identifier aliases between LiteSpec releases would promise a continuity the model does not offer. A consumer product keeps its own API compatibility, migration, deprecation, and rollback provisions for its own users.

provisions.heading: Exclude Generated Regions from Prose Checks
provisions.evidence: Do any findings point inside generated-region fences? Check the findings the checks report.
provisions.statement: An authoring check MUST skip every generated region.
provisions.rationale: A generated region holds tool output: no author wrote it, and no author can fix it by editing the page. Checking it would fail pages for words outside author control, and writers would learn to ignore diagnostics.

provisions.heading: Exclude Historical Transition Material
provisions.evidence: Does any active file carry history-specific paths, aliases, or migration material? Check the files the change adds.
provisions.statement: Current standards material MUST NOT contain history-specific paths, IDs, terms, aliases, replacement maps, release migration material, compatibility rules, or transition checks other than the generated provision identifier list in the changelog.
provisions.rationale: A snapshot that carries aliases, maps, migration notes, or transition checks for other releases forces every reader to learn releases they did not pin. The published snapshot states its own contract and nothing else. An extension's `Baseline Relationship` section names a provision it replaces inside this release, which is a current replacement rather than history. The changelog's generated list of added, removed, and renamed provision identifiers states a fact about the release it ships in; it offers no alias, mapping, or migration path, so it stands as the one exception this provision allows.

provisions.heading: Generate the Provision Diff for Each Release
provisions.evidence: Was any changelog identifier typed by hand, or does any name an identifier that comparing the two provision indexes does not produce? Check the changelog entry against the provision index at the previous tag and the provision index of the release.
provisions.statement: The changelog for each LiteSpec release MUST list the provision identifiers the release adds, removes, and renames, generated from the provision index at the previous tag and the provision index of the release.
provisions.rationale: A consumer cites provision identifiers in code marks, records, and waivers. A release that removes or renames an identifier without naming it leaves every citation pointing at nothing, with no way to find what changed. The generated list states a fact about the release it ships in and nothing more: it carries no alias, no replacement map, and no migration path, and no provision depends on an earlier release to state its own contract. The list derives from the two provision indexes, so a tool generates it; a list typed by hand goes stale with the next provision edit. This provision is the exception to `litespec/core/authoring#exclude-historical-transition-material`, and it extends to no other history material.
provisions.example: `litespec-maintain changelog --from v3.0.0` writes the list into the changelog entry for a release, with `litespec/core/scope#claim-the-record-layers-the-project-uses` under Added when that provision first ships, and a major release lists each identifier it removes or renames under Removed and Renamed in the same entry.

provisions.heading: Keep a Pinned Release for as Long as It Serves
provisions.evidence: Does any provision oblige a move to a later release? Check the Statements the change adds.
provisions.statement: A LiteSpec release MUST NOT oblige a consumer to move to a later release.
provisions.rationale: Adoption is the consumer's decision. If a repository change could oblige a move, every LiteSpec edit would become a deadline for every consumer. A published release stays usable for as long as it serves, which decouples the consumer's schedule from the standard's.

provisions.heading: Keep Authored Prose ASCII-Safe
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `PROSE_NON_ASCII` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Authored prose MUST contain only ASCII unless code, data, or mathematical content requires another character.
provisions.rationale: A curly quote renders in one reader and breaks in another: terminals, diffs, generated context, and plain-text tools each handle non-ASCII characters differently, and a character that is unreadable in one is a silent mismatch in another. ASCII prose renders the same everywhere the standard is read or checked.
provisions.example: Write a hyphen or a comma where a typographic dash would go.

provisions.heading: Keep Each Standard to One Obligation
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `STANDARD_LABEL_INVALID`, `STANDARD_LABEL_ORDER`, `STANDARD_LABEL_DUPLICATE`, `STANDARD_MISSING_DEVIATION`, `STANDARD_UNEXPECTED_DEVIATION`, `STANDARD_MISSING_REQUIREMENT`, `STANDARD_REQUIREMENT_COUNT`, or `STANDARD_UNLABELED_CONTENT` diagnostic, and reports `STANDARD_SENTENCE_COUNT`, `STANDARD_MODAL_COUNT`, `STANDARD_MODAL_VOCABULARY`, `STANDARD_DEVIATION_NORMATIVE`, `STANDARD_DEVIATION_SENTENCE`, and `PROVISION_RESTATES_HEADING` as warnings.
provisions.statement: A Standards provision MUST follow the Standard contract this page defines.
provisions.rationale: One provision with one obligation has one authority, one identifier, and one verification line. A provision that bundles two obligations leaves a project half-compliant, with no identifier for the half it missed.
provisions.example: `### Keep Business Invariants in Domain` owns one obligation about where invariants are enforced.

provisions.heading: Keep Identifiers Out of Provision Headings
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_IN_HEADING` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision heading MUST carry no identifier text.
provisions.rationale: The page path with the heading already states the identifier. An identifier written into the heading repeats it at best; at worst, a rename touches one and misses the other, and the two contradict each other.

provisions.heading: Keep Principle Pages Free of Stack Detail
provisions.evidence: Does any principle page name a framework, package, or language construct? Check the principle pages the change touches.
provisions.statement: A principle page MUST NOT name a framework, a package, or a language-specific construct.
provisions.rationale: A principle holds for every stack only while it names none of them. Stack-specific technology belongs on stack pages; a framework name in a principle binds every stack to one choice.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Provision as Checked or Reviewed
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `VERIFY_MISSING_ID` for a provision whose verification line opens with any other label.
provisions.statement: A verification line MUST open with `Checked by` for a provision a tool checks or `Reviewed for` for one a person judges.
provisions.rationale: The label tells a reader who judges the provision: a tool (`checkable`) or a person (`guidance`). Without the label, a team automates a judgment call or hand-reviews what a command already proves.

provisions.heading: Match Strength to the Modal Word
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` confirms each Standards provision carries the modal its Strength line grades.
provisions.statement: A Standards provision MUST use the modal word its Strength line grades.
provisions.rationale: The Strength line grades how binding a provision is. The modal in its Statement says the same thing in words: a required provision obliges with must or must not, while an advisory one advises with should, should not, or may. When the two disagree, each reader picks the reading that suits the change, and the grade means nothing. A lone permission looks like optional advice under a required label, so a permission either joins the provision it relaxes or becomes an obligation of its own. Settled by [decision/0082-give-every-rule-one-home-and-one-strength](decision/0082-give-every-rule-one-home-and-one-strength).
provisions.example: A required provision states with must that a use case declares its kind, while an advisory provision suggests a naming shape with should.

provisions.heading: Name Observable Evidence in Verification Lines
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `VERIFY_COMMAND` or `CHECKED_BY_UNKNOWN` diagnostic, and reports `VERIFY_GENERIC_EVIDENCE`, `VERIFY_TEMPLATED_EVIDENCE`, and `VERIFY_DUPLICATE_EVIDENCE` as warnings.
provisions.statement: A verification line MUST name the observable evidence and where the reviewer looks.
provisions.rationale: A line that restates its Statement gives the reviewer nothing to check beyond the rule's own words. Naming the artifact and its location turns the line into an instruction the reviewer follows.

provisions.heading: Name the Command That Performs Each Step
provisions.evidence: Does every added step name the repository command that performs it? Check the steps the change adds.
provisions.statement: A tutorial step or how-to step MUST name the repository command that performs it, where one exists.
provisions.rationale: When a procedure spells out what a command already does, the page becomes a second copy of the command's behavior. The copy drifts from the tool, and readers follow stale steps. Naming the repository command delegates the steps to the tool that performs them.
provisions.example: A step reads ``Run `./shop up` `` rather than listing the compose start, the readiness wait, and each process launch.

provisions.heading: Name the Owning Page in the Identifier
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_PAGE_FILENAME` or `ID_DUPLICATE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision ID's page segment MUST be its page's path under `docs/` without the `.md` extension.
provisions.rationale: The page segment is both the file a reader opens and the address the provision carries on the published site. Deriving it from the path keeps the identifier and the file from disagreeing.
provisions.example: `litespec/core/backend-architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case` and `litespec/core/backend-application#organize-application-by-use-case` are on two different pages.

provisions.heading: Open Each Page with a Lead
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `PAGE_LEAD_MISSING` for a page with no paragraph between its title and its first H2.
provisions.statement: Every documentation page MUST open with a lead of one or more paragraphs between its title and its first H2 that tells the reader what the subject is and why it matters to them.
provisions.rationale: A reader who arrives from a link reads the lead first and decides from it whether the page answers the question. A lead that states the subject helps that reader; a summary of the page's headings does not, and the headings already show the outline. The lead takes no heading of its own, so the page starts with its answer.
provisions.example: The model page opens with "A LiteSpec project describes itself with records" and the problem the records solve, then goes straight to its sections.

provisions.heading: Order Glossary Groups Alphabetically
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `GLOSSARY_ORDER` diagnostic and reports `GLOSSARY_DEFINITION` as a warning.
provisions.statement: Glossary groups MUST stand in alphabetical order, each opening with one intro sentence.
provisions.rationale: A reader guesses where a term lives before reading any term. Alphabetical groups put each term where that guess expects it, and the opening sentence gives each group its shared context. An unordered group hides its terms from a reader who looks in the wrong place, and a group without its sentence opens with terms that share no stated context.
provisions.example: The code, product, and standard term groups open the glossary in that order, each with one sentence saying what its terms name.

provisions.heading: Place Each Stack Binding on Its Stack Page
provisions.evidence: Does any shared page carry a stack-specific section? Check the shared pages the change touches for stack sections.
provisions.statement: A stack-specific section MUST live on its stack page rather than on a shared page.
provisions.rationale: A reader following one stack finds its detail in one place. Each stack page carries its own bindings, and shared pages stay neutral across stacks.

provisions.heading: Place the ID Under Every Provision Heading
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_LINE_MISSING` or `ID_LINE_MISMATCH` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Every provision heading MUST be followed by an ID line holding the provision's identity.
provisions.rationale: A reader who cites a provision copies its ID from where the provision stands, instead of deriving a slug by hand or looking it up elsewhere. The ID line is the identity: a heading may change without changing it, so an ID line that reads differently from its heading still holds.
provisions.example: `### Compose Each Route from One Locked Archetype` on `docs/core/ui-ia.md` is followed by the ID line `litespec/core/ui-ia#compose-each-route-from-one-locked-archetype`.

provisions.heading: Prefer Direct Action Headings
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `HEADING_ACTION` as a warning.
provisions.statement: Start a Standard or Convention heading with a concrete action verb.

provisions.heading: Publish Each Release as a Complete Contract
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` checks every page of the release in one run, and the manifest names one version for the whole contract.
provisions.statement: A LiteSpec release MUST state every active provision without depending on an earlier release.
provisions.rationale: A consumer pins one snapshot and reads it as the whole obligation. If a release depended on another, the consumer would pin and read two contracts to know either. Stating every active provision in each release keeps one snapshot sufficient.

provisions.heading: Record Each Setting on a Configuration Page
provisions.evidence: Does every setting the change adds appear on a configuration page with its default, scope, and overrides? Check the settings the change adds against the configuration pages.
provisions.statement: A configuration setting a reader can change MUST appear on a configuration page with its default, its scope, and what overrides it.
provisions.rationale: A setting introduced inside a procedure is found only by the reader who already knows which procedure mentioned it. A configuration page with the default, the scope, and the overrides puts every setting where a reader looks it up.

provisions.heading: Record the Reviewed LiteSpec Release
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `release-drift` when `reviewedLiteSpecVersion` names no release or a release other than the installed tool release.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST record the LiteSpec release it adopts in `reviewedLiteSpecVersion` within `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: A provision can gain force while keeping its ID. Without a recorded release, a waiver written against one release could apply to a rule nobody reread. Recording the adopted release in `reviewedLiteSpecVersion` makes adoption an explicit act and tells every reader which contract the project reviewed.

provisions.heading: Regenerate the Provision Index
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain provisions --check` exits zero.
provisions.statement: A standards change MUST leave `docs/reference/provisions.md` equal to the output of `litespec-maintain provisions`.
provisions.rationale: One generated page resolves every identifier to its heading and page, so a reader follows a citation in one step. It also carries each provision's scope and strength, so the CLI reads one file instead of parsing every page. Regenerating it with `litespec-maintain provisions` on every standards change keeps the index and the pages from disagreeing.

provisions.heading: Restrict Normative Language to Standards and Conventions
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `PROSE_NORMATIVE_LOCATION` and `STANDARD_INFORMATIVE_NORMATIVE` as warnings.
provisions.statement: A capitalized modal MUST appear only in a Statement, a Default, or a Replacement.
provisions.rationale: When an obligation sits in Concepts, a Rationale, or an example, a project can miss it because the labeled assertions never state it. One location for every modal lets readers and tools find each obligation in the same place. A prohibition written as `cannot` and a rule written as `never` belong in the same labels.

provisions.heading: Route the Reader Before Listing Pages
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `INDEX_MISSING_ROUTING` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A documentation root index MUST state which page style answers which reader question before its first navigation group.
provisions.rationale: Without a mapping from question to page, a reader cannot tell which page answers the question. Naming each style in the reader's terms before the first navigation group sends each question to the page that answers it.
provisions.example: A `Which Page Do You Want` section names each style in the reader's terms, one sentence each.

provisions.heading: Run Repeatable Authoring Checks
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate`, `dotnet test --solution LiteSpec.slnx` and `git diff --check` exit zero.
provisions.statement: A standards change MUST pass the repository validator, the test suite, and `git diff --check`.
provisions.rationale: Structure, behavior, and whitespace each need their own check: the repository validator, the test suite, and `git diff --check` each catch what the others miss. Passing all three on every standards change keeps the standard checkable by anyone who runs the same commands. Diagnostics that judge wording print as warnings and do not fail the run; every other diagnostic fails it. The tools check every schema with LiteSpec's own evaluator, so running them needs no paid license, settled by [decision/0022-own-schema-evaluator](decision/0022-own-schema-evaluator) on the evidence in [research/schema-evaluator-evidence](research/schema-evaluator-evidence). The change report lists every skipped check with its reason. The [command index](../tools/README.md) and the [maintainer index](../maintain/README.md) name each check and its command. Settled by [decision/0035-bind-docs-to-tools-and-example](decision/0035-bind-docs-to-tools-and-example), which checks each tool fact the pages cite against the tools' own data.

provisions.heading: Split Extension Dependencies into Three Labeled Lines
provisions.evidence: Does every Dependencies section carry the Packages, Related extensions, and Guides lines? Check each page under an `ext/` folder.
provisions.statement: An extension Dependencies section MUST carry the lines Packages, Related extensions, and Guides.
provisions.rationale: Fixed labels separate package needs from related extensions and guides. A line with nothing to name holds `None.`.

provisions.heading: State One Tier per Page
provisions.evidence: Does any command page mix mechanism into sections other than Underneath? Check outside the Underneath section of each command page the change touches.
provisions.statement: A page MUST NOT describe both a command and the mechanism that command runs, outside an `Underneath` section.
provisions.rationale: A reader who wanted the command reads mechanism detail as noise, and a reader who wanted the mechanism reads the command wrapper as an obstacle. One tier per page serves each reader, and the `Underneath` section holds the mechanism for the reader who asks for it.

provisions.heading: State What the Command Runs Underneath
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `PAGE_MISSING_SECTION` diagnostic for a command page.
provisions.statement: A command page MUST state under `Underneath` what the command runs or the sentence `Nothing beneath this command is separately runnable.`.
provisions.rationale: When a command fails, the reader needs a command to run by hand and a tier to inspect. A command that states nothing beneath it leaves them with neither. Stating what the command runs, or that nothing beneath it is separately runnable, gives every failure a next step.
provisions.example: A command with nothing separately runnable writes `Nothing beneath this command is separately runnable.` under `Underneath`.

provisions.heading: Use Controlled Capitalization
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `PAGE_TITLE_CASE` and `PAGE_HEADING_CASE` as warnings.
provisions.statement: A page MUST use Title Case for its title and every heading.
provisions.rationale: A reader meets titles and headings in indexes, tabs, and search results, where they read as names. One casing rule keeps them uniform there. Title Case capitalizes every word except articles (`a`, `an`, `the`), coordinating conjunctions (`and`, `but`, `for`, `nor`, `or`, `so`, `yet`), and prepositions of four letters or fewer (`as`, `at`, `by`, `for`, `from`, `in`, `into`, `of`, `off`, `on`, `onto`, `over`, `per`, `to`, `up`, `upon`, `via`, `with`); the first and last words stay capitalized, and code, identifiers, and file names keep their own case.

provisions.heading: Use One Mark for One Fact Across Pages
provisions.evidence: Does any shared fact carry different marks on different pages? Compare the verification lines that name one check, using the provision index.
provisions.statement: One observable fact MUST carry one mark across pages.
provisions.rationale: When one page marks a fact for a tool and another marks the same fact for a person, each reviewer is unsure which judgment holds.

provisions.heading: Use One Normative Vocabulary
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `STANDARD_MODAL_COUNT` and `STANDARD_MODAL_VOCABULARY` as warnings.
provisions.statement: A Standards provision MUST use exactly one listed capitalized modal and no other capitalized normative term.
provisions.rationale: A reader decides from one word whether a provision obliges or suggests. That works only when each strength word means exactly one thing, as the listed modals do under their RFC meaning. A second capitalized term would add a shade of obligation that no contract defines.

provisions.heading: Use One Term for One Concept
provisions.evidence: Does every concept in the change go by one name? Check the terms the change adds against the glossary.
provisions.statement: Authored prose MUST name each concept with its one glossary term.
provisions.rationale: When one concept carries two names, each reader looks for a distinction the writer never meant. One term per concept means each term is defined once and checked once. Settled by [decision/0018-one-record-language](decision/0018-one-record-language) on the evidence in [research/naming-grammar-evidence](research/naming-grammar-evidence).

provisions.heading: Use the Declared Identifier Grammar
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` or `ID_DUPLICATE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision ID MUST be `litespec/<page>#<slug>` as its ID line states it.
provisions.rationale: The page segment names the file and the ID line states the slug, so a citation resolves with no lookup table. One grammar keeps every identifier writable by hand and checkable by tool. The ID line is the identity: a reworded heading leaves it unchanged, and no two provisions share one.
provisions.example: `litespec/core/ui-ia#fill-only-declared-slots-with-matching-guardrails` is the ID line under its heading on the user interface information architecture page.

provisions.heading: Use the Declared Page Contract
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `PAGE_MISSING_SECTION`, `PAGE_SECTION_ORDER` or `PAGE_UNKNOWN_SECTION` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: An authored page MUST use the sections, in order, of its page style.
provisions.rationale: Readers learn the page shape once and tools find each section without guessing, because the authority, the context, the defaults, and the evidence sit in the same place on every page. A page that invents its own order forces readers and tools to search. A record file carries its type's fields in canonical key order instead of sections.

provisions.heading: Validate Current Standards Material
provisions.evidence: Does the validator read anything outside the working tree? Check the paths the validator reads.
provisions.statement: The standards validator MUST evaluate only current standards material.
provisions.rationale: Each pinned release is a complete snapshot, so the validator judges the working tree alone. Reading history would let a provision pass on the strength of a release nobody pinned. Git history and the changelog still give readers release context; they stay outside validation.

provisions.heading: Validate Each Template Against the Record Schema
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `TEMPLATE_SCHEMA` diagnostic, and `litespec model check` reports `template-value-unchanged` on a scaffold that keeps a copied value.
provisions.statement: Each record template in `templates/consumer/` MUST satisfy `schemas/record.schema.yaml` with a placeholder value in every field, and a scaffold that `litespec new` writes keeps no copied text or number.
provisions.rationale: A template teaches the shape of its record type, so the record schema is its contract: a template that satisfies the schema stays teachable while the example product changes beside it. Each field shows a placeholder value, so nothing in the template reads as a decided value, and the Claimwick example beside it shows realistic values in one coherent product. `litespec model check` reports `template-value-unchanged` on a scaffold that keeps a copied value, so a copied period or a copied statement cannot pass as a decision. Settled by [decision/0093-check-templates-against-the-record-schema](decision/0093-check-templates-against-the-record-schema).

provisions.heading: Write Each Convention with a Default and a Replacement
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `CONVENTION_MISSING_DEFAULT` or `CONVENTION_MISSING_REPLACEMENT` diagnostic, and reports `CONVENTION_DEFAULT_SENTENCE`, `CONVENTION_REPLACEMENT_SENTENCE`, `CONVENTION_REPLACEMENT_WAIVER`, and `PROVISION_RESTATES_HEADING` as warnings.
provisions.statement: A Convention provision MUST follow the Convention contract this page defines.
provisions.rationale: A project replaces a default by citing it, which works only when each default has an identifier. Without the contract, defaults hide in prose and replacements cite paragraphs instead of identifiers.

provisions.heading: Write None in an Empty Required Section
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `PAGE_EMPTY_SECTION` or `PAGE_EMPTY_SECTION_TEXT` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A required section with nothing to say MUST contain only `None.`.
provisions.rationale: One marker reads the same on every page and gives the validator one shape to accept.

provisions.heading: Decide Current Truth in the Owning Module
provisions.evidence: Is every decision that needs current truth decided in the owning module? Check the reads beside the declared `queries` edges.
provisions.statement: A decision that needs current truth MUST be decided in the owning module, never from a read model.
provisions.rationale: A read model lags by its freshness. Revoked permissions, available funds, reservations, and period locks move after the copy was taken, so deciding from a copy accepts a stale answer where the business needs the current one. The owning module decides instead, through its public query the command sends with a declared `queries` edge, or by its own invariant. A read model serves reads the consumer reshapes and keeps locally.
provisions.example: The library refuses a hold on a lent copy by asking the lending module for current availability through its public query instead of reading a reporting copy.

provisions.heading: Declare Each Read Model Field from a Published Field
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` (level G) for a `from`, `erasedBy` or `removedBy` naming no module event or integration event, or a field the event does not carry, `read-model-key-invalid` (level G) for a `keyedBy` naming an aggregate of the read model's own module, and `read-model-unused` (level G) for a read model no use case reads.
provisions.statement: Each read model MUST name in `keyedBy` an aggregate of another module and, on each field, name in `from` the module event or integration event and the published field the field comes from.
provisions.rationale: A read model is a copy, and a copy with no stated source drifts: nobody can tell which event fills a field, so a renamed published field breaks the read model without a finding. Naming the event and its field makes every crossing of the module boundary a declared edge the check reads, the same way an effect names its target. A read model keyed by its own module's aggregate copies state the module already reads directly. A use case names the read model in `reads`, and a read model no use case reads is kept current for no reader. Settled by [decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model](decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model). Settled by [decision/0084-give-read-models-their-semantics](decision/0084-give-read-models-their-semantics).
provisions.example: `read-model/reporting.reimbursed-expense` is keyed by `aggregate/spending.expense`, and its `amount` field comes from `module-event/spending.expense-reimbursed#amount`.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Reaction and Job Edge in Effects
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a reaction or job with no `effects` or with a top-level effect verb.
provisions.statement: Each reaction and each job MUST declare its edges in `effects`, with exactly one verb per entry.
provisions.rationale: A reaction or job with no declared edge observes and never acts, and an edge written outside `effects` hides behavior the checks never see. Declaring each edge in `effects`, with exactly one verb of `runs`, `sends`, `calls`, `queries`, or `commands`, keeps every consequence beside the trigger or schedule, in the one grammar every record with edges shares, as the [use cases](use-cases.md) page defines.

provisions.heading: Declare the Outcomes of Each Reaction and Job
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a reaction or job without `outcomes` or with a name outside the closed set.
provisions.statement: Each reaction and each job MUST declare its run endings in `outcomes` from the closed set.
provisions.rationale: A run without declared endings leaves each reader guessing: a skipped item looks like a failure, and a suppressed send looks like a bug. Declaring each ending with its meaning states what a run produces: `completed` for work done, `skipped` for work set aside by its skip condition, `suppressed` for a send held by suppression, `failed` for work ending in refusal or error, `retry-scheduled` for work waiting on another attempt, and `nothing-selected` for a run finding no item. Scenarios end in one of these endings or in a run use case result, so every run has a proof. Settled by [decision/0081-own-scenarios-and-declare-outcomes](decision/0081-own-scenarios-and-declare-outcomes).
provisions.example: The send-due-notice reaction declares `completed` for a sent notice and `suppressed` for a notice held because the reader opted out.

provisions.heading: End Reaction and Job Scenarios in the Run Result
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a reaction or job scenario ending outside the run use case results and the declared outcomes.
provisions.statement: Each scenario on a reaction or job MUST end in a result of a use case its effects run or in one of its outcomes.
provisions.rationale: A reaction or job scenario ending anywhere else proves another behavior story: it covers the trigger or schedule and asserts an ending no run use case declares and no outcome names. Ending in a run use case result or in a declared outcome keeps the scenario a proof of the reaction or job consequence. A send-only reaction or job ends its scenarios in outcomes, with no invented command.

provisions.heading: Erase a Read Model Personal Field with Its Owner
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `read-model-erasure-missing` (level G) for a `personal` or `sensitive` read model field with no `erasedBy`.
provisions.statement: Each `personal` or `sensitive` read model field MUST name in `erasedBy` the module event or integration event whose arrival erases it.
provisions.rationale: A read model copies data out of the module that owns its erasure. A copy without an erasure trigger outlives the owner's erasure and keeps personal data the product promised to remove. Naming the erasing event ties the copy to the owner's erasure position, and the projection for that event clears the field. The erased key keeps a tombstone that a rebuild applies, so no rebuild restores the erased field. Settled by [decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model](decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model).
provisions.example: The `employeeId` field of `read-model/reporting.reimbursed-expense` is personal, so it names `module-event/spending.expense-personal-data-erased` in `erasedBy`, and the projection for that event clears it.

provisions.heading: File Every Reaction and Job with the Module It Changes
provisions.evidence: Does every reaction and job sit with the module whose own records it changes, or with the sending module when it changes another module only through that module's public command? Check the reactions and jobs beside the modules whose records they change and the public commands they send.
provisions.statement: Each reaction and each job MUST live with the module whose own records it changes, with the sending module when it changes another module only by sending that module's public command, or with the module owning the notification when it only sends one.
provisions.rationale: Filing by trigger spreads one module's work across many trigger pages, so no page shows the module whole. Filing each reaction and job with the module whose records it changes keeps each module's behavior in one place. A module changes another module only through that module's public command, sent from a reaction or job, usually a reaction to the sender's own fact. The sending module holds that fact and its reaction, so the reaction sits with the sender. Its event handler or job class lives in that module's code with what it runs: in the folder of the use case it runs, or with the notification it sends or the system it calls (`litespec/workspace/naming#place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs`). The trigger page lists the reactions answering its event, derived from records.

provisions.heading: Keep Failure Handling on the Reaction or Job
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `on-failure-placement-invalid` (level G) for a reaction or job whose effect entry carries `onFailure`.
provisions.statement: A reaction or job MUST state its failure handling once, in `onFailure` on the record and never in an effect entry.
provisions.rationale: A reaction or job runs one use case and owns the failure of the whole run. The record's `onFailure` states the mode, the retry and the dead-letter beside the trigger or schedule, where a reader looks for it. Repeating the shape on an effect entry leaves two places to change and two answers to the same failure, so the entry is not a second home for it. A use case has no record-level `onFailure`; its effect entries each carry their own, as [Use Cases](use-cases.md) states.
provisions.example: Claimwick's reaction `reaction/spending.release-hold-on-rejection` states its retry and dead-letter in `onFailure` on the reaction record. Copying that object into its `runs` effect entry is reported.

provisions.heading: Keep Job Fields off Reactions
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a reaction carrying `kind`, `schedule`, `runbook`, `runsWhen`, `cursor`, `selection`, `lease`, `batchSize`, `serviceLevel`, or `evidence`.
provisions.statement: A reaction MUST NOT carry `kind`, `schedule`, `runbook`, `runsWhen`, `cursor`, `selection`, `lease`, `batchSize`, `serviceLevel`, or `evidence`.
provisions.rationale: Run fields describe work over time: the kind, the schedule, what each run selects, how many items per batch, the lock, where resume state lives, the condition it runs under, the promised service level, and the evidence the run leaves. A reaction answers one event and carries none of that. A run field on it claims a schedule the trigger never states. Settled by [decision/0015-automations-and-sagas](decision/0015-automations-and-sagas) on the evidence in [research/lower-layers-practice](research/lower-layers-practice).
provisions.example: The send-due-notice reaction answers its event with no `selection` and no `schedule`.

provisions.heading: Keep Validity Apart from Storage
provisions.evidence: Does every expiring credential and session refuse use from expiry, with a cleanup job removing expired records within a stated interval? Check the expiry rules beside the cleanup jobs.
provisions.statement: Each expiring credential or session MUST refuse its use from its expiry and be removed by a cleanup job within a stated interval.
provisions.rationale: An expiry that only deletes leaves a window where an expired credential still works, and a check without cleanup leaves dead rows forever. Refusing the use from the expiry keeps validity at the moment of use, and a cleanup job removing expired records within a stated interval reclaims storage. The two stay separate: the check refuses, and the job removes.
provisions.example: A library session past its expiry is refused at its next use, and the expire-sessions job removes expired sessions within one day.

provisions.heading: Move a State by Time with a Timed Transition
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` (level G) for a timed transition naming a missing state or a job no record declares.
provisions.statement: Each transition that time moves MUST name its duration from entering its source state in `after` and the moving job in `movedBy`.
provisions.rationale: A deadline with no stated duration and no moving job has no defined moment to expire: holds linger, and reservations never release. Naming the duration and the job states the timed move beside the lifecycle. The job selects instances past their window and runs the moving command once per instance. States, reactions, and timed transitions cover long-running work with no process record.
provisions.example: The hold transition from Ready to Expired carries `after: P7D` and `movedBy: job/lending.expire-lapsed-holds`, and the job runs the expire-holds command once per lapsed hold.

provisions.heading: Name Each Job for the Use Case It Runs
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `job-name-invalid` (level G) for a job outside `<verb>-<what>` with the verb of the use case it runs or its own verb when it runs none.
provisions.statement: Each job MUST be named `<verb>-<what>` with the verb of the use case it runs, or with its own verb when it runs no use case.
provisions.rationale: A job selects items and runs one command for each. Naming it for that command lets a reader go from the schedule to the behavior in one step, as `litespec/core/language#use-the-declared-record-identifier-grammar` states. A job that only sends or calls takes its own verb, since no use case verb names it.
provisions.example: `job/lending.expire-lapsed-holds` runs `use-case/lending.expire-holds`.

provisions.heading: Name Each Reaction for Its Act and Its Trigger
provisions.evidence: Does every reaction name state its act and its trigger? Check the reaction names beside their triggering events.
provisions.statement: Each reaction MUST be named `<verb>-<what>-on-<fact>` with a declared verb.
provisions.rationale: A reaction runs because something happened, and a name without its trigger hides why it runs: `send-due-notice` could fire on a borrow, a hold, or a reminder run. Naming the act and the fact lets a reader find every consequence of a fact by its name, as `litespec/core/language#use-the-declared-record-identifier-grammar` states.
provisions.example: `reaction/lending.send-due-notice-on-loan-borrowed` answers `domain-event/loan.loan-borrowed`.

provisions.heading: Name the Step a Compensating Reaction Undoes
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `compensation-target-invalid` (level G) for a `compensates` naming a use case that is not a command or the same use case the reaction runs, `compensation-trigger-invalid` (level G) for a compensating reaction answering an event the compensated use case lists in `raises`, and `reference-unknown` (level G) for a `compensates` naming no written record. The trigger check is a minimum: a reviewer confirms the trigger reports a later step's failure.
provisions.statement: A reaction that undoes a committed step of a multi-step process MUST name the undone use case in `compensates`, run a use case other than the one it names, and answer an event the undone use case does not raise.
provisions.rationale: A multi-step process commits each step before the next runs, so a later failure cannot roll the earlier steps back, and each committed step needs an undo that runs only when a later step fails. Without the link, a reader sees a reaction running an undoing command and cannot tell which committed step it reverses. Running the named use case again redoes the step instead of undoing it, and answering an event the undone step raises undoes every success. Naming the undone step in `compensates` states the undo beside the reaction, with its own trigger and failure handling.
provisions.example: The library reserves a copy with `use-case/lending.reserve-copy`, which commits the reservation. When the later charge fails, `use-case/lending.record-charge-failure` raises `domain-event/charge.charge-failed`. The reaction `reaction/lending.release-copy-on-charge-failed` answers that event, runs `use-case/lending.release-copy`, and carries `compensates: use-case/lending.reserve-copy`, so a reader sees which committed step the release undoes.

provisions.heading: Publish Every Module Event from the Event It Translates
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a module event without `translates` or `fields`, `event-field-uncarried` (level G) for a field name its translated domain event does not carry, `event-publisher-invalid` for a module event with a second publishing module, and `effect-undeclared` for an event a handler, event handler or job publishes itself; `dotnet build` reports `LS2022` for an event published by user code.
provisions.statement: Each module event MUST name in `translates` the domain event of its own module it carries, and is published only from that domain event, by the pipeline step that stages raised events.
provisions.rationale: When a handler builds a module event from whatever the aggregate holds after the act, it publishes state the act never announced, and a second handler can publish the same event with different fields. Deriving the event from the one domain event it translates keeps every published field a field of the announced fact. The publishing use cases then follow from `raises`, with no second declaration to drift, and the domain event carries every field its module events publish, as typed fields. A publish call in user code is an edge no record can declare, so the stack reader reports it. Settled by [decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers](decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers).
provisions.example: Claimwick's `module-event/spending.expense-approved` translates `domain-event/expense.approved`, so `use-case/spending.approve-expense`, which raises that event, publishes it, and its handler publishes nothing. The payouts module answers the module event from a reaction.

provisions.heading: Raise Completion Only When Every Module Is Done
provisions.evidence: Does spanning work raise completion only after every module reports done, with progress in a record the work does not delete? Check the completion reactions beside the module reports.
provisions.statement: Work that spans modules MUST raise its completion fact only after every module reports its part done.
provisions.rationale: A completion raised early declares done while parts remain: erased data returns, and closed work reopens. Each module's reaction erases or closes its part and reports done, and the completion is raised only when every report arrived. A report to an upstream module travels as its public command that the reporting module calls, under `litespec/core/backend-application#confirm-downstream-completion-through-an-upstream-command`. Progress lives in a record outliving the deleted data, and the requesting state blocks new writes until completion.
provisions.example: Erasing a departed employee's personal data enters Erasing, which blocks new writes. The spending reaction erases expenses and the access reaction erases sessions, each reporting done. The employee becomes Erased only when both report, and the erasure record keeps the fact and date outside the erased data.

provisions.heading: Run at Most One Use Case from a Reaction or Job
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a reaction or job with more than one `runs` entry.
provisions.statement: A reaction or job MUST run at most one use case, a job running it once per selected item.
provisions.rationale: A reaction or job is an entry point: it turns one fact or one selected item into one message, as an endpoint turns one request into one message. A reaction that ran two use cases would decide their order and their joint failure in code no record states, and the second would fail after the first committed. Two follow-on acts are two reactions to the same fact, each with its own failure handling. A reaction or job that only sends or calls runs no use case. Settled by [decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers](decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers).
provisions.example: The erase-expired-personal-data job selects decided expenses past retention and runs `use-case/spending.erase-personal-data` once for each.

provisions.heading: Run Each Effect on Its Own
provisions.evidence: Does every effect of each reaction and job run, retry, and deduplicate on its own? Check the effects beside their failure handling and idempotency.
provisions.statement: Each effect of a reaction or job MUST run, retry and deduplicate on its own, with any order expressed by chaining facts.
provisions.rationale: Effects that share one retry decide their joint failure in code no record states: the second send waits on the first, and a retry doubles the first while fixing the second. Running each effect on its own keeps each consequence independent, with its own idempotency and its own failure handling. An order between effects is a fact the first produces and the second answers, never an assumed sequence.
provisions.example: The loan-borrowed reaction sends the due notice and calls the statistics system as two independent effects; a retry of the call never resends the notice.

provisions.heading: Run Every Job from Its Declared Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `schedule-invalid` (level G) for a schedule neither an `every` duration, a `cron` expression, nor `at: startup`, and fails a job without its `kind` or a scheduled job without `schedule`.
provisions.statement: Each job MUST declare its `kind` of `scheduled` or `one-off` with its `schedule` where scheduled.
provisions.rationale: A job without a kind has no defined moment to run: it never runs, or it runs whenever its author remembered. Naming the kind states when it runs. A scheduled job carries its `schedule`, with an `every` duration, a `cron` expression and timezone, or `at: startup` for a run once at deployment start. A `one-off` job runs once.
provisions.example: `job/lending.expire-lapsed-holds` runs every six hours over open holds past their window.

provisions.heading: Settle Every Async Outcome in Visible States
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `async-pending-missing` (level G) for a `settles` with a pending or done state that names no state or names one state twice, or with a pending state that no earlier transition reaches, `async-refused-unrecorded` (level G) for a run with no refused state and no declared retry, or a refused state that repeats pending or done, and `reference-unknown` (level G) for a `settles` naming no written aggregate or state. A run with no `settles` states nothing, because the model cannot tell whether a reader waits on it. A reviewer confirms each query reading the settled aggregate returns its state.
provisions.statement: Each reaction and each job whose outcome a reader waits on MUST name in `settles` the aggregate it writes with its pending state and its done state, and its refused state except where another attempt returns the run to pending.
provisions.rationale: A result produced after the commit arrives later: the command commits, and a reaction or job settles the outcome afterwards. A reader that meets the record meanwhile sees neither done nor refused, and reads the absence as whichever ending fits the screen: a payout still travelling reads as refused, or a refused payout reads as still travelling. Naming the pending state the run leaves, the done state it enters, and the refused state a terminal refusal enters keeps the three endings apart on the written aggregate. Where every failure earns another attempt, the run returns to pending instead, and the declared retry states that no terminal refusal exists. A run writing no aggregate settles nothing, and a run writing several is reviewed with its atomicity rule. A query reading the settled aggregate returns its state, so the reader sees which of the three holds.
provisions.example: Claimwick's erase job runs the erase-personal-data command over decided expenses past retention. It settles the expense from pending Reimbursed to done Erased, and names no refused state: its retry returns each failed expense to Reimbursed for the next nightly run.

provisions.heading: State the Failure Handling of Every Reaction and Job
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` fails a reaction or job with `onFailure` outside the one failure shape, and reports `record-invalid` for prose handling, a missing or malformed retry, and a malformed duration. A reaction or job that states `onFailure` in an effect entry is reported as `on-failure-placement-invalid`.
provisions.statement: Each reaction and each job MUST declare its `onFailure` in the one failure shape and its idempotency.
provisions.rationale: A failed reaction or job without handling retries forever or drops silently: notices double-send, and holds never clear. Declaring `onFailure` states the failure shape beside the trigger or schedule: `mode` of `retry`, `skip-and-log`, or `discard`; `retry` with `maxAttempts`, `initialDelay`, `maxDelay`, and `backoff` of `exponential` or `fixed`; `ifExhausted` of `dead-letter`; `deadLetter` carrying `after` with the action a person takes; `surfacesIn` naming the entry point showing the failure, and `runbook` the recovery procedure. `retry` and `ifExhausted` are required with `mode: retry`; `deadLetter`, `surfacesIn`, and `runbook` are optional. Delays and `after` are ISO 8601 durations, and prose handling is refused. The one shape also serves the effect entries of a use case; a reaction or job states failure handling once on the record, as [Keep Failure Handling on the Reaction or Job](#keep-failure-handling-on-the-reaction-or-job) states. The idempotency mode, usually `state`, states how repeated runs collapse.

provisions.heading: Subscribe to Every Module Event
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `module-event-unused` (level G) for a module event that no reaction in `triggeredBy`, no read model field in `from`, `erasedBy` or `removedBy`, and no other consumer names.
provisions.statement: Each module event MUST be named by a reaction, a read model projection or another consumer that answers or copies it.
provisions.rationale: A module event is a contract between modules. Publishing one nobody consumes stages an event on every commit that no work reads, and a reader cannot tell whether the fact matters or the consumer was forgotten. Naming the consumer makes the crossing complete: the reaction answers the fact, or the projection copies it into the reading module's own store. A direction may describe a planned event, but it justifies no published record; only a waiver sets this rule aside for an event waiting on a consumer.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `module-event/spending.expense-approved` is named by the payouts reaction that pays the reimbursement. A second event with no reaction or read model is reported until its consumer is written or the event is removed.

provisions.heading: Trigger Every Reaction from Its Declared Events
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` (level G) for a trigger naming an unknown event, `reaction-trigger-foreign` (level G) for a trigger naming another module's domain event, and fails a reaction without a `triggeredBy` list.
provisions.statement: Each reaction MUST declare in `triggeredBy` the domain events of its own module, the module events of upstream modules of the product, or the inbound integration events it answers.
provisions.rationale: A reaction without a trigger has no defined moment to run: it never runs, or it runs whenever its author remembered. Naming the events states when it fires, as one id or a list. The reaction answers the domain events of its own module, upstream module events, or inbound integration events, never another module's domain event and never a downstream module's fact. Answering another module's domain event would couple it to state its module does not own; the owning module publishes a module event instead. A module event is itself the declared crossing between modules, as `litespec/core/model#connect-across-modules-only-through-declared-dependencies` states, so a reaction may answer an upstream one without a module dependency, under `litespec/core/backend-architecture#send-commands-and-queries-upstream`. A `skippedWhen` clause states when the reaction skips.
provisions.example: In the library product, `reaction/lending.send-due-notice-on-loan-borrowed` answers `domain-event/loan.loan-borrowed` and runs the send-due-notice command.

provisions.heading: Write Every Runbook to Run or Recover
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a runbook page without `impact`, `prerequisites`, `procedure`, `verification`, `recovery`, or `escalation`.
provisions.statement: Each runbook MUST state its `impact`, `prerequisites`, `procedure`, `verification`, `recovery`, and `escalation`.
provisions.rationale: A runbook named by a job, a failure policy, or an alert is the answer a person opens under pressure. Its `impact` says what breaks, `prerequisites` say what to hold, `procedure` says each step, `verification` says how to confirm, `recovery` says how to undo, and `escalation` says who to call. A runbook missing one leaves the reader guessing at the worst moment.
provisions.example: The clear-stuck-reimbursements runbook states its impact on waiting expenses, its prerequisites, its procedure, its verification query, its recovery, and its escalation to the spending team.

provisions.heading: Write No Aggregate Directly from a Reaction or Job
provisions.evidence: Does every reaction and job write aggregates only through the use case it runs? Check the reaction and job effects beside the use cases.
provisions.statement: A reaction or job MUST NOT write an aggregate except through the use case it runs.
provisions.rationale: A direct write splits the write path: the same aggregate changes through a reviewed command and through an unreviewed reaction or job, each with its own guards. Running a small command keeps every write behind a use case, with its access, consistency, results, and scenarios.

provisions.heading: Apply Only Coarse Policies at the Endpoint
provisions.evidence: Does any endpoint policy decide target authorization instead of coarse authentication, role, or scope? Look at the endpoint policies beside the application guard.
provisions.statement: A WebApi endpoint MUST enforce only coarse authenticated, role, or scope policies, leaving target decisions to the application guard.
provisions.rationale: Authentication establishes who is calling, not whether the caller may act on this specific resource. An endpoint that decided target authorization would duplicate the business data access the guard already owns. Coarse policies at the endpoint check the caller; the application guard decides the target from the `access` the use-case record declares. `litespec/core/backend-application#enforce-target-authorization-in-the-pipeline` states target authorization. An operation applies a stable forbidden or not-found policy when revealing that a resource exists would leak information.

provisions.heading: Apply PATCH to a Partial Update
provisions.evidence: Does every partial update arrive as PATCH with the merge-patch media type? Look at the partial update requests.
provisions.statement: A WebApi operation MUST apply a partial update with PATCH and the `application/merge-patch+json` media type.
provisions.rationale: A partial update names only the fields it changes. Sending them with PATCH and the merge-patch media type gives those semantics a standard meaning. A PUT body for a partial change either repeats fields the caller does not change or invents merge semantics per field. [RFC 5789](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5789) defines PATCH and [RFC 7386](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7386) defines the merge-patch media type.
provisions.example: A partial update sends only the changed members with `Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json`, and the endpoint reads the body as a sparse patch. A PUT replaces the whole resource ([RFC 9110 section 9.3.4](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#section-9.3.4)), and DELETE remains a hard-state transition.

provisions.heading: Authorize Every File Download Through Its Owning Use Case
provisions.evidence: Is every stored file reachable only through a download use case with its declared access? Look at the download endpoints and the storage addresses beside each owning use case.
provisions.statement: A caller MUST reach a stored file only through a download use case authorized from the access that use case declares.
provisions.rationale: A stored file carries the data of the record it belongs to. A direct storage address would serve that data to anyone holding the address, skipping the owning use case's grant and tenant scope. Routing each download through its owning use case keeps one authorization decision for the file and for the record it belongs to.
provisions.example: A Claimwick receipt photo downloads through the use case that owns the expense, so only an actor its access allows reads the photo, and no storage address serves it on its own.

provisions.heading: Avoid Noise Words in Field Names
provisions.evidence: Does any field name in contract schemas carry a type prefix or noise word? Look at the field names.
provisions.statement: Field names carry no type prefix and no noise word.
provisions.rationale: A type prefix repeats what the schema already declares, and a noise word names nothing an integrator acts on: `customerInfo` carries no more meaning than `customer`. The noise words are `data`, `info`, `item`, `object`, `value`, and `thing`; the type prefixes are `str`, `int`, `bool`, `num`, `obj`, and `arr`.
provisions.example: `customerInfo` becomes `customer`.

provisions.heading: Bound Collection Queries
provisions.evidence: Does every collection response apply deterministic order with the declared default and maximum limits? Look at the collection responses beside their records.
provisions.statement: A collection endpoint MUST apply deterministic ordering, its record's declared default limit, and its record's declared maximum limit of 100 or lower.
provisions.rationale: An unbounded collection read lets one caller cause unbounded database and serialization work. Deterministic ordering keeps pages stable, the declared default limit bounds the common case, and the declared maximum of 100 or lower caps the worst case. The use-case record declares its paging with order, cursor or offset, default limit, and maximum limit, and the endpoint applies exactly that. `litespec/core/backend-api#use-opaque-cursors-for-collection-paging` and `litespec/core/backend-api#version-cursors-with-stable-sort-values` state the cursor mechanics.

provisions.heading: Bound Every File Upload
provisions.evidence: Does every upload operation declare its size and media-type bounds, and refuse files outside them? Look at each upload endpoint beside its use-case record.
provisions.statement: A file upload operation MUST accept no file larger than the size its use-case record declares and no media type outside the media types its use-case record declares.
provisions.rationale: An upload without a declared size or media-type bound lets one caller send work the server never agreed to store or inspect. Declaring both bounds on the use-case record lets the server refuse an oversize file or an undeclared type before storage, and lets a reviewer see the limit beside the use case that owns the file.
provisions.example: The Claimwick submit-expense upload declares the size and the image media types a receipt photo may carry. The server refuses a larger file or another media type before it stores anything.

provisions.heading: Commit the Generated Contract Its Consumers Read
provisions.evidence: Does every frontend or external consumer read a committed, current OpenAPI artifact? Look at the committed artifact beside its consumers.
provisions.statement: An application MUST commit its generated OpenAPI artifact when a frontend or external consumer reads it.
provisions.rationale: Without a committed file, a breaking contract change hides inside a code change. A committed artifact makes every contract change visible in review and lets CI fail when the document was not regenerated. Consumers read the artifact through the generated client, model, schema, and query-option packages.

provisions.heading: Declare a Smaller Collection Maximum
provisions.evidence: Does every lowered collection maximum carry its value and reason on the use-case record? Look at each lowered maximum.
provisions.statement: A use case with stricter needs declares its smaller maximum in its record's `paging` and states the reason on its use-case record.
provisions.rationale: Some collections cost more per item than others. A use case with stricter needs declares its smaller maximum in its record's `paging` with the reason on its use-case record, and the endpoint enforces it under `litespec/core/backend-api#bound-collection-queries`.

provisions.heading: Declare Stable Operation Metadata in the Contract
provisions.evidence: Does every operation in the generated contract declare its operationId, authorization, request, success, failure, and summary entries? Look at the operations in the generated contract.
provisions.statement: An operation MUST declare a stable `operationId`, its authorization, request, success, and Problem Details metadata, and a summary.
