This is the practice known as event-carried state transfer, declared as a record so a check can prove every field has a source. Settled by [decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model](decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model).
provisions.example: The reporting module's list-reimbursed-expenses query reads `read-model/reporting.reimbursed-expense`, which its projections fill from the spending module's expense-reimbursed module event. It calls no spending reader.

provisions.heading: Read Settings Through Typed Options
provisions.evidence: Does every handler read its settings through a typed options value or stored tenant data, with no raw lookup? Look at each setting read in the handlers.
provisions.statement: A handler MUST read a setting record through a typed options value, or through stored tenant data where the record's `setBy` is `tenant`.
provisions.rationale: A raw configuration lookup bypasses the type, the range, and the bound the setting record owns, so no handler uses one. Binding decider-set and operator-set values to typed options the host validates at startup fails a bad value before traffic arrives. A setting record owns its type, its default, its range, its unit, and what happens at the bound. Tenant-set values are data nobody reviews: they live in stored tenant state the handler reads per tenant.
provisions.example: The receipt threshold binds to a spending options value. The handler reads the bound and refuses past it with `outOfRange: refuse`.

provisions.heading: Read Time from the Scoped Clock
provisions.evidence: Which handlers read the system clock directly, or take more than one timestamp for one message? Look at the clock reads in each handler.
provisions.statement: Each handler MUST read the message timestamp from the scoped clock the pipeline stamps once per message.
provisions.rationale: A handler that reads the clock two or three times in one decision records different times for one act, sometimes with an outside call in between. One timestamp per message fixes the moment the message starts, and every decision in the handling answers to the same time. The shared clock stays for infrastructure only.
provisions.example: The approve handler stamps its approval with the handled clock, not with a fresh clock read.

provisions.heading: Record a Decision for Closed-Set Narrowing
provisions.evidence: Does every narrowed closed set have a recorded decision with an updated specification? Look at each narrowed set beside the decision records.
provisions.statement: A layer MUST NOT narrow a Domain closed set without a recorded decision and an updated specification.
provisions.rationale: Narrowing silently drops cases the Domain can produce, so a caller meeting a dropped case gets a shape the contract left undescribed. A recorded decision with an updated specification makes the dropped cases visible and owned. The decision follows `litespec/core/model#record-each-technical-choice-as-a-decision`.

provisions.heading: Refuse a Lost Race as a Conflict
provisions.evidence: Does every command that loses a race at commit end with its use case conflict refusal? Look at the race outcomes beside the use case refusals.
provisions.statement: Each command that loses a race at commit MUST end with its use case's conflict refusal.
provisions.rationale: A duplicate key or a stale version reaches the commit as a store fault, and the pipeline classifies it as the use case's named conflict refusal, so the caller learns what happened and may reread and retry. No reservation, re-read, or retry lives in the handler. The store enforces uniqueness under `litespec/core/backend-persistence#enforce-uniqueness-in-the-store` and versions every aggregate under `litespec/core/backend-persistence#version-every-aggregate`.
provisions.example: Two clerks register the same book barcode at once. The second commit violates the barcode unique index, and the command refuses with `book-barcode-taken`.

provisions.heading: Report Input Problems as Validity Findings
provisions.evidence: Does every validator report validity findings with a member, a code, and a message, and no transport status? Look at the findings each validator reports.
provisions.statement: A validator MUST report its findings as validity findings, with each finding carrying a member, a code, and a message, and no transport status.
provisions.rationale: When validation stops at the first problem, one form turns into repeated round trips. Running every validator and merging the findings tells the caller everything wrong with the form in one answer. Each finding carries a member naming the input member, a code naming the stable reason, and a message explaining the problem in caller-safe language. Findings carry no transport status, because Application answers no transport.
provisions.example:
A submit request with an empty expense identifier and an empty employee identifier reports one finding per member, two in total, with no transport status:

```json
[
  { "member": "ExpenseId", "code": "required", "message": "An expense is required." },
  { "member": "EmployeeId", "code": "required", "message": "An employee is required." }
]
```

The caller sees both problems at once, and the pipeline refuses the request before Domain runs.

provisions.heading: Return Only Declared Results and Refusals
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `result-undeclared` (level S) for a code a handler produces that no declared result names; a handler returns only the results and codes its record lists.
provisions.statement: A handler MUST return only the results, refusals, and codes its use-case record declares.
provisions.rationale: An observable outcome no result declares is behavior the specification hides, so the stack reader fails `result-undeclared` on it. Refusals return in the precedence order the record lists, first match wins, and a success carrying `codes` returns only those codes. Generic refusals derive from `access`, `input`, and the knowledge the use case reads, and need no declaration. A use case refuses only with refusals its own module declares: when another module's public query answers nothing, the use case refuses with its own declared refusal, never with the other module's exception.
provisions.example: A handler that returns a code its record never lists fails the check, even when the code is spelled correctly.

provisions.heading: Return Only What the Caller Needs
provisions.evidence: Does any Application result return more than the caller needs? Look at each result beside its caller.
provisions.statement: Return only the values the caller needs from an Application result.
provisions.rationale: A result carries only what the caller needs. An aggregate, session, provider response, or transport result leaving Application makes an inner concern part of the outward contract, and every change to that concern breaks callers.

provisions.heading: Run Each Job Within Its Declared Selection
provisions.evidence: Does every scheduled or one-off job run within its selection, batch size, lease, and cursor? Look at each job run beside its record.
provisions.statement: A scheduled or one-off job MUST run its declared commands once per item in its record's `selection`, honoring its batch size, lease, and cursor.
provisions.rationale: The job record owns what each run selects, how many items each batch takes, the lease that keeps two runs apart, and the cursor where a run resumes. The job runs its `effects` entries once per item, records its evidence where the record states, and follows its `onFailure` when an item fails. One execution host runs the job under `litespec/core/backend-architecture#name-the-host-for-work-that-outlives-a-request`. The job class lives in the `Application/` folder of the use case it runs, so the use case folder shows every way it starts.
provisions.example: The erase-expired-data job selects decided expenses past retention in batches of 200 under its lease, runs one erase command per expense, and resumes from its cursor.

provisions.heading: Run Heavy Work as a Request Then a Build
provisions.evidence: Does any command assembling a large artifact skip the recorded request and building job? Look at each heavy command.
provisions.statement: Record the request behind a command that assembles a large artifact, and let a job build the artifact for the requester to read back.
provisions.rationale: A command that reads many repositories to assemble a large response holds the caller waiting and times out under load. Recording the request answers at once, the build runs in the background, and the requester reads the state of its own request. Which artifact counts as large depends on the data and the load of the project, so that bound sits in the shape the project names.
provisions.example: The export-expenses command records its request, and a job builds the file the requester then downloads.

provisions.heading: Send Cross-Module Queries and Commands Through the Mediator
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` (level S) for another module's public query or public command sent with no declared edge, and `effect-unimplemented` (level S) for a declared `queries` or `commands` edge no send takes, and `dotnet build` reports `LS2029` for another module's public query or query result named outside a handler, reaction, or job, and for another module's public command or command result named outside a reaction or job.
provisions.statement: A use case, reaction, or job MUST reach another module's public query or public command only through the mediator with a declared edge: a handler, reaction, or job sends another module's public query with a `queries` edge, and only a reaction or job sends another module's public command with a `commands` edge.
provisions.rationale: A module reaches another module through the provider's Contracts and the mediator, never through a port of its own: `Ports/` holds driven ports only, and a port or adapter folder named for a provider module is a placement finding. Provider result types appear in Application code, while Domain takes plain values and identifiers, never a provider's result. A handler never sends its own module's queries: it reads those through its repository or the read session. An endpoint sends only its own use case's command. The sending use case, reaction, or job declares each query edge as `effects.queries` naming the provider's public query use case, and the sending reaction or job declares each command edge as `effects.commands` naming the provider's public command use case. Settled by [decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data](decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, a reimbursement command sends spending's public read-expense query through the query mediator with a declared `queries` edge, and a reporting reaction sends spending's public command through the command mediator with a declared `commands` edge.

provisions.heading: Send Notifications Through the Messenger Port
provisions.evidence: Does every `sends` effect run in an event handler through the messenger port, after the commit? Look at each send beside its record's `sends` entry.
provisions.statement: Each `sends` effect MUST run in an event handler or job through the messenger port, after the commit of the command that raised its trigger.
provisions.rationale: A command handler changes only its aggregate under `litespec/core/backend-application#dispatch-only-declared-effect-edges`, so a notification send runs in an event handler after the commit. The notification record owns the template, the audience, the channel, the consent rule, the frequency, the dedup key, and the claims each message keeps. The `sends` edge names the notification, and the notification record carries its suppression in `suppressedWhen`. The messenger port carries the send with project-owned types. A reaction or job that only sends lives in the `Application/Notifications/` folder named for its notification, beside the notification's message model and any type only that notification uses. A send no edge declares fails `effect-undeclared`, and a second send of a `once` notification with the same dedup key sends nothing.
provisions.example: The due-notice event handler sends the loan-due notification through the messenger port. The template and consent rule stay on the notification record, not in the handler.

provisions.heading: Send Public Commands in Process
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2029` for another module's public command or command result named outside a reaction or job.
provisions.statement: A reaction or job MUST send another module's public command in process and synchronously through the command entry point.
provisions.rationale: A public command travels like a public query: the reaction or job sends the owner's command through the command entry point, and the owner runs its ordinary command handler through its own pipeline, with authorization, audit, idempotency, and validation. A command handler never sends a command, so each command commits in its own pipeline. Durable asynchronous sending stays a later step; the records and contracts do not change when it comes. Settled by [decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data](decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, reporting's close-period reaction sends spending's close-expenses command through the command entry point, and the spending handler runs the change through spending's own pipeline.

provisions.heading: Separate Input Validation from Invariants
provisions.evidence: Does every validator check structural input only, leaving aggregate state to Domain? Look at each validator body.
provisions.statement: A validator MUST limit its checks to structural input, leaving aggregate state decisions to Domain.
provisions.rationale: Structural input and aggregate state fail for different reasons at different times. Malformed input is rejected before Domain runs, while a state refusal needs the loaded aggregate. A validator that checked state would need the aggregate, which pulls persistence into validation and judges one input in two layers. Validators stay with structural input, an empty title, a malformed identifier, or an invalid page size, and leave state decisions, such as whether an expense above the threshold carries a receipt, to Domain. Every validator for a message reports validity findings under `litespec/core/backend-application#report-input-problems-as-validity-findings`, so the caller learns the whole form in one answer.
provisions.example: Take the Claimwick expense submission, `use-case/spending.submit-expense`. Its command carries an expense identifier and an employee identifier, plus the amount, currency, and receipt. The validator checks the shape of that input: it rejects an empty expense identifier or an empty employee identifier, and it accepts every well-formed pair. It does not ask whether an expense above the threshold carries a receipt, because that is an aggregate state decision. Domain makes that call and rejects a receipt-less expense above the threshold with `result/submit-expense.receipt-missing`, which carries the stable code `spending.receipt-missing`.

provisions.heading: Shape Query Results from Declared Output
provisions.evidence: Does every query result type carry its declared `include` groups with their fields, freshness, and visibility? Look at each result type beside its record's `output`.
provisions.statement: A query result type MUST carry the `include` groups its record's `output` declares, with their fields, freshness, and visibility.
provisions.rationale: The record's `output` names each group with its fields, their classification, the aggregates it reads, and the freshness the caller can rely on: `immediate`, `snapshot`, or `eventual` with its `within`. The result type carries one member per group, with its fields, freshness, and visibility, so the caller reads what the record promises and nothing more. A group with `visibleWhen` appears only when its condition holds, and a group wider than its `reads` names the approved requirement widening it in `widenedBy`. A group showing a figure a command re-decides names the deciding command use case or its aggregate in `decidedBy`, as `litespec/core/use-cases#name-the-use-case-that-decides-a-stale-figure` states. A query whose `timing` is asynchronous carries an `eventual` freshness with its `within` and a lag scenario.
provisions.example: The expense-list result carries its `rows` group with the declared fields, freshness, and visibility.

provisions.heading: Stage Declared Module and Integration Events in the Commit
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2022` for an event published outside the platform, and `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` for an event a handler, event handler or job publishes itself.
provisions.statement: Each module event and each outbound integration event MUST leave the commit only through the one pipeline step that stages raised domain events, built from the domain event its record `translates`, so no user code publishes an event.
provisions.rationale: When user code publishes events, two handlers publish one fact with two payloads, and a publisher in a handler emits state the act never announced. One global step, running in the command pipeline before the commit, stages each raised domain event for the reactions of its own module, each module event whose record translates that domain event, and each outbound integration event whose record translates it, built by each event's own mapping from the domain event alone. All three commit with the business work, and the outbox extension delivers them. A command handler changes only its aggregate under `litespec/core/backend-application#dispatch-only-declared-effect-edges`, so the aggregate raises its fact and the pipeline does the rest. The domain event therefore carries every field its module and integration events publish. Settled by [decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers](decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers).
provisions.example: The expense raises its reimbursed fact, and the staging step stages it, `module-event/spending.expense-reimbursed`, and the outbound `integration-event/expense-reimbursed`, each built from that fact, in the same commit. The reimburse handler publishes nothing.

provisions.heading: Use This Use-Case Layout
provisions.evidence: Does every use-case path, layer folder, trigger folder, and result part name follow the layout? Look at each path under the modules.
provisions.statement: Place each use case in one folder per layer that serves it, inside the plural aggregate folder of its aggregate, with a module-level read dropping the aggregate segment in each: `Application/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` with its message, result, handler, validator, pipeline definitions, own steps and triggers, and `WebApi/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` with its endpoint and transport models when it has an endpoint; place every port of the module in its own `Ports/{Port}/` folder with its adapter in `Infrastructure/{Port}/`.
provisions.rationale: One folder per use case inside the plural aggregate folder in each layer that serves it holds everything a reviewer needs to judge it in one set of folders, and the module tree lets a reader move from a handler to its endpoint without a map. The layer folders state each file's layer in the path and show by their presence whether the use case has an endpoint. The module `Ports/` folder lists every port of the module with its adapter in `Infrastructure/`. The reactions and job that run the use case sit in its `Application/` folder, so the folder shows every way the use case starts. Settled by [decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs](decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs).
provisions.example:
The layout reads as follows:

```text
{Product}/
  Application/                            product layer folder: pipeline positions and pipeline stages, and nothing else
  Posts/                                  one aggregate: every layer holds the plural aggregate folder
    Contracts/
      Posts/          PostId, OnPostPublished/PostPublishedModuleEvent, ReadPost/ (query and result)
    Domain/
      Posts/                              Post, PostState, and the post repository contract
    Application/
      Posts/
        CreateDraft/                      Command, Result, Handler, Validator, mapping
        GetPost/
        ListPosts/
          ListPostsQueryResultItem        a result part named after its result
        ArchiveStalePost/                 no WebApi folder: no endpoint reaches this use case
          ArchiveStalePostsJob            the job that runs this use case once per stale post
          ArchiveStalePostOnPostReportedHandler   a reaction that runs this use case
        ExportPosts/                      query, handler, definitions, result
      Notifications/
        NewPost/
          NotifySubscribersOnPostPublishedHandler   a reaction that only sends the new-post notification
    Ports/
      PostsArchive/                       IPostsArchive with its signature types in Models/
    Infrastructure/
      Persistence/                        module-wide store setup, with one folder per aggregate
        Posts/                            PostRepository with its stored documents and mapping
      PostsArchive/                       PostsArchiveWriter, one writer per section
    WebApi/
      Posts/
        CreateDraft/                      Endpoint, RequestModel, ResponseModel
        GetPost/
        ListPosts/
        ExportPosts/                      endpoint
  Customers/                              two aggregates: Domain holds one plural folder per aggregate
    Contracts/
      CustomerAccounts/  CustomerAccountId, one On{Fact}/ folder per fact, and the public queries and public commands of the account aggregate
      Consents/          ConsentId, one On{Fact}/ folder per fact, and the public queries and public commands of the consent aggregate
    Domain/
      CustomerAccounts/
      Consents/
    Application/
      CustomerAccounts/
        RestrictAccount/
      Consents/
        GrantConsent/
      ReadModels/
        OrderHistories/                   a read model of another module's published facts
    WebApi/
      CustomerAccounts/
        RestrictAccount/
      Consents/
        GrantConsent/
```

Module, aggregate, and use case order follow `litespec/core/backend-architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`.

Only a use case gets a folder named for it in an `Application/` or `WebApi/` folder, so every such folder name names one use case.

A use case's own models stay in its folder under `litespec/core/backend-architecture#give-each-use-case-its-own-models`, and any other type sits in the node layer folder that owns it, chosen by `litespec/core/backend-architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`. An event handler or job lives with what it runs, under `litespec/workspace/naming#place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs`, with its mark under `litespec/core/backend-application#answer-each-reaction-in-one-marked-class`. A folder named for a fact, a service, or a caller, or a grouping outside the closed sets, breaks that reading; it is drift rather than a second convention.

provisions.heading: Validate Query Input
provisions.evidence: Does every query with paging, filters, or ranges declare a query validator? Look at each such query beside the pipeline validators.
provisions.statement: Each query carrying paging, filters, or ranges MUST declare a query validator run by the pipeline.
provisions.rationale: An unvalidated page size or range reaches the store unchecked, and each query handler clamps its own input or none does. A query validator runs in the same pipeline step as command validators, so reads and writes answer to the same input rule.
provisions.example: The list-expenses query validates its page size through its query validator.

provisions.heading: Write Only Aggregates the Record Names
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `write-undeclared` (level S) for a handler that takes a repository whose aggregate sits outside the aggregates its record names in `writes` and `reads`; one domain repository serves each named aggregate.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST write only the aggregates its record's `writes` names, through one domain repository per aggregate.
provisions.rationale: A write outside `writes` is behavior the record hides, so the stack reader fails `write-undeclared` on it. Under `litespec/core/backend-application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage`, the handler normally takes one domain repository for the one aggregate it changes, and stages only that aggregate. A use case whose record declares `consistency: atomic` over several aggregates, named with its invariant by a decision record, takes one repository per named aggregate and stages each one. A query handler likewise projects only over the aggregates its record's `reads` names, through the read session.
provisions.example: The `approve-expense` handler takes the expense repository and no other. Staging a second aggregate fails the check unless the record declares `consistency: atomic` over both with its decision.

provisions.heading: Carry Cross-Module Text References as Contract Types
provisions.evidence: Is any cross-module identifier or reference built or parsed outside the one contract type in its publishing module's Contracts folder? Look at each text reference beside the publishing module's Contracts folder.
provisions.statement: An identifier or reference that crosses modules as text MUST be a contract type with one parser and one formatter in the publishing module's Contracts folder.
provisions.rationale: Two modules that each build and parse one reference with string interpolation hold two copies of its shape. One module writes a segment the other reads differently, and the reference then points nowhere. One contract type in the publishing module's Contracts folder holds the one parser and the one formatter, so every module builds and reads the reference through the same code.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, a payout reference travels from spending to reporting as text. Spending publishes the reference as a contract type with one parser and one formatter, and reporting builds and reads it only through that type. No module interpolates or splits the reference text on its own.

provisions.heading: Compose Each Process Explicitly
provisions.evidence: Is any host composing its process without calling the shared entry points, or building a second provider mid-registration? Look at each host entry point.
provisions.statement: A host MUST register its own transport services and call the shared composition entry points without building a second provider.
provisions.rationale: Each host registers its own services and calls the shared entry points, so the full composition of a process is visible in one place. A second provider built mid-registration resolves a different object graph than the one the host runs. WebApi and Worker are the only composition roots. Domain contains no registration code, and Application exposes contracts without resolving services.

provisions.heading: Create a Worker Project When Background Work Needs Its Own Process
provisions.evidence: Is any background work that needs independent scaling, deployment, or isolation running outside a Worker project? Look at the execution-host decision beside the solution project list.
provisions.statement: An application MUST create a Worker project when background work needs independent scaling, independent deployment, or isolation from request-path resource limits.
provisions.rationale: A shared process couples scaling, deployment, and resource limits. A restart to deploy an endpoint change interrupts a dispatch loop, and request load and dispatch load compete for one thread pool, so neither scales alone. When background work needs independent scaling, deployment, or isolation, it gets its own process. A product with one deployable unit and modest background load accepts that coupling deliberately, which is why the choice is declared rather than assumed.
provisions.example: An application whose outbox dispatches a few messages each minute can run it in WebApi. An application that dispatches continuously, or whose dispatch needs to survive an endpoint deployment, creates the Worker project.

provisions.heading: Give Each Use Case Its Own Models
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2019` for a use case folder referencing a type in another use case folder, and `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for a message, result or transport-model file outside a use-case folder.
provisions.statement: A message, result, result part, transport model or mapping MUST belong to exactly one use case and sit in its folder, so two use cases that need the same shape each declare their own.
provisions.rationale: A shared shape couples two use cases that change for different reasons: one use case adds a field, and the other starts returning it. Counting consumers for shapes moved messages and results out of their use cases into module folders as soon as a second caller referenced them, until those folders held more models than behavior. A copied shape costs a few lines and cannot drift into a wrong answer, because a shape decides nothing. A rule is different: two copies of a rule disagree, so a rule lives in one place in Domain under `litespec/core/backend-architecture#repeat-coordination-never-a-rule`. Settled by [decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs](decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs). Kernel values are the exception: money, typed identifiers, dates, and closed sets the Kernel owns are referenced directly from any layer the layer table allows, and copying one into a use case folder breaks the rule.
provisions.example: The submit-expense and approve-expense use cases each return the expense they acted on. Each declares its own result with the fields its caller needs, and neither result lives in `Domain/Expenses/`.

provisions.heading: Give Every Module Relationship One Direction
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `module-dependency-invalid` for a cycle in the module dependency graph over Contracts references, `queries` edges, `commands` edges, and reactions to facts.
provisions.statement: Every relationship between two modules MUST have one direction, so the module dependency graph over Contracts references, `queries` edges, `commands` edges, and reactions to facts holds no cycle.
provisions.rationale: A relationship with two directions says each module builds on the other, so neither has a seam to split along. One direction per relationship keeps the graph acyclic: A depends on B when A references B's Contracts, sends B's public queries or public commands, or reacts to B's facts, and no chain of such edges returns to its start. A cycle means a concept is split across two modules, and the fix moves the concept into one module, under `litespec/core/backend-architecture#merge-modules-that-need-each-others-model`. Settled by [decision/0110-module-dependencies-form-a-dag](decision/0110-module-dependencies-form-a-dag).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, reporting depends on spending through its declared edges to spending's public queries, and spending depends on nothing. A spending edge back to reporting would close a cycle and is reported naming both modules and the edges.

provisions.heading: Group a Folder That Holds Past Twenty Files
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `folder-ungrouped` for a folder past 20 files that holds none of its allowed groupings.
provisions.statement: A folder that holds past 20 files MUST hold the grouping folders the closed set of its place allows.
provisions.rationale: A folder past 20 files with no groupings reads as one long listing: a reader finds a file only by search, and review misses what the folder holds. Each kind of place has a short closed list of grouping folders, and an agent never invents another. A `Domain/{Aggregates}/` folder groups into `{Act}/` per root action, `Parts/`, `Facts/`, `Events/`, and `Exceptions/`; a `Ports/{Port}/` folder groups its signature types into `Models/`; an `Infrastructure/{Port}/` folder groups its wire types into `Models/` and the collaborators its adapter needs into `Parts/`; an `Infrastructure/Pipeline/` folder past 20 files groups into one folder per protocol. A use case folder holds everything flat with no groupings: it stays small once fan-out lives in a reaction or a job.
provisions.example: A `Domain/Entries/` folder past 20 files groups each root action into its own `{Act}/` folder, so `Domain/Entries/PostInvoice/` mirrors `Application/Entries/PostInvoiceEntry/`.

provisions.heading: Keep Business Invariants in Domain
provisions.evidence: Is any state transition or invariant enforced outside its aggregate or value object, or repeated in a handler? Look at the handlers beside the aggregates they call.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, command-handler, job, query-handler, reaction, value-object
provisions.statement: An aggregate or value object MUST be the only place that enforces a state transition or invariant.
provisions.rationale: The aggregate or value object that owns data is the only code that sees every change to it. A rule duplicated in a handler drifts from the aggregate that owns it: one path allows what the other refuses.

provisions.heading: Keep Implementations Hidden and Closed
provisions.evidence: Is any handler, validator, definition, persistence implementation, or endpoint implementation visible outside its own layer, or inheritable? Look at the implementations in each layer.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, endpoint, query-handler, reaction, repository, validator
provisions.statement: An application MUST keep each handler, validator, definition, persistence implementation, and endpoint implementation inside its own layer and closed to extension.
provisions.rationale: Hidden implementations limit each layer's surface to the contracts other layers actually use. A public handler allows direct construction that bypasses the pipeline, and an inheritable one allows overrides that split behavior across subclasses. Messages, results, and ports stay public only when another layer uses them, and automatic discovery is not a reason to widen visibility.

provisions.heading: Keep Service Registration in Hosts
provisions.evidence: Is any service registered outside host entry points and host registration modules? Look at the registration calls in each layer.
provisions.statement: Keep service registration in host entry points and host registration modules.
provisions.rationale: Registration lives where the process is composed, so hosts and their registration modules hold every registration call. A registration call inside Domain or Application inverts the dependency direction, because those layers declare abstractions.
provisions.example:
Each outer layer keeps one registration entry point, so the call order stays visible.

```text
infrastructure: register providers and options
webapi: register transport, authentication, and documentation
```

The Infrastructure entry point receives the configuration and host environment values needed to bind and validate provider options. The WebApi entry point owns error details, authentication, authorization, endpoint discovery, and API documentation.

provisions.heading: Merge Modules That Need Each Other's Model
provisions.evidence: Do any two modules need each other's model without merging or moving the shared concept? Look at the module pairs with edges both ways beside the module records.
provisions.statement: Two modules that need each other's model MUST merge into one module or move the shared concept into the module that owns it.
provisions.rationale: Two modules that each need the other's model have no seam between them: whatever the boundary, each side reaches across it. Merging them into one module, or moving the shared concept into the module that owns it, gives every concept one owner and every relationship one direction, under `litespec/core/backend-architecture#give-every-module-relationship-one-direction`. Sharing identifiers through the Kernel instead hides the cycle while the split concept stays split. Settled by [decision/0110-module-dependencies-form-a-dag](decision/0110-module-dependencies-form-a-dag).
provisions.example: Two modules passing each other's identifiers both ways merge into one module, and the shared concept lives in one aggregate with one owner.

provisions.heading: Name the Host for Work That Outlives a Request
provisions.evidence: Does any durable dispatch, queue consumption, or scheduled work run without a Decision naming its execution host? Look for the decision record under `.litespec/intent/decisions/`.
provisions.statement: An application MUST declare the execution host that runs its durable dispatch, queue consumption, and scheduled work.
provisions.rationale: The declared host is either the WebApi process or a Worker project. A rule that only constrains a Worker, when one exists, leaves unsaid where the work runs without one, so a project can host background services inside WebApi while breaking no named rule and recording no decision. Naming the host makes the choice visible either way. The declaration lives in a Decision record, following `litespec/core/model#record-each-technical-choice-as-a-decision`. Durable dispatch and queue consumption follow the outbox extension, and scheduled work follows the jobs extension. The host is a composition decision, not a code-placement decision. A job class lives with the use case it runs. The outbox dispatcher and the scheduler that drive reactions and jobs live in Worker when that project exists, otherwise in Infrastructure, and the host registers them.
provisions.example: A Decision naming WebApi as the execution host states that durable dispatch shares the request process and what that costs when the process is unavailable.

provisions.heading: Organize Code by Module, Aggregate and Use Case
provisions.evidence: Is any module, aggregate, use case, notification, external-system, or read-model folder without a declared record, with a forbidden folder name, or with a technical-grouping name? Look at the folder paths in each module.
provisions.statement: Every module MUST organize its code as the module tree with one `Contracts/` folder, one `Domain/` folder holding one folder per declared aggregate in the plural, one `Ports/` folder holding one folder per driven port of the module, the `Application/` and `WebApi/` layer folders holding one plural aggregate folder with one folder per use case inside it plus one folder per module-level read, and one `Infrastructure/` folder holding `Persistence/` nested by aggregate, `Messaging/`, `Pipeline/`, and one adapter folder per port, using only the folder names its level allows.
provisions.rationale: One plural folder per declared aggregate under `Domain/`, one folder per driven port under `Ports/` with its adapter in `Infrastructure/`, `Messaging/` with the module's message pipeline pieces, one folder per aggregate under `Persistence/`, `Pipeline/` with the module's HTTP pipeline pieces, and one plural aggregate folder with one folder per use case inside each layer that serves it fix every type's address: a reader moves from a Domain aggregate to its handler, its repository, and its endpoint without a map. The closed folder names at each level keep that reading exact, because a folder outside the allowed set is refused and no second organization grows beside the tree. A module publishes what other modules may reference in its `Contracts/` folder grouped by aggregate, every use case sits in the aggregate folder its record names or directly in the layer folders when its record is a module-level read, and each reaction and job sits in the folder of the use case it runs. A folder named for a fact would reference the commands of other use cases and pull them out of their folders, and a fact's reactions span modules, so no fact folder could ever show them all. Every module keeps its plural aggregate folder in every layer, whatever its number of aggregates and even when the aggregate's name equals the module's. Settled by [decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs](decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs). The module tree shape is settled by [decision/0107-kernel-platform-and-one-project-per-module](decision/0107-kernel-platform-and-one-project-per-module). A folder named for a technical grouping rather than a module defeats the rule: the next unrelated type fits it too. `Shared`, `Common`, `Util`, `Helpers`, `Core`, and `Misc` inside a layer are the names that do this.
provisions.example:
```text
# one aggregate: every layer holds the plural aggregate folder, even when the aggregate's name equals the module's
Organizations/
  Contracts/
    Organizations/            the identifier, one On{Fact}/ folder per fact, and the public queries and public commands of the organization aggregate
  Domain/
    Organizations/            Organization, OrganizationState, the organization repository contract
  Application/
    Organizations/
      CreateOrganization/     Command, Result, Handler, Validator
  WebApi/
    Organizations/
      CreateOrganization/     Endpoint, RequestModel, ResponseModel

# multi-aggregate module: Domain holds one plural folder per aggregate, each layer holds one plural aggregate folder with one folder per use case inside it
Spending/
  Contracts/
    Expenses/                 ExpenseId, OnExpenseReimbursed/ExpenseReimbursedModuleEvent, ReadExpense/ (query and result)
    Policies/                 the identifier, one On{Fact}/ folder per fact, and the public queries and public commands of the policy aggregate
  Domain/
    Expenses/                 Expense, the expense repository contract, and the act, part, fact, event, and refusal groupings
    Policies/
  Application/
    Expenses/
      SubmitExpense/
      ErasePersonalData/      the erase command, its handler, and the job that runs it
    ReadExpenseDirectory/     a module-level read: no aggregate folder
    Notifications/
      ApprovalReminder/       the reaction that only sends the approval reminder
  Ports/
    {Port}/                   I{Port} with its signature types in Models/
  Infrastructure/
    Persistence/              module-wide store setup, with one folder per aggregate
      Expenses/               the expense repository with its stored documents and mapping
    Messaging/                the domain-to-module event mapping, audit writers
    Pipeline/                 middleware, authorization conditions, authentication handlers
    {Port}/                   the adapter implementing Ports/{Port}/, same folder name, with its wire types in Models/ and its collaborators in Parts/
  WebApi/
    Expenses/
      SubmitExpense/
```

The placement check asserts these folder names directly: a rule that only a reviewer checks stops holding at the first missed file.

```text
fail when a type path contains Shared, Common, Util, Helpers, Core, or Misc
```

provisions.heading: Own Each Layer's Contract Types
provisions.evidence: Is any inner layer's type reused as an outward contract, or any other module's port answer returned as-is, outside Kernel values and aggregate typed identifiers? Look at the results and transport models in each layer's folders.
provisions.statement: A layer MUST define its own outward contracts rather than reuse an inner layer's type or another module's contract type, except for Kernel values and aggregate typed identifiers.
provisions.rationale: When each layer defines its own outward contracts, a change to an inner shape stops at the boundary instead of forcing changes in every outer layer. Kernel values cross layer boundaries because the Kernel is shared by definition, and aggregate typed identifiers cross them because messages need to identify their targets. The module boundary works the same way: a provider's public query or public command answer stays inside the consumer's Application code, and a use case returns it in no result or transport model of its own, so the owner can change its answer without changing the reader's contract. Domain takes plain values and identifiers, never a provider's result.

provisions.heading: Place a Type at the Lowest Folder That Holds Its Consumers
provisions.evidence: Is any type sitting above the lowest folder holding every consumer that references it? Look at each type beside its consumers, watching for Shared, Common, Util, Helpers, Core, or Misc folders.
provisions.statement: A type that is not a use case's own model MUST live at the lowest folder containing every consumer that names it.
provisions.rationale: Counting consumers gives each type exactly one folder, so placing a type needs no judgment. The lowest folder is the use case folder when one use case references the type, the module folder when several use cases of one module reference it, and the product layer folder when several modules reference it with no module between them. A domain rule several use cases of one aggregate reference lives in that aggregate's `Domain/{Aggregates}/` folder. Every port of a module lives in the module `Ports/` folder instead, whether one use case or many call it, with its adapter in `Infrastructure/`, under `litespec/core/backend-application#declare-every-port-in-the-module-ports-folder`, so the consumer count never places a port. A type another module references is published by its owning module in `Contracts/`; across modules a type is never shared. A use case file's layer comes from its top folder in the module, and a type only Infrastructure references is an Infrastructure type. Two kinds of type follow something else instead of their own consumer count. A type that exists only to shape one contract's input or output stays with that contract, and a closed enumerated set stays whole. A use case's own models are never counted: a message, result, result part, transport model, or mapping belongs to one use case under `litespec/core/backend-architecture#give-each-use-case-its-own-models`, so the count places behavior such as ports, rule calculations, and adapters. A type's private shapes stay private beside it instead of moving up the count. The product layer folders hold what remains after the count; they are not a destination anyone chooses. A folder named for no reason (`Shared`, `Common`, `Util`, `Helpers`, `Core`, `Misc`) accepts every type placed in it, until a tenth of the layer sits outside the module tree, unreviewed and belonging to no aggregate. The Kernel values are the one product `Domain/` folder a solution keeps. Its membership is closed by `litespec/core/backend-architecture#own-each-layers-contract-types`; it is not a place for types that fit nowhere else. A service that coordinates several aggregates lives in the module that owns the aggregates it reads and writes, not with whichever module calls it first.

provisions.heading: Point Dependencies Inward
provisions.evidence: Is any outer layer referenced from an inner one? Look at the reference graph in the code.
provisions.statement: A reference MUST point inward, so Domain references no outer layer and WebApi composes the process.
provisions.rationale: Inner code references no outer code, so business rules compile and test without adapters or hosting. An outward reference would place technical concerns in Domain or coordination in Infrastructure. Application coordinates Domain, Infrastructure implements the boundaries both declare, and the reference matrix in [Dependencies](../workspace/dependencies.md) applies as written.
provisions.example:
Every reference points from an outer layer to an inner one: Application references Domain, Infrastructure references both, and Domain references neither.

![The four layers and their references: WebApi references Application and WebApi, and from Domain only typed identifiers and Kernel values; Infrastructure references Domain, Application, and Infrastructure; Application references Domain and Application; Domain references only Domain.](../assets/diagrams/backend-dependencies.svg)

provisions.heading: Produce File Formats in Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Does any Application folder produce a file format, render, or parse, instead of calling an Infrastructure port? Look for archive, CSV, JSON-writer, PDF, and rendering libraries in the Application folders.
provisions.statement: Production of a file format, rendering, and parsing MUST live in Infrastructure behind a module port, even when the code uses only the base class library.
provisions.rationale: An archive, CSV, PDF, or audit-file writer that only uses the base class library passes every layer check while doing infrastructure work, and the use case folder fills with code the use case only calls. The module declares the port in its `Ports/` folder and hands the gathered input to it; Infrastructure implements the writer, split by section, with the small shapes as private nested types. A use case folder then reads as the use case: its message, handler, validator, definitions, and result.
provisions.example: The export-expenses use case declares `IExpensesArchive` in `Ports/ExpensesArchive/` and hands it the gathered lines; the writer lives in `Infrastructure/ExpensesArchive/`, split into one writer per archive section.

provisions.heading: Read Another Module Only Through Its Contracts
provisions.evidence: Does any cross-module read load another module's aggregate or repository, or call a general reader instead of a public query sent with a declared edge, a read model, or a screen joining owner queries? Look at the cross-module reads beside the declared edges.
provisions.statement: A module needing another module's data MUST read it through the provider's public query sent with a declared `queries` edge, through its own read model built from the owner's module events, or, on a screen, through the owner's own query.
provisions.rationale: A module that loaded another module's aggregate or repository would couple its reads to the owner's consistency boundary and storage. A general reader in the owner's `Contracts/` is the same coupling one step removed: it grows a method per caller, and no record says which fields cross. The three allowed paths each state what crosses. The provider's public query answers with the owner's current value, sent with a declared `queries` edge, under `litespec/core/backend-application#send-cross-module-queries-and-commands-through-the-mediator`. A read model states each field it copies from a published event, under `litespec/core/backend-application#read-another-modules-state-through-a-read-model`. A screen joins each owner's query, under `litespec/core/ui-ia#compose-each-screen-from-its-owners-queries`.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, the reporting module reads the current expense through spending's public read-expense query, sent with a declared `queries` edge. It keeps its own `read-model/reporting.reimbursed-expense`, filled from the spending module's expense-reimbursed module event, only for the reshaped rows its lists show. It loads no spending aggregate, no spending repository, and no spending reader.

provisions.heading: Repeat Coordination, Never a Rule
provisions.evidence: Is any shared Application type only coordinating, or any use-case step repeating a decision made elsewhere? Look at the shared Application types beside the use cases that call them.
provisions.statement: A step two use cases share MUST live once in Domain, or behind the owning module's port, when it decides something, while each use case holds its own copy of a step that only coordinates.
provisions.rationale: A step that decides, such as whether an expense needs a receipt, is a rule: two copies drift until one path allows what the other refuses, so the rule lives once on its aggregate, in a domain service marked with its `rule/`, or in the owning module behind its public query or public command. A step that only coordinates, such as mapping a request or loading two records in order, decides nothing, and a shared coordinator couples the use cases that call it. Once a reaction runs each follow-on act, most shared coordinators disappear: the act raises its fact, and the other use case answers it.
provisions.example: The receipt threshold check lives once on the expense aggregate, while submit-expense and attach-receipt each map their own request.

provisions.heading: Restrict Commands to Their Own Module Aggregates
provisions.evidence: Is any command writing an aggregate outside its own module, or reaching another module outside a public command sent upstream or a fact a downstream reaction answers? Look at each command handler beside its module.
provisions.statement: A command MUST change only the aggregates of its own module, so an act on another module's aggregate runs as that module's public command sent upstream, or as a downstream reaction to the fact the command raised.
provisions.rationale: Each module guards its own consistency boundaries, so a command from another module that wrote its aggregates would bypass the owning module's rules. An act on an upstream module's aggregate is that module's public command instead: the caller's reaction or job sends it through the mediator, the owning module runs its own handler through its own pipeline, and the owning module enforces its own invariants. The caller declares the send as `effects.commands` naming the owner's public command use case. An act on a downstream module's aggregate is a fact the command raises and the downstream module's reaction answers, under `litespec/core/backend-architecture#send-commands-and-queries-upstream`.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, a reporting reaction that needs an expense changed sends spending's public command through the mediator, and the spending handler runs the change through spending's own pipeline. The reaction writes no spending aggregate itself. A spending command that changes what reporting keeps raises its fact, and reporting's reaction answers the published module event.

provisions.heading: Run Every Spanning Process from Its Most Downstream Participant
provisions.evidence: Does every process spanning modules run from its most downstream participant or a process module through public commands, with choreography only where it creates no cycle? Look at the spanning processes beside their participants' public commands.
provisions.statement: A process spanning modules MUST run from its most downstream participant, or from a process module depending on every participant, through the participants' public commands, with choreography only where it creates no cycle.
provisions.rationale: A spanning process needs one driver: the most downstream participant, which already depends on every other participant, or a process module that depends on all of them. The driver runs the process through the participants' public commands and follows their facts, so every edge points upstream and the graph holds no cycle. Choreography, where each participant reacts to the others' facts, stays allowed only where it creates no cycle: two participants answering each other's facts depend on each other both ways. Settled by [decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data](decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, a period close spanning spending and reporting runs from the reporting module, which sends spending's public commands for each spending step and follows spending's facts. Spending answers no reporting fact.

provisions.heading: Send Commands and Queries Upstream
provisions.evidence: Does any module query, command, or react to a downstream module instead of sending upstream and following upstream facts? Look at the cross-module edges beside the module dependency graph.
provisions.statement: A module MUST send another module's public queries and public commands only upstream, follow only upstream facts, and direct no query, command, or reaction at a downstream module.
provisions.rationale: The direction rule is what makes one direction per relationship hold in practice. A downstream module sends an upstream module's public queries and public commands and reacts to its facts. An upstream module never queries, commands, or reacts to a downstream module: choreography across the boundary makes two modules depend on each other, which the direction rule forbids. When an upstream module must know downstream work finished, the downstream module calls its public command, under `litespec/core/backend-application#confirm-downstream-completion-through-an-upstream-command`. Settled by [decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data](decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, the reporting module sends spending's public read-expense query and spending's public commands through the mediator, and follows spending's published facts. Spending sends nothing to reporting and answers no reporting fact.

provisions.heading: Separate Command and Query Behavior
provisions.evidence: Is any command changing outside one aggregate or skipping the domain repository, or any query loading an aggregate or writing? Look at the command and query handlers in Application.
provisions.statement: A command MUST mutate one aggregate through its domain repository while a query projects read results without loading an aggregate or writing.
provisions.rationale: Loading aggregates for a read enforces invariants the read does not need, and writing from projections enforces rules against stale shapes. Commands change one aggregate through its domain repository, following `litespec/core/backend-application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage`, with a use case declaring `consistency: atomic` over several aggregates and named with its invariant by a decision record as the declared exception. Queries project read results without loading an aggregate and write nothing, following `litespec/core/backend-application#keep-query-handlers-free-of-writes`. An enabled persistence extension may replace the read boundary for named aggregate paths, but a command still enforces no invariant from a read projection.

provisions.heading: Subscribe Across Modules Only to Module Events
provisions.evidence: Is any reaction triggered by another module's domain event instead of its published module event? Look at each reaction trigger beside the module events.
provisions.statement: A reaction to another module's fact MUST subscribe only to the published module event.
provisions.rationale: A domain event stays inside the module that raised it, while the published module event carries the fact to the other modules of the product. A reaction that subscribed to another module's domain event would couple to the owner's internals and break when they change. The module event is the stable cross-module fact, so cross-module reactions answer it. A reaction answers the module events of upstream modules only, under `litespec/core/backend-architecture#send-commands-and-queries-upstream`. A fact from outside the product still arrives as an inbound integration event.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, a reaction in the reporting module answers the published expense reimbursed module event, not the spending domain event behind it.

provisions.heading: Test Structural Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does any structural boundary lack both an analyzer or `model check` finding and an architecture test, or does any architecture test repeat a boundary a check covers? Look at the architecture tests beside the analyzer and `model check` runs.
provisions.statement: A structural boundary that no LiteSpec analyzer or `model check` finding covers MUST have an architecture test.
provisions.rationale: Layer references, package boundaries, visibility, module folders, and aggregate inheritance are invisible at runtime: the application runs the same with or without them. Without mechanical proof on every run, each one erodes unnoticed. The analyzers and `model check` already prove the boundaries a stack page names as checked, and the rows in the table below. A check over method bodies, for example, reports an outer-layer call inside a method, which a test over compiled signatures misses. An architecture test that repeats a covered boundary holds a second copy of a rule the build or the check already enforces, and the copy drifts while the analyzer or the check keeps reporting the breach. Architecture tests hold the rest: a boundary the checks cover only in part, and a structural decision the project itself made that no LiteSpec tool names. | Structural boundary | Covered by | |:---|:---| | A folder sits outside the closed set its level allows, or a module folder names no declared module | `record-placement-invalid` from `litespec model check` | | A marked code element, test, or folder sits outside the folder its record names, or a folder names no declared record | `mark-folder-drift` and `code-placement-drift` from `litespec model check` | | A folder or type carries a technical grouping name such as `Shared`, `Common`, or `Helpers` outside the declared Kernel | `name-reason-missing` from `litespec model review` |
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, no architecture test repeats the checks that report an outer-layer type in Domain, an enum in Domain, a command handler that holds a write session, or a handler that authorizes itself, because the stack's checks report each one. The architecture suite keeps a test that no module reaches another module outside its `dependsOn`, with a type in the other module's `Contracts/` folder staying allowed.

provisions.heading: Align ID Representations at Every Boundary
provisions.evidence: Is any identifier unreadable as the same value across Domain, persistence, transport, or generated clients? Look at one identifier in each boundary form.
provisions.statement: Represent an identifier the same way in Domain, persistence, transport, and generated clients.
provisions.rationale: One identifier takes a different form at each boundary, and each form is correct in its own place. Alignment means every form still reads as the same value, so a reader tracing one identifier follows it across boundaries without translation.
provisions.example: Domain and Application hold the typed identifier; the [HTTP API](backend-api.md) states the route, query, JSON, and contract forms, and [Persistence](backend-persistence.md) states the stored form.

provisions.heading: Change Each Aggregate Through Its Marked Act
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-act-missing` (level S) for a command handler changing an aggregate that calls no root method marked with its use case. The check runs in the CLI only, with no analyzer rule: the handler and the root method sit in different projects, and one compilation sees one project.
provisions.statement: A command handler changing an aggregate MUST change it by calling a root method marked with the handler's use case.
provisions.rationale: The use case declares an act, and the aggregate performs it. The mark on the root method says which act the method performs. A handler that changes its aggregate only through methods marked for other use cases performs an act its record never declared, and a reader has no way to tell from the use case which method to open. The use-case verb, the method name, and the raised event's tense agree under `litespec/core/backend-domain#raise-the-past-tense-of-a-methods-own-verb`. This provision states the marked form of `litespec/core/backend-application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage`. A command that only runs other commands and lists nothing in `writes` performs no act on a root, so it needs no marked call.
provisions.example: The handler for `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` calls `Reimburse` on the expense root, and `Reimburse` carries the mark `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense`.

provisions.heading: Compare Collection Values by Their Content
provisions.evidence: Is any collection value compared by reference instead of content, or missing a matching hash for its declared ordering rule? Look at each collection value beside the module terms.
provisions.statement: A value object containing a collection MUST implement content equality and a matching hash for its declared ordering rule.
provisions.rationale: Default structural equality compares collection references rather than contents, so two value objects holding equal lists compare as different. Content equality with a matching hash compares what the value means. Creation copies incoming mutable collections, and members return read-only views, so later changes by the caller leave the value unchanged. The module terms state whether order is part of the value.
provisions.example: A post-tags value holding an ordered list compares element by element with a matching hash. Where order is not part of the value, creation normalizes to the documented comparison order before storing values.

provisions.heading: Create Valid Aggregates Through Named Factories
provisions.evidence: Can any aggregate root be created through a constructor or a factory that is not named for its business action? Look at the creation paths of each root.
provisions.statement: An aggregate root MUST create instances only through a factory named for its business action.
provisions.rationale: A constructor carries no business name, so creation through constructors spreads creation rules across call sites. A factory named for its business action accepts typed identifiers, rejects empty identity and violated creation rules, selects the initial state, records the required events, and returns a complete aggregate. A root created with its children composes them inside the same factory call. The factory builds the children itself from typed values the caller supplies, because a caller holding an already built child could change it after the invariant was checked.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `use-case/spending.submit-expense` creates its expense through a factory named for submitting. The factory takes the expense and employee identifiers, rejects an empty identity, selects the submitted state, and records the submitted event.

provisions.heading: Declare Cross-Record Keys on the Aggregate
provisions.evidence: Is any cross-record uniqueness rule missing its `UniquenessKeys` declaration, or enforced by other code in Domain? Look at each aggregate with such a rule.
provisions.statement: An aggregate needing a cross-record uniqueness key MUST expose its current keys through `UniquenessKeys`.
provisions.rationale: `UniquenessKeys` is the only uniqueness code in Domain. The aggregate declares its current keys through it, and persistence claims and releases them in the commit that changes the aggregate, following `litespec/core/backend-persistence#claim-a-cross-record-key-at-commit`. The aggregate computes keys from its own state and validates nothing about other records, because only the store sees every concurrent write and arbitrates the race.
provisions.example: In the library product, a book holding a list of copy barcodes returns each barcode from `UniquenessKeys`, so adding a copy claims the new barcode at commit. In the Claimwick product, a payout carrying a reference that is unique across payouts and adjustments returns that reference, so a duplicate reference fails the commit on either record.

provisions.heading: Document Every Public Domain Contract
provisions.evidence: Is any public Domain type or member missing documentation of its business constraint, result, or refusal, or documented with a restated name? Look at the documentation on each public member.
provisions.statement: Every public Domain type and member MUST carry documentation stating the business constraint, result, or refusal it represents.
provisions.rationale: A reader meeting a public Domain member needs the business rule behind it, not just its signature. Documentation states the business constraint, result, or refusal the member represents. A mutation method names its source states, resulting state, protected invariant, and recorded event. A summary that restates the member name adds nothing.

provisions.heading: Express Transitions Through Business Methods
provisions.evidence: Does any public mutation skip its state check or invariant, or any lifecycle move skip replacement or its transition event? Look at the public mutation methods of each aggregate.
provisions.statement: A public aggregate mutation method MUST check current state and protect its invariants, replacing state and recording its transition event when it moves the lifecycle.
provisions.rationale: A business-named method lets the handler call the publish behavior without testing the state first: the method checks the current state and protects its invariants, then replaces state and records the transition event when it moves the lifecycle. A generic `Set`, `Update`, `Process`, or `Handle` name hides which business action ran. A mutation that changes no lifecycle state, such as `ChangeTitle` on a draft, checks state and assigns without recording a transition. Checks run before replacement, and replacement runs before recording: a method that replaces state before checking an invariant leaves a rejected aggregate holding the new state.
provisions.example:
In the Claimwick product, `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` ends with `result/reimburse-expense.reimbursed` when the expense is approved, and with `result/reimburse-expense.not-approved` when it is not. The handler calls one business method, and the method checks the state, replaces it, and records `domain-event/expense.reimbursed`.

An unapproved expense keeps its state, and the refusal carries the stable code `spending.not-approved`.

provisions.heading: Give Each Use Case Its Own Act
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-count-invalid` (level S) for a root method carrying more than one use-case mark, and `mark-unknown` (level S) for a mark on a method that changes no state.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate root method that changes state MUST perform the act of exactly one use case.
provisions.rationale: Each use case is its own path, with its own caller, setup, refusals, events, and scenarios. A method two use cases share couples them: a change made for one silently changes the other, and neither scenario set describes the method. One method per act keeps each path readable on its own; logic the acts share moves into a private method of the root that each act calls. A method that only reads or computes performs no act and carries no mark.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, a manager approving an expense and a delegate approving it for an absent manager both record an approval. The expense root offers `Approve` marked `use-case/spending.approve-expense` and `ApproveOnBehalf` marked `use-case/spending.approve-expense-on-behalf`: each raises its own event, and both call a private `RecordApproval`.

provisions.heading: Identify Each Aggregate with a Typed Version 7 Identifier
provisions.evidence: Does any aggregate identity escape the dedicated version 7 type, or does any conversion, alias, or creation path bypass its validation? Look at each identity type and its creation paths.
provisions.statement: An aggregate identity MUST be a dedicated type wrapping one version 7 UUID, with no conversion, alias, or creation path that bypasses its validation.
provisions.rationale: A bare identifier type lets one aggregate's identifier pass where another's is expected: an expense id is passed to a parameter typed for an employee id, and the compiler stays silent. A dedicated identity type wrapping one version 7 UUID makes that a compile error. With no conversion, alias, or creation path around its validation, no path back to a bare value skips validation. The type rejects the empty value, and each factory also rejects its default. New values arrive from the caller: a factory takes its identifier as an argument, and a method that needs several identifiers takes a generator. Domain reads no clock and calls no static source of time or randomness, so every Domain call stays a pure function of its inputs. Version 7 values come from the caller-supplied generator, so Domain observes no business time and decides nothing about clocks. Persistence rejects a duplicate key and the write fails, which follows the same path as any other write conflict, with the violation mapped to the use case conflict refusal under `litespec/core/backend-persistence#map-a-constraint-violation-to-its-refusal`.
provisions.example: A post identifier wraps one version 7 UUID, rejects the empty value, and parses from text through a named method.

provisions.heading: Keep Binary Floating Point Out of Exact Quantities
provisions.evidence: Is any monetary amount, rate applied to one, or exactly-compared quantity held in a binary floating-point type? Look at the field, parameter, and return types in Domain.
provisions.statement: A Domain value MUST NOT use binary floating point for a monetary amount, a rate applied to one, or a quantity compared for exact equality.
provisions.rationale: Binary floating point represents most decimal fractions only approximately, so two amounts a person reads as equal compare as different, and totals drift by fractions of a cent. Exact decimal types keep equality and arithmetic exact.
provisions.example: A tax rate multiplied into a `Money` amount uses an exact decimal type. A measured latency in a diagnostic log is not a Domain quantity and sits outside this rule.

provisions.heading: Keep Child Entities Inside the Aggregate Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does any child entity expose mutable state outside its root, including through a writable collection? Look at the child entities beside their root, including their collections.
provisions.statement: A child entity MUST expose no mutable state outside its aggregate root, surfacing its collection as a read-only collection.
provisions.rationale: A child that exposed mutable state would let outside code change aggregate data without passing the root's checks. The root creates, finds, and changes children through business methods, and collections surface as read-only collections. A child entity and the values only it holds sit in the part folder named for its data group, under `litespec/core/backend-domain#organize-a-module-by-aggregate-and-concept`. A child with lifecycle states uses the same state types and no enumeration.

provisions.heading: Keep Domain Independent of Outer Layers
provisions.evidence: Does any Domain type reference code outside the language standard library and project-owned Domain types? Look at the references in the Domain code.
provisions.statement: The Domain code MUST reference only the language standard library and project-owned Domain types.
provisions.rationale: Domain that references only the language standard library and its own types compiles and tests with no infrastructure at all. Each banned reference would bring one outer concern into the business model: persistence metadata couples a rule to a store format, and dispatch plumbing couples it to delivery. Infrastructure registers a persisted discriminator instead, so Domain carries no serialization metadata.

provisions.heading: Limit Each Repository to One Aggregate
provisions.evidence: Is any domain repository serving more than one aggregate, exposing non-Domain types, or offering a composable query, session, or generic CRUD surface? Look at each repository interface.
provisions.statement: A domain repository MUST serve exactly one aggregate root, exposing only aggregate and Domain types, with no composable query, session, or generic CRUD surface.
provisions.rationale: One domain repository per aggregate keeps the write side shaped by the aggregates it loads. A required load looks the aggregate up by identity and reports a missing aggregate through the missing-resource refusal, so a handler repeats no absence check. An optional lookup is reserved for cases where absence is normal. A composable query, session, or generic CRUD surface would expose store mechanics to every handler. This boundary is the write side only: a query uses a read model owned by Application and shaped by Infrastructure, with no Domain contract on that path. A repository that gained a projection method would put query shapes in Domain, which is the coupling this layer exists to prevent. A flow that finds a record or creates it is two use cases that the boundary owning the flow chooses between, following `litespec/core/backend-application#implement-one-outcome-path-per-command`.
provisions.example: A post repository loads a post by identity, reports a missing post through the missing-resource refusal, and stages the loaded aggregate through a staging call. The Infrastructure implementation owns the refusal, the command pipeline owns the commit, and the staging call stages the aggregate through the selected provider.

provisions.heading: Model Every Aggregate Lifecycle with State Types
provisions.evidence: Is any lifecycle exposed outside one state property and one closed hierarchy of per-state types? Look at the lifecycle declarations in each aggregate.
provisions.statement: An aggregate MUST expose its lifecycle only through one state property backed by one closed hierarchy of per-state types.
provisions.rationale: Each lifecycle state can carry different facts: a published post carries its publication time, and a draft has none. An enumeration, a string discriminator, a boolean flag, a parallel nullable field, or a computed state carries no state-specific data. State types hold each state's data on the state itself, and aggregate methods own the transitions between them. A switch over the state types gives each case its own arm where the language requires a fallback, and a case with no arm reaches that fallback at run time.
provisions.example:
A post defines one abstract post state with draft and published cases, and the published case carries its publication time. An aggregate with one current state still defines the hierarchy, so the second state has a home.

In the Claimwick product, `aggregate/spending.expense` records the `Submitted`, `Approved`, `Refused`, and `Reimbursed` states with their transitions: Submit from `use-case/spending.submit-expense` creates Submitted, Approve from `use-case/spending.approve-expense` moves Submitted to Approved, Refuse from `use-case/spending.refuse-expense` moves Submitted to Refused, and Reimburse from `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` moves Approved to Reimbursed. The approved case carries the approver and the decided time, and the reimbursed case carries the reimbursed time.

![Submit from submit-expense creates a Submitted expense, Approve from approve-expense moves it to Approved carrying the approver and the decided time, Refuse from refuse-expense moves it to Refused carrying the reason, and Reimburse from reimburse-expense moves an Approved expense to Reimbursed carrying the reimbursed time.](../assets/diagrams/backend-aggregate-lifecycle.svg)

provisions.heading: Model Every Closed Set as a Type Hierarchy
