provisions.evidence: Is any closed set kept outside one type hierarchy with named label lookups? Look at each closed set and its boundary lookups.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST model a closed set as one type hierarchy whose cases the type system can enumerate.
provisions.rationale: A closed set with case data needs a type per case. An enumeration carries no case data, admits undefined values, and forces parallel nullable fields the moment one case gains data. A closed hierarchy gives each case a named type with its own arm in a switch, and a case with no arm reaches the switch fallback at run time. A label arriving from outside converts to its case through a named lookup rather than through a string conversion, and an unrecognized label fails validation rather than landing on a default case.
provisions.example:
A refund outcome defines pending, succeeded, failed, and reversed cases, and each case carries its own data.

This provision owns the Domain form. Application mirrors the set in its result under `litespec/core/backend-application#mirror-a-domain-closed-set-in-the-result`, the wire mirrors it as a transport model of the same shape under `litespec/core/backend-api#mirror-each-closed-set-on-the-wire`, and storage mirrors it as a stable string discriminator under `litespec/core/backend-persistence#keep-serialization-behavior-out-of-domain`. Label-only sets cross the boundary as plain enumerations under `litespec/core/backend-api#publish-label-only-sets-as-string-enums`. A transport label converts to its type case before it reaches a Domain method.

provisions.heading: Model Money with Exact Decimal Values
provisions.evidence: Is any monetary amount held outside the shared `Money` value, missing its currency, or serialized in another shape? Look at each monetary amount in Domain.
provisions.statement: A monetary amount MUST use an exact decimal type inside one shared `Money` value object carrying an ISO 4217 currency code and serializing as `{ "amount": "12.50", "currency": "EUR" }`.
provisions.rationale: Money needs exact arithmetic and an explicit currency on every value, and one shared `Money` object gives both. The owning module record defines supported currencies, scale, rounding, sign rules, and cross-currency arithmetic, and Infrastructure maps that precision explicitly. A use case fixed to one currency accepts an amount alone and states that currency in its record.
provisions.example:
```json
{ "amount": "12.50", "currency": "EUR" }
```

The amount serializes as a string, so no reader parses it as binary floating point.

provisions.heading: Name Domain Types from Their Aggregate Root
provisions.evidence: Is any Domain name breaking the cited workspace naming provisions, or any state case breaking the one kept form? Look at each Domain name.
provisions.statement: Derive each Domain type name from the aggregate root it belongs to, following the workspace naming provisions cited below.
provisions.rationale: Aggregate-prefixed names keep each type readable at its call site without its namespace. Aggregate-owned names follow `litespec/workspace/naming#anchor-aggregate-owned-types-on-the-aggregate-root`, architectural suffixes follow `litespec/workspace/naming#use-architectural-suffixes`, and refusal names follow `litespec/workspace/naming#name-exceptions-by-failed-rule`. A project names every state case in one form and keeps it.
provisions.example: A post title reads as `PostTitle` at its call site, and a published post state as `PostPublishedState`. The stack page states the declaration form each name takes.

provisions.heading: Organize a Module by Aggregate and Concept
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` (level S) for a domain event outside its aggregate's `Events` folder, for a state beside its aggregate root, and for a second store interface of one aggregate, and `folder-ungrouped` for a folder past 20 files that holds none of its allowed groupings.
provisions.statement: Give each aggregate a `Domain/` folder named with its plural root name, holding the root's main file, the repository interface as the aggregate's only store interface, and the root's partial files for a concern no single act owns at its top with the groupings `{Act}/`, `Parts/`, `Facts/`, `Events/`, and `Exceptions/`.
provisions.rationale: Each aggregate `Domain/` folder holds everything one aggregate owns: its states, events, refusals, and concepts. A reader finds the full aggregate in one place instead of hunting shared folders. Every aggregate keeps its own folder, whatever the module's number of aggregates. Each root action groups into its own `{Act}/` folder with its partial file, its inputs, its private rules, and the steps only it calls; entities, value objects, state types, and the stateless rules several acts share sit in `Parts/`; values passed in from other modules or the country pack sit in `Facts/`; domain events sit in `Events/` and refusals in `Exceptions/`. A part is a data group the aggregate record declares with dotted field names, such as `parcel.*`. The part's child entity and the values only that child holds sit in `Parts/`, while the part's events and refusals stay in the aggregate's `Events/` and `Exceptions/` folders.
provisions.example:
```text
{Product}/
  Domain/                         the shared kernel: the root, event, identity, and refusal contracts
  Posts/                          one aggregate: every layer holds the plural aggregate folder
    Domain/
      Posts/
        Post                      the root's main file
        PostRepository            the repository interface
        CreateDraft/              the act's partial file, inputs, and private rules
        Publish/
        Parts/
          PostId
          PostTitle
          PostState
          PostDraftState
          PostPublishedState
          PostArchivedState
        Events/
          PostCreatedDomainEvent
          PostPublishedDomainEvent
        Exceptions/
          PostIdentityRequired
          PostAlreadyPublished
  Shipping/                       one aggregate whose name differs from the module
    Domain/
      Shipments/
        Shipment
        ShipmentRepository
        RecordOutcome/
        Parts/
          ShipmentId
          ShipmentOutcome
          ShipmentDeliveredOutcome
          ShipmentReturnedOutcome
          ShipmentLostOutcome
          ShipmentState
          ShipmentPendingState
          ShipmentDispatchedState
          ShipmentDeliveredState
        Events/
          ShipmentOutcomeRecordedDomainEvent
        Exceptions/
  Customers/                      more than one aggregate: one plural folder per aggregate
    Domain/
      CustomerAccounts/
        CustomerAccount
        CustomerAccountRepository
        Restrict/
        Parts/
          CustomerAccountId
          CustomerAccountState
          CustomerAccountClaimedState
        Events/
          CustomerAccountRestrictedDomainEvent
        Exceptions/
      Consents/
        Consent
        ConsentRepository
        Grant/
        Parts/
          ConsentId
          ConsentState
          ConsentGrantedState
        Events/
          ConsentGrantedDomainEvent
        Exceptions/
```

Each aggregate's domain repository stays with the aggregate it loads. The module, aggregate, and use case order follows `litespec/core/backend-architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`. Each stack page states the file names and extensions that carry this layout.

provisions.heading: Pass Nondeterministic Values into Domain
provisions.evidence: Is any clock read, random source, or new identifier reached from inside Domain instead of passed in as an argument? Look at the calls Domain code makes.
provisions.statement: Domain behavior MUST receive time, randomness, and new identifiers as arguments rather than read them, and read no clock.
provisions.rationale: Domain behavior that reads a clock or generates identifiers returns different results for the same call, which makes tests nondeterministic: the same test passes and fails with no code change. Receiving time, randomness, and new identifiers as arguments keeps every Domain call a pure function of its inputs: a test supplies explicit values and stays deterministic. Application obtains each value through an owned port and passes it in. A method that needs more than one value receives a clock or a generator through its arguments, and version 7 identifiers come from the caller-supplied generator.

provisions.heading: Place Every Part Type in Its Aggregate's Folder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `part-parent-missing` (level S) for an unmarked Domain type whose folder holds no aggregate root and is not the product `Domain/` folder, and the model output lists each part under its aggregate.
provisions.statement: A Domain part type, meaning an identifier, a state type, a closed set, a child entity, a value object, or a repository interface, MUST sit in the `Domain/` folder of the aggregate it belongs to, or in the product `Domain/` folder, and a row or projection a port returns is no part.
provisions.rationale: A part serves no record of its own: it belongs to its aggregate, whose record states the states, transitions, and data the part holds. A mark on each part would write that fact a second time, and the two copies would drift. The folder shows which aggregate a part belongs to, so the builder derives the link from it. A type in a folder that holds no aggregate root, and that is not the product `Domain/` folder, is the one place the derivation fails. A domain service that holds one rule calculation is not a part: it carries its `rule/` mark. A row or projection a port returns is not a part either: it is the port's answer, shaped for a reader, and it sits with its port.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `IExpenseRepository` sits beside the `Expense` root in `Spending/Domain/Expenses/`, `ExpenseState` sits in its `Parts/` grouping, and both carry no mark; the builder lists them as parts of `aggregate/spending.expense`. `Money` sits in the product `Domain/` folder and belongs to no aggregate.

provisions.heading: Raise Immutable Facts as Domain Events
provisions.evidence: Is any domain event mutable, named for the wrong aggregate or fact, or carrying more than business data? Look at each domain event.
provisions.statement: A domain event MUST be immutable and carry business data only.
provisions.rationale: A domain event records a completed fact for reactions to consume. The event carries business data only: typed identifiers and the values its reactions need, with no aggregate, session, service, mutable collection, or thrown error, because any of those would couple reactions to the raising aggregate. Envelope identity, such as message identity and causation identity, lives on the published integration event that carries the fact outside the process. That integration event points to the domain event in its `translates` field. The event name states the aggregate and the completed fact, following `litespec/workspace/naming#anchor-aggregate-owned-types-on-the-aggregate-root` and `litespec/workspace/naming#use-architectural-suffixes`, so a reader knows which aggregate raised the fact without opening the file.

provisions.heading: Raise the Declared Events from the Marked Act
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `act-event-undeclared` (level S) for a marked method raising an event its use case does not list, and `act-event-unimplemented` (level S) for a listed event no marked method raises.
provisions.statement: The root methods marked with a use case MUST together raise exactly the events that use case lists in `raises`.
provisions.rationale: The use case record states the facts its act leaves behind, and reactions subscribe to those facts. A marked method that raises an event the record does not list starts a consequence nobody reviewed, and a listed event that no marked method raises is a promise the code does not keep. Each raised event carries every field its module and integration events publish, because each module and integration event is built from its domain event alone under `litespec/core/backend-application#stage-declared-module-and-integration-events-in-the-commit`.
provisions.example: `use-case/spending.submit-expense` lists `domain-event/expense.submitted` in `raises`, and the `Submit` method marked with it raises `ExpenseSubmittedDomainEvent` and nothing else.

provisions.heading: Raise the Past Tense of a Method's Own Verb
provisions.evidence: Does any state-changing aggregate method raise an event named for a different verb than its own? Look at the events each changed aggregate method raises.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate method that changes state MUST raise a domain event named for the past tense of its verb.
provisions.rationale: The command raises nothing; the aggregate root raises its domain event inside its own method. An event named for another verb tells the reader the act finished under a name no method carries, and reactions subscribe to a vocabulary the aggregate does not own. The event name takes the past tense of the act's verb, as `litespec/core/domain-model#name-every-event-in-the-past-tense` requires for every event. The name may place the past tense as a whole word followed by a complement that opens with a preposition or particle. A method that sets a state names that state in its event, and a method may raise further events for the consequences of its act, as long as one of its events names the act itself.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `Approve` on an expense raises `domain-event/expense.approved` and passes. `Approve` raising `domain-event/expense.signed-off` fails review, because that name belongs to another act.

provisions.heading: Reach an Aggregate Only Through Its Root
provisions.evidence: Does every caller reach the aggregate only through its root? Look at the callers of each aggregate beside its root's factories and methods.
provisions.statement: Code outside an aggregate MUST reach the aggregate only through its root's named factories and methods, passing plain inputs.
provisions.rationale: The root is the one entry point to its aggregate: it alone decides how the aggregate's state changes. When a caller builds an entity or value object of the aggregate, or calls a service that produces part of the aggregate's state, the aggregate's behavior splits across layers. The caller chooses which rule applies and in which order, and a later caller can skip a step. Passing plain inputs, such as typed identifiers, values, and input records, keeps that knowledge inside the root. The root alone records the aggregate's domain events, following `litespec/core/backend-domain#raise-the-past-tense-of-a-methods-own-verb`. The parts of this rule that own their own provision stay there: one repository per root under `litespec/core/backend-domain#limit-each-repository-to-one-aggregate`, typed-identifier references under `litespec/core/backend-domain#reference-other-aggregates-by-id`, and child entities with no mutable surface under `litespec/core/backend-domain#keep-child-entities-inside-the-aggregate-boundary`. Settled by [decision/0104-reach-each-aggregate-only-through-its-root](decision/0104-reach-each-aggregate-only-through-its-root).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, the submit-expense handler calls `Expense.Submit` with the expense and employee identifiers, the lines, and the submitted time. The root computes the cost-center allocation inside its own method and records the submitted event. No handler builds an allocation line, and no service produces part of the expense.

provisions.heading: Reference Other Aggregates by ID
provisions.evidence: Does any aggregate field hold another aggregate as an object reference instead of a typed identifier? Look at the fields of each aggregate.
provisions.statement: An aggregate MUST store another aggregate's typed identifier rather than an object reference.
provisions.rationale: An object reference between aggregates loads one aggregate's data through another, which couples their consistency boundaries and their storage. A typed identifier keeps each aggregate loadable on its own, and Application loads each side through its own domain repository when a command coordinates several aggregates, with `consistency: atomic` citing the rule in `boundBy` and the decision in the rule's `basedOn`.

provisions.heading: Reject Business Violations with Dedicated Refusals
provisions.evidence: Is any rejected business rule ending outside a dedicated refusal with its stable code, or carrying transport status? Look at each rejection beside its refusal.
provisions.statement: A rejected business rule MUST end its use case in a dedicated refusal carrying its stable code.
provisions.rationale: One refusal per rejected rule lets each boundary map outcomes without parsing messages: the refusal names the failed rule, and the stable code travels to the caller. The name leads with the aggregate root. Domain raises no standard library, validation, transport, or provider failure for a business rejection, and carries no transport status: the host maps refusals to transport errors through the mapping the API page documents under `litespec/core/backend-api#defer-error-mapping-to-the-global-handler`. Refusal names follow `litespec/workspace/naming#name-exceptions-by-failed-rule`; this provision owns the one-refusal-per-rule shape and the code each refusal carries.
provisions.example:
A refund allocation rule ends its use case in its own refusal, rather than sharing one refusal with a code passed at the call site.

Two rules that share a caller-visible refusal code because a boundary maps them to one response still get two refusals. The shared code lives in the two refusals, not in a value passed by the aggregate. One refusal serves more than one input only when one rule fails from more than one input and the differing values arrive as creation parameters.

Application validators handle malformed caller input through validity findings. Aggregate and value-object refusals remain the last defense when direct Domain use violates a rule. Command handlers do not catch expected Domain refusals.

provisions.heading: Reuse the Shared Domain Contracts Across Modules
provisions.evidence: Is the root, event, identity, or refusal contract declared more than once across modules? Look at those contracts in each module.
provisions.statement: Declare the shared Domain contracts once in the product `Domain/` folder and reuse them across every module.
provisions.rationale: One declaration keeps the root, event, identity, and refusal mechanics identical in every module. A second declaration drifts from the first with the next fix.
provisions.example:
The shared contracts are the aggregate root, the domain event, the typed identity, and the refusal.

Event clearing is delivery mechanics, not a business mutation. Infrastructure calls it only after delivery accepts the pending events.

provisions.heading: Store Each State the Reader Sees
provisions.evidence: Is any state a reader sees inferred from the absence of another record instead of stored on its aggregate? Look at each displayed state beside its aggregate.
provisions.statement: An aggregate MUST store each state a reader sees instead of inferring it from the absence of another record.
provisions.rationale: A state inferred from absence reads two stores to answer one question: the aggregate and the record whose absence means the state. The two disagree under concurrent writes, and a reader that checks only the aggregate reads the wrong state. Storing the state on the aggregate keeps the answer in one place. The automation rule `litespec/core/automation#settle-every-async-outcome-in-visible-states` states how pending, done, and refused read apart; this provision states the domain side: the state lives on the aggregate.
provisions.example: In the library product, a loan that charged its overdue fee records that fact on the loan. A reader sees the charged state on the loan itself instead of inferring it from the absence of a pending charge record. In the Claimwick product, a reimbursed expense carries the reimbursed state with its time; no reader infers reimbursement from the absence of an outstanding payout.

provisions.heading: Take Identity and Events from the Shared Root Contract
provisions.evidence: Does any aggregate root take identity or event mechanics from outside the project-owned root contract? Look at each aggregate root declaration.
provisions.statement: An aggregate root MUST take its identity and event mechanics from the project-owned root contract.
provisions.rationale: One shared root contract gives every aggregate the same identity and event mechanics, so Infrastructure collects pending events from any aggregate the same way. The contract stays small on purpose: it owns typed identity, pending events, recording, and clearing, plus the aggregate version as persistence metadata that Domain never reads or sets. A timestamp, audit, tenant, lifecycle, or other persistence behavior would couple every aggregate to a concern only some need.

provisions.heading: Treat Aggregates as Consistency Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Can any invariant be changed through a public mutation outside its aggregate root? Look at the public mutation entry points of each aggregate.
provisions.statement: An aggregate root MUST be the only public mutation entry point for every invariant its transaction protects.
provisions.rationale: If outside code could set properties or call child mutations directly, it would change data around the root's checks. With the root as the only public mutation entry point, every change passes the invariant its transaction protects. A command with `consistency: atomic` changes every aggregate listed in its `writes` in one transaction, citing the rule in `boundBy` and the decision in the rule's `basedOn` when it changes more than one.

provisions.heading: Use Immutable Value Objects for Domain Concepts
provisions.evidence: Is any value object mutable, comparing by less than its complete value, or creatable without validation? Look at each value object and its creation paths.
provisions.statement: A value object MUST be immutable, compare by its complete value, and validate every value at creation.
provisions.rationale: Immutability with comparison by complete value lets two instances with the same data stand in for each other. The value exposes no mutation and no implicit conversion, because a primitive conversion hides validation and a value conversion erases the domain type. Readers use the wrapped value or its text form, and creation through a named creation path keeps every value under the validation the type declares.
provisions.example: A post title accepts only non-blank text up to 200 characters: blank or longer input fails creation, and two titles with the same text compare as equal.

provisions.heading: Use One Ubiquitous Language
provisions.evidence: Does every Domain name match a term in the project glossary? Compare the Domain names with `glossary.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A Domain name MUST match a term in the project glossary.
provisions.rationale: When code and records use different names for one action, every reader translates between them. `SetStatus` in code hides which business action ran. With one shared name from the project glossary on both sides, the record and the code describe the same action in the same words.
provisions.example: The glossary names the business action `Publish`, so the root method is `Publish`, not `SetStatus`.

provisions.heading: Use Stateless Domain Services for Ownerless Rules
provisions.evidence: Is any domain service stateful, taking or returning non-Domain values, or calling persistence, messaging, logging, clock, authorization, or a provider? Look at each domain service and its calls.
provisions.statement: A domain service MUST be stateless, hold only a calculation that spans aggregates with no owning aggregate, accept and return Domain values, and perform no persistence, messaging, logging, clock, authorization, or provider call.
provisions.rationale: Some calculations span concepts with no natural aggregate owner. Forcing one into an aggregate couples that aggregate to another's data. A stateless service holds the calculation instead, accepting and returning Domain values with no persistence, messaging, logging, clock, authorization, or provider call. A calculation one aggregate owns stays in that aggregate's root. The root calls the service inside its own method, or Application passes the service's plain result into a root method as an input. A result that carries part of an aggregate's state never crosses that boundary: the aggregate's parts are built inside the root. A domain service takes no port and holds no state, so its tests are Domain tests: they sit beside the aggregate tests in the unit tests mirroring the module tree, with no harness, no substitute, and no fixture. Settled by [decision/0104-reach-each-aggregate-only-through-its-root](decision/0104-reach-each-aggregate-only-through-its-root).
provisions.example: An order-pricing service takes order lines and a currency and returns their total as `Money`, with no domain repository, clock, logger, or provider client. The order root calls it inside `ConfirmPrice`, or Application supplies the lines and passes the returned total into `ConfirmPrice` as an input. The service returns no order line and no other part of the order.

provisions.heading: Add Read Documents for Query-Shaped Data
provisions.evidence: Is any read document missing recorded consistency and rebuild behavior beside its owning use case? Look at each read document.
provisions.statement: Add a module-owned read document for repeated cross-aggregate composition, deep traversal, or a distorting index shape.
provisions.rationale: Aggregate documents serve simple reads. Repeated cross-aggregate composition or deep traversal through them loads whole aggregates to show a few fields. A module-owned read document carries that shape directly. Its owning use case defines its consistency and rebuild behavior.

provisions.heading: Assign Document Numbers from a Sequence
provisions.evidence: Is any legal document number allocated outside a per-owner sequence taken in the command transaction? Look at each number allocation.
provisions.statement: Each legal document number MUST allocate from a per-owner sequence taken in the command transaction.
provisions.rationale: A number computed from a count plus one gives two concurrent issues the same legal number. A per-owner counter row taken in the command transaction allocates each number once, no matter what races it.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command takes its number from the spending payout sequence, not from a list count.

provisions.heading: Claim a Cross-Record Key at Commit
provisions.evidence: Is any cross-record uniqueness rule missing declared keys, or claiming and releasing them outside the committing transaction? Look at each such rule beside its commit.
provisions.statement: A uniqueness rule that no single-record constraint can express MUST be declared by the aggregate as a key and claimed and released by persistence in the commit that changes the aggregate.
provisions.rationale: Some rules fit no single-record constraint: a value held in a list inside the aggregate, or a value that is unique across two record kinds. A check in code sees only its own transaction. It passes two racing writers. For those rules, the aggregate declares its current keys through `UniquenessKeys` (see `litespec/core/backend-domain#declare-cross-record-keys-on-the-aggregate`). Persistence compares the keys at load with the keys at commit, inserting the added keys and deleting the removed ones in the same transaction. The database still arbitrates the race.
provisions.example: In the library product, a book holds a list of copy barcodes and each barcode belongs to one book: the book declares each barcode as a key, and the commit that adds a copy claims the new barcode while releasing a removed one. In the Claimwick product, a payout reference that is unique across payouts and adjustments is declared by each aggregate that carries it, so a reference already used by either record blocks the other at commit.

provisions.heading: Collect Events Without a Public Unit of Work
provisions.evidence: Is any touched aggregate missing from the internal event buffer, or any event mechanics exposed through a public type? Look at the repository staging calls beside the post-handler.
provisions.statement: A repository MUST register each touched aggregate with the internal event buffer that the post-handler drains.
provisions.rationale: Pending events leave the process exactly when their write commits. The post-handler drains the buffer and commits in one place. A public unit-of-work type would expose that mechanism to every handler. The internal buffer keeps it inside the pipeline. Async delivery leaves after the commit succeeds.

provisions.heading: Commit Each Command Pipeline Once
provisions.evidence: Does any pipeline commit outside one command post-handler, or do any handlers, repositories, validators, reactions, jobs, or endpoints commit? Look at the commit calls in each pipeline.
provisions.statement: Exactly one global command post-handler MUST commit the session for a command pipeline.
provisions.rationale: One commit point makes the transaction boundary visible. Everything the handler staged succeeds or fails together, and a failed command leaves the session uncommitted. If handlers or repositories committed, a later failure in the same pipeline would leave a partial write behind. Handlers, repositories, validators, reactions, jobs, and endpoints commit nothing. Every command runs as a top-level pipeline with its own commit, because no handler sends a command. A command uses no caller's commit. A declared consistency mode other than `atomic` splits work across commands. Each command still commits once.
provisions.example:
In the Claimwick product, `use-case/spending.submit-expense` stages the expense through its Domain repository, and one post-handler commits once after the handler returns:

```text
handler stages the expense through its repository
post-handler collects the pending events
post-handler commits the session once
```

A failed submission leaves the session uncommitted, so no partial expense is stored.

provisions.heading: Control Production Schema Changes
provisions.evidence: Is any hosted schema change applied outside a reviewed step before traffic shifts, or from a starting replica? Look at the deployment steps beside the startup paths.
provisions.statement: A hosted environment MUST apply schema changes through a reviewed step before traffic shifts, not from a starting replica.
provisions.rationale: A schema change that runs from a starting replica races every other starting replica. The winner is nondeterministic. A reviewed step produces the migration artifact instead. A deployment step applies that artifact before traffic shifts. Development and disposable integration databases still apply schema automatically. A tool that alters the schema from application startup is no reviewed step, whichever provider runs it.

provisions.heading: Enforce Uniqueness in the Store
provisions.evidence: Is any uniqueness rule missing a store unique index or an owner-derived identity, or indexing a denormalized field? Look at the store configuration for each rule.
provisions.statement: Each uniqueness rule MUST be enforced by the store, through a unique index over the stored value or, for a record that exists at most once per owner, through an identity derived from its owner.
provisions.rationale: The store is the only place that sees every concurrent write. A check in code sees only its own transaction. Two commands that both check and then both write store the same value twice. A unique index or an owner-derived identity makes the second write fail in the store instead. When the rule ignores case or spacing, the stored value is normalized before writing and the index covers the normalized field. Differently cased writes still collide.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, each payout carries a legal document number that is unique per spending owner. The store holds a unique index over the owner and number pair, so two concurrent reimbursements collide on the index and the loser ends with the use case conflict refusal instead of sharing one number. In the library product, each book barcode is unique across books: two clerks registering the same barcode at once collide on the barcode unique index, and the second commit refuses with `book-barcode-taken`.

provisions.heading: Evolve Stored Document Contracts Explicitly
provisions.evidence: Is any rename, removal, type change, member move, or discriminator change shipping without a reviewed transformation or an expand-and-contract rollout? Look at each stored-contract change.
provisions.statement: A rename, removal, type change, member move, or discriminator change MUST have a reviewed data transformation or an expand-and-contract rollout.
provisions.rationale: Stored JSON member names, required values, and discriminator values are database schema. Old documents stay on disk after the code changes. Without a reviewed transformation or an expand-and-contract rollout, a rename or type change makes old documents unreadable. An additive member still defines its behavior for documents written earlier. An additive change is the only kind that needs no transformation. It counts as additive only when every earlier document stays valid. A new member with a defined absent-value behavior qualifies. A new required member, a narrowed type, or a new discriminator value that an earlier reader rejects does not.

provisions.heading: Honor the Declared Consistency Mode
provisions.evidence: Is any command committed in a shape its record's `consistency` mode does not declare? Look at each commit beside the record's mode.
provisions.statement: Persistence MUST commit a command exactly as its use-case record's `consistency` mode states.
provisions.rationale: Under `atomic`, everything the handler staged commits in one unit of work, citing the rule in `boundBy` and the decision in the rule's `basedOn` when `writes` names more than one aggregate. When `consistency` names `guards`, the guarded read holds each guard to commit by a lock, a version check, or serializable isolation, and the stack page fixes which. Under `per-record`, each record's command commits alone, and the job resumes from its cursor after a failure. A second commit inside one command splits one unit of work across two transactions. A failure between them leaves a partial write.
provisions.example: The erase-expired-data job commits each expense alone under `per-record`, while the submit-expense command commits its staged aggregates together under `atomic`.

provisions.heading: Keep Mappings and Aliases Explicit
provisions.evidence: Is any stored aggregate missing a stable document alias, a typed-identifier mapping, or the indexes its accepted queries need? Look at the store configuration for each aggregate.
provisions.statement: Each stored aggregate MUST declare a stable document alias, typed-identifier mapping, and the indexes its accepted queries need.
provisions.rationale: Document types and collection names are storage identity. If they followed code names, renaming a class would orphan every stored document. An explicit alias, identifier mapping, and index list keeps storage identity independent of code names. The store configuration owned in Infrastructure holds all three.

provisions.heading: Keep Serialization Behavior Out of Domain
provisions.evidence: Is any serialization metadata sitting on a Domain type, or any stored JSON contract owned outside Infrastructure? Look at the Domain types beside the Infrastructure JSON contract.
provisions.statement: Infrastructure MUST own the JSON contract for stored documents, including member names, constructors, converters, and polymorphic registration.
provisions.rationale: Serialization metadata on Domain types couples the business model to one store's format. Changing the format then means editing the rules. Infrastructure owns member names, constructors, converters, and polymorphic registration. Domain stays free of serialization metadata. Every concrete type behind a base or interface is registered, because an unregistered subtype fails at read time. Registration covers the types this store actually persists. The store that writes a union referenced from another aggregate registers it once, instead of every store that names the referencing type. A type reachable only through an identifier is persisted by no store here, so it needs no registration.

provisions.heading: Keep Unbounded Collections Out of Aggregate Documents
provisions.evidence: Is any collection with no accepted business bound embedded in an aggregate document? Look at the embedded collections in each document.
provisions.statement: An aggregate document MUST NOT embed a collection that has no accepted business bound.
provisions.rationale: A document grows with every write to its collection. An unbounded embedded collection eventually exceeds size limits and slows every load of its aggregate. Data with no accepted business bound belongs in another aggregate, an owned document record, or a separate query-shaped document, depending on the consistency boundary it needs.

provisions.heading: Keep Uniqueness Out of Handlers
provisions.evidence: Is any handler reserving, claiming, checking, or releasing a uniqueness key? Look at each handler body.
provisions.statement: A handler MUST NOT reserve, claim, check or release a uniqueness key.
provisions.rationale: A reservation made in a handler runs outside the commit that needs it. It can leak when the command fails later. It also teaches every later handler to coordinate with the store directly. The store enforces the rule at commit through `litespec/core/backend-persistence#enforce-uniqueness-in-the-store` and `litespec/core/backend-persistence#claim-a-cross-record-key-at-commit`. The pipeline turns a lost race into the use case conflict refusal under `litespec/core/backend-application#refuse-a-lost-race-as-a-conflict`, so the handler carries no reservation, check, or cleanup.
provisions.example: The register-reader handler creates the reader aggregate and stages it through its Domain repository. It reserves no card number and checks no registry first. When two registrations race for one card number, the second commit violates the unique index and refuses with the use case conflict, with no reservation or cleanup code in the handler. The submit-expense handler likewise stages the expense and leaves the payout number to the store sequence.

provisions.heading: Map a Constraint Violation to Its Refusal
provisions.evidence: Is any unique constraint missing a conflict refusal mapping for the use cases that can violate it? Look at the fault classification map.
provisions.statement: Each unique constraint MUST map by name to the conflict refusal of the use cases that can violate it.
provisions.rationale: When the store refuses a commit, pipeline fault classification turns that fault into the use case named conflict refusal, following `litespec/core/backend-application#refuse-a-lost-race-as-a-conflict`. The map keys each unique constraint by name. The classifier then knows which refusal the violation answers. An unmapped violation still fails the commit, but it reaches the caller as a generic conflict that names no rule and suggests no next step. A classifier that builds the code from the lost key, one code per key scope, declares its template in the project file `refusals.composed`. The model checks then read each code as raised where its key scope is declared.
provisions.example: The barcode unique index is named `uq_book_barcode`, and the map pairs it with `book-barcode-taken`, so a registration that loses the barcode race refuses with that code. The payout number index is named `uq_payout_owner_number`, and the map pairs it with the reimburse conflict refusal, so each racing command names the number it lost.

provisions.heading: Model a Once-Only Rule as Aggregate State
provisions.evidence: Is any at-most-once rule held outside its aggregate's state, or any repeated action escaping the refusal? Look at each such rule beside its aggregate.
provisions.statement: Each rule that an action happens at most once for a record MUST be state on that record's aggregate.
provisions.rationale: A flag on the aggregate travels with the record it guards. The rule is then checked where the record is changed. The aggregate sees the earlier action in its own state and refuses the repeat, or leaves it without effect. A counter or marker kept anywhere else splits the rule from the record. The two disagree under concurrent writes.
provisions.example: In the library product, a loan charges its overdue fee at most once. The loan records that it charged the fee, and a repeat command finds the flag and refuses with the loan conflict refusal. In the Claimwick product, an expense is reimbursed at most once: the reimbursed state carries the fact, so a second reimbursement finds an already reimbursed expense and ends with `spending.not-approved`.

provisions.heading: Page and Filter Collection Queries in the Store
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `query-filter-invalid` (level S) for a query handler filtering a repository list in memory.
provisions.statement: Each collection query MUST page and filter in the store, never load a whole list to shape it in memory.
provisions.rationale: A query that loads a whole list to filter, sort, or page it in memory pays the full read on every call. It breaks when the data grows. Repository list methods take the scope and the page and filter in the database instead, through the shared page request and page shapes.
provisions.example: The list-expenses query passes its employee scope and page to the repository. A handler that filters a full list in memory is reported.

provisions.heading: Persist One Explicit State Object
provisions.evidence: Is any aggregate document flattening its state object, or any state failing to round-trip through the serializer? Look at each stored state in the integration tests.
provisions.statement: Persist the aggregate state object itself rather than a flattened projection, round-tripping every state object through the configured serializer in integration tests.
provisions.rationale: The stored state object keeps the aggregate's lifecycle and its state-specific facts in one value. A read then materializes the same state the command stored. A flattened projection splits that value across members the store cannot version together. A flag beside the object disagrees with it after the next transition.

provisions.heading: Query Through the Read Session
provisions.evidence: Is any query handler projecting outside the read session, or applying filter, scope, ordering, or limit after materialization? Look at each query handler body.
provisions.statement: A query handler MUST project through the read session, applying filter, scope, ordering, and limit before materialization.
provisions.rationale: The session already projects, filters, and pages. A read-store interface per aggregate, a generic read repository, or a callback wrapper adds a layer that only repeats it. Applying filter, scope, ordering, and limit before materialization keeps that work in the database. Materializing first loads rows the caller does not see. Ordering and paging follow `litespec/core/backend-api#bound-collection-queries`.

provisions.heading: Review Query Plans for New Indexes
provisions.evidence: Is any new index missing an accepted query or a justifying plan on representative data? Look at each new index beside its query.
provisions.statement: Add an index only from an accepted query or a measured operating need, and inspect its plan on representative data.
provisions.rationale: Every index costs write throughput on each change to its table. An index added without reading its plan on representative data pays that cost for a read with no measured need. So each index starts from an accepted query or a measured operating need.

provisions.heading: Serialize Every Persisted Payload with One Configuration
provisions.evidence: Does any persisted payload serialize outside the one shared configuration, or any store carry converters the others lack? Look at the document store, the outbox store, and the scheduled-job store beside the shared configuration.
provisions.statement: The document store, the outbox, and any scheduled-job store MUST serialize every persisted payload through one shared serializer configuration.
provisions.rationale: A typed identifier or money value that serializes one way in the document store and another way in the outbox arrives in a different shape than the store wrote. Two configurations drift with the first converter added to one and not the other: an identifier that survives the store arrives empty through the outbox. One shared configuration with the same converters keeps every persisted payload round-tripping the same everywhere.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, the expense document, the expense-reimbursed outbox envelope, and the erase-expired-data job payload each carry the expense identifier and money amounts. All three serialize through the one product serializer configuration, so the identifier and the amounts read back identically from each store.

provisions.heading: Stage Aggregate Writes Through Domain Repositories
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `repository-unimplemented` (level S) for an aggregate a use case changes that has no Infrastructure repository implementing its domain repository, and `code-placement-drift` for a repository implementation outside its aggregate's `Persistence/` folder.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST reach persistence only through a Domain repository, never through the session directly.
provisions.rationale: The repository is the one reviewable path from a handler to the store, shaped around one aggregate type. Without it, handlers reach the session directly, bypass aggregate loading, and scatter store calls through Application. Infrastructure implements each repository with the command session. The repository exposes no session, generic query, or save operation.
provisions.example: The submit-expense handler stages the new expense through the expense repository; it names no session and issues no store call of its own.

provisions.heading: Test Persistence Against the Pinned Database
provisions.evidence: Is any repository behavior, projection, mapping, correctness index, commit behavior, or schema application tested outside the pinned database, or against an in-memory substitute? Look at the persistence test fixtures.
provisions.statement: Repository behavior, projections, mappings, correctness indexes, commit behavior, and schema application MUST run against the pinned database.
provisions.rationale: Only the pinned database runs the real query planner, constraints, and type behavior. An in-memory substitute proves the test's own model of the database. A query that passes against it fails in production. HTTP integration through the real host is covered under `litespec/core/testing#test-http-integration-through-the-real-application-host`.

provisions.heading: Use Database Naming Conventions
provisions.evidence: Is any schema, table, column, index, constraint, document alias, or SQL identifier breaking `snake_case`? Look at the schemas, tables, columns, and indexes.
provisions.statement: A database schema, table, column, index, constraint, document alias, or SQL identifier MUST use `snake_case`.
provisions.rationale: One casing rule lets anyone predict a table or column name from the code type without opening the mapping. Code types keep normal language naming while the mapping layer converts once. The store configuration sets the casing. No configuration repeats the rule per entity.

provisions.heading: Use One Persistence Folder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for a repository implementation outside its aggregate's `Persistence/` folder, for a use-case model or adapter file in `Persistence/`, and for any other file directly in `Persistence/` outside module-wide store setup.
provisions.statement: Place store setup in the product `Infrastructure/` folder, each module's store setup in its own `Infrastructure/Persistence/` folder, and each aggregate's repository implementation, stored documents, and mapping in `Infrastructure/Persistence/{Aggregates}/`.
provisions.rationale: The product `Infrastructure/` folder holds store setup, session and commit plumbing, and serialization shared by every module. Every persistence type then has one discoverable home. Each module keeps its store setup in its own `Infrastructure/Persistence/` folder, and each aggregate's repository implementation, stored documents, and mapping in `Infrastructure/Persistence/{Aggregates}/`, so every layer nests by aggregate. Scattered configuration hides the provider setup across the product.
provisions.example:
```text
{Product}/
  Infrastructure/                   store setup: registration, configuration, commit handler, event buffer
    StoreServiceRegistration
    StoreConfiguration
    Commands/
      CommitCommandPostHandler
    Events/
      DomainEventBuffer
  Posts/                            one aggregate: every layer holds the plural aggregate folder
    Infrastructure/
      Persistence/
        Posts/
          PostRepository
          PostStoreConfiguration
  Customers/                        two aggregates: one folder per aggregate
    Infrastructure/
      Persistence/
        CustomerAccounts/
          CustomerAccountRepository
          CustomerAccountStoreConfiguration
        Consents/
          ConsentRepository
          ConsentStoreConfiguration
```

The module folders follow `litespec/core/backend-architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`: each module keeps its repositories in its `Infrastructure/Persistence/{Aggregates}/` folders.

Aggregate-specific configuration sits beside its aggregate's repository. Session and commit plumbing sit under the product store root.

provisions.heading: Use One Session per Command
provisions.evidence: Is any command resolving more than one session across its repositories and commit handler? Look at the session wiring in each command.
provisions.statement: Resolve one session for the repositories and the commit handler in one command.
provisions.rationale: One session per command means the repositories and the commit handler stage and commit the same unit of work. Two sessions in one command commit separately. A failure between them leaves a partial write behind.

provisions.heading: Version Every Aggregate
provisions.evidence: Is any stored aggregate committed without a compared version, or any stale write escaping the use case conflict refusal? Look at each stored aggregate beside its commit.
provisions.statement: Each stored aggregate MUST carry a version that the store compares at commit, so a lost update fails the commit.
provisions.rationale: Without a compared version, two commands can load the same aggregate and both commit. The second silently overwrites the first. The store compares the version each command loaded with the version it commits against. A stale write fails the commit instead of erasing newer work. A failed comparison ends with the use case conflict refusal, following `litespec/core/backend-application#refuse-a-lost-race-as-a-conflict`.
provisions.example: Two approvers open the same submitted expense. The first approval commits and moves the version forward, and the second approval fails its version comparison and refuses with the approve conflict instead of overwriting the first decision. In the library product, two clerks extending one loan race the same way, and the loser re-reads the loan before deciding again.

provisions.heading: Illustrate Pages with Examples from the Cast
provisions.evidence: Does every module, aggregate, and use-case explanation file carry an Example section from the cast where a case would add to the records? Check the Example sections against the record files, or against the recorded project convention.
provisions.statement: Each module, aggregate, and use-case explanation file carries an Example section drawn from the cast, removed where no case adds to the records.
provisions.rationale: Fields state rules, states, and mappings, but none says when the behavior happens or who is under pressure while it runs. An occasion drawn from the one shared cast lets a reviewer judge the behavior against the world it serves, and lets readers carry the same people and figures from page to page.

provisions.heading: Keep Design Choices Out of the Records
provisions.evidence: Does any record page declare a child entity or value object as a record type? Check the record types against the aggregate pages.
provisions.statement: Child entities and value objects MUST appear only in code and the glossary, never as records.
provisions.rationale: The design inside an aggregate changes without changing its business meaning, so a record for every child entity and value object would triple the tree in size without adding one decision a reviewer judges. Keeping those choices in code and the glossary puts them where builders and readers meet them, and leaves records for what carries business meaning.
provisions.example: Order lines live as a child of the order aggregate, and money as a value with its glossary entry; neither is a record.

provisions.heading: Shape Each Module Page
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a module record file missing a required field.
provisions.statement: A module MUST state its `summary` and its `dependsOn` in fields.
provisions.rationale: The module names one product area of the bounded context, so Intent, Behavior, and code share one name for one area. `summary` states what the area covers in one place, and `dependsOn` names the modules it builds on, so a reader learns where each area sits once and finds its records under one folder. Cross-cutting work sits at product level, never in a module that borrows it. The module is declared in Behavior, beside the aggregates it groups, because it is a code boundary. Proposed by [decision/0051-declare-modules-only-in-behavior](decision/0051-declare-modules-only-in-behavior).
provisions.example: The spending module covers expenses, receipts, and the policy, with an empty `dependsOn` where it stands alone.

provisions.heading: Apply HTTP Version Preconditions
provisions.evidence: Does every versioned HTTP operation return a strong persistence-derived `ETag` and require `If-Match` on writes? Check the versioned endpoints.
provisions.statement: An HTTP operation requiring a caller version MUST return a strong persistence-derived `ETag` and require `If-Match` on writes.
provisions.rationale: The caller reads the current state with its strong persistence-derived `ETag` and sends it back in `If-Match` on the write. The server compares what the caller saw with what is stored. The round trip carries the version through HTTP headers instead of a second contract field.
provisions.example: A current `ETag` permits the write; a changed entity version rejects it.

provisions.heading: Build Fingerprints from Canonical Request Data
provisions.evidence: Does every fingerprint derive from canonical input, route identity, and actor identifier, with no credentials and no client key? Check the fingerprint derivation.
provisions.statement: An idempotency implementation MUST derive its fingerprint from canonical mapped command input, route identity, and the authenticated actor identifier, excluding credentials and the client key.
provisions.rationale: The fingerprint decides whether two requests under one key carry the same intent. Canonical mapped command input, route identity, and the authenticated actor identifier make equivalent requests produce one value. The actor identifier is in the fingerprint because two actors can present the same client key, and a fingerprint without it would replay one actor's stored response to another. The credential that proved the actor stays out, since a cookie and a signature each change between two requests this rule treats as equal.

provisions.heading: Compare Caller and Stored Versions in One Transaction
provisions.evidence: Does every caller-version comparison run inside the transaction carrying its change? Check the conflicting-write paths.
provisions.statement: An implementation MUST compare the caller-supplied version with the stored version in the same transaction as the change.
provisions.rationale: The caller-supplied version marks which write the caller saw, and the stored version marks what the database holds. Comparing the two in the same transaction as the change detects a competing accepted write against the same state, through the selected persistence model. A comparison outside that transaction can miss a competing write that commits between the comparison and the change.

provisions.heading: Declare Applicable Headers
provisions.evidence: Does every applicable operation expose the idempotency header in the generated OpenAPI, or a recorded header-declaration convention naming how contracts expose it? Check the generated OpenAPI document beside that convention.
provisions.statement: Declare the idempotency header as required on each applicable HTTP operation.
provisions.rationale: Each HTTP operation that accepts a client key declares the header as required. Generated API contracts then expose the requirement to every client author, under `litespec/core/backend-api#publish-precise-complete-schemas`. An undeclared header reaches only the callers who read the implementation.

provisions.heading: Define Concurrent Retry Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every idempotent use case define whether a concurrent request waits, reports in-progress, or returns a stable conflict? Check the idempotent use case pages.
provisions.statement: An idempotent use case MUST define whether a concurrent request waits, reports in-progress, or returns a stable conflict.
provisions.rationale: An identical request can arrive while the first is still running. The use case states whether that concurrent request waits, learns the work is in progress, or receives a stable conflict. Without one documented result, each implementation invents its own and callers handle all of them.

provisions.heading: Delay Irreversible Provider Calls
provisions.evidence: Does any irreversible provider call run before its business transaction commits? Check the idempotent operation paths.
provisions.statement: An idempotent operation MUST NOT perform an irreversible provider call before its business transaction commits.
provisions.rationale: A provider call that cannot be undone follows the commit. A call made before commit fires even when the transaction then rolls back. The business change would vanish while its external effect stands.

provisions.heading: Discard Failed Replay State
provisions.evidence: Does every failed pre-commit request leave neither a business change nor a completed replay record? Check the failure paths.
provisions.statement: A failed pre-commit idempotent request MUST leave neither the business change nor a completed replay record.
provisions.rationale: A request that fails before commit changed nothing, so it leaves neither the business change nor a completed replay record. A leftover completed record would replay success for work that never happened. Clean state lets a later retry perform the operation for the first time.

provisions.heading: Document Write Conflict Behavior
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `field-extension-unselected` for a `conflicts` entry written when `concurrency` is not selected, and `record-invalid` for a `conflicts` entry that names no `subject`, no `winner`, or no `refusal`, or a `winner` outside `first-write`, `last-write`, and `merge`.
provisions.statement: A command that can conflict with another accepted write MUST state `conflicts` naming what conflicts in `subject`, which write wins in `winner`, and the refusal id the loser gets in `refusal`.
provisions.rationale: Version coordination exists to protect one invariant. The `subject` entry names the conflicting operations and the invalid combined result they would leave, so an implementation distinguishes a conflict it rejects from contention it absorbs. The `winner` entry names which write wins: `first-write` keeps the accepted change and refuses the late write, `last-write` lets the late write replace the accepted change, and `merge` combines both writes. The `refusal` entry names the refusal id the loser gets from its aggregate's refusal set, or from the module's set for a refusal no aggregate raises, so the caller learns the loss as a declared refusal with its stable code. Every command whose writes can conflict declares `conflicts`.
provisions.example: Claimwick's approve-expense command states `conflicts` with `subject` naming a second approval of the same expense, `winner: first-write`, and `refusal` naming the refusal id the late approval gets.

provisions.heading: Enforce Key Uniqueness
provisions.evidence: Does every idempotency store enforce the unique constraint on tenant, actor, operation, and client key? Check the store schema.
provisions.statement: An idempotency store MUST enforce a unique constraint on tenant, actor, operation, and client key.
provisions.rationale: Two concurrent requests can arrive with the same key before either commits. The unique constraint on tenant, actor, operation, and client key admits one winner and rejects the other at the store. Application code alone cannot order two requests that arrive together. A project without the tenancy extension uses one fixed tenant value.

provisions.heading: Exclude Failures and Secrets from Replays
provisions.evidence: Does any replay return an authentication failure, a transient failure, a cookie, a hop-by-hop header, a token, or a secret? Check the replayed responses.
provisions.statement: An idempotent implementation MUST NOT replay authentication failures, transient server failures, `Set-Cookie`, `Cache-Control`, `Vary`, `Expires`, `Age`, hop-by-hop headers, tokens, or secrets.
provisions.rationale: Authentication failures and transient server failures describe one exchange rather than the accepted result, so replaying them answers a new request with an old failure. Tokens, secrets, cookies, and hop-by-hop headers each belong to the exchange that produced them. The caching headers are computed for the response that produced them, so replaying them hands a later caller freshness instructions from an earlier moment. [RFC 9111](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9111) makes each one a property of the exchange rather than of the result, so the replayed response computes its own.

provisions.heading: Hash Sensitive Fingerprint Data
provisions.evidence: Does any idempotency store keep original sensitive content that support never needs? Check the fingerprint store.
provisions.statement: An idempotency implementation MUST store a cryptographic hash when support does not require original sensitive request content.
provisions.rationale: The fingerprint has to compare requests, not to show what they contained. A cryptographic hash preserves the comparison while the original sensitive content stays out of the store. The store keeps original content only where support needs the original.

provisions.heading: Hide Provider Version Values
provisions.evidence: Does any transport model expose a provider-specific version value outside the `ETag`? Check the public transport models.
provisions.statement: An HTTP API MUST NOT expose a provider-specific version value in another contract field.
provisions.rationale: The `ETag` is the one contract field that carries the persistence version. A provider-specific version leaked into another field gives callers a second version to depend on. Hiding it keeps the persistence version behind one contract field, so the project can change it without breaking callers.

provisions.heading: Keep Idempotency Persistence in Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Does every idempotency persistence and transaction handling sit in Infrastructure, or under a recorded idempotency-store convention naming where its state lives? Check the idempotency store code beside that convention.
provisions.statement: Keep idempotency persistence and transaction handling in Infrastructure.
provisions.rationale: Idempotency state lives in provider transactions guarded by store constraints. That machinery belongs in Infrastructure, where provider details live. Application and Domain stay free of the store mechanics behind their operations.

provisions.heading: Keep Keys Until Callers Stop Retrying
provisions.evidence: Does any key expire before the documented safe retry time? Check the retention settings beside the idempotent use cases.
provisions.statement: An idempotency owner MUST NOT expire a key before callers can safely retry.
provisions.rationale: Callers retry inside a documented window after an uncertain response. A key that expires inside that window is gone when the retry arrives, so the retry runs as new work. Retention covers the whole window the project promises.

provisions.heading: List Which Statuses and Headers Replay
provisions.evidence: Does every idempotent use case list the statuses and headers stored for replay? Check the idempotent use case pages.
provisions.statement: An idempotent use case MUST list the statuses and headers stored for replay.
provisions.rationale: A completed retry reproduces the stored statuses and headers instead of the live ones. The declared list states which statuses and headers the store holds. A reviewer reads that list to learn exactly what a retry can return.

provisions.heading: Map Replay Responses at the API Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does every replay response mapping sit at the API boundary, or under a recorded replay-mapping convention naming where it lives? Check the replay mapping code beside that convention.
provisions.statement: Keep replay response mapping at the API boundary.
provisions.rationale: Replaying a stored result means rebuilding its statuses and headers. Those are transport concerns, so the mapping lives at the API boundary. Application code then deals in operation results, never in wire shapes.

provisions.heading: Reject Conflicting Key Reuse
provisions.evidence: Does every reuse of one key with a different fingerprint meet the documented rejection? Check the key-reuse paths.
provisions.statement: An idempotent operation MUST reject reuse of one key with a different request fingerprint.
provisions.rationale: A key reused with a different request fingerprint names two different intents under one key. Accepting both would replay the first intent's result for the second intent's request. Rejecting the reuse keeps one key bound to one intent.

provisions.heading: Reject Silent Overwrites
provisions.evidence: Does any conflicting write silently replace the accepted change? Check the conflict outcomes.
provisions.statement: An implementation MUST NOT silently overwrite a conflicting accepted change.
provisions.rationale: A conflicting write that silently replaces the accepted change destroys work another caller committed, and the losing caller never learns its change is gone. Rejecting the conflict instead hands the caller the facts it needs to reconcile.

provisions.heading: Remove Expired Keys Within Fixed Bounds
provisions.evidence: Does every expired-record cleanup run as a bounded maintenance process? Check the cleanup jobs.
provisions.statement: An idempotency owner MUST remove expired records through a bounded maintenance process.
provisions.rationale: Expired keys accumulate without cleanup, and cleanup without bounds takes capacity from live work. A bounded maintenance process removes expired records within fixed limits on rate and batch. The store stays small without starving the application.

provisions.heading: Replay Completed Results
provisions.evidence: Does every completed idempotent retry return the original response status and body? Check the replay paths.
provisions.statement: A completed idempotent retry MUST return the original response status and body.
provisions.rationale: The first attempt performed the state change, and the retry performs it no second time. Returning the original response status and body gives the retry the accepted result. The caller sees one execution no matter how many times the network retried.

provisions.heading: Replay the Winner for Losing Concurrent Requests
provisions.evidence: Does every losing concurrent request with a matching fingerprint reload and replay the winning record? Check the concurrent retry paths.
provisions.statement: A losing concurrent idempotency request MUST reload and replay the winning record when its fingerprint matches.
provisions.rationale: The unique constraint admits one winner among concurrent same-key requests. A losing request whose fingerprint matches reloads the winning record and replays its result. The loser then returns the accepted outcome instead of an error for work that succeeded.

provisions.heading: Require Caller Versions Only for Declared Conflicts
provisions.evidence: Does every caller-version requirement have a `conflicts` entry on its command? Check the versioned operations beside the use case records.
provisions.statement: An implementation MUST NOT require a caller-supplied version without a `conflicts` entry on its command.
provisions.rationale: Every stored aggregate already carries a baseline version that the store compares at commit, so the version itself needs no record. Requiring the caller to supply a version adds a rejection path the caller has to handle: a missing or stale caller version refuses an otherwise valid write. The `conflicts` entry is the condition for that caller burden: without an entry, the implementation requires no caller version.

provisions.heading: Return 409 for Failed Version Checks
provisions.evidence: Does every failed expected version return 409 Problem Details with its stable code? Check the conflict responses.
provisions.statement: An HTTP API MUST map a failed expected version to status 409 Problem Details with a stable code.
provisions.rationale: A caller that loses a version race retries by reading again, applying again, and sending again. Status 409 with a stable Problem Details code names the loss as a conflict, distinct from validation and authorization failures. Without that stable code, the caller guesses which failure it met.

provisions.heading: Return Precondition Outcomes
provisions.evidence: Does every versioned operation return 428 `precondition_required` for a missing `If-Match` and 409 `version_conflict` for a stale version? Check the precondition responses.
provisions.statement: An HTTP API MUST return 428 `precondition_required` for missing `If-Match` and 409 `version_conflict` for stale versions.
provisions.rationale: A missing `If-Match` and a stale version are different caller mistakes with different fixes: send the version, or read again and retry. Status 428 `precondition_required` names the omission and 409 `version_conflict` names the stale version. One code for both would leave the caller guessing which fix applies.

provisions.heading: Route Required External Effects Durably
provisions.evidence: Does every required external effect use the outbox or a documented provider idempotency contract? Check the idempotent operation paths.
provisions.statement: An idempotent operation MUST use the outbox extension or a documented provider idempotency contract for required external effects.
provisions.rationale: A required external effect has to survive retries without duplicating. The outbox extension delivers it durably after commit, or a documented provider idempotency contract lets the provider absorb the replay. An effect with neither path fires once per retry.

provisions.heading: Run Idempotency in the Pipeline
provisions.evidence: Does every idempotent operation run idempotency in a pipeline stage after authorization and validation, before the handler? Check the pipeline stage order.
provisions.statement: Idempotency MUST run as a pipeline stage after authorization and validation, before the handler.
provisions.rationale: Authorization and validation run first, so a denied or invalid attempt neither consumes a client key nor replays a stored result. The handler runs after, so a replayed key returns the stored response without running the handler again. Any other order either spends keys on attempts the pipeline would refuse, or runs work the store already accepted.

provisions.heading: Scope Client Keys
provisions.evidence: Does every idempotent operation scope its client key to tenant, authenticated actor, and operation? Check the keyed operations.
provisions.statement: An idempotent operation MUST scope its client key to the tenant, authenticated actor, and operation.
provisions.rationale: A client key alone proves nothing about who sent it: two callers can pick the same key. Scoping the key to tenant, authenticated actor, and operation stops one caller's key from replaying another caller's operation. A project without the tenancy extension uses one fixed tenant value.

provisions.heading: Set Key Retention
provisions.evidence: Does every key retention cover the caller retry window and the business risk? Check the setting record beside the idempotent use case.
provisions.statement: An idempotency owner MUST record key retention as a setting record set from the caller retry window and business risk.
provisions.rationale: A key that expires too early turns a legitimate retry into duplicate business work. Retention therefore spans the caller retry window plus the business risk of a late duplicate. The setting record states that span where reviewers and operators read it.

provisions.heading: Store Idempotency State Atomically
provisions.evidence: Does every idempotent operation store its fingerprint, state, response, and expiry with its business change in one transaction? Check the keyed write paths.
provisions.statement: An idempotent operation MUST store its fingerprint, state, response status, response body, and expiry with its business change in one provider transaction.
provisions.rationale: The fingerprint, state, response status, response body, and expiry describe the accepted change, so they commit with it in one provider transaction. One transaction leaves neither a completed record without its change, nor a change without its replay record. A retry then replays exactly what the first attempt accepted.

provisions.heading: Store Only Fields That Replay Needs
provisions.evidence: Does every stored replay field serve a result callers reproduce? Check the replay store.
provisions.statement: An idempotent implementation MUST store only safe response fields required to reproduce an accepted result.
provisions.rationale: The store holds what a retry needs to reproduce the accepted result, and nothing more. Each extra field widens the sensitive data held under the key's retention. A field that serves no replay need stays out.

provisions.heading: Use the Standard Idempotency Header
provisions.evidence: Does every applicable operation accept `Idempotency-Key` within its bounds, or a recorded client-key convention naming its header and value bounds? Check the operations beside that convention.
provisions.statement: Use `Idempotency-Key` for HTTP commands that accept client keys, bounded to 255 characters of visible ASCII.
provisions.rationale: The `Idempotency-Key` header makes client-key behavior recognizable at the HTTP boundary. [The IETF draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header/) leaves the value opaque, so a server stores whatever a client sends. The 255-character visible-ASCII bound stops an unbounded key from becoming an unbounded store entry, and it keeps control characters out of log lines.

provisions.heading: Change Every Instance of a Shape in One Change
provisions.evidence: Does a search of the repository for the old shape's name return nothing after the change? Run `git grep` for the old field, folder or type name.
provisions.statement: A change to a shape, such as a field, a folder, a section or a name, MUST change every instance of it in LiteSpec in the same change (the schema, the tools, the templates, the Claimwick example, the test fixtures and the pages) and add a check or a validator where one is cheap and sure, so the old shape cannot come back.
provisions.rationale: A shape changed in some places and not others leaves two answers to one question, and the next maintainer copies whichever one they find first. LiteSpec ships no compatibility path, so the change is whole or it is not made. Settled by [decision/0116-write-the-design-rules-down](decision/0116-write-the-design-rules-down).
provisions.example: When rule sets were removed, the schema, the folder table, the scaffolder, the templates, Claimwick, every test fixture and every page that showed a rule-set file changed together, and the schema rejects a rule-set file.

provisions.heading: Deliver Each Record Type Complete
provisions.evidence: Does the change that adds or moves a record type touch every part this provision lists? Walk the list against the diff.
provisions.statement: A change that adds a record type or moves it to another home MUST ship, in the same change, its schema definition, its home in the folder table, its explanation sections, its link phrases, its field-table rows, its template copied from a Claimwick record, an instance in the Claimwick example, its book placement, the checks that read it, and the pages that teach it.
provisions.rationale: A type that ships part of its shape teaches consumers a half: a schema with no home, a home with no template, or a template no example shows. Each missing part is a question every consumer answers on their own. Settled by [decision/0116-write-the-design-rules-down](decision/0116-write-the-design-rules-down).
provisions.example: The rule type's move into its own folders shipped the `rulePage` schema definition, its homes, its Rationale, Example and Limits sections, the `rule.yaml` and `rule.md` templates, Claimwick's rules split into folders, and the pages that describe them.

provisions.heading: Give a Record with Its Own Reasoning Its Own Folder
provisions.evidence: Does a new or changed record type that carries a rationale, sources or examples have a named home in the folder table, and does every type left as an entry carry no reasoning of its own? Read `RecordFolders.cs` and the type's schema definition.
provisions.statement: A record type whose records carry reasoning of their own, such as a rationale, sources, an example or limits, MUST give each record its own folder holding its record file and its explanation file, and only a closed list whose entries carry no reasoning of their own MAY hold its records as entries in a set or in their parent's file.
provisions.rationale: An entry has no explanation file, so its reasons end up in the parent's explanation, mixed with every other entry, or get lost.
