A shared file also grows with every entry, and a change to one entry rewrites the whole file and its history. Settled by [decision/0115-give-reasoned-records-their-own-folder](decision/0115-give-reasoned-records-their-own-folder), following [decision/0045-keep-each-requirement-in-its-own-folder](decision/0045-keep-each-requirement-in-its-own-folder).
provisions.example: A Claimwick rule sits at `aggregates/expenses/rules/reimbursed-once/reimbursed-once.yaml` with its explanation beside it, while the refusal codes the spending module raises stay as entries in its `refusals.yaml`.

provisions.heading: Give Every Type, Field and Value a Reader
provisions.evidence: Which check, book page, command or citing record reads each new type, field and value, and does an existing type already carry it? Search the tools for the field name.
provisions.statement: A new record type, field or enumeration value MUST have a reader (a check, the book, a command or a citing record), carry no shape an existing type already carries, and go in the same change that removes its last reader.
provisions.rationale: A shape nothing reads teaches consumers to write facts no tool will ever hold them to, and a second shape for one concept makes them choose between two answers. Settled by [decision/0025-remove-fields-nothing-reads](decision/0025-remove-fields-nothing-reads) and [decision/0076-remove-shapes-nothing-needs](decision/0076-remove-shapes-nothing-needs).
provisions.example: A `priority` field on Claimwick's requirements that no check, book page or citing record reads is not added; a field the book shows on the requirement page is.

provisions.heading: Hold One Thing in Each Record
provisions.evidence: Does each record of a new or changed type hold one thing? Read the type's statement field and ask whether a second sentence could carry its own refusal, value or scenario.
provisions.statement: A record type MUST be shaped so that each record holds one thing: one condition, one commitment, one failure case, one event or one choice, so that a second thing with its own refusal, derived value, dates or proof is a second record.
provisions.rationale: A citation, a scenario step or a code mark can rest on exactly the thing it depends on only when each record holds one thing. A record holding several makes every citation vague and reopens all of them when one changes. Settled by [decision/0116-write-the-design-rules-down](decision/0116-write-the-design-rules-down), which generalizes [decision/0114-one-condition-per-rule](decision/0114-one-condition-per-rule).
provisions.example: A Claimwick rule that held both "an expense is reimbursed at most once" and "an expense is reimbursed only after approval" is two rules, because each has its own refusal.

provisions.heading: Shape Each Record Type for Its Next Field
provisions.evidence: Would adding a field to the type change one record's file or a shared one? Read the type's home in `RecordFolders.cs`.
provisions.statement: A record type SHOULD be shaped so that adding a field, a link or an explanation section to it changes one record's file, never a whole set of records in one file.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec keeps adding facts to its record types. A type held in sets makes each addition lengthen every set for every consumer, and a type held one per file lets the record grow where it lives.
provisions.example: Adding an optional `limits` explanation section to Claimwick's rules touched only the rules that have limits to state.

provisions.heading: State Each Deviation from a Design Rule
provisions.evidence: Does each decision behind a change that departs from a rule on this page name the rule and the reason? Read the decision's Decision section.
provisions.statement: A change that sets a design rule aside MUST say so in the decision record behind it, naming the provision and why the rule does not fit.
provisions.rationale: A rule broken without a word teaches the next maintainer that the rule does not hold. A stated deviation keeps the rule and records its known exception.
provisions.example: A decision that keeps Claimwick's refusal codes in one refusal set names `litespec/core/designing#give-a-record-with-its-own-reasoning-its-own-folder` and states that a refusal code carries no reasoning of its own.

provisions.heading: Update a Design Rule That Keeps Bending
provisions.evidence: Has this rule been set aside by earlier decisions? Search `docs/intent/decisions/` for the provision ID.
provisions.statement: When two changes have set the same design rule aside, the next change SHOULD amend the rule on this page, or record why it still holds, rather than set it aside a third time.
provisions.rationale: A rule bent again and again no longer describes how LiteSpec is designed. Amending it keeps this page true; recording why it holds keeps the exceptions from becoming the rule.
provisions.example: If two decisions each keep a reasoned record type as entries, the next maintainer amends the folder rule to name the case, or records why both were exceptions.

provisions.heading: Append Released Reference Rows
provisions.evidence: Does any released row carry an edited value? Check each row's value beside its git history: a new value arrives as a new row with the old row end-dated.
provisions.statement: A released reference-data row MUST stay unchanged, with a new value arriving as a new row and the old row taking an end date.
provisions.rationale: A row is released once the product reads it. Stored records keep the rule version they were made with: an expense decided under the five-day target still points at that row after the target moves to three days. Editing the released row rewrites what those records decided under. The old row keeps its dates and takes its end date, and the new row carries the new value from its start date.
provisions.example: Claimwick's five-day row keeps 2026-01-01 to 2026-12-31 while the three-day row starts 2027-01-01.

provisions.heading: Bind a Reference-Data Table to an External Pack
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-data-pack-missing` (level G) for a reference-data table whose `pack` names no file that exists.
provisions.statement: A reference-data table that names a `pack` MUST point at a file that exists.
provisions.rationale: A pack such as a country list can carry thousands of values, so copying the whole list into a record would bury the dates and sources a reader needs. Naming the file beside the table keeps one source of truth and lets the table state only the values the product uses. A path that names no file leaves the table pointing at values nobody can read, so the check reports it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `reference-data/spending.country` names `pack: data/country-pack.csv` and holds only the rows whose effective dates and sources the product states. A table naming `data/countries.csv` when no such file exists is reported.

provisions.heading: Bind Every Atomic Write Group in Its Rule
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `atomicity-drift` (level G) for an atomic use case whose `writes` differs from its rule's `binds`, and `atomicity-invalid` (level G) for a group binding more than 4 aggregates.
provisions.statement: Each atomicity rule MUST name the aggregates it binds in `binds` and the decision behind the group in `basedOn`.
provisions.rationale: An atomic write across aggregates stays allowed only through its rule and its decision. The rule states the group and why, such as an order without its hold overselling, names in `basedOn` the decision recording why the invariant needs one transaction, and the use case commits exactly that group, as the [use-cases page](use-cases.md) states. A group above 4 aggregates is a coordination candidate, and the check reports it at level G.
provisions.example: The library's hold rule binds the hold and the copy aggregates, so a hold without its copy never stands.

provisions.heading: Cite Varying Values from Reference Data
provisions.evidence: Does a rule statement write a rate, threshold, deadline, or other value that varies by date, jurisdiction, or tenant? Check that it cites the reference-data table holding the value, or scopes the value to where it holds when no table exists yet.
provisions.statement: A rule SHOULD cite the reference-data table that holds a value varying by date, jurisdiction, or tenant, such as a rate, threshold, or deadline, instead of writing the value into its statement.
provisions.rationale: A value written into a statement is true only until its law, contract, or tenant changes it, and then the rule, its scenarios, and its code drift apart with no dated row to show when the value changed. A cited table holds each value with its effective dates and source, so the rule states the condition once and stays true across every period and jurisdiction the table covers. A value with no table yet stays in the statement, scoped to where it holds.
provisions.example: Claimwick's receipt rule says "an expense above the policy threshold needs a receipt" and leaves the amount to the policy, so a new threshold changes a row, not the rule.

provisions.heading: Close the Value Set of Every Meaning Column
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-data-value-invalid` (level G) for a row whose value is outside the table's `choices`.
provisions.statement: Each reference-data table whose meaning column changes behavior MUST list every allowed value in `choices`.
provisions.rationale: A free string compared in code compiles against any spelling, so a value goes unhandled or means two things in two rows. The closed set in `choices` names every spelling the product handles, the `reference-data-value-invalid` check reports a row outside it, and code enumerates the set instead of comparing strings.
provisions.example: The library's membership table lists `choices: [child, adult, senior]`, and a row holding `guest` is reported.

provisions.heading: Compute Shared Values from One Calculation Rule
provisions.evidence: Do the query and the command behind one value cite the same calculation rule in `computedBy`? Check the use cases beside the calculation rule.
provisions.statement: A value shown by a query and recorded by a command MUST cite the same calculation rule in `computedBy` on both use cases.
provisions.rationale: Two computations of one value drift: the screen shows one figure while the ledger records another, and each side cites its own code. Citing the same calculation rule on both use cases keeps one computation behind the shown and the recorded value. Code carries a mark naming the rule; the rule never names code.

provisions.heading: Connect Every State Through Transitions
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `state-unreached` (level G) for a state reached by no transition, a creation included, and `reference-unknown` (level G) for a transition naming a missing state, or a `movedBy` naming no use case or job.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate MUST list every allowed state change with the use case or job moving it in `transitions`, including the creation that enters its first state.
provisions.rationale: States without transitions list names with no path between them: a reviewer sees where an aggregate can stand but never how it moves. Listing every allowed change with the use case or job moving it in `movedBy` shows the whole lifecycle beside the states, and leaves no state reachable only by a path no record names. A transition moved by time names the job in `movedBy` with the duration from entering its source state in `after`. The `state-unreached` and `reference-unknown` checks report a state no transition reaches and a transition naming a missing state, use case, or job.

provisions.heading: Cover Every Date in Use
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-data-coverage-missing` (level G) for dates between rows with no row in force and for a cast `today` no row covers.
provisions.statement: Each reference-data table MUST cover every date the product reads with a row in force, at least the date the cast declares as `today`.
provisions.rationale: A read past the covered dates finds no row, and without a rule it crashes or silently takes a default. Full coverage leaves no such read: every date the product reads has a row in force. The `reference-data-coverage-missing` check reports dates between rows with no row in force and a cast `today` no row covers, and a read past the covered dates stays a refusal with a reason.
provisions.example: Claimwick's decision-target rows run from 2026-01-01 to 2026-12-31 and from 2027-01-01 on, leaving no date without a target.

provisions.heading: Date Every Reference-Data Row
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a reference-data row without `effectiveFrom` or `source`.
provisions.statement: Each reference-data row MUST state the date its value takes effect in `effectiveFrom` and the record behind its value in `source`.
provisions.rationale: A value without its date cannot be looked up for a past moment, and a value without its source cannot be defended or updated when the outside rule moves. The table keeps each value once with both, so every lookup answers with the value in force and the record behind it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's decision-target row states five business days from 2026-02-10 with `research/approval-time-benchmarks` as its source.

provisions.heading: Define Every Behavior Term in the Glossary
provisions.evidence: Does every term the Behavior records name have a glossary entry stating its meaning? Check the records beside the project glossary.
provisions.statement: Each term a Behavior record names MUST have a glossary entry stating its meaning.
provisions.rationale: Records and code share one language only when each word is defined once. A term used without an entry means whatever each reader guesses, while the entry fixes the meaning, the rejected synonyms, and the wider and narrower terms, so reviewers and checks read the same word the same way.
provisions.example: Claimwick's glossary defines `receipt` as "proof of payment accepted for an expense", so every record naming a receipt means that proof.

provisions.heading: Keep Each Rule Statement Short
provisions.evidence: `litespec model review` reports `rule-statement-wide` (level R) for a rule whose statement is longer than 600 characters.
provisions.statement: A rule statement SHOULD stay within 600 characters.
provisions.rationale: A statement past a few sentences almost always holds several conditions, or a list of values that a reference-data table or a calculation's examples hold better. The length is only the signal: a long statement that does state one condition, such as one calculation over a closed list of cases, stays whole, and the finding never blocks.
provisions.example: A Claimwick rule that stated the receipt duty, the approval chain, and the reimbursement limit of every expense category in one statement would report `rule-statement-wide`; as one rule per category and duty, each statement stays within a sentence or two.

provisions.heading: Keep Model Invariants in Rules
provisions.evidence: Does any setting hold a model invariant? Check the settings beside the rules.
provisions.statement: A model invariant MUST live as a rule, never as a setting.
provisions.rationale: A setting tunes and a rule holds. An invariant filed as a setting reads as tunable, and a later operator tunes away what the model guaranteed. Keeping invariants in rules keeps what holds apart from what varies.

provisions.heading: Keep One Home for Each Rule, Calculation, and Projection
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `logic-duplicate` (level S) for one method or local-function body of at least 6 statements or 80 tokens carried in two or more different folders.
provisions.statement: Each slice MUST call every rule, calculation, or projection from its one home in the aggregate, a domain service, or the knowledge model, instead of carrying a copy of another slice's logic.
provisions.rationale: A rule copied into several slices is fixed several times: each change must be found and made in every copy, and one copy drifts while the others move. Vertical slices multiply whatever the first slice did, so a copied projection or test spreads with every new slice. One home keeps the rule, the calculation, or the projection behind one call, so a change lands once and every slice moves together.
provisions.example: Claimwick reads the per-diem rate for an expense day when submitting and when approving the expense. Both slices call one calculation on the travel knowledge model with the day and the country, instead of each carrying its own walk over the per-diem rows. A copy of the walk in the approval slice would report `logic-duplicate`.

provisions.heading: Keep Reference-Data Rows from Overlapping
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-data-period-invalid` for rows of one key whose validity periods overlap, naming both rows and the overlap, or whose `effectiveTo` is no later than `effectiveFrom`.
provisions.statement: The validity periods of the rows of one key of a reference-data table MUST NOT overlap within one variant.
provisions.rationale: Two rows of one key in force on one date give two answers to one lookup, and the reader guesses which holds. One row in force per date and key keeps every lookup single-valued. Rows of different keys, different roles when rows carry no key, or different variants run on their own timelines, so they never overlap each other. A row without `effectiveTo` stays in force, so it overlaps any later row of its key until it gains an end date.
provisions.example: Claimwick's German full-day per-diem rows share one key: the 28 EUR row runs 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-31 and the 30 EUR row runs from 2026-01-01, so each date answers one row.

provisions.heading: Keep Technical State Out of Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does any Behavior record state technical mechanism state, such as outbox rows, idempotency keys, caches, sessions, leases, or provider delivery logs? Check the aggregates beside the stack and extension pages and the technical decisions.
provisions.statement: State that exists only because of a technical mechanism MUST NOT be written as a Behavior record.
provisions.rationale: State the business cares about is an aggregate with its invariants. State that exists only because of a technical mechanism, such as outbox rows, idempotency keys, caches, sessions, leases, or provider delivery logs, is infrastructure: a Behavior record for it promises business meaning nothing guards, and it drifts with every mechanism change. The stack and extension pages and technical decisions govern such state instead. When such state holds personal data, its retention is stated where the mechanism is stated. Settled by [decision/0092-module-events-and-business-state](decision/0092-module-events-and-business-state).
provisions.example: Claimwick records each manager's reminder choice as `aggregate/spending.reminder-preference`, one per manager with the single state `Active`: a rule states that only the manager or an admin holding the named permission changes it, a use case changes it with its refusals, access, and audit, and its data classes carry an erasure position. The outbox rows carrying the reminder facts are mechanism state, so no Behavior record states them and the outbox extension governs them.

provisions.heading: Keep the Negation Word in the Rule Name
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `rule-name-invalid` for a rule whose statement says `not`, `no`, `never`, or `cannot` while its name keeps no restricting word or uniqueness.
provisions.statement: A rule whose statement says `not`, `no`, `never`, or `cannot` MUST keep a restricting word in its name: `no`, `never`, `not`, `cannot`, `none`, `nothing`, `without`, `unless`, `non`, `refused`, `refuses`, `refusal`, `forbidden`, `blocked`, or `rejected`, a limit `only`, or a uniqueness `one-...-per-...`.
provisions.rationale: A name that drops the negation reads as its own opposite: a rule named `cancel-after-shipment` whose statement says "never" allows what it forbids. A restricting word keeps the name a true sentence, which a reviewer trusts without opening the statement. A uniqueness name such as `one-grant-per-account` already says what "an account never holds two grants" says.
provisions.example: The rule is named `rule/order.cancel-never-after-shipment`.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Term with Its Layer
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `glossary-invalid` for a glossary term without `layer`, and each behavior term lists the synonyms its readers know in `aliases`.
provisions.statement: Each glossary term MUST carry its record layer, intent, behavior, or implementation, with the established synonyms its readers know in `aliases`.
provisions.rationale: Each layer's words change for their own reasons: a business term changes when the market changes, a design term when the model changes, and an implementation term when the code changes. The record layer tells each reader what kind of change moves the word, and the aliases let industry readers find LiteSpec's own words without learning a second vocabulary first.
provisions.example: The term `refusal` carries `layer: behavior` with `aliases: ["rejection", "error"]`, so readers who know rejections and errors find it.

provisions.heading: Model Each Aggregate Lifecycle with States
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an aggregate page without `states` entries carrying a name and a meaning.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate MUST declare its lifecycle as `states` entries with a name and a meaning, and an aggregate with no lifecycle declares the single state `Active`.
provisions.rationale: A bare state name tells a reviewer nothing: `rejected` without its meaning hides what rejection costs and allows. A name with a meaning makes each lifecycle step reviewable on the page and gives `transitions` states to connect. An aggregate with no lifecycle declares the single state `Active`, so every aggregate carries states.
provisions.example: The library's hold queue aggregate declares `Requested`, `Ready`, `Collected`, `Cancelled`, and `Lapsed`, each with one sentence saying what the hold awaits or has received. Claimwick's reminder-preference aggregate declares the single state `Active`.

provisions.heading: Name Each Module After Its Capability
provisions.evidence: Does every aggregate in this module serve the capability the module name states? Check the aggregates beside the module name.
provisions.statement: Name each module after one capability the software offers, not after a company function or a catch-all, and split a module whose aggregates serve more than one capability into sibling modules.
provisions.rationale: Modules mark the areas of the bounded context: where a monolith would later split, and how a reader finds a use case by module, then aggregate, then use case. A capability name keeps one module cohesive. A company function or a catch-all such as `platform`, `sales`, `operations`, or `misc` gathers unrelated aggregates that change for unrelated reasons. Splitting such a module into siblings keeps each module one capability with aggregates that serve it.
provisions.example: A finance module holds payout and ledger aggregates serving finance, while a misc module holding lending and catalog aggregates splits into lending and catalog siblings.

provisions.heading: Name Every Event in the Past Tense
provisions.evidence: Does every event name read as a completed fact rather than an order? Check the event records beside their raising acts.
provisions.statement: Each domain event MUST be named in the past tense.
provisions.rationale: An event names a fact that completed, so the past tense tells a reader the business already moved: `submitted` reports, while `submit` orders. The past tense also pairs each event with the act raising it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense aggregate raises `domain-event/expense.submitted` for a completed submission.

provisions.heading: Name Every Spanned Aggregate in Binds
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `rule-binds-missing` (level G) for a rule whose `governs` names more than one aggregate while `binds` names none or not all of them.
provisions.statement: Each rule whose `governs` names more than one aggregate MUST name every governed aggregate in `binds`.
provisions.rationale: No rule across aggregates is held by one aggregate alone: a state guard or an atomicity rule holds it. Naming every reached aggregate in `binds` shows the rule's reach beside the rule, so a reader sees which aggregates change together.
provisions.example: `rule/spending.receipt-filed-once` states that a receipt file supports one expense across spending, and names `aggregate/spending.expense` and `aggregate/spending.receipt` in `binds`.

provisions.heading: Name the Record Each Law Rule Restates
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a rule with `source: law` and no `cites`.
provisions.statement: A rule with `source: law` MUST name the restated constraint or research record in `cites`.
provisions.rationale: A law claim without its record cannot be checked: no reader can tell which outside rule the statement restates, so a change to the outside rule never reaches the rule. Naming the restated record ties each law rule to the constraint or research it carries, and the model checks the link resolves. Settled by [decision/0099-rule-sources](decision/0099-rule-sources).
provisions.example: Claimwick's erased-after-retention rule cites `constraint/tax-receipt-retention`, the tax rule its seven years restate.

provisions.heading: Name the Refusal a Broken Rule Produces
provisions.evidence: Does every guarded rule name its refusal in `refusal`? Check the rule records beside the results citing their refusal.
provisions.statement: Each rule whose breach refuses a use case MUST name the refusal in `refusal` by the refusal's id.
provisions.rationale: A guarded rule without a named refusal leaves the ending unnamed, and callers branch on a refusal the records never predicted. Naming the refusal from its aggregate's refusal set ties the rule to every result citing that refusal, so the breach and the ending stay one fact. The [Use Cases page](use-cases.md) states the refusal set.

provisions.heading: Raise Every Event Through Its Aggregate Root
provisions.evidence: Is every event raised through the root of its aggregate? Check the aggregate code beside the event records.
provisions.statement: Each event MUST be raised through its aggregate root.
provisions.rationale: The root is the one type through which outside behavior changes the aggregate, so it sees every change worth announcing. Raising each event there keeps the fact and its announcement in one step, and no event is announced for a change the aggregate never made.

provisions.heading: Record When Each Frozen Value Freezes and Where It Lives
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a frozen-value rule without `frozenWhen` or `retainedIn`.
provisions.statement: Each frozen-value rule MUST name when the value freezes in `frozenWhen` and where its retained facts live in `retainedIn`.
provisions.rationale: A price, fee, or rate read live changes under settled business: a refund follows today's price instead of the price at sale. Naming when the value freezes pins each reading to its moment, and the retained link keeps the earlier values reachable for audit and dispute.

provisions.heading: Release Every Reservation by a Named Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reservation-release-missing` for a reservation rule whose `releasedBy` names neither a use case nor `{ "mode": "never", "reason": "..." }` with its cost.
provisions.statement: Each reservation rule MUST name the use case releasing it in `releasedBy`, or `{ "mode": "never", "reason": "..." }` with its cost.
provisions.rationale: A held claim with no release keeps places, funds, or names locked past their need, and nobody owns freeing them. Naming the releasing use case states the end of the hold beside its start. A hold that truly lasts is admitted with `{ "mode": "never", "reason": "..." }` and its cost on record. Persistence claims the added keys and releases the removed ones in the commit that changes the aggregate (`litespec/core/backend-persistence#claim-a-cross-record-key-at-commit`).

provisions.heading: State Each Event with Meaning and Carries
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an event record without `meaning` or `carries`, and `event-field-uncarried` for an integration-event payload field its translated domain event does not carry.
provisions.statement: Each event MUST state its meaning and the typed fields it carries.
provisions.rationale: An event without a meaning is a name every reaction interprets alone, while facts without a carries list are reconstructed from code at each reaction. Stating the meaning with the typed `carries` fields lets each reaction trust what happened and what arrived with it. An integration event publishes only fields its translated domain event carries.

provisions.heading: State Each Rule with Its Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a rule record without `kind` or `statement`.
provisions.statement: Each rule MUST state its kind and its statement.
provisions.rationale: The kind decides how the rule is proved: an invariant on every change, a precondition before the behavior, a calculation through its examples, an atomicity rule through its bound group, a reservation through its release, and a frozen-value rule through its frozen value. A rule without a kind leaves each reader proving it a different way, and the checks with no place to confirm it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's invariant `rule/expense.reimbursed-once` states "an expense is reimbursed at most once", and every reimbursement checks it.

provisions.heading: State Each Rule's Source
provisions.evidence: Does each rule that restates an outside rule or makes a product choice state its source? Check `source` on the rule records.
provisions.statement: Each rule SHOULD state in `source` whether it restates the law, a contract, or a product choice.
provisions.rationale: A product simplification later gets mistaken for law: a future maintainer reads a rule that claims legal backing and will not change it, even when the product owner could, or changes a real legal rule believing it is a product choice. Stating the source keeps each kind changeable on its own terms: the law changes with the statute, and a product choice changes with the owner. Settled by [decision/0099-rule-sources](decision/0099-rule-sources).
provisions.example: Claimwick's erased-after-retention rule states `law` and cites the tax constraint. A rule making a product choice states `product-choice` with no `cites`.

provisions.heading: State One Condition per Rule
provisions.evidence: Does each rule statement hold one condition? Read each sentence after the first and check that it narrows the first; a sentence that holds a case with its own refusal, derived value, dates, or scenario belongs in a rule of its own, cited by the records that rest on it.
provisions.statement: Each rule MUST state one condition: one thing that holds, guards, or is derived, whose first sentence states it and whose further sentences only narrow its scope, its unit, or an exception without a refusal of its own.
provisions.rationale: A rule is what refusals, scenario steps, and code marks cite. A rule that holds several conditions makes each of those citations vague: a scenario step that cites it does not say which condition it proves, a code mark does not say which branch it carries, and a change to one condition reopens every record that cites the others. A case with its own refusal, its own derived value, its own dates, or its own scenario is a condition of its own, and one rule for it lets each citation name exactly what it rests on. Proposed by [decision/0114-one-condition-per-rule](../intent/decisions/0114-one-condition-per-rule/0114-one-condition-per-rule.md).
provisions.example: Claimwick states `rule/expense.reimbursed-once` ("an expense is reimbursed at most once") and `rule/expense.approved-before-reimbursement` ("an expense is reimbursed only after approval") as two rules with two refusals, not as one paragraph about reimbursement.

provisions.heading: State the Sign of Every Amount
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `amount-sign-drift` (level G) for amount fields one calculation rule computes that state differing conventions or none.
provisions.statement: Each use-case amount field whose sign carries meaning MUST state its convention in `sign`.
provisions.rationale: A bare amount reads two ways: positive as money in or money out, and each consumer assumes one. The convention in `sign` fixes the reading on the field, so every consumer reads it from the record. The `amount-sign-drift` check blocks where the use cases computing one value through one calculation rule state differing conventions or none; a field no second use case computes is judged by review.
provisions.example: The library computes its fine total through one calculation rule: the payment command and the payout report both state `money-in-positive` on it, and a report stating `money-out-positive` is reported.

provisions.heading: State What an Empty Table Will Hold
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a reference-data table with no rows and no summary.
provisions.statement: Each reference-data table with no rows MUST state in `summary` what rows it will hold.
provisions.rationale: A table with no rows and no summary leaves a reader guessing whether the table is new, abandoned, or waiting on another team. The summary names the values the rows will state and who will state them, so an empty table reads as a promise instead of a gap.
provisions.example: Claimwick's accepted-agencies table holds no rows and states in `summary` that each country will name the agencies it accepts bookings from.

provisions.heading: State What Each Rule Governs
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `rule-governs-drift` for `governs` disagreeing with the links that name the rule, counting a use case's `computedBy` as a calculation link that reaches the rule.
provisions.statement: Each rule MUST name what it constrains in `governs`.
provisions.rationale: A rule that names no governed record constrains nothing a reader can find. Naming the constrained aggregates and use cases in `governs` pins each rule to its records. The governed records match the links that name the rule: input `rules`, consistency bindings, a use case's `computedBy` as its calculation link, scenario `exercises`, and result refusals. A calculation rule cited only through `computedBy` reaches the use case whose value it computes. A module rule governs records of its own module; a product-level rule governs records in any module and names each aggregate it governs.
provisions.example: The reimbursed-once rule governs the expense aggregate and the reimburse-expense command, matching the refusal results that cite its refusal.

provisions.heading: Tabulate Every Calculation with Examples
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `calculation-table-missing` for a calculation rule with no scenario examples table.
provisions.statement: Each calculation rule MUST be proven by a scenario carrying an `examples` table.
provisions.rationale: A calculation stated only as a sentence hides its edge cases, so reviewers agree on the words while each pictures other numbers. An `examples` table shows those edge cases, and the scenario proving the rule pins them as checked facts.

provisions.heading: Cite the Requirement Behind Every Notification Claim
provisions.evidence: Does every notification claim cite the requirement behind it? Check the claims beside each notification.
provisions.statement: Each claim a notification makes MUST cite its requirement.
provisions.rationale: A message can promise what no requirement holds: the text assures a refund the policy never states. Citing the requirement behind each claim keeps every assured sentence a carried promise.

provisions.heading: Describe Every External System Operation
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an external system operation without action, timeout, timeout handling, response, or cache.
provisions.statement: Each external system MUST describe its operations with action, timeout, timeout handling, response, and cache.
provisions.rationale: Without a declared shape, an outside call fails unpredictably: timeouts hang, retries double-charge, and responses fail to parse. Describing each operation with its action of `send` or `receive`, its timeout with its timeout handling, its response, and its cache states the coupling beside the system. The `retries` prose states the retry behavior in words beside `onTimeout`, while the retry count lives on the calling edge in `onFailure.retry.maxAttempts`.

provisions.heading: Describe Every Integration Event the Product Sends or Receives
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an integration event without action, CloudEvents identity, typed payload, trust, or `through`.
provisions.statement: Each integration event MUST declare its action, its CloudEvents identity, its typed payload, the trust its readers place in it, and the external system it travels through in `through`.
provisions.rationale: Without a stated action, a published fact is read both ways: an outbound notice is answered as an order, and an inbound claim is taken as authoritative. The action, the CloudEvents identity, the typed payload, the trust level, and the external system in `through` state what the fact is, how far readers follow it, and what it travels through. Each payload field carries the field types use-case inputs use, as `litespec/core/use-cases#describe-every-use-case-input-with-origin-and-classification` states, and a money field carries an amount with an ISO 4217 currency, as the [Record Language](language.md) states. An event may name the `dataschema` URL its payload follows. An inbound event also declares its `correlation` and its `arrivesThrough`, while an outbound event declares its `translates` domain event and its optional `requires`.

provisions.heading: Describe Every Notification with Audience Channel and Consent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `notification-effect-missing` for a notification no use case, reaction, or job sends, and fails a notification without its declared fields.
provisions.statement: Each notification MUST declare its template, audience, channel, consent rule, frequency, deduplication key, parameters, locale, and delivering system.
provisions.rationale: A message without a declared audience and consent reaches the wrong actors, ignores consent, and repeats without control. Declaring the template with its parameters and locale, the audience, the channel of `email`, `sms`, or `push`, the consent rule in `consentRule`, the frequency of `once` or `per-attempt`, the deduplication key, and the delivering system in `deliveredThrough` puts the message beside its promise. A notification is a message to a person; a webhook to a system is an outbound integration event. Suppression lives on the notification in `suppressedWhen`, and suppression scenarios show the message sending nothing. A use case that needs consent names the same rule in its `consentRule`.

provisions.heading: Give Each Entry Point a Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an entry point without `kind` or `authentication`.
provisions.statement: Each entry point MUST declare its kind and its `authentication`.
provisions.rationale: An entry point with no kind is entered any way: a webhook is called as a page, and a device as a browser. Declaring the kind, one of `browser`, `api`, `webhook`, `device`, `cli`, or `mcp`, together with its `authentication`, states how callers arrive and how they prove themselves.

provisions.heading: Give Every Browser Step a Screen
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `step-screen-missing` (level G) for a step a browser or device use case serves that no screen serves.
provisions.statement: Every flow step a use case serves through a browser or device entry point MUST be served by at least one screen.
provisions.rationale: A step a person achieves in a browser happens on some page. A step that no screen serves is either carried by a page nobody recorded or not reachable at all, and then the book cannot tell the reader where it happens. Two findings sit side by side: `step-use-case-missing` names a step no use case serves, and `step-screen-missing` names a step that a browser or device use case serves and no screen serves.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `step/submit-and-reimburse.submit-expense` is served by the expense form.

provisions.heading: Give Every Page Its Screen Record
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `screen-unimplemented` (level S) for a screen no route marks, and `behavior-unrecorded` (level S) for a route with no mark or a mark naming no screen.
provisions.statement: Every route a browser or device entry point serves MUST be the implementation of exactly one screen record.
provisions.rationale: A page is where a person meets the product. An unrecorded page offers use cases nobody reviewed as a page: what it lets someone start, which flow step it carries, and which refusal it shows. One record per page, with one mark on the route, makes the page a reviewable promise, and lets every other link (calls, results, and flow coverage) be computed from it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's web route `/expenses` carries `implements: "screen/claimwick-app.expense-list"`, and the screen record at `behavior/entry-points/claimwick-app/screens/claimwick-app.expense-list/claimwick-app.expense-list.yaml` offers `use-case/spending.list-expenses`.

provisions.heading: Give Every Screen a Route or a Host
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a screen without exactly one of `route` and `host`.
provisions.statement: Each screen MUST carry exactly one of `route` and `host`.
provisions.rationale: A route screen without a route is unreachable, and an overlay with one is two pages fighting over a route. A route places a screen on its route, while a host places an overlay on the screen it opens on. Exactly one of the two places every page once.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list carries the route `/expenses`, and its confirm overlay names the expense list in `host` instead.

provisions.heading: Limit Each Screen to Steps Its Use Cases Serve
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `screen-serves-drift` (level G) for a served step no offered use case serves.
provisions.statement: A screen's `serves` MUST name only flow steps that a use case it offers serves through a browser or device entry point.
provisions.rationale: A person achieves a flow step through use cases, and reaches those use cases on a screen. Naming the step on the screen lets the book say where each step happens. Checking it against the offered use cases catches a screen that claims a step its use cases do not carry.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense form serves `step/submit-and-reimburse.submit-expense` because it offers `use-case/spending.submit-expense`, which serves that step.

provisions.heading: Match a Screen's Offers to Its Calls
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `screen-offers-drift` (level S) for a screen whose `offers` miss a use case its route's own calls reach, or name a use case neither its route nor its layouts reach, naming each use case on one side only.
provisions.statement: A screen's `offers` MUST name every use case the route's own calls reach, by client call or by navigation to a marked endpoint route, and no use case neither the route nor its layouts reach.
provisions.rationale: `offers` is the recorded promise of what a person can start on the page, and the calls are what the page actually does. When the two differ, the page either gained a capability nobody recorded or the record promises one the page dropped. Comparing them on every run keeps the record honest without anyone re-reading the page. A layout read serves every screen under it: the session, the permissions, and the workspace the frame loads for all pages. Holding every screen to those reads would repeat one frame read on each screen record. The layout call still counts as reached, so the entry point's use cases stay covered and a screen that offers one reports no drift.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense list offers `use-case/spending.list-expenses`, and its route calls `ListExpenses` through the generated client. The root layout's session read counts as reached for every screen under it, but no screen offers it.

provisions.heading: Match Notification Templates to the Template Store
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `template-unimplemented` (level S) for a declared key the store the stack page names lacks, and `template-unrecorded` (level S) for a stored key no notification declares, in a project whose stack configuration names a template store.
provisions.statement: The `template` keys the notification records declare and the keys the project's template store holds MUST be the same set.
provisions.rationale: The template key is the one join between a notification's promise and the text a person receives. A declared key the store lacks fails at send time, and a stored template no notification declares is text nobody reviewed. The store is the stack's own file, so the check reads it where it is instead of copying the keys into a record. A notification whose body the sender composes at send time declares `template: none` and stays out of the comparison.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `notification/spending.receipt-reminder` declares `template: receipt-reminder-manager`, which the template store holds.

provisions.heading: Name Each External System for Its Role
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an external system whose name equals its vendor, ignoring case and separators.
provisions.statement: Each external system MUST be named for the role the system plays, never for its vendor.
provisions.rationale: A record named for its vendor ties the specification to one provider: changing vendors renames the record, its identifier, and every citation. A record named for the role keeps its name while vendors change, and the vendor sits in one `vendor` field beside it. A record whose name equals its vendor is a finding.
provisions.example: `external-system/identity-provider` names the role, with the vendor in `vendor`; `external-system/kinde` names the vendor and is reported.

provisions.heading: Name Each Template for Its Subject, Event and Audience
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `template-key-invalid` (level G) for a template key ending in no name the notification declares in `audience`.
provisions.statement: Each notification template key MUST read `<subject>-<event>-<audience>`, with the audience name the record declares in `audience`.
provisions.rationale: A key that names its subject, its event, and its audience tells every reader what the message is about and who receives it. A key that names none of the three hides both.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `receipt-reminder-manager` names the receipt, the reminder, and the manager audience, while `email-change-confirmation` names no audience and is reported.

provisions.heading: Name How Every Inbound Integration Event Arrives
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an inbound integration event without `arrivesThrough` naming a webhook entry point or a subscribed external system.
provisions.statement: Each inbound integration event MUST name how it arrives in `arrivesThrough`.
provisions.rationale: An inbound fact with no stated arrival is accepted anywhere: each handler invents its own intake, with its own trust decision. Naming the arrival gives each inbound fact one entry point with one authentication, where trust and correlation hold. That is either the `webhook` entry point a provider calls or the external system whose broker or stream the module subscribes to. Settled by [decision/0075-draw-the-boundary-around-outside-traffic](decision/0075-draw-the-boundary-around-outside-traffic).
provisions.example: Claimwick's receipt-scan-available event names the scanning provider webhook entry point in `arrivesThrough`, and the payout-settled event names the payout bank stream the spending module subscribes to.

provisions.heading: Name Published Events in the Domain's Words
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `integration-event-name-invalid` (level G) for an outbound event named with an internal word.
provisions.statement: Each outbound integration event SHOULD be named for the business fact, without internal words.
provisions.rationale: An integrator reads the published name as the business fact. Words like `staged`, `dispatch`, or `outbox` describe the machinery that delivered it instead of the fact itself. A name that carries the fact travels across the boundary unchanged. The internal words are `staged`, `dispatch`, `dispatched`, `outbox`, `handler`, `queued`, `worker`, and `job`.
provisions.example: Claimwick names its event `expense-reimbursement-requested` for the requested reimbursement, while `expense-reimbursement-staged` names the staging step and is reported.

provisions.heading: Name the Actor Each External System Represents
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an external system without `represents`, and `reference-unknown` for a `represents` naming no written actor.
provisions.statement: Each external system MUST name the actor it represents in `represents`.
provisions.rationale: An outside system that acts in a flow is an actor of kind `system`. Every link points from the lower or later record to the higher or earlier one, so the Behavior system record names its Intent actor in `represents` instead of the flow naming the system. The reverse view is gathered for `model query` and the book, never stored.
provisions.example: The text gateway record names the text gateway actor in `represents`, and the flow step sending the overdue notice names that actor in `actor`.

provisions.heading: Publish Every Outbound Integration Event from the Event It Translates
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an outbound integration event without `translates`, `event-field-uncarried` (level G) for a payload field its translated domain event does not carry, and `effect-undeclared` for an event a handler, event handler or job publishes itself; `dotnet build` reports `LS2022` for an event published by user code.
provisions.statement: Each outbound integration event MUST name in `translates` the domain event it carries, and is published only from that domain event, by the pipeline step that stages raised events.
provisions.rationale: When a handler builds an integration event from whatever the aggregate holds after the act, it publishes state the act never announced, and a second handler can publish the same event with a different payload. Deriving the event from the one domain event it translates keeps every published field a field of the announced fact. The publishing use cases then follow from `raises`, with no second declaration to drift, and the domain event carries every field its integration events publish, as typed fields. A publish call in user code is an edge no record can declare, so the stack reader reports it. Settled by [decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers](decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers).
provisions.example: Claimwick's `integration-event/expense-submitted` translates `domain-event/expense.submitted`, so `use-case/spending.submit-expense`, which raises that event, publishes it, and its handler publishes nothing.

provisions.heading: Resolve Late Arrivals Against Owner-Written Facts
provisions.evidence: When one module acts on a fact another module owns, which owner-written moment or public query settles a late arrival? Check the timestamps and declared `queries` edges beside each cross-module read.
provisions.statement: Each module that acts on a fact another module owns SHOULD resolve late arrivals against facts the owning modules wrote themselves, or confirm with the owner before acting.
provisions.rationale: The owner's event can arrive after the reader acts, so an arrival the reader takes at face value lands in the wrong period. Comparing moments each owner wrote, such as an approval moment against a recorded close, classifies each arrival without a lock. Where moments cannot settle the act, confirming with the owner before committing keeps the decision on current truth, as `litespec/core/automation#decide-current-truth-in-the-owning-module` states.
provisions.example: Claimwick counts an expense approved after the recorded March close toward April, even when its event arrives with late March events.

provisions.heading: Serve Static Files as Served Content
provisions.evidence: Is every static script and legal text served through a browser entry point's `servedContent` list, with its path, content type, cache control, and versioning? Check the static files beside the `servedContent` entries.
provisions.statement: A static script or legal text MUST be served through a browser entry point's `servedContent` list, with its path, content type, cache control, and versioning, never as a use case.
provisions.rationale: A static file modeled as a use case invents behavior where none exists: results, scenarios, and handlers for bytes that are served unchanged. Serving it as content keeps content apart from behavior.

provisions.heading: State Every Boundary Check as a Rule of Its Module
provisions.evidence: Does every module confirming work for another state the receiving preconditions as its own rules? Check the rules at each module boundary against the receiving module's rules.
provisions.statement: A module that confirms work for another module MUST state the receiving module's preconditions as its own rules at its boundary.
provisions.rationale: Each module refuses at its own boundary: the confirming module states the receiving module's preconditions as its own rules and names the receiving rules in prose, and the receiving module checks again when it acts. The second check guards against changes between the two acts, so the pair is two boundaries, not one rule written twice. A rule governs another module's records only through a declared dependency, as `litespec/core/model#connect-across-modules-only-through-declared-dependencies` states; without one, each module states the check at its own boundary.
provisions.example: Claimwick's payout module confirms each transfer before calling the bank. It states its own rule that a transfer settles only a payable reimbursement, naming spending's reimbursed-once rule in prose, and spending checks the rule again when it posts the settlement.

provisions.heading: State the Density and Voice of Each Entry Point
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a browser or device entry point without `density` or `voice`, and `record-invalid` for a `density` outside public-light, application-balanced, and admin-dense.
provisions.statement: Each browser or device entry point MUST state its density in `density` and how the product addresses its audience in `voice`.
provisions.rationale: Each audience reads its own screens: a public page shows little, an application screen balances work and guidance, and an admin screen packs dense rows. One density per entry point keeps every screen of one audience at the same weight, and one voice keeps the product addressing that audience the same way on each screen. Both sit on the entry point record, because the audience is what an entry point models. Proposed by [decision/0089-specify-the-ui-as-a-blueprint](decision/0089-specify-the-ui-as-a-blueprint).
provisions.example: The Claimwick employee app entry point states `application-balanced` in `density`, with the `voice` "Claimwick addresses the employee plainly and names the next step on every screen."

provisions.heading: State the Outcome of Every Outside Call
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an external-system operation without separated `rejected`, `accepted`, and `unknown` outcomes or with an `unknown` case naming no `onUnknown` handling.
provisions.statement: Each external-system operation MUST separate its `rejected`, `accepted`, and `unknown` outcomes, with the `unknown` case naming its handling in `onUnknown`.
provisions.rationale: An outside call that ends unknown is neither done nor safe to repeat: a timeout after the provider charged double-charges on retry, while a drop after no charge loses the act. Separating the three outcomes states what each ending means, and naming the unknown handling in `onUnknown` states how the product recovers: `dedupe-key` for a provider idempotency key, `reconcile` for a later comparison, or `retry-safe` for a call the receiver tolerates twice.
provisions.example: Claimwick's payout-bank charge operation names `rejected` for a refused charge, `accepted` for a queued payout, and `unknown` with `onUnknown: dedupe-key` for a timeout retried with the provider key.

provisions.heading: State the Vendor of Each External System
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an external system without `vendor`.
provisions.statement: Each external system MUST state its vendor in `vendor`.
provisions.rationale: The vendor is the provider behind the role: who operates the system the record names. Stated in one field, a vendor change edits that field and the one adapter folder, and every operation, erasure position, and port name stays put.
provisions.example: `external-system/identity-provider` carries its provider in `vendor`.

provisions.heading: Use Every Declared Template Parameter
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `template-param-drift` (level S) for a declared parameter whose placeholder, in the case the stack page states, appears in none of its template's texts.
provisions.statement: Every parameter a notification declares in `parameters` MUST appear as a placeholder in at least one of its template's texts.
provisions.rationale: A declared parameter is part of the message's promise: the order number in a confirmation, or the name in a reminder. A parameter the template never uses is a promise the message does not keep, and it usually means someone rewrote the template without updating the record.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `notification/spending.receipt-reminder` declares the parameter `submitterName`, and the `receipt-reminder-manager` template renders it as `{{SubmitterName}}`.

provisions.heading: Write the Sentence a Person Reads on Each Refusal
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `refusal-sentence-missing` for a refusal result of a use case a screen offers that carries no `sentence`.
provisions.statement: Every refusal result of a use case a screen offers MUST carry the sentence a person reads in `sentence`.
provisions.rationale: A refusal a person can trigger on a page is part of what the page says to them. Without a sentence, the person sees a code or a generic error. The sentence sits on the result in the product's language, with one sentence per language beside it in `sentences`, the way glossary terms carry `labels`. That makes the wording a person reads record data the check reads beside the refusal. The sentence is required only where a screen can reach the refusal, so refusals no person meets need none. Proposed by [decision/0089-specify-the-ui-as-a-blueprint](decision/0089-specify-the-ui-as-a-blueprint).
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense form offers `use-case/spending.submit-expense`, whose `spending.receipt-missing` refusal result carries "Attach the receipt for this expense, then submit again." in `sentence`.

provisions.heading: Call Only Declared Operations
provisions.evidence: Does every `calls` effect name an operation its cited external system declares? Check each effect beside its external system record.
provisions.statement: A `calls` effect MUST name an operation the cited external system declares.
provisions.rationale: The effect names the system and its operation, and the operation states the action, timeout, retry, response, and cache, so each call to the outside is a declared edge. A call to an undeclared operation ships as an unreviewed dependency. `litespec/core/use-cases#declare-every-effect-with-one-verb-and-its-timing` states the effect verbs, and the `effect-undeclared` check reports an edge the records never declared.
provisions.example: The Claimwick payout effect cites `calls` on the payout bank `send-batch` operation with its timeout and retry count.

provisions.heading: Configure External Clients Through Validated Options
provisions.evidence: Does every external client bind its base address, credentials, timeout, and policy through validated options? Check the client registrations.
provisions.statement: An external client MUST bind its base address, credentials, timeout, and policy through validated options.
provisions.rationale: Base address, credentials, timeout, and policy decide where the client calls and how it behaves. Validated options check each value at startup. A missing or invalid value then fails fast instead of misdirecting the first live call.

provisions.heading: Cover Provider Failure Modes
provisions.evidence: Does the suite test every declared failure mode: timeout, connection failure, transient response, permanent response, malformed payload, rate limit, duplicate delivery, and unexpected response shape? Check the integration test suite.
provisions.statement: An integration test MUST cover timeout, connection failure, transient response, permanent response, malformed payload, rate limit, duplicate delivery, and unexpected response shape.
provisions.rationale: Timeout, connection failure, transient and permanent responses, malformed payloads, rate limits, duplicate delivery, and unexpected shapes each exercise a different path through retry, mapping, and idempotency. A mode without a test leaves its path unverified, so the suite covers all eight and each path proves itself. The timeout mode exercises the unknown outcome: the test shows which `onUnknown` handling the retry follows. An unexpected response shape is the mode a provider produces without failing. A well-formed response can carry a field that moved, a type that changed, or a value no one planned for. The response parses, but the behavior is still wrong, while every other listed mode reports that response as an error. A provider that versions its API changes shape on a schedule, and a pinned version still changes on the day the provider raises it.

provisions.heading: Declare Trust for Inbound Integration Events
provisions.evidence: Does every inbound integration event declare trigger-only or payload trust with its correlation? Check each inbound integration event record.
provisions.statement: An inbound integration event MUST declare `trust` as trigger-only or payload with its correlation.
provisions.rationale: An inbound fact carries one of two trusts: trigger-only wakes a read of the source, while payload is fit to act on. The `trust` declaration states which one, and the correlation states how the event matches, so no handler guesses how far to trust the event's fields. `litespec/core/edges#describe-every-integration-event-the-product-sends-or-receives` states the record, and `litespec/core/edges#name-how-every-inbound-integration-event-arrives` states how each inbound fact arrives. The record names in `arrivesThrough` the webhook entry point the provider calls or the external system whose broker or stream the module subscribes to, and every integration event names in `through` the external system it travels through.

provisions.heading: Define Business-Action Ports
provisions.evidence: Is every port named for its business action, with no provider in its name or signature? Check each port.
provisions.statement: The module MUST own a public external-service interface named for its business action.
provisions.rationale: What the use case needs is a behavior, such as sending a payout, not a provider. Naming a public interface for that business action states the need without naming a provider, so the module depends on the behavior while providers change behind it.
provisions.example: `IPayoutSender` describes the business action without exposing a payout-bank client.

provisions.heading: Isolate Provider Implementations
provisions.evidence: Does any Application layer code reference a provider SDK or transport type? Check the Application layer folders.
provisions.statement: Infrastructure MUST own provider clients, SDKs, authentication, and transport models.
provisions.rationale: Provider clients, SDKs, authentication, and transport models name provider things in provider terms, so they live in Infrastructure, outside the Application business boundary. A provider SDK upgrade then touches Infrastructure instead of the use case.
provisions.example: `IPayoutProviderClient` is provider infrastructure rather than a port.

provisions.heading: Keep Provider Components Together
provisions.evidence: Does every provider adapter folder hold its options, client, models, mappings, and registration, or follow another grouping the project documentation names? Check each provider adapter folder.
provisions.statement: Keep one options class, client, transport models, mappings, and registration module in each provider's `Infrastructure/{Port}/` adapter folder.
provisions.rationale: When the provider changes, its options, client, transport models, mappings, and registration module change together. Keeping them in the provider adapter folder keeps each change in one place, while a registration module stored elsewhere is easy to miss when the provider changes.

provisions.heading: Keep Provider Internals from API Responses
provisions.evidence: Does any API response expose provider bodies, credentials, headers, exception types, or internal account identifiers? Check the API responses.
provisions.statement: An API MUST NOT expose provider bodies, credentials, headers, exception types, or internal account identifiers.
provisions.rationale: Secrets, implementation details, and sometimes another account's data arrive in provider bodies, headers, exception types, and account identifiers. An API that returns them exposes all three to its callers. The mapped project-owned outcome carries the meaning without the internals.

provisions.heading: Process Duplicate Messages Safely
provisions.evidence: Does every inbound provider handler leave exactly one accepted effect for a duplicate event? Check the duplicate-delivery paths.
provisions.statement: An inbound provider handler MUST store or process duplicate events idempotently.
provisions.rationale: After a timeout or an acknowledgement failure, the provider repeats delivery and the same event arrives twice. Idempotent storage or processing leaves one accepted effect. A handler without that protection pays, ships, or notifies twice.

provisions.heading: Protect Non-Idempotent Calls
provisions.evidence: Does every retried non-idempotent provider call rest on provider idempotency and documented replay behavior? Check the retry paths.
provisions.statement: An external client MUST NOT retry a non-idempotent provider call without provider idempotency and documented replay behavior.
provisions.rationale: Retrying a payout, a shipment, or any irreversible provider call can perform it twice. The retry is safe only with provider idempotency behind it and documented replay behavior stating what a repeat does. Without both, one failed call becomes two completed effects.

provisions.heading: Record Each Provider as an External System
provisions.evidence: Does every provider have an external system page in the Behavior external systems naming its operations and erasure? Check the external system pages.
provisions.statement: An integration MUST record its provider as an external system naming its operations and erasure.
provisions.rationale: The external-system record draws the boundary around the dependency. Its summary names the party behind the provider, `litespec/core/edges#describe-every-external-system-operation` names every operation the product may call, and `litespec/core/access#declare-erasure-for-every-external-system` names how personal data leaves it. A provider with no record gains new messages and fallbacks without review.

provisions.heading: Reject Formula-Leading Import Values
provisions.evidence: Does every CSV or spreadsheet import reject or neutralize each formula-leading value? Check the import boundaries.
provisions.statement: A CSV or spreadsheet import MUST reject or neutralize a value that begins with a formula-leading character.
provisions.rationale: The formula-leading characters are the equals sign, the plus sign, the minus sign, the at sign, the tab, and the carriage return. Escaping on export protects the user of that export, but not the reader of the next one: a different report can re-export an unchanged imported value without escaping it. [CSV injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/CSV_Injection) travels through the store, so the boundary that admits the value is where it stops.
provisions.example: An import that rejects the value reports the row and the field. An import that neutralizes it records what it changed. A silently altered value is a data defect nobody can trace.

provisions.heading: Reject Per-Request HTTP Clients
provisions.evidence: Does any HTTP integration construct a new HTTP client per request? Check the HTTP call sites.
provisions.statement: An HTTP integration MUST NOT construct a new HTTP client for each request.
provisions.rationale: Each per-request client skips the central handler configuration and opens sockets the process never reuses. Under load, those exhausted sockets fail calls the provider would have served. Managed clients reuse what per-request construction throws away.

provisions.heading: Retry Transient Failures with Bounded Attempts
provisions.evidence: Which external clients retry without a cap on attempts or without jitter? Check each client's retry policy.
provisions.statement: An external client MUST retry transient failures with bounded attempts and jitter.
provisions.rationale: When a provider fails, every caller retries at once, and the synchronized retries hit the provider the moment it recovers. Bounded attempts cap that load, and jitter spreads it over time. Without a bound, the retries become a second outage.

provisions.heading: Run Provider Calls from Event Handlers or Jobs
provisions.evidence: Does every provider call run from an event handler or a job, or carry a waiver naming its compensation? Check the provider call sites beside the waiver records.
provisions.statement: A provider call SHOULD run from an event handler or a job, although a query may call a provider inline within its own handling, and a command never calls a provider before its commit.
provisions.rationale: A command handler changes its aggregate and nothing else, and each consequence runs after the commit, as `litespec/core/backend-application#call-external-systems-through-their-ports` requires. An event handler or a job calls the provider after the outbox delivers the fact, with one delivery per handler under `litespec/core/outbox#give-each-handler-its-own-delivery`. A provider failure then retries without rolling back the accepted change. When the command needs the provider result before it can answer, it records the intent first and an event handler calls the provider. A query changes nothing, so an inline call that fails fails only that read.
provisions.example: The Claimwick reimburse-expense command records a pending payout on the expense, and the event handler for the recorded fact calls the payout provider through the business-action port.

provisions.heading: Simulate Integration Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does every integration test run against WireMock.Net or a protocol-specific local endpoint instead of a live provider? Check the integration test suite.
provisions.statement: An integration test MUST use WireMock.Net or a protocol-specific local endpoint.
provisions.rationale: A live provider account makes tests slow, flaky, and expensive, and some failure modes never occur on demand. WireMock.Net or a protocol-specific local endpoint simulates the network contract under test control, so the suite covers provider behavior without calling the provider.

provisions.heading: Translate Provider Failure Outcomes
provisions.evidence: Does every provider error map to a rejected, accepted, or unknown outcome with a project-owned result and stable diagnostics, and does every unknown case name its `onUnknown` handling? Check the integration failure mappings.
provisions.statement: An integration MUST map each provider error to a rejected, accepted, or unknown outcome with its project-owned result and stable diagnostics, and name the handling of the unknown case in `onUnknown`.
provisions.rationale: Each provider reports failure in its own codes and shapes. Mapping them to project-owned results with stable diagnostics keeps the project failure contract steady while providers change theirs. A rejected outcome names the provider refusal, an accepted outcome names what the provider took, and an unknown outcome names a call whose effect stayed uncertain, such as a timeout. The unknown case names its handling in `onUnknown`: `dedupe-key` reuses the provider deduplication key on retry, `reconcile` settles the effect out of band, and `retry-safe` repeats a call the receiver tolerates twice. The stable codes live in the project error catalog, and `litespec/core/backend-api#return-stable-problem-details` returns a code from that catalog. An integration that invents one code per provider creates one code space per provider, and a client that branches on failure then learns every code space. The provider error taxonomy feeds the mapping; it is not the mapping's output.
provisions.example: A rejected Claimwick payout file and an unsettled batch both map to the project `payout-refused` code, while the provider's own code travels in diagnostics. A payout call that times out maps to unknown with `onUnknown: dedupe-key`, so the retry reuses the provider key instead of paying twice.

provisions.heading: Use Managed HTTP Clients
provisions.evidence: Does every HTTP integration use `HttpClientFactory` and applicable service discovery? Check the HTTP registrations.
provisions.statement: An HTTP integration MUST use `HttpClientFactory` and applicable service discovery.
provisions.rationale: `HttpClientFactory` centralizes handler lifetime in one place, and service discovery resolves provider addresses in one place. Together they keep HTTP construction out of the use case, where hand-built clients would repeat both at every call site.

provisions.heading: Verify Inbound Provider Messages
provisions.evidence: Does every webhook inbound handler run the checks its arrival requires, and does every subscription inbound handler verify event identity, schema, size, and replay protection? Check the inbound handlers.
provisions.statement: An inbound provider handler MUST verify signature, timestamp tolerance, replay protection, content type, size, schema, and event identity before processing on a webhook arrival, and event identity, schema, size, and replay protection on a subscribed broker or stream arrival.
provisions.rationale: An inbound message arrives from the network, where anyone can send bytes. Signature, timestamp tolerance, replay protection, content type, size, schema, and event identity each guard a different part of that trust boundary, and skipping any one leaves its attack open. A subscribed broker or stream arrival authenticates at the subscription, so each message carries no per-message signature, and the handler verifies event identity, schema, size, and replay protection on each message. Order matters on a webhook arrival: verify the signature first, over the raw body, before parsing the body or running any other check. An unauthenticated caller can reach a parser that runs first. A deserialized body is not the bytes the signature covered.
provisions.example: A failed signature returns `401` with no body. A message that names the failed check tells an unauthenticated caller how to pass it.

provisions.heading: Admit Only Outside Pains as Problems
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `problem-sufferer-invalid` for a problem whose primary sufferer is no person or organization outside the team; `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a problem record file missing `affects`, `summary` or `statement`; `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a problem record file missing `failureCases`, `workaround`, `cost`, or `resolutionCriteria`.
provisions.statement: A problem MUST name in `affects` a primary sufferer that is a person or organization actor outside the team building the product, state the pain in `summary` and `statement` in fields, carry graded evidence, state its failure cases in `failureCases`, its workaround in `workaround`, its cost in `cost`, and its resolution criteria in `resolutionCriteria`.
provisions.rationale: A problem is a pain someone outside the team has today. The first `affects` entry is the primary sufferer, so who has the pain is the first fact a reader meets. The `statement` names the sufferer, the condition, and the consequence in one sentence, with the product never as its subject; the `summary` states the pain in one paragraph: when it happens and what the person was trying to do, never a bare pointer to another page. The graded evidence shows the pain is real, as [Grade Problem Evidence by Kind](#grade-problem-evidence-by-kind) states. The `failureCases` state each failure that can happen on its own as its own sentence, with what is missing or wrong, how the sufferer finds it, and what follows when they do not. The `workaround` states what the sufferer does instead today, with the burden that work carries. The `cost` states what the pain costs the sufferer, with time, money, and risk kept apart. The `resolutionCriteria` state one observable outcome per failure case, with no solution named. The explanation file restates each of these fields in its fixed sections. Content that is no problem goes to its own record: a solution in disguise becomes a feature, a worry about what might happen becomes a decision or a goal, an internal limit becomes a limit on the plan written outside Intent, a market fact becomes research, and a legal duty becomes a constraint.
provisions.example: In the library product, readers losing track of due dates is a problem whose primary sufferer is the reader. The library having too few staff for the summer is an internal limit, not a problem.

provisions.heading: Answer Every Constraint
