provisions.heading: Exclude Machine-Local Time
provisions.evidence: Is every production job source free of machine-local clock reads? Check the job sources for local time calls.
provisions.statement: Scheduled-job production code MUST NOT depend on machine-local time.
provisions.rationale: Machine-local time follows each host's configuration, so production code that reads it schedules differently on a developer machine, in staging, and in production. Schedules read their time from the injected clock and the declared zone instead.

provisions.heading: Generate Monotonic Fencing Values
provisions.evidence: Does every fencing value in the store rise per occurrence, with no stale value completing? Check the store write path and its fencing tests.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job store MUST generate each fencing value monotonically per occurrence.
provisions.rationale: Each fencing value rises monotonically per occurrence, so a later claim always presents a higher value than an earlier one. A Worker that lost its lease presents a stale value, and `litespec/core/jobs#allow-completion-only-with-a-current-fencing-value` refuses completion on a stale value.

provisions.heading: Keep Jobs off Direct Storage and Web Endpoints
provisions.evidence: Is every job source free of direct Marten session or DbContext mutations and WebApi endpoint calls? Check the job sources and their imports.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST NOT mutate a Marten session or DbContext directly, bypass Domain behavior, or call WebApi endpoints.
provisions.rationale: A job that mutates a Marten session or DbContext directly, bypasses Domain behavior, or calls WebApi endpoints skips the command boundary. That boundary carries the authorization, transaction, and validation the job needs. Jobs enter through use case messages like every other caller.

provisions.heading: Keep Raw SQL in Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Does all raw report SQL and connection handling sit inside Infrastructure code? Check the report query sources.
provisions.statement: Infrastructure MUST own raw reporting SQL and connection handling.
provisions.rationale: Raw SQL names tables, dialects, and connection handling that belong to one provider. Keeping it in Infrastructure lets Application and Domain state what the report means, without depending on how one database phrases it.

provisions.heading: Keep Report Definitions in Application
provisions.evidence: Does every report definition sit inside its module, when the report-definition convention names no other place? Check the report definition sources.
provisions.statement: Keep report definitions in Application under their module.
provisions.rationale: What a report means and who may run it are business choices. Keeping the definition in Application under its module puts those choices beside the module's other rules, instead of buried in query code.

provisions.heading: Keep Report Providers in Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Does all SQL and storage code sit inside Infrastructure, when the report-provider convention names no other place? Check the report provider sources.
provisions.statement: Keep SQL, row mappings, and storage providers in Infrastructure.
provisions.rationale: SQL text, row mappings, and storage calls change per provider, while the report's meaning stays fixed. Keeping them in Infrastructure swaps the provider without touching the report's business rules.

provisions.heading: Keep Schedule Definitions Separate from Commands
provisions.evidence: Does any schedule definition sit inside Command behavior, when the project keeps them apart from it? Check the handler code and the schedule records.
provisions.statement: Keep schedule definitions separate from Command behavior.
provisions.rationale: Timing policy changes when operations needs a new schedule; Command behavior changes when the business needs a new outcome. Keeping schedule definitions separate from Command behavior lets each change alone. A schedule inside the handler makes every timing change a code change.

provisions.heading: Keep Worker Orchestration Separate from Report Rules
provisions.evidence: Does any Worker orchestration code sit inside report rules, when the report-orchestration convention names no other place? Check the report rule sources.
provisions.statement: Keep the scheduling, chunking, and progress tracking of a report in Worker code, apart from the rules that define the report.
provisions.rationale: Scheduling, chunking, and progress tracking run the report; they don't define it. Keeping Worker orchestration apart from the report's rules lets either change without changing the other.

provisions.heading: Limit Job Duration
provisions.evidence: Does every job declare a duration bound, with completions recorded inside it? Check the handler code and the occurrence store.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST complete within a bounded duration.
provisions.rationale: Each job bounds its duration, so a Worker can stop without leaving running work it can no longer monitor.

provisions.heading: Limit Job Retries with Backoff and a Poison State
provisions.evidence: Does every schedule declare bounded attempts, cancellation-aware backoff, and a poison state? Check the schedule records and the retry code.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST use bounded attempts, cancellation-aware backoff, and a poison state for permanent failure.
provisions.rationale: Without the bound, one poison occurrence consumes the Worker's whole capacity. Bounded attempts with cancellation-aware backoff cap what one failed occurrence consumes, and a poison state parks the permanently failing occurrence instead of retrying it forever.

provisions.heading: Name a Varying Time Zone by Its Source
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a schedule timezone that is neither a zone name nor a setting or field reference.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST state its time zone as a literal IANA zone or as the setting or aggregate field holding the zone.
provisions.rationale: A literal zone on every job freezes one country into each schedule: tenants in other countries run on the wrong day boundary, and a second country arrives as edits to every job. Naming the setting or the tenant field holding the zone keeps the schedule once while each run reads its own zone. A job with one zone keeps its literal.
provisions.example: Claimwick's nightly close names `setting/reporting.close-time-zone` instead of a literal zone, so the operator moves the close with one setting.

provisions.heading: Observe Job Cancellation
provisions.evidence: Does every job handler wait with cancellation and end its current step when cancellation fires? Check the handler code and its cancellation tests.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST observe cancellation.
provisions.rationale: Each job observes cancellation, so an occurrence ends its current step instead of running past the moment an operator asked it to stop.

provisions.heading: Parameterize Report SQL
provisions.evidence: Does every report query pass actor, tenant, filter, range, sort, and pagination values as parameters instead of SQL text? Check the query code.
provisions.statement: A reporting query MUST parameterize every actor, tenant, filter, range, sort, and pagination value.
provisions.rationale: A report feeds actor, tenant, filters, ranges, sorting, and pagination into SQL that reads across the database. Binding each of those values as a parameter keeps tenant and actor isolation intact, and closes the injection hole string concatenation opens.

provisions.heading: Persist Occurrence Recovery Points
provisions.evidence: Does every occurrence row carry a last scheduled, started, and completed time? Check the occurrence table schema.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job store MUST persist each occurrence's last scheduled, started, and completed time.
provisions.rationale: After a restart, the Worker must tell missed work from completed work. Last scheduled, started, and completed times persist per occurrence to mark that boundary. Memory alone can't hold it, because the restart wipes it.

provisions.heading: Persist Occurrence State
provisions.evidence: Does every occurrence row carry a scheduled, processing, completed, or dead-letter state, with only safe execution details? Check the occurrence rows.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job store MUST persist scheduled, processing, completed, and dead-letter state with safe execution details.
provisions.rationale: Operators and recovery code need to see where each occurrence stands. The four states persist with attempt, lease, start, completion, and safe error data: scheduled, processing, completed, and dead-letter. Without them, work in flight is indistinguishable from work not yet started.

provisions.heading: Place Handlers with Owned Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every job handler sit in the folder of what it runs, when the project names no other job handler layout? Check the handler folders beside the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Place each job handler in the `Application/` folder of the use case it runs, or with the notification it sends or the system it calls when it runs none.
provisions.rationale: A job handler lives in the `Application/` folder of the use case its `runs` entry names, so the use case folder shows every way the use case starts. One that runs no use case lives in the `Application/Notifications/` folder of the notification it sends, or the `Application/ExternalSystems/` folder of the system it calls, under `litespec/workspace/naming#place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs`. The module owns both the business action and what its schedule means. A handlers folder far from the behavior separates each schedule from its reason.

provisions.heading: Prefer UTC Schedules
provisions.evidence: Does every schedule state UTC or a business-local time requirement with its IANA time zone? Check each schedule record.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST use a UTC schedule unless its specification names a business-local time requirement and its IANA time zone.
provisions.rationale: A daylight-saving transition makes a wall clock run one hour twice and skip another. A local schedule therefore runs twice on one date each year and skips an hour on another. That behavior is correct for a job whose meaning is local, such as a nightly statement at 9 AM for a user, and a defect for every other job. Naming the time zone in the specification states the transition behavior for a later reader.

provisions.heading: Prevent Duplicate Completion
provisions.evidence: Does any lease path admit more than one completion per occurrence across overlapping replicas? Check the lease claim code and its concurrency tests.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job lease MUST prevent two replicas from completing the same occurrence.
provisions.rationale: Overlapping replicas must not complete the same occurrence twice. The lease admits one completion per occurrence. Two completions would bill, notify, or reconcile the same planned work twice.

provisions.heading: Protect Export Output
provisions.evidence: Does every export output sit in approved object storage with a named contact, an expiry, and a short-lived authorized download? Check the export storage configuration.
provisions.statement: An export worker MUST store output in approved object storage with a named contact, an expiry, and a short-lived authorized download.
provisions.rationale: An export file concentrates sensitive rows into one downloadable object that outlives the request that built it. Approved object storage with a named contact, an expiry, and a short-lived authorized download gives that object controlled access and a defined end instead of a permanent public link.

provisions.heading: Record the Schedule on the Job Record
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `schedule-invalid` (level G) for a job schedule that is neither an `every` duration nor a `cron` expression; each scheduled job record states its timezone.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST record its schedule in structured form with its timezone on its job record.
provisions.rationale: Tools can't parse prose for a schedule. The job record states when the work runs as `every` or `cron` with its timezone, which tools read directly. A schedule kept outside the record has no recorded moment attached, so misfire behavior has no stated time to measure against. The [automation page](../core/automation.md) states the record fields, and the `schedule-invalid` check reports a schedule no tool can read.

provisions.heading: Record Why Each Report Needs Its Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Does every report use case page record the report, volume, plan, target, maximum, and operator? Check each use case page.
provisions.statement: A reporting proposal MUST record the report, representative data volume, plan or limitation, latency target, maximum result, and operator.
provisions.rationale: Reporting infrastructure costs a Worker, storage, and operating attention. Before building any of it, the team writes down the report, a representative data volume, the plan or limitation, the latency target, the maximum result, and the operator. The use case page carries that record, with why a normal request projection cannot serve it.

provisions.heading: Remove Occurrences Past Retention
provisions.evidence: Is every stored occurrence within its schedule's retention setting record? Check the store rows beside the setting records.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job store MUST remove occurrences older than the schedule's retention setting record.
provisions.rationale: Occurrences older than the retention setting record leave the store so the key space stays bounded. The key space grows with the schedule's frequency and its retention: a per-second schedule kept for a year holds more than 30 million rows. [Quartz states the same practice](https://quartz-scheduler.net/documentation/best-practices.html) for a persistent job store.
provisions.example: A daily schedule that retains occurrences for 90 days holds 90 rows. A minute schedule with the same retention holds more than 100,000 rows. That is a different storage decision.

provisions.heading: Renew Only Owned Leases
provisions.evidence: Does any replica renew a lease after a failed renewal, or keep running an occurrence it lost? Check the replica logs and the renewal tests.
provisions.statement: A Worker replica MUST renew only its active lease and stop when renewal fails.
provisions.rationale: A failed renewal means another replica owns the occurrence now. A replica that kept going would complete work it no longer owns. The replica that lost the lease stops instead, so each replica renews only the lease it holds, and only while it stays active.

provisions.heading: Resolve Dependencies Inside an Execution Scope
provisions.evidence: Does every occurrence resolve scoped dependencies inside a disposed execution scope, when the project names no other scope boundary? Check the job execution code and the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Resolve scoped dependencies inside an execution scope and dispose the scope after the Command completes.
provisions.rationale: Each occurrence resolves its scoped dependencies inside one execution scope, disposed after the Command completes. The scope isolates one occurrence's dependencies from the next. A shared scope would leak one occurrence's state into another.

provisions.heading: Resume Batch Work from Its Cursor
provisions.evidence: Does every batch job name its resume position in its cursor, with a scenario for the remainder after a halfway failure? Check the job records and the scenario tests.
provisions.statement: A job that works through items in batches MUST name where resume state lives in its `cursor`.
provisions.rationale: A batch that fails halfway resumes instead of restarting. The cursor holds where the run stopped. Without it, the next run replays finished items or skips unfinished ones, and a scenario covering the remainder has no stated position to assert.

provisions.heading: Review Report Plans
provisions.evidence: Does every report have a review record showing query plans and indexes checked against representative data? Check the review records.
provisions.statement: Each report SHOULD have its query plans and indexes reviewed against representative data.
provisions.rationale: A query that runs quickly over a hundred local rows can scan millions in production. Reviewing query plans and indexes against representative data shows the true cost before the report ships, rather than after it slows the database.

provisions.heading: Run One Command per Selected Item
provisions.evidence: Does every job run one command per item in its `selection` within its `batchSize`, each in its own unit of work? Check the job record selection and the handler code.
provisions.statement: A job MUST run one command per item in its `selection` within its `batchSize`, each in its own unit of work.
provisions.rationale: The selection states what each run selects, the batch size bounds how many items one batch takes, and `runs` names the command run per item. Each item runs as one command in its own unit of work, as `litespec/core/backend-application#issue-per-record-work-from-a-job` requires, so a failed item replays without replaying its batch.

provisions.heading: Run Over-Budget Exports in the Worker
provisions.evidence: Does every export past its request budget run in a Worker, with the budget in a setting record? Check the export use cases and their setting records.
provisions.statement: An export exceeding its request budget MUST run through Worker, with the budget a setting record the export's use case names.
provisions.rationale: An export that outlasts its request budget holds an HTTP connection open while the user waits. Running it in a Worker returns the request immediately. The budget in its setting record tells the team exactly when an export outgrows the request path.

provisions.heading: Run Scheduled Jobs in Worker
provisions.evidence: Does every scheduled job run in the Worker sources, outside WebApi request handling? Check the Worker project and the WebApi endpoints.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST run in Worker outside WebApi request handling.
provisions.rationale: Scheduled work needs two things request handling doesn't have: a scheduler that owns each schedule's lifetime, and a shutdown order that stops replicas in a controlled way. That is why scheduled work runs in a Worker, outside WebApi request handling.

provisions.heading: Scope Command Idempotency by Occurrence
provisions.evidence: Does every retry of one occurrence use its occurrence identity as the idempotency key scope? Check the command idempotency keys.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST use its occurrence identity as the command idempotency key scope.
provisions.rationale: Every retry of one occurrence replays the same scheduled business action. The occurrence identity scopes the command idempotency key to make that hold. A key scoped any wider would merge separate occurrences into one.

provisions.heading: Scope Export Output to the Tenant
provisions.evidence: Does every export store output under a tenant-scoped path in object storage? Check the export storage paths.
provisions.statement: An export MUST store its output under a tenant-scoped object-storage path.
provisions.rationale: Export addresses are predictable. In a shared folder, one tenant can guess another tenant's file name. A tenant-scoped storage path puts each tenant's exports under its own prefix, so a guessed address stays inside the guesser's own data.

provisions.heading: Scope Occurrences and Leases by Tenant
provisions.evidence: Does every occurrence and lease row carry tenant scope in a product that isolates tenants? Check the occurrence and lease table schemas.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job occurrence and its lease MUST carry tenant scope when the product isolates tenants.
provisions.rationale: In a product that isolates tenants, one tenant's schedules must trigger, block, and expose only that tenant's work. Scoping each occurrence and its lease to one tenant keeps that boundary. Unscoped leases would let a replica mix tenants inside one occurrence.

provisions.heading: State Clock Behavior for Business-Local Schedules
provisions.evidence: Does every business-local schedule record its IANA zone and the skipped and repeated local-time behavior? Check each schedule record.
provisions.statement: A business-local schedule MUST record an IANA time-zone identifier and define skipped and repeated local-time behavior.
provisions.rationale: Daylight-saving transitions omit one local hour and repeat another. A business-local schedule records its IANA time-zone identifier and defines what happens to occurrences in the skipped and repeated hours. Without that definition, each transition silently drops or doubles the local work.

provisions.heading: State How Missed Occurrences Recover
provisions.evidence: Does every schedule state skipped, once-replayed, or interval-replayed behavior for missed occurrences? Check each schedule record.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job specification MUST define skipped, once-replayed, or interval-replayed behavior for missed occurrences.
provisions.rationale: Downtime and delay leave occurrences past their time. The specification states whether each missed occurrence is skipped, replayed once, or replayed per interval. The choice controls the business effect: a skipped reminder stays silent, while a replayed one arrives late.

provisions.heading: Stop Jobs During Graceful Shutdown
provisions.evidence: Does every Worker shutdown path drain running occurrences before stopping schedule polling? Check the shutdown code in the Worker.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST stop accepting new work during graceful shutdown.
provisions.rationale: A job that keeps accepting work during shutdown delays every deploy until that work ends. Stopping intake lets the running occurrences drain, and the Worker stop.

provisions.heading: Store Execution Leases
provisions.evidence: Does every lease row in PostgreSQL carry an owner, an expiry, and a fencing value? Check the lease table schema.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job store MUST record lease owner, expiry, and fencing value in PostgreSQL.
provisions.rationale: Each planned occurrence carries a lease with its owner, expiry, and fencing value in PostgreSQL. The lease names the one replica that may complete that occurrence. The `lease` field on the job record names the lock each run claims. The outbox extension cites this definition for its own claims.

provisions.heading: Support Report Cancellation
provisions.evidence: Does every report honor a cancel request and remove expired output? Check the cancellation tests.
provisions.statement: A report implementation MUST support cancellation and remove expired outputs.
provisions.rationale: Closing the tab leaves the report running, and an export nobody downloads still occupies storage. Cancellation stops the abandoned work, and expiry removes the abandoned file, so neither consumes resources indefinitely.

provisions.heading: Test Time Transitions
provisions.evidence: Does every job test use an injected clock and cover representative time-zone transitions? Check the job test sources.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job test MUST use an injected clock and representative time-zone transitions.
provisions.rationale: Tests on the real clock can only wait for the next transition to arrive. An injected clock moves time to any transition on demand, so representative time-zone transitions run deterministically instead of once a year in production.

provisions.heading: Tolerate Duplicate Execution
provisions.evidence: Does any job Command or side effect record more than one accepted effect after a replayed occurrence? Check the replay tests.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job Command and side effect MUST tolerate duplicate execution after lease or process failure.
provisions.rationale: A lease or process failure can replay a job whose completion stayed uncertain. The job Command and its side effects tolerate that duplicate execution. Work that assumes exactly-once execution breaks on the first uncertain failure.

provisions.heading: Treat Unavailable Schedule Stores as Outages
provisions.evidence: During a store outage, is every Worker log entry backed off and rate-limited, with no occurrence poisoned? Check the Worker logs and the outage tests.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST treat an unavailable scheduler store as the store outage `litespec/core/outbox#report-store-outages-separately-from-delivery-failures` defines, with backed-off, rate-limited logging.
provisions.rationale: An unavailable scheduler store is an outage of the dependency, not a failed occurrence. The Worker treats it as the store outage `litespec/core/outbox#report-store-outages-separately-from-delivery-failures` defines, with backed-off, rate-limited logging. Retry and poison outcomes belong to claimed occurrences, not to a store the Worker cannot reach.

provisions.heading: Write Runbooks for Inspection, Replay, and Disable
provisions.evidence: Does every schedule have a runbook record for inspection, manual replay, and disable? Check the runbook records beside the schedules.
provisions.statement: Each schedule MUST have Runbook records for inspection, manual replay, and disable.
provisions.rationale: Stalled, failed, or unsafe schedules need controlled operator actions: inspection, manual replay, and disable. Runbook records carry those procedures, because an operator without them works directly against the store during the incident. Each procedure names the interface that performs it: a command, an endpoint, or a configuration value. A procedure that says "disable the schedule" without naming the switch stays undiscovered until the incident it was written for. Writing straight to the schedule store instead would bypass the occurrence identity `litespec/core/jobs#derive-stable-occurrence-identity` depends on.
provisions.example: Claimwick's disable procedure names the configuration value or the administrative endpoint that stops the schedule, and states what happens to an occurrence already claimed.

provisions.heading: Check Shape at Compile Time and Dates at Startup
provisions.evidence: Is any date rule left to a compile-time check, or any shape rule left to a startup check? Look at the build diagnostics beside the startup validation of each set.
provisions.statement: Shape and cross-references in code MUST be checked at compile time, while overlaps, gaps, and coverage of the current period are checked at startup.
provisions.rationale: Row types, roles, and references between model types are fixed by the code, and the compiler proves them on every build. Dates depend on the rows a set ships, so only loading the set can prove that its periods do not overlap, leave no gap, and cover today. Startup is the first moment the whole set is known, and a failure there names the row before any request uses it. A set that fails startup validation raises a startup configuration failure, not a business refusal, so `LS1005` does not apply inside a knowledge model.
provisions.example: Claimwick's build proves that every per-diem row carries a country, an amount, dates, and a source. At startup the travel model rejects a German row that overlaps another or leaves the current year uncovered, and the product does not serve until it is fixed. The rejection raises `InvalidOperationException`, as `TravelRegistry.Validate` does.

provisions.heading: Give Each Knowledge Area One Model
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `knowledge-set-missing` for a variant an area names with no set, and `knowledge-variation-undeclared` for rows that differ by variant without a declared dimension.
provisions.statement: A knowledge area MUST have one knowledge model and one knowledge set per variant of its dimension, keeping its one table in the model when it varies by nothing.
provisions.rationale: One model gives every caller the same types and lookups, and one set per variant keeps values for a country or a branch apart without copying the types into each set. An area that varies by nothing needs no set: a second shape for one table would leave readers unsure which holds the values. A set project sits under `Knowledge/` beside its model and references that model; anything else the tools never treat as a set.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `travel` area has the `Claimwick.Travel` model and a set for each country its rates cover, while its approval-target table, which varies by nothing, stays in the model.

provisions.heading: Keep Knowledge in the Backend Language
provisions.evidence: Is any knowledge table kept in a data format without the stated need, or shipped in code when non-developer editors change it? Look at each knowledge set beside the project's backend documentation.
provisions.statement: Keep knowledge in the backend language when only the backend reads it and it ships with the release.
provisions.rationale: Values written as code travel with the release, compile with the model, and need no loader or schema of their own. A data format earns its place when the people who own the values are not developers, when a value must change between releases, or when another reader needs the same table; in those cases the project names the format and its home.
provisions.example: Claimwick's travel rows with their dates and sources live in the backend language and ship with each release. A table that editors outside the team maintain between releases is recorded as a data format.

provisions.heading: Keep Knowledge Sets Free of Logic
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2039` for a method or property body in a knowledge set that does more than return or construct rows; a static `Parse`, `From`, `FromCode`, `Of` or `Create` call on a named type with only literal arguments, such as a typed key built from its text, counts as constructing.
provisions.statement: A knowledge set MUST hold only rows built through its model's constructors, with any behavior a variant needs added as a case in the model's closed set of strategies.
provisions.rationale: A set that decides something splits one rule into one copy per variant, and the copies drift. Rows built through model constructors carry the model's types and validation. When a country or a branch needs a treatment data cannot express, a case in the model's strategy set holds the rule and the set selects it, so every variant shares the same behavior.
provisions.example: Claimwick's Germany and Netherlands sets list dated per-diem rows and nothing else. When a country needs a different rounding of a partial day, the rule becomes a case in the model's rounding strategy set, selected by the set's data.

provisions.heading: Keep Overrides and Integration Catalogs Out of Knowledge
provisions.evidence: Is any tenant override held in a knowledge set, any connection setting held in a knowledge model, or any provider fact a use case reads held only in an adapter? Look at the settings and adapter configuration beside the knowledge sets.
provisions.statement: Per-tenant overrides and the settings an adapter needs to connect to an outside system MUST stay outside knowledge, as a setting on an operational aggregate and as adapter configuration; facts about outside providers that the product itself reasons about or shows are knowledge.
provisions.rationale: An override belongs to one tenant and changes through that tenant's use case, so it needs the aggregate's rules and access, not a released table. An endpoint, a credential or the wire format an adapter parses concerns only the adapter that connects; it changes with the outside system, and no use case reads it. Which providers the product accepts or offers, and what it promises about them, is different: use cases read it, screens show it, and it varies like any other knowledge, so it belongs in a knowledge area read through its model.
provisions.example: A Claimwick tenant that pays a higher partial-day rate keeps that rate in its own policy aggregate through a use case. The endpoint and file layout Claimwick's import adapter uses to fetch travel bookings stay in that adapter's configuration, while the travel agencies Claimwick accepts bookings from, which an employee picks on the expense form, live in a knowledge area.

provisions.heading: Model Reference Data as Domain Values
provisions.evidence: Does any caller interpret reference-data rows outside the domain values, or does infrastructure decide behavior from them? Check the readers of each reference-data table beside the domain values.
provisions.statement: Each reference-data table MUST be read through domain values that carry the behavior its values decide, with infrastructure only loading the rows.
provisions.rationale: A row of free strings means whatever each caller guesses: one value reads two ways in two callers, and a new caller adds a third reading. A domain value types what the table holds and carries the behavior each reading needs, so every caller decides the same way. Infrastructure loads rows and parses them into those values, and decides nothing from them.
provisions.example: Claimwick's decision target is read through a domain value carrying days: the approval rules interpret the days, and the loader that reads the table's rows interprets nothing.

provisions.heading: Name a Role Not a Row
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-data-role-missing` (level G) for a required role played by no row.
provisions.statement: Each reference-data table MUST list in `requiredRoles` the roles its citing rules read, with each role played by a row in `role`.
provisions.rationale: A data key names one row of one data set, so code naming the key breaks when another data set keys its rows differently or not at all. A role names what the product needs, such as the standard target, and each data set says which row plays it. The `reference-data-role-missing` check reports a required role no row plays, and code asks for the role instead of the key.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `reference-data/spending.decision-target` lists `requiredRoles: [standard]`, and both its rows play `standard`, so the approval rules read the standard target without naming a row.

provisions.heading: Read Knowledge by Role and Date
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2040` for a knowledge key built from a string literal outside a knowledge set.
provisions.artifact: knowledge-model, knowledge-set, command-handler, query-handler, reaction, job
provisions.statement: Operational code MUST read knowledge by role and date through the model's typed keys, naming no set and building no key from a string literal.
provisions.rationale: A data key names one row of one set, so code naming it breaks when another set keys its rows differently. A role states what the caller needs, and each set says which row plays it. A typed key built through the model keeps the caller from spelling a country or a date into a raw string.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense submission asks the travel model for the `FullDay` per-diem role on the travel date. It builds the key through the model and names neither Germany nor a row key. A literal such as `new TravelKey("DE")` is reported.

provisions.heading: Read Knowledge Through Its Model
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2038` for a module assembly referencing a knowledge set assembly: a project under `Knowledge/` named `<Product>.<Area>.<Variant>` of the same product that references its model, so another vendor's packages never count. It reports `LS1001` for an outer-layer reference in a model outside the dependency-injection, logging and options libraries.
provisions.artifact: knowledge-model, knowledge-set, command-handler, query-handler, reaction, job
provisions.statement: A module MUST reach a knowledge area through its knowledge model, leaving a set to be referenced only by a host that registers it.
provisions.rationale: A module that names a set binds its code to one country or branch, so adding a variant means editing the module. The model gives modules one stable surface, and a host registers each set with that model at startup. The dependency runs from the Kernel to the model to the modules, and from a set to its model and the Kernel only. The model owns its registry, its composition and its startup validation, so it references the dependency-injection, logging and options libraries those need.
provisions.example: Claimwick's spending module asks `Claimwick.Travel` for a per-diem role on the expense date and names no country project. The API host registers `Claimwick.Travel.Germany` and `Claimwick.Travel.Netherlands` with the model at startup. The `Claimwick.Travel` model registers its sets through `TravelComposition`, which takes an `IServiceCollection` and validates the registered sets at startup.

provisions.heading: Refuse a Missing Rule with a Reason
provisions.evidence: Does any knowledge lookup return a null or a default when no row is in force, or end without naming the missing rule? Look at each lookup beside the use-case refusals.
provisions.statement: A lookup with no row in force MUST end its use case in a refusal naming the missing role, date, and variant.
provisions.rationale: A null or a default value makes the caller spend a value no rule supports, with no record of why. A refusal with a reason points the operator at the row that is missing, and the use case records the refusal beside its other endings. The model derives that ending as `result/<use-case>.rule-not-stated`. The model throws the product's rule-not-stated refusal type, which derives the kernel's domain exception.
provisions.example: If no German per-diem row covers a travel date, Claimwick's submission ends in a refusal naming the `FullDay` role, that date, and Germany, rather than paying zero. Claimwick's travel model throws `TravelRuleMissingException`, which derives the kernel `DomainException` and carries the code `travel.rule-missing`.

provisions.heading: Seed Operational Records from Templates
provisions.evidence: Does any operational record still read its template after it was created, or does any record skip the one-time copy? Look at the creation use case beside the template it seeds from.
provisions.statement: A template MUST seed an operational record once, after which the copy is operational and no longer reads the template.
provisions.rationale: A starting chart or default policy gives a new record a valid beginning without asking the operator to enter every value. If the copy kept reading the template, a later template change would rewrite a record the business already uses. Copying once makes the record own its values and its own use cases.
provisions.example: In the library product, a new branch starts from a template of loan limits. The clerk copies it when the branch opens; later edits to the branch's limits go through the branch's own use case, and a change to the template does not touch that branch.

provisions.heading: Use an Aggregate for Edited Reference Data Only
provisions.evidence: Does any reference-data table take edits at runtime, or does any aggregate hold a published table nobody edits? Check each table beside the use cases that write it.
provisions.statement: Reference data MUST live as an aggregate only when people edit it at runtime, on the owner who edits it rather than on the published table.
provisions.rationale: A published table changes by release: its rows are written with the product and read as written. An aggregate changes by use case: it guards each change with rules, refusals, and access. Making a published table an aggregate promises guarding nothing performs, and leaving runtime-edited values in a table leaves their changes unguarded. The aggregate sits on the owner who edits the values, such as a tenant's own overrides, rather than on the published table.
provisions.example: Claimwick's receipt threshold lives on the policy aggregate because managers change it through `use-case/spending.change-receipt-threshold`, while the decision target stays a reference table nobody edits at runtime.

provisions.heading: Validate Reference Data Before Serving
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-data-key-unknown`, `reference-data-value-invalid`, and `reference-data-role-missing` (level G) for a cross-reference to a missing key, a value outside `choices`, and a required role played by no row.
provisions.statement: Each reference-data table MUST hold only rows that resolve their cross-references, stay within its closed set where one is listed, and play its required roles.
provisions.rationale: A broken cross-reference, an unlisted value, or a missing role each fails at read time, far from the row that caused it. Validating the whole table before serving it moves each failure to startup, naming the file and row. The record checks report `reference-data-key-unknown`, `reference-data-value-invalid`, and `reference-data-role-missing`, and the host refuses to start until the tables it loads validate.
provisions.example: A Claimwick row referring to `reference-data/spending.decision-target#target-2030` is reported, naming the file and row, before the product serves the table.

provisions.heading: Version Each Set and Freeze What Records Used
provisions.evidence: Does any operational record name a knowledge value without the key, value, and version in force when it was made? Look at each record beside the set version it cites.
provisions.statement: Each knowledge set MUST carry a version that an operational record keeps with the key and value it used.
provisions.rationale: A rate that changes after an expense was decided must not rewrite that decision. The set's version pins the row in force at the time, and the record keeps the key, value, and version so a reader can defend the figure. Row effectivity and sourcing follow `litespec/core/domain-model#date-every-reference-data-row`, and released rows stay unchanged under `litespec/core/domain-model#append-released-reference-rows`.
provisions.example: A Claimwick expense submitted under the 2026 per-diem row keeps that row's key, value, and set version. When a 2027 row takes effect, the expense still shows the figure it used.

provisions.heading: Cite Shared Provisions in Their Published Form
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A shared provision citation MUST use its published identifier.
provisions.rationale: A shared provision is cited across projects, so its identifier looks the same everywhere. The published `litespec/<page>#<slug>` form stays fixed, while project records use the type forms above.

provisions.heading: Exclude Declared Content Paths from the ASCII Check
provisions.evidence: Does any non-ASCII prose sit outside the paths the project record declares? Check the content files against the declaration.
provisions.statement: An ASCII check MUST exclude only the natural-language content paths that the project record declares.
provisions.rationale: A product whose subject is another language carries that language in its content files, where a diacritic is part of a word rather than a styling choice. Excluding only the declared content paths keeps the check strict everywhere else: documents about that content stay in scope, so styled prose filed beside content still meets the check.

provisions.heading: Keep Names an Outside Standard Fixes
provisions.evidence: Was any fixed name renamed to fit the grammar? Check the Gherkin fields and CloudEvents attributes the change touches.
provisions.statement: Every name an outside standard fixes MUST stay exactly as that standard spells it.
provisions.rationale: A name an outside standard fixes belongs to that standard: renaming `given` to fit the word classes breaks every Gherkin reader. The grammar stays complete by exempting exactly these names instead of adding a list of exceptions. Gherkin and CloudEvents names are the only exemptions.
provisions.example: A Claimwick scenario keeps `given`, `when`, and `then`, which the word-class table gives no class.

provisions.heading: Keep Wire Codes Stable
provisions.evidence: Does any wire code in the contract break the values deployed clients branch on? Check the wire codes in the contract against the deployed clients.
provisions.statement: A wire code MUST stay unchanged once clients read it.
provisions.rationale: Wire codes travel to deployed clients, which branch on their exact values. Renaming a code that clients already read breaks every deployed reader that compares the old value, with no record the reader opens to learn the new one.

provisions.heading: List the Compounds a Rejection Does Not Cover
provisions.evidence: Does any compound use a rejected word for another concept without an `except` entry? Check the compounds against the rejection's `except` list.
provisions.statement: A glossary rejection MUST list, in `except`, every compound in which a rejected word names a concept other than the one the rejection is about.
provisions.rationale: A rejection matches a word, and a word can belong to more than one term: Claimwick rejects `docket` in favor of `receipt` for payment proof while a docket still names the shipping list. Without the `except` list, the check would force the project to rename an unrelated concept or drop a sound rejection.
provisions.example:
The exemption covers the compound only, so the bare word stays rejected.

```json
{ "word": "docket", "reason": "one word for a payment receipt and a shipping list",
  "scope": "^.litespec/domain/modules/spending/", "except": ["shipping docket"] }
```

provisions.heading: Name a Boolean as a Predicate
provisions.evidence: Does every boolean field read as a predicate with no `is` or `has` prefix? Check the boolean fields the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every boolean field MUST read as a present-tense predicate that is true about the record when the value is true.
provisions.rationale: A boolean without a prefix is a fact about the record: `applies` says the constraint applies, and `recorded` says the entry is recorded. An `is` or `has` prefix adds a word that repeats what the value already says. The predicate form keeps every boolean readable in a sentence about its record.
provisions.example: Claimwick marks an applying constraint with `applies: true` instead of `isApplicable: true`.

provisions.heading: Name Commands as Verbs and Flags by What They Set
provisions.evidence: Does every subcommand read as a verb and every flag as its mode or value? Check the commands and flags the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every subcommand MUST read as a verb and every flag as the mode or value it sets.
provisions.rationale: A verb names what the command does, so `check` names an action without reading its arguments. A flag that names its mode or value reads the same way at every call site, and kebab-case keeps multiword flags writable without quotes. Stable exit codes let scripts distinguish a clean run, a blocking finding, and bad arguments.
provisions.example: The release check runs as `litespec model check --release` and exits 1 on a blocking finding.

provisions.heading: Name Each Date by What It Marks
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `FIELD_NAME_SHAPE` diagnostic for a date field.
provisions.statement: Every date field MUST end in `On` for a recorded date or carry a name that states what the date does.
provisions.rationale: A recorded date says when something happened or until when it holds: `readOn` says when an outside source was read, and `expiresOn` says when a waiver ends. `effectiveFrom` opens a validity span. The shape shows which dates record the world and which open a span.
provisions.example: A Claimwick constraint carries `readOn` on each source with the date the source was read, and a waiver carries `expiresOn` with the date it ends.

provisions.heading: Name Each Field by Its Word Class
provisions.evidence: Does every field use the name its word class gives it? Check the field names the change adds against the word-class table.
provisions.statement: Every record field MUST use the name its word class gives it in the word-class table.
provisions.rationale: One grammar means a reader who learned `serves` on a flow understands `serves` on a use case the same way. Each class answers one question about the field: whether it identifies, links, classifies, narrates, conditions, or reasons. Only names an outside standard fixes stand outside this grammar. Settled by [decision/0006-one-field-naming-grammar](decision/0006-one-field-naming-grammar) on the evidence in [research/field-naming-evidence](research/field-naming-evidence) and [research/cross-layer-trace-evidence](research/cross-layer-trace-evidence).
provisions.example: The Claimwick flow `submit-an-expense` names its goal in `serves` and states each step in `statement`.

provisions.heading: Name Each Finding Code by Subject and Problem
provisions.evidence: Does every finding code read as subject-problem with a problem word from the table? Check the finding codes the change adds against the problem-word table.
provisions.statement: Every finding code MUST read as `<subject>-<problem>` with the problem drawn from the problem-word table.
provisions.rationale: A code in subject-problem form tells a reader what the finding is about and what is wrong with it without opening the message. A closed set of problem words, each with one meaning, keeps codes comparable across tools: one word for absent, one for expired, and no synonyms. The problem-word table lists each word with its meaning and an example.
provisions.example: A use case with no scenario takes the code `use-case-scenario-missing`.

provisions.heading: Read Each Field Name in Its Record Type
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `FIELD_NAME_SHAPE` for a field named after a record type that holds anything but links to that type, for a link verb that holds no links, and for a date name that holds no date, and reports a field name defined with two shapes and a field outside the field table. One meaning per name is held by the table itself, which carries exactly one row per field name.
provisions.statement: Every field name MUST carry the one meaning and shape the field table states for it, reading naturally in each record type that carries it, and hold links to a record type when it names that type, in the singular or the plural.
provisions.rationale: A reader meets a field inside one record, so each name reads naturally where it stands. Its meaning and shape stay fixed across every record type: one name carries one meaning, so `excludes` states what a record does not cover on a product, a feature, a module, a role, an aggregate, an entry point, and a permission set alike, and `key` carries only an idempotency key. The field table holds one row per field name with its meaning, its shape, and the record types that use it. One concept keeps one name, so `summary` and `fulfills` read the same everywhere, and a name that names a record type, such as `rules`, always holds links to that type. A Claimwick constraint states its legal rules in `obligations`, because `rules` holds links to rule records. Settled by [decision/0096-read-field-names-in-their-record-type](decision/0096-read-field-names-in-their-record-type).
provisions.example: A module states what its area covers in `covers` and what it does not cover in `excludes`. An actor states the acts the product holds it to in `responsibilities`, the one record type that carries that name. A setting names its configuration path in `configurationPath`, and a research source carries its label in `name`.

provisions.heading: Record the Project Vocabulary as Data
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `glossary-invalid` for a glossary that fails the glossary schema.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST record each term, its rejected synonyms, the scope of each rejection, and its mannered terms in the project glossary satisfying `schemas/glossary.schema.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: A glossary column headed "Avoid" helps a reader but gives a tool nothing to check. A rule held as data reaches the reader and the validator alike, so the same rejection appears in prose guidance and in diagnostics.
provisions.example:
A rejection carries the scope that binds it, because a word that is right in one module is wrong in another.

```json
{ "id": "term/customer", "term": "customer", "meaning": "A person or company that buys.",
  "rejected": [{ "word": "client", "scope": "^domain/modules/orders/",
    "reason": "client names the API consumer" }] }
```

provisions.heading: Reject a Recorded Synonym Inside Its Scope
provisions.evidence: Does any word on the page use a synonym the glossary rejects for this scope? Check the page against the project glossary.
provisions.statement: Authored prose MUST NOT use a synonym that the project glossary rejects for the scope the page sits in.
provisions.rationale: Term drift is invisible one page at a time and plain across a module: each page looks fine while the project slowly uses two words for one concept. A synonym that is a defined term elsewhere costs the most, because one word then names two things and every reader guesses which one.

provisions.heading: Resolve Every Identifier Citation
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a citation naming no written record.
provisions.statement: Every identifier citation MUST resolve to a written record.
provisions.rationale: A citation is a promise that a record exists at the other end. A citation that names nothing sends the reader searching for a record nobody wrote, so the model check fails it.

provisions.heading: Review Each Term for Its Lookalikes
provisions.evidence: Does any term differ from another only in hyphenation, spelling, plurality, or a compound split? Check the terms the change adds against the glossary.
provisions.statement: A project MUST resolve each pair of terms that differ only in hyphenation, spelling variant, plurality, or a compound split.
provisions.rationale: Two spellings of one concept split every search and every listing, and a reader cannot tell whether they name one concept or two. One spelling per concept keeps each term defined once and checked once. A hyphenated pair whose first part is a function word is two words side by side, not one compound split in two, so the check skips it: `a`, `an`, `as`, `at`, `by`, `in`, `of`, `on`, `or`, `to`, and `with`.
provisions.example: The notification `send-receiptreminder-confirmation` and the reaction `send-receipt-reminder-on-expense-submitted` name one concept with two spellings; the project picks one and renames the other. `send-on-line-notice` beside `send-online-notice` is not reported, since `on` opens no compound.

provisions.heading: State Mannered Terms Literally
provisions.evidence: Does any mannered term stand where the glossary asks for the literal word? Check the page against the project glossary.
provisions.statement: Authored prose MUST NOT use a mannered term the project glossary lists.
provisions.rationale: A metaphor or stock phrase hides what the project means: each reader understands a different act behind the same phrase. The glossary lists each mannered term with the literal phrase that carries its meaning, so the check names the mannered term and the plain words to use instead.
provisions.example: The glossary lists `{ "term": "leverage", "instead": "use" }`, so prose reads "use the retry queue" rather than "leverage the retry queue".

provisions.heading: Use Every Identifier Once
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-duplicate` for an identifier used twice.
provisions.statement: A record identifier MUST name exactly one record.
provisions.rationale: An identifier used twice names two records at once, so every citation of it points to both records. One use per identifier keeps each citation single-valued.
provisions.example: Two records named `use-case/spending.submit-expense` leave the model check reporting the duplicate on the second record.

provisions.heading: Use the Declared Record Identifier Grammar
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-invalid` for a record identifier outside the declared grammar.
provisions.statement: A consumer record identifier MUST use the form the Project Model states for its type, as `type/home.name` in kebab-case, with its name in the name form the record-name table gives its type and one to six lowercase hyphenated words.
provisions.rationale: The type names the record kind and `home.name` names the owning module or set, so an identifier resolves with no lookup table: a reader who sees `use-case/spending.submit-expense` knows it is a use case in the spending module without opening it. If two types shared one form, a citation needs its surrounding page to make sense, and search returns the wrong records. One grammar for every record kind keeps identifiers writable by hand and checkable by tool. The [Project Model](model.md) states the form each type uses, and the Identifier Forms section above states the name rules and checks. A name in the word class of what the record is shows the type without opening the record: a verb opens a use case, a noun phrase opens a goal, and a past participle opens a domain event. One name form per type keeps listings scannable and citations writable by hand. The record-name table lists the Intent, Behavior, and governance forms together. Settled by [decision/0077-use-the-standard-term-for-each-concept](decision/0077-use-the-standard-term-for-each-concept). A short hyphenated name is easy to read aloud in review and stays stable when the wording of the record changes. A long name gets shortened differently at each citation, and the shortcuts become competing names for one record.
provisions.example: `reaction/spending.send-receipt-reminder-on-expense-submitted` is a reaction owned by the spending module, and `step/submit-and-reimburse.attach-receipt` is the step where the employee attaches the receipt. Claimwick names the flow `submit-an-expense`, the use case `submit-expense`, and the setting `receipt-threshold`, each in one to six words. `decision/0001-receipt-threshold` counts its number as one word.

provisions.heading: Write Each Finding Message as a Fact
provisions.evidence: Does every finding message state one present-tense fact opening with the subject and identifier? Check the messages the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every finding message MUST state one present-tense fact that opens with the subject title and its quoted identifier.
provisions.rationale: A message that states a fact reads the same in the terminal and the book: both show what is true. Advice belongs in the finding table on the [model command page](../tools/model.md), where it is written once beside the code instead of repeated in every occurrence. Analyzer diagnostics keep their `LS` numbers and follow the same message rule.
provisions.example: A flow step with no serving use case reports `Flow step 'step/book-a-room.confirm-booking' is served by no use case.`

provisions.heading: Write Each Text Kind in Its Own Form
provisions.evidence: Does every text use the form of its kind? Check the statements, steps, and meanings the change adds against the text-kind table.
provisions.statement: Every project text MUST use the form the text-kind table gives its kind.
provisions.rationale: Each kind of text has one reader and one job: a requirement promises, a domain event reports, and a runbook step instructs. One form per kind means the tense and voice show what the text does from its form alone. Record values stay in the third person, Intent chapter prose says `we` for the business, and no record says `you`; tutorial and how-to pages may.
provisions.example: A Claimwick requirement states "An expense above the threshold waits for its approver."

provisions.heading: Write Each Value in the Value Style
provisions.evidence: Does every statement, meaning, rationale, condition, failure, and title value use its row's style? Check the values the change adds against the value-style table.
provisions.statement: Every `statement`, `meaning`, `rationale`, `*Because`, `*When`, `condition`, `failure`, and `title` value MUST use the value style the value-style table states.
provisions.rationale: Values are read far more than they are written, in records, in the book, and in tool output. One written form per value means a period or a capital letter is never a styling choice but part of the value. The value-style table ends each row with the mechanical test the value meets. Settled by [decision/0011-one-grammar-for-names-and-values](decision/0011-one-grammar-for-names-and-values) on the evidence in [research/naming-grammar-evidence](research/naming-grammar-evidence).
provisions.example: A Claimwick flow step states "The traveller pays for the booking."

provisions.heading: Write in American English
provisions.evidence: Does any word use British spelling? Check the field names, enum values, and prose the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every field name and enum value MUST use American spelling.
provisions.rationale: One spelling per word keeps each term defined once and checked once: `license` in one record and `licence` in another split every search and every listing. American spelling is the project spelling for field names and enum values; prose spelling follows the [Writing Standard](writing.md). Each British form is a rejected word beside its American spelling.
provisions.example: Claimwick writes `license` and `pseudonymize` in field names, values, and prose.

provisions.heading: Write Quantities in Standard Units
provisions.evidence: Does every quantity use a standard unit? Check the dates, durations, money values, and numbers the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every quantity in a record MUST use an ISO 8601 date, an ISO 8601 duration, an amount with an ISO 4217 currency, or a number with its unit.
provisions.rationale: Free-text quantities vary with local habits: one record writes `7 years`, another writes `seven years`, and a check matches neither. ISO dates, ISO durations, and ISO currency codes give every quantity one written form across records and tools. Prose keeps numbers readable by writing each with its unit.
provisions.example: Claimwick holds a room for `PT10M` and writes "95 percent of checkouts complete" in prose.

provisions.heading: Add Behavior Detail When Specifying Intent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `record-link-missing`, `step-use-case-missing`, `erasure-undeclared`, or `setting-requirement-missing` finding across Behavior records.
provisions.statement: Behavior that fulfills an Intent record MUST add the states, invariants, refusals, consistency, data classes with erasure positions, freshness, and tenant-scoped access that the Intent record implies but leaves unstated.
provisions.rationale: An Intent promise says what the product owes in product words, without saying how the system keeps it. Behavior turns each promise into the states, invariants, refusals, consistency, data classes with erasure positions, freshness, and tenant-scoped access that keep it. A detail counts as implied when every faithful fulfillment of the promise needs it and no actor meets it as an outcome, limit, or figure the promise does not name. Only Behavior records fulfill a requirement, as `litespec/core/intent#restrict-requirement-fulfillment-to-behavior` states. Without that detail, each implementer fills the gap with a guess, and two guesses about the same promise diverge.
provisions.example: Claimwick's reimbursement promise gains an entity with Approved and Reimbursed states, a refusal for an expense that is already reimbursed, and atomic consistency over one aggregate.

provisions.heading: Build Ahead of a Regulation Only Under Its Constraint
provisions.evidence: Does every anticipatory behavior cite its constraint without blocking a release before the statutory date? Check the regulation-driven Behavior records against the constraint and its date.
provisions.statement: Behavior that anticipates a regulation with a deadline MUST follow that regulation's constraint.
provisions.rationale: A regulation with a deadline needs working behavior before its requirement exists, so the constraint carries the rule in the meantime, with its statutory date in `effectiveFrom`. The release stays shippable until the statutory date, and only then does the missing behavior block it. Without this path, teams either ship late or build the rule where no record owns it.
provisions.example: A privacy regulation taking effect next year enters as a Claimwick constraint with its statutory date, and the anticipatory erasure behavior follows that constraint until the requirement exists.

provisions.heading: Enter World Facts as Cited Research or Constraints
provisions.evidence: Did every world fact enter as a cited and dated research or constraint record? Check the provider, regulation, and incident facts the change relies on.
provisions.statement: A fact learned from the world MUST enter Intent as research, or as a constraint whose `sources` cite its source with the date it was read.
provisions.rationale: Commitments flow down, and facts from the world flow up: a provider's behavior, a regulation, or an incident enters Intent where people can weigh it. The citation and the `readOn` date show where the fact came from and when someone read it, so a later change rechecks the source instead of trusting memory. A constraint names the research it rests on in `basedOn`, as the constraint fields state. Proposed by [decision/0047-cite-a-source-for-each-constraint-rule](decision/0047-cite-a-source-for-each-constraint-rule).
provisions.example: Claimwick's observed two-day payout settlement window enters as research, then as a constraint citing that research.

provisions.heading: Implement Only Declared Behavior
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `behavior-unrecorded`, `use-case-unrecorded`, `reaction-unrecorded`, `job-unrecorded`, `write-undeclared`, `result-undeclared`, `effect-undeclared`, or `refusal-unimplemented` finding across the implementation.
provisions.statement: Implementation MUST add only the code shapes its stack pages fix and no observable outcome, edge, write, or access grant its Behavior records leave undeclared.
provisions.rationale: Stack pages fix the code shapes: the handler, the repository call, and the published domain event each have one prescribed form. An extra outcome, edge, write, or access grant splits the project into a specification that says one thing and code that does another. A handler that authorizes itself is one such extra grant, which analyzer `LS2012` reports. A record sentence describing a possible future is not a specification. Code builds no interface, provider list, or hook for a feature no record specifies.
provisions.example: Claimwick's submit-expense handler returns a code no result declares. The run fails `result-undeclared`, and the fix declares the result or removes the code. A record sentence saying a country pack may add a national audit file specifies no feature: the code builds no audit file provider for it, and the national audit file arrives as its own specified feature.

provisions.heading: Prove Each Scenario Through the Public Boundary
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `use-case-scenario-missing` or `proves-unreached` finding across scenarios and tests.
provisions.statement: At large size or with the `bdd` extension, each scenario MUST be proved by one test through the public boundary.
provisions.rationale: Small projects carry no scenarios unless the `bdd` extension enables them, so the rule binds large projects and small projects with the extension. A scenario is the leaf of the record tree, so one test through the public boundary connects each leaf to running behavior.
provisions.example: Claimwick, a large project, carries a scenario for its missing-receipt refusal, and one test proves it by submitting an expense without a receipt through the endpoint.

provisions.heading: Raise Open Needs as Owner Questions or Backlog Items
provisions.evidence: Does every need the upper layer neither states nor implies have a question to the owner with a recommendation or a backlog item? Check the added records from a lower record layer beside the owner questions and the backlog.
provisions.statement: A need that the upper record layer neither states nor implies, such as a refusal, eligibility condition, limit, or a figure the owner sets, MUST travel up as a question to the owner with a recommendation or as a backlog item, never as a record or code.
provisions.rationale: The lower layer does not decide what the upper layer neither states nor implies, so the need travels up with its context instead of turning into a guess. A question carries product choices to the person who answers for them. A backlog item holds the rest where it stays visible until it is specified. The specification is closed: an agent builds what it states and nothing more. A figure the owner sets is one such need: the [Project Model](model.md) holds the one list of owner-set figures, and each one binds the product to buyers, markets, or law, so only an accountable person decides it. A figure the business changes while the system runs is aggregate data, not a setting: its range is a rule with a refusal, and its change is a use case with access and audit. A setting is operator configuration the running system reads. An agent that fixed a figure would hide a commitment in a Behavior record nobody chose. A question carries a recommendation with each figure: a figure without one asks the owner to research from nothing, while a recommendation gives a default to accept or correct. Grouping figures by subject lets the owner answer one set at a time.
provisions.example: Claimwick's agent meets a need for a refusal of expenses with a future date, which the receipt promise neither states nor implies, so the need becomes a question to the owner instead of a rule the agent writes. A receipt threshold the promise leaves unnamed travels up as a question with a recommended figure the same way.

provisions.heading: Write Each Layer from the Layer Above It
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `behavior-unrecorded` finding for a refusal literal or a screen that calls no endpoint, and reports `mark-missing` for a code element that carries no mark.
provisions.statement: Each record below Intent MUST be written from a record in the record layer above it.
provisions.rationale: Without a parent above it, a lower record could carry a promise from above or invent a new one, and reviewers cannot tell which. Implementers then build from guesses, and two guesses about the same gap diverge. Writing each record from the layer above keeps one chain from promise to proof, so a gap shows as a missing parent instead of silent invention. Derivation between records follows the same direction: generic refusals derive from `access`, `input`, and the knowledge the use case reads without new records.
provisions.example: Claimwick's submit-expense handler holds a positivity guard with no rule above it. The agent writes the missing rule or reports the gap, and the guard stays until the record is written. Behavior with no parent is recorded or reported, never deleted for lacking one. A test with no record above it is a finding the team resolves by writing the missing record or reporting the gap. It is deleted only when a reviewer establishes that the behavior it protects is obsolete, redundant or wrong, and the pull request says so.

provisions.heading: Align Backup Deletion Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every backup and replica operation follow the documented deletion guarantee? Check the backup and replica procedures.
provisions.statement: Backup and replica operations MUST follow the documented deletion guarantee.
provisions.rationale: Every copy the product keeps falls under the deletion promise, including backups and replicas that restore for months after the live row disappears. When backup behavior stays undocumented, the team promises erasure it cannot deliver and learns the gap during an audit or a restore.

provisions.heading: Audit Lifecycle Changes
provisions.evidence: Does every lifecycle operation write an audit record, or a standalone record where audit is not selected? Check each operation's writes.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle operation MUST record its audit as an audit record when audit is selected and a standalone record otherwise.
provisions.rationale: A subject-access or legal-hold dispute asks first who deleted what and when. The audit entry lets a reviewer answer from the record.

provisions.heading: Authorize Lifecycle Access Paths
provisions.evidence: Does every administrative or restore query run on a named path with explicit authorization? Check the query paths and their authorization.
provisions.statement: An administrative or restore query MUST use a named path with explicit authorization.
provisions.rationale: Restore and administration queries reach records normal queries cannot see, so they need a path of their own with checks of their own. Without the named path, a privileged read hides inside normal query code and inherits normal authorization, which grants too much to too many callers.

provisions.heading: Authorize Lifecycle Changes
provisions.evidence: Does every lifecycle operation check its documented authorization before changing the record? Check each operation's authorization check.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle operation MUST apply its documented authorization.
provisions.rationale: Deleting or restoring the wrong record harms a customer or breaks a legal duty. The authorization check runs before the record changes, because a check that runs after can only report harm it already allowed.

provisions.heading: Default to Hard Delete
provisions.evidence: Does every deletion with no retention or restore requirement remove the row in the delete transaction? Check the delete transaction code.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle implementation MUST use hard delete when no accepted retention or restore requirement applies.
provisions.rationale: When no use case needs the data back, removing the row deletes the least and keeps the least: no hidden state, no filtered queries, and no purge job to write and watch. A team that keeps deleted rows just in case pays for retention without a requirement and answers subject-access exports with data it promised to delete.
provisions.example: A Claimwick expense deleted without a retention duty removes the expense row in the delete transaction.

provisions.heading: Define Document Lifecycle Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every document implementation define document state, filtered queries, indexes, purge transformations, and contract evolution? Check each document implementation.
provisions.statement: A Marten lifecycle implementation MUST define document state, filtered queries, indexes, purge transformations, and contract evolution.
provisions.rationale: A document store keeps whatever the aggregate writes. The team states how each lifecycle state lands in the document: which state the document carries, which queries filter it, which indexes serve those queries, how a purge rewrites the document, and how the contract changes when the shape does. Without those choices, the business transition lands in storage by accident and each query invents its own filter.

provisions.heading: Define Post-Deletion References
provisions.evidence: Does every specification define post-deletion behavior for references, exports, and unique constraints? Check each specification's deletion section.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle specification MUST define post-deletion behavior for cross-aggregate references, exports, and unique constraints.
provisions.rationale: Other records can point at the deleted one, exports can carry its values, and a unique value such as an expense reference number can become available again. When the specification does not define the behavior, each developer guesses: one nulls the reference, another keeps it, and a duplicate value slips through or a report breaks. Writing the behavior down gives every reference, export, and constraint one answer.

provisions.heading: Define Relational Lifecycle Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every relational implementation define columns, query filters, partial indexes, migrations, and named filter behavior? Check each relational implementation.
provisions.statement: A relational lifecycle implementation MUST define columns, query filters, partial indexes, migrations, and named filter behavior.
provisions.rationale: A relational table keeps retained rows beside active ones. The team states which columns mark the state, which query filters hide retained rows, which partial indexes keep active values unique, which migrations add all of it, and what each named filter means. Without those choices, a unique constraint blocks a legitimate reuse or a query returns rows the lifecycle retired.

provisions.heading: Exclude Inactive Records from Normal Reads
provisions.evidence: Is every normal query free of deleted or archived records? Check the query filters beside the active state.
provisions.statement: A normal query MUST exclude deleted or archived records.
provisions.rationale: An employee browsing expenses expects live data. Deleted and archived records in that list confuse the employee and leak data the lifecycle retired. Normal queries therefore read only the active state, while the named privileged paths serve the records outside it.

provisions.heading: Exclude Persistence-Only Lifecycle Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every lifecycle transition run through behavior beyond persistence filters or property setters alone? Check the transition code and the persistence filters.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle rule MUST NOT rely only on persistence filters or property setters.
provisions.rationale: A query filter or a property setter runs without the business checks. It filters rows in storage while the aggregate never learns the transition happened. The product then enforces lifecycle in two places that disagree, and a new query that skips the filter exposes data the lifecycle retired.

provisions.heading: Keep Archive Records Module-Owned
provisions.evidence: Does every archive record sit under its owning module, or in the shared archive area the project keeps? Check the module folders.
provisions.statement: Keep archive records under the owning module.
provisions.rationale: The module that defines what a record means also defines what its archive means and who may read it. An archive kept elsewhere sits under two modules, and its access checks drift from its home module.

provisions.heading: Keep Purge and Archive Work Bounded and Observable
provisions.evidence: Does every purge and archive run resume after interruption within declared bounds and show progress? Check the purge and archive tests.
provisions.statement: A purge or archive operation MUST be resumable, bounded, cancellation-aware, and observable.
