provisions.rationale: A purge or archive job can run for hours across millions of rows, and a deployment, a failure, or an operator stops it midway. Resumable, bounded, cancellation-aware work restarts where it stopped instead of from the beginning, and observable progress tells the operator whether it moves or stalls.

provisions.heading: Model Lifecycle Operations in Domain
provisions.evidence: Does every aggregate expose delete, archive, and restore methods where those operations apply? Check each aggregate's methods.
provisions.statement: A Domain aggregate MUST expose delete, archive, and restore as explicit behavior when those operations apply.
provisions.rationale: Delete, archive, and restore change what the business promises about a record. The aggregate owns them the way it owns any rule: one method per operation, with the checks beside the change. When the operation lives anywhere else, two callers implement it two ways and the checks drift apart.

provisions.heading: Model Retained Lifecycle States
provisions.evidence: Does every retained record carry a business reason and a named state transition? Check each retained record beside its state transitions.
provisions.statement: A soft-deleted or archived record MUST have a business reason and explicit state transition.
provisions.rationale: A record that stays after deletion or moves to an archive still affects the product: it appears in some reads, skips others, and can return. A named state with a named transition shows that behavior in the aggregate itself, so a reader sees which transitions exist and which checks each one runs. Without the transition, the retained data is a row that code handles with special cases in scattered places.
provisions.example: `Archive` changes aggregate state after the authorization and audit checks succeed.

provisions.heading: Name Soft-Delete Timestamps
provisions.evidence: Does every soft-delete timestamp use `deleted_at_utc`, or another column the documentation names? Check the schema columns.
provisions.statement: Use `deleted_at_utc` when a soft-delete timestamp is required.
provisions.rationale: One name for the deletion timestamp lets every reader and query recognize it on sight. The name states the event and the unit, removing two guesses a reviewer otherwise makes.

provisions.heading: Preserve Legal-Hold Data
provisions.evidence: Does every retention run preserve held data past its retention date? Check the retention run code beside the hold records.
provisions.statement: A retention job MUST preserve data under legal hold.
provisions.rationale: A legal hold suspends the duty to delete. The named data stays until the hold releases, even when its retention date passes. A retention job that ignores the hold destroys evidence the organization had a duty to keep.

provisions.heading: Record Lifecycle Scope
provisions.evidence: Does every lifecycle record name classification, retention, deletion trigger, hold, export, restore, and backup? Check each lifecycle record.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle record MUST name classification, retention, deletion trigger, hold, export, restore, and backup.
provisions.rationale: A record's lifetime raises one set of choices: what kind of data it is, how long it stays, what triggers deletion, and how holds, exports, restores, and backups behave. Naming them all in one lifecycle record keeps them reviewable together. Without that record, the choices scatter across tickets and memory, and a deletion runs before anyone checks the retention bound. Retention bounds live in setting records.

provisions.heading: Record Retention Progress
provisions.evidence: Does every retention run persist progress for the next run to resume from? Check the retention run code.
provisions.statement: A retention job MUST record its progress.
provisions.rationale: A retention run can stop midway through millions of rows. Recorded progress tells the next run where to resume, and observable progress tells the operator whether the job moves or stalls.

provisions.heading: Record the Release of a Legal Hold
provisions.evidence: Does every legal-hold release record the actor, data covered, reason, and resumed retention? Check the release records.
provisions.statement: A legal-hold release MUST record actor, data covered, reason, and resumed retention: an audit record when audit is selected, a standalone record otherwise.
provisions.rationale: A hold suspends the duty to erase, and releasing it resumes that duty from a date the team can name. Without a release record, nobody can state when the suspension ended. A subject [erasure request](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/) then has no answer date, and the next retention run cannot tell which data is deletable again. The record also tells the retention job exactly which data resumed which retention date.
provisions.example: A release record names the hold, the release date, and the retention date the covered data carries.

provisions.heading: Reject Hidden Lifecycle Flags
provisions.evidence: Does every lifecycle transition run through explicit behavior instead of a storage-only flag? Check the transition code.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle implementation MUST NOT use a hidden boolean as its sole lifecycle behavior.
provisions.rationale: A boolean column that only the storage layer reads can flip without running the business checks: no authorization, no audit entry, and no named transition a reviewer can find. The record then looks deleted in one query and active in another, depending on which filter each query applies. An explicit lifecycle operation keeps the flag, where one exists, as an effect of the transition rather than the transition itself.

provisions.heading: Separate Query-Shaped History
provisions.evidence: Does every query-shaped history live in a read model instead of on its aggregate, unless the project keeps it on the aggregate? Check the aggregate code beside the read models.
provisions.statement: Use a separate read model when archived history is query-shaped instead of an aggregate invariant.
provisions.rationale: History kept for display, such as a list of past expenses, constrains nothing the aggregate protects. It costs less as a read model beside the record. Folding it into the record widens the transaction boundary for data no invariant needs.

provisions.heading: Test Provider Lifecycle Paths
provisions.evidence: Does the suite test the normal and lifecycle query paths on the selected provider? Check the lifecycle tests.
provisions.statement: A selected persistence provider MUST test normal and lifecycle query paths.
provisions.rationale: Filters, indexes, and migrations behave differently per provider: a filter that works on documents can fail on tables. Tests that read through both the normal path and the lifecycle path on the selected provider catch the difference before a customer does.

provisions.heading: Avoid Catalog-Only Locale Claims
provisions.evidence: Does every shipped locale come from the locale decision rather than from catalog files alone? Check the shipped locales beside the locale decision.
provisions.statement: A product MUST NOT infer supported locales from catalog files alone.
provisions.rationale: A catalog file shows only that someone wrote translations. It says nothing about routes, fallback, selection, or detection, so a product that counts locales by counting files claims a locale its routes cannot serve and its fallback never reaches.

provisions.heading: Avoid Duplicate Localized URLs
provisions.evidence: Does every localized content item serve from exactly one indexable URL? Check the served URLs of each content item.
provisions.statement: A localized application MUST NOT publish multiple indexable URLs for the same localized content.
provisions.rationale: When two addresses serve the same locale, search engines split the page's rank between them, and canonical links point in two directions. One indexable address per locale keeps search, sharing, and caching on the same page.

provisions.heading: Complete or Fall Back Catalog Values
provisions.evidence: Does every supported locale contain its required keys or resolve them through its declared fallback? Check each locale catalog beside the fallback chain.
provisions.statement: Each supported locale MUST contain required keys or use its declared fallback.
provisions.rationale: A missing translation with no declared fallback reaches the interface with no chosen outcome: the interface shows a key, an empty string, or the wrong language. The declaration states the fallback locale and what a missing key does at build time. A key missing from the default locale fails the build. No fallback exists for it, and the interface renders its identifier. A key missing from a non-default locale reports a warning and falls back. Shipping one untranslated string costs less than blocking a release on it.
provisions.example: A catalog check runs in the frontend lint gate, so a missing key fails or warns before review, not in a browser.

provisions.heading: Define One Locale Route Shape
provisions.evidence: Does every locale reach the application through the documented route shape? Check the route definitions.
provisions.statement: A localized application MUST define one documented locale route shape.
provisions.rationale: Users, links, crawlers, and caches address a localized page, so one route shape gives each locale one predictable address. A path segment is the default shape: every localized page gets a distinct address that links, crawlers, and cache entries can each name. A cookie or header shape serves every locale from one address instead, so a shared cache and a search index each see only one locale. A product with no public pages, whose locale belongs to the signed-in account, documents one of those shapes instead of inventing a fourth.
provisions.example: `/nl/orders/42` places the locale in the documented path segment, so a crawler and a shared cache each address one locale.

provisions.heading: Follow the Validation Message Grammar
provisions.evidence: Does every validation message state the field label, the fault, and the accepted input without technical wording? Check the validation messages in each locale.
provisions.statement: A validation catalog MUST state the field label, what is wrong, and what is accepted, without technical wording.
provisions.rationale: A validation message that names the field, the fault, and the accepted input tells the user how to fix the entry in any language, while a message with only one of the three does not. The three-part shape holds across languages; each language's sentence pattern is recorded in the labels of the field's glossary term and the language's writing page.
provisions.example: The glossary term for a Claimwick expense field records the sentence pattern for each supported language.

provisions.heading: Format Values with Active Locale
provisions.evidence: Does every date, number, currency, plural, list, and relative time render through the active-locale formatters? Check the formatting calls.
provisions.statement: A localized interface MUST format dates, times, numbers, currency, plurals, lists, and relative time by active locale.
provisions.rationale: Dates, times, numbers, currency, plurals, lists, and relative time each follow the user's conventions, and a date the user misreads becomes a missed appointment or a wrong payment. The platform supplies all of them. [The `Intl` namespace](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl) has `DateTimeFormat`, `NumberFormat`, `PluralRules`, `ListFormat`, and `RelativeTimeFormat`. Each one uses the locale data the browser already ships. A project-written formatter for any of these is a second locale database that no one updates. Its plural rules are wrong for the first language with more than two forms.
provisions.example: Create one formatter instance per locale and reuse it. Construction is the expensive part.

provisions.heading: Handle Unavailable Locale Segments
provisions.evidence: Does every unsupported or missing locale segment redirect under the documented product policy? Check the redirect tests.
provisions.statement: A localized application MUST redirect unsupported or missing locale segments according to product policy.
provisions.rationale: Readers mistype addresses and follow stale links, so a locale segment can name a locale the product never shipped, or go missing entirely. Without a documented policy, each route responds differently: one shows the default locale, another shows an error, and a crawler indexes both as content.

provisions.heading: Keep Locale Selection Explicit
provisions.evidence: Does every request carry the locale in the URL or a documented session preference instead of ambient request state? Check the request handling for the locale.
provisions.statement: Keep locale selection in the URL or documented session preference.
provisions.rationale: A locale stored in the URL or a documented session preference travels with the request, so any developer can see which locale a page serves and link to it. An implicit global locale hides in process state, where one request can read another's locale and no link reproduces the page.

provisions.heading: Keep Stable Error Codes Locale-Neutral
provisions.evidence: Is every stable API error code identical across locales? Check the error code values in each locale's responses.
provisions.statement: A stable API error code MUST NOT change by locale.
provisions.rationale: Integrations and support tools match on the error code. A code that changes per language forces every consumer to list every translation before handling one failure. The code stays fixed while the human-readable message beside it translates.

provisions.heading: Localize Public Presentation Content
provisions.evidence: Do public metadata, form labels, validation messages, and user-safe errors all follow the active locale? Check each rendered page.
provisions.statement: Public metadata, form labels, validation messages, and user-safe errors MUST follow the active locale.
provisions.rationale: A Dutch page with an English title, English form labels, or an English error tells the user the translation stopped halfway and tells a search engine the page serves two languages. Metadata, labels, validation messages, and user-safe errors follow the active locale together with the surrounding page.

provisions.heading: Name Messages by Meaning
provisions.evidence: Does every catalog key use a semantic name citing a glossary term instead of a source-language sentence? Check the catalog keys.
provisions.statement: A locale catalog MUST use semantic keys that cite glossary terms rather than source-language sentences.
provisions.rationale: A key that copies the English sentence loses its meaning when English is reworded: every other language still refers to the old sentence. A semantic key names the intent instead, citing the glossary term that holds the word's labels per language, so wording changes in any language without disturbing the key.
provisions.example: `orders.cancel.confirmation` identifies intent without copying the English sentence.

provisions.heading: Preserve Locale-Neutral Business Data
provisions.evidence: Is every domain value and API contract locale-neutral outside an explicitly localized exchange? Check the domain values and contracts.
provisions.statement: Domain values and API contracts MUST remain locale-neutral unless a use case explicitly exchanges localized content.
provisions.rationale: An expense state or a price stored in Dutch breaks when an English speaker opens it, and an API contract that shifts per language forces every consumer to handle wording before reading data. Business values and wire contracts stay in one neutral form, and only the interface translates them for display. A use case that genuinely exchanges localized content, such as a product description the merchant writes per language, names that exchange explicitly.

provisions.heading: Record Supported Locale Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does the locale decision list the supported locales, the default locale, the fallback chain, user selection, and browser detection? Check the locale decision record.
provisions.statement: A localization decision MUST list supported locales, default locale, fallback chain, user selection, and browser detection.
provisions.rationale: Catalogs, routes, and formatters read the same five choices, and the choices interact. Writing them once in the decision, before building any of the three, gives all three one contract to follow. Without it, each part guesses its own fallback, and the product handles each missing translation differently.

provisions.heading: Resolve Every Shown Identifier
provisions.evidence: Does every screen render glossary labels instead of raw codes, outside user-facing reference numbers? Check the rendered screens.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST resolve every closed-set code it renders to its glossary label and never render the raw code, excluding user-facing reference numbers.
provisions.rationale: A code such as a refusal ground or a billing state is a contract value built for systems, while the glossary label beside it is copy built for users. A screen that renders the raw code shows one untranslated fragment in an otherwise translated page and forces the user to decode it. Resolving every shown code keeps the whole screen in the user's language, except reference numbers the user quotes back.
provisions.example: A Claimwick shipment row shows the glossary label for `shipment-delayed` in the active locale.

provisions.heading: Split Catalogs by Module When Needed
provisions.evidence: Is every catalog whole unless measured size calls for a split, or the project chose a feature split from the start? Check the catalog files beside the size measurements.
provisions.statement: Split catalogs by module only when catalog size requires it.
provisions.rationale: Small catalogs read better whole: one file per locale shows every key at a glance and survives a rename without cross-file edits. Splitting waits until measured size, such as slow loads or conflicting edits, proves one file no longer serves.

provisions.heading: Store User-Facing Copy in Catalogs
provisions.evidence: Does every user-facing sentence live in the locale catalogs instead of source code? Check the source files for literal copy.
provisions.statement: A localized application MUST store user-facing copy in locale catalogs.
provisions.rationale: Copy in source code reaches translators only through developers, and each wording change becomes a code change with a review, a build, and a deployment. Holding every user-facing sentence in one catalog per locale lets translators edit wording while developers edit behavior.

provisions.heading: Use BCP 47 Identifiers
provisions.evidence: Does every locale identifier use BCP 47, or another identifier form the documentation names? Check the locale identifiers in the catalogs and routes.
provisions.statement: Use BCP 47 locale identifiers.
provisions.rationale: BCP 47 is the identifier form routes, catalogs, browsers, and libraries recognize: one tag such as `nl` passes unchanged from the address bar to the catalog lookup. A home-grown form needs conversion at every boundary and confuses every new developer.

provisions.heading: Use One Catalog Root
provisions.evidence: Does every catalog sit under the application-owned root, or under another root the documentation names? Check the catalog folders.
provisions.statement: Keep catalogs under one application-owned locale root.
provisions.rationale: One application-owned root tells every developer and tool where catalogs live, so a new locale sits beside the old ones instead of in a folder nobody checks. Scattered catalogs split the set, and one of them misses the fallback check.

provisions.heading: Derive a General Rule from a Consumer Need
provisions.evidence: Does a change prompted by one consumer name the general need and check the rule against products unlike that consumer? Check the change's wording, the products it tests, and any need left in the consumer as a convention or waiver.
provisions.statement: A change prompted by one consumer's need MUST state the general need behind it, design and check the rule against products unlike that consumer, apply the rule only where it makes sense across them, and leave a need that holds for one consumer alone in that consumer as a project convention or waiver rather than in LiteSpec.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec is a contract many unrelated products adopt. A rule shaped around one product's domain misfits every other product and teaches their readers a world they do not have. Check the rule against an expense product, a library product, a consumer app with no organization, and a client-only app with no hosted sign-in, where the provision could apply, so the rule holds for each.
provisions.example: A consumer asks for development seed data. LiteSpec adds a cast-based seeding default that works for an expense product and a library product alike, not a rule about one product's records, and a need that only that consumer has stays in its project as a convention or waiver.

provisions.heading: Keep Consumers Out of LiteSpec
provisions.evidence: Does the change name a consumer project or carry a consumer's domain vocabulary? Grep the change for consumer names and for vocabulary of a consumer's domain.
provisions.statement: Every page, provision, example, test fixture, template, decision, changelog entry, and tool message in LiteSpec MUST name no consumer project and carry no consumer domain vocabulary, records, flows, figures, people, or products, drawing examples only from the Claimwick expense product or the library product.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec serves many projects in unrelated business areas. A reader who meets one consumer's name or domain vocabulary has to learn a world they do not work in, and a rule shaped around that domain misfits every product that does not share it. Claimwick and the library product are the shared examples, so every reader meets the same expenses and library holdings whatever product they build.
provisions.example: A page that explains a rule shows a Claimwick expense submitted by Ava for Harbor or Pine, or a library patron borrowing a book, rather than an example lifted from a consumer's records.

provisions.heading: Keep Provision Identifiers Stable Within a Major Version
provisions.evidence: Did a minor release remove or rename any provision identifier? Compare the provision index at the previous tag with the provision index of the release, beside the changelog entry that lists the generated diff.
provisions.statement: A minor LiteSpec release MUST keep every provision identifier of its major version, adding provisions and rewording provision text without removing or renaming an identifier.
provisions.rationale: Consumers cite provision identifiers in code marks, records, and waivers, each written against the major version the project pins. A minor release that removes or renames an identifier breaks those citations inside a version line the consumer took as stable, with no major release to signal the break. A major release may remove or rename identifiers, and the generated provision diff in its changelog lists every added, removed, and renamed identifier, so a consumer moving across a major version finds each change in one place.
provisions.example: A minor release adds `litespec/core/scope#claim-the-record-layers-the-project-uses` and rewords a neighboring provision; both keep their identifiers, so every mark and waiver written against the major version still resolves.

provisions.heading: List Every Stack, Shape, and Extension in the Manifest
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits `EXTENSION_UNLISTED` for an extension page no manifest entry lists, `LAYER_UNREACHABLE` for a page no stack selection reaches, and `MANIFEST_ANALYZER_PIN` for an analyzer pin that differs from the analyzer project version.
provisions.statement: The LiteSpec manifest MUST list every stack, shape, extension, and version pin the release carries.
provisions.rationale: The manifest is the release record that tools read: stacks and shapes decide which pages apply, extensions decide which conditional bundles a project selects from, and pins decide which versions build. A stack, shape, extension, or pin the manifest omits is one no consumer selects and no tool resolves. Listing all of them in one file keeps the release reproducible from its tag.
provisions.example: The manifest lists the `delivery` extension with its page path `docs/ext/delivery.md` and its `project` activation scope.

provisions.heading: Mark the Tools with the Provisions They Follow
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits `MARK_MISSING` for a class with a method and no `follows` mark in a source project under `apps/`, and `MARK_UNRESOLVED` for a `follows` or `proves` mark in a .NET project under `apps/`, outside its `Fixtures` folders, that names no provision in `docs/reference/provisions.md`.
provisions.statement: Every top-level class that declares a method in a .NET source project under `apps/`, and every test that verifies a provision, MUST name its provision in a mark: a `follows` mark on the class and a `proves` mark on the test.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec's own tools are technical classes: they serve no product record, and each exists because a provision requires a check, a reader, or a generator of its shape. A `follows` mark is the reverse index from that code to the provision, so a retired or renamed provision finds every class still built for it. A `proves` mark finds the tests that verify its check. LiteSpec keeps the research and decisions behind its provisions as records under `docs/intent/`, in the shapes a consumer uses; its provisions remain its specification, and the marks point at them directly. The site under `apps/site` is TypeScript with no mark form in the maintainer tool, so it carries no marks.
provisions.example: The .NET scenario reader carries `/// <follows>litespec/core/model#name-the-lowest-record-each-test-proves</follows>`, and the test that confirms a scenario driven through a shared probe step carries `/// <proves>litespec/core/model#name-the-lowest-record-each-test-proves</proves>`.

provisions.heading: Model a Reported Spec Gap Before More Code
provisions.evidence: Does each reported spec gap have a LiteSpec model change that cites the gap before the consumer writes more code around it? Check the gap report beside the record type, field, or provision that answers it.
provisions.statement: When a consumer's agent reports a spec gap, a maintainer MUST model the missing concept in LiteSpec as a record type, a field, or a provision, with the change citing the gap, before the consumer writes more code around it.
provisions.rationale: An agent that meets a concept LiteSpec cannot express stops instead of bending the code, so the gap is a request for a contract change. Answering the question alone leaves the next agent to meet the same gap, and the consumer's substitutes grow. Modelling the concept in LiteSpec gives every consumer one decided shape, and citing the gap in the change shows which need the provision answers. Check the rule against products unlike the consumer that reported it, as `litespec/core/maintaining#derive-a-general-rule-from-a-consumer-need` states.
provisions.example: An agent reports that Claimwick's per-diem rates have no home because the checks accept a rate table only as an external system. The maintainer adds the dated reference data and the rule that cites it, cites the gap in the change, and only then does the consumer replace the substitute.

provisions.heading: Publish a LiteSpec Release from a Tag
provisions.evidence: `dotnet test --solution LiteSpec.slnx` fails `ReleaseVersionTests` when the changelog, the template, or either package version differs from the manifest version, and `.github/workflows/release.yml` refuses a tag that does not name the manifest version, a release tag whose commit is not on `main`, and a candidate tag whose commit is not on `release/<version>`.
provisions.statement: A LiteSpec tag that publishes MUST be `v<version>` on `main`, or a release candidate `v<version>-rc.<n>` on `release/<version>`, and the changelog entry, the consumer template version, and the tool and analyzer package versions name the same manifest version.
provisions.rationale: A git tag is the only durable artifact that names a release: branches move and files change, but the tag stays. Reading the current release from the highest tag gives maintainers, consumers, and tools one shared answer. Writing that version into the manifest, the changelog, the template, and the tool package in the same release keeps the four consistent. A candidate lets a consumer test the packages a release will publish before the release branch merges. Its suffix keeps its packages apart from the release's, and the committed files keep the plain version, so a candidate never changes what `main` names. Each release publishes the CLI as one native executable per platform, in the tool packages and in standalone archives, so the version reaches a consumer with or without .NET, settled by [decision/0021-native-command-line](decision/0021-native-command-line) on the evidence in [research/native-command-line-evidence](research/native-command-line-evidence).

provisions.heading: Publish Each Release Candidate from Its Release Branch
provisions.evidence: Does every release candidate tag name a commit on `release/<version>`, with no candidate packages published from `main`? Check the candidate tags and the release workflow runs that published them.
provisions.statement: Every release candidate MUST publish from its release branch, `release/<version>`, and no candidate publishes from `main`.
provisions.rationale: A consumer validates a candidate before the final release reaches `main`, so the candidate must hold the release branch's commit and nothing newer on `main`. Publishing from the branch means the tested packages are the packages the release will publish, and the release's final tag still comes from `main`. Proposed by [decision/0059-publish-candidates-from-release-branches](decision/0059-publish-candidates-from-release-branches).

provisions.heading: Record the Reasoning Behind Each Release
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `RECORD_SCHEMA`, `RECORD_ID_MISMATCH`, `RECORD_SOURCE`, `RECORD_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE`, or `RECORD_DECISION_UNCITED` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A maintainer MUST keep the research and decisions behind each release as records under `docs/intent/`.
provisions.rationale: Provisions state obligations without the questions, sources, or conclusions behind them. Without that reasoning on record, a later change cannot tell why a rule reads as it does. Settled by [decision/0001-keep-release-reasoning-as-records](decision/0001-keep-release-reasoning-as-records) on the evidence in [research/comparable-rationale-practice](research/comparable-rationale-practice).
provisions.example: Claimwick states its five-day reimbursement target in a provision, with the benchmark behind the number in a research record beside it.

provisions.heading: Replace Every Citation on a Rename
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision rename MUST replace every citation of the old identifier in one change.
provisions.rationale: An identifier rename changes the ID line, and no alias covers a missed citation. Every citation the rename misses names a provision that no longer exists, and readers following it find nothing. Replacing all of them in one change keeps the repository resolvable at every commit. A heading reword leaves the identifier unchanged, so it needs no citation changes.
provisions.example: A rename changes the ID line and every citation of it in the same change.

provisions.heading: State the Provision Lifecycle
provisions.evidence: Does every provision sit in exactly one lifecycle state, with no citations to retired identifiers? Check the provisions beside their citations.
provisions.statement: A maintainer MUST keep each provision in exactly one of three states: draft, active, or retired.
provisions.rationale: The three states tell a maintainer what an identifier promises. An active identifier names a rule that holds, with its verification line saying how to check it. A retired identifier names nothing, so a citation to it is a defect rather than a reference. Without the lifecycle, a half-written provision and a removed one look identical to a cited one.
provisions.example: A new provision starts in draft. When its verification line is written, it becomes active. When a richer provision folds its assertion in, it retires.

provisions.heading: Add a Missing Fact to LiteSpec Before the Book Shows It
provisions.evidence: Does every fact the book shows come from LiteSpec? Look at the book beside the model output and the finding codes: each fact is a record field, a computed status, or a check.
provisions.statement: A fact the book needs that LiteSpec does not define MUST become a record field, a computed status, or a check in LiteSpec before the book shows it.
provisions.rationale: Rendering the book is a probe: what it cannot show is a gap in the specification. Closing the gap in LiteSpec gives every project the fact, checked; closing it in the book gives one view an unchecked fact. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence/check-coverage-evidence.md).
provisions.example: The book needs to say that a refusal has no scenario, so LiteSpec gains a check for it, and the book shows that check's findings.

provisions.heading: Block Every Finding That Predicts a Runtime Failure
provisions.evidence: Does every check block when ignoring its finding fails at runtime, and does level R hold only prose quality? Read each finding code's meaning in `FindingCodes.cs` against the runtime-failure test: a refused call, a crash, or a wrong result.
provisions.statement: A check MUST block when ignoring its finding fails at runtime; prose quality only a person can weigh is reported by `litespec model review` at level R and never blocks.
provisions.rationale: A finding nobody must act on teaches its readers to ignore findings. When a finding predicts a refused call, a crash, or a wrong result, moving on ships the failure: a command whose idempotency states no replay ignores its report, and a repeat then fails instead of returning the first result. Blocking the finding holds the run until the record or the code answers what the repeat brings. Level R stays for prose quality no caller meets at runtime, which a person weighs through `litespec model review`.
provisions.example: Claimwick's reimburse-expense command states `replay: refuses` with the state it checks in `recognizedBy`. A command stating no replay is reported and blocks until the replay is stated.

provisions.heading: Cite Reference Data Instead of Literal Values
provisions.evidence: Does any rule statement state a value a reference-data table holds? Check the rule statements beside the reference-data tables.
provisions.statement: A rule SHOULD cite the reference-data table holding a value instead of stating the value in its statement.
provisions.rationale: A value written into prose drifts: each statement holding it needs its own edit when the value changes, and no check sees which statements hold it. One table with dated rows keeps each value once with its source, and the model checks that every cited table exists. Settled by [decision/0098-reference-data-tables](decision/0098-reference-data-tables).
provisions.example: The approval rule cites `reference-data/spending.decision-target` instead of stating five business days.

provisions.heading: Classify Every Specification File
provisions.evidence: a file under the documentation root that is neither a record file, an explanation beside its record file, nor a document, and sits under no declared unstructured path.
provisions.statement: Every file under the consumer documentation root MUST be a record file, an explanation file beside its record file, or a document, or sit under a declared unstructured path.
provisions.rationale: A file the validator leaves unclassified is skipped, and a skipped file looks sound: its errors stay hidden. Requiring every file to be a record file, an explanation, or a document, or to sit under a declared unstructured path, leaves no page unchecked. A directory index that owns no record uses the index style, and a `README.md` with no frontmatter is a document.

provisions.heading: Compute Completion in the Builder
provisions.evidence: Which features read below `verified`, and which children hold each one back? Look at `completion` on each feature in the model.
provisions.statement: The builder MUST compute one completion stage for every requirement, use case, flow, feature and goal, and write it as `completion` with `stage`, `proof`, `heldBy`, `parkedBy` and `counts`, with a parent only as far as its weakest in-scope child, `heldBy` naming at most ten in-scope children at that stage, and `counts` holding `inScope`, `parked` and `total`.
provisions.rationale: Completion is a fact the builder can count from fulfillment, code, and proof, so no record carries a shorthand saying how far it is. One ladder reads the same everywhere: `unfulfilled` when no Behavior record fulfills a record, `specified` when it is fulfilled and no code is found, `coded` when code is found for every in-scope child, and `verified` when every in-scope child is verified with fresh proof. When the model holds no test run, a coded record stays `coded` with proof `unknown`, so proof unknown never reads as a failure. A requirement a waiver parks stays out of the stage and counts as parked: `heldBy` lists only in-scope records holding the stage back, and `parkedBy` lists parked records with the waiver that parks each and its `expiresOn`. The book shows "verified, 12 of 14; 2 parked", with a parked list naming each waiver and expiry. A goal's completion shows delivery only; its outcome reads `not measured` until the goal records `observations`.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, `feature/expense-submission` shows `coded` with proof `unknown` before any test run, held by the one requirement with no fulfiller; after a passing run proves every fulfiller, the same feature shows `verified` with no held-by entries.

provisions.heading: Compute Proof Statuses in the Builder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-unimplemented`, `proves-unreached`, and `refusal-unimplemented` for a use case whose handler, proof, or refusal code is missing, and `proof-invalid` (level S) for a test that both passed and failed within the runs read.
provisions.statement: Coded, verified, tested, exercised, stale, flaky, and reachable MUST come from the builder, never from handwriting.
provisions.rationale: Handwritten state drifts: a record marked coded stays marked after its handler is deleted. Computed state cannot drift, because the builder re-derives it from handlers, routes, scenarios, and test runs on every run. A use case reads coded when a handler, reaction, job, or endpoint marked with it carries it out, verified when every scenario has a passing proof through the public boundary that is not stale, and stale when its run commit is behind HEAD with a changed path outside the record and documentation paths, or when its run commit is unknown. A run records its commit. A requirement reads verified when everything fulfilling it is verified and its measure's check passes. A record reads tested when a passing test that asserts something links to it. A flow step reads exercised when a passing proof of a use case, reaction, or job serves it. A proof reads flaky when its test both passed and failed within the runs read. Nothing above Implementation is computed from code: derivation from code into any other record is forbidden, and code-computed facts live in the book and the model output. Settled by [decision/0017-proof-that-holds](decision/0017-proof-that-holds) on the evidence in [research/lower-layers-practice](research/lower-layers-practice).
provisions.example: A use case reads coded when its handler exists.

provisions.heading: Connect Across Modules Only Through Declared Dependencies
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `link-locality-invalid` for a record under a module that is linked from another module with no declared dependency, module event, or integration event. A queries edge to a public query that lists the consuming module passes, and so does a commands edge to a public command that lists the sending module; a queries edge to a query use case whose `reachedThrough` does not name the consuming module is reported as `query-target-invalid`, and a commands edge to a command use case whose `reachedThrough` does not name the sending module is reported as `command-target-invalid`.
provisions.statement: Within one layer, a record under a module MUST be linked from another module only along a declared module dependency, through a module event, through an integration event, through a queries edge to a public query that lists the consuming module in `reachedThrough`, or through a commands edge to a public command that lists the sending module in `reachedThrough`.
provisions.rationale: A record linked from another module with no declared tie is not local: it belongs at product level. The declared dependency, the module event, or the integration event names the tie, so the seam where a monolith would split stays visible. A queries edge to a public query that lists the consuming module names its own tie: the consuming module's `queries` edge names the query, and the query's `reachedThrough` names the consuming module back. A commands edge to a public command that lists the sending module names its own tie the same way. Links from one layer down to the next may cross modules, because that is how one capability spans modules. This provision is the one rule for links across modules.
provisions.example: A spending rule cited from the finance module with no `dependsOn` tie and no module or integration event between them is reported; the rule moves to product level or the modules declare the tie. Reporting's reimbursement command declares a `queries` edge to spending's read-expense query, which lists `module/reporting` in `reachedThrough`, so the edge passes with no `dependsOn` tie. Reporting's close-period command declares a `commands` edge to spending's close-expenses command, which lists `module/reporting` in `reachedThrough`, so that edge passes the same way.

provisions.heading: Connect Every Behavior Record to Intent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-link-missing` for a use case, reaction, job, notification, or setting with neither `serves` nor `fulfills`, and `use-case-flow-missing` (level G) at large size for a use case that no reaction, job or other use case runs and that serves no flow step.
provisions.statement: A use case, reaction, job, notification, or setting MUST carry `serves`, `fulfills`, or both.
provisions.rationale: A behavior record with no served flow step and no fulfilled requirement answers to nothing above it: no promise explains why it exists. Pointing up with `serves` or `fulfills` ties every behavior to the Intent that asks for it. A use case is background-only when a reaction or job runs it, so `use-case-flow-missing` skips it.

provisions.heading: Declare Cross-Module References in DependsOn
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `module-reference-undeclared` (level G) for an `input`, `output`, or `steps` entry that names another module's record with no declared dependency. A field stating `held: opaque` passes unless the use case also reads or writes the named record or a step cites it.
provisions.statement: An `input`, `output`, or `steps` entry of a use case MUST name a record of another module only when the use case's module lists that module in `dependsOn` or when the entry is an input or output field stating `held: opaque` for an identifier the module stores and passes without loading, querying, or reasoning about the named aggregate.
provisions.rationale: The link checks read a use case's top-level links, but an entry inside `input`, `output`, or `steps` can name another module's record without appearing in any of them. Such a reference is a dependency the record graph does not declare, so the module seam stays invisible to a reader and to a check. Naming the dependency in `dependsOn` states the tie where module ties belong; a module event, an integration event, or a public edge states the crossing when the two modules should not depend on each other. A module that only stores and passes an identifier needs no tie to the owning module: the value arrives through an event, a public query result, or the caller, and the module never follows it into the aggregate. Declaring `dependsOn` for such a carried identifier would tie modules that never call each other and can close a dependency cycle. The field states `held: opaque` to record the carrying, and it still states how the value arrives: an input keeps its `origin`, and a query output group keeps its `reads`. The exemption ends where use begins: a use case that also reads or writes the named aggregate, or whose step cites it, still declares the dependency.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, an input of `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` names `aggregate/reporting.reimbursed-expense` in `identifies`. Module `spending` does not list `module/reporting` in `dependsOn`, so the entry is reported; the modules either declare the tie or the use case reads the value through a public query. When a reporting use case takes the expense identifier its row came from as an input it only stores and passes, the input states `held: opaque` and needs no `dependsOn` tie to spending. When the same use case also reads the expense aggregate or a step cites it, the input is reported like any other cross-module reference.

provisions.heading: Declare One Mark Style
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-style-invalid` (level S) for a mark written in a form its language does not take.
provisions.statement: A project MUST write each C# mark in the one style that `marks` in `.litespec/project.yaml` declares, each TypeScript mark as a typed constant, and each operations mark as a comment.
provisions.rationale: Two styles in one language are two ways to do one job: a reader learns both, a check covers both, and a search for a record finds half its code. The C# style is a project choice made once, so every tool reads it from the project file and refuses the other style within C#. TypeScript and operations files have one form each, so a typed constant beside a C# documentation tag is two languages, not two styles. A code fix converts a mark to the form its language takes.
provisions.example: The Claimwick product declares `"marks": "xml"`, so its submit-expense handler carries a documentation tag naming `use-case/spending.submit-expense`, and an attribute naming the same use case is reported. Its use-case module carries the same identifier as a typed constant, and its deployment file carries its `follows` mark as a comment.

provisions.heading: Declare Size and Stacks
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `size-type-missing` and `record-invalid` for a project missing its declaration or a required type.
provisions.statement: A project MUST declare its size and stacks.
provisions.rationale: Size decides which record types and test projects the checks require, while stacks decide which technology pages and checks apply. Without the declaration, the builder cannot tell a missing record from one the project never needed.
provisions.example: The running Claimwick example declares large with a server shape and two stacks.

provisions.heading: Derive a Computed Fact Instead of Restating It
provisions.evidence: Does every count, census, and membership list name its source or command? Look at the numbers the change adds.
provisions.statement: A specification MUST name the source or the command that produces any count, census, or membership list derived between records.
provisions.rationale: A restated number is right until the next unrelated edit changes the records it counts, and nothing reports when it goes stale. Naming the source or the command gives every reader the current figure instead of the figure from commit day. Derivation between records is allowed: generic refusals derive from `access`, `input`, and the knowledge the use case reads, and computed completion appears in the book and the model output only.
provisions.example:
A chapter states where its numbers come from rather than copying them.

```markdown
The figures below render from the retention schedule at build time.
```

provisions.heading: Explain Each Record Beside Its Record File
provisions.evidence: Does every Markdown file under a record root sit beside its record file or carry frontmatter? Look at the Markdown files beside the record files.
provisions.statement: An explanation file MUST sit beside its record file in the record's own folder, with the same name, and hold plain Markdown with no frontmatter.
provisions.rationale: The shared file name is the link: no field joins the two files, so a rename moves both and nothing else. Plain Markdown with no frontmatter stays readable in any reader and tells every check to read fields from the record file only. The file opens with the record title and uses H2 sections, so each explanation has one shape.
provisions.example: `submit-expense.yaml` explains its Example and Notes in `submit-expense.md` beside it.

provisions.heading: Explain the Book from LiteSpec Definitions
provisions.evidence: Does every book explanation come from a LiteSpec definition? Look at the book's explanations beside the glossary and the record type table.
provisions.statement: Every explanation the book shows MUST come from the glossary definition of the term or from the question its record type answers on this page.
provisions.rationale: The book explains itself so nobody needs a learning curve, and the explanation stays true only when it has one source. An explanation written for the book drifts from the definition the records follow. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence/check-coverage-evidence.md). Settled by [decision/0090-make-the-book-an-explorer](decision/0090-make-the-book-an-explorer): the book states a definition on hover and in the lexicon, and shows no teaching text beside each use.
provisions.example: The book explains a waiver with the glossary definition of Waiver.

provisions.heading: Follow the Authority Order
provisions.evidence: When records conflict, does the decision name the higher record that won? Look at the conflict decisions under `.litespec/intent/decisions/`, in the order this page states.
provisions.statement: A conflict MUST resolve toward the higher authority.
provisions.rationale: Intent records outrank Behavior records: constraint over product, product over requirement, requirement over rule, rule over use case, use case over result, and result over scenario. A use case asking for behavior its rule forbids loses to the rule, and the contradiction is reported and resolved by updating the inconsistent records. Where Intent has spoken, the specification wins over code; where the specification is silent, an agent builds nothing, as the Authority section states. Goals, problems, features, flows, actors, research, and prose carry no authority, so none outranks the ladder. Only an explicit product `excludes` overrides a requirement.

provisions.heading: Generate Record-Determined Code from the Records
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `generated-drift` for each file `litespec generate` writes that is missing or differs from what the records render now.
provisions.statement: Code that the records fully determine MUST come from `litespec generate`, written again in the same change as the record and never typed by hand.
provisions.rationale: A typed copy of a record fact drifts the first time the record changes and the copy does not: a refusal code typed into an exception and into the web, a permission name typed into a policy, an event decision typed into startup code. A generator removes the typing, and the drift check removes the drift. The records stay the one source, and the generated files carry no fact of their own.
provisions.example: The spending refusal codes live in a generated class, with one constant per refusal holding its code. When the receipt rule gains a refusal, the same change runs `litespec generate` and the exceptions read the new constant.

provisions.heading: Give Every Record One Parent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-placement-invalid` (level G) for a record whose required parent is missing.
provisions.statement: Every record except the product MUST have exactly one parent from the Placement Table on this page.
provisions.rationale: A record with no parent has no place in the book, and a record with two parents appears twice. One parent per record places every record exactly once: the container is the parent, so an entry sits under the record file that holds it, a scenario sits under its use case, reaction, or job, and a record file sits under its scope node. A feature requirement sits under its feature in its own folder, and types at product level, including a product-level requirement, sit under the product with no field written. The product is the root of the tree and stands above every record layer, settled by [decision/0091-place-the-product-above-layers](decision/0091-place-the-product-above-layers). Settled by [decision/0002-parent-for-every-record](../intent/decisions/0002-parent-for-every-record/0002-parent-for-every-record.md) on the evidence in [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), [research/intent-hierarchy-evidence](../intent/research/intent-hierarchy-evidence/intent-hierarchy-evidence.md), [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), and [research/established-traceability-practice](../intent/research/established-traceability-practice/established-traceability-practice.md).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `requirement/approval-reminders.receipt-over-threshold` sits under `feature/approval-reminders` in `intent/problems/expenses-wait-weeks/features/approval-reminders/requirements/receipt-over-threshold/`; `use-case/spending.submit-expense` sits beside its aggregate; and `scenario/submit-expense.submitting-with-a-receipt-succeeds` sits in the file of `use-case/spending.submit-expense`.

provisions.heading: Hold Every Record File and Frontmatter Block to the Schema
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for each record file and document frontmatter block that fails the record schema.
provisions.statement: Every record file and every document frontmatter block MUST satisfy the record schema for its declared type.
provisions.rationale: The record schema owns the field list of every record type and page style. A record file is one YAML mapping with its entries in `records`, holding no Markdown and no frontmatter fences. A document frontmatter block is YAML between two lines that hold only `---`, holding only the page style and its common fields. This page states the record types and their homes.
provisions.example:
A use-case record file opens with its identity fields.

```yaml
type: use-case
id: use-case/spending.submit-expense
title: Submit Expense
```

provisions.heading: Hold Module Rules in Rule Folders
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-placement-invalid` for a rule in `module.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A module-level rule MUST live in its own folder under `behavior/modules/<m>/rules/<name>/`, never in `module.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: The module record declares the module; rules are behavior and live with Behavior. A rule written into `module.yaml` hides behavior in a declaration no rule check scans.
provisions.example: A spending rule lives in its own folder under `behavior/modules/spending/rules/`, as `reimbursed-once/reimbursed-once.yaml`; the same rule written into `module.yaml` is reported.

provisions.heading: Implement Each Mapped Behavior Record Behind a Mark
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `aggregate-unimplemented`, `reaction-unimplemented`, `job-unimplemented`, `external-system-unimplemented`, and `use-case-endpoint-missing` (level S) for a record no mark names, where `aggregate-unimplemented` fires only for an entity aggregate, and `use-case-unreached` (level S) for a browser use case no screen calls; a request pipeline handler carrying the use case mark serves as its endpoint and needs no screen call.
provisions.statement: Every entity aggregate, every reaction, job, and external system, and every use case reached through a `browser` or `api` entry point, MUST be named by a mark on the code element the marks table gives it.
provisions.rationale: A mark points up, so a check reading marks alone finds code nobody recorded but misses a record nobody built. Checking each record that the marks table maps to code from the top closes the loop in the other direction: an entity aggregate with no root, a reaction with no event handler, a job with no host, an external system with no port, and a use case people reach with no endpoint. A use case with no screen calling it blocks at level S: the link between a use case and the screens that call it always blocks.
provisions.example: `reaction/spending.send-approver-reminder-on-expense-submitted` has no event handler carrying its mark, so the check reports `reaction-unimplemented` and blocks.

provisions.heading: Keep Code Out of Intent and Behavior Fields
provisions.evidence: Does any Intent or Behavior field copy a value from code? Look at the fields the change fills, beside the implementation.
provisions.statement: A project MUST fill no field on an Intent or Behavior record from code.
provisions.rationale: Code implements Behavior, so a field filled from an implementation restates what already ships instead of stating the promise under review. A fact learned from the world enters Intent as research or a constraint, cited and dated, and a need the upper record layer does not state becomes a backlog item outside the repository. Derivation between records stays allowed.
provisions.example: A positivity guard found in a handler becomes a backlog item for a rule, while the code stays untouched until the rule lands.

provisions.heading: Keep Each Name Unique in Its Record Type
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-key-duplicate` for a name that occurs twice in one record type, and for a use case, reaction or job name that occurs in another of the three types.
provisions.statement: Each name MUST stay unique in its record type.
provisions.rationale: Short identifiers resolve with no lookup table only when each name means one record of its type. Two records of one type with one name collide everywhere the identifier is read, while two records of different types with one name coexist: `actor/owner` and `role/owner` are different records. Folders do not narrow uniqueness within a type. Use case, reaction, and job names share one namespace, so a scenario cites its parent without ambiguity.
provisions.example: Claimwick names one feature `approval-reminders`; a second feature with that name is reported even though the folders differ. An actor named `owner` and a role named `owner` coexist.

provisions.heading: Keep Module Dependencies Free of Cycles
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `module-dependency-invalid` for a module dependency cycle.
provisions.statement: Module dependencies MUST NOT form a cycle.
provisions.rationale: A dependency cycle says each module builds on the other, so neither has a seam to split along. The graph runs over Contracts project references, `queries` edges, `commands` edges, and reactions to another module's facts, beside the `dependsOn` links. A cycle means a concept is split across two modules, and the fix moves the concept into one module, never through a shared identifier. Settled by [decision/0110-module-dependencies-form-a-dag](decision/0110-module-dependencies-form-a-dag).
provisions.example: Spending depends on finance and finance depends on spending, so the cycle is reported naming both modules and the edges that close it.

provisions.heading: Keep Rules and Targets Out of Technical Decisions
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `decision-basis-missing` (level G) for a technical decision whose `basedOn` names nothing, and counts a quality requirement as fulfilled when a technical decision names it in `basedOn`.
provisions.statement: A technical decision MUST leave each rule the product obeys whatever its design to a constraint and each measurable target to a quality requirement, and name the ones it serves in `basedOn`.
provisions.rationale: A technical decision chooses one way among alternatives, and a better alternative may replace it tomorrow. A rule such as keeping personal data in the European Union, or a target such as answering checkout within two seconds, does not change when the library does: overriding it needs a business, legal, or organizational change. Written inside a decision, the rule disappears the day the decision is replaced, and nobody holds it as the promise it is. Kept in Intent, the rule and the target stand as the promises they are, the decision points up to them, and the chain runs unbroken from code through the decision to the constraint or requirement and the goal above it. A decision with no basis blocks at level G, like a product decision that no settled record names. A technical choice among equal options may serve no rule or target yet and still govern the code that follows it, but a product decision that settles no record governs nothing.
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps each receipt for the tax file because `constraint/tax-receipt-retention` requires it, and answers submissions quickly because `requirement/approval-reminders.month-end-submission` sets the target. `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` names the constraint in `basedOn`, and `decision/0004-serve-receipts-behind-one-proxy` names the requirement in `basedOn`; neither the seven years nor the two seconds is written in a decision.

provisions.heading: Keep Shape Rules in the Schema
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a record that breaks a shape rule and `record-key-duplicate` for two entries of one record that share a key, and the parity test `RecordSchemaParityTests` fails when the schema and the model check disagree on a rule both carry.
provisions.statement: Each rule on the shape of one record MUST be written in the record schema, and each rule on the graph between records stays in the model check.
provisions.rationale: An editor validates a record against the schema alone, so a shape rule the schema lacks lets a record pass in the editor and fail in the check. Graph rules, such as reference resolution, ownership, and consistency across records, need every record at once, which a schema cannot read. The schema holds required properties, minimum counts, conditional requirements, and allowed values. A list of objects does not use `uniqueItems`, since that compares whole objects, so the model check reports each key that two entries of one record share. Proposed by [decision/0058-keep-shape-rules-in-the-schema](../intent/decisions/0058-keep-shape-rules-in-the-schema/0058-keep-shape-rules-in-the-schema.md) on the disagreements between the schema and the check.
provisions.example: A Claimwick research record with an empty `sources` list fails the schema in an editor and the model check alike, and a research record that names source name `benchmark-report` twice is reported as `record-key-duplicate`.

provisions.heading: Keep the Whole Specification in the Records
provisions.evidence: Does every explanation section rest on filled backing fields, with no fact beyond the record and the records it cites? Compare each explanation file with its record file.
provisions.statement: Every fact an agent needs to build the product MUST stand in a record field, and no fact MAY stand only in an explanation file.
provisions.rationale: An agent builds from the records, and a check reads only fields. A fact written only in prose reaches neither: the agent builds without it, and no finding notices when it changes. Keeping every fact in a field makes the YAML a complete specification on its own, and leaves the explanation file free to restate and elaborate it for people. Settled by [decision/0095-keep-the-whole-specification-in-the-records](decision/0095-keep-the-whole-specification-in-the-records).
provisions.example: Claimwick's `problem/expenses-wait-weeks` states its failure cases in `failureCases` and the condition that ends the problem in `resolutionCriteria`. Its explanation's Failure Cases section restates those cases and walks through one with the cast.

provisions.heading: Mark Every Check with Its Level
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reader-missing` (level S) for a frontend whose reader is missing or failing, prints the level beside each finding, prints `inspection incomplete: reader for <frontend> missing, <N> findings not blocking` as its last line when any reader was missing with one clause per frontend, and exits with code 3 when no finding blocks but the inspection was incomplete. `litespec model check --release` blocks on `reader-missing` for a claimed layer. `litespec model review` reports the level R findings and exits zero.
provisions.statement: Every check MUST carry one of the levels G, S or R, where `litespec model check` blocks on G findings and on S findings whose reader is qualified, and only `litespec model review` reports R findings, without blocking.
provisions.rationale: The level tells a reader what a finding rests on: G rests on records only, S rests on code read through a stack reader, and R rests on prose quality a person weighs. `litespec model check` prints the level beside each finding, so a reader tells what each finding rests on at a glance. A missing required link is level G.

provisions.heading: Match Each Backend Mark to Its Folder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-folder-drift` (level S) for a handler, endpoint, event handler, job host or aggregate root whose mark names a record outside its module and folder, and `code-placement-drift` (level S) for a code element, test, or folder outside the code folder its record's placement names.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, query-handler, endpoint, reaction, job, aggregate
provisions.statement: A backend handler, endpoint, event handler, job host or aggregate root MUST carry a mark naming a use case, reaction, job, or aggregate in the module and folder it sits in.
provisions.rationale: Copying a handler and forgetting its mark is the most common agent mistake, and the folder already says what the mark should be. A handler that sits in one use-case folder while naming another sends readers and checks to the wrong record. An aggregate method and a technical class carry the mark of the use case that calls them, which may sit in another module, so their folder says nothing about their mark. The frontend mirror already compares each mark with its module; the backend check applies the same comparison to handlers, endpoints, and aggregates.
provisions.example: A handler in `Booking/Holds/HoldRoom/` marked `use-case/booking.release-hold` is reported, because the folder holds `use-case/booking.hold-room`.

provisions.heading: Move Each Identifier with Its Module
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-placement-invalid` for an identifier whose home segment disagrees with its folder.
provisions.statement: A record that moves to another module MUST change the module segment of its identifier and every citation in the same change.
provisions.rationale: The folder decides: an identifier whose home segment disagrees with its folder names a home the record left. Only identifiers whose first segment names a module change with a module move. A rule identifier keeps its home segment, because the segment names the aggregate or module the rule is about rather than the folder that holds it. A move between product and module level changes no identifier, so no citation changes.
provisions.example: Claimwick moves `use-case/spending.submit-expense` from the spending module to the finance module, so the use case becomes `use-case/finance.submit-expense` and every citation changes in the same change.

provisions.heading: Name Book Labels with LiteSpec Terms
provisions.evidence: Does every book label use a LiteSpec term? Look at the book beside the glossary and the Links table: each label is a record type, a field name, a computed state, a glossary term, or a reads-as phrase.
provisions.statement: Every label in the book MUST be a record type, a field name, a computed state, a glossary term, or the reads-as phrase the Links table states for a connection.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec already names every concept once, for people and agents alike. A friendlier synonym in the book, such as promise for requirement, is a second word for one concept: the reader learns it, then meets the real word in the records and the checks, and has to translate. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence/check-coverage-evidence.md).
provisions.example: A use case page heads its results "Results" and its scenarios "Scenarios", never "Endings" and "Examples".

provisions.heading: Name Each Identifier from Its Title
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-title-invalid` for a page record whose identifier name is no word subsequence of its title, or whose record file is named for neither its identifier name nor the fixed file name of its type, and for a flow step whose act is no word subsequence of its title.
provisions.artifact: record:product, record:goal, record:direction, record:problem, record:feature, record:requirement, record:constraint, record:decision, record:research, record:flow, record:step, record:actor, record:role, record:module, record:aggregate, record:use-case, record:reaction, record:job, record:notification, record:reference-data, record:integration-event, record:entry-point, record:screen, record:external-system, record:runbook, record:waiver
provisions.statement: Every page record and every flow step MUST take its name from the words of its title in title order: a page record its identifier name, and so its folder and file names, and a flow step the act in its identifier.
provisions.rationale: Readers browse the folders before they open a record, so the folder name must say what the record says. A retitle that keeps the identifier leaves the folder and file saying the old name while the record says the new one, and no listing shows the gap. Taking the name from the title's words keeps the identifier, the file, and the folder on what the record says. A step lives in its flow's file, so only its act faces its title. Proposed by [decision/0061-name-each-identifier-from-its-title](../intent/decisions/0061-name-each-identifier-from-its-title/0061-name-each-identifier-from-its-title.md).
provisions.example: Claimwick titles a requirement "Nobody Approves Their Own Expense", so the requirement is `requirement/approval.nobody-approves-own-expense` in `nobody-approves-own-expense/nobody-approves-own-expense.yaml`. The name `no-self-approval` holds words the title does not hold, so it is reported. Claimwick titles a step "Submit Expense", so the step is `step/submit-and-reimburse.submit-expense`.

provisions.heading: Name Records in Prose by Their Identifiers
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a backticked identifier that names no written record and for a backticked provision the carried release does not ship.
provisions.statement: Prose in a record field, an explanation file, a document, or the `AGENTS.md` file at the consumer root MUST name every record by its identifier in backticks and every provision by the published identifier the carried release ships.
provisions.rationale: A name in plain words, such as a decision number without its identifier, cannot be resolved: nothing tells whether the record still exists after a rename or a move. The identifier in backticks is the one form every check reads, so a stale name fails the check at the line that names it instead of sending the reader after a record nobody wrote.
provisions.example: A waiver `exitWhen` reads "The gap closes when `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` lands." rather than "The gap closes when Decision 5 lands."

provisions.heading: Name the Field to Use Instead in Schema Errors
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` naming the field to use instead.
provisions.statement: A schema error on a rejected field or a link in the wrong field MUST name the field to use instead.
provisions.rationale: Some fields read naturally but belong elsewhere: `heldBy` on a permission, `required` on an output field, a notification under a step's `carries`. The record schema lists each rejected field with the field to use instead, and the link checks name the field for a misplaced link, so the error moves the author forward instead of leaving them to guess which of the many shapes they broke.
provisions.example: `heldBy` on a permission reports that the permission names its roles in `grantedTo`.

provisions.heading: Name the Lowest Record Each Test Proves
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` and `mark-unknown` (level S) for a test that names no record or a record of a kind a test does not take.
provisions.statement: Every test MUST name in a `proves` mark the lowest record it verifies, from the kinds the marks table on this page lists for a test.
provisions.rationale: A test outside the record tree is either proof of something the specification forgot to state or a test that verifies nothing anyone promised. Naming the lowest record it verifies places each test: a scenario or rule for behavior, a quality requirement for how well the product behaves, a technical decision for a technical choice, an external system or integration event for an agreement with the outside, a provision for a structural rule the code must keep, and a project convention for a standing rule the code must keep. A test that verifies a choice no record states shows a missing record, which is written at the level where the choice lives, as safety-critical standards resolve derived requirements; a test with no record above it is a finding to resolve by writing the missing record or reporting the gap. It is deleted only when a reviewer establishes that the behavior it protects is obsolete, redundant or wrong, and the pull request says so. Proof stays layered: only scenario and rule proofs verify a use case, and a passing test that asserts something links to a quality requirement, a technical decision, an external system, an integration event, or a provision marks that record tested, so "the adapter is right" never reads as "the promise is kept". A background use case is verified through the passing proofs of the use cases it serves. A browser success proof asserts the result sentence or the scenario Then text.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, the submit-expense acceptance test proves `scenario/submit-expense.submitting-with-a-receipt-succeeds`; a load test of month-end submissions proves `requirement/approval-reminders.month-end-submission`; a receipt-rendering test proves `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf`; and the layering test that Domain references no persistence package proves `litespec/core/backend-architecture#point-dependencies-inward`.

provisions.heading: Name What Every Decision Decides
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `decision-decides-missing` for a product decision that no settled record names in `basedOn`.
provisions.statement: Every product decision MUST be named in `basedOn` by at least one record it settles.
provisions.rationale: A decision that no settled record names governs nothing. Every link points from the lower or later record to the higher or earlier one, so the settled record names its decision in `basedOn` instead of the decision naming the record. A technical decision governs the code that follows it instead.

provisions.heading: Organize the Book by the Record Layers
provisions.evidence: Which book headings or groupings are not a record layer, a record type, or a record the identifier names? Look at the book's outline beside this page's record type table.
provisions.statement: The book MUST outline a project by the four record layers, with the governance records beside them, and place each record under the record its folder and links name, or at the top of its own layer when the product parents it.
provisions.rationale: The book is how people read the model, so it shows the model's own hierarchy. A reader who learns Intent, Behavior, Implementation, and Proof in the book reads the same structure in the docs folder, in the model output, and in every other LiteSpec project. An outline of the book's own invention is a second hierarchy to learn, and it drifts from the one the records keep. Settled by [decision/0002-parent-for-every-record](../intent/decisions/0002-parent-for-every-record/0002-parent-for-every-record.md) on the evidence in [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), [research/intent-hierarchy-evidence](../intent/research/intent-hierarchy-evidence/intent-hierarchy-evidence.md), [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), and [research/established-traceability-practice](../intent/research/established-traceability-practice/established-traceability-practice.md).
