Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence/check-coverage-evidence.md). Settled by [decision/0088-serve-the-book-live-and-export-it](decision/0088-serve-the-book-live-and-export-it).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `use-case/spending.submit-expense` sits under Behavior, its module and its aggregate; its results under it; each scenario under the result it shows; and the handler that carries its mark under Implementation.

provisions.heading: Place a Record by Its Content and Link It by Its Reason
provisions.evidence: Does any record sit under a record that holds only part of its content, and does any record type in the Placement Table take a parent whose scope is narrower than its content? Compare each record's folder with the records it cites and the records that serve it.
provisions.statement: A record MUST nest under another record only when its whole content lies within that record, and otherwise sit at the lowest scope node that holds all of its content and name the record it exists for in a link field.
provisions.rationale: A folder states that everything inside it belongs to the record above it. Content is what a record states and what it changes; its links are its reasons, not its content. A record filed under one of several records its content spans claims a scope it does not hold, and a reader looking for every record of its type must search the folder of every possible parent. The reason a record exists can change while its content stays the same, so a link field keeps that change to one line where a folder would move the record. Settled by [decision/0078-place-each-record-by-its-content](decision/0078-place-each-record-by-its-content).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `flow/submit-and-reimburse` carries requirements of both `feature/approval` and `feature/approval-reminders`, so it sits in `intent/flows/` under the product and names its goal in `serves`. A reaction answering another module's integration event sits with the module whose records it changes, and names the event in `triggeredBy`.

provisions.heading: Place Child Records in Typed Folders
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-placement-invalid` for a child record outside its typed folder, and for a module subfolder that names no typed folder.
provisions.statement: A project MUST hold each child record stored as its own file in a folder named for its type in the plural, inside its parent's folder, and each child stored as an entry in its parent's file.
provisions.rationale: A reader who opens a parent folder sees its own files with each kind of child kept apart, without opening each file. One rule for every parent replaces a placement sentence per type and gives every module one layout. A child stored as an entry has no file of its own, so a folder for it would hold nothing. Proposed by [decision/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders](decision/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders).
provisions.example: A feature's requirements sit in `features/approval/requirements/`, and an aggregate's use cases sit in `aggregates/expenses/use-cases/`, while a result stays in its use case file.

provisions.heading: Point Every Book Entry to Its Source
provisions.evidence: Does every book entry link to its file and line? Look at the book's record, code, test, and finding entries.
provisions.statement: Every record, code element, test and finding the book shows MUST link to the file and line it comes from.
provisions.rationale: The book is where a reader notices what to change, and the source is where the change is made. A link to the file and line makes the next step one click, and it shows that every entry comes from a written record or from code, not from the book. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence/check-coverage-evidence.md).
provisions.example: The submit-expense use case page links to `.litespec/behavior/modules/spending/aggregates/expenses/use-cases/submit-expense/submit-expense.yaml` at its first line, and its handler to the handler file at the class.

provisions.heading: Point Every Link Up
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `link-direction-invalid` (level G) for a link from a higher layer to a lower one.
provisions.statement: Every link MUST point from the lower or later record to the higher or earlier one, with no exceptions.
provisions.rationale: A link from a higher layer to a lower one makes the layers depend both ways: an Intent record cannot be written or read before the Behavior records it names. Each permission names the roles that grant it in `grantedTo`, each settled record names its decision in `basedOn`, and each external system names the actor it represents in `represents`, so every record is written before the records above it read it. The reverse views are gathered for `model query` and the book, never stored. `holds` stays: actor and role are both Intent, so it is not a layer down-link.
provisions.example: `permission/request-expense` names `role/employee` in `grantedTo`, and the book gathers the employee role's permissions from the permissions naming it.

provisions.heading: Publish Each Integration Event from One Module
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `event-publisher-invalid` for an integration event with a second publishing module.
provisions.statement: An integration event MUST have exactly one publishing module.
provisions.rationale: An event with two publishers has two writers of one fact: readers cannot tell which module states it. One publishing module gives the fact one home, and every other module reads it through the event. The publishers follow from the records: the use cases whose `raises` holds the domain event the integration event `translates`.
provisions.example: `integration-event/expense-submitted` translates `domain-event/expense.submitted`, which only spending use cases raise, so the spending module publishes it.

provisions.heading: Record Each Screen's Captures from the Gallery
provisions.evidence: Which screens with a route have no capture? Look at `captureState` `route-not-captured` on screen records in the model.
provisions.statement: The builder MUST record each screen's captures from the gallery folders and file-name pattern the project file names, as `captures` with `path`, `theme`, `width` and `capturedOn`, and its `captureState` as `captured`, `route-not-captured` or `no-route`.
provisions.rationale: A reader judging a screen needs to see it, and a capture named by its route, theme, and width is the copy the built screen makes. The route slug names the file the same way everywhere: the leading slash dropped, segments joined with a hyphen, a parameter reduced to its name, and the root route named `home`. A missing gallery folder captures nothing and fails nothing, so a project with no photography yet still builds its model.
provisions.example: The Claimwick web gallery holds `expenses--light--1440.png`, so `screen/expenses.list` at `/expenses` shows that capture at theme `light` and width 1440 with `captureState` `captured`; a screen with no route shows `no-route`.

provisions.heading: Record Each Technical Choice as a Decision
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `decision-unimplemented` (level S) for a technical decision that no code element follows. It reports `decision-kind-missing` (level G) for a technical decision with no `kind`, `decision-scope-invalid` (level S) for a technical decision whose followers all sit in one module and each already carry an `implements` mark, and `decision-home-drift` (level S) for a technical decision kept at a level its followers do not match. The check runs in the CLI only, with no analyzer rule: whether any code follows a decision is known only across every project, and one compilation sees one project.
provisions.statement: A technical choice of one of the six kinds that code follows and no LiteSpec provision makes MUST be a decision under `.litespec/implementation/decisions/` that at least one code element follows.
provisions.rationale: Why a pattern, a library, or a configuration value was chosen is the first thing a maintainer asks before changing it. Written in a comment, the answer drifts and no tool finds it. Written as a decision, it carries its options, what speaks for and against each, and what would reopen it, and every code element shaped by it names it in a `follows` mark. A choice a LiteSpec provision already makes needs no decision, because the provision is the record. The six kinds are provider, package, format, boundary, topology, and replacement, as the [decision records page](../reference/decision-records.md) states: a choice of no kind is not a decision. A choice of no kind states its reason in the class documentation, and the mark on the class names the record the class serves. Technical decisions sit under Implementation because they name technologies and code, which Intent never holds, and they share the numbered sequence of product decisions, so all decisions share one identifier space. Settled by [decision/0040-decisions-only-for-six-kinds-of-choice](decision/0040-decisions-only-for-six-kinds-of-choice).
provisions.example: Claimwick renders each receipt as a PDF file. `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` weighs a PDF library against an HTML-to-PDF browser, chooses the PDF library, and names what reopens the choice: receipts no longer needing a downloadable file. The decision carries `kind: package`. The receipt PDF renderer carries `/// <follows>decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf</follows>`.

provisions.heading: Render Generated Regions from the Model
provisions.evidence: Does any generated region outside an index region render code-computed facts? Look inside the generated fences beside the book and the model output.
provisions.statement: A generated region renders only facts derived from records, and a `decision-index` or `waiver-index` region also renders the computed follower facts its rows name.
provisions.rationale: A generated region sits inside a record page, so everything in it reads with record authority. Facts computed from code, such as coded and verified counts, describe the world rather than the promise, and rendering them beside records would lend them authority they do not hold. The book and the model output carry code-computed facts where readers meet them as computed. An index region is the exception: it lists the records beside it, so each row names the computed followers, concerns, and flags the reader needs to read the list. Settled by [decision/0072-generate-the-links-table-from-the-schema](decision/0072-generate-the-links-table-from-the-schema).

provisions.heading: Report One Shape in Schema Errors
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` naming only the errors of the selected shape, and the full shape list with `--verbose`.
provisions.statement: A schema error on a value matching no allowed shape MUST report only the errors of the one shape its discriminating field selects, falling back to the closest shape by error count, with the full list behind the `--verbose` flag.
provisions.rationale: A record declares its shape in `type`, so listing every shape the value is not wastes the reader's time: the cause sits in one shape's errors, buried under missing-property notes from shapes that never applied. Reporting only the selected shape's errors shows the cause first. The discriminating field is the `type` field, or the field the value carries that only one shape declares. The closest shape by error count is the best guess when neither selects one, and `--verbose` keeps the full list for the case the guess is wrong.
provisions.example: A rule record with a misspelled field reports that field under its rule shape, not under every other shape in the schema.

provisions.heading: Report Unverified Use Cases
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-unverified` (level S) for a use case whose scenarios are not all proved.
provisions.statement: A use case whose scenarios are not all proved MUST be reported as `use-case-unverified`.
provisions.rationale: An unverified use case is a promise with no proof, so the finding blocks until every scenario has a passing proof or a waiver parks the use case. The waiver keeps daily work loose where proof cannot land yet, and the release stays honest because no unverified use case passes the check unparked.
provisions.example: Claimwick adds `use-case/spending.export-expenses` with two scenarios and one passing proof: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-unverified` (level S) for it and exits 1, until a passing proof or a waiver covers it.

provisions.heading: Require Explanation Files on the Layers a Project Names
provisions.evidence: Does every record page carry its explanation file with the required H2 sections in order? Look at the record files beside their explanation files.
provisions.statement: A record page on a layer the project lists in `explanations.layers` MUST carry its explanation file with the required H2 sections.
provisions.rationale: On a complex product, every record needs explaining for people who did not write it. Listing a layer in `explanations.layers` makes the explanation a gate instead of a habit. The layers a project can list are `intent`, `behavior` and `governance`, and every record file on a listed layer carries its explanation file, requirements and waivers included. On a layer the project does not list, the explanation file is optional for every record type, including research and decision records.
provisions.example: Claimwick lists `intent` and `behavior` in `explanations.layers`, so its problem `problem/expenses-wait-weeks` carries `expenses-wait-weeks.md` with the sections Affected Users, Failure Cases, Current Workaround, Cost, Evidence and Resolution Criteria. A problem without that file, or without one of those sections, fails the check. When Claimwick lists `governance`, its waiver `waiver/export-expenses-unimplemented` carries its explanation file with Provision, Reason, Risk and Expiry.

provisions.heading: Resolve Every Page Link
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `link-unknown` for a link that resolves to no file and no written record identifier.
provisions.statement: Every Markdown link outside code in a record field, an explanation file, or a document MUST resolve to an existing file or to a written record identifier.
provisions.rationale: A link that points at a moved file or an unknown identifier reads as navigation and leads nowhere. A link whose target is a record identifier cites that record: link checks resolve it against the model's identifiers, citation checks count it, and the book links it to the record. Prose cites a record by its identifier, never by its file path.
provisions.example: The Claimwick receipt rule is cited as `[the receipt rule](rule/expense.approver-is-not-submitter)`.

provisions.heading: Rewrite Every Link on a Rename
provisions.evidence: `litespec rename` leaves no citation of the old identifier, and `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: An author MUST rename a record identifier with `litespec rename <old> <new>`, which rewrites every link and keeps the record at its level and in its owner's folder unless `--move` names another owner.
provisions.rationale: An identifier rename touches the record file, its explanation file, and every record that points at it. Rewriting every link in the same command leaves no citation pointing at the old name, so the repository stays resolvable at every commit. When the file name follows the identifier, both files move together. A plain rename changes no owner, so a record never changes level by accident, and a move to another owner is an explicit choice. Proposed by [decision/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders](../intent/decisions/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders.md).
provisions.example: `litespec rename use-case/spending.close-run use-case/spending.complete-run` updates the page and every citation together.

provisions.heading: Scaffold Pages and Reserve Identifiers
provisions.evidence: Does every new page carry a reserved identifier? Look for pages created without `litespec new`.
provisions.statement: An author MUST scaffold a new page with `litespec new <type> <id>`, which reserves its identifier.
provisions.rationale: Two agents working in parallel mint the same identifier when each writes a file by hand, and the collision surfaces only at merge time. Scaffolding reserves the identifier before any prose exists, so the second author learns the clash at creation and picks another name. For an article type the command also writes the explanation file, and for a document style it writes the document.
provisions.example: `litespec new reaction spending.send-receipt-reminder-on-expense-submitted` creates the reaction record file with its reserved identifier.

provisions.heading: Serve Every Flow Step
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `step-use-case-missing` for a flow step with no serving use case, reaction, or job, beside `step-screen-missing` for a step a browser or device use case serves that no screen serves, and beside `step-implementation-missing` (level S) for a step whose serving use cases have no implementing code.
provisions.statement: Every flow step MUST have a serving use case, reaction, or job.
provisions.rationale: A step no use case, reaction, or job serves promises a moment the product never builds. Use cases, reactions, and jobs point up with `serves`, so each step id collects the behaviors that carry the actor through it. Three findings cover the three gaps: `step-use-case-missing` names a step no use case, reaction, or job serves, `step-screen-missing` names a step a browser or device use case serves that no screen serves, and `step-implementation-missing` names a step whose serving use cases have no implementing code. Reworded by [decision/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences](decision/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences).

provisions.heading: Show Only Computed Judgments in the Book
provisions.evidence: Does every status, count, order, and finding in the book come from the builder or a check? Look at the book beside the model output.
provisions.statement: Every status, count, order and finding the book shows MUST be one the builder or a check computes.
provisions.rationale: The book is a view of the model, not a second authority. A judgment only the book makes, such as its own idea of what to do next, cannot be checked, cannot fail a build, and cannot be found by an agent reading the model output. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence/check-coverage-evidence.md).
provisions.example: The book orders features by the completion the builder computes.

provisions.heading: Split Record Fields from Explanation
provisions.evidence: Does any explanation file state a fact a check reads, or any page carry field values outside the record file? Compare each explanation file with its record file.
provisions.statement: A fact a check reads MUST live as a field in the record file, the page's only metadata carrier.
provisions.rationale: Two metadata carriers on one page disagree sooner or later: source links, paths, and evidence drift between the record file and the explanation file. One record file keeps every field a check reads in one place: fields are checked and prose is not, so a check-read fact sitting in prose is invisible to its check. The page explanation cites entries by identifier, so entries need no file of their own. A generated region that `model render` writes from the record file is not a second carrier, because no person edits it and `model check` reports any drift from the record. The source-links region of a research or constraint explanation is one such region.
provisions.example: The submit-expense summary lives in the `summary` field of `submit-expense.yaml`, while why the flow reads well lives under Notes in `submit-expense.md`.

provisions.heading: Start Each Explanation File with Its Title
provisions.evidence: Does every explanation file open with its H1 title and section content under H2? Look at the explanation files beside the changed record files.
provisions.statement: An explanation file MUST open with one H1 title and section its content with H2 sections.
provisions.rationale: One shape puts the title and each section in the same place on every explanation. The H1 carries the record title, and each H2 carries one section from the table on this page or a free section; Notes take free `###` headings under their H2.

provisions.heading: State the Common Fields on Every Record
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a record missing a common field.
provisions.statement: Every written record MUST carry its type, identifier, and title.
provisions.rationale: Type, identifier, and title are the fields every join needs. Without them on every record, the builder cannot connect decisions to requirements, scenarios to results, or records to terms, and the model falls apart into loose pages. A record adds `terms` when it uses glossary terms and `records` when it holds entries.

provisions.heading: State What a Reader Needs on the Record and Check Each Copy
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `rule-governs-drift`, `exposure-reference-drift`, `exposure-missing`, `classification-drift` and `data-class-fields-drift` for a stated copy that differs from its source.
provisions.statement: A record MUST state the links and facts a reader needs to read it alone, with every stated fact the model can also derive held by a check that reports a difference.
provisions.rationale: An isolated file reads whole by eye and by tool, without opening the files it links to. The copy stays honest because a check compares it with its source on every run: `governs` against the links naming the rule, `exposure` against the entry points and permissions the use case declares, a field `classification` against its data class, a data class `fields` list against the fields naming the class, and a screen `serves` against the steps its use cases serve. Judgments stay computed and are never typed: completion, coverage, proof status, counts, and censuses. Settled by [decision/0070-keep-one-source-for-each-fact](decision/0070-keep-one-source-for-each-fact).
provisions.example: The Claimwick submit-expense use case states its `exposure` in plain words, and `exposure-reference-drift` reports an entry point it names that `reachedThrough` lacks.

provisions.heading: State What Happens in Every Behavior Statement
provisions.evidence: Does any rule statement, scenario step, result meaning, or result sentence hide its behavior behind a vague word? Look at the statements the change adds.
provisions.statement: A rule statement, scenario step, result meaning, and result sentence SHOULD avoid words that hide behavior.
provisions.rationale: The vague words are handle, handles, handled, process, processes, manage, manages, various, etc., appropriate, appropriately, properly, as needed, and so on: each says that something happens without saying what. A reader cannot check a statement that hides its behavior, so each statement names the act in words a test could assert.
provisions.example: A scenario step reads "The member borrows the copy" rather than "The member handles the copy".

provisions.heading: Take Decision Numbers from One Sequence
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-key-duplicate` for two decisions sharing one number.
provisions.statement: A decision number MUST come from one sequence across every home, with each decision folder named `<four-digit number>-<name>/` holding its record file.
provisions.rationale: Product and technical decisions share one identifier space, so a number identifies one decision wherever it sits. `litespec new decision` takes the next free number, and no two decisions share it. Each decision folder is named `<four-digit number>-<name>/` and holds its record file `<four-digit number>-<name>.yaml`, with `decision/<four-digit number>-<name>` as its identifier. Numbers order decisions by when each choice was proposed, giving every record a short stable name a citation can carry. The number counts as a word, so digits never stand alone in the identifier.
provisions.example: `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` is the fifth decision, whether it sits under Intent or under Implementation.

provisions.heading: Validate a Single Page Before Committing
provisions.evidence: Does the change report show each touched page passing single-page validation before commit?
provisions.statement: An author MUST validate a single page before committing it.
provisions.rationale: Full validation walks the whole repository, which grows slow exactly when many authors commit often. A single-page check reports shape and link errors for the page at hand in seconds, so each commit arrives already sound.
provisions.example: The author validates the touched page, fixes the reported diagnostics, and commits only when the page passes.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record File in Canonical Form
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `format-drift` for a record file whose text differs from its canonical form.
provisions.statement: Every record file MUST match the canonical text the record writer produces for it.
provisions.rationale: One layout for every record keeps diffs small and readers on content: a change shows the moved fact, never reflowed prose or reordered keys. The tool owns the layout, so `litespec model format` rewrites every record file into canonical form and the check reports any file that differs.
provisions.example: A use-case file opens with `type`, `id`, and `title`, holds its own fields in schema order, and closes with `records`.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record in Its Home
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-placement-invalid` for a folder outside the closed set of its layer and level, `record-placement-invalid` for a `modules` folder naming no declared module, and `record-placement-invalid` for a record outside its home.
provisions.statement: A project MUST keep every record in the home its type names.
provisions.rationale: A fixed home tells a reader where to open a record and tells the builder where to read it. A record kept anywhere else misses the checks that scan its home, so it looks sound while nothing validates it. Settled by [decision/0042-record-named-folders](../intent/decisions/0042-record-named-folders/0042-record-named-folders.md), which puts each named record in its own folder beside its explanation.
provisions.example: A decision lives at `.litespec/intent/decisions/0001-receipt-threshold/0001-receipt-threshold.yaml`.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record in Its Record File
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a record file that does not parse or whose top level names no record type or container page style.
provisions.statement: Every record page MUST live in one record file holding one YAML mapping with its entries in `records`.
provisions.rationale: One file per page tells a reader where to open a record and tells the builder where to read it. The mapping holds exactly the fields the schema defines for its type, with entries in `records`, so every record has one shape and the checks read every record the same way. A record kept anywhere else misses the checks that scan its home. Settled by [decision/0020-records-in-yaml](decision/0020-records-in-yaml) on the evidence in [research/record-format-evidence](research/record-format-evidence).
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps `use-case/spending.submit-expense` in `.litespec/behavior/modules/spending/aggregates/expenses/use-cases/submit-expense/submit-expense.yaml`, with its results and scenarios in `records`.

provisions.heading: Write Links on the Record That Points
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a link whose target no record carries.
provisions.statement: A link MUST live as a field on the record it starts from, with an inverse stated only where a reader needs it and held by an agreement check.
provisions.rationale: One writing site keeps a link and its source in one edit: changing the source updates the link in the same change. Links written on the target instead would scatter each relationship across every page it touches. A record states the inverse only when a reader needs it there, and the agreement check holds the copy to its source, as `litespec/core/model#state-what-a-reader-needs-on-the-record-and-check-each-copy` states. The Links table states how each link reads in both directions. Settled by [decision/0002-parent-for-every-record](../intent/decisions/0002-parent-for-every-record/0002-parent-for-every-record.md) on the evidence in [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), [research/intent-hierarchy-evidence](../intent/research/intent-hierarchy-evidence/intent-hierarchy-evidence.md), [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), and [research/established-traceability-practice](../intent/research/established-traceability-practice/established-traceability-practice.md).

provisions.heading: Accept Repeated Delivery
provisions.evidence: Does every event handler keep correct state when the same message arrives twice? Check the handler tests that deliver a message twice.
provisions.statement: An event handler that receives an outbox delivery MUST handle the same message more than once.
provisions.rationale: The target can accept a message while the Worker crashes before recording completion, and the requeued claim then dispatches it again. Delivery is at-least-once, so every event handler handles the same message more than once without corrupting its state.

provisions.heading: Audit Outbox Replay
provisions.evidence: Does every replay record its actor, reason, time, and failure without editing the payload? Check the replay code and its audit records.
provisions.statement: An outbox replay MUST record actor, reason, time, and failure without editing the payload: an audit record when audit is selected, a standalone record otherwise.
provisions.rationale: A replay dispatches a message the system already handled or dead-lettered. The team records who replayed it, why, when, and which failure it addresses. Without that record, a duplicate delivery looks like a dispatcher bug rather than an operator's decision, and no one can reconstruct the choice.

provisions.heading: Avoid Automatic Durable-Bus Adoption
provisions.evidence: Does every dispatcher run on project-owned records, or on a durable bus with a pinned manifest entry and a documented choice? Check the manifest and the dispatch transport.
provisions.statement: Use project-owned Marten records and Worker dispatch unless a manifest-pinned durable package passes a shared-transaction integration test.
provisions.rationale: A durable bus package is adopted only when an integration test proves it commits the message in the same transaction as the business work. Until that evidence exists, project-owned Marten records with Worker dispatch handle delivery without depending on behavior no one verified.

provisions.heading: Classify Message Kinds
provisions.evidence: Does every outbox record name its message kind, with each module and integration event citing its record? Check the record type and the messages staged.
provisions.statement: An outbox record MUST name its message kind as module event, integration event, flow-step command, or provider side effect, with a module event citing its module-event record and an integration event citing its integration-event record.
provisions.rationale: Each kind dispatches through its own owner: a module event in process to its subscribed handlers, an integration event through its transport, a flow-step command through the mediator, and a provider side effect through its integration, so the record names which one it holds. The module event cites its module-event record and the integration event cites its integration-event record, so the staged message traces to the published fact it carries.

provisions.heading: Cover Undispatched Records in the Rollback Runbook
provisions.evidence: Does every rollback runbook cover the records the new writer staged but no one dispatched? Check each rollback runbook record.
provisions.statement: A rollback Runbook MUST include records created by the new writer but not yet dispatched.
provisions.rationale: Rolling back the deployment does not roll back the store. Records the new writer staged but no one dispatched stay behind. The rollback Runbook names how the previous version handles them. Without that plan, they sit undispatched with no owner and no reader.

provisions.heading: Decide Every Domain Event Outcome
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `domain-event-outcome-missing` (level G) for a domain event no reaction or translating event consumes that states no `ignored`, `domain-event-outcome-drift` (level G) for a domain event stating `ignored` that a reaction or translation consumes, and `outbox-decision-drift` (level S) for a code decision contradicting the records and `outbox-decision-missing` (level S) for a domain event type with no outbox decision.
provisions.statement: Each domain event MUST reach exactly one decided outcome in the records: a reaction or a translating module or integration event consumes it, or its record states `ignored: true`, and the code's outbox decision matches that outcome.
provisions.rationale: A staged event with no handler fails every command that raises it at commit time, while an event the code drops although the records consume it silently skips its reaction. Deciding each event once in the records, and matching that decision in code, keeps the staging and the handling one fact.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `domain-event/expense.submitted` is answered by the approver-reminder reaction and translated by the expense-submitted integration event, so it states no `ignored`; `domain-event/expense.approved` states `ignored: true` because nothing answers it. The outbox registration translates the submitted event and ignores the approved event.

provisions.heading: Declare Published Facts as Integration Events
provisions.evidence: Does every delivered integration event have a record carrying action, payload, trust, and, for an outbound event, `translates`? Check each event type beside its record.
provisions.statement: Each integration event the outbox delivers MUST have an integration-event record carrying action, payload, trust and, for an outbound event, the domain event it translates.
provisions.rationale: A published fact without a record leaves readers depending on fields no page states, and a field change breaks them without a diff. The integration-event record states the direction, the payload with its classifications, and the trust readers place in it. The [edges page](../core/edges.md) states the declaration and the record.

provisions.heading: Define Claim Ownership
provisions.evidence: Does every claim take an owner, expiry, and fencing value inside a short transaction? Check the claim code in the outbox store.
provisions.statement: An outbox claim MUST use a short transaction with the lease owner, lease expiry, and fencing value that `litespec/core/jobs#store-execution-leases` defines.
provisions.rationale: Several Workers poll the same store, so each dispatch attempt needs one owner. The lease owner, the lease expiry, and the fencing value name that owner. The short transaction takes the claim without holding locks into the delivery itself.

provisions.heading: Deliver Module Facts in Process Without a Broker
provisions.evidence: Does any delivery between modules of one product leave the process or name a broker? Check the dispatch transports beside the module events.
provisions.statement: Facts between modules of one product MUST travel in process through the outbox, with no broker.
provisions.rationale: A module event is a contract between modules of one product, delivered from the same database that holds the business work. A broker between modules adds transport, operations, and failure modes for a hop that never leaves the process. An integration event still crosses the bounded context through the transport its record names in `through`.

provisions.heading: Deploy Readers Before Writers
provisions.evidence: Does every release plan deploy compatible readers before its additive writers? Check the deployment order in the release runbook.
provisions.statement: A release MUST deploy compatible readers before writers for additive event versions.
provisions.rationale: In a mixed-version rollout, old and new records sit in one store. Deploying compatible readers before the writers that emit new shapes keeps every record dispatchable at each step. The reverse order leaves new records without a reader until the readers catch up.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Claimed Records in Worker
provisions.evidence: Does every Worker loop dispatch a bounded batch and record each outcome? Check the dispatcher's claim and batch code.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST claim pending outbox records, dispatch a bounded batch, and record success or retry information.
provisions.rationale: Dispatch needs time, retries, and network calls that no request transaction can hold. The Worker claims pending records, dispatches a bounded batch, and records each outcome. The request then commits fast while delivery proceeds on its own schedule.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Flow-Step Commands in a New Scope
provisions.evidence: Does every flow-step command dispatch through `ICommandMediator` in a fresh Worker scope, or is inline running a documented choice? Check the dispatcher's flow-step code.
provisions.statement: Dispatch a flow-step command through `ICommandMediator` in a fresh Worker scope.
provisions.rationale: A flow-step command is a full command with validation, authorization, and its own transaction, not a subroutine of the dispatcher. Sending it through `ICommandMediator` in a fresh Worker scope runs the whole application pipeline for it.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Projections Immediately After Commit
provisions.evidence: Is every projection the caller reads dispatched in process after the commit with the processor as fallback? Check each such projection beside the dispatch registration.
provisions.statement: A projection a caller reads when the command returns MUST dispatch in process after the commit, with the outbox processor retrying whatever the immediate dispatch misses.
provisions.rationale: A read-model projection the next screen reads is visible when the command returns, but a dispatch without retry loses the projection on a crash. An immediate in-process dispatch after the commit gives read-your-writes for projections, and the outbox processor stays the fallback, so retry is never given up. The command's outcome never changes on a failed immediate dispatch.

provisions.heading: Document Delivery Guarantees Before Sending
provisions.evidence: Does every durable-delivery specification document its guarantee, downstream boundary, duplicate behavior, retry horizon, and recovery runbook? Check each specification.
provisions.statement: A durable-delivery specification MUST document delivery guarantee, downstream boundary, duplicate behavior, retry horizon, and recovery runbook.
provisions.rationale: Delivery crosses a system boundary, so the team agrees before sending on the guarantee, the boundary, the duplicate behavior, the retry horizon, and the runbook that recovers when delivery fails. Without that agreement, the writer assumes once-only delivery while the target assumes retries, and both discover the mismatch in production. The agreement comes before the first message.

provisions.heading: Emit Excluded Reactions and Jobs After Commit
provisions.evidence: Does every fact raised under an excluded reaction or job publish after the commit succeeds, with no outbox record staged? Check the pipeline's publish step for the use cases those reactions and jobs run.
provisions.statement: The facts raised by the use case a reaction or job the outbox excludes runs MUST be published after that use case's commit succeeds, without staging an outbox record.
provisions.rationale: Without an outbox record, nothing survives a crash between the commit and the publish, so the pipeline publishes the raised facts right after the commit succeeds and accepts the loss. Publishing before the commit would be worse: it would fire for a change the database then rolls back. The reaction or job itself publishes nothing; the pipeline's staging step does.

provisions.heading: Exclude Request-Transaction Dispatch
provisions.evidence: Does any request path dispatch a durable message inside the request transaction? Check the endpoint and command handler paths.
provisions.statement: WebApi MUST NOT dispatch a durable message inside the request transaction.
provisions.rationale: A network call inside the request transaction holds database locks while it waits for the target, and a slow target slows every request behind it. The request commits only to make the message eligible. The Worker performs the delivery later.

provisions.heading: Give Each Handler Its Own Delivery
provisions.evidence: Does every handler receive its own delivery with its own retries and dead letter? Check the outbox delivery records for each handler.
provisions.statement: The outbox MUST deliver an event to each of its handlers as a separate delivery with its own retries and dead letter.
provisions.rationale: One delivery shared by all handlers retries every handler when one fails. Each handler therefore gets its own delivery with its own retries and dead letter. Each of those deliveries still ends in repeat-safe handling, under `litespec/core/outbox#accept-repeated-delivery`.
provisions.example: In the library product, a loan-borrowed event feeds a due-notice handler and a statistics handler. The notice delivery retries on its own schedule while the statistics delivery stays complete.

provisions.heading: Group Outbox Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Does every outbox infrastructure file sit under `Infrastructure/Messaging/Outbox/` or another home named in the documentation? Check the outbox code folders and the project's documentation.
provisions.statement: Keep outbox record, storage, claim, and dispatch infrastructure under `Infrastructure/Messaging/Outbox/`.
provisions.rationale: The outbox record, storage, claim, and dispatch code form one mechanism with one owner. Keeping it under `Infrastructure/Messaging/Outbox/` keeps every persistent dispatch file in one folder instead of scattered across the project.

provisions.heading: Identify Repeated Delivery
provisions.evidence: Does every event handler check the message ID or business key at its Command or side-effect boundary? Check each handler's boundary.
provisions.statement: An event handler that receives an outbox delivery MUST use message ID or a business idempotency key at its Command or side-effect boundary.
provisions.rationale: Handling a repeat means recognizing it: the message ID or a business idempotency key gives the event handler a stable identity to check at its command or side-effect boundary. Without that key, the handler processes the repeat as new work and pays, notifies, or ships twice.

provisions.heading: Isolate the Worker Host
provisions.evidence: Does the outbox Worker host live in its own project, or is the shared hosting a documented choice? Check the solution's projects.
provisions.statement: Keep the outbox Worker host in its own project.
provisions.rationale: The Worker runs as its own process with its own lifetime, scaling, and configuration, apart from the request host. Its own project keeps that independence visible and stops request concerns from leaking into dispatch configuration.

provisions.heading: Keep Provider Mapping with Integration
provisions.evidence: Does every provider mapping live in the integration that owns its side effect, or is shared-path hosting a documented choice? Check the dispatch code and the integration projects.
provisions.statement: Keep Integration Event-to-provider mapping in the integration that owns the side effect.
provisions.rationale: Each provider uses its own transport with its own mapping, retries, and quirks. The integration that owns the side effect owns that mapping, so a provider change touches one integration instead of the shared dispatch path.

provisions.heading: Keep Published Events Available for Read Model Rebuilds
provisions.evidence: Is every module or integration event a read model names kept apart from delivery for as long as a rebuild may need it, with erased fields removed or the key shredded? Check the event log's retention beside the read models that read it.
provisions.statement: A project MUST keep every module or integration event a read model names in `from`, `erasedBy` or `removedBy` apart from the outbox's delivery records for as long as a read model may need rebuilding from it, with erased personal fields removed or the event key shredded.
provisions.rationale: A new read model, or a changed one, fills from the events the owner already published. An outbox that deletes delivered records after a few days leaves a new read model nothing to replay, and every new read model then needs a hand-written backfill from the owner's tables, which is the coupling the read model exists to remove. Keeping the published events in a log apart from delivery lets a projection replay history. The log holds personal fields, so the erasing event a read model names in `erasedBy` also erases the field in the log. A retained event keeps its shape with the erased personal fields removed, or with its key shredded, so no rebuild restores them. The read model keeps an erasure tombstone for the erased key and applies it on rebuild, under `litespec/core/automation#erase-a-read-model-personal-field-with-its-owner`. Settled by [decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model](decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model).
provisions.example: In Claimwick, the reporting module rebuilds its reimbursed-expense read model by replaying the kept expense-reimbursed module events, while the outbox deletes its delivery records after seven days. A retained event for an erased expense replays without the erased personal fields.

provisions.heading: Model Outbox Lifecycle States
provisions.evidence: Does every outbox state have a sealed record under the abstract base with a documented transition? Check the outbox state types and their transitions.
provisions.statement: An outbox record MUST model its lifecycle as an abstract state base with one sealed record for each of pending, processing, dispatched, and dead-letter.
provisions.rationale: `pending` becomes `processing`, and `processing` becomes `dispatched`, `pending`, or `dead-letter`, while audited replay moves `dead-letter` back to `pending`. Three of the four states carry data the others do not: `processing` holds a lease expiry, `dispatched` holds a dispatch time, and `dead-letter` holds a failure reason and an attempt count. A four-value label forces those onto nullable columns that mean something in one state each. That is the shape `litespec/core/backend-domain#model-every-closed-set-as-a-type-hierarchy` removes everywhere else.
provisions.example: `OutboxState.Processing` carries one unexpired lease before a dispatcher records `OutboxState.Dispatched` or a retry state.

provisions.heading: Preserve Message Identity During Retry
provisions.evidence: Does any retry or replay path mint a new message ID? Check the dispatcher's retry and replay code.
provisions.statement: An outbox dispatcher MUST preserve message ID across retry and replay.
provisions.rationale: The target suppresses a repeat by recognizing its identity. That works only when every retry and replay carries the same message ID. A dispatcher that mints a new ID per attempt turns each retry into a new message the target processes again.

provisions.heading: Protect Active Worker Compatibility
provisions.evidence: Can every active Worker read the type and schema version of each new message the WebApi emits? Check the Worker's readers against those messages.
provisions.statement: New WebApi code MUST emit a message only after every active Worker can read its type and schema version.
provisions.rationale: WebApi writers and Worker dispatchers deploy independently, so a writer can run ahead of the oldest active Worker. When the writer emits a shape that Worker cannot read, those messages dead-letter on arrival even though their shape is valid.

provisions.heading: Publish Backlog Indicators
provisions.evidence: Does the deployment publish all six backlog indicators? Check the metrics the Worker exports.
provisions.statement: An outbox deployment MUST publish pending count, failed count, oldest pending age, attempts, dispatch duration, and success rate.
provisions.rationale: Pending count, failed count, oldest pending age, attempts, dispatch duration, and success rate together show whether delivery keeps up. Growth in the backlog or its age reveals a stall, while duration and success rate reveal a struggling target. Without these indicators, the first sign of failure is a customer asking where their message went.

provisions.heading: Read Records from Every Coexisting Version
provisions.evidence: Does the dispatcher hold a reader for every application version that can coexist? Check the dispatcher's version selection and its tests.
provisions.statement: A deployed dispatcher MUST process records from every application version that can coexist during rollout or rollback.
provisions.rationale: During rollout and rollback, several application versions share one store and write different valid shapes into it. The dispatcher reads from every version that can coexist, or the deployment itself causes delivery failures. Each message record therefore carries its own shape version, and the dispatcher picks a reader from that value. Adding an optional member with a defined absent-value behavior needs no new version. Removing a member, renaming one, narrowing a type, or changing a discriminator needs a new version, and the reader for each version stays until no record carries that version.

provisions.heading: Reduce Polling When the Store Is Unavailable
provisions.evidence: Does every Worker loop back off and rate-limit its logging when the store is unavailable? Check the Worker's poll loop and its outage tests.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST apply bounded backoff and rate-limited logging when its outbox store is unavailable.
provisions.rationale: A Worker that polls a dead store on a tight loop writes an exception per iteration, filling disks and log quotas before anyone reads the first one. Bounded backoff with rate-limited logging keeps the Worker alive and quiet until the store returns.

provisions.heading: Reject Independent Outbox Commits
provisions.evidence: Does any outbox writer use a separate connection or commit? Check each writer source and its path into the business session.
provisions.statement: An outbox writer MUST NOT use another connection or independent commit for required durable delivery.
provisions.rationale: Two commits on two connections can split around a crash: the business change persists while the message rolls back, or the message persists for a change that never happened. Sharing one PostgreSQL database does not make separate transactions atomic, so the message joins the business transaction instead.

provisions.heading: Release Claim Transactions Before Calls
provisions.evidence: Does any claim transaction stay open across a network call? Check the Worker's dispatch path.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST NOT hold an outbox claim transaction open during a network call.
provisions.rationale: A network call to a slow target can last seconds or minutes. Holding the claim transaction open across that call pins database locks and connection slots, starving the Workers behind it. Releasing the claim first lets the database serve other work while the call runs.

provisions.heading: Report Store Outages Separately from Delivery Failures
provisions.evidence: Does every outbox metric use the right instrument type for store availability and claimed-message outcomes? Check the metrics the outbox publishes.
provisions.statement: A dispatcher MUST distinguish an unavailable outbox store from a failed claimed message.
provisions.rationale: A dead outbox store and a failed delivery need different recoveries: the first needs a database restored, the second needs one destination investigated. Each carries its own signal. The store's availability is a gauge the readiness endpoint reads, while a claimed message's outcome is a counter carrying the result, following [the OpenTelemetry metrics specification](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/metrics/). A single error counter cannot tell an operator whether to restore a database or investigate one destination.

provisions.heading: Requeue Expired Claims
provisions.evidence: Does every expired claim return to eligible work? Check the requeue query in the outbox store and its tests.
provisions.statement: An outbox store MUST return expired claims to eligible work.
provisions.rationale: A Worker can die between claiming a record and dispatching it. Returning expired claims to eligible work lets a live Worker pick them up. One crash then delays a message instead of losing it.

provisions.heading: Restrict Completion to Current Lease Owners
provisions.evidence: Does every record update check the current lease and fencing value? Check each update statement in the outbox store.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST update an outbox record only while it owns the matching lease and fencing value.
provisions.rationale: A Worker that lost its lease through a crash, a pause, or an expiry can wake up after another Worker claimed the same record. Checking the lease and fencing value before each update stops the stale Worker from overwriting the current owner's result.

provisions.heading: Restrict Message Retry to Claimed Records
provisions.evidence: Does any retry or poison-handling path act on a record that holds no claim? Check the dispatcher's retry and poison code.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST apply message retry and poison handling only to claimed outbox records.
provisions.rationale: Retry and poison handling act on a claimed message. When the store itself is down, no claim exists and no message waits for delivery. Running retry logic against the outage double-counts attempts and can dead-letter messages whose only fault was an unreachable store.

provisions.heading: Retry Delivery with Bounded Backoff and Jitter
provisions.evidence: Does every retry schedule use a bound, backoff, and jitter? Check the dispatcher's retry code.
provisions.statement: An outbox dispatcher MUST use bounded exponential backoff with jitter.
provisions.rationale: A failing target with ten thousand pending messages meets a retry storm when every message retries at once on a fixed interval. Bounded exponential backoff with jitter spreads those retries over time and caps the total, so the target recovers instead of failing under the load.

provisions.heading: Serialize Durable Messages
provisions.evidence: Does every pending durable message reach a serialized outbox record? Check the outbox writer and its record type.
provisions.statement: An outbox writer MUST serialize each pending durable message into an outbox record.
provisions.rationale: The command scope ends when the request ends. Dispatch happens later, in a Worker that runs after the request ends. Serializing the message into an outbox record gives that Worker everything it needs once the scope is gone.

provisions.heading: Set Delivery Alerts
provisions.evidence: Does every alert threshold sit in a setting record derived from a use-case delivery target? Check the setting records beside each use case.
provisions.statement: An outbox deployment MUST set alert thresholds as setting records from its use-case delivery target.
provisions.rationale: A shipment notice delayed an hour and a receipt delayed a week carry different business consequences. Each use case therefore sets alert thresholds from its own delivery target. Setting records hold those thresholds, so the alert fires when a delay passes what the business accepted.

provisions.heading: Skip the Outbox for Manually Repeatable Work
provisions.evidence: Does any reaction or job whose loss the operators accept still carry outbox records? Check the outbox records and the reactions and jobs they name.
provisions.statement: A project MUST NOT activate outbox for a reaction or job whose loss the operators accept and which they can repeat manually.
provisions.rationale: Outbox storage, dispatch, retries, and replay exist to prevent loss. A reaction or job whose loss the operators accept, and which they can repeat by hand, needs none of that machinery. Its `onFailure` states how failures are handled, and the use case page records that the loss is accepted.

provisions.heading: Stage After-Commit Effects in the Outbox
provisions.evidence: Does every raised domain event and translated module and integration event stage in the transaction of its aggregate changes, through the one global step? Check the pipeline's staging step and the outbox writes beside it.
provisions.statement: A use case MUST stage each domain event its act raises, each module event translating one of them, and each integration event translating one of them, in the outbox in the same transaction as its changes.
provisions.rationale: A raised fact means what follows it runs: staged in the same transaction, the change and its message commit or roll back together. One global pipeline step stages each raised domain event for the reactions of its module, each module event whose record translates it, and each integration event whose record translates it, each built from the domain event alone, as `litespec/core/backend-application#stage-declared-module-and-integration-events-in-the-commit` requires. No user code stages or publishes, so this step is the only code that stages. A message sent from memory instead would be lost on a crash between the commit and the send, and every follow-on act runs from a reaction to a staged fact.

provisions.heading: Stage Messages with Business Work
provisions.evidence: Does every pending durable message stage inside the scoped session of its aggregate changes? Check each command post-handler and its session.
provisions.statement: A command post-handler MUST stage pending durable messages in the same scoped business session as its aggregate changes.
provisions.rationale: The business change and its message commit together: both persist or neither does. Staging the message in the same scoped business session as the aggregate changes puts both under one commit, so a crash can never leave an accepted change without its message or a message without its change.

provisions.heading: Stop Dispatch When the Host Is Not Ready
provisions.evidence: Does every unready host stop dispatching and polling stores that cannot serve requests? Check the readiness check and the Worker's dispatch loop.
provisions.statement: A Worker host exposing readiness MUST gate dispatch and stop polling stores that cannot serve requests.
provisions.rationale: A host that reports unready still serves traffic it cannot finish when its Workers keep polling dead stores. Gating dispatch on readiness stops that polling, so the host fails fast and recovers instead of polling storage that cannot serve requests.

provisions.heading: Stop Retrying Permanent Failures at the Bound
provisions.evidence: Does every permanent failure stop at its retry bound with its investigation and replay data kept? Check the dispatcher's failure classification and its tests.
provisions.statement: An outbox dispatcher MUST classify permanent failures, stop automatic retry at its retry bound, and retain safe investigation and replay data.
provisions.rationale: Some failures never clear on retry: a deleted destination, a rejected payload, or a revoked credential. Retrying those forever wastes resources and hides the real backlog. The dispatcher classifies them, stops at its retry bound, and keeps the evidence an operator needs to investigate and replay safely.

provisions.heading: Store Failure and Completion Evidence
provisions.evidence: Does every outbox record keep its last error summary and completion time? Check the record type and its update code.
provisions.statement: An outbox record MUST retain its last error summary and completion time.
provisions.rationale: When delivery stalls, the operator opens the record first. The last error summary says why the previous attempt failed, and the completion time says which records finished. Without that evidence on the record, each investigation starts from scattered logs instead.

provisions.heading: Store Required Message Fields
provisions.evidence: Does every outbox record carry identity, kind, type, schema version, time, payload, tenant, state, attempt, and next-attempt data? Check the outbox record type.
provisions.statement: An outbox record MUST contain message identity, kind, stable type, schema version, time, payload, tenant, state, attempt, and next-attempt data.
provisions.rationale: Three readers share the record: the dispatcher, the retry logic, and the operator. Identity and type route the message, the schema version picks its reader, time and tenant scope it, and state, attempt, and next-attempt data drive the retry. A field stored nowhere forces one of those readers to guess.

provisions.heading: Version Message Types
provisions.evidence: Does every outbox message carry a stable type name and an explicit schema version? Check each outbox message type.
provisions.statement: An outbox message MUST use a stable type name and explicit schema version.
provisions.rationale: An outbox record outlives the deployment that wrote it, so the dispatcher meets records written by several versions at once. A stable type name with an explicit schema version tells the dispatcher which reader parses each record. Without that pair, one shape change breaks every record written before it.

provisions.heading: Wait for Target Acceptance Before Completing
provisions.evidence: Does any outbox record mark completion before the target accepts the message? Check the Worker's completion code and the target's acceptance response.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST NOT mark an outbox record complete before the target boundary accepts it.
provisions.rationale: Marking a record complete before the target accepts it declares a delivery that never happened. No retry follows, because the record looks done. The Worker therefore waits for the target boundary's acceptance before recording completion.

provisions.heading: Add New Machinery Only for a Current Requirement
provisions.evidence: Does each added package, project, wrapper, process, cache, queue, or pattern cite a current use case, decision, or requirement? Check the added machinery beside the use cases, decisions, and requirements it cites.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST add packages, projects, wrappers, background processes, caches, queues, or distributed patterns only for a current documented requirement, and never for a direction alone.
provisions.rationale: Each package, project, wrapper, background process, cache, queue, or distributed pattern adds maintenance, failure modes, and concepts every later reader learns. A current use case, decision, or requirement justifies that cost by naming the activation criterion. Preference and possible future need justify nothing, so speculative machinery stays out. A direction may justify the shape of a record or a model, such as a field that keeps a later way of growing reachable, but it activates no machinery: that cost waits for the requirement that cites the direction.

provisions.heading: Avoid Generic Boundary Names
provisions.evidence: Does each changed boundary name carry the narrowest accurate business name, with no bare `bus`, `manager`, `helper`, `processor`, or `service`? Check the changed names for bare mechanism words.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST NOT use generic `bus`, `manager`, `helper`, `processor`, or `service` names when a narrower name exists.
provisions.rationale: Names such as `bus`, `manager`, `helper`, `processor`, and `service` say nothing about the business action, so unrelated responsibility collects behind them with every change. The narrower name keeps each boundary to the action it names.
provisions.example: Claimwick's receipt-reminder notifier names its action, while one named only `service` does not.

provisions.heading: Complete Work Before Merging
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` blocks on unreached records, such as `intent-unreached` and `constraint-unreached`, in every run, locally and in the pull-request check alike.
provisions.statement: What merges MUST be complete.
provisions.rationale: A branch may be incomplete, but what merges is complete. A record that must stay unreached past a merge carries a gap waiver with `expiresOn` and `closedBy`, which parks reachability for that record until the waiver expires.
provisions.example: A Claimwick use case with no endpoint stays on its branch until the endpoint lands, or until a gap waiver with `expiresOn` and `closedBy` parks it.

provisions.heading: Compute Completion from Code and Tests
provisions.evidence: Does any record state its own completion? Compare the record fields with the completion the model computes.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST NOT write completion by hand, because the model computes it from code, tests, and passing scenarios.
provisions.rationale: A reader's first question is how much of a thing is coded and verified. Completion typed by hand answers with a report the next commit falsifies. The [model page](model.md) defines what the model computes.
provisions.example: Claimwick's book marks a use case complete when its handler exists and its scenarios pass, with the model deriving that from the runs.

provisions.heading: Compute Nothing Above Implementation from Code
provisions.evidence: Does every record above Implementation state a decided promise rather than restating code? Compare each new record with the code beside it.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST NOT compute a record above Implementation from code.
provisions.rationale: A record computed from code turns what exists into what is promised: drift becomes the plan, and the record restates what the code already does. Records above Implementation state decided promises instead, and code points up to the record it serves through a mark that names that record.

provisions.heading: Confine Atomic Consistency to One Use Case
provisions.evidence: Does every atomic use case rely only on its own writes, with every rule across use cases held by a state guard? Check the consistency field and the rules it cites beside the reactions that follow.
provisions.statement: Atomic consistency MUST cover only the writes of one use case, never an edge to another record.
provisions.rationale: Every edge crosses a commit boundary, so work past it can fail after the caller succeeded. Atomic consistency promises one shared outcome, and that promise holds only inside the one commit a use case owns. A rule that spans two use cases is held by a state guard instead: the later act refuses until the earlier fact arrived.
provisions.example: The library's hold request waits for its copy in an awaiting-copy state, and lending the copy refuses until the hold fact arrives.

provisions.heading: Cover Other Mechanisms with Extensions
provisions.evidence: Does every mechanism outside the favored set have an extension? Check the selected extensions beside the changed records.
provisions.statement: A mechanism outside modules, aggregates, domain events, use cases, reactions, and jobs MUST live in an extension.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec favors one set of mechanisms and states that choice openly instead of claiming neutrality. An extension states how its mechanism composes with the core fields, so a project that needs it selects one place holding the whole contract.

provisions.heading: Derive Records Only from Records
provisions.evidence: Can every derived value be traced to the record that authors it? Trace each derived value to the record it cites.
provisions.statement: A record MUST take each derived value from another record.
provisions.rationale: Derivation between records keeps one authored source behind every value: the source changes once, and each derived read model follows. Generic refusals derive from access, input, and the knowledge the use case reads, and each read model derives from the records it lists, so readers trace every derived value to the record that states it.

provisions.heading: End Every Effect Cycle in a Domain Event
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports no `effect-loop-invalid` finding on the changed records.
provisions.statement: An effect graph MUST NOT hold a cycle except through a domain event with a stated end condition.
provisions.rationale: A cycle without an end condition runs until something outside the records stops it, so no reader can say when the work finishes. Routing each cycle through a domain event with a stated end condition names the loop and its exit in the records the graph checks.

provisions.heading: Follow Intent Where It States the Promise
provisions.evidence: Does the changed code agree with the Intent records it serves? Compare the changed code with the stated promises.
provisions.statement: Behavior and Implementation MUST follow Intent where Intent states the promise.
provisions.rationale: Intent holds the decided promises, and Behavior and code keep one chain from promise to product by following them. Where Intent states the promise, code that disagrees is the defect, and the fix changes the code.

provisions.heading: Keep Git as the Decision Record
provisions.evidence: Did every changed record go through its pull request? Check the pull request behind the change.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST treat a record in the repository as decided, with the pull request that changes it as its review.
provisions.rationale: A record in git is the decision, and the pull request that changes it is its review. A record nobody wants is deleted, while git keeps who changed what and when, so records carry no history of their own.
provisions.example: A Claimwick feature nobody wants is deleted from the repository, and its history stays in git.

provisions.heading: Keep One Authored Source
provisions.evidence: Does every fact on the changed pages trace to one authored source, with every stated copy equal to its source under its check? Check the changed pages against their sources and checks.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST author each fact once as its source and state it elsewhere only under a check that compares the copy with the source.
provisions.rationale: One source behind every fact lands each change in one place: the source changes once, and each stated copy follows under its check. A record repeats a fact from another record only when a reader needs it there, and the check reports a copy that drifts from its source. Judgments stay computed: completion derives from the model, and nobody types it by hand. Settled by [decision/0069-state-each-copy-under-a-check](decision/0069-state-each-copy-under-a-check).

provisions.heading: Keep Tools Small
provisions.evidence: Does every added command, check, generated file, or package have an owner approval and a user? Check the tooling the change adds beside its users.
provisions.statement: A command, check, generated file, or package MUST exist only while the owner approves it and something uses it.
provisions.rationale: Each command, check, generated file, or package adds maintenance, failure modes, and concepts every later reader learns. A tool nothing uses is removed instead of kept beside its replacement. Settled by [decision/0029-delete-the-unwired-language-checker](decision/0029-delete-the-unwired-language-checker), [decision/0031-remove-only-the-timing-variable](decision/0031-remove-only-the-timing-variable), and [decision/0034-measure-mutation-before-gating](decision/0034-measure-mutation-before-gating), and the same rule removes project fields in [decision/0025-remove-fields-nothing-reads](decision/0025-remove-fields-nothing-reads).
provisions.example: A Claimwick check nobody runs goes away with its command.

provisions.heading: Locate Package Versions in the Manifest
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `dependency-version-drift` for a package whose version differs from its manifest pin, and `stack-invalid` for a named stack the manifest does not ship.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST resolve the standards-selected stack versions from `litespec.manifest.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: The manifest is the version authority for the stacks the standards select, so every consumer resolves the same tested combination. A version pinned in prose or remembered by an agent drifts from that authority with the next manifest change. Consumer dependencies still live in package manifests and lockfiles: only the standards-selected stack versions resolve from `litespec.manifest.yaml`.

provisions.heading: Name Boundaries for Their Business Action
provisions.evidence: Does each changed boundary name state its business action? Check the changed boundary names against the actions they guard.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST use business operation names, specific command and query mediators, and business-action external ports at boundaries.
provisions.rationale: Components meet at boundaries, and future readers orient themselves there. Business operation names, specific command and query mediators, and business-action external ports state the purpose at that meeting point, so a newcomer places the interaction without opening either side.

provisions.heading: Prefer Direct Owned Dependencies
provisions.evidence: Does each new abstraction name the boundary that justifies it, or the wrapping convention that permits it? Check the new abstractions beside their boundaries and the wrapping convention.
provisions.statement: Use a selected framework type directly inside the architecture layer that owns it until an architectural boundary exists.
provisions.rationale: Using a selected framework type directly keeps one concept instead of two: the abstraction and what it hides. A project-owned abstraction earns its place for provider replacement, a test boundary, a stable domain concept, or an architecture boundary. Wrapping the framework everywhere else doubles the API the team maintains without isolating any real change.

provisions.heading: Prefer Local Code Until Reuse Is Real
provisions.evidence: Does each new shared unit serve two real consumers under one accurate name, or fall under the sharing convention? Check the new shared units beside their consumers and the sharing convention.
provisions.statement: Keep operation-specific code in its operation folder until two real consumers need the same precise behavior.
provisions.rationale: Operation-specific code kept beside its operation stays easy to change with the operation. Shared code needs a name and a responsibility that stay accurate for both consumers, but the first consumer rarely knows what the second needs. Holding out for two real consumers means the shared unit covers behavior both actually need.

provisions.heading: Prove Enforceable Boundaries Mechanically
provisions.evidence: Does each changed enforceable boundary name a reference, test, or lint rule that proves it? Check the changed boundaries beside their references, tests, and lint rules.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST prove each enforceable boundary mechanically: a reference, visibility, an architecture test, a behavior test, or a lint rule.
provisions.rationale: A boundary stated only in prose holds until the first commit that ignores it. Mechanical proof fails the build or the check the day the boundary breaks. Specifications then explain the decisions that need judgment, while tools guard the constraints that do not. Enforceable boundaries include project and package references, compiler visibility, permission guards, store constraints, and lint rules.
provisions.example: A project-reference test proves Claimwick's Domain has no Infrastructure reference.

provisions.heading: Record Stricter Edge Rules as Conventions
provisions.evidence: Does every stricter edge rule have a cited convention? Check the project conventions beside the changed records.
provisions.statement: A project that keeps a stricter edge rule MUST record it as a cited convention.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec checks declared edges and leaves stricter taste to each project. A stricter rule recorded as a cited convention stays visible and checkable beside the records it constrains, instead of surviving as habit in a few heads.

provisions.heading: Share No Transaction Across an Edge
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an effect entry that names `sharesTransaction` or a use case that `runs` another use case; `dotnet build` reports `LS2021` for a command or event mediator held outside an endpoint, event handler, or job, and `LS2022` for an event published by user code.
provisions.statement: An edge between records MUST NOT share a transaction, so each use case commits only its own writes.
provisions.rationale: An edge that shares its caller's transaction makes two use cases one unit of work: the called use case depends on a commit it does not own, a failure in either rolls back both, and neither use-case record says what it commits anymore. Running every follow-on act from a reaction to the fact the first act raised gives each use case its own commit, its own failure handling, and its own record.
