The schema offers no field for transaction sharing, so a record cannot declare a shared transaction. Settled by [decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers](decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers).
provisions.example: Claimwick's reimbursement commits the expense and raises its reimbursed fact, and a reaction in the reporting module answers the published fact in its own transaction.

provisions.heading: State the Strength of Every Provision
provisions.evidence: Does every added provision state its strength and scope? Check the provisions the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every provision MUST state whether it is required, a default, or advisory, and where it applies.
provisions.rationale: Strength words work only when each one means exactly one thing. With the strength stated, an agent tells binding from advisory without a check existing, and a check stays an aid where one is cheap and sure, never the condition for a provision to exist.

provisions.heading: Take Every Name from the Intent Above It
provisions.evidence: Does every act carry the name the record above it states in its use case, method, event, permission, route, and screen label? Compare the names of one act across its record, its handler, its endpoint, and its screen.
provisions.statement: Every layer below a record MUST carry the name that record gives an act, a name chosen for what the act does in the business.
provisions.rationale: A name states what happens, so the right name comes from asking what the act really does, including how it can end. The record that states the act decides the name, and the use case, the aggregate method, the event, the permission, the route, and the screen label repeat it. A check that reports two names for one act reports drift, not the answer: the fix brings every layer to the name the intent states, and the intent changes first when its own word is wrong. A rename that only clears the check finding leaves one act with two names, as does a name kept in one layer while the others move. Settled by [decision/0026-one-name-for-each-concept](decision/0026-one-name-for-each-concept).
provisions.example: In Claimwick, finance staff send an approved expense's payout to the bank, and the bank can refuse it when the company account cannot cover it. The act is a submission, not a payment, so the use case is `submit-payout`, the method `SubmitPayout`, the event `PayoutSubmitted`, the permission `submit-payout`, and the screen button reads "Submit payout". A later command records whether the bank paid or refused.

provisions.heading: Treat Code Beyond Silent Intent as Evidence for an Owner Question
provisions.evidence: Does every piece of working code outside Intent have an owner question carrying it? Check the owner questions beside the uncovered code.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST treat working code that Intent does not cover as evidence for a question to the owner, not as a defect to delete and not as a source to copy into Intent.
provisions.rationale: When Intent is silent and working code exists, a decision went unrecorded. Deleting the code destroys behavior users rely on, and copying it quietly into Intent turns code into a promise nobody stated. A question carries the behavior to the owner with the code as evidence, and the answer lands in Intent first.
provisions.example: A positivity guard in Claimwick's submit-expense handler that no rule states becomes an owner question citing the guard, while the code stays until the answer lands in Intent.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record About the Software
provisions.evidence: Does every new record state the software rather than company business? Compare each new record with the code, results, tests, or infrastructure it translates into.
provisions.statement: Every record MUST state behavior the application performs, data it holds, a refusal it raises at runtime, infrastructure it runs on, or a limit it enforces.
provisions.rationale: A goal, problem, feature, research record, or constraint qualifies when it translates into code, results, tests, or infrastructure. Running the company stays out: it enters only as a constraint or as dated research.
provisions.example: A Claimwick goal that translates into payout code and tests qualifies, while a sales target does not.

provisions.heading: Accept Every Retained Personal Data Class in Intent
provisions.evidence: Does every pseudonymized, retained, or exempt personal or sensitive class name its accepting requirement or decision? Check `basedOn` on each data class.
provisions.statement: Each personal or sensitive data class kept with `pseudonymize`, `retain`, or `exempt` MUST name the Intent requirements or decisions accepting it in `basedOn`.
provisions.rationale: Keeping personal data past erasure is a business choice, not a technical default: the statute or the business accepts it, with the reason on record. Pseudonymized data stays personal data, so it needs the same acceptance as retained data. Naming the accepting requirements or decisions in `basedOn` keeps the choice reviewable where the promise lives.

provisions.heading: Classify Every Aggregate Data Field
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `classification-drift` for a field whose `classification` differs from its data class.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate MUST list its data fields with their meaning, classification, and data class in `data`.
provisions.rationale: Without a classification, personal facts sit beside public ones with nothing marking which is which, and every handler guesses. A meaning with a classification of public, internal, personal, or sensitive tells every later reader how each field is handled, and the data class ties the field to its erasure position and its retention. The classification of a field matches its data class, and the fields live in `data` on the aggregate record file.

provisions.heading: Complete the Subject Export Before Erasure
provisions.evidence: Does every export-first class complete its export before an erasure run? Check the run evidence beside each class.
provisions.statement: A data class with `exportFirst` MUST complete the subject export before its erasure runs.
provisions.rationale: Erasure destroys the only copy of data the subject may still want: identity documents, message history, and purchase records. Completing the export first gives the subject that data while it still exists, so erasure never destroys what the subject asked to keep elsewhere.
provisions.example: Claimwick makes finance download the tax-relevant data before a shredder runs, and refuses to shred when anything changed after that download.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Data Class with Its Erasure Position
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `erasure-undeclared` for a personal or sensitive field with no declared position, `retention-enforcement-missing` for a class nothing enforces, and `data-class-fields-drift` for a data class `fields` list differing from the fields naming the class.
provisions.statement: Each data class MUST declare its classification, its fields, its purpose, its erasure position, its basis, its retention period with the date it counts from, and the enforcement that carries it out.
provisions.rationale: Erasure declared per field drifts: one field keeps a new position while another field in the same class keeps the old one. Declaring the position once per class, with per-field exceptions beside it, keeps one decision in one place. The position is `erase`, `pseudonymize`, `anonymize`, `retain`, `exempt`, `tombstone`, `discard`, `cascade-only`, or `transferred`. The `basis` names the constraint, requirement, and decision identifiers behind the retention; the period is an ISO 8601 duration or `{ "mode": "none", "reason": "..." }` with its start in `periodStartsAt`; the enforcement names the `job/` or `use-case/` identifiers carrying out the erasure. A pseudonymized class stays personal with its basis, and an anonymized class can no longer identify anyone. The `erasure-undeclared` check reports a personal or sensitive field with no declared position, and `retention-enforcement-missing` reports a class nothing enforces.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, the submitter-contact class declares `personal`, `pseudonymize`, its purpose, and its accepting requirement, while the expense-ledger class declares `internal`, `retain`, a statutory seven years from the financial year end, and the finance expiry job.

provisions.heading: Discard Rows That Leave No Trace
provisions.evidence: Does any `onErasure` entry keep a marker where no marker duty exists? Check the entries on the aggregate pages.
provisions.statement: A data class with no duty to keep a marker MUST use `onErasure: discard`.
provisions.rationale: A tombstone is still a row: it takes storage, appears in counts, and invites readers to treat a gone subject as present. Where no reference and no audit needs the marker, deleting the row outright leaves nothing behind.
provisions.example: Lago discards a customer: the profile is hidden and its relations end, while finalized invoices and credit notes stay as the ledger.

provisions.heading: Enforce a Data Class Through Its Aggregate
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `enforcement-job-unreached` (level G) for a data class whose `enforcedBy` names a job that runs or sends no use case writing the aggregate holding the class.
provisions.statement: When a data class names a job in `enforcedBy`, that job MUST run or send a use case writing the aggregate holding the data class.
provisions.rationale: An enforcement job that never reaches the aggregate leaves the retention promise unkept: the class states a period and an erasure position, but no command in the job's run path touches the rows the period covers. Following the job's `runs` and `commands` effects to the use cases they send and those use cases' `writes` shows whether the job can erase the class it claims to enforce. A job writing a different aggregate enforces that aggregate's data, not this one. An enforcement use case needs no job, because its `writes` states the aggregate directly.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense-ledger data class names the finance expiry job. That job runs the erase-expired-expenses command, whose `writes` names `aggregate/spending.expense`, so the job reaches the class it enforces. A job running only the session cleanup command would be reported.

provisions.heading: Keep a Tombstone Where Deletion Stays Visible
provisions.evidence: Does every class referenced after erasure carry a tombstone marker with its kept fields? Check the marker entries on the aggregate pages.
provisions.statement: A data class whose rows outlive erasure as references MUST use `onErasure: tombstone` with the fields its marker keeps.
provisions.rationale: Some rows stay referenced after they are gone: remote servers hold copies, audit trails cite row ids, and support tools link to deleted accounts. Erasing the row breaks those references, while keeping it breaks the erasure duty. A tombstone keeps the row id and the erasure date and drops every other field, so references resolve to a marker that says the subject is gone.
provisions.example: ZITADEL deletes a user by moving it to a terminal state and deleting its read-model rows while the events stay for audit, and Sentry writes a tombstone for a discarded issue so that later events for it are dropped at intake instead of stored again.

provisions.heading: Keep Tombstone Fields Minimal
provisions.evidence: Does every tombstone entry keep only the row id and the erasure date, unless the project lists wider fields with their rules? Check the entries beside the project listing.
provisions.statement: A tombstone keeps the row id and the erasure date, and no other field.
provisions.rationale: Every field on a tombstone is data kept past erasure. The row id and the date satisfy references and audits; anything wider needs its own rule.

provisions.heading: Move Data to Its Next Controller Instead of Erasing
provisions.evidence: Does every handed-over class entry name its receiver and handover record? Check the entries on the aggregate pages.
provisions.statement: A data class handed to another controller MUST use `onErasure: transferred` with the receiver and the handover record.
provisions.rationale: Custody does not always end in erasure: a branch closes and a successor takes its readers, a company is acquired, or a contract moves to a new processor. The data survives under a new controller, so the record names the receiver and the handover both sides signed instead of a deletion that never happened.
provisions.example: A library support tool sends a loan summary and the reader message to a hosted AI model to draft a reply; the position names the model provider, its region and its retention, and the product stores none of it.

provisions.heading: Pause Deletion While a Hold Stands
provisions.evidence: Does every data class under audit, objection, or dispute carry its hold with its reason and start date, with deletion paused until the hold lifts? Check `retentionHolds` on each data class beside the enforcement runs.
provisions.statement: A data class MUST pause deletion while a retention hold stands, with each hold's reason and the date the hold starts on record.
provisions.rationale: A tax audit, an objection, or a dispute stops deletion: a product that deletes records during an audit breaks the law even though it followed its retention period exactly. The hold states its reason with the date it starts in `heldOn`, and deletion resumes only when the hold lifts with its date in `liftedOn`. The enforcement named in `enforcedBy` skips held rows, so the hold pauses every erasure path of the class. Settled by [decision/0100-retention-holds-and-rounded-starts](decision/0100-retention-holds-and-rounded-starts).
provisions.example: Claimwick's finance team places a hold on the expense ledger while the tax office audits the year, and the expiry job leaves held rows until the hold lifts.

provisions.heading: Purge Erased Data from Restored Backups
provisions.evidence: Does every restore runbook name its sweep job? Check the restore runbooks.
provisions.statement: A restore runbook MUST name the sweep job that re-applies erasure after the restore.
provisions.rationale: A backup holds data as it was, including rows erased since. Restoring it brings back rows the product promised to erase. The sweep job re-applies every erasure decided before the restore, so the restore brings the system back without bringing the erased data back with it.
provisions.example: The database restore runbook names `job/privacy.sweep-restored-erasure`, which runs before traffic returns and deletes every row erased since the backup.

provisions.heading: Record Which Duty Wins Each Conflict
provisions.evidence: Does every data class `exceptions` entry name its winning duty with its basis? Check the `exceptions` on each data class.
provisions.statement: Each retention conflict MUST name the winning duty and its basis in the data class `exceptions`.
provisions.rationale: Keeping for audit and erasing for the subject collide on the same row: the invoice the statute keeps sits beside the name the subject erases. Without a recorded winner, each implementer picks one. Naming the winning duty with its basis in the data class `exceptions` keeps one decision where every reader finds it.
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps the expense ledger for seven years under tax law while erasing the submitter contact. ZITADEL keeps its audit events while erasing the user they describe, under the same rule.

provisions.heading: Remove Child Rows Through Their Parent Only
provisions.evidence: Does every child class entry carry cascade-only with its parent class, with parent erasure tests that clear the children? Check the entries and tests beside each child class.
provisions.statement: A data class erased only as a cascade from a parent erasure MUST use `onErasure: cascade-only` with the parent it follows.
provisions.rationale: Some rows have no subject of their own: line items belong to an invoice, receipt files belong to an expense, and usage rows belong to a customer. A direct erasure request names the parent, never the child, so the child follows the parent erasure and refuses a request addressed to itself.
provisions.example: Cal.com deletes a user by removing the account and letting the database cascade remove the rows that hang off it, with no retention schedule. A product following this rule declares cascade-only and names the cascade path.

provisions.heading: Require a Fresh Export After Changes
provisions.evidence: Does every erasure run after mid-window edits wait for a fresh export completed first? Check the run evidence beside each erasure.
provisions.statement: Erasure under `unchangedSinceExport` MUST stop and ask for a fresh export when the data changed since the last export.
provisions.rationale: An export taken last month does not cover rows written yesterday. Erasing on that stale copy destroys rows the subject never received. Stopping for a fresh export keeps the export-first promise true at the moment of erasure.
provisions.example: A reader who corrected their address after exporting it gets a fresh export first, and the erasure waits for it.

provisions.heading: Round an Event Start to a Calendar End
provisions.evidence: Does every retention period counted from a rounded event name its event and rounding? Check `periodStartsAt` on each data class.
provisions.statement: A retention period that rounds an event start up to a calendar end MUST name its event and its rounding in `periodStartsAt`.
provisions.rationale: The law starts counting when a record stops being current: an asset invoice when the asset leaves, a lease when it ends. The start then rounds up to the end of the year, so every record of one year shares one expiry. Naming the event with its rounding states both halves: the event that starts the count and the calendar end it rounds to. A start naming only the event expires each record on its own date. Settled by [decision/0100-retention-holds-and-rounded-starts](decision/0100-retention-holds-and-rounded-starts).
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps a receipt seven years from the end of the year its expense was reimbursed: `periodStartsAt` names `domain-event/expense.reimbursed` with `rounding: financial-year-end`.

provisions.heading: Route Every External Erasure Through an Operation or Event
provisions.evidence: Does every external system declare its erasure call, forwarding event, or reason mode with acceptance? Check the external systems beside their erasure routes.
provisions.statement: Each external system MUST declare its erasure as `{ "mode": "call", "operation": "external-system/<name>#<operation>" }`, `{ "mode": "event", "event": "integration-event/<name>" }`, or `{ "mode": "unsupported", "reason": "..." }`, `{ "mode": "manual", "reason": "..." }`, or `{ "mode": "not-applicable", "reason": "..." }`, each with its acceptance.
provisions.rationale: Personal data forwarded to a processor without an erasure route stays there past erasure: the product erases its copy while the processor keeps its copy. Declaring the call operation, the forwarding integration event, or one of the three reason modes with its reason and its Intent acceptance states the route beside the system.

provisions.heading: Run One Sweep Job per Data Class
provisions.evidence: Does every sweep job page cover one data class, unless the project names the classes each job covers? Check each sweep job page beside the project naming.
provisions.statement: Each sweep job covers one data class.
provisions.rationale: One sweep per class keeps a failure small: a broken sweep delays one class while the others complete. A shared sweep is one failure away from resurrecting every class at once.

provisions.heading: Scope Erasure to What the Subject Requested
provisions.evidence: Does every erasure use case cite the request it answers and touch only the data in it? Check the erasure use cases beside their requests.
provisions.statement: Erasure that answers a subject request MUST use `reach: requested` and touch only the data the request names.
provisions.rationale: A subject who asks to delete one order does not ask to delete the account, and a subject who asks to delete the account names everything. The requested reach ties the erasure to the request it answers, so a narrow request cannot widen into a broad deletion and a broad request cannot stop at one row.
provisions.example: A request naming one hold erases that hold and leaves the reader's other loans untouched.

provisions.heading: State the Erasure Sentence in Intent
provisions.evidence: Does every Intent requirement carry the confirmation sentence before the release that shows it? Check the requirement beside the release.
provisions.statement: The literal sentence the subject reads about an erasure MUST stand in Intent before the erasure ships.
provisions.rationale: The sentence on the confirmation screen is the promise: what goes, what stays, and for how long. Only the product team decides what the product promises, so Behavior cannot word it. Stating it in Intent puts the exact sentence readers see beside the requirement it fulfills.
provisions.example: Mastodon shows on its account deletion form that content other servers have cached may persist, next to the promise that the account and its posts are removed; that sentence is the user-facing copy for a requested reach.

provisions.heading: Apply Release Access Controls
provisions.evidence: Does every restricted release path carry authentication and authorization? Check the guards on each restricted path.
provisions.statement: A release with restricted access MUST provide authentication and authorization.
provisions.rationale: Restricted behavior without authentication accepts callers nobody identified, and without authorization it accepts actions nobody permitted. Both decisions call for a trusted identity and a declared permission before the behavior ships.

provisions.heading: Check Intent and Behavior Changes with the Book
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` exits zero when it reports no G finding, such as `record-invalid`, and the inspection was complete.
provisions.statement: An Intent or Behavior change MUST pass the G checks with the book.
provisions.rationale: G checks read records only: shape, references, links, reachability, coverage, and the Behavior rules the check list names. Without them, a renamed record or a moved file silently breaks the references other pages rely on, and the book renders a graph that no longer holds. `litespec model check --since <ref>` blocks only on findings about records and code changed since `<ref>` and reports the rest, so an adopting project clears new findings first.

provisions.heading: Identify Immutable Release Artifacts
provisions.evidence: Does every release record name its source commit and artifact reference? Check the record header beside each artifact.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST name its source commit and its immutable artifact reference.
provisions.rationale: Without both references, evidence from one build can stand in for another, and nobody can tell which build a record proves. The source commit names the verified input and the artifact reference names the deployed output, which binds the record to one build.

provisions.heading: Keep Generated Contracts Stable
provisions.evidence: Does any contract diff hold timestamps, machine paths, or unstable order? Check the generated diff beside each contract.
provisions.statement: A generated application contract MUST be stable and exclude timestamps, machine paths, and nondeterministic ordering.
provisions.rationale: Timestamps, machine paths, and unstable ordering make every regeneration look like a behavior change. Deterministic output keeps contract diffs reviewable, so a reviewer sees only the changes that matter.

provisions.heading: Keep Release Records Non-Authoritative
provisions.evidence: Does any release record restate a specification or copy a scenario? Check the record against the linked specifications.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST NOT restate a specification or copy a scenario.
provisions.rationale: Specifications own behavior and scenarios. A release record that restates them becomes a second copy, and the copies drift until nobody knows which one holds. Linking outward keeps one home for each fact.

provisions.heading: List Included Release Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every record list each included flow, use case, and extension? Check the behavior list on each release record.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST list included flows, use cases, and selected applicable extensions.
provisions.rationale: Operators and reviewers need to know what an artifact contains and, by omission, what it does not. Listing the flows, use cases, and extensions states the behavior boundary exactly.

provisions.heading: Qualify Each Stack Reader with Fixtures
provisions.evidence: Does every gating S reader show passing fixture runs? Check the fixture results beside the stack reader.
provisions.statement: A stack reader MUST pass its known good and known bad fixtures before it gates with S checks.
provisions.rationale: An unqualified reader blocks on noise or passes on silence, and each mistake trains the team to ignore its findings. Passing a known good tree and reporting each planted defect in a known bad tree proves the reader sees what it claims before it blocks any change.
provisions.example: The .NET reader passes the clean tree and reports the planted undeclared write before its S findings block.

provisions.heading: Record the Release Artifact
provisions.evidence: Does every release show one record naming its immutable artifact? Check the release records beside each artifact.
provisions.statement: A release MUST create one release record for its immutable artifact.
provisions.rationale: Evidence scattered across builds and reports leaves no one place that says what one artifact proved. One release record per immutable artifact binds every result to the exact output it proves, so each artifact carries its own evidence.

provisions.heading: Regenerate Application Contracts
provisions.evidence: Does any committed contract differ from a fresh generation? Check the contract diff beside the source change.
provisions.statement: A source change MUST regenerate OpenAPI and frontend API types when it changes their source contract.
provisions.rationale: OpenAPI and frontend API types derive from a source contract, and clients build against the committed copies. A source change that leaves those copies stale ships clients built against a contract the server no longer honors.

provisions.heading: Report Verification Exactly
provisions.evidence: Does every completion report name its commands, outcomes, scope, omissions, differences, limits, and covered use cases? Check the report beside the change.
provisions.statement: A completion report MUST name exact commands, outcomes, evidence scope, skipped checks, generated differences, scope limits, and covered use cases.
provisions.rationale: A vague report lets unrun checks hide among completed ones. Naming exact commands, outcomes, scope, omissions, and limits tells a reviewer precisely what the evidence covers and what it does not.

provisions.heading: Resolve Release Blockers
provisions.evidence: Does any release depend on an expired waiver or an external claim without excluding the behavior? Check the waivers and claims beside the owning records.
provisions.statement: A release MUST settle every expired waiver and every external claim it depends on, or exclude the affected behavior from every owning record.
provisions.rationale: An expired waiver is a promise past its date, and an unverified external claim behind released behavior is a promise with unsettled terms: a provider fact, a law text, or a term nobody rechecked. Settling each one, or excluding the affected behavior from every owning record, keeps the Intent and release records agreeing on what shipped. `waiver-expired` reports every expired waiver.

provisions.heading: Run Boundary-Selected Checks
provisions.evidence: Does every change show a passing result for each check its boundaries select? Check the change report against the boundary table.
provisions.statement: A release change MUST run every check selected by its changed backend, frontend, flow, Intent, Behavior, and extension boundaries.
provisions.rationale: Each boundary carries failures the others can't see: frontend checks say nothing about migrations, and backend suites say nothing about rendered screens. Running every check the changed boundaries select keeps each change evidenced where its failure lives. A narrow category that passes alone certifies only part of the change. The release build catches the conditional and optimization-gated breaks a debug build hides; frozen installation, lint, type checking, tests, and the production build each guard one failure class of a frontend; and an affected extension's stated verification is the only evidence written for its surface.

provisions.heading: Run One LiteSpec Build
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `toolchain-drift` when any two of the three name different builds.
provisions.statement: A project MUST run one LiteSpec build at a time: the `LiteSpec.Cli` version the tool manifest pins, the `LiteSpec.Analyzers` version the build references, and the CLI running the checks name the same build.
provisions.rationale: Checks written against one build misread code written against another. An old tool reports findings the current build fixed, and a lagging analyzer never runs its newest rules, so the team fixes findings that do not apply and misses the ones that do. Moving the tool manifest, the analyzer reference, and the running CLI together keeps every finding about the build the code follows.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense product pins `LiteSpec.Cli` 7.0.0 in `.config/dotnet-tools.json`, references `LiteSpec.Analyzers` 7.0.0 from its central package file, and runs the checks with the 7.0.0 CLI.

provisions.heading: State Each Release as a Complete Record
provisions.evidence: Does any release record depend on an earlier record to be judged? Read the record alone beside its links.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST state its complete behavior and evidence without depending on an earlier release record.
provisions.rationale: A release judged from fragments forces the reader to dig through other records to fill the gaps. A complete record lets one reader judge one release from one page, with no upgrade guide filling in.

provisions.heading: Store Release Records Together
provisions.evidence: Does every release record sit under `.litespec/releases/`, or does a recorded release path convention name where it lives? Check the release paths against the convention.
provisions.statement: Keep release records under `.litespec/releases/`.
provisions.rationale: One folder for release records tells a maintainer where to find the evidence for any artifact. A record filed elsewhere looks missing while readers open the folder and find nothing there.
provisions.example: `.litespec/releases/2026-08-21.md` records one immutable artifact and its evidence.

provisions.heading: Verify Connected Flows
provisions.evidence: Does every completed flow show a passing test through the deployed boundary, and every flow change its passing flow tests? Check the flow tests beside each included flow.
provisions.statement: A completed flow MUST connect verified use cases to one observable outcome through a deployed public boundary, proved by its flow tests.
provisions.rationale: Use cases that pass in isolation can still fail together: wiring, permissions, and data cross boundaries the isolated tests never touch. A flow test that runs verified use cases to one observable outcome through the deployed public boundary proves the connected path customers actually take. A flow change alters the connected path, so only a flow test through the deployed public boundary proves it still reaches its outcome; narrower suites keep passing while the flow itself breaks.

provisions.heading: Answer the Constraints Question
provisions.evidence: Does `.litespec/project.yaml` state which outside constraints apply, or record an empty answer? Check the project file.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST state in `.litespec/project.yaml` whether any outside constraint applies to the project.
provisions.rationale: A product can break a law the team never named. An empty answer proves the team asked the question and found no outside rule binding the project. A later reader can then tell a project with no constraints apart from one that never looked.
provisions.example: A clinic booking system records that medical-device regulation does not apply to appointment scheduling.

provisions.heading: Claim Conformance Only When Every Applicable Provision Holds
provisions.evidence: Does the project meet every provision that applies to each layer it claims? Check `layers` in `.litespec/project.yaml`, the waiver records under `.litespec/governance/waivers/`, and the checks that run for those layers.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST meet every provision that applies to each layer it claims in `layers` before claiming conformance to LiteSpec for those layers.
provisions.rationale: A conformance claim tells a reader that the whole claimed part of the contract holds, not only the parts the project chose to follow. A claim of `intent` and `behavior` takes in the provisions about the record model, and a claim of `implementation` or `proof` also takes in the provisions that tie each layer to the records. A [waiver](waivers.md) outranks the provision or findings it covers while it stands, so a project that records each waiver still meets this provision. A waiver past its expiry date reports `waiver-expired` and no longer outranks them. An unrecorded gap in a claimed layer breaks the claim for that layer, and leaves any layer the project does meet untouched.
provisions.example: A consumer claims all four layers with `litespec`, selects the dotnet stack and the caching extension, and claims conformance when every page those selections apply holds and their checks pass, with each waiver recorded. A consumer that claims `intent` and `behavior` claims conformance when the provisions about the record model hold, while its own code layout and tooling stay outside the claim.

provisions.heading: Claim the Record Layers the Project Uses
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a project file without `layers`, with a value other than those the table allows, or with a layer whose parent is not claimed.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST name each record layer it claims in `layers` in `.litespec/project.yaml`, with `litespec` or `own` for Implementation and Proof, leaving layers out only from the bottom.
provisions.rationale: Teams adopt LiteSpec in parts: the record model alone, records with marked code, records with acceptance tests, or all of it, with their own architecture or test practice where they have one. Naming each layer lets every tool check exactly the part the team uses, so a missing test project is not a finding for a team that claims no Proof, and a team that keeps its own code layout still gets its marks checked. Leaving layers out from the bottom keeps every remaining link whole, because each layer points up to the one above it. Settled by [decision/0027-projects-claim-record-layers](decision/0027-projects-claim-record-layers).
provisions.example: The running Claimwick example claims all four layers with `litespec`. A product that marks its code in its own layout and proves no scenarios yet claims `intent`, `behavior`, and `implementation: own`, and `model check` reports no `use-case-unverified` finding for it.

provisions.heading: Declare a Consumer That Has No Backend
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `stack-invalid` for a `client-only` project that names a backend stack.
provisions.statement: A consumer with no server of its own MUST declare the `client-only` shape and record a decision naming the surfaces left without coverage.
provisions.rationale: The shape decides which backend pages still apply. A `client-only` product keeps a domain model, so the backend architecture, domain, and application pages that the manifest lists under `shapes` still apply to it. Persistence, the HTTP API, and API testing have no target without a server, and the decision names those uncovered surfaces. Adding a server only to obtain conformance contradicts `litespec/core/principles#add-new-machinery-only-for-a-current-requirement`, which permits new machinery only for a current documented requirement.
provisions.example: `litespec/quality/ci#run-applicable-gates-on-every-pull-request` already permits skipping a gate whose surface does not exist, so a missing backend gate is a recorded consequence rather than an unexplained absence.

provisions.heading: Keep Every LiteSpec File Under One Folder
provisions.evidence: Does any LiteSpec record, document, explanation file, or generated file sit outside `.litespec/` or at the repository root? Look at the repository tree beside the project's `.litespec/` folder.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST hold every LiteSpec record, document, explanation file, and generated file under one folder, `.litespec/`, at the repository root.
provisions.rationale: When LiteSpec material scatters across the repository, readers and tools hunt the tree for it. One folder with one name in every consumer makes the material identifiable at a glance: a reader, a tool, or an agent finds the whole contract in one place, moves or deletes it without hunting, and keeps it apart from application code, tests, contracts, and `AGENTS.md`, which keep their own homes. Generated output inside it stays covered by its `.gitignore`, so a checkout never mixes committed records with built files. Every path in `.litespec/project.yaml` stays relative to the repository root, so moving the folder never rewrites the paths inside it. A command finds the consumer by walking up from the working folder to the first folder that holds `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.example: Claimwick holds its project file, glossary, cast, and its Intent, Behavior, Implementation, Proof, and Governance folders under `examples/claimwick/.litespec/` (in a real consumer, at its repository root), beside its application code, tests, contracts, and `AGENTS.md`, which keep their own homes. An agent asked to read the contract opens that one folder, instead of collecting a root project file, a documentation tree, a model folder, and a book folder from four places.

provisions.heading: Keep One Bounded Context
provisions.evidence: Does the project keep one business language and one deployment boundary? Check the module pages and `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST keep one business language and deployment boundary.
provisions.rationale: One business language and one deployment boundary keep every module, record, and use case in a single consistent model. Modules organize related language, models, use cases, and code without becoming independent services or bounded contexts. A second language or boundary splits the project into systems the records, links, and checks can no longer hold together.
provisions.example: A publishing product keeps Posts, Authors, and Comments as modules in one context, with one shared language.

provisions.heading: Measure Capacity Before Expansion
provisions.evidence: Does each added cache, replica, queue, or partition follow recorded load, latency target, and observed constraint, or a capacity convention? Check the capacity records beside each expansion.
provisions.statement: Record current load, latency target, and observed constraint before adding caches, replicas, queues, or partitioning.
provisions.rationale: Caches, replicas, queues, and partitioning each answer a different limitation, and only measurements show which one the project hit. Expanding first and measuring later adds machinery that can hide the real bottleneck. Recording current load, the latency target, and the observed constraint before expanding proves the added capacity answers the observed limit.

provisions.heading: Point Behavior Docs at the Behavior Root
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a project record without `paths.behaviorDocs`.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST set `paths.behaviorDocs` in `.litespec/project.yaml` to the folder that holds its Behavior records.
provisions.rationale: Tools never see a Behavior tree the project record does not name, so its records skip every check. The builder joins records, queries, diffs, and the book from one declared root. One declared folder keeps authors and tools on the same tree.
provisions.example:
```yaml
paths:
  behaviorDocs: .litespec/behavior
```

provisions.heading: Record Selected Extensions
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a selection without a criterion.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST list every selected extension in `selectedExtensions` in `.litespec/project.yaml`, each with its criterion.
provisions.rationale: Without a written selection, extensions drift in through dependencies and prose while the checks apply a different set. A later reader cannot tell which condition justified each extension, or whether it still holds. Writing each selection with its criterion keeps the project record as the one place that decides which extension boundaries apply.

provisions.heading: Record Unsupported Scope Decisions
provisions.evidence: Does a project decision name each architecture outside the supported boundary the project adopts? Check the project decisions.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST record a separate project decision for microservices, multiple contexts, native clients on a platform with no mobile stack, other platforms, event sourcing, active-active regions, or large pipelines.
provisions.rationale: Each of these architectures changes the assumptions this page rests on: one language, one deployment, one API, and one database. Without a recorded decision, the project drifts outside the supported scope while claiming its checks still apply. A separate project decision records that the team saw the boundary and chose deliberately.

provisions.heading: Select a Size, a Shape and Stacks
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `stack-invalid`, when the project claims Implementation or Proof, for a shape whose backend stack count is wrong and a platform that names no frontend stack.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST select a size, a shape, one stack per frontend, and one backend stack unless the shape is client-only or the project claims neither `implementation` nor `proof` in `layers`.
provisions.rationale: When size and stacks stay undeclared, each agent infers the architecture from the directory tree, and two agents infer two architectures. Declared once, they tell every check which records and pages apply: the size decides which record types the project carries and which test projects prove them, and each stack decides which technology pages and checks apply. A project with no Implementation or Proof claim needs no code reader, so it may leave stacks empty or absent, or name them for information alone. A project that claims either layer names the stacks the code reader and the checks govern.
provisions.example:
A project with one web frontend and no flows selects small with the svelte stack. The running Claimwick example has flows, so it selects large.

The running Claimwick example declares large with a server shape and two stacks in `.litespec/project.yaml`:

```yaml
size: large
shape: server
stacks:
- dotnet
- svelte
layers:
  intent: litespec
  behavior: litespec
  implementation: litespec
  proof: litespec
```

Size selects the large record set, shape selects a backend stack, and each stack selects its technology pages, which satisfies this provision.

The diagram below shows what each choice decides.

![Size, shape and stacks and what each decides: size, small or large, decides the record types and the test projects, with large adding goals, problems, features, flows, and scenarios; shape, server or client-only, decides whether the project names a backend stack; stacks, one backend stack and one stack per frontend, decide the technology pages and the checks that apply.](../assets/diagrams/core-scope-selection.svg)

provisions.heading: Select Conditional Extensions Explicitly
provisions.evidence: Does `selectedExtensions` list exactly the extensions whose criteria hold? Check each entry against the extension catalog.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST select every extension whose activation criteria apply, and no extension whose criteria do not.
provisions.rationale: Conditional capabilities stay inactive until a documented product or engineering condition applies, so no project carries caching, messaging, or tenancy machinery it never justified. Selecting exactly the extensions whose criteria hold keeps the active rule set minimal and reviewable. The manifest's extension list is the closed set to select from, so no informal extension slips in. Settled by [decision/0030-limit-the-jobs-extension](decision/0030-limit-the-jobs-extension) for the jobs extension, which holds it to subjects a small team can follow.
provisions.example: Caching, durable messaging, and multitenancy are extensions. The extension index lists each with its activation criteria.

provisions.heading: Start with One API and Database
provisions.evidence: Does the topology hold one API deployable and one database, or does a topology convention record what runs instead? Check the topology and the project conventions.
provisions.statement: Use one API deployable and one database.
provisions.rationale: Each additional deployable or store adds deployment, data-consistency, and operations work that a project rarely needs at the start. One API deployable and one database keep the first architecture reviewable and operable by a small team. A background job appears only when a process continues without an HTTP request.

provisions.heading: Write Every Hand-Written LiteSpec File in YAML
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a project file that is not `.litespec/project.yaml` or lacks `schemaVersion`; scope: the project file.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST write every structured LiteSpec file a person edits, the project file, the records, the glossary, and the pattern catalog, in YAML that states its `schemaVersion` and names its schema in a first-line `# yaml-language-server: $schema=<url>` comment.
provisions.rationale: Without one syntax, readers learn a new format per file, and edits hide in brace noise. People write these files and review them in pull requests, so one syntax with comments keeps every edit readable, and one syntax across the folder means a reader learns it once. The schema comment gives an editor completion and validation without a key in the data, and `schemaVersion` tells a tool which shape the file holds. Structured LiteSpec data is YAML; explanation files are Markdown, as the [model page](model.md) states. Files that programs exchange, such as check results, the model, and `--format json` output, stay JSON, which every tool reads without a parser of its own. Settled by [decision/0023-every-handwritten-file-in-yaml](decision/0023-every-handwritten-file-in-yaml).
provisions.example: Claimwick's `.litespec/project.yaml` starts with the comment naming `https://litespec.dev/<version>/schemas/litespec-project.schema.yaml`, then `schemaVersion: 1`, and lists its layers, size, shape, and stacks as YAML keys. Its explanation files beside the records are Markdown. Its check results under `.litespec/proof/checks/` stay JSON, written by its harness.

provisions.heading: Declare the Page Scope
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_BLOCK` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Each page that owns provisions MUST declare its stack and concern in a `**Stack:**` line and a `**Concern:**` line directly under its title.
provisions.rationale: Without it, the page's provisions stay unfiled. Retrieval cannot tell which change they govern, so it shows them everywhere or nowhere. One block under the title tells every reader and tool which situation the page governs, with no need to read further. Declaring both fields once keeps the page, rather than each provision, as the home of the shared scope.

provisions.heading: Give Every Provision Its Layer and Trace
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_VALUE` diagnostic for a `layer` or `trace` value.
provisions.statement: Every provision MUST carry the record layer of its page, or state its own layer as a `layer` field on its Applies to line when that layer differs from its page layer; a provision that ties its layer to the records states `trace: yes` on that line.
provisions.rationale: A tool reporting only the part of the record model a project claims reads each provision's layer and trace from the provision index. A provision with no layer, or with a layer copied from its page, gives the tool no exact part to report. The page gives the default, one field states the exception, and the index carries the result beside the artifact, so no reader composes the layer by hand.
provisions.example: A provision about expense records on a page under `docs/core/` carries `any` from its page and states no field. A provision that requires code marks on the same page states `**Applies to:** layer: implementation; trace: yes`. Its index row carries `implementation` and `yes`.

provisions.heading: Name the Artifact of Every Provision on a Page That Names One
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_ARTIFACT` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: On a page where one provision names an `artifact`, every provision MUST name the kinds of file it governs, or `artifact: any` when it governs every file of its layer.
provisions.rationale: `litespec rules` matches a provision to a file by the kind of file the provision names. A provision naming none on a page of named kinds matches every file of the layer. A handler receives the validator and port provisions beside its own, and an agent reads provisions that do not govern the file in front of it.
provisions.example: On the application page, the provision for validators names `artifact: validator`. The provision for the whole application concern names `artifact: any`. Running `litespec rules` on a command handler returns the second and leaves out the first.

provisions.heading: Record Each Replaced Default
provisions.evidence: Is every choice against a default recorded where its provision's Replacement names? Check each replaced default's recording place.
provisions.statement: A project that chooses otherwise than a provision of Strength default MUST record its choice where the provision names.
provisions.rationale: Without the record, a reader cannot tell a deliberate choice from a provision nobody read. A default holds until the project says otherwise in writing. The provision names the recording place in its Replacement, so each choice sits where its provision points. An advisory provision asks for no record, which is what sets the two strengths apart.
provisions.example: A project keeps its pattern catalog outside the default path, and records the path in `paths.uiPatterns`, as the provision's Replacement names.

provisions.heading: Set a Rule Aside Only Through a Recorded Waiver
provisions.evidence: Does every waiver from a provision of Strength `required` name a provision, page, or finding code, and give a reason? Check each file under `.litespec/governance/waivers/`.
provisions.statement: A project that sets aside a provision of Strength `required` MUST record a waiver whose `waives` names the provision, with a reason.
provisions.rationale: A rule binds every project it reaches. If a project quietly skips a required rule, its records claim it follows the standard when it doesn't. The [waiver record](waivers.md) names the provision and the reason. A gap waiver's expiry date marks a gap the team means to close, so the waiver stays visible and ends instead of lingering.
provisions.example: Claimwick ships its weekend export without the review step. It records a waiver whose `waives` names the authorization provision and whose reason states the choice.

provisions.heading: State Applies to Only When Narrower
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_NARROW` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision MUST carry an Applies to line only when its scope is narrower than its page scope, its layer or trace differs from its page, or it marks its concern-wide scope with `artifact: any` on a page where another provision names a kind.
provisions.rationale: The page scope already governs every provision on the page. Repeating it on each provision gives one fact two homes, and the copies disagree at the next edit. Widening it misfiles the provision under situations the page never governed. A line that appears only when narrower, at a different layer or trace, or marking concern-wide scope beside a named kind keeps retrieval exact.
provisions.example: On a page scoped to `concern: domain`, a provision for aggregates carries `**Applies to:** artifact: aggregate`. A provision for the whole domain concern carries no line. On an application page where a provision names `artifact: validator`, a provision for the whole application concern carries `**Applies to:** artifact: any`. On a record-model page, a provision about marks carries `**Applies to:** layer: implementation; trace: yes`.

provisions.heading: Use Only Declared Scope Values
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_VALUE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A Scope block and an Applies to line MUST use only the stack, concern, artifact, layer, and trace values this page lists.
provisions.rationale: Retrieval matches situations to values. A value invented on one page matches nothing, and its provisions never surface for the change they govern. One closed vocabulary keeps every value comparable across pages. A new situation earns its value on this page first, then uses it on its page.
provisions.example: A provision about the expense aggregate narrows with `artifact: aggregate` rather than inventing `artifact: receipt`. A provision about marks on a record-model page states `trace: yes` rather than inventing a trace value.

provisions.heading: Apply the Complete Stack
provisions.evidence: Does the project apply every page its stack selection brings in? Compare the files against the stack folders, the folders above them, and their stackless subfolders.
provisions.statement: A consumer selecting a stack MUST apply the pages in its folder, every folder above it, and their subfolders that hold no stack.
provisions.rationale: The stack is the unit of conformance: a consumer cannot claim a stack while silently omitting an applicable page. Applying the folder, every folder above it, and their stackless subfolders keeps inherited principles in force without restating them. A deeper page replaces only the provisions it names, so everything it leaves unnamed keeps applying.

provisions.heading: Keep the Stack Visible
provisions.evidence: Does `.litespec/project.yaml` name each selected stack, and does the root `AGENTS.md` name the solution, applications, and commands? Check both files against the project layout.
provisions.statement: Name each selected stack in `.litespec/project.yaml` and the solution, applications, and commands in the root `AGENTS.md`.
provisions.rationale: When `.litespec/project.yaml` names each selected stack and the root `AGENTS.md` names the solution, applications, and commands, an agent resolves the project placeholders directly. Inferring the selection from the directory tree fails whenever folders outnumber stacks or names overlap. A visible selection also tells a human reader what the project runs before opening any code.

provisions.heading: Name Every Provision a Replacement Replaces
provisions.evidence: Does every extension and waiver name each baseline provision it replaces? Check each replacement against the baseline provisions it touches.
provisions.statement: An extension or a waiver MUST name every baseline provision ID it replaces.
provisions.rationale: Naming every replaced provision ID draws the exact boundary of the change: everything unnamed stays active. A waiver names the provision in `waives`, and `rules <path>` shows the waiver in place of the provision. Without the list, a replacement silently widens its scope with each reading, and reviewers cannot tell which baseline provisions still bind the project.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Edge Between Records
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `effect-undeclared` or `effect-loop-invalid` finding across use cases, reactions, jobs, notifications, and integration events, and reports `effect-unimplemented` (check level S) for a declared edge no code takes.
provisions.statement: Every edge between use cases, reactions, jobs, notifications, integration events, and external systems MUST be declared in a record and checked.
provisions.rationale: The declared edges form the effect graph the checks verify, and an undeclared edge is the defect, not the mechanism that carries it. Cycles in the graph end in a domain event with a stated end condition, as `litespec/core/principles#end-every-effect-cycle-in-a-domain-event` states. No edge shares a transaction: a use case commits its own writes, only a reaction or job runs a use case, and an outbound integration event follows from the domain event it translates. The [behavior page](behavior.md) states the edge fields, and the [layers page](layers.md) states how Implementation is checked against them.

provisions.heading: Deliver One Complete Use Case
provisions.evidence: Does every use case page show behavior, persistence, entry points, tests, and operating records? Check the use case page against its records.
provisions.statement: A use case MUST complete with behavior, persistence, entry points, evidence, and operating impact.
provisions.rationale: A use case is done only when a caller can run it and operations can support it: behavior, storage, entry points, automated evidence, and operating impact together. Accepting a thinner slice leaves the missing parts for later, and later rarely itemizes what shipped half-built. Placeholder work leaves the use case unimplemented. Multi-step product outcomes belong to a flow rather than stretching one use case across several goals.
provisions.example: The Claimwick `use-case/spending.submit-expense` use case without its tests and operating records is not complete.

provisions.heading: Group Module Use Case Files by Aggregate
provisions.evidence: Does every use case folder sit in its aggregate subdirectory? Check each use case folder, holding its `<use-case>.yaml`, against the module layout.
provisions.statement: Group each module use case in its own folder under a plural kebab-case aggregate subdirectory, which holds the aggregate's `aggregate.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: Each aggregate needs its own directory for its `aggregate.yaml` and use cases, so grouping use case folders under a plural kebab-case aggregate subdirectory gives every aggregate one home. The use case identifier stays `use-case/<module>.<name>`; only the directory changes. Each module keeps the same typed layout, so a module with one aggregate has the same folders as any other. Proposed by [decision/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders](decision/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders).

provisions.heading: Keep Decision Authority with Accountable People
provisions.evidence: Does every change report name the unknown fact, the person asked, and the record carrying the answer? Check the change report beside the change.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST stop affected work and take to an accountable person an unknown fact that changes behavior, money, data, access, or recovery.
provisions.rationale: Agents meet unknowns in the middle of a task: an unknown access rule, an unclear retention limit, a missing recovery target. When the answer changes behavior, money, data, access, or recovery, only an accountable person can give it. Stopping and taking the question to that person keeps the choice visible instead of buried in code nobody stated. Accountable people decide outcomes, terms, policies, and criteria, and an agent contribution stays a proposal until one of them accepts it.

provisions.heading: Keep Operational and Security References Under Operations
provisions.evidence: Does all operating and security reference prose sit under `.litespec/implementation/operations/`, or does the project documentation name a replacement home? Check the prose against that folder and the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Keep operating and security reference prose under `.litespec/implementation/operations/`.
provisions.rationale: One home for operating and security reference prose means an on-call reader looks in `.litespec/implementation/operations/` first and finds the runbooks, limits, and inventories there. Scattering that prose across product and domain pages buries it where an incident never looks. Enforceable security and privacy rules still belong to their owning use case fields and rules, since those are what the code and tests prove.

provisions.heading: Point Code and Tests up to Records
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing`, `mark-unknown`, and `mark-count-invalid` (check level S) for a code element with no mark, a mark naming no record of the type its element takes, or a handler marking other than one record.
provisions.statement: Every code element the marks table on the [model page](model.md) assigns a mark MUST carry one naming the record it serves, with each handler marking exactly one record.
provisions.rationale: A folder or a type name only resembles its record, and a resemblance drifts with the next rename. The mark is the link from Implementation to Behavior and from Proof to the scenario it proves, in the two kinds the [model page](model.md) states: `implements` names the record served and `follows` names the choice followed. The mark holds the identifier, so the checks, the analyzers, and the editor follow the same link without guessing. One record per handler keeps each file answerable to one use case. Nothing above Implementation is computed from code, so the link points up and the records stay the authority.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense handler carries a mark naming `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense`, the `Reimburse` method on the expense root carries the same mark, and the reminder event handler carries a mark naming `reaction/spending.send-approver-reminder-on-expense-submitted`.

provisions.heading: Point Every Technical Class up to Its Record or Choice
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` and `mark-unknown` (check level S), and `dotnet build` reports `LS5001` and `LS5002`, for a technical class with no mark, an `implements` mark naming no Behavior record, or a `follows` mark naming no provision of the carried release, no decision, waiver, or project convention, or a provision on a page the project's stacks do not apply.
provisions.statement: Every technical class the marks table on the [model page](model.md) names MUST carry at least one mark: an `implements` mark naming a Behavior record it serves, or a `follows` mark naming the LiteSpec provision, decision, waiver, or project convention that shapes it.
provisions.rationale: Every class in the outer layers exists for a record or for a reason. An input validator or a read model serves one use case, and a repository serves one aggregate, so each names that record in `implements` like the handler beside it. Code that serves no record still exists for a reason: a provision requires it, a technical decision chose it, a waiver allows it, or a project convention states it, and a `follows` mark names that reason by identifier. The named target is the reason for the shape the class carries, so review judges a `follows` mark by whether its target requires that shape. A reader asking why the command pipeline commits once, or why the repository stores documents, follows the link instead of guessing, and a check finds the code that still follows a deleted decision. A class may carry both kinds when it serves a record in a chosen way.
provisions.example: The Claimwick submit-expense validator carries `/// <implements>use-case/spending.submit-expense</implements>`. The receipt PDF renderer carries `/// <follows>decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf</follows>`, and the command pipeline's commit step carries `/// <follows>litespec/core/backend-persistence#commit-each-command-pipeline-once</follows>`. The payout bank port carries `/// <follows>claimwick/conventions#confirm-large-payouts</follows>`.

provisions.heading: Update Records with Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every behavior change update its use case page, tests, product records, decision, flow, and operating records? Check the behavior change against its records.
provisions.statement: An observable behavior change MUST update its use case page, implementation, tests, product records, decision, flow, and operating records together.
provisions.rationale: Records map to current names and paths only when each behavior change carries them along. A change that moves code but leaves the use case page, the tests, or the flow behind splits the project into stated fiction and unstated fact. Updating the records in the same change keeps the change to behavior and the change to its description in one place.

provisions.heading: Use Established Technical Terms
provisions.evidence: Does the prose use aggregate, command, query, reaction, job, repository, projection, outbox, idempotency, and transaction with their accepted meanings?
provisions.statement: Use aggregate, command, query, reaction, job, repository, projection, outbox, idempotency, and transaction with their accepted technical meanings.
provisions.rationale: Names such as aggregate, command, query, reaction, job, repository, projection, outbox, idempotency, and transaction carry established meanings that developers and agents already share. Replacing one with a softer synonym hides the pattern and forces every reader to guess what the new word covers. When a term is unfamiliar, explain it and give an example instead of renaming it.

provisions.heading: Use Ordinary Capitalization in Prose
provisions.evidence: Does the prose keep module, aggregate, use case, flow, rule, domain event, and decision lowercase outside names and identifiers?
provisions.statement: Write module, aggregate, use case, flow, rule, domain event, and decision as ordinary nouns in prose.
provisions.rationale: Lowercase module, aggregate, use case, flow, rule, domain event, and decision read as ordinary nouns, while exact record types and code types keep their declared capitalization. The contrast tells a reader whether a word names the concept or the artifact. Capitalizing both blurs that distinction on every page.

provisions.heading: Use the Docs Layout on the Model Page
provisions.evidence: Does the `docs/` tree match the layout the model page states, or does the project documentation record a replacement? Check the tree against the model page layout and the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Use the docs layout the [model page](model.md) states under The Docs Layout, creating a directory only when its first real artifact exists.
provisions.rationale: One home for the docs layout means the folders and the record layers stay in one table. A second tree beside it drifts with the next reorganization, and readers follow the stale one.

provisions.heading: Apply Cross-Tenant Disclosure Policy
provisions.evidence: Does every cross-tenant response follow the documented not-found or forbidden policy? Check the API tests.
provisions.statement: A cross-tenant resource response MUST use the documented not-found or forbidden policy.
provisions.rationale: A caller that names another tenant's resource forces an answer. The product either pretends the resource does not exist or admits it exists and refuses. It documents one policy and applies it to every cross-tenant response, so callers cannot probe for resources through inconsistent answers.

provisions.heading: Audit Actions Taken Under Delegation
provisions.evidence: Does every action taken under delegation record the delegation grant used? Check the audit records of delegated actions.
provisions.statement: An action that an actor takes under delegation MUST record the delegation grant used.
provisions.rationale: An acted-for action without a marker reads exactly like the delegator's own action, and a reviewer then cannot tell who actually acted. Recording the delegation grant used puts the acting party on the record beside the delegator. `litespec/core/audit#mark-actions-taken-under-a-support-grant` states the same marker for administrative grants.

provisions.heading: Avoid Unplanned Isolation Models
provisions.evidence: Does every mixed isolation model trace to a decision with a data evolution plan? Check each mixed model beside its decision.
provisions.statement: A multi-tenant system MUST NOT mix isolation models without a decision and data evolution plan.
provisions.rationale: One part of the product on shared tables and another on separate databases decide which rows each tenant sees in two different ways. Without a decision and a data evolution plan for the mix, backup, restore, and incident response each guess which guarantee covers which data.

provisions.heading: Define Tenant Isolation
provisions.evidence: Does the adoption decision name its isolation model with its guarantee and operating trade-off? Check the adoption decision.
provisions.statement: A multi-tenant decision MUST define shared-table, schema, or database isolation and state its guarantee and operating trade-off.
provisions.rationale: Shared tables, separate schemas, and separate databases isolate differently and operate differently, and each choice moves work between queries, migrations, backups, and scaling. Naming the model with its guarantee and its operating trade-off tells every later choice which isolation it can rely on.

provisions.heading: Isolate Administrative Cross-Tenant Access
provisions.evidence: Does every administrative cross-tenant use case require a platform-scope permission, with an audit record for every run? Check the use case permissions beside the audit trail.
provisions.statement: An administrative cross-tenant operation MUST require a permission the actor holds through a role whose scope is platform, writing an audit record.
provisions.rationale: Support and operations sometimes reach across tenants, and that reach needs exceptional control: a permission held through a role whose scope is `platform`, with an audit record for every use. Without both, one support login gains unrestricted access to every customer's data, with no record of what it touched. Grants that let one tenant act for another follow `litespec/core/access#grant-across-tenants-only-through-declared-delegation` instead.

provisions.heading: Limit Every Delegation in Time
provisions.evidence: Does every delegation carry an expiry or a revocation path? Check each delegation record.
provisions.statement: A delegation MUST carry an expiry or a revocation path.
provisions.rationale: Without an end, a grant outlives its reason: the assistant keeps acting after the engagement ends, and no date prompts anyone to reopen the pairing. An expiry ends the pairing on its date, and a revocation path ends it on demand. Either way, the grant states its own end, so the pairing ends on its terms instead of running until an incident exposes it.

provisions.heading: Pass Tenant Scope Explicitly
provisions.evidence: Is the Domain free of ambient tenant state reads, or does the tenant-scope convention name how the Domain receives scope? Check the Domain code.
provisions.statement: Pass tenant scope through Application messages or trusted ports rather than ambient Domain request state.
provisions.rationale: Domain logic that reads the tenant from ambient request state depends on the host to run at all, which complicates tests and reuse. Passing the scope through Application messages or trusted ports keeps the tenant visible in the call and the Domain free of host state.

provisions.heading: Protect Tenant Diagnostics
provisions.evidence: Is every error, log, metric, and trace output free of another tenant's identifiers and data? Check the output samples in the tests.
provisions.statement: Errors, logs, metrics, and traces MUST NOT reveal another tenant's business identifiers or data.
provisions.rationale: Errors, logs, metrics, and traces travel to people the API never authorized, on support screens, dashboards, and log stores shared across tenants. Scrubbing other tenants' identifiers and data from diagnostics keeps the disclosure policy whole past the API boundary.

provisions.heading: Record an All-Tenant Operation
provisions.evidence: Does every all-tenant run record the actor, operation, reason, tenant count, and reached tenant identifiers up to the adoption bound? Check the run records.
provisions.statement: An all-tenant operation MUST record actor, operation, reason, tenant count, and reached tenant identifiers up to the adoption decision bound.
provisions.rationale: A documented scope states what an operation may touch. It does not state what one run touched, and the run is what a tenant asks about after an incident. An all-tenant run is also the one case where no single tenant's audit trail holds the whole event. [The OWASP logging guidance](https://owasp.org/www-project-cheat-sheets/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet) treats an administrative action over many subjects as one event to record: actor, operation, reason, tenant count, and reached tenant identifiers up to the adoption decision bound. When the `audit` extension is selected, the record is an audit record; otherwise it stays a standalone record.
provisions.example: A support export covering every tenant records the operator, the export, the tenant count, and the incident it was run for.

provisions.heading: Record Delegation Grants with Roles
provisions.evidence: Does every delegation grant sit on its role page, or where the delegation-records convention names? Check the role pages beside that convention.
provisions.statement: Record each delegation grant on the role page that holds it.
provisions.rationale: Each grant qualifies its role: the delegator role names who may be acted for, and the acting role names who may act. Recording the grant on its role page keeps the pairing beside the permission it extends, so a review reads both at once.

provisions.heading: Record the Tenant Adoption Decision
provisions.evidence: Does the tenant adoption decision name the source, storage model, isolation guarantee, administrative access, evolution path, and enumeration bound? Check the decision under `.litespec/intent/decisions/`.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST record a decision naming tenant source, storage model, isolation guarantee, administrative access, evolution path, and enumeration bound.
provisions.rationale: Tenant source, storage model, isolation guarantee, administrative access, and evolution path interact across every boundary, so one decision records them together before code assumes any of them. The enumeration bound caps how many tenant identifiers an all-tenant record lists.

provisions.heading: Reject Unrestricted Tenant Input
provisions.evidence: Does any tenant resolver path accept a tenant identifier from request data? Check the tenant resolver code.
provisions.statement: A tenant resolver MUST NOT accept an unrestricted tenant ID from request data.
provisions.rationale: Any caller can name any tenant when the tenant ID comes directly from request data. Rejecting unrestricted input keeps the request from choosing a data boundary outside its authenticated context.

provisions.heading: Resolve Tenant Identity from Trusted Context
provisions.evidence: Does every trusted host boundary resolve the tenant from an authenticated source? Check each boundary's tenant resolution.
provisions.statement: A trusted host boundary MUST resolve tenant identity from verified claims, host mapping, or another authenticated source.
provisions.rationale: The tenant decides which data the request may touch, so only a trusted host boundary resolves it: verified claims, host mapping, or another authenticated source. A tenant identifier the caller supplies in request data is caller-chosen, not authenticated.

provisions.heading: Scope Delegated Grants to Named Permissions
provisions.evidence: Does every delegation name its delegated permissions, with none opened to all permissions? Check each delegation's permission list.
provisions.statement: A delegation MUST name the permissions it delegates, never all permissions.
provisions.rationale: A delegation open to every permission hands the whole tenant to the acting party. One pairing meant for reading reports also moves money. Naming each delegated permission bounds the pairing to what the delegator intended. Each new permission then needs its own review in the pull request before the acting party holds it.

provisions.heading: Scope Persistence Sessions to the Tenant
provisions.evidence: Does every session-creation path resolve the tenant through its provider's own tenancy support? Check each provider's session creation.
provisions.statement: A multi-tenant persistence implementation MUST resolve its tenant at session creation through the selected provider's own tenancy support.
provisions.rationale: A session opened without a tenant serves its next query without scope. Resolving the tenant at session creation, through the selected provider's own tenancy support, scopes every query the session runs, so no query needs its own check. Filtering per query instead means any query that omits the filter reads across tenants. The baseline provider resolves the tenant from the registered tenancy at session creation; an Entity Framework Core implementation resolves it when the context is created and applies it through a query filter convention.

provisions.heading: Scope Tenant Operations
provisions.evidence: Does every backup, restore, replay, deletion, export, support, and investigation procedure document one-tenant or all-tenant scope? Check each procedure.
provisions.statement: Backup, restore, replay, deletion, export, support access, and incident investigation MUST document one-tenant or all-tenant scope.
provisions.rationale: Each of backup, restore, replay, deletion, export, support access, and incident investigation touches more data than one normal request. Documenting each as one-tenant or all-tenant tells the operator how much data the run touches before it starts.

provisions.heading: Scope Tenant-Owned Records
