provisions.evidence: Does every tenant-owned document, query, constraint, cache key, outbox record, reaction, job, export, and storage path in code carry tenant scope? Check the code for each kind.
provisions.statement: Every tenant-owned document, query, unique constraint, cache key, outbox record, reaction, job, export, and object-storage path MUST include tenant scope.
provisions.rationale: Documents, queries, unique constraints, cache keys, outbox records, reactions, jobs, exports, and object-storage paths can each carry one tenant's data into another tenant's reach. Leaving tenant scope out of any one of them discloses or mixes customer data through exactly that gap.

provisions.heading: Use One Tenant Accessor
provisions.evidence: Does every trusted host boundary read the current tenant through one accessor, or through the place the tenant-access convention names? Check the tenant accessors in code.
provisions.statement: Use one current-tenant accessor at the trusted host boundary.
provisions.rationale: Every boundary reads the current tenant. Two accessors can disagree about which tenant is current, so one accessor at the trusted host boundary gives every reader the same answer from the same trusted source.

provisions.heading: Use Typed Tenant Identities
provisions.evidence: Does every tenant reference carry the `TenantId` type, or another type the tenant-identity convention names? Check the tenant references in code.
provisions.statement: Represent tenant identity with a strongly typed `TenantId`.
provisions.rationale: A bare string tenant ID passes anywhere a string passes. It can land in an actor field, an aggregate key, or a log line. A strongly typed `TenantId` turns each of those mistakes into a compilation failure instead of a production failure.

provisions.heading: Verify Actor and Target Tenancy
provisions.evidence: Does every protected operation refuse when the actor and target tenants mismatch? Check the authorization tests.
provisions.statement: A protected multi-tenant operation MUST confirm actor and target tenancy, with the needed permission held at the resolved scope and the target belonging to it.
provisions.rationale: Checking the caller alone leaves the target unchecked. An authorized caller can still name a resource from another tenant. The operation confirms both sides through one chain: the actor holds a role for the resolved tenant, the permission names the role in `grantedTo`, the use case declares that permission in its grant, and the target belongs to the same scope.

provisions.heading: Isolate Integration State
provisions.evidence: Is any mutable business state shared across tests, or any reset strategy missing from the testing documentation? Look at the tests beside the testing documentation.
provisions.statement: An integration test MUST reset database state between tests through one documented strategy and depend on no test order.
provisions.rationale: Two tests that share mutable business state pass or fail depending on which runs first, and the failure disappears when either test runs alone. One documented reset strategy removes that coupling, so order stops mattering. Container and host fixtures stay shared for cost, because only mutable business state leaks between tests. The default strategy is one database per test class, cloned from a migrated template. The harness applies the schema once per run to a template database. Each test class then receives its own database cloned from that template and drops it when the class finishes. A clone takes milliseconds, so every class starts from an empty migrated schema without a second container. A project that resets tables between tests instead records that strategy in its testing documentation.

provisions.heading: Keep Assertions Focused
provisions.evidence: Is any test body asserting outside its named outcome, or snapshotting whole objects? Look at each test body.
provisions.statement: Assert only the state, event, call, response, or error that the test covers.
provisions.rationale: A focused assertion fails only when the behavior it covers breaks. A broad object snapshot fails on an unrelated field addition, which trains readers to update it without reading it.

provisions.heading: Keep the Test Suites the Size Requires
provisions.evidence: Is any required suite missing a folder, or any extra folder holding an unnamed suite? Look at the test folders beside the declared project size.
provisions.statement: A backend codebase MUST hold exactly the test suites its size requires: architecture and integration for small, adding acceptance for large.
provisions.rationale: Each suite owns one boundary and one harness, so a project that keeps exactly its suites knows where each new test belongs. A missing suite pushes its tests into another suite with the wrong fixtures: an integration test in a unit harness gets no database. An extra suite with no stated boundary collects the tests nobody placed, and nobody knows what those tests prove. Unit suites stay optional at both sizes, and acceptance stays optional at size small. An acceptance suite without the executable BDD extension is an unnamed baseline suite: the project either selects the extension or names the suite for what it actually is.
provisions.example:
These are the suite folders:

```text
architecture-tests/
integration-tests/
acceptance-tests/
```

A small codebase holds the first two. The acceptance folder appears when the executable BDD extension activates.

provisions.heading: Match Tests by Fully Qualified Name
provisions.evidence: Is any test result matched by a short name, or carrying data-row arguments? Look at the test result files.
provisions.statement: A test run MUST match results to tests by fully qualified name.
provisions.rationale: Result files name each test in full: its namespace, its containing types joined with dots, and its method, without data-row arguments. A renamed test then matches nothing instead of matching another test's same-named method, so the rename fails loudly instead of lingering as an awaited run. Matching by short name hides the rename behind a passing name the test no longer owns.
provisions.example: A renamed submit-expense test leaves its old qualified name with no matching result, so the use case stays coded until the new name runs and passes.

provisions.heading: Mirror Production Module Names
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for a test folder under `{Module}/{Aggregates}/` naming no declared aggregate or use case, and `use-case-unimplemented` for a use case with scenarios and no `Application/` folder.
provisions.statement: Mirror the production module, aggregate, and use case folder names inside each test suite, so acceptance tests mirror `{Module}/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` with no layer segment.
provisions.rationale: When test folders mirror production folders, a reader finds the tests for a module without searching. Harness and flat files stay exempt: a `Support` folder and flat Architecture test files need no production counterpart. Adapter tests sit under the adapter's `Infrastructure/` path and are exempt by kind, because they prove a scenario through an adapter that owns no use case folder.
provisions.example:
Each test tree mirrors the production module folders, with no layer segment:

```text
Unit tests/
  Posts/
    Posts/
      CreateDraft/
      GetPost/
Integration tests/
  Posts/
    Posts/
      CreateDraft/
  Support/
Architecture tests/
```

The same module names appear in every test tree, apart from the exempt harness files and adapter tests.

provisions.heading: Name Tests by Observable Behavior
provisions.evidence: Is any test name missing operation, condition, or expected result, or any test class missing its production type? Look at the test names.
provisions.statement: Name a test `{MethodOrOperation}_{Condition}_{ExpectedResult}` and its class after the production type it covers.
provisions.rationale: The failing test name is often the first thing anyone reads in a broken build. A name that states operation, condition, and expected result identifies the broken behavior without opening the file. A name such as `Test1` or `HappyPath` describes the author's intent instead of the behavior that failed, so the reader opens the file to learn what broke.

provisions.heading: Prove Every Aggregate with a Model-Based Test
provisions.evidence: Is any aggregate at size large missing a model-based test walking its declared transitions? Look at the aggregates beside their model-based test files and the declared project size.
provisions.statement: Prove every aggregate with a model-based test generated from its declared transitions at size large; model-based tests stay optional at size small.
provisions.rationale: The transitions table declares every allowed move between states. A model-based test walks generated sequences through that model, checking that allowed moves succeed and rejected moves refuse. Generating from the declared table keeps the model and the test in agreement by construction. The table lives on the aggregate page, as `litespec/core/domain-model#connect-every-state-through-transitions` requires.
provisions.example: An expense test generates walks across submitted, approved, refused, and reimbursed, checking each move against the declared transitions. A walk attempting reimbursement from submitted ends in the refusal the transitions table allows.

provisions.heading: Prove Every Calculation with Property Tests
provisions.evidence: Is any calculation rule at size large missing property tests seeded from its scenario examples? Look at the calculation rules beside their property test files and the declared project size.
provisions.statement: Prove every calculation rule with property tests seeded from its scenario examples at size large; property tests stay optional at size small.
provisions.rationale: An examples table holds the debated rows, and property tests range beyond them: each generated input checks the same stated property the rows illustrate. Seeding from the table ties the properties to reviewed values instead of invented ones. The table itself lives on a scenario proving the rule, as `litespec/core/domain-model#tabulate-every-calculation-with-examples` requires.
provisions.example: A rounding rule with three reviewed rows seeds a property test that asserts the rounded total against the stated bound for every generated input.

provisions.heading: Share One Production-Faithful Integration Harness
provisions.evidence: Is any integration suite missing its container fixture, host factory, or isolation helper, or holding a second of one? Look at the integration suite.
provisions.statement: The integration suite MUST own one database container fixture, one application host factory, and one database isolation helper.
provisions.rationale: One fixture, one host factory, and one reset helper give every integration test the same database and configuration. A container per test group multiplies run time by the group count and buys no isolation that a cloned database lacks. The fixture starts the pinned PostgreSQL once per test run and supplies each test group its connection string before the host builds. An activated BDD extension brings its own host for the acceptance suite, because the two suites run different lifetimes. That host reuses this fixture's container and reset helper instead of starting another database.

provisions.heading: Test Domain in Isolation
provisions.evidence: Is any Domain test using a database, HTTP host, container, clock, or mock instead of explicit inputs alone? Look at the Domain test files.
provisions.statement: A Domain test MUST use explicit inputs with no database, HTTP host, container, clock, or mock.
provisions.rationale: Domain behavior is deterministic: the same explicit inputs produce the same new state or the same refusal. A database, host, container, clock, or mock in a Domain test hides nondeterminism behind the call, so the same test passes and fails without a code change. The suite covers factories, every lifecycle state, allowed and rejected transitions, invariants, value equality, collections, money rules, exceptions, and raised events.

provisions.heading: Test HTTP Integration Through the Real Application Host
provisions.evidence: Is any HTTP integration test bypassing the real host factory or production configuration, or skipping Problem Details, authentication, or resource authorization? Look at the HTTP integration tests.
provisions.statement: An HTTP integration test MUST run through the real application host with the real configuration, covering Problem Details, authentication, and resource authorization.
provisions.rationale: The real host is the only place where routing, serialization, authentication, and authorization are wired together. A test that bypasses the host proves the handler a second time and misses the boundary where status codes, Problem Details shapes, and policy denials actually come from. Persistence behavior runs against PostgreSQL under `litespec/core/backend-persistence#test-persistence-against-the-pinned-database`, and both run on the harness that `litespec/core/testing#share-one-production-faithful-integration-harness` owns.

provisions.heading: Use Builders for Valid Defaults
provisions.evidence: Is any test data builder starting outside valid state, or customizing without business names? Look at each builder.
provisions.statement: Create a test data builder that produces valid state by default and exposes business-named customization.
provisions.rationale: A builder that starts from valid state keeps each test focused on the one value it changes. Building state by bypassing Domain methods is reserved for a persistence compatibility test, because only that test needs state the Domain would refuse.

provisions.heading: Limit Each Non-Hub Screen to Four Offered Commands
provisions.evidence: Does every non-hub screen offer at most 4 commands, with only explicitly typed read-only lookups excluded? Check each screen record beside its route.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST offer at most 4 commands in `offers`, not counting read-only lookup queries explicitly typed as queries.
provisions.rationale: Each offered command is a job the page claims to serve. A fifth offer is a second job sharing the page, and the page then needs the decomposition table again. Counting every command except explicitly typed read-only lookups keeps the cap honest: an untyped read is an offer until proven otherwise.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense detail offers open, approve, request changes, and reimburse: 4 offers. A fifth offer, such as editing workspace settings, moves to its own settings sub-route.

provisions.heading: Limit Visual Sections to Three per Screen
provisions.evidence: Does every route render at most 3 top-level sections with no nested surfaces? Check each route at desktop and mobile widths.
provisions.statement: A route MUST render at most 3 top-level visual sections across cards, panels, and drawers combined with no nested surface.
provisions.rationale: Each added surface splits attention: a fourth card or a drawer inside a card asks the person to track two hierarchies at once. Three flat sections fit one job, and a job that needs more is two jobs. A nested surface hides the hierarchy instead of simplifying it, so the ban is absolute.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense detail renders its header, its main sections, and one history aside: 3 sections. A nested card inside the history panel becomes a labeled subsection divider or moves to a tab.

provisions.heading: Compose Each Route from One Locked Archetype
provisions.evidence: Does every route compose exactly one archetype and fill only its declared slots? Check each route against its archetype row.
provisions.statement: A route MUST compose exactly one of the six locked archetypes using only its declared slots.
provisions.rationale: Unconstrained composition drifts: a list page grows a second form, a record page stacks drawers, a settings page buries a table. One archetype per route fixes the slots up front, and filling only declared slots keeps each job in the shape the product approved. The two minimal utility frames, `AuthPage` and `OutcomePage`, cover sign-in and plain confirmations and carry no other job.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense list composes `ListPage` and fills `header`, `filterBar`, `table`, and `pagination`. A secondary form below the table is refused in review.

provisions.heading: Compose Each Screen from Its Owners Queries
provisions.evidence: Does every screen join each owner's query, with no query that only shows another module's data? Check each screen beside the owning modules.
provisions.statement: A screen that shows data owned by several modules MUST join each owner's query, and a query that only shows another module's data belongs to that module.
provisions.rationale: A screen that copies another module's data into its own query duplicates ownership: two queries answer the same question and drift apart. Joining each owner's query keeps one owner per fact while the screen shows them together. A query that only reshapes another module's data is filed in the wrong module, so the rule files it with its owner.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense detail joins the spending query for the expense with the payouts query for its reimbursements instead of copying payout fields into a spending query.

provisions.heading: Declare Each Screen Job and Archetype
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a screen without `route`, `archetype`, `job`, `offers`, `primaryAction`, `states`, or `leadsTo`, and for an `archetype` outside the six locked archetypes.
provisions.statement: Each screen MUST declare `route`, its optional sub-nav parent in `section`, its `archetype` from the six locked archetypes, its `job` as one plain sentence naming the single user job, its `offers`, its `primaryAction`, its `states`, and its `leadsTo`.
provisions.rationale: A screen without a stated job and archetype is reviewed by feel: nobody can say whether it does one thing or which structure it should follow. Declaring the job in one sentence forces the one-job decision up front, and declaring the archetype fixes which slots and guardrails the route review checks. `primaryAction`, `states`, and `leadsTo` state what the person starts, what the page looks like while busy or empty, and where each path continues.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense list declares `route: /expenses`, `archetype: ListPage`, `job: "Find one expense among many and open it."`, `offers` with the list query and the new-expense command, `primaryAction: new-expense`, `states` for empty and loading, and `leadsTo` with the expense detail route.

provisions.heading: Declare Navigation on Each Browser Entry Point
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a browser entry point without `navigation`, and for a primary sidebar with more than 3 groups or more than 10 items.
provisions.statement: Each browser entry point MUST declare its `navigation` groups for daily work, periodic work, and settings, with `sections` for multi-facet areas carrying their ordered sub-nav items.
provisions.rationale: Navigation declared on the entry point is one reviewed list instead of one invented sidebar per route. Named groups keep daily and periodic work apart, and `sections` give multi-facet areas such as settings one ordered sub-nav. Without the declaration, each route adds its own links and the product grows two navigations.
provisions.example: The Claimwick employee app declares daily work (`Home`, `Expenses`, `Approvals`), periodic work (`Reports`, `Close`), and settings (`Settings`, opening `/settings/business` with its ordered sub-nav).

provisions.heading: Map Every Screen to Its Job Table Structure
provisions.evidence: Does every screen use the structure its job shape maps to? Check each screen against the decomposition table.
provisions.statement: Each screen MUST match the Required Structure its User Job Shape maps to in the decomposition table.
provisions.rationale: Without a fixed mapping, each route author re-derives the structure from taste, and the same job shape gets a dialog in one place and a sub-route in another. The table fixes each shape to one structure, so review checks the row instead of re-arguing the shape. A shape the table does not cover is a gap in this page, not a free choice.
provisions.example: Claimwick's workspace configuration follows the first table row: one `SettingsPage` with left sub-navigation and one focused sub-route per facet. Its expense creation follows the last row: one `FormPage` capped at `max-w-2xl`.

provisions.heading: Use Only Declared Slots with Matching Guardrails
provisions.evidence: Does every filled slot honor its archetype guardrails? Check each route against its row in the archetype table.
provisions.statement: Each filled slot MUST honor its archetype guardrails: at most 1 work queue card plus 1 symmetric KPI strip on a home page, a single table surface with no stacked forms on a list page, a 2-column split with at most 1 active form on a work page, at most 2 main sections with URL-backed tabs for peer facets on a record page, one facet per sub-route on a settings page, and capped form width with uniform 36px control height on a form page.
provisions.rationale: Slots without guardrails fill up: a second queue card appears on the home page, a form lands below the table, a record page stacks a third section. Each guardrail caps the failure its archetype invites, so the common drift of that shape is refused by rule instead of by taste.
provisions.example: Claimwick's home page renders 1 waiting-expenses queue card and 1 symmetric 4-up KPI strip. A proposed second queue becomes a second route or waits for the sitemap review.

provisions.heading: Keep Backend-Mirrored Folders to Clients and Fetching Adapters
provisions.evidence: Do backend-mirrored folders hold only clients and fetching adapters, or does a layout convention name another home? Check the mirrored folders beside the sitemap.
provisions.statement: Backend-mirrored folders hold only API clients and data-fetching adapters (`lib/modules/` or `packages/api/`).
provisions.rationale: Mirrored folders tempt authors to mirror backend structure in pages too. Restricting them to clients and adapters keeps the fetching code findable by module while routing decisions stay in the sitemap.

provisions.heading: Keep One Editing Mechanism per Section
provisions.evidence: Do peer facets of one entity or settings group share one editing mechanism? Check the sibling routes beside each other.
provisions.statement: Peer facets of one entity or settings group MUST use the same editing mechanism: all inline section forms, all dedicated sub-routes, all modal dialogs, or all drawers.
provisions.rationale: Mixed mechanisms teach a different gesture per sibling: one facet saves inline while its neighbor opens a dialog and a third navigates away. The person learns three interactions for one kind of change. One mechanism per section keeps every sibling predictable once the first is learned.
provisions.example: Every Claimwick settings sub-route saves its own inline section form. No sibling mixes a dialog edit beside an inline edit.

provisions.heading: Keep Route Files Small
provisions.evidence: Does every route file stay under 350 lines, or does a waiver decision record the reason? Check the route file sizes beside the waiver records.
provisions.statement: A route file MUST stay under 350 lines with an explicit waiver decision covering any file above that limit.
provisions.rationale: A route file of 500 to 1,500 lines is not a long page but a missing decomposition: several jobs, modes, or facets stacked in one file. The line count is the cheapest proxy for that defect. Keeping each route small forces modes into isolated sub-components and facets into sub-routes, where the archetype guardrails check them. Teams treat 250 lines as the practical target, with the 350-line limit as the defect boundary.
provisions.example: Claimwick's flagged-expense review stays under 250 lines per mode view by isolating `Match`, `Split`, and `Reject` into their own components behind route-backed mode tabs.

provisions.heading: Organize Pages by User Job
provisions.evidence: Does the navigation follow jobs, cadence, and focus, with backend-mirrored folders holding only clients and fetching adapters? Check the sitemap beside the module folders.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST organize its routes and navigation by user job, cadence, and focus instead of deriving page, tab, or navigation structure from backend module folders.
provisions.rationale: Backend modules bound writes, while pages serve people. A navigation tree copied from module folders forces a person to learn the code layout to find a job, and two jobs with different cadences land on one page. Organizing by job, cadence, and focus puts daily work, periodic work, and settings where each is looked for. Backend-mirrored folders keep their one role: API clients and data-fetching adapters.
provisions.example: Claimwick groups daily expense work apart from periodic close and reports, and keeps its workspace settings under one settings section instead of beside the expense list.

provisions.heading: Approve the Sitemap Before Any Frontend Code
provisions.evidence: Was the sitemap approved with one job per page before the first route was written? Check the approval beside the route history.
provisions.statement: No frontend code MUST be written or refactored before the owner approves the sitemap and jobs table with one clear job per page and commands of at most 4.
provisions.rationale: Code written before the sitemap bakes unreviewed jobs into routes: two jobs share a page, a page has no archetype, navigation grows a second copy. Approving the table first makes every later route a fill-in of an approved row. The review stays short because the table shows only the job, the grouping, and the command count.
provisions.example: Claimwick's sitemap review approves `/expenses` as a `ListPage` serving "Find one expense among many and open it." with 2 commands before any route file exists.

provisions.heading: Build Routes Only from Locked Archetypes
provisions.evidence: Is every route built from the sitemap with locked archetypes only, within the line budget? Check the routes beside the sitemap rows.
provisions.statement: Every route MUST be built or migrated from the approved sitemap using only locked archetypes and layout primitives, guarded by the route layout rule, the 350-line route budget, and post-write checks.
provisions.rationale: An approved sitemap without build guards drifts on the first busy week: a route adds a second form, a raw spacing utility, a nested surface. Building only from locked archetypes with continuous guards keeps each route a fill-in of its row. The layout rule, the line budget from `litespec/core/ui-ia#keep-route-files-small`, and the post-write checks catch the drift at write time.
provisions.example: Claimwick's settings migration builds each `/settings/*` sub-route from the locked settings screen, one facet per sub-route, with no raw layout utilities inside route files.

provisions.heading: Update Golden Screens in Plain Words
provisions.evidence: Did calibration stay on the five screens with plain-word feedback, or does a convention name another approver? Check the baseline history.
provisions.statement: The owner gives plain visual feedback on the five golden screens ("too cramped", "buttons misaligned", "too noisy") and the agent iterates only those five until they read as sharp.
provisions.rationale: Plain words keep calibration open to an owner with no interface vocabulary: nobody needs to name a token or a component. Iterating only the five screens bounds the work, so calibration ends with a locked baseline instead of a running redesign.

provisions.heading: Pin Five Golden Archetype Screens
provisions.evidence: Do five locked PNG sets sit under `.agents/ui-baseline/`, one per archetype at three widths in both modes? Open the baseline folder.
provisions.statement: The product MUST lock five real browser-rendered archetype screens (app shell with navigation and workspace switcher, list, record detail with URL tabs, settings with left sub-navigation, and complex form or workbench) at `1440px`, `1280px`, and `390px` in light and dark modes, with the rendered PNGs stored under `.agents/ui-baseline/`.
provisions.rationale: Five locked screens fix the product look once: density, rhythm, control sizes, and navigation behavior. Every later route copies them instead of inventing its own spacing. Rendering them in a real browser at three widths in both modes proves the look holds where people see it, and the stored PNGs give every later comparison a fixed target.
provisions.example: Claimwick locks its expense list at all three widths in both modes. Its later reimbursement screens copy the list density instead of re-deciding it.

provisions.heading: Review Changed Routes with an Independent Visual Critic
provisions.evidence: `litespec ui review --since <base>` records the critic score per dimension for every changed route and files defect tickets for failing scores.
provisions.statement: Every new or changed route MUST be reviewed by an isolated vision-capable critic context that never built the route, scoring alignment, spacing rhythm, visual hierarchy, symmetry, golden archetype consistency, and single-job focus, with `litespec ui review --since <base>` capturing fresh screenshots beside the locked golden archetype screenshots.
provisions.rationale: The builder cannot judge its own rendering: it reads its intent instead of the pixels. An isolated critic sees only the screenshots and the golden baseline, so it reports what a person would see. Scoring the six named dimensions keeps the review on the product look instead of personal taste. A failing score produces concrete defect tickets that agents fix before the owner reviews anything. Settled by [decision/0119-audit-the-rendered-page](decision/0119-audit-the-rendered-page).
provisions.example: The critic scores Claimwick's new mileage claim route against the locked expense form baseline and files "primary and cancel buttons differ in height by 4px" instead of asking the owner to look.

provisions.heading: Run Geometry Sensors on Every Route
provisions.evidence: `litespec ui review` reports the failing sensor with its measured value for every route outside tolerance.
provisions.statement: Every route MUST pass the deterministic geometry and health sensor suite at `1440x900`, `1280x800`, and `390x844` in light and dark modes: column edges within 1px, control height with 0 variance and centers within 1px, balanced grids with no orphan cell, form containers within 720px, non-list screens within 2.2 viewport heights, at most 3 top-level sections with 0 nested surfaces, and the baseline health checks.
provisions.rationale: Geometry a person sees is measurable: aligned edges, uniform controls, symmetric grids, capped widths, bounded length, flat surfaces. Numeric tolerances turn each into a pass or fail with no argument about taste. The baseline health checks (errors, overflow, contrast, heading order, focus, hidden commands) run in the same pass, so one suite proves both geometry and accessibility on every route.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense form passes with its `max-w-2xl` container, uniform 36px controls, and one `h1` at all three viewports in both modes.

provisions.heading: Bind Every Keyed Setting in One Marked Element
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `setting-unimplemented` (level S) for a keyed setting no marked element implements, and `setting-key-drift` (level S) for a marked element whose name does not spell the setting's `configurationPath`.
provisions.statement: A setting with a `configurationPath` MUST be bound in code by one element that carries an `implements` mark naming the setting and whose name spells the path.
provisions.rationale: A setting reaches the running product through configuration, and the code reads it as a typed value. The code element holding that value is where the record and the configuration meet, so marking it with the setting it implements names the promise the element holds. Comparing the element name with the record path finds a renamed section or a typo before the product starts on a default nobody chose. Each stack states the shape of the element.
provisions.example: Claimwick's approval-reminder-delay setting carries `configurationPath` `Spending:ApprovalReminderDelay`. One element carries an `implements` mark naming `setting/spending.approval-reminder-delay`, and its name spells the path.

provisions.heading: Bound Every Caller-Supplied Input Value
provisions.evidence: Does every caller-supplied money or access input cite its bounding rule? Look beside each input with `origin: caller` on a money or access path.
provisions.statement: Each input value with `origin: caller` on a money or access path MUST cite the rule bounding it.
provisions.rationale: A caller-asserted figure on a money or access path arrives unchecked: a replacement amount arrives negative, a quantity arrives absurd, and the code accepts them. Citing the rule bounding it ties each such value to the guard holding it.
provisions.example: The replacement net amount cites the positivity rule bounding it.

provisions.heading: Carry Every Key Placeholder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `idempotency-key-uncarried` (level G) for each key placeholder that no input of a use case, no field of a reaction's triggering event, and no input of a job's run use case carries.
provisions.statement: Each idempotency or deduplication key MUST name only placeholders that the record carries: an input of a use case, a field of an event a reaction answers, or an input of a use case a job runs.
provisions.rationale: A key template is evaluated when a repeat arrives. A placeholder naming no value the record carries is never filled, so every call computes the same key or no key at all: distinct expenses collapse onto one replay, and a reaction never deduplicates the fact it answers. A use case carries its input field names. A reaction carries the fields of the domain event, module event or integration event in `triggeredBy`. A job carries the input field names of the use cases it runs or sends. Naming only carried fields keeps each key unique to the work it guards.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, `use-case/spending.submit-expense` keys repeats on `{expenseId}`, an input it carries. A key on `{attemptId}` would be reported, because no input or triggering event supplies an attempt identifier.

provisions.heading: Change One Aggregate in Each Command
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-writes-invalid` for a command whose `writes` names more than one aggregate without a `boundBy` rule that governs the use case and names a decision in `basedOn`, and `record-placement-invalid` for a command use case at module level.
provisions.statement: Each command MUST name one aggregate in `writes`, live under that aggregate, and change one instance, unless a rule that governs the use case is named in its consistency `boundBy` and names in `basedOn` the decision recording the invariant needing more in one transaction, its record states `consistency: per-record` for independent instances, or it changes no aggregate and declares `writes: []`.
provisions.rationale: A command that changes two aggregate types in one transaction couples their consistency boundaries: one failing part rolls back work that had no reason to fail with it, and the change cannot move to eventual consistency later. One aggregate type per command keeps each transaction on one boundary. The command changes one instance; when its record states `consistency: per-record`, each instance it changes is independent with no invariant spanning two, and it may stage several in one commit. A command that changes two instances under one invariant, such as an original and its reversal or two statements resolving one duplicate, is split by reaction like two aggregates, or the invariant moves into a unique constraint the record names. A command that changes no aggregate, because it verifies or reports and raises a fact, is allowed and declares `writes: []`. Another aggregate of the same module follows through a reaction to the domain event, with its own commit, and time-based work is a job that selects instances and sends one command per instance. A command writing more than one aggregate type is usually a sign the aggregate boundary is drawn wrong; it stays allowed only when a rule that governs the use case is named in its consistency `boundBy`, stating the invariant needing both in one transaction, and names its decision in `basedOn`. Every command belongs to the aggregate it changes, so a command at module level is a finding, and module level keeps only module-wide reads such as an export archive.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command names `aggregate/spending.expense` in `writes` and lives under the expenses aggregate. The reporting reaction to its reimbursed fact answers in its own transaction instead of joining the write. The attach-receipt command names two aggregates with its atomicity rule in `boundBy` naming the decision that records the invariant.

provisions.heading: Cite the Invariants Most Writers Cite
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `rule-sibling-uncited` for a command writing an aggregate without citing an invariant most commands writing that aggregate cite.
provisions.statement: Each command MUST cite every invariant rule that governs an aggregate it writes when most commands writing that aggregate cite the rule.
provisions.rationale: A command that writes an aggregate can break every invariant governing it, and the sibling commands writing the same aggregate show which invariants those writes meet. When most of them cite an invariant, the outlier posts without the checks the others apply. A command cites a rule in its steps' cites, its input rules, its consistency boundBy, or a result carrying the rule's refusal code. Only invariants qualify, since any other kind constrains single commands, while an invariant holds on every change. Settled by [decision/0101-check-rule-citations](decision/0101-check-rule-citations).
provisions.example: Three library commands write the loan aggregate. Two cite the one-hold-per-copy invariant, and the third does not, so the third is reported.

provisions.heading: Declare Consistency on Multi-Aggregate Commands
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `consistency-cites-missing` for an atomic multi-aggregate write with no `boundBy`, `atomicity-drift` for `writes` differing from the bound group, `atomicity-invalid` (level G) for a group above 4 aggregates, and `atomicity-duplicate` (level G) for a command saving more than one atomic write group; `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a query carrying `consistency`.
provisions.statement: Each command writing two or more aggregates, or reading an aggregate whose rule guards its write, MUST declare its write consistency in `consistency`.
provisions.rationale: Consistency left unsaid is read as atomic until a multi-aggregate write fails halfway. Declaring the mode states the promise: `atomic` commits every write in `writes` as one group, and `per-record` commits each write on its own. A command that writes one aggregate and reads an aggregate whose rule guards its write declares `atomic` with the guarding aggregates in `guards`, so the guard still holds when the command commits. An atomic write across aggregates cites its `atomicity` rule in `boundBy`, and `writes` holds exactly the aggregates the rule binds. The command also needs its decision, as `litespec/core/use-cases#change-one-aggregate-in-each-command` states. A guarded command cites the guarding rule in `boundBy` and names in `guards` the aggregates it reads, and does not write. A group above 4 aggregates is reported. Atomic consistency never spans an `async` edge. A command writing one aggregate and reading no guarding aggregate is atomic by definition and carries no `consistency`, and a query carries none. [Domain Model](domain-model.md) states the `atomicity` rule. The `consistency-cites-missing` check reports an atomic multi-aggregate write with no `boundBy`, `atomicity-drift` reports `writes` differing from the bound group, and `atomicity-invalid` reports a group above 4 aggregates. Settled by [decision/0076-remove-shapes-nothing-needs](decision/0076-remove-shapes-nothing-needs).
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command declares atomic consistency citing the reimbursed-once rule. The self-checkout scan declares per-record consistency across its attempts. The submit-expense command writes the expense and reads the report, so it declares atomic consistency citing the open-report rule with the report in `guards`.

provisions.heading: Declare Each Aggregate's Refusals Once
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a result refusal missing from its aggregate's refusal set, `record-invalid` for a refusal entry without `id` or `title`, and `code-placement-drift` or `record-placement-invalid` for a refusal and its exception declared under different homes: a refusal declared under an aggregate whose exception lives under another aggregate or outside `Domain/`, or an aggregate's exception whose refusal is declared at module level.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate MUST declare the refusals its rules raise once in `behavior/modules/<m>/aggregates/<aggregates>/refusals.yaml`, with each entry carrying its `id` and `title`.
provisions.rationale: Refusals declared per use case drift: one use case retires a code while its neighbor keeps it, and the same breach reports two refusals. Declaring each refusal once beside the aggregate whose rules raise it, mirroring `Domain/{Aggregates}/Exceptions/`, keeps one refusal and one meaning behind every result citing it. Each entry carries its `id` as `refusal/<module>.<name>` and its `title` like every other entry; the code is the id's name, so the code `spending.receipt-missing` stays the API's problem code and the audit trail's stored value. A result's `refusal` names a refusal from its aggregate's set, and a rule's `refusal` names the same refusal, so every result carrying it is that rule's refusal in that use case. Settled by [decision/0073-type-every-output-and-declare-refusal-sets](decision/0073-type-every-output-and-declare-refusal-sets).
provisions.example: The expense aggregate declares `refusal/spending.receipt-missing` with its meaning. The submit-expense refusal cites that id.

provisions.heading: Declare Each Module's Refusals Once
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a result refusal missing from its module's refusal set, `record-placement-invalid` for a module-level refusal raised by exactly one aggregate, and `code-placement-drift` for a module-level refusal carried outside `Domain/` or directly in `Domain/`.
provisions.statement: Each module MUST declare in `behavior/modules/<m>/refusals.yaml` only refusals no aggregate raises, with each code's meaning.
provisions.rationale: A refusal an aggregate's rules raise is declared in that aggregate's set, as `litespec/core/use-cases#declare-each-aggregates-refusals-once` states. The module's set keeps only the refusals no aggregate raises: a file refused before any aggregate exists, or a module-wide refusal. Each exception carrying a module-level refusal sits under `Domain/{Aggregates}/Exceptions/` like any other exception. The project declares `problemTypeBase` once in `.litespec/project.yaml`: the problem type of a code is the base followed by the code's part after its module, and the code's part after its module as a short RFC 9457 type name where no base is declared. The book joins the meaning onto each result citing the refusal. Settled by [decision/0073-type-every-output-and-declare-refusal-sets](decision/0073-type-every-output-and-declare-refusal-sets).
provisions.example: The spending module declares a module-wide refusal with its meaning. With a `problemTypeBase` of `https://claimwick.example/problems/`, its problem type is the base followed by the code's part after the module, and without a base it is the short name, the part after the module.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Effect with One Verb and Its Timing
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` for an edge the records never declared and `effect-timing-invalid` for a command `sends` or `calls` effect with `inline` timing; `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an effect entry without exactly one verb or its timing.
provisions.statement: Each effect entry MUST carry exactly one verb and its timing.
provisions.rationale: An edge no record declares stays hidden: calls between use cases, reactions, jobs, notifications, integration events, and external systems that no reader can see. Declaring each edge with exactly one verb, its timing, and its failure handling turns every coupling into data. The verb is `sends`, `calls`, `queries`, or `commands`. The timing is `inline`, `after-commit`, or `async`, and timing is required on every use-case effect. On a command, a `sends` or `calls` effect carries `after-commit` or `async` timing, and an event handler runs the consequence after the commit. A `queries` entry names the public query use case of another module the behavior reads and carries `inline` timing: the read runs within the handling. A `commands` entry names the public command use case of another module the behavior sends and carries `inline` timing: the send runs within the handling. A use case declares no `runs`, no `emits`, and no `commands`. A reaction to its raised fact runs the follow-on work, and the integration events it publishes follow from `raises` and the `translates` field of each outbound integration event. The `effect-undeclared` check reports an edge the records never declared.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command declares no effect. It raises its reimbursed fact, the expense-reimbursed integration event translates that fact, and the reporting module's read model answers the published event.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Query Output
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `query-output-missing` for a query with no declared output.
provisions.statement: Each query MUST declare its output in named `include` groups.
provisions.rationale: A query without a declared output returns whatever its author fetched. Readers and screens guess the shape from code. Declaring the output in named groups with fields, classifications, the aggregates each group reads, and freshness states what readers receive, so the shape is reviewable before anything implements it. The `query-output-missing` check reports a query with no declared output.
provisions.example: The list-expenses query declares open and decided groups, each with `{ "mode": "immediate" }` freshness.

provisions.heading: Declare Paging on Every Collection Query
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `paging-undeclared` for a collection query with no paging.
provisions.statement: Each collection query MUST declare its paging with `mode` of `pages`, or `{ "mode": "none", "reason": "..." }` with its reason.
provisions.rationale: A collection without paging works until the data outgrows it: the first hundred rows return, and the next ten thousand time out. Declaring the order, the cursor or offset, and the default and maximum limits with `mode` of `pages` states the paging beside the read. The value `{ "mode": "none", "reason": "..." }` with its reason states why a query returns one object. The `paging-undeclared` check reports a collection query with no paging.

provisions.heading: Declare the Result a Scenario Ends In
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `scenario-result-unknown` (level G) for a scenario ending in a result id that no result record declares and is not a derived generic refusal.
provisions.statement: The result a scenario names MUST be declared by the use case: a written result, or one of the generic refusals the model derives.
provisions.rationale: A scenario whose ending no result declares asserts an outcome the use case never promises, so its test proves a story nobody wrote down. A written result is a child record of the use case, and a derived generic refusal follows from the access and inputs. Pointing the scenario at `result/<use-case>.<name>` with no such result leaves the proof attached to nothing. Naming a declared ending ties each scenario to an outcome the use case owns.
provisions.example: A Claimwick scenario for `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` that ends in `result/reimburse-expense.already-reimbursed` needs a written result with that id. Ending in `result/reimburse-expense.not-found` needs none, because the model derives that refusal.

provisions.heading: Derive Generic Refusals Instead of Writing Them
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `refusal-generic-written` for a use case writing a generic refusal as a record.
provisions.statement: A use case MUST NOT write a generic refusal as a record.
provisions.rationale: Hand-written generic refusals multiply: hundreds of pages each declare their own forbidden, and each drifts in wording and code. Deriving them keeps one of each per use case, current with the grant, the inputs, the target, the state, the knowledge, the caller, and the sign-in. The builder derives `result/<use-case>.forbidden`, `result/<use-case>.invalid-input`, `result/<use-case>.not-found`, `result/<use-case>.conflict`, `result/<use-case>.unauthenticated`, `result/<use-case>.sign-in-too-old`, and `result/<use-case>.rule-not-stated`. Scenarios point at the derived results without anyone writing them. A derived `not-found` result carries the refusal of the product-level rule taken on an input, and a derived `rule-not-stated` result carries the refusal of the product-level rule that triggers it, so the product code is declared on every use case taking the rule without restating it; the checks treat that code as declared by the derived result. Each result keeps its generic id, title, meaning, and status. A rule stating no refusal keeps the generic code, and a module rule keeps its written result. A rule naming the generic refusal itself is carried like a product-level rule, since no written result may state a generic refusal.
provisions.example: The library takes `rule/library.unknown-copy` on the id input of every use case that loads a copy. Each use case derives `result/<use-case>.not-found` carrying `refusal/library.unknown-copy`, so a handler throwing `library.unknown-copy` is declared with no written result.

provisions.heading: Describe Every Use Case Input with Origin and Classification
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a use-case input without name, meaning, or type, without `identifies` on an `id` field, without `rowShape` on a `list` field, without `choices` on a `choice` field, or with `identifies`, `rowShape`, or `choices` on another type, and `reference-unknown` for an `identifies` naming an aggregate part the aggregate does not declare with identity.
provisions.statement: Each use-case input MUST declare its name, meaning, type, origin, and classification.
provisions.rationale: An input without an origin is trusted on faith: caller-asserted values pass as verified claims, and money moves on an unchecked figure. Declaring the name, the meaning, the type, the origin, and the classification states what arrives, what it is, and how far to trust it. The type comes from `text`, `integer`, `decimal`, `money`, `boolean`, `date`, `date-time`, `duration`, `email`, `choice`, `file`, `list`, and `id`. The origin is `caller`, `claim`, `verified-claim`, or `derived`. An `id` field names the record it refers to in `identifies`, or an identified part of an aggregate as `aggregate/<module>.<aggregate>#<part>` when the aggregate declares that part with `identity: true`, a `choice` field names its allowed values in `choices`, a `file` field names its media types in `contentTypes` with its limit in `maxSize`, and a `list` field names its row shape in `rowShape`. Other types carry no `identifies`, no `rowShape`, and no `choices`. A `verified-claim` input names the entry point or external system that validated it in `verifiedBy`, as [Mark Every Provider-Verified Input](#mark-every-provider-verified-input) states. The `rules` field names the `rule/` identifiers bounding the value, and `required` states whether the caller sends the field. A money field carries an amount with an ISO 4217 currency, as [Record Language](language.md) states. A type on each field lets the builder compare the records with the generated contract and lets agents generate the right code first time. Settled by [decision/0016-typed-contracts-and-privacy](decision/0016-typed-contracts-and-privacy) on the evidence in [research/lower-layers-practice](research/lower-layers-practice).
provisions.example:
```json
"input": [
  { "name": "expenseId", "type": "id", "identifies": "aggregate/spending.expense", "origin": "caller" },
  { "name": "amount", "type": "money", "rules": ["rule/spending.positive-amount"], "origin": "caller" },
  { "name": "lines", "type": "list", "rowShape": { "fields": [{ "name": "amount", "type": "money", "required": true, "meaning": "The line amount." }], "minItems": 1 }, "origin": "caller" }
]
```

provisions.heading: End Every Use Case in Named Results
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-success-missing` for a use case with no success result; each refusal result on the use-case page carries its `refusal`.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST declare its success result and, on every refusal result, its `refusal`.
provisions.rationale: Callers branch on named endings: success, or one refusal result with its stable code. Without a named success, readers guess what good looks like. Without a refusal id on a refusal result, each architecture layer reports the same breach another way. The `use-case-success-missing` check reports a use case with no success result, and `result-undeclared` reports a refusal the records never declared.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command declares `reimbursed`, with the refusal results citing `refusal/spending.not-approved` and `refusal/spending.already-reimbursed`.

provisions.heading: Exercise Rules from Scenarios
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `scenario-rule-unexercised` for a refusal scenario whose result's rule is not in `exercises`, or an input rule no scenario of the use case exercises, and `exercises-uncited` (level G) for a scenario exercising a rule its use case cites nowhere in its steps, inputs, or results.
provisions.statement: A scenario MUST name the rules it shows in `exercises`.
provisions.rationale: A rule proved only through a test mark hides which example walks it: readers open the rule and find no scenario showing it. Naming the shown rules in `exercises` ties each example to the rules it walks, and every rule meets its scenarios. A refusal scenario names the rule behind its result. The scenarios of a use case together walk every rule its inputs cite. An `exercises` entry naming a rule the use case never applies inflates coverage and sends a test author looking for behavior the scenario never shows. Settled by [decision/0101-check-rule-citations](decision/0101-check-rule-citations).
provisions.example: In the library product, a scenario walking a second hold on one copy names `rule/lending.one-hold-per-copy` in `exercises`.

provisions.heading: Give Each Rule Boundary Its Own Scenario
provisions.evidence: Does every exercised rule boundary have its own scenario at the boundary? Look at `exercises` beside the scenarios of the use case.
provisions.statement: Each rule boundary a use case exercises MUST have its own scenario at the boundary.
provisions.rationale: A boundary shown only from the safe side proves nothing about the edge. Expiry, attempt limits, and one-time use each fail exactly at the line. Giving each boundary named in `exercises` its own scenario at the line pins the edge as a checked fact. Settled by [decision/0071-give-every-stated-rule-a-field](decision/0071-give-every-stated-rule-a-field).
provisions.example: The hold expiry rule carries one scenario collecting on the last pickup day, and one collecting after the lapse.

provisions.heading: Give Each Use Case a Command or Query Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a use-case page without `kind` or with an unknown kind.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST declare one kind: command or query.
provisions.rationale: A use case with no kind reads as able to do anything, and the checks have no shape to confirm. The kind decides what the use case may touch: a command changes, a query reads. Work that runs when an event arrives, and work without a request, are reaction and job records, as [Automation](automation.md) states.

provisions.heading: Give Every Tenant Setting a Change Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `tenant-setting-change-missing` (level G) for a setting with `setBy: tenant` that no `change-*` use case names in `reads`.
provisions.statement: A setting with `setBy: tenant` MUST be changed by a `change-*` use case that names it in `reads`.
provisions.rationale: A tenant setting holds configuration the tenant's administrator changes while the system runs. The schema admits `setBy: tenant` beside `product` and `operator`, so a tenant setting is a record, not aggregate data; without a use case that changes it, the value can never move and the default becomes a permanent figure. Naming the setting in `reads` of the `change-*` use case states who changes it and under which access, so the change has the audit and refusal handling every command carries. A product or operator setting names a configuration path instead, as [Name the Configuration Key of Every Operator Setting](#name-the-configuration-key-of-every-operator-setting) states for the operator.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `setting/spending.claim-approval-limit` is set by the tenant, and `use-case/spending.change-claim-approval-limit` names it in `reads`. A tenant setting with no such use case is reported.

provisions.heading: Hold Every Cross-Aggregate Guard Until Commit
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `guard-undeclared` (level G) for a command whose `boundBy` rule governs an aggregate the command reads but does not write, and whose `consistency.guards` does not name that aggregate, and `guard-module-foreign` for a guard naming an aggregate of another module, or a bound rule over one the command reads but does not write.
provisions.statement: Each command whose `boundBy` rule governs an aggregate of its own module that the command reads but does not write MUST name that aggregate in `consistency.guards`.
provisions.rationale: A guard read at the start of a command can change before the command commits: submit-expense reads the report as open, close-report closes it and commits, and submit-expense then commits an expense on a closed report. Naming the guarding aggregate in `guards` states that the rule must still hold when the command commits. Mode `atomic` with `guards` means the guard holds at commit. The stack page states how the guarded read holds the guard, by a lock, a version check, or serializable isolation. No guard reaches into another module: the guard holds at commit, and no commit spans modules. A command bound by a rule over another module's aggregate is reported, and [Edges and Screens](edges.md) states how the two modules keep the fact consistent without a lock.
provisions.example: The submit-expense command reads the report and writes the expense, with the open-report rule in `boundBy`. It names the report in `guards`, so a racing close-report commit either waits or makes submit-expense refuse.

provisions.heading: Justify Every Wider Visibility
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `widening-cites-missing` for a widened include group with no cited requirement.
provisions.statement: Each include group visible to more roles than the aggregates it reads MUST cite the requirement widening it in `widenedBy`.
provisions.rationale: A read showing more than the aggregates it reads widens without a recorded choice: roles see figures their own grants never allowed, and no requirement states the view. Citing the requirement in `widenedBy` keeps the widening a decided choice. The `visibleWhen` field states the condition where one narrows it. The `widening-cites-missing` check reports a widened group with no cited requirement.

provisions.heading: Keep Each Scenario Inside Its Operation
provisions.evidence: Does every scenario assert only its own operation in `then`? Look at `then` beside the scenario's own operation.
provisions.statement: Each scenario MUST assert only its own operation's results, state, and raised events in `then`.
provisions.rationale: A scenario that asserts a later operation's effect ties two operations in one test. When the first operation changes, the second breaks, and the failure points at the wrong record. Asserting only the scenario's own results, state, and raised events keeps each test on its record. An effect of a later operation belongs to a flow test. Settled by [decision/0081-own-scenarios-and-declare-outcomes](decision/0081-own-scenarios-and-declare-outcomes).
provisions.example: The submit-expense scenario asserts the stored expense and its submitted fact. It leaves the approver payout to the flow test walking both operations.

provisions.heading: Keep One Kind per Verb
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-verb-invalid` for a use case opening with a verb of the other kind.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST open with a verb of its own kind, or with an either verb.
provisions.rationale: A query named `change-...` or a command named `read-...` mislabels what the use case may touch in every listing. The first word is the first thing a reader trusts, so a mismatched first word teaches readers to trust no name. The baseline vocabulary gives each verb a kind of query, command, or either, and an either verb opens either kind. A project declares the kind of each of its verbs in its glossary verb term. Proposed by [decision/0062-declare-project-verbs-in-the-glossary](decision/0062-declare-project-verbs-in-the-glossary).
provisions.example: `use-case/lending.list-loans` is a query and passes. The name `use-case/lending.answer-inquiry` opens either kind on an either verb and passes. The name `use-case/lending.read-overdue-count` declared as a command is reported, and so is `use-case/lending.change-copy` declared as a query.

provisions.heading: List Recorded Outcomes Inside Success Codes
provisions.evidence: Does every success result with recorded outcomes list them in `codes`? Look at the success results beside their use-case pages.
provisions.statement: Each success result with recorded outcomes MUST list them in `codes`.
provisions.rationale: A success hiding several recorded outcomes forces callers to guess: borrow and renew both succeed, but the due date and the analytics differ. Listing the closed codes inside the success states each recorded outcome beside the ending.
provisions.example: The checked-out result lists `borrow` and `renew` as its recorded outcomes.

provisions.heading: List the Consumer Modules of a Public Query
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a `queries` edge naming no written use case, `query-target-invalid` for a `queries` edge to a use case that is not a query or whose `reachedThrough` names no calling module, and `query-consumer-missing` for a public query no module queries.
provisions.statement: Each public query MUST list every consuming module in `reachedThrough`.
provisions.rationale: A `queries` edge names the public query use case it reads, and the public query names the modules allowed to read it. When the two lists disagree, the edge is declared on one side only: a `queries` edge to a use case whose `reachedThrough` does not name the calling module reads a query that names no such reader, and a public query no module reads is published for no reader. Settled by [decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data](decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data).
provisions.example: Spending's read-expense query lists `module/reporting` in `reachedThrough`, and reporting's reimbursement command declares `effects.queries` naming `use-case/spending.read-expense`. A second consumer joins by adding its module to the list.

provisions.heading: List the Sending Modules of a Public Command
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a `commands` edge naming no written use case, `command-target-invalid` for a `commands` edge to a use case that is not a command or whose `reachedThrough` names no sending module, and `command-consumer-missing` for a public command no module commands.
provisions.statement: Each public command MUST list every sending module in `reachedThrough`.
provisions.rationale: A `commands` edge names the public command use case it sends, and the public command names the modules allowed to send it. When the two lists disagree, the edge is declared on one side only: a `commands` edge to a use case whose `reachedThrough` does not name the sending module sends a command that names no such sender, and a public command no module sends is published for no caller. Settled by [decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data](decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data).
provisions.example: Spending's close-expenses command lists `module/reporting` in `reachedThrough`, and reporting's close-period job declares `effects.commands` naming `use-case/spending.close-expenses`. A second sender joins by adding its module to the list.

provisions.heading: Mark Every Provider-Verified Input
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `input-claim-unverified` for a claim-shaped input with `origin: caller` on an entry point that authenticates through a provider.
provisions.statement: Each input carrying a claim a provider validated MUST declare `origin: verified-claim` with the entry point or external system that validated it in `verifiedBy`.
provisions.rationale: A provider claim filed as caller input is trusted on faith: a forged subject or email passes as verified, and access follows. Declaring the claim with the entry point or external system that checked its issuer, audience, signature, and expiry ties each trusted value to the boundary that earned the trust. A caller never supplies such an input.
provisions.example: The library sign-in command declares the provider subject with `origin: verified-claim`. Its `verifiedBy` names the provider sign-in entry point.

provisions.heading: Name a Use Case for the Act Its Aggregate Performs
provisions.evidence: Does every aggregate method a command handler calls start with the use-case verb or `Request`? Look at the methods each command handler calls.
provisions.statement: Each command use case MUST share its verb with the aggregate method its handler calls.
provisions.rationale: A different word in the use-case name and in the act means two meanings have merged, or the use case is misnamed. Each reader then guesses which word to trust. The use case names one aggregate act, so the two share their verb. A handler calling no aggregate method answers to no act, so queries and ports stay out of this rule. A command that records a request for work an event handler finishes after the commit, as `litespec/core/backend-application#call-external-systems-through-their-ports` requires, performs the request, so its method starts with `Request` and passes.
provisions.example: `use-case/orders.void-order` whose handler calls `Abandon` is reported. The project renames the use case to the domain word, or the method and its event to `Void` and `OrderVoidedDomainEvent`.

provisions.heading: Name Each Refusal Code for the State That Refuses
provisions.evidence: Does every refusal id read `refusal/<module>.<noun>-<state>` and name its state? Look at the refusal ids on each use-case page.
provisions.statement: Each refusal id MUST read `refusal/<module>.<noun>-<state>` and name the state, not the failure.
provisions.rationale: The code is the id's name, and it is a public contract. The words `invalid`, `failed`, or `error` tell an integrator nothing to do. A code naming the state tells what holds and what to change. The module segment names the module that owns the refused state, which may differ from the module of the refusing use case. A code built at run time from a key, such as the conflict for a lost uniqueness key, declares its template in `refusals.composed`.
provisions.example: `refusal/spending.receipt-missing` names the missing receipt. The id `refusal/spending.receipt-invalid` hides the state behind a vague word and is reported.

provisions.heading: Name Every Aggregate a Use Case Writes or Reads
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `write-undeclared` for a write outside `writes` and `reference-unknown` for an unknown aggregate.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST name every aggregate it writes in `writes` and every aggregate it reads in `reads`.
provisions.rationale: A write no record names is invisible: the handler touches a second aggregate, the second aggregate changes, and no diff shows it. Naming every touched aggregate states the read and write footprint beside the behavior. The `write-undeclared` check reports a write outside `writes`.

provisions.heading: Name Only a Provided Way Out in Each Refusal Sentence
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `refusal-next-step-unknown` (level G) for a refusal sentence naming a `use-case/`, `screen/`, or `setting/` id no record holds, or carrying `instead`, `alternatively`, `you can also`, or `or you can`.
provisions.statement: Each refusal sentence that names a next step SHOULD name a use case, screen, setting, or input that exists.
provisions.rationale: The refusal sentence is what the user reads. When it promises a way out the product lacks, the user follows the advice into the same refusal: the sentence says to submit the expense to the next open report instead, but the command takes no report. Naming only a use case, screen, setting, or input that exists keeps every promised step one the user can take.
provisions.example: Claimwick's closed-report refusal carries "This expense falls in a closed report. Reopen the report and submit again." only when the reopen use case exists; otherwise it carries "This expense falls in a closed report, so it cannot be submitted."

provisions.heading: Name the Configuration Key of Every Operator Setting
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `setting-key-missing` (level G) for a setting with `setBy: operator` and no `configurationPath`.
provisions.statement: A setting the operator sets MUST name its configuration path in `configurationPath`.
provisions.rationale: An operator setting reaches the product through configuration. The record and the configuration meet at one path: the record states the default and the bounds, and the configuration names the value. Without the path, a renamed section silently falls back to a default nobody chose, and no reader can tell which configuration value a promise rests on. A setting a tenant or the product sets names no configuration path; a tenant setting is changed by a `change-*` use case, as [Give Every Tenant Setting a Change Use Case](#give-every-tenant-setting-a-change-use-case) states.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `setting/spending.approval-reminder-delay` is set by the operator. It carries `configurationPath` `Spending:ApprovalReminderDelay`.

provisions.heading: Name the Entry Points and Modules That Reach Each Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a live use case that names no entry point and that nothing runs, and `reference-unknown` for a `reachedThrough` entry naming no entry point or module.
provisions.statement: Each use case a caller reaches from outside MUST name the entry points that reach it in `reachedThrough`.
provisions.rationale: A use case with no named entry point is reachable from anywhere or nowhere. Readers cannot tell a public operation from an internal one. Naming the entry points shows how callers arrive at each behavior. A public query names the consuming modules beside or instead of entry points, under `litespec/core/use-cases#list-the-consumer-modules-of-a-public-query`, and a public command names the sending modules, under `litespec/core/use-cases#list-the-sending-modules-of-a-public-command`, so the provider side of every synchronous cross-module edge is declared. A use case that only a reaction or a job runs has no entry point of its own, and the `runs` edge of that reaction or job already shows how it is reached. A use case a provider callback runs names the entry point the host serves: the provider redirects the browser to the host callback, and the pipeline handler in the module `Infrastructure/Pipeline/` folder runs the use case under its mark. That handler is the use case endpoint, so the use case needs no mapped endpoint route and no screen call.
provisions.example: The library `complete-sign-in` use case names the library app entry point in `reachedThrough`. The provider redirects the browser to the host callback, where the ticket handler in the `Infrastructure/Pipeline/` folder runs the use case under its mark. No endpoint maps the callback route and no screen calls the use case.

provisions.heading: Name the Events Each Use Case Raises
provisions.evidence: Does every use case name the domain events it raises in `raises`? Look at `raises` beside each use-case page.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST name the domain events it raises in `raises`.
provisions.rationale: An event raised but unnamed leaves reactions waiting on a fact no behavior admits raising. Naming the raised events ties each fact to the behavior that announces it.

provisions.heading: Name the Idempotency of Every Command
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a command without an idempotency mode or without the key, key scope, or reason its mode needs; `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a key with no `{field}` placeholder or a key scope outside `tenant`, `account`, `login`, and `global`; `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a query carrying `idempotency`. `litespec model check` reports `idempotency-key-uncarried` for a key placeholder naming no carried field.
provisions.statement: Each command MUST declare its idempotency mode with the key, key scope, or reason that mode needs.
provisions.rationale: A retried call without a stated idempotency runs twice: a double payout, a double loan, a double notice. Declaring the mode states how repeats collapse. The mode is `key`, `state`, or `none`, with its key template and key scope. Mode `none` carries the reason repeats cannot happen. The `key` templates `{field}` placeholders over the record's `input` field names, and the `keyScope` is `tenant`, `account`, `login`, or `global`. A query carries no `idempotency`, since a read is idempotent by kind. A reaction or job carries its own `idempotency`, as [Automation](automation.md) states. The self-checkout scan keys on `{nonce}` scoped to the login.

provisions.heading: Name the Result Each Scenario Ends In
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a scenario entry without `result`, and `reference-unknown` for a scenario ending in another use case's result. `litespec model check` reports `scenario-result-unknown` for a result id no record declares.
provisions.statement: Each scenario MUST name the result it ends in, written or derived.
provisions.rationale: A scenario that names no result reads well and proves nothing: it illustrates behavior without asserting an ending. Naming the result ties each example to the ending it walks toward, so every test knows what to assert. A reaction or job scenario names a result or an outcome instead, as [Automation](automation.md) states. The `reference-unknown` check reports a scenario ending in an unknown result.

provisions.heading: Name the Settings Each Use Case Reads
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `setting-unused` for a setting no record `reads`.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST name the settings it reads in `reads`.
provisions.rationale: A setting a use case reads but no record names is a coupling no one can see: the tunable moves, the use case reading it breaks, and no diff shows the pair. Naming the settings in `reads` beside the use case states the coupling beside the behavior that reads it, so each change to the range or default meets the use cases that read it. The setting's readers are computed as the inverse, never written. A setting no use case, reaction, or job reads is a finding. Settled by [decision/0012-use-cases-read-their-settings](decision/0012-use-cases-read-their-settings) on the evidence in [research/behavior-containment-evidence](research/behavior-containment-evidence) and [research/field-naming-evidence](research/field-naming-evidence).
provisions.example: The send-approver-reminders reaction names `setting/spending.approval-reminder-delay` in `reads`. A move of the delay then meets the reaction that reads it.

provisions.heading: Name the Use Case That Decides a Stale Figure
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `freshness-decider-invalid` (level G) for a `decidedBy` naming a query or a use case or aggregate outside the module that owns the figure's source, and `record-invalid` for a `decidedBy` with `immediate` freshness.
provisions.statement: Each query output group and each read model whose figure a command re-decides at write time MUST name in `decidedBy` that command use case or its aggregate, in the module that owns the figure's source.
provisions.rationale: A stale figure without a named decider leaves the reader guessing who settles it: the page shows seat availability, and nothing says the hold command re-decides it at write time. Naming the deciding command use case, or its aggregate, states the link beside the figure, so the reader follows it to the current truth. The schema allows `decidedBy` only with `snapshot` or `eventual` freshness, since an `immediate` figure is current and names no decider. A query decides nothing, so a `decidedBy` naming one is reported. The decider sits in the module that owns the figure's source, as `litespec/core/automation#decide-current-truth-in-the-owning-module` states.
provisions.example: The reimbursed-expenses list carries `snapshot` freshness and names `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` in `decidedBy`. A reader seeing a stale row follows the link to the command that decides each reimbursement.

provisions.heading: Name What a Use Case Acts on from the Model
provisions.evidence: Does every use-case name carry an aggregate, a declared part, or a glossary term after its verb? Look at the words after the verb in each use-case name.
