provisions.rationale: A structural comparison never compiles a client. Compiling each first-party generated client against the changed document, and running its changed operations, lets the client compiler and its exhaustive switches catch breaking changes the comparison cannot detect.

provisions.heading: Treat Errors as Contracts
provisions.evidence: Did every type, code, field-code, or status change ship inside versioning? Check the versioned error surface.
provisions.statement: An API owner MUST treat Problem Details type, code, field-error codes, and documented statuses as versioned contract elements.
provisions.rationale: Error handling is consumer code, and it branches on Problem Details type, code, field-error codes, and documented statuses. When those elements change outside versioning, the consumer failure path breaks, and that path has the least test coverage. Versioning error shapes with the contract keeps that handling working across releases.

provisions.heading: Treat Removed Behavior Fields as Breaking Changes
provisions.evidence: Does every removed output field, refusal code, or integration-event payload field carry a breaking verdict? Check the change reviews.
provisions.statement: An API change reviewer MUST classify removal of a query output field, a refusal code, or an integration-event payload field as breaking.
provisions.rationale: Consumers read query output fields, branch on refusal codes, and parse integration-event payloads, so a removed field breaks every consumer that relied on it while the route stays green. Calling each such removal breaking routes it to versioning and notice instead of silent release.

provisions.heading: Use One Diff Tool
provisions.evidence: Do the local runs and the CI runs share the diff tool the local convention records? Check the local runs and the CI runs.
provisions.statement: Use the same OpenAPI diff tool in local verification and continuous integration.
provisions.rationale: The local run and continuous integration need one shared meaning of breaking. Using one diff tool in both places gives each change one classification. Two tools disagree on edge cases, and developers learn to distrust a check that answers differently in each place.

provisions.heading: Version Breaking Contracts
provisions.evidence: Does every breaking contract ship behind a new route or a documented media-type version? Check the versioned API surface.
provisions.statement: An API owner MUST use a new route or documented media-type version for a breaking contract.
provisions.rationale: Breaking changes need a boundary: a new route or a documented media-type version. Both contracts then serve at once, and each consumer moves on its own schedule. Without the boundary, one contract serves two incompatible expectations.

provisions.heading: Version Breaking Integration Events
provisions.evidence: Does every breaking event change ship in a new version beside the retained one? Check the integration event versions.
provisions.statement: An API owner MUST carry a breaking integration-event change in a new event version beside the retained version.
provisions.rationale: Consumers the project does not deploy move on their own release cadence. Shipping the breaking change in a new event version, beside the retained version, lets each consumer move on its own schedule. Without the retained version, one event has to serve two incompatible expectations.

provisions.heading: Accept Every Shipped Package License Explicitly
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `dependency-license-unknown` (level S) for a direct package whose license the project does not accept and no `admits` entry names.
provisions.statement: Every direct package in the project's generated bill of materials MUST carry a license the project accepts in `dependencies.licenses`, or one its `admits` entry names.
provisions.rationale: A copyleft or commercial license binds the product the day the package ships. When nobody accepted the license at the change that brought it, the license is discovered at an audit instead. Listing the accepted licenses once, and naming any other license on the admitting decision, keeps each license choice a decision that names the person who made it.
provisions.example: Claimwick accepts `MIT`, `Apache-2.0`, and `BSD-3-Clause` in `dependencies.licenses`, so a direct package under `AGPL-3.0-only` that no decision admits is reported.

provisions.heading: Allow Time for Graceful Shutdown
provisions.evidence: Does every deployment set a shutdown grace period longer than measured request or Worker stop time? Check the deployment manifests beside the measured stop times.
provisions.statement: A deployment MUST set a shutdown grace period longer than measured request or Worker stop time.
provisions.rationale: Stopping a replica interrupts its in-flight requests and Worker operations. A grace period longer than the measured stop time lets that work finish, or record a safe interruption. A shorter period kills work the system then has to reconcile.

provisions.heading: Apply OCI Release Labels
provisions.evidence: Does every release image carry OCI source, revision, version, and created-time labels? Check the built images.
provisions.statement: A release image MUST include OCI source, revision, version, and created-time labels.
provisions.rationale: Labels in the OCI standard form connect each image to the commit and release that produced it: source, revision, version, and created time. An incident responder reads the running image's labels and opens the exact source. Without labels, joining a running image to its source takes guesswork.

provisions.heading: Ask Only Unanswered Questions
provisions.evidence: Do the worker's questions stay within what the brief leaves unanswered? Check the worker questions beside the brief.
provisions.statement: A worker MUST ask no question its brief answers.
provisions.rationale: The brief settles the questions the handing-off agent already answered. A worker that re-asks them spends a round trip on a reading failure. Questions are for what the brief leaves genuinely unanswered.

provisions.heading: Attach Dashboard Links to Production Objectives
provisions.evidence: Does every production objective in the book link to its dashboard? Check the objective pages in the book.
provisions.statement: Each production objective MUST link to its dashboard in the book.
provisions.rationale: The book states intent while dashboards show production truth, and the link joins them: a reviewer clicks from the objective to the numbers behind it. Copying numbers into the page instead would freeze production truth at commit time.

provisions.heading: Build from the Workspace Root
provisions.evidence: Does every image build that needs shared inputs start from the workspace root, or does a build-context convention name another context? Check the image build commands.
provisions.statement: Build images from the workspace root when shared project or package files are required.
provisions.rationale: Shared project and package files sit above any one application, so the build starts from the workspace root to reach them. The Dockerfile excludes what the build does not need, including unrelated secrets. A narrower context would copy shared inputs into each build or miss them.

provisions.heading: Build Release Images in Stages
provisions.evidence: Does every release image use multi-stage builds and pinned base-image digests? Check the Dockerfiles.
provisions.statement: A release image MUST use multi-stage builds and pinned base-image digests.
provisions.rationale: Build tooling has no place in a runtime image: each compiler and package cache widens the attack surface of every deployment. Multi-stage builds leave that tooling in the build stage. A pinned base-image digest fixes the exact reviewed base, so a rebuild months later starts from the same bytes.

provisions.heading: Check Implementations Against Held-Back Example Rows
provisions.evidence: Was every refusal or calculation implementation checked against rows its worker never saw? Check the held-back rows and the check runs.
provisions.statement: An agent handing off work MUST check a refusal or calculation implementation against example rows held back from the worker that wrote it.
provisions.rationale: Example rows given to the implementing worker become the values the implementation is tuned to pass, so the check proves nothing. Rows held back from the worker stay an independent verdict: the handing-off agent runs them after the worker finishes, and the implementation passes or fails on unseen cases.

provisions.heading: Close Incident Waivers Within Seven Days
provisions.evidence: Does every incident fix that shipped before its records carry a waiver, with none expired? Check the waiver records beside each fix.
provisions.statement: A production incident fix that ships before its records are updated MUST carry a gap waiver expiring within seven days.
provisions.rationale: A production incident ships its fix at once, before the records catch up. The gap waiver records what shipped and why, and names the records to update in `closedBy`. Those records are updated before the waiver expires, and an expired waiver is a blocking finding, so the gap stays visible until the records close it.

provisions.heading: Copy Only Runtime Files
provisions.evidence: Does every runtime image contain only the files the declared runtime manifest names? Check the image file listing beside the declared runtime manifest.
provisions.statement: A runtime image MUST contain only files required to run the deployed application.
provisions.rationale: Every file in the runtime image ships to every replica, where an attacker can read it. Copying only the files the application needs keeps the image small, quick to transfer, and quick to inspect. Each extra file adds cost with no runtime purpose.

provisions.heading: Cover Every Quality Requirement with an Alert or a Check
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `quality-alert-missing` (level G) for a quality requirement that no alert rule names in its `requirement` label, whose `check` matches no measured-check or check result the model read, and that no waiver covering `quality-alert-missing` lists in its `appliesTo`.
provisions.statement: Every quality requirement that is not retired MUST be named by at least one alert rule or check result, or covered by a waiver.
provisions.rationale: A quality requirement nobody watches is a promise checked only when a customer notices it broken. An alert watches it in production by naming the requirement, and a check result, from a measured check or a drill, shows it was measured before release by naming it through its `check`. A requirement that can't be watched yet says so as a gap waiver, with a reason, an exit, closing records, and an expiry date, instead of passing silently.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `requirement/approval-reminders.month-end-submission` is named by the alert `submission-acknowledgement-slow` and by the k6 result its `check` names.

provisions.heading: Cover the Baseline Alert Set
provisions.evidence: Does the alert set cover all five baseline failures: readiness failures, unexpected HTTP errors, release-flow latency, PostgreSQL outages, and failed deployments? Check the alert rules.
provisions.statement: Baseline coverage MUST include sustained readiness failures, unexpected HTTP errors, release-flow latency, PostgreSQL outages, and failed deployments.
provisions.rationale: Five failures end a release when nobody observes them: readiness that never recovers, unexpected HTTP errors, a slowing release flow, a lost database, and a deployment that failed partway. Naming them as the minimum coverage keeps a team from declaring alerts only for the failure it just survived.

provisions.heading: Declare Writable Paths and Limits
provisions.evidence: Does every deployment declare writable paths and record CPU and memory bounds as setting records? Check the deployment manifests beside the setting records.
provisions.statement: A deployment MUST declare writable paths and record CPU and memory bounds as setting records.
provisions.rationale: Declared writable paths name the mutable storage the application needs. CPU and memory bounds as setting records cap what one deployment can consume, which protects the node's capacity from one replica consuming more than its share, and tells the next reader what the application was sized for.

provisions.heading: Define Actionable Baseline Alerts
provisions.evidence: Does every baseline alert declare an owner, threshold, window, severity, and runbook? Check each alert rule.
provisions.statement: A baseline alert MUST declare owner, threshold, evaluation window, severity, and runbook before a production release.
provisions.rationale: Each declared field answers one failure mode: - An alert with no owner waits for somebody to adopt it. - An alert with no threshold or evaluation window fires on noise. - An alert with no severity waits in the wrong queue. - An alert with no runbook asks its receiver to invent the response. Declaring all five before the production release makes each alert answerable the first time it fires.

provisions.heading: Define Backup and Restore Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does the release documentation state a backup owner, schedule, retention, encryption, location, restore command, and recovery objective? Check the release documentation.
provisions.statement: A release MUST document backup owner, schedule, retention, encryption, location, restore command, and recovery objectives.
provisions.rationale: A backup is only as good as its restore. Without a named owner, a schedule, a retention bound, encryption, a location, a restore command, and recovery objectives, nobody knows what is kept, who restores it, or how much loss is accepted. Writing all seven down before production data arrives leaves nothing to decide during the incident.
provisions.example: Claimwick's release names its backup owner, its nightly schedule, its 30-day retention, its encryption, its storage location, its restore command, and its recovery objectives.

provisions.heading: Enforce the Supply-Chain Gate
provisions.evidence: Does every supply-chain report show scan, pin, inventory, and license evidence, with a waiver covering each unhandled high-severity advisory? Check the supply-chain report beside the artifact.
provisions.statement: CI MUST enforce the supply-chain gate on every pull request.
provisions.rationale: When a new advisory names a component and a version range, the team needs one fast answer: does any running release contain it. Without a component inventory beside the artifact, finding that answer means rebuilding the dependency graph from a commit that somebody must first identify. [NIST SP 800-218](https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-218/final) states the practice, and the frozen lockfile the build resolved is what the inventory is generated from. OSV-Scanner matches dependencies against OSV.dev advisories, and Gitleaks scans for leaked secrets, so advisories and secrets each have one evidence tool.
provisions.example: Claimwick's build job generates its inventory from the same frozen lockfile it built from, and stores that inventory beside the artifact under the release version.

provisions.heading: Exclude Build Material from Runtime Images
provisions.evidence: Is every runtime image free of source, tests, package caches, and local configuration? Check the runtime image contents.
provisions.statement: A runtime image MUST NOT contain source, tests, package caches, or local configuration.
provisions.rationale: Source, tests, package caches, and local configuration serve the build and never the running application. Carrying them into production leaks internals to anyone who pulls the image. Secrets stay out under `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data`.

provisions.heading: Exclude Build Timestamps from Contracts
provisions.evidence: Is every published OpenAPI document and generated client free of build timestamps? Check the generated contracts.
provisions.statement: A published OpenAPI document or generated client MUST NOT contain a build timestamp.
provisions.rationale: A generated-at field or a build-time comment changes the OpenAPI document and generated clients on every build. The diff then reports change where no contract changed, and that noise hides real breaking changes. Contracts carry version identity instead of build time.

provisions.heading: Exclude Environment Configuration from Images
provisions.evidence: Is every release image free of environment-specific configuration? Check the release image contents.
provisions.statement: A release image MUST NOT contain environment-specific configuration.
provisions.rationale: One immutable image deploys unchanged into staging and production. Environment values baked into the image break that promise, because the tested bytes and the deployed bytes differ. External values keep the image identical everywhere it runs.

provisions.heading: Expose Release Health and Diagnostics
provisions.evidence: Does every release expose health signals and trace diagnostics, and keep secrets outside source control? Check the operating evidence beside the release.
provisions.statement: A release MUST expose liveness, readiness, and trace-correlated diagnostics, and keep secrets outside source control.
provisions.rationale: Operators cannot keep a product they cannot see: liveness and readiness signals drive restarts and traffic, and trace-correlated diagnostics connect each failure to its cause. Secrets stay outside source control because anything committed there is exposed to everyone who can read it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's release exposes liveness, readiness, and trace-correlated diagnostics, with its database password supplied outside source control.

provisions.heading: Give Each Jobs-Table Job Its Own Workflow
provisions.evidence: Does every consumer workflow file match a jobs-table job and name, or does a workflow-layout convention name another arrangement? Check the workflow files beside the jobs table.
provisions.statement: Keep one workflow per job the jobs table lists and use the job names the jobs table states.
provisions.rationale: One workflow per job keeps each gate readable, runnable, and skippable on its own. When containerized integration tests or browser tests join CI, they join as jobs the table names, not as hidden steps inside another job, so the selection rules and the branch protection keep working unchanged. Hidden steps would run without a name the release job or branch protection can require.

provisions.heading: Keep a Canonical Job Graph
provisions.evidence: Does every consumer workflow use only the job names and responsibilities the jobs table states? Check the workflow files.
provisions.statement: Consumer CI MUST use the job names and responsibilities the jobs table on the [Continuous Integration page](../quality/ci.md) states.
provisions.rationale: The release job reruns the table's jobs by name, and the branch protection settings require them by name. When a consumer renames a job or moves its checks elsewhere, those references point at a job that no longer exists. The gate then stops checking without failing. Fixed names and responsibilities keep every reference pointed at the checks the table states.
provisions.example: Claimwick's CI uses the jobs table names, so its release job and branch protection resolve every job.

provisions.heading: Keep a First-Release Readiness Record
provisions.evidence: Does every pre-release consumer keep dated rehearsals, green gates, and a rehearsal owner? Check the readiness record beside the project.
provisions.statement: A consumer before its first production release MUST keep a readiness record with dated rehearsals, green gates, and a rehearsal owner.
provisions.rationale: A release record binds evidence to one artifact, so a product with no artifact yet has nothing to record in one. The readiness record instead states the evidence that the product is ready to take data: dated rehearsals, green gates, and a rehearsal owner responsible for the backup and restore rehearsal.
provisions.example: Claimwick's readiness record names its rehearsal owner and dates its backup and restore rehearsal before the first customer data arrives.

provisions.heading: Keep Deployment Descriptors Together
provisions.evidence: Does every deployment descriptor sit under one `deploy/` tree, or does a deployment-layout convention name another arrangement? Check the repository layout.
provisions.statement: Keep compose files, proxy configuration, the environment example, database setup, observability, DNS records, alert definitions, service definitions, and bootstrap scripts under one `deploy/` tree.
provisions.rationale: A deployment spreads across compose files, proxy configuration, environment examples, database setup, observability, DNS records, alert definitions, service definitions, and bootstrap scripts. Scattered across the workspace, one of them is always the file nobody finds during the incident. One `deploy/` tree keeps every descriptor where the operator looks first.

provisions.heading: Keep Deployment, Limits, and Runbooks Ready
provisions.evidence: Does every release ship with deployment, rollback, limits, and runbooks? Check the delivery evidence beside the release.
provisions.statement: A release MUST ship with tested deployment and rollback paths, current operating limits, and the runbooks those limits name.
provisions.rationale: Tested deployment and rollback paths, current limits, and the runbooks those limits name make every release repeatable and every failure recoverable. Without tested paths, each deployment is improvised; without current limits and their runbooks, each incident is handled without a procedure.
provisions.example: Claimwick's release ships its deployment script, its rollback runbook, its current memory and CPU limits, and the runbooks those limits name.

provisions.heading: Keep Frontend Secrets Out of Arguments, Files, and Layers
provisions.evidence: Is every frontend image build free of `ARG`, copied environment files, and image layers carrying secrets? Check the frontend image builds.
provisions.statement: A frontend image build MUST NOT use `ARG`, copied environment files, or image layers for secrets.
provisions.rationale: `ARG` values, copied environment files, and image layers all persist into the image history, so a secret delivered through any of them stays readable to anyone who pulls the image. Secrets stay out of layers under `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data`.

provisions.heading: Keep Mutable Data Outside the Container
provisions.evidence: Does any mutable data live inside a container filesystem? Check the application storage design.
provisions.statement: A containerized application MUST keep mutable data outside its container filesystem.
provisions.rationale: The platform recreates replicas at will: each deploy, scaling event, and node failure replaces containers with fresh ones. Mutable data kept inside the container filesystem dies with its replica. External storage keeps the data alive across every recreation.

provisions.heading: Keep Release Data Recoverable
provisions.evidence: Does every release provide repeatable schema setup, backup instructions, and a tested restore? Check the recovery evidence beside the release.
provisions.statement: A release MUST provide repeatable schema creation or upgrade, backup instructions, and a tested restore.
provisions.rationale: A product that cannot recreate its schema, back up its data, and restore from backup holds customer data it cannot recover. Repeatable setup plus a tested restore makes recovery a rehearsed procedure.
provisions.example: Claimwick's release ships its schema creation script, its backup instructions, and the log of its latest restore rehearsal.

provisions.heading: Keep Rollback Ready to Run
provisions.evidence: Does every rollback runbook state its artifact reference, command, compatibility, data condition, expand-and-contract sequence, and, for a container release, the previous image digest? Check each rollback runbook.
provisions.statement: The rollback runbook MUST state the previous artifact reference, command, configuration and schema compatibility, data recovery condition, and the expand-and-contract sequence for destructive schema work, and name the previous image digest for a container release.
provisions.rationale: Rollback is written during the incident if it is not written before it, and an incident is the worst time to work out which artifact was live, which command restores it, and whether the schema still fits. Stating the previous artifact reference, the command, the configuration and schema compatibility, the data recovery condition, and the expand-and-contract sequence for destructive schema work keeps each answer ready before it is needed. For a container release the runbook names the previous image digest, which names one immutable image where a tag alone could have moved since the release went out. Rollback is a required runbook, so `litespec/ext/delivery#rehearse-every-runbook-before-release` rehearses it.

provisions.heading: Keep Scripts at the Root
provisions.evidence: Does every bootstrap, release, or CI helper script sit under root `scripts/`, or does project documentation name another script layout? Check the repository layout.
provisions.statement: Keep bootstrap, release, and CI helper scripts under root `scripts/`.
provisions.rationale: Bootstrap, release, and CI helper scripts serve the whole workspace, so the root `scripts/` folder keeps them where every caller looks. A script that only one application calls can stay inside that application.

provisions.heading: Limit Container Privileges
provisions.evidence: Does every deployment use a read-only filesystem and drop unnecessary capabilities where the application permits the limits? Check the deployment manifests.
provisions.statement: A deployment MUST use a read-only filesystem when the application permits it and drop unnecessary capabilities.
provisions.rationale: A read-only filesystem and dropped capabilities shrink what a compromised process can do next: no writes outside declared paths, no privileged calls the application never needed. The limits apply where the application permits them, and each kept capability is an action an attacker inherits.

provisions.heading: Link Each Operations File to Its Decision
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` (level S) for a file in `paths.operations` with no `follows` mark and `mark-unknown` (level S) for a mark naming no decision, waiver, or provision, and counts the file toward `decision-unimplemented`.
provisions.statement: Every deployment, proxy, host, and CI workflow file the project lists in `paths.operations` MUST carry a `follows` mark naming the technical decision, waiver, or provision it carries out.
provisions.rationale: Operations files hold choices as consequential as code: the proxy's security headers, the backup schedule, the gates a pull request passes. Their reasons usually live in comments no tool reads, so when a decision retires, its configuration stays behind unnoticed. A `follows` mark in the file's own comment syntax is the same link a technical class carries, so `decision-unimplemented` and `mark-unknown` cover these files too.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `deploy/Caddyfile` opens with `# <follows>decision/0004-serve-receipts-behind-one-proxy</follows>`.

provisions.heading: Link Every Runbook to Its Caller
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `runbook-unused` (level G) for a runbook record that no alert label, job, reaction or failure policy names.
provisions.statement: Every runbook record MUST be named by at least one alert, job, reaction, or failure policy.
provisions.rationale: A runbook nobody names answers no failure. An alert, a job, a reaction, or a failure policy is the caller that sends a person to the procedure. Without that link, the procedure waits undiscovered while the failure it answers gets handled from memory. Naming each runbook from at least one caller keeps every procedure reachable from the event that needs it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's job `send-event-change-notices` names `runbook/clear-stuck-notices` in its `runbook` field, so the procedure is reachable from the work that needs it.

provisions.heading: Match Every Shipped Package to Its Pin
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `dependency-version-drift` (level S) for a direct package whose version is outside its manifest pin.
provisions.statement: Every direct package in the project's generated bill of materials that the manifest pins MUST ship within its pin: a stable release of the pinned major, or the exact version where the manifest pins one.
provisions.rationale: The bill of materials (SBOM) is the computed list of what ships, so it is the one place a pin can be checked instead of trusted. A version outside its pin carries a major's breaking changes, or a prerelease's behavior, that the release never reviewed. The bill is generated, so the fact stays written once; a record per package would rewrite hundreds of facts on every update.
provisions.example: Claimwick's bill of materials sits at `.litespec/proof/sbom/api.spdx.json`, the project file names that folder in `paths.sbom`, and a direct `pkg:nuget/Marten` at 10.0.0 is reported because the manifest pins `9.x`.

provisions.heading: Meet Release Readiness Gates
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` blocks on `use-case-unverified` (level S).
provisions.statement: A release MUST show green G checks, verified scenarios, and green S checks where the reader is qualified.
provisions.rationale: The three parts prove the three risks are closed: G checks prove the record graph holds, verified scenarios prove each behavior through the public boundary, and S checks prove the code matches the records where a qualified reader exists. A release missing any part ships with that risk unchecked. `litespec model check --release` makes `reader-missing` block for a claimed layer, so the gate runs as a command.
provisions.example: Claimwick's reimbursement release shows green G checks, every scenario verified, and green S checks on the .NET reader.

provisions.heading: Name the Requirement and Runbook on Every Alert
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `alert-link-missing` (level S) for an alert rule in the files `paths.alerts` names whose `requirement` label is missing or names no quality requirement, or whose `runbook` label is missing or names no runbook.
provisions.statement: Every alert rule MUST carry a `requirement` label naming the quality requirement it measures and a `runbook` label naming the runbook that answers it, both as record identifiers.
provisions.rationale: An alert watches a quality requirement at runtime: it fires when the measure the requirement promises is breached, and the runbook says what a person does next. When that link is a file path or missing entirely, no tool can follow it. An alert can then outlive its requirement, a requirement can lose its last alert, and a renamed runbook breaks silently. Record identifiers in the alert's own labels keep the link in the file the alert lives in, in the syntax its tool already reads, and let the model check both ends. A baseline alert also carries its window and severity, as `litespec/ext/delivery#define-actionable-baseline-alerts` states.
provisions.example: Claimwick's alert rule `submission-acknowledgement-slow` carries `requirement: requirement/approval-reminders.month-end-submission` and `runbook: runbook/slow-submissions` in its labels.

provisions.heading: Pass Frontend Secrets by Mount or Runtime Injection
provisions.evidence: Does every frontend secret travel through a mount or runtime injection? Check the frontend image build.
provisions.statement: A frontend image build MUST use secret mounts or runtime injection for secrets.
provisions.rationale: Secret mounts and runtime injection hand secrets to the build without writing them into a layer. Nothing secret then persists in the image history. A pulled image reveals its layers to anyone, so image history stays free of secrets.

provisions.heading: Place Dockerfiles Beside Their Applications
provisions.evidence: Does every deployable application keep a Dockerfile beside it, or does a dockerfile-layout convention name another place? Check each application folder.
provisions.statement: Keep one Dockerfile beside each deployable application.
provisions.rationale: The image definition belongs with the project that defines its runtime output. One Dockerfile beside each deployable application puts the build next to the code it ships, where the reader looks first. A shared folder of Dockerfiles separates each build from its owner.

provisions.heading: Promote Verified Artifacts
provisions.evidence: Does every staging or production deployment reference the artifact the release job passed? Check the deployment references.
provisions.statement: CI MUST build one immutable artifact and promote that same artifact through staging and production.
provisions.rationale: Staging tests prove something about the artifact they ran against. When production deploys a fresh build from the same branch instead, it ships code the tests never saw, because the branch may have moved between the two builds. Promoting the one tested artifact through staging and production keeps the tested code and the shipped code identical.
provisions.example: Claimwick's release job builds one image, staging tests that image, and production deploys that same image.

provisions.heading: Protect the Default Branch
provisions.evidence: Does the default branch require the jobs-table entries, a reviewed pull request, and a clean merge state? Check the branch protection settings.
provisions.statement: The default branch MUST require the jobs table entries for the project's size, a reviewed pull request, and a clean merge state.
provisions.rationale: Every environment deploys from the default branch. A commit that lands there unreviewed or unchecked reaches production with no further review. Requiring the jobs table entries for the project's size, a reviewed pull request, and a clean merge state keeps every commit on the branch reviewed and verified. Only a documented repository recovery action may push directly or bypass a check.

provisions.heading: Publish a Book Preview for Every Change
provisions.evidence: Does every pull request link to a book preview built from the change? Check the pull request description.
provisions.statement: CI MUST publish a preview of the book for every change.
provisions.rationale: The intent diff names what changed, while the preview shows it rendered, with the changed records readable beside their neighbors. The reader clicks from the comment into the preview for full context.
provisions.example: Claimwick's pull request comment links to a preview where the changed requirement reads beside its feature.

provisions.heading: Record Each Drill Run as a Check Result
provisions.evidence: Does every drill or measuring harness run write a check result file naming the requirement's `check` under `paths.checkResults`? Check the harness run records beside the files under `paths.checkResults`.
provisions.statement: A drill or measuring harness that checks a quality requirement MUST write each run as a check result naming the requirement's `check`, kept under the project's `paths.checkResults`.
provisions.rationale: A drill rehearses a procedure against a running deployment, and a harness measures it from outside. Neither is a test, and neither runs in the test job. Without a result file, the outcome lives only in a terminal or a pasted note that no tool reads. Writing each run as a small result file in Proof gives the quality requirement the same evidence a measured check gives it: the same `check` name, the date it ran, and the value it saw.
provisions.example: Claimwick's month-end load harness writes `.litespec/proof/checks/2026-11-20-month-end-load.json` holding `"check": "month-end-load"`, `"passed": true`, `"value": "99.4 percent acknowledged within two seconds"`, and `"ranOn": "2026-11-20"`, and `requirement/approval-reminders.month-end-submission` names `month-end-load` in its `check`.

provisions.heading: Record Every Branch Protection Bypass
provisions.evidence: Does every bypass entry name its actor, reason, and admitted change? Check each bypass entry in the operations log or the recovery decision.
provisions.statement: A direct push or bypassed check on the default branch MUST produce a record naming the actor, the reason, and the change it admitted.
provisions.rationale: Gates can't run during some recoveries, so the bypass permission lets a recovery proceed. An unrecorded recovery is indistinguishable from skipping the gates by habit, so the next reviewer cannot tell which commits on the branch were reviewed. The record names the actor, the reason, and the admitted change, which is the attribution [NIST SP 800-218](https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-218/final) states for the same event.
provisions.example: Where a recovery decision exists, it serves as the record. A bypass smaller than a decision takes a dated entry in the operations log at `.litespec/implementation/operations/log/`.

provisions.heading: Record Image Digests
provisions.evidence: Does every release record store the deployed image digest rather than only a tag? Check the release records.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST store the deployed image digest rather than only an image tag.
provisions.rationale: A tag can move to a newer image after release, so a tag alone no longer says what went out. The digest names the exact bytes that shipped, which makes the deployed artifact reproducible and the rollback target exact.

provisions.heading: Record Operating Readiness
provisions.evidence: Does every release record list limits, alerts, runbooks, conditions, and skipped checks? Check the readiness list on each release record.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST list operating limits, alerts, runbooks, known operating conditions, and skipped checks.
provisions.rationale: Limits, alerts, runbooks, known conditions, and skipped checks tell the maintainer what to watch, what to run, and what remains unverified after release. Without them, the release hands over an artifact with no operating instructions.
provisions.example: Claimwick's release record lists its memory limits, its slow-submission alert, the runbook that answers it, and the checks it skipped.

provisions.heading: Record Release Evidence
provisions.evidence: Does every release record list a result for each evidence kind? Check the evidence list on each release record.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST list build, test, contract, security, flow, schema, backup, deployment, readiness, diagnostics, smoke-test, and rollback results.
provisions.rationale: Build, test, contract, security, flow, schema, backup, deployment, readiness, diagnostics, smoke-test, and rollback results together show the artifact works and can be operated. A missing kind means nobody produced that evidence.
provisions.example: Claimwick's release record lists a result for each kind, from build through rollback.

provisions.heading: Rehearse a Restore Before the First Production Data
provisions.evidence: Does the operations log show a restore rehearsal on representative data before the first production data? Check the operations log entries.
provisions.statement: A project MUST rehearse a restore on representative data before its first deployment holds production data.
provisions.rationale: Backups fail in ways only a restore reveals: a missing key, a wrong permission, a dump the new version can't read. A rehearsal on representative data finds those failures while they cost nothing, before production data arrives.

provisions.heading: Rehearse Every Runbook Before Release
provisions.evidence: Does every required runbook carry a dated rehearsal in the operations log? Check the operations log entries.
provisions.statement: Each required runbook MUST carry a dated rehearsal in the operations log before a production release, with restore rehearsed on representative data.
provisions.rationale: A runbook nobody has run is a claim: steps go stale, commands change, and permissions lapse. A dated rehearsal in the operations log proves each required runbook still works against the current system. The restore rehearsal is the one `litespec/ext/delivery#rehearse-a-restore-before-the-first-production-data` requires.

provisions.heading: Repeat Every Deployment from Named Inputs
provisions.evidence: Does every deployment use a versioned artifact, declared configuration, a schema step, readiness checks, and a passing release job? Check the deployment definitions.
provisions.statement: A deployment MUST use versioned artifacts, declared configuration, a schema step, readiness checks, and a passing release job.
provisions.rationale: A repeatable deployment names everything it ships: a versioned artifact, declared configuration, a schema step, readiness checks, and a passing release job. Deploying from an uncommitted tree or a mutable branch reference makes the deployed content unknowable afterwards, because the same reference points at different code a week later. Named inputs let any deployment run again, and let any incident trace back to its exact content.

provisions.heading: Report Liveness from Every Recurring Job
provisions.evidence: Does every recurring job report liveness that pages a person when the job goes silent? Check each job and its alert rules.
provisions.statement: Every recurring job MUST report liveness that pages a person when the job goes silent.
provisions.rationale: A recurring job with nothing to do is quiet, and a recurring job that stopped is quiet too. Without a liveness signal that pages a person on silence, the two stay indistinguishable until somebody notices the missing output.

provisions.heading: Restrict a Worker to Its Paths
provisions.evidence: `git diff --name-only` lists only the brief's named paths. The worker commits nothing.
provisions.statement: A worker MUST stay inside the paths its brief names and commit nothing.
provisions.rationale: The brief names the paths the worker may change. A worker that stays inside them can't rewrite what another worker owns. One that roams the whole tree overwrites parallel work and commits what nobody asked for.

provisions.heading: Review Schema Artifacts
provisions.evidence: Does every persistence change publish a schema artifact that lists each destructive operation with its reason? Check the schema artifact beside each change.
provisions.statement: A persistence change MUST publish a schema artifact that lists every destructive operation with its reason.
provisions.rationale: A persistence change reaches production data, so the reviewer needs to see exactly what the database will do before it runs. The schema artifact shows that: the Marten schema plan and document transformation, or a generated relational migration with its SQL. Listing every destructive operation with its reason forces the author to name data loss where every reader sees it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense-table change publishes its Marten schema plan with the dropped column listed as destructive, with its reason.

provisions.heading: Route Each Severity to a Declared Destination
provisions.evidence: Does every severity state a destination and an expected response time on the limits page? Check the limits page.
provisions.statement: An alert inventory MUST state, for each severity it uses, the destination that receives the alert and the response time expected of it.
provisions.rationale: A severity with no destination is only a label: every alert lands in the same place, and the page that should wake somebody sits beside the ticket that can wait. Routing each severity to its destination, with the response time expected of it, separates the page from the ticket, which is the separation [Prometheus alerting practice](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/alerting/) states. The limits page declares the routing beside the generated inventory.
provisions.example: Claimwick's two-severity inventory routes `page` to the on-call destination with a stated response time, and `ticket` to the queue reviewed each working day.

provisions.heading: Run Images as Non-Root
provisions.evidence: Does every release image run its application with a non-root user? Check the Dockerfiles and image configuration.
provisions.statement: A release image MUST run its application with a non-root runtime user.
provisions.rationale: A compromised application process inherits the rights of its runtime user. A non-root user confines the attacker to what that user can access. Root would expose the whole container.

provisions.heading: Run the Application as PID 1
provisions.evidence: Does every container run the application as its entry process? Check the image entrypoints.
provisions.statement: A container MUST run the application as its entry process.
provisions.rationale: The platform stops a container by signaling its entry process. An application running as PID 1 receives that signal and shuts down on purpose. A wrapper that swallows the signal leaves the platform waiting until it kills the container mid-work.

provisions.heading: Run the End-to-End Suite After Traffic Shifts
provisions.evidence: Does every release run its recorded end-to-end suite after traffic shifts? Check the release evidence.
provisions.statement: A release deployment MUST run the release's recorded end-to-end suite after traffic reaches the new version.
provisions.rationale: An image that builds can still fail where it runs, because routing, configuration, and data differ from the build machine. Running the release's recorded end-to-end suite after traffic shifts tests the deployed path itself. The release record names the suite, so the same tests run every release.

provisions.heading: Separate Public Configuration from Runtime Secrets
provisions.evidence: Does every frontend build keep public configuration separate from server-only secrets? Check the frontend image build.
provisions.statement: A frontend image build MUST distinguish public build-time configuration from server-only runtime secrets.
provisions.rationale: A frontend build produces a browser bundle that anyone can download. Public build-time configuration belongs in that bundle, while server-only runtime secrets travel through mounts or runtime injection instead. The build distinguishes the two classes, so each value lands in its own delivery.

provisions.heading: State Availability Objectives as OpenSLO Files
provisions.evidence: Does every OpenSLO file pass Sloth validation with its generated alerts loaded? Check the Sloth validation output.
provisions.statement: A production release MUST state its availability and latency objectives as OpenSLO files compiled by Sloth.
provisions.rationale: OpenSLO files state objectives as code, and Sloth validates them in CI and compiles them into Prometheus recording rules and burn-rate alerts. OpenTelemetry supplies the signals the objectives read, as `litespec/quality/operations#emit-correlated-diagnostics` states. Sloth and OpenTelemetry are free and maintained under Apache-2.0. Availability is evidenced in production only.

provisions.heading: Supply Runtime Configuration Externally
provisions.evidence: Do the connection strings, OIDC settings, exporter endpoints, and secrets all live outside the image? Check the deployment manifests.
provisions.statement: A deployment platform MUST supply connection strings, OIDC settings, exporter endpoints, and secrets outside the image.
provisions.rationale: Connection strings, OIDC settings, exporter endpoints, and secrets differ by environment. Supplying them outside the image lets one image serve every environment. Baking them in would force a rebuild and retest for each environment the image enters.

provisions.heading: Tie Alert Thresholds to Requirement Measures
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `alert-threshold-drift` (level G) for an alert rule whose own text carries none of the decimal numbers its requirement's `measure` names.
provisions.statement: An alert rule MUST state every number its requirement's `measure` names in its own expression or threshold.
provisions.rationale: The requirement's measure states the agreed target, and the alert is the one place that target is enforced at runtime. When the requirement changes, nobody re-reads the alert, so a measure that says two seconds and an alert that fires at five drift apart silently. Comparing the numbers is coarse because a measure is prose, so the check compares only the decimal numbers the measure names with the alert's own text, and blocks when the alert carries none of them.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `requirement/approval-reminders.month-end-submission` measures "at least 99 percent within two seconds", and its alert's expression compares the 0.99 quantile against 2.

provisions.heading: Treat Check Warnings as Failures
provisions.evidence: Does any build pass with unreviewed warnings outside recorded suppressions? Check the build logs beside the warnings convention.
provisions.statement: Treat build and lint warnings as failures unless the build configuration records a narrow suppression with its reason.
provisions.rationale: Warnings nobody reviews accumulate until a real defect hides among them. Failing on warnings forces each one to be fixed, or narrowly suppressed with its reason, so a changed compiler, linter, or dependency boundary surfaces immediately.

provisions.heading: Use Stable Service Names
provisions.evidence: Do service, resource, meter, and trace-source names stay identical across environments, or does a service-naming convention name another arrangement? Check the environment configurations.
provisions.statement: Keep service, resource, meter, and trace-source names identical across environments.
provisions.rationale: Dashboards and alerts reference services by name. When a name changes with each deployment, every reference breaks, and each one must be rebuilt before the new deployment can be watched. Identical names across environments keep one dashboard and one alert set working everywhere.

provisions.heading: Verify Before Accepting Worker Output
provisions.evidence: Does every accepted output show a watched verification run? Check the verification runs the agent handing off the work reports.
provisions.statement: An agent handing off work MUST re-run the verification its brief names before accepting worker output.
provisions.rationale: The agent handing off the work owns the result. It re-runs the verification the brief named and watches it pass, because a done claim without that run is unverified. Accepting on trust moves the worker's defect into the handing-off agent's change.

provisions.heading: Wait for Replica Readiness
provisions.evidence: Does every deployment wait for new replicas to reach readiness before shifting traffic? Check the deployment controller behavior.
provisions.statement: A deployment controller MUST start new replicas and wait for readiness before shifting traffic.
provisions.rationale: New replicas need time to load before they serve, and a replica that receives traffic mid-startup fails its first requests. The controller starts the new replicas, waits for readiness, and only then shifts traffic, so the new version proves it can serve before it takes traffic.

provisions.heading: Write a Brief Before Handing Off
provisions.evidence: Does every brief state goal, context, sources, and output? Check the briefs the agent starting the handoff wrote.
provisions.statement: An agent that starts another agent MUST give it a written brief stating goal, context, sources, and output.
provisions.rationale: Two agents sharing one tree collide without a written split of work. The brief states what the worker owns and what it builds on: its goal, context, sources, and output. When workers collide, the defect lies in the brief rather than in either worker.
provisions.example:
A brief carries four sections, each answering one question for the worker.

```text
Goal: the change the worker owns.
Context: the repository facts the change builds on.
Sources: the records and pages to read first.
Output: the files to change and the report to write.
```

provisions.heading: Write Runtime Logs to Streams
provisions.evidence: Does every containerized application write logs to standard output or standard error? Check the application logging configuration.
provisions.statement: A containerized application MUST write logs to standard output or standard error.
provisions.rationale: A container filesystem vanishes with its replica, so a log file inside the container is lost with it. Standard output and standard error hand each line to the platform's log collection, which keeps logs past the life of any one replica.

provisions.heading: Hide Unentitled Actions on Screens
provisions.evidence: Does any screen offer an action the acting plan does not entitle? Read each screen's actions.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST NOT offer an action the acting plan does not entitle.
provisions.rationale: The server refuses what the plan does not entitle, and the screen reflects that refusal before the call. A button for an unentitled action leads to a failure the product already decided. Hiding or disabling the action shows each plan only what it may run.

provisions.heading: Record Each Plan Once
provisions.evidence: Does every plan have its own record with its entitlements? Read the requirement pages under `.litespec/intent/`.
provisions.statement: A consumer selecting `plans` MUST record each plan once with its name and entitlements.
provisions.rationale: A plan named in two places disagrees when one updates without the other: one record allows what the gate refuses. One record per plan holds the name and the entitlements, so a plan change is one edit in one place.
provisions.example: The team plan's record names the export use case it unlocks and the row cap it allows.

provisions.heading: Resolve the Acting Plan from Trusted Context
provisions.evidence: Does every acting plan resolve from verified subscription state rather than caller input? Read the plan resolution code.
provisions.statement: The product MUST resolve the acting plan from verified subscription state, never from caller input.
provisions.rationale: The plan decides what runs, so only verified subscription state resolves it: a plan the caller supplies itself is a choice, not a fact. The [multitenancy extension](../core/tenancy.md) treats tenant identity the same way.

provisions.heading: Resolve the Acting Plan in the Authorization Pipeline
provisions.evidence: Does every use case find the acting plan in the authorization pipeline, or does a plan-resolution convention name where? Read the authorization pipeline and that convention.
provisions.statement: Resolve the acting plan where the pipeline authorizes the use case.
provisions.rationale: Authorization already runs in the pipeline with the actor and the target available. Resolving the plan there gives every use case the same answer from the same verified state, instead of each handler querying subscriptions its own way.

provisions.heading: Authenticate and Authorize Subscriptions
provisions.evidence: Does any connection test accept an unauthenticated connection, or a scoped subscription without an authorization check? Read the connection and subscription tests.
provisions.statement: A realtime server MUST authenticate each connection and authorize every user-, tenant-, or resource-scoped subscription.
provisions.rationale: A connection proves who the caller is; it says nothing about which user's, tenant's, or resource's updates the caller may hear. Each user-, tenant-, or resource-scoped subscription checks its own authorization, so one valid connection cannot receive another tenant's data.

provisions.heading: Bound Realtime Resources
provisions.evidence: Does each of the four deployment bounds have a setting record beside the deployment? Read the setting records and the deployment configuration.
provisions.statement: A realtime deployment MUST set four setting-record bounds: concurrent connections per host, receive message size, parallel invocations per connection, and client timeout.
provisions.rationale: Each open connection holds memory and each message costs CPU, so a flood of either starves the host. The deployment sets four bounds as setting records: concurrent connections per host, receive message size, parallel invocations per connection, and client timeout. Each value comes from the deployment's own connection count and message size and the observation behind it. [The platform's realtime security guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/signalr/security) names the same settings.

provisions.heading: Declare Realtime Freshness
provisions.evidence: Does every realtime-served query declare immediate freshness on its output? Read the served query beside the realtime use case.
provisions.statement: A query served over realtime MUST declare a `freshness` object with `mode` of `immediate` on its output.
provisions.rationale: A realtime channel delivers an update seconds after the change, so the served query declares that speed on its output as `{"mode": "immediate"}`. Without that declaration, a client reading the live value has no way to know how stale it may be.

provisions.heading: Measure Polling Before Choosing Realtime
provisions.evidence: Does every realtime use case page record polling behavior, measured cost, update target, expected connections, and recovery behavior? Read each realtime use case page.
provisions.statement: A realtime use case MUST document polling behavior, measured cost, update target, expected connections, and recovery behavior.
provisions.rationale: Open connections cost memory, CPU, and operating attention on every host, so the team writes down what polling costs, what the update target requires, how many connections to expect, and how recovery works before choosing transport. The use case page holds that record, so a later reviewer sees which measurements justified the choice.

provisions.heading: Place Realtime Code at Outer Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does any realtime transport code sit outside the documented boundaries without a realtime-placement convention? Check the WebApi, Infrastructure, and `lib/realtime/` folders.
provisions.statement: Keep hubs or endpoints in WebApi, publication adapters in Infrastructure, and browser connections under `lib/realtime/`.
provisions.rationale: Hubs, endpoints, publication adapters, and browser connections contain transport and provider detail, not business rules. Keeping them at the outer boundaries leaves each business feature owning only the narrow functions it calls.

provisions.heading: Reconnect and Refresh Authoritative State
provisions.evidence: Does every client reconnect with bounded backoff and refresh authoritative state after a gap? Read the recovery tests.
provisions.statement: A realtime client MUST reconnect with bounded backoff and refresh authoritative state after a connection gap.
provisions.rationale: Connections drop, and notifications sent during the gap are lost. Bounded backoff reconnects without overloading the server, and refreshing authoritative state after the gap replaces whatever the missed notifications would have changed.

provisions.heading: Record the Transport and Its Platform Support
provisions.evidence: Does every realtime use case page name its transport choice and expected hosted-platform support? Read each use case page.
provisions.statement: A realtime use case MUST record its transport choice and expected hosted-platform support.
provisions.rationale: Hosted platforms cap connection duration, idle timeouts, and transport upgrades, and each host caps them differently. Recording the transport choice with its expected platform support reveals the mismatch before deployment instead of during the first long-lived connection.

provisions.heading: Reject Cosmetic Realtime Adoption
provisions.evidence: Does every realtime decision cite a measured update requirement? Read the use case page beside each realtime transport.
provisions.statement: A product MUST NOT activate realtime only to make an interface feel immediate.
provisions.rationale: Realtime transport that serves only a feeling of immediacy spends connection capacity and operating attention without meeting any update target. The extension asks for a measured update requirement first, so polling stays where polling suffices.

provisions.heading: Reject Unbounded Slow-Client Buffering
provisions.evidence: Does any server code path buffer a slow client's stream without a bound or backpressure? Read the connection and send code.
provisions.statement: A realtime server MUST NOT buffer an unbounded stream for a slow client.
provisions.rationale: A client that reads slower than the server writes grows its buffer without end, consuming host memory meant for every subscriber. Bounded buffering with backpressure disconnects the slow client or slows delivery to it, so one slow reader does not starve the rest.

provisions.heading: Revalidate Long-Lived Access
provisions.evidence: Does any connection keep streaming after its token or session expires? Read the revalidation tests.
provisions.statement: A realtime server MUST revalidate long-lived access according to token and session lifetime.
provisions.rationale: A connection can outlive the grant that opened it: tokens expire, roles change, and sessions end. Revalidating access on token and session lifetime closes the connection whose grant ended instead of streaming updates to a caller who no longer qualifies.

provisions.heading: Subscribe Through Narrow Functions
provisions.evidence: Does any feature subscribe to the raw connection instead of a use-case-specific function? Read each feature module's realtime calls.
provisions.statement: Let feature modules subscribe through narrow use-case-specific functions.
provisions.rationale: A feature using the raw connection directly spreads subscription strings and payload shapes through business code. Narrow use-case-specific functions show each subscription's inputs and effects beside the feature that owns them.

provisions.heading: Tolerate Notification Ordering Differences
provisions.evidence: Does any duplicate or reordered notification leave client state wrong? Read the client state tests.
provisions.statement: A realtime client MUST safely handle duplicate and out-of-order notifications.
provisions.rationale: The transport can deliver a notification twice or deliver two of them out of order. A client that applies each notification as an absolute update corrupts its state on the first duplicate. A client built for repeats and reordering reaches the correct state either way.

provisions.heading: Use Server-Sent Events for Notifications
provisions.evidence: Do all one-way notifications travel over server-sent events? Read the notification endpoints in code.
provisions.statement: A one-way server notification use case MUST use server-sent events.
provisions.rationale: A notification that flows one way, from server to browser, has no use for a bidirectional channel with groups and fallback. Server-sent events carry it over plain HTTP, which passes through proxies and firewalls without extra negotiation.

provisions.heading: Use SignalR for Interactive Messaging
provisions.evidence: Does every bidirectional use case run on SignalR? Read each use case's hub code.
provisions.statement: A use case requiring bidirectional messages, server groups, or transport fallback MUST use SignalR.
provisions.rationale: Two-way messages, server-managed groups, and transport fallback need a channel built for interaction, which one-way events cannot provide. SignalR supplies all three, so the use case that needs them takes SignalR instead of forcing one-way events to carry interaction.

provisions.heading: Call the Server Only Through the Generated Client
provisions.evidence: Does every backend call in a `server` app go through the generated client in `{ProjectName}.Client`? Check the backend call sites.
provisions.statement: A `server` consumer's app MUST call the backend only through the generated client in `{ProjectName}.Client`.
provisions.rationale: The generated client owns the base address, the credentials, the headers, and the mapping from a failure to a result. A call that builds its own request opts out of all four at once: it can point at the wrong host, miss the session, and surface a raw failure outside the handler's result shape. Routing every backend call through the one client keeps those decisions in one place.

provisions.heading: Copy Picked Media into the App
provisions.evidence: Does every media import copy the media into app-private storage instead of storing the picker's URI? Check the media imports.
provisions.statement: Media picked from the device MUST be copied into app-private storage on import rather than kept as a reference to the picker's URI.
provisions.rationale: The platform can revoke a picker's URI when the picker closes, and the source file can move or vanish. A screen holding only the URI shows a broken image after either. Copying the media into app-private storage on import keeps the app's copy under the app's own control.

provisions.heading: Keep Persisted State in App-Private Storage
provisions.evidence: Does all persisted state and user-added media live in app-private storage, written through a temporary file? Check the storage writes.
provisions.statement: Persisted state and media the user adds MUST live in the app's private storage, written atomically.
provisions.rationale: App-private storage keeps the user's data inside the app's own sandbox, away from other apps and from the shared media library. A crash mid-write leaves a half-written file, so each write lands in a temporary file that then replaces the target, keeping the previous complete file until the new one is whole. Media the user adds travels with the state that references it, so an export or a reinstall keeps both together.
provisions.example: A filed Claimwick expense report persists as versioned durable state in app-private storage, with its photographed receipts beside it in the same private files.

provisions.heading: Load Persisted State Once
provisions.evidence: Does all persisted state load once at startup into the typed store, with screens showing a loading state until it is ready? Check the startup sequence and the screen loading states.
provisions.statement: Persisted state MUST load once at startup into a typed store that screens read from, with screens showing a loading state until it is ready.
provisions.rationale: Storage reads are slow and can fail, so the app reads once at startup into a typed store that screens read from. A screen that reads storage on render pays an input-output call per frame and can render half-loaded state. A screen renders its loading state until the store finishes loading, so it never shows an unloaded store as ready.

provisions.heading: Refuse Commands While Offline
provisions.evidence: While offline, does every screen show its failure state and queue only what a recorded local convention names with its replay order? Check the command call sites and the offline screens.
provisions.statement: While the network is unavailable, a screen shows its failure state and queues no command; the user retries the command in the foreground when the network returns.
provisions.rationale: A command queued offline runs later against state the user cannot see, so an expense submitted on a train can land after its trip closed or its approval policy changed. Showing the failure state keeps the refusal on the screen that caused it, and queuing nothing keeps every command tied to the screen that sent it. A project that needs offline capture writes its own convention with its replay rules, instead of letting each screen improvise a queue.
provisions.example: With no network, filing expense EXP-1042 for the Rotterdam client visit shows the failure state on the expense screen and sends nothing; the user submits the expense again when the network returns.

provisions.heading: Return Every Refusal in a Typed Result
provisions.evidence: Does every handler return a typed union of success and each named refusal, with every screen mapping each refusal to a message? Check the handler result types and the screens.
provisions.statement: A handler MUST return a typed result union covering success and each named refusal, with each screen mapping every refusal to a message.
provisions.rationale: Signaling a refusal through `null`, an empty collection, or a bare boolean tells the caller that something was refused but not what. Every caller then guesses, and two callers guess differently. A typed result union names success and each refusal, so each screen maps every refusal to the message the application holds for it, with one failure type per refusal.

provisions.heading: Declare Only Used Permissions
provisions.evidence: Does every permission in the app manifest serve a current feature? Check the app manifest beside the features.
provisions.statement: The app manifest MUST declare only the permissions the app's current features use.
provisions.rationale: Each declared permission is a promise the app's features must keep: a declaration without a feature asks for trust no feature uses. Stale declarations accumulate as features leave, and each one asks the user a question no feature needs. Declaring only what current features use keeps the manifest an honest list of the app's needs.

provisions.heading: Hold Audio Focus While Playing Sound
provisions.evidence: Does every audible playback request audio focus first and pause on focus loss? Check the playback code.
provisions.statement: An app playing audible sound MUST request audio focus and pause when it loses focus.
provisions.rationale: One speaker serves every app, so playback without focus talks over navigation prompts, calls, and other players. Requesting focus before playing lets the platform arbitrate between them. Pausing on focus loss yields to whatever took it, and resuming waits for focus to return rather than grabbing it back.

provisions.heading: Keep Device Work in the Foreground
provisions.evidence: Does every background service, scheduled job, and push handler have a project decision naming it? Check the background work beside the decision records.
provisions.statement: Run no background service, scheduled job, or push handler without a project decision naming it.
provisions.rationale: Background work runs where the user cannot see it, spending battery and data on a schedule the app chose. A project decision naming the service, job, or handler records why the work cannot wait for the foreground and what it costs. Without that decision, every device feature runs while the app is visible and stops with it.

provisions.heading: Pause Media in the Background
provisions.evidence: Does all sound and video pause when the app leaves the foreground and resume only on return? Check the lifecycle handling.
provisions.statement: Sound and video MUST pause when the app leaves the foreground and resume only when it returns.
provisions.rationale: An app the user cannot see goes quiet: background sound from a hidden app reads as a bug, and background video decodes frames nobody watches. Pausing when the app leaves the foreground frees the speaker and the decoder for the app now in front, and resuming only on return keeps playback tied to the visible screen.

provisions.heading: Pick Media Through Permissionless System Pickers
provisions.evidence: Does every photo and file pick go through the permissionless system picker where the platform offers one? Check the picking call sites.
provisions.statement: An app MUST pick photos and files through the system picker that needs no storage permission when the platform offers one.
provisions.rationale: A permissionless system picker shows the user exactly what the app receives: the chosen items and nothing else. Requesting broad storage access instead asks for the whole library to read one photo, which the user has good reason to refuse. Using the permissionless picker where the platform offers one keeps the app's access to what the user chose.

provisions.heading: Request a Permission at the Point of Use
provisions.evidence: Is every runtime permission requested from the action that needs it, none at launch? Check the permission requests.
provisions.statement: A runtime permission MUST be requested when the user starts the action that needs it, never at launch.
provisions.rationale: Asked at launch, a permission arrives before the user knows what it is for, so the safe answer is no. Asked when the user starts the action that needs it, the same permission answers a question the user just asked. Each request names the feature waiting on it, so refusing it disables that feature rather than the app.

provisions.heading: Draw Edge to Edge with Insets
provisions.evidence: Does every screen draw edge to edge with its controls and text inside the system bar and cutout insets? Check the screen layouts.
provisions.statement: Screens MUST draw under the system bars and apply the system bar and cutout insets to their controls and text.
provisions.rationale: Drawing under the system bars uses the whole display, but controls and text under a bar or a cutout are unreadable and untappable. Applying the system bar and cutout insets moves controls and text into the visible area while backgrounds keep the full-bleed look. Each stack page names the inset source for its platform.

provisions.heading: Follow the System Back Gesture
provisions.evidence: Does the back gesture close the overlay first, step back one screen, and leave only from the first screen? Check the back handling.
provisions.statement: The system back gesture MUST close the open overlay first, then step back one screen, and leave the app only from the first screen.
provisions.rationale: Users learn one back behavior per platform: the gesture dismisses what is on top before it leaves where they are. An app that leaves from a deeper screen, or that traps the gesture on the first screen, breaks a habit the whole platform teaches. Closing the overlay first, then stepping back one screen, then leaving from the first screen matches that habit on every screen. Each stack page names how the platform's back signal reaches the controller.

provisions.heading: Honor Reduced Motion
provisions.evidence: With animations off, does every screen replace looping motion and video with a still state? Check the screens with animations off.
provisions.statement: When the system turns animations off, a screen MUST replace looping motion and video with a still state.
provisions.rationale: Some users turn animations off because motion causes discomfort, so a screen that keeps looping motion ignores an explicit request. A still state shows the same content without the movement: the final frame, the resting layout. Applying the system's setting on every screen keeps the whole app honoring one choice.

provisions.heading: Meet Touch and Text Accessibility
provisions.evidence: Does every interactive view carry a content description and the platform-minimum touch target, with text scaling with the system font scale? Check the views, the text styles, and the accessibility device tests the Mobile Testing page names.
provisions.statement: Every interactive view MUST carry a content description, meet a minimum touch target of 48 dp on Android or 44 pt on iOS, and scale its text with the system font scale.
provisions.rationale: A view without a content description is silent to a screen reader, and a target below the platform minimum is too small to tap reliably. Text fixed at one size ignores the user who enlarged the system font to read. Meeting the platform target size and scaling with its font scale keeps every screen usable with the platform's own accessibility settings. The device tests on the [Mobile Testing](testing.md) page prove each screen against this rule.

provisions.heading: Own Navigation in One Controller
provisions.evidence: Does all navigation state live in the one controller, with screens raising events instead of navigating? Check the controller and the screens.
provisions.statement: The current screen, the open overlay, and the history MUST live in one controller per app, with screens raising events instead of navigating.
provisions.rationale: A screen that navigates itself keeps a second history nobody else reads, so back behavior and deep links disagree with what the screen shows. Holding the current screen, the open overlay, and the history in one controller gives navigation one answer for every question. Events keep screens decoupled from the controller, so the controller alone decides what each event opens.

provisions.heading: Release Media with Its Screen
provisions.evidence: Is every player, animator, and decoded image released or cancelled when its view leaves the window? Check the view teardown.
provisions.statement: A player, animator, or decoded image MUST be released or cancelled when its view leaves the window.
provisions.rationale: Media holds memory and hardware that the app stops showing once its view leaves the window. A player that keeps playing, an animator that keeps running, or a decoded image that stays resident drains the battery and starves the screen the user now sees. Releasing or cancelling with the view ties each resource's life to the screen that uses it.

provisions.heading: Render with the Platform's Own Views
provisions.evidence: Does every product screen render with the platform's native UI toolkit, none in a WebView or cross-platform layer? Check the screen implementations.
provisions.statement: A mobile app MUST render every screen with the platform's native UI toolkit, with no product screen in a WebView or a cross-platform UI layer.
provisions.rationale: The platform's native toolkit gives each screen the platform's behavior for focus, text input, and accessibility without extra work. A WebView or a cross-platform layer reimplements that behavior and lags behind it, so the screen feels foreign on its own platform. One toolkit also keeps every screen testable through the platform's own device tests.

provisions.heading: Restore the User's Place
provisions.evidence: Does every process recreation return to the screen the saved navigation state names? Check the saved-state handling.
provisions.statement: Save the controller's navigation state in the platform's saved-state mechanism so a process recreation returns to the same screen.
provisions.rationale: The platform destroys background processes when memory runs short. Without saved state, recreation drops the user on the first screen; with the controller's navigation state in the platform's saved-state mechanism, the user returns to the same screen with the same overlay and history. Each stack page names the saved-state mechanism for its platform.

provisions.heading: Route App Links to Flow Entry Screens
