provisions.evidence: Does every app link open the flow entry screen and record it names, resolved through the one controller? Check the app link handling and the controller.
provisions.statement: A screen a flow can be entered from MUST open directly from its app link, with the controller resolving the link to that screen and its record.
provisions.rationale: A flow that starts outside the app, in a message or a browser page, lands on the screen the link names rather than on the first screen with the work still to find. The controller resolves the link, so a cold start and a link that arrives while the app runs open the same screen with the same history behind it. Each stack page names how its platform delivers the link to the controller.
provisions.example: A Claimwick approval message for expense EXP-1042 carries an app link that opens the approval screen for EXP-1042, with the expenses list behind it for back.

provisions.heading: Accept App Links in the Host Activity
provisions.evidence: Does the host Activity receive app links on both a cold start and while running? Check the intent filter and both overrides.
provisions.statement: The host Activity MUST receive app links in `OnCreate` and `OnNewIntent`, through an `IntentFilter` with `AutoVerify` set.
provisions.rationale: Handling both entry points lets a cold start and a link that arrives while the app runs open the same screen, and `AutoVerify` lets the platform open the app instead of a browser.
provisions.example: A link to `https://claimwick.example/claims/` opens the claim screen its path names, whether the app was closed or open.

provisions.heading: Apply System Insets to Each Screen
provisions.evidence: Does every screen keep its controls and text clear of the system bars and cutouts? Check the screen layouts and the inset handling.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST apply the system bar and display cutout insets it reads from `WindowInsets` to its controls and text.
provisions.rationale: The window supplies these insets, so reading them from `WindowInsets` keeps controls and text clear of the bars and cutouts on every device.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense claim screen pads its submit button by the system bar inset while its background draws full bleed.

provisions.heading: Declare Android Outside the Controlled UI Contract
provisions.evidence: Does every Android frontend declare an entry point record naming Android and its replacement boundaries? Check the entry point records.
provisions.statement: An Android frontend MUST declare an entry point record naming Android and the boundaries that replace the controlled UI contract.
provisions.rationale: The shared contract covers the Svelte web stack, so an Android frontend with no declaration reads as a frontend with nothing to check. Naming Android and its replacement boundaries reports it as a frontend with named replacements instead.
provisions.example: The Claimwick Android entry point record names Android and the native view review standing in for the controlled contract.

provisions.heading: Hold One Navigation Controller in the Platform Project
provisions.evidence: Does navigation run through the one controller owned by the host Activity, with no screen navigating on its own? Check the screen classes and the host Activity.
provisions.statement: The Android app MUST hold its navigation controller in one class in the platform project, owned by the host Activity.
provisions.rationale: One controller holds the current screen, the open overlay, and the history, so no screen navigates on its own.
provisions.example: The Claimwick host Activity creates the one controller class, and every expense screen raises events to it.

provisions.heading: Keep Android Core Test Mocks to the Owned Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does any core test replace a Domain type or an Application handler? Check the test doubles.
provisions.statement: A core test MUST NOT replace the Domain types or the Application handlers it proves.
provisions.rationale: A stand-in for the code under test proves the stand-in, so the test reaches the rule only through the real types and handlers.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense claim test builds a real Domain claim and calls the real submit handler, replacing only the platform storage adapter.

provisions.heading: Keep Hosts and Failure Views Unmarked
provisions.evidence: Do any host Activities or failure views carry a screen mark? Check the platform project.
provisions.statement: A host Activity or a failure view MUST NOT carry a screen mark.
provisions.rationale: A host or failure view draws no screen of its own, so a mark on it links an address to a screen it does not show.
provisions.example: The Claimwick host Activity class carries no `<implements>` mark.

provisions.heading: Keep Screen Styles in Resources
provisions.evidence: Does every screen take its colors and text styles from `Resources/values/styles.xml`, with none set in code? Check the screen classes.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST take its colors and text styles from `Resources/values/styles.xml` and set no style value in code.
provisions.rationale: Resources hold every color and text style in one place, and a screen that sets a value in code is a second style that no resource answers to.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense total uses the `TotalText` style from `Resources/values/styles.xml`, setting no color in its screen class.

provisions.heading: Keep the Android Frame, Routes, and Modules
provisions.evidence: Does every screen class sit under `Screens/` and call Application handlers instead of holding use-case logic? Check the platform project and the core projects.
provisions.statement: An Android frontend MUST hold its frame in the host code of the platform project, its routes as screen classes under `Screens/`, and its use-case code as Application handlers, with no module mirror: each screen maps to the records it serves through its mark.
provisions.rationale: Three fixed locations let a reader and a tool find the frame, the screens, and the use-case code in the same place in every Android app. The three-segment module mirror does not apply on this stack: screens group by module under `Screens/`, and each screen class carries the mark of the screen it renders.
provisions.example: The Claimwick Android app keeps its navigation host in `Claimwick.Android`, its expense list screen in `Screens/Expenses/`, and its expense handlers in the Application project.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Android Screen with Its Screen Record
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for a screen mark outside the `Screens/` root.
provisions.statement: A screen class under `Screens/` MUST carry the `<implements>` mark of the screen it renders, in the form the .NET stack states.
provisions.rationale: The mark links the screen to its record the way a .NET handler carries its use-case mark, so the builder and the check read one link.
provisions.example: The Claimwick `ExpenseListScreen` carries `/// <implements>screen/claimwick-app.expense-list</implements>`.

provisions.heading: Read Android Copy Through the Generated Resource Class
provisions.evidence: Does every screen read its copy through the generated `Resource` class? Check the screen classes and the layouts.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST read every copy string through the generated `Resource` class, with its fallback in `Resources/values/strings.xml`.
provisions.rationale: The generated class gives every copy key a typed name, and the default values folder gives every key a fallback when a language lacks it.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list reads its empty-state sentence as `Resource.String.ExpenseListEmpty`, with the Spanish file supplying the translation.

provisions.heading: Request Audio Focus Before Playing Sound
provisions.evidence: Does every screen that plays sound request audio focus first and pause on focus loss? Check the playback call sites.
provisions.statement: A screen that plays sound MUST request audio focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` before it plays, and pause when focus is lost.
provisions.rationale: One speaker serves every app, so the platform arbitrates only the apps that ask for focus, and pausing on loss yields to navigation prompts and calls.
provisions.example: The Claimwick confirmation chime plays only after the app holds audio focus, and a phone call pauses it.

provisions.heading: Request Permissions at the Point of Use
provisions.evidence: Is every runtime permission requested through `RequestPermissions` when its action starts, none in `OnCreate`? Check the host Activity and the action handlers.
provisions.statement: The Android app MUST request each runtime permission through `RequestPermissions` when the action that needs it starts, never in `OnCreate`.
provisions.rationale: A request at the point of use arrives when the visitor knows what it is for, and the same permission answers a question the visitor just asked.
provisions.example: The Claimwick app requests the camera permission when the visitor taps Scan receipt, not at launch.

provisions.heading: Route the Back Gesture Through the Activity Dispatcher
provisions.evidence: Does every back gesture reach the controller through the Activity's dispatcher, leaving the app only from the first screen? Check the host Activity and the controller.
provisions.statement: The host Activity MUST deliver the system back gesture to the navigation controller through its `OnBackInvokedDispatcher`.
provisions.rationale: The dispatcher is the platform's own path for the back signal, so predictive back reaches the controller as the same overlay-then-screen-then-leave order on every screen.
provisions.example: On the Claimwick expense detail screen, a back gesture closes an open overlay first, then steps back to the expense list.

provisions.heading: Run Android Core Tests on xunit.v3
provisions.evidence: Does every core test run in a plain .NET test project on the pinned `xunit.v3`, with no emulator? Check the core test projects.
provisions.statement: The Android app MUST run its core tests as plain .NET test projects on `xunit.v3`, the version `packages.nuget` pins.
provisions.rationale: Core tests need no emulator, so a plain .NET runner keeps them fast, and one pinned runner keeps every core project on the same version.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense claim rule has its test in an xunit.v3 project beside the Domain project it proves.

provisions.heading: Store Navigation State in the Activity Bundle
provisions.evidence: Does the host Activity save and restore the controller's navigation state through its `Bundle`? Check the host Activity and the controller.
provisions.statement: The host Activity MUST save the navigation controller's state in its `Bundle` from `OnSaveInstanceState` and restore it in `OnCreate`.
provisions.rationale: The platform ends the process in the background when memory runs short, and the saved bundle returns the visitor to the same screen with the same overlay and history.
provisions.example: When the platform ends the Claimwick process, the app reopens on the expense detail screen with its overlay still open.

provisions.heading: Store Persisted State in App-Private Storage
provisions.evidence: Does all persisted state and user media live under `Context.FilesDir`, written atomically? Check the storage adapters.
provisions.statement: Persisted state and user media MUST live under `Context.FilesDir`, written atomically.
provisions.rationale: The app's own sandbox keeps the data away from other apps and the shared media library, and an atomic write keeps the previous complete file if a write stops midway.
provisions.example: The Claimwick receipts the visitor adds are copied into the app's files directory, replacing their previous copy only after the new one is whole.

provisions.heading: Use the System Pickers for Media
provisions.evidence: Does every screen pick photos and files through the system pickers, with no storage permission requested for it? Check the picking call sites and the manifest.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST pick photos through the Photo Picker action `android.provider.action.PICK_IMAGES` and files through `android.intent.action.OPEN_DOCUMENT`.
provisions.rationale: Both pickers grant access to the chosen items only, so the app needs no storage permission to read one receipt.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick app, adding a receipt photo opens the Photo Picker, and the visitor's choice is the only image the app receives.

provisions.heading: Keep Core Projects Platform-Free
provisions.evidence: Does every core project target plain .NET with no platform SDK reference? Check the core project files and sources.
provisions.statement: Domain, Application, Infrastructure, and Client core projects MUST target plain .NET and reference no platform SDK type.
provisions.rationale: A core project that names a platform SDK type compiles only for that platform, so a second platform app copies the core instead of reusing it. Targeting plain .NET with no platform reference keeps the core compiling for every platform unchanged, with platform differences behind the interfaces Application owns and the adapters in the platform projects.

provisions.heading: Match Core Projects to the Product Shape
provisions.evidence: Does every `client-only` solution hold Domain, Application, and Infrastructure projects, and every `server` solution the Client project with no Domain copy? Check the solution tree.
provisions.statement: A mobile consumer MUST hold Domain, Application, and Infrastructure core projects in the `client-only` shape, and a `{ProjectName}.Client` core project with the generated API client instead of them in the `server` shape.
provisions.rationale: Where the rules live decides what the app holds. A product with no server carries its own domain model in Domain, Application, and Infrastructure projects. A product with a server keeps its rules there, and the app holds a Client project with the generated API client instead, reaching every rule through that client. A copy of the rules in the app drifts from the server's rules on the first change, and the app then enforces a rule the server does not hold.

provisions.heading: Organize Screens by Module
provisions.evidence: Does every screen sit under `Screens/`, in its module folder in a multi-module product? Check the platform project tree.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST live under `Screens/` in the platform project, in a folder for its module when the product has more than one module.
provisions.rationale: A reader holding a module record finds its screens by path when screens group by module. One folder for a single-module product would add a level that distinguishes nothing, so its screens sit directly under `Screens/`. Use-case code reached from a screen lives in Application, so the screen folder holds the screen and the handler holds the behavior. The three-segment module mirror does not apply: each screen maps to the records it serves through its mark, as the [Android Stack](stack.md) states.

provisions.heading: Place Platform Adapters in the Platform Project
provisions.evidence: Does every platform API surface have one adapter type in the platform project behind an interface Application owns? Check the platform project adapters.
provisions.statement: Place adapters for players, pickers, sensors, and storage locations in the platform project behind an interface Application owns, one type per platform API surface.
provisions.rationale: Each platform API surface gets one adapter type in the platform project, implementing an interface declared in Application. That puts every platform call behind a testable boundary the core tests can substitute. The platform project is the only layer naming the platform SDK, so each adapter resolves to its platform API by name.

provisions.heading: Use the Mobile Solution Tree
provisions.evidence: Does every mobile app live in the one solution at `apps/mobile/`, with core projects under `src/` and one `{ProjectName}.{Platform}` app project per platform? Check the `apps/mobile/` tree.
provisions.statement: A consumer selecting a mobile stack MUST hold its mobile apps in one solution at `apps/mobile/` with core projects under `src/` and one app project per platform named `{ProjectName}.{Platform}`.
provisions.rationale: One solution gives every platform app one core to share, so a second platform reuses the domain model unchanged. Core projects under `src/` separate shared code from the platform apps that consume it, and one app project per platform named `{ProjectName}.{Platform}` makes each platform's screens findable by name. A reader moves from the solution to a screen by rule rather than by search. This replaces the API solution path in `litespec/workspace/structure#use-the-canonical-root-tree`, because a client-only consumer has no API directory.
provisions.example:
```text
apps/mobile/
  {ProjectName}.Mobile.slnx
  src/
    {ProjectName}.Domain/
    {ProjectName}.Application/
    {ProjectName}.Infrastructure/
    {ProjectName}.Android/
  tests/
    {ProjectName}.Domain.Tests/
    {ProjectName}.Application.Tests/
    {ProjectName}.Android.Tests/
```

The framework-generated `bin`, `obj`, and `publish` folders stay untracked.

provisions.heading: Prove Screens on a Device or Emulator
provisions.evidence: Does every screen a use case reaches have a device test driving it on an emulator or a device? Check the device tests beside the screens.
provisions.statement: Each screen a use case reaches MUST have a device test that drives it on an emulator or device.
provisions.rationale: Screens render through the platform toolkit, so only a device test meets them where users do: layout, insets, back behavior, and accessibility. A screen no device test drives is proved by nothing, whatever the core tests cover. Driving each screen a use case reaches on an emulator or device keeps every reachable screen proved.

provisions.heading: Prove Touch and Text Accessibility on a Device
provisions.evidence: Does every screen have a device test checking content descriptions, platform-minimum touch targets, and text scaling with the system font scale? Check the device tests beside the screens.
provisions.statement: A device test for each screen MUST check that every interactive view carries a content description and the platform-minimum touch target, and that text scales with the system font scale.
provisions.rationale: A screen that looks right at the default font size can still hide its commands from a screen reader, offer a target too small to tap reliably, or clip text a reader enlarged. Checking descriptions, targets, and scaling on a device meets the screen with the platform accessibility settings its visitors use, not the settings the developer happened to keep. This proves `litespec/packs/android/screens#meet-touch-and-text-accessibility` on each screen.

provisions.heading: Test the Core as Plain .NET
provisions.evidence: Does every core test project run on the plain .NET runner with no emulator? Check the core test projects.
provisions.statement: Domain, Application, Infrastructure, and Client tests MUST run as plain .NET test projects with no emulator.
provisions.rationale: Core tests need no emulator, device, or platform host, because the core holds no platform type. Plain .NET test projects in xunit.v3, the framework the manifest pins, keep them fast. A core test that needs a device proves the layering already broke, and the fix belongs in the layering rather than in the test setup.

provisions.heading: Try the Release Build on Hardware Before Publishing
provisions.evidence: Does every release record one physical device per platform with the result of the hand check? Check the release records.
provisions.statement: Install the release build and try it by hand on one physical device per platform before publishing, and record the device and result.
provisions.rationale: Emulators approximate performance, sensors, and vendor behavior, and hardware differs on all three. Trying the release build by hand on one physical device per platform meets the app as users will. The recorded device and result make the check reviewable; a release without that record ships on emulator evidence alone.

provisions.heading: Approve Five Golden Archetype Screens
provisions.evidence: Do the five golden screens carry recorded approval on the stated viewport in both themes? Check the recorded baseline beside the emulator screenshots.
provisions.statement: The team MUST approve five golden screens before building all routes: shell with bottom navigation, list, record detail, settings drill-down, and form, each on the 1080 by 2400 emulator viewport in light and dark.
provisions.rationale: Five approved screens lock the look early: spacing, type, color, and navigation read in pixels, not prose. Later screens copy approved patterns instead of inventing new ones.
provisions.example: The Claimwick team approves the golden expense list on the emulator in both themes before building the remaining screens.

provisions.heading: Record Emulator Screenshots in UI Review
provisions.evidence: Does every new or changed screen carry a fresh capture beside its golden archetype? Check the review output.
provisions.statement: `litespec ui review` MUST capture emulator screenshots of new or changed screens beside their golden archetype screen.
provisions.rationale: A side-by-side capture shows drift the text review misses: misaligned columns, uneven rhythm, or a new pattern beside the approved one. Capturing on the same viewport in both themes keeps the comparison honest.
provisions.example: A new Claimwick report screen captures beside the golden list screen at 1080 by 2400 in light and dark.

provisions.heading: Show One Settings Facet per Screen
provisions.evidence: Does any settings screen hold two configuration facets? Check each settings screen under `Screens/`.
provisions.statement: Settings MUST open as a hub list that pushes one focused drill-down screen per configuration facet, with no screen holding two facets.
provisions.rationale: A hub list names every facet in one place, and each drill-down edits one facet with one save path. Two facets on one phone screen stack long forms that bury the second facet below the fold.
provisions.example: The Claimwick business settings hub pushes one drill-down for invoicing details and another for senders, each with its own save.

provisions.heading: Keep 48dp Minimum Touch Targets
provisions.evidence: Does every interactive view meet the 48dp minimum? Check the device tests beside the screens.
provisions.statement: Every interactive view MUST offer a touch target of at least 48dp.
provisions.rationale: A smaller target misses taps, especially while walking. The 48dp minimum matches the platform rule the device tests prove.
provisions.example: The Claimwick approve button keeps its full 48dp target even where its visible shape is smaller.

provisions.heading: Keep Drill-Down Depth Shallow
provisions.evidence: Does any settings path run deeper than hub, facet, and one detail without a recorded map? Check the settings screens.
provisions.statement: Keep settings drill-downs to hub, facet, and at most one deeper level, with a visible back path at each level.
provisions.rationale: Each level buries the hub one step further, and the visitor loses the path back. Three levels stay navigable: the hub, the facet, and one detail. Deeper trees need their own recorded map.
provisions.example: The Claimwick invoicing drill-down opens numbering as its one deeper level, each with a visible back path.

provisions.heading: Keep One Job per Screen
provisions.evidence: Does any screen serve two jobs or carry more than three actions? Check each screen class under `Screens/`.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST serve one job with at most three actions.
provisions.rationale: A phone screen shows less than a desktop page, so a second job crowds out the first. One job per screen keeps each screen focused enough to finish with a thumb. A job that needs more actions splits into two screens.
provisions.example: The Claimwick approval screen shows one approval with approve, refuse, and history actions only.

provisions.heading: Keep Spacing and Type in Resource Tokens
provisions.evidence: Does every spacing and type value resolve to a named resource token? Check the screen classes and layouts beside `dimens.xml` and `styles.xml`.
provisions.statement: Spacing and type MUST resolve to named resource tokens: spacing to the 4dp, 8dp, 16dp, and 24dp steps in `Resources/values/dimens.xml`, and type to the styles in `Resources/values/styles.xml`.
provisions.rationale: Named tokens keep every screen on one rhythm: two screens from different authors still align. Inline values drift one screen at a time until the app holds a dozen near-equal paddings.
provisions.example: The Claimwick list screen pads rows 16dp from `dimens.xml` and draws titles in the agreed style from `styles.xml`.

provisions.heading: Keep the Bottom Bar on Top-Level Screens
provisions.evidence: Does the bar stay visible on every top-level destination with a back path on deeper screens? Check the navigation controller.
provisions.statement: Top-level destinations MUST keep the bottom bar visible, with drill-down and form screens showing a back path instead.
provisions.rationale: The bar orients the visitor among destinations, so it stays where destinations change. A drill-down or form has one job with one way back, so a back path replaces the bar and keeps the focus on the task.
provisions.example: The Claimwick list screens keep the bar visible, while the filing form shows a back path to the list.

provisions.heading: Mirror Desktop Jobs on Mobile
provisions.evidence: Does every mobile screen name a desktop job, with differences recorded? Check the screens beside the product record.
provisions.statement: Name each mobile screen for the same job its desktop archetype serves, with fewer actions and a narrower layout.
provisions.rationale: One job vocabulary across platforms keeps records, tests, and support speaking one language. The phone layout narrows the presentation but keeps the job name, so a record still maps to one screen on each platform.
provisions.example: The Claimwick mobile expense list serves the same list job as desktop with search and open actions only.

provisions.heading: Keep Primary Navigation in the Bottom Bar
provisions.evidence: Does primary navigation run through a bottom bar of three to five destinations on top-level screens? Check the navigation controller and the host Activity.
provisions.statement: Primary navigation MUST run through bottom navigation with three to five destinations, visible on top-level screens.
provisions.rationale: The bottom bar sits under the thumb and stays visible, so the visitor always knows where they are and where they can go. A drawer hides destinations behind a gesture, and more than five items shrink below tappable width.
provisions.example: The Claimwick app navigates between home, documents, entries, and settings through four bottom destinations.

provisions.heading: Show Every Screen in Both Themes
provisions.evidence: Does every screen carry light and dark previews from the emulator? Check the review evidence.
provisions.statement: Preview every screen on the emulator in light and dark before sending it to review.
provisions.rationale: A screen approved in one theme can fail in the other: light text on a light fill, or a dark fill that swallows the divider. Previewing both themes before review catches the failure where the fix is cheap.
provisions.example: The Claimwick filing form previews in both themes on the emulator before review, catching a low-contrast hint in dark mode.

provisions.heading: Refuse Inline Sizing in Screens
provisions.evidence: The Roslyn analyzer reports inline sizing in screen classes, and review refuses any `Screens/*.cs` change that sets a size, margin, or color.
provisions.statement: C# screen classes MUST NOT set pixel sizes, margins, or colors inline.
provisions.rationale: An inline value bypasses the tokens review approved, so the screen drifts from the baseline one value at a time. Refusing inline values forces every value through a named token a reviewer can check.
provisions.example: A Claimwick screen that needs wider padding adds a token to `dimens.xml` instead of setting pixels in `Screens/`.

provisions.heading: Match Type to the System Setting
provisions.evidence: Does any text clip or overlap at enlarged font scales? Check the device tests beside the screens.
provisions.statement: Text MUST scale with the system font scale without clipping or overlap.
provisions.rationale: Readers who enlarge system text do so to read. Fixed-size text ignores their choice, and clipped text hides the words they enlarged to see. Fluid layouts with scaled type keep every screen readable at every setting.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense total wraps instead of clipping when the reader enlarges system text.

provisions.heading: Show One Primary Action per Screen
provisions.evidence: Does any screen offer two primary actions? Check each screen class under `Screens/`.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST offer at most one primary action, placed where the thumb reaches it.
provisions.rationale: Two primaries force the visitor to weigh buttons instead of acting. One primary action names the screen's job: everything else stays secondary or moves to another screen.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list offers New filing as its single primary action, with search and open as secondary.

provisions.heading: Use Material 3 Color Roles
provisions.evidence: Does any screen class set a hardcoded color? Check the screen classes beside the declared color roles.
provisions.statement: Screen colors MUST come from Material 3 color roles declared in resources, never from hardcoded color values in screen code.
provisions.rationale: Color roles carry both light and dark values with the contrast each pair promises. A hardcoded color fixes one theme and breaks the other, so dark mode shows unreadable text on dark fills.
provisions.example: The Claimwick warning banner uses the warning role, which resolves to its light value in day mode and its dark value at night.

provisions.heading: Compose the Host in Program.cs
provisions.evidence: Does `Program.cs` hold the recorded composition order with every step present? Look at `Program.cs`.
provisions.statement: `Program.cs` calls `AddPlatform` and `AddModules`, then holds middleware order, endpoint mapping, health endpoints, OpenAPI, and host startup, ending with an empty partial `Program` class.
provisions.rationale: Middleware runs in registration order, so authentication registered after endpoints does not run. When one file shows the whole sequence, a reviewer sees the order at a glance; when registration scatters across files, a misplaced call is hard to spot. This file binds `litespec/core/backend-architecture#compose-each-process-explicitly` for WebApi.
provisions.example: The visible order is the `AddPlatform` and `AddModules` calls, then trusted forwarded headers, exception handling, transport security, authentication, authorization, endpoints, and then health. Forwarded headers appear only when the deployment boundary requires trusted proxies. OpenAPI and Scalar map only in Development.

provisions.heading: Convert Money with the Platform Converter
provisions.evidence: Does every `Money` value on the wire pass through the platform converter, with a string amount and a three-letter code in both directions? Look at the converters registered for the host and the monetary fields in the contract.
provisions.statement: WebApi MUST convert `Money` through the platform converter, which writes the amount as an invariant decimal string, reads only a string amount with a three-letter currency code, and registers once through `AddPlatform`.
provisions.rationale: A `decimal` property serializes as a JSON number, breaking the wire shape `{ "amount": "12.50", "currency": "EUR" }` that `litespec/core/backend-domain#model-money-with-exact-decimal-values` fixes. One converter in `Platform/Http`, registered once for the host, keeps every serializer producing the contracted shape, including a test client using default options. It reads only a string amount with a three-letter code, so a number amount or a code of another length is refused instead of parsed.

provisions.heading: Declare Operation Metadata in the Contract
provisions.evidence: Does every operation declare a stable `operationId`, a summary, authorization, request, success, and Problem Details metadata, and typed results or `Produces` entries? Look at each operation.
provisions.statement: An operation MUST declare a stable `operationId`, a summary, its authorization, request, success, and Problem Details metadata, and typed results or `Produces` metadata.
provisions.rationale: Generated clients name their calls from `operationId`, so an unnamed or unstable operation breaks every client regeneration. Authorization and Problem Details metadata tell a client which policies apply and which failures to handle; without them the client guesses. Route-lambda comments do not reach the contract, so the summary is declared explicitly. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-api#declare-stable-operation-metadata-in-the-contract` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Derive HTTP Statuses from Refusal Codes
provisions.evidence: Does every refusal code map to its outcome-table status in the one `IExceptionHandler`? Look at the WebApi global handler.
provisions.statement: WebApi MUST map each refusal code to its HTTP status in one global handler.
provisions.rationale: The specification records each refusal with its stable `code` and no transport status, so each stack derives the status its transport needs. The outcome-to-status assignment is stated in `litespec/core/backend-api#use-consistent-status-codes`; this provision binds it for .NET. The handler uses ASP.NET Core `AddProblemDetails` with one `IExceptionHandler`: - Validation failures answer 400. - Missing targets answer through the operation's 404 policy. - Forbidden failures answer 403 or the declared 404 disclosure policy. - Conflicts and state rejections answer 409. - Unexpected failures answer 500 with code `internal_error`. The derived `invalid-input` refusal answers 400 under the project's `refusals.invalidInput` code, and the derived `forbidden` refusal answers 403 or the declared 404 under the project's `refusals.forbidden` code. The derived `rule-not-stated` refusal answers 409. Known Domain exception types map individually, and a cancellation from a disconnected request is not reported as an application error.

provisions.heading: Exclude MVC Controllers from the Stack
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2003` for a WebApi class deriving from `ControllerBase` or carrying `ApiController`.
provisions.statement: WebApi code MUST NOT route requests through MVC controllers or `ControllerBase`.
provisions.rationale: Controllers and endpoint classes route, filter, and map errors through different models. When both exist, a reviewer checks two mappings for every behavior, and error responses drift apart. With one model, one place defines how requests reach handlers and how failures reach clients.

provisions.heading: Map Failures to Statuses in the Global Exception Handler
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2035` for an exception type the global handler leaves outside the status map.
provisions.statement: The one `IExceptionHandler` MUST map each failure to the status the exception-to-status map declares for it.
provisions.rationale: This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-api#map-every-failure-to-its-declared-status` for .NET: the one `IExceptionHandler` registered through `AddExceptionHandler` carries the whole map, so each failure reaches the client through the one map. The 500 problem detail names the exception type and message only when the host runs in the Development environment; a hosted environment answers the stable code with no exception detail.
provisions.example: The global handler answers an unknown expense with 404 and its problem detail, a malformed expense identifier with 400, and a fault no refusal covers with 500. That 500 carries the exception type and message when the host runs in Development, and the stable `internal_error` code with no exception detail in any other environment.

provisions.heading: Use One Endpoint per Operation
provisions.evidence: Does every mapped route run through one `IEndpoint` type that converts input, dispatches, and maps the result? Look at the endpoints in the use case folders.
provisions.statement: A WebApi endpoint MUST implement `IEndpoint`, map one route operation, convert input to an Application message, dispatch through its mediator, and map the result.
provisions.rationale: When one class serves one route, a reviewer finds the input mapping, the dispatch, and the result mapping for that route in one place. Without that rule, operations share classes or helpers, so a change to one route silently affects another, and a second routing pattern grows beside the first unnoticed. A use case a provider callback runs is the exception: the pipeline handler in the module `Infrastructure/Pipeline/` folder carries the use case mark as its endpoint, so it implements no `IEndpoint` and no screen calls it. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-api#map-one-operation-per-endpoint` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Bind Command Handlers to Load, Call, and Stage
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2012` for a handler that throws a forbidden refusal or takes the authorization guard, `LS2013` for an audit call that reads the message, `LS2014` for a find followed by a create, `LS2015` for a store inside a loop, and `LS2021` for a handler holding a command or event mediator.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST load or create one aggregate through its repository, call one domain method on it, stage it, and return the result.
provisions.rationale: The handler body has three steps: the load or creation, the one domain call, and the stage. A required load uses the throwing `GetByIdAsync`, and an optional lookup uses the nullable `FindBy...Async`, under `litespec/packs/dotnet/domain#keep-repository-interfaces-in-domain`. The message carries the pipeline-stamped timestamp as `HandledAt` under `litespec/core/backend-application#read-time-from-the-scoped-clock` (see `litespec/packs/dotnet/application#bind-the-pipeline-to-the-pinned-litebus-apis`), so the handler stamps decisions without reading a clock. Validation, authorization, idempotency, audit, holds, and the commit are pipeline stages, not handler code. Messages, provider calls, and writes to other aggregates run in event handlers after the commit, under `litespec/packs/dotnet/application#dispatch-declared-effects-through-their-entry-points`. The handler takes no `ICommandMediator` or `IEventMediator`; it takes `IQueryMediator` only to send another module's public query with a declared `queries` edge. A use case whose record declares `consistency: atomic` over several aggregates is the one exception: the handler loads, calls, and stages each aggregate its `writes` names, one method each. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage` and `litespec/core/backend-application#load-a-required-record-or-refuse-it` for .NET, where `GetByIdAsync` and `FindBy...Async` are the forms.

provisions.heading: Bind the Pipeline to the Pinned LiteBus APIs
provisions.evidence: Does every pipeline position use its pinned LiteBus API? Check the command pipeline composition.
provisions.statement: An Application MUST compose its command pipeline through the LiteBus APIs this provision names for commit, authorization, audit, idempotency, fault classification, delivery, event staging, immediate dispatch, and the timestamp.
provisions.rationale: One pinned binding per position keeps every project's pipeline identical: - The commit runs through `commands.UseMartenUnitOfWork()`, which registers the LiteBus `IUnitOfWork` at `HandlerPriorities.UnitOfWork`, so the pipeline commits once under `litespec/packs/dotnet/persistence#commit-once-in-the-command-pipeline`. - Authorization runs through a guard derived from `LiteBus.Messaging.Abstractions.AuthorizationGuard<TMessage>`, which reads the declaration through `DeclarationGuard<TMessage, TValue>`. The guard reads the declaration from the message's `{Message}AuthorizationDefinition`, which implements `IAuthorizationDefinition<TMessage>` beside the message under `litespec/core/backend-application#enforce-target-authorization-in-the-pipeline`. The project's `AuthorizeAsync(policy, message, cancellationToken)` answers whether the caller holds the declared policy; LiteBus carries the policy and never evaluates it. - Audit runs through `AuditDeclaration.Audited(...).WithTargetFrom<TCommand>(...).WithReasonFrom<TCommand>(...)` in the message's `{Message}AuditDefinition`, which implements `IAuditDefinition<TCommand>` from `LiteBus.Messaging.Abstractions.Auditing`, declaring the target and reason beside the message under `litespec/core/backend-application#declare-the-audit-target-and-reason-beside-the-message`. - The audit chain runs through `AddAuditing(auditing => auditing.UseMartenStore().UseHashChain(chain => ...))`, with `UseMartenStore` from `LiteBus.Auditing.Storage.Marten`. The chain writes its records in the Marten session of the business unit of work, so a captured record commits or rolls back with the change. `StoreAs<TDocument, TMapper>()` names the stored document and its `IAuditRecordMapper<TDocument>`, `SegmentBy<TSegmenter>()` the `IAuditSegmenter<TDocument>`, `SignCheckpointsWith<TSigner>()` the `ICheckpointSigner`, `CheckpointWhen(...)` the `ICheckpointPolicy`, `PublishCheckpointsTo<TPublisher>()` the `ICheckpointPublisher`, and `VerifyAgainst<TSource>()` the `ICheckpointSource`. The Marten store registers its `IAuditCanonicalizer<TDocument>` as a replaceable default. - Idempotency runs through the message's `{Message}IdempotencyDefinition`, which implements `IIdempotencyDefinition<TMessage>`, declaring the message's idempotency beside the message. A record of mode `key` keys the message with its key template. A record of mode `key` with `replay: returns-first-result` declares `replayResult: true`, so a repeat returns the first result; with `replay: refuses` or `replay: acts-again` it declares `replayResult: false`, so a repeat brings no stored result. A keyed declaration that omits the flag replays nothing, so `model check` reports `idempotency-replay-drift` when its record states `returns-first-result`. A record of mode `state` or `none` declares an exemption: a state command recognizes the repeat by the state its `recognizedBy` names, and a pipeline key would outlive that state, so a grant, a revoke and a second grant would replay the first answer. - Fault classification runs through `UseFaultRefusalClassifierInstance(new PostgreSqlConstraintRefusalClassifier(map))`, mapping each store fault to its refusal under `litespec/core/backend-persistence#map-a-constraint-violation-to-its-refusal`. - Delivery runs through `outbox.EnablePerHandlerDelivery()`, reaching each handler separately, one envelope per subscribed handler so one failing handler retries alone, under `litespec/core/outbox#give-each-handler-its-own-delivery`. - Event staging runs through `outbox.StageCollectedEvents()`, which drains the facts `IDomainEventCollector` holds and stages them in the same commit as the aggregate change. Harvesting moves the domain events an aggregate raised into that collector before the drain, so a handler does not call `Collect` for them: - `outbox.HarvestDomainEvents(...)` on the outbox builder names the aggregate root base. Its open generic definition, such as `typeof(AggregateRoot<>)`, covers every aggregate built on the base and gives the accessor that reads and clears its buffered events. An aggregate that implements `IHasDomainEvents` harvests without it. - The Marten harvester is registered on the storage builder: `postgres.UseDataSource(dataSource).UseMartenTransactionalOutbox().HarvestDomainEvents()`. - Each domain event type takes one decision. `TranslateDomainEvent<TEvent>(...)` stages the module events and integration events it translates, and `IgnoreDomainEvent<TEvent>()` drops it. `RequireDomainEventDecision()` makes staging fail before the commit when a harvested event has no decision. A translation builds each module event by its static `From` method from the domain event alone. - Hand collection stays on `IDomainEventCollector` in three cases: a deletion by predicate or by id, which carries no document for the harvester to read; a carrier type that is never stored; and an event raised outside an aggregate. - In-process dispatch runs through `outbox.UseInProcessDispatch()` with `outbox.EnableOutboxProcessor()`, delivering module events and domain-event reactions inside the process against the product's PostgreSQL database. A Marten project stores outbox rows in its own session and transaction through `LiteBus.Outbox.Storage.Marten` (`outbox.UsePostgreSqlStorage(postgres => postgres.UseDataSource(dataSource).UseMartenTransactionalOutbox().HarvestDomainEvents())`), and a project that persists through Entity Framework Core uses `LiteBus.Outbox.Storage.EntityFrameworkCore`. Envelopes commit with the business work; the processor retries a failed handler with the configured backoff and dead-letters at the bound. No broker is needed for anything inside the bounded context. An outbound integration event uses a transport dispatcher (`LiteBus.Outbox.Dispatch.Amqp` or `LiteBus.Outbox.Dispatch.Kafka`) toward the external system its record names in `through`. - Immediate dispatch runs through `outbox.EnableImmediateDispatch(...)` with `[DispatchImmediately]` on the handlers the caller reads when the command returns, under `litespec/packs/dotnet/application#dispatch-read-model-projections-immediately`. - The timestamp runs through `IExecutionContext.HandledAt`, stamping each message once for the handler to read as `HandledAt` under `litespec/core/backend-application#read-time-from-the-scoped-clock`. Each message declares its pipeline positions in definition classes in its use case `Application/` folder: `{Message}AuthorizationDefinition`, `{Message}AuditDefinition`, and `{Message}IdempotencyDefinition`, each in its own file and implementing exactly one definition interface. LiteBus verifies at composition through `RequireDeclaration` that every message carries them. A definition carries no LiteSpec mark; the handler carries the use case mark. A project declares authorization, audit, and idempotency only through definitions, never through attributes or custom guards. Settled by [decision/0103-dotnet-stack-binding](decision/0103-dotnet-stack-binding).

provisions.heading: Call Shared Logic Instead of Copying It
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `logic-duplicate` (level S) for one method or local-function body of at least 6 statements or 80 tokens carried in two or more different folders.
provisions.statement: A command handler, query handler, event handler, or job MUST call shared logic from its one home, the aggregate, a domain service, or the knowledge model, instead of carrying a copy of another slice's method body.
provisions.rationale: A handler body has three steps: the load, the one domain call, and the stage. A rule, calculation, or projection copied into the handler adds a fourth step that no record owns and no other slice shares, so each fix lands in every copy or misses one. Calling the aggregate method, the domain service, or the knowledge model keeps the handler at its three steps and the logic behind one call. This provision binds `litespec/core/domain-model#keep-one-home-for-each-rule-calculation-and-projection` for .NET.
provisions.example: Claimwick's submit-expense handler calls `Expense.Submit` with the receipt threshold it loaded, and the approve-expense handler calls `expense.Approve`: each handler holds its three steps while the expense aggregate holds the rules. A per-diem walk copied into both handlers would report `logic-duplicate`; both call the travel knowledge model instead.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Declared Effects Through Their Entry Points
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` for a dispatch no record declares, and `dotnet build` reports `LS2021` for a command or event mediator held outside an endpoint, event handler or job and `LS2022` for an event published outside the platform.
provisions.statement: An event handler or job MUST dispatch each declared `sends` effect through the messenger port, each declared `calls` effect through its external-system port, its one declared `runs` effect through `ICommandMediator`, and each declared `commands` edge through `ICommandMediator`, after the commit that stored the fact it answers, while the pipeline stages each raised domain event, each module event translating it, and each outbound integration event translating it in the same commit.
provisions.rationale: A command handler changes its aggregate and returns; it dispatches nothing. The aggregate raises its facts, and the outbox stages them in the same commit through `outbox.StageCollectedEvents()` (see `litespec/packs/dotnet/application#bind-the-pipeline-to-the-pinned-litebus-apis`). The same commit stages each module event and each outbound integration event whose record translates a raised domain event. The platform collects each one beside its domain event. Each is built by its static `From` method from that domain event alone, so no module code publishes. After that commit, an event handler answers each fact through its entry point: the messenger port for `sends`, its external-system port for `calls`, and `ICommandMediator` for `runs` and for each declared `commands` edge, sending each command in its own pipeline and commit. A scheduled or one-off job dispatches through the same entry points. Each handler gets its own delivery under `litespec/core/outbox#give-each-handler-its-own-delivery`, so one failing handler retries alone. An undeclared dispatch fails `effect-undeclared`, whatever its entry point. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-application#dispatch-only-declared-effect-edges` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Read-Model Projections Immediately
provisions.evidence: Does every handler the caller reads when the command returns carry `[DispatchImmediately]` with immediate dispatch registered, and does every other handler leave it off? Check each event handler beside the outbox registration.
provisions.statement: A handler whose effect the caller reads when the command returns, such as a read-model projection the next screen reads, carries `[DispatchImmediately]`, and the outbox registers immediate dispatch with a ten-second timeout and a thirty-second fallback delay.
provisions.rationale: LiteBus dispatches those envelopes in process after the unit of work commits and before `SendAsync` returns, so the caller reads its own write. A failed or timed-out dispatch is left to the outbox processor's retry, and the command's outcome never changes. Immediate dispatch needs a registered unit of work (`commands.UseUnitOfWork<...>()`), an outbox dispatcher, and a store implementing `IOutboxTargetedLeaseStore`, which the shipped PostgreSQL, Entity Framework Core, and in-memory stores do. The fallback delay stays greater than the timeout.

provisions.heading: Keep Query Handlers Free of Repositories and Writes
provisions.evidence: Does every query handler project through `IQuerySession`, with no repository and no stage, store, delete, or dispatch? Check each query handler; `dotnet build` reports LS2011 for a repository in a query handler and LS2012 for a forbidden refusal or the authorization guard.
provisions.statement: A query handler MUST take no repository and stage, store, delete, or dispatch nothing.
provisions.rationale: A read path acts on no invariant, so a repository in a query handler loads an aggregate the query has no write to justify. The handler projects through the read session under `litespec/packs/dotnet/persistence#query-through-iquerysession`. A read that writes makes retries and caching unsafe: repeating the query would repeat the write. An audited read is the pipeline's work, not the handler's. `dotnet build` reports a repository in a query handler as `LS2011`. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-application#project-queries-directly` and `litespec/core/backend-application#keep-query-handlers-free-of-writes` for .NET.
provisions.example: The list-expenses query projects its rows through `IQuerySession`, taking no repository and staging nothing.

provisions.heading: Name Every Outbox Subscriber
provisions.evidence: Does every event handler of a module event or domain event carry its subscriber name? Check each event handler.
provisions.statement: Every event handler of a module event or domain event MUST carry `[SubscriberName("<module>.<handler-name>")]`.
provisions.rationale: Under per-handler delivery, each handler gets its own envelope, so one failing handler retries alone. The subscriber name keeps envelopes reaching the handler after the class is renamed. LiteBus validates the names at composition when per-handler delivery is on.
provisions.example: The handler that schedules a payout when spending approves an expense carries `[SubscriberName("payouts.schedule-payout")]`.

provisions.heading: Pass Explicit Mediation Settings to Nested Use Cases
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2034` for an event handler running a nested use case without explicit mediation settings.
provisions.statement: An event handler that runs a nested use case MUST pass explicit mediation settings carrying the identity the nested use case runs as.
provisions.rationale: A nested command sent with ambient settings runs as whoever the outer pipeline authorized, or as no identity at all. The nested use case then passes an access check meant for another caller or fails one it was meant to pass. Explicit mediation settings state the identity on the send, so the nested pipeline authorizes the identity the handler names.
provisions.example:
In the library product, the handler that answers `domain-event/loan.loan-borrowed` runs the mark-book-lent use case with explicit settings carrying the system identity:

```csharp
await _commandMediator.SendAsync(
    new MarkBookLentCommand(@event.BookId, @event.LoanId),
    mediationSettings,
    cancellationToken);
```

The settings carry the identity the nested command runs as, so its access check authorizes that identity.

provisions.heading: Report Immediate Dispatch Beside the Backlog
provisions.evidence: Does the deployment report the immediate dispatch count with its outcome tag and the immediate dispatch duration beside the backlog indicators? Check the exported metrics beside the outbox dashboard.
provisions.statement: A deployment that dispatches projections immediately MUST report the immediate dispatch count with its outcome and the immediate dispatch duration beside the outbox backlog indicators.
provisions.rationale: The backlog indicators of `litespec/core/outbox#publish-backlog-indicators` show whether the outbox processor keeps up. Immediate dispatch adds a path in front of the processor, so its own instruments show how often it runs and how long it takes, and a slow immediate dispatch reads as duration rather than as a backlog. `AddLiteBusOutboxMetrics()` from `LiteBus.Outbox.Extensions.OpenTelemetry` reports the counter `litebus.outbox.immediate_dispatch.count`, tagged `litebus.outbox.immediate_dispatch.outcome` with `published`, `failed`, `skipped` or `timed_out`, and the histogram `litebus.outbox.immediate_dispatch.duration`.
provisions.example: Claimwick's reporting projection dispatches immediately. Its dashboard shows the immediate dispatch count by outcome and its duration beside the pending count and oldest pending age, so a run of `timed_out` outcomes explains a rising backlog.

provisions.heading: Report Input Problems as Validity
provisions.evidence: Does every validator report through `Validity`, with member, code, and message on each finding and no HTTP status? Check each validator.
provisions.statement: A validator MUST report its findings as Validity, with each ValidationFailure carrying a member, a code, and a message, and no HTTP status.
provisions.rationale: Every validator for the message runs, and the pipeline merges the findings before it refuses the request, so the caller fixes the whole form at once. The member tells the caller which input failed, the stable code lets a client branch on the reason, and the message explains the problem in words safe to show. Validity values come from the pinned mediator's abstractions, named in `litespec/packs/dotnet/application#use-the-pinned-mediator-entry-points`, so every project reports the same shape. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-application#report-input-problems-as-validity-findings` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Run Reactions in Dedicated Handlers
provisions.evidence: Does every reaction run in one handler class with its record's mark, sending at most one command from the folder of what it runs? Check each event handler beside its reaction record.
provisions.statement: A reaction MUST run in one class carrying one mark naming its reaction record.
provisions.rationale: One class per reaction answers the trigger the record names in `triggeredBy`, and dispatches only through its `effects` entries. The class carries the mark `reaction/<module>.<name>` in the declared style, so the stack reader links it without guessing. It sits in the `Application/` folder of the use case it runs, or in the `Application/Notifications/` or `Application/ExternalSystems/` folder of the notification it only sends or the system it only calls, under `litespec/workspace/naming#place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs`. It never writes an aggregate directly: a reaction that needs a write sends one command. It honors the record's `reads`, its idempotency, and its `onFailure`. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-application#answer-each-reaction-in-one-marked-class` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Run Scheduled Jobs as Hosted Operations
provisions.evidence: Does every scheduled or one-off job run as one marked hosted operation honoring selection, batch size, lease, and cursor? Check each such job.
provisions.statement: A scheduled or one-off job MUST run as one hosted operation carrying one mark naming its job record.
provisions.rationale: The hosted operation sits in the `Application/` folder of the use case it runs, or in the `Application/Notifications/` or `Application/ExternalSystems/` folder of the notification it only sends or the system it only calls. It registers on the declared execution host. It honors its record's selection, batch size, lease, and cursor, so a restart resumes where the last run stopped instead of reprocessing or skipping items. It sends its one command once per selected item, and records its evidence where the record states. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-application#run-each-job-within-its-declared-selection` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Subscribe Each Reaction Handler to Its Declared Triggers
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reaction-subscription-drift` (level S) for a marked handler subscribed to an event outside its reaction's `triggeredBy`, and `reaction-trigger-unhandled` (level S) for a declared trigger with no marked handler subscribed to it.
provisions.statement: The event handlers marked with a reaction MUST together subscribe to exactly the events the reaction names in `triggeredBy`.
provisions.rationale: The reaction record states the facts its handlers answer, and each handler subscribes by implementing its event-handler interface for one event type. A handler subscribed to an event the record does not name answers a fact nobody reviewed, while a named trigger with no subscribed handler is a promise the code does not keep. The check resolves each subscribed type through the event's own mark, so the mark on the event class is the link the reader follows. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-application#answer-each-reaction-in-one-marked-class` for .NET, where the subscription is the event type of the handler's event-handler interface.
provisions.example: Claimwick's reaction `reaction/spending.send-approver-reminders-on-expense-submitted` names `domain-event/expense.submitted` in `triggeredBy`: `SendApproverRemindersOnExpenseSubmittedHandler` implements `IEventHandler<ExpenseSubmittedDomainEvent>`, and `ExpenseSubmittedDomainEvent` carries the mark `domain-event/expense.submitted`.

provisions.heading: Use the Pinned Mediator Entry Points
provisions.evidence: Does every dispatch site use `ICommandMediator.SendAsync` or `IQueryMediator.QueryAsync` from the pinned LiteBus version? Check each dispatch site.
provisions.statement: Dispatch a command through `ICommandMediator.SendAsync` only from an endpoint, an event handler, or a job, and a query through `IQueryMediator.QueryAsync` from those or from a handler with a declared `queries` edge, from the LiteBus version the manifest pins.
provisions.rationale: With one pinned library, every dispatch site in every project reads the same way, and an agent finds all callers of a message with one search. A project that replaces the default still keeps commands and queries on separate entry points: that separation is required by `litespec/core/backend-application#dispatch-commands-and-queries-through-separate-entry-points`, and no replacement removes it.

provisions.heading: Verify Durable Contracts, Event Decisions, and Reference Data at Startup
provisions.evidence: Does every host composition verify its durable contracts, event decisions, and reference data, failing startup with the contract or row it names? Look at the composition code beside the durable contracts, the event decisions, and the reference data load.
provisions.statement: The host MUST verify every durable message contract, every staged domain event decision, and the loaded reference data when it composes, failing startup with a message that names the contract or row.
provisions.rationale: A durable message contract that fails a round trip, a staged domain event with no handler and no explicit ignore, and a reference row that fails validation each surface at runtime as a failed delivery, a dropped fact, or a wrong answer. Composition-time verification moves each one to startup: (a) every durable message contract survives a serialize-and-deserialize round trip with its identifiers intact; (b) every domain event the outbox may stage has a handler or an explicit ignore; (c) the reference data the product loads validates fully under `litespec/core/knowledge#validate-reference-data-before-serving` and covers every date in use under `litespec/core/domain-model#cover-every-date-in-use`. The verification runs with the host composition and carries no dedicated tests, because startup itself runs it on every boot. A startup failure names the contract or row, so the breakage points at its fix.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, composition builds one instance of each durable contract, serializes and deserializes it, and compares the identifiers; it lists every domain event the outbox may stage and confirms each one has a handler or an explicit ignore; and it loads the reference data and validates each row. When the expense-reimbursed envelope loses its expense identifier in the round trip, startup fails with a message naming that contract.

provisions.heading: Compile Module Contracts as Sibling Projects
provisions.evidence: Does any module project reference another module project, does any Contracts project reference a module project or name a domain type, and do the Contracts projects reference each other without a cycle? Check the project references of each module and Contracts project.
provisions.statement: Compile each module's contracts as a sibling `{Product}.{Module}.Contracts` project beside the module project under `Modules/`, referencing only the Kernel and the Contracts projects whose identifiers its public types name, and let each module project reference the Contracts projects of the modules it reaches instead of their module projects.
provisions.rationale: Project references cannot form a cycle, and neither can module dependencies: Contracts references, `queries` edges, `commands` edges, and reactions to facts form a directed acyclic graph, and a cycle means a concept is split across two modules. With one project per module and module projects referencing each other, the first cross edge fails the build. A Contracts project depends on no module project, so any module can reference the Contracts of the modules below it, and the module projects never reference each other. An identifier that two modules carry lives in the Contracts project of the module that owns its aggregate; it moves to the Kernel only with a decision record naming the Contracts cycle it breaks, under `litespec/packs/dotnet/architecture#keep-each-identifier-with-its-owner`. A Contracts project holds no domain type: a fact that a domain event produces is mapped inside the publishing module, never by a factory in the Contracts project that names the domain event.
provisions.example:
```text
Modules/Claimwick.Spending/
  Claimwick.Spending.csproj                 references Kernel, Platform, Claimwick.Spending.Contracts,
                                            Claimwick.Reporting.Contracts
  SpendingModule.cs
  Domain/  Application/  Ports/  Infrastructure/  WebApi/
Modules/Claimwick.Spending.Contracts/
  Claimwick.Spending.Contracts.csproj       references Kernel and the Contracts projects its public types name
  Expenses/
    ExpenseId.cs  OnExpenseReimbursed/ExpenseReimbursedModuleEvent.cs  ReadExpense/
```

The Contracts project sits beside the module project: a nested project would need the outer project to exclude its files item by item, would put its build output inside the module tree, and shows awkwardly in IDEs.

provisions.heading: Compile Each Knowledge Area as a Model Project with Its Set Projects
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for a folder under `src/Knowledge/` that is neither a `<Product>.<Area>/` model project nor a `<Product>.<Area>.<Variant>/` set project of a model the folder holds, and for a file directly in the Knowledge root. Review each host `Program.cs` for the `Add<Area>` call registering the sets the host runs, and each set for slice folders mirroring its model.
provisions.statement: Each knowledge area MUST compile as one `<Product>.<Area>/` model project with one `<Product>.<Area>.<Variant>/` set project per variant under `src/Knowledge/`, with slice folders by subject mirrored in each set and host composition through `services.Add<Area>(x => x.Add<Variant>())`.
provisions.rationale: One model project gives every module the same types and lookups for an area, and one set project per variant keeps the values of each country or branch apart without copying the types into each set. Slice folders by subject, mirrored in each set, put the same subject in the same folder in the model and in every set, so a reader moves from a row type to its rows by folder name. The host registers the sets it runs with the model at startup, so adding a variant touches the host and adds a set project, while each module keeps referencing the model. This provision binds `litespec/core/knowledge#give-each-knowledge-area-one-model` for .NET.
provisions.example:
Claimwick's travel area compiles as:

```text
src/Knowledge/Claimwick.Travel/                the model: row types, roles, keys, lookups, the registry, composition, validation
  PerDiem/  Mileage/                           one folder per subject
src/Knowledge/Claimwick.Travel.Germany/        one set per variant
  PerDiem/  Mileage/                           the same subjects
src/Knowledge/Claimwick.Travel.Netherlands/
```

Each host registers the sets it runs:

```csharp
services.AddTravel(x => x.Add<Germany>().Add<Netherlands>());
```

provisions.heading: Expose One Public Entry Type per Module
provisions.evidence: Does each module project expose exactly its entry type as its one public marker, with no unneeded marker elsewhere? Check each project for its marker.
provisions.statement: Expose the module entry type as the one public marker of each module project for host composition, endpoint discovery, and scanning.
provisions.rationale: Scanners and the host need an assembly reference, and without a marker developers make handlers public to supply one, widening visibility for tooling convenience. Each module project's entry type gives the host and the scanners their reference while every handler stays internal. The platform discovers the internal endpoints in every module assembly the host adds.

provisions.heading: Expose Only Contracts and the Entry Point
provisions.evidence: Is any type in a module project outside the entry type public? Look at the visibility modifiers in each module project.
provisions.statement: Every type in a module project outside its module entry type MUST be internal.
provisions.rationale: With one project per module, visibility is the module boundary: a public Contracts project and one public entry type, everything else internal, so no module names another module's internals and the compiler refuses the reference. Endpoints stay internal while the platform discovers them in every module assembly the host adds. A project that keeps one modules project holding every module keeps the same visibility inside each module folder, with `LS2020` as the boundary.

provisions.heading: Follow Declared Module Dependencies
provisions.evidence: Does every cross-module reference name a module its owner declares in `dependsOn`, with no dependency cycle? Check the cross-module references beside the module records.
provisions.statement: A module MUST reference only modules its record names in dependsOn.
provisions.rationale: The `dependsOn` list states which modules a module may reference. An undeclared edge crosses a boundary the design does not allow. The rule covers code references and record links alike: Contracts project references, `queries` edges, `commands` edges, and reactions to another module's facts. The dependency graph stays acyclic: a cycle means a concept is split across two modules, and the fix moves the concept, under `litespec/core/model#keep-module-dependencies-free-of-cycles`. Settled by [decision/0110-module-dependencies-form-a-dag](decision/0110-module-dependencies-form-a-dag).

provisions.heading: Follow Layer Direction in Every File
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1001` for a Domain type naming an outer-layer type, `LS2018` for an Application, Ports, or WebApi type naming a type outside its layer, `LS2025` for an adapter in `Infrastructure/{Port}/` naming a Domain type outside those or a WebApi type, and `LS2029` for another module's public query or query result named outside a handler, reaction, or job, and for another module's public command or command result named outside a reaction or job.
provisions.statement: A type MUST reference only the layers its own layer allows under the layer table of [Backend Architecture](../../core/backend-architecture.md).
provisions.rationale: Layers are roles played by folders, whatever project holds them: a file takes its layer from its top folder in the module. Global usings import namespaces for every file, so the rule covers them too: a global using hides no coupling. The dependency rules below bind the layer table to projects and folders. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-architecture#point-dependencies-inward` for .NET. | From | May reference | Enforced by | |---|---|---| | Kernel | the base class library only | project references | | Platform | Kernel and its libraries; never a module | project references | | A module | Kernel, Platform, and other modules' Contracts projects | project references plus visibility: only the Contracts project and `{Module}Module` are `public`, everything else `internal` | | A knowledge model | Kernel and its libraries | project references | | A knowledge set | Its model and the Kernel | project references | | `Domain/` | Kernel and the module's own `Domain/`, and the identifiers in other modules' Contracts projects | analyzer (folder) | | `Ports/` | Kernel, the module's `Domain/` types, the identifiers in other modules' Contracts projects, Platform abstractions; never `Application/`, `Infrastructure/` or `WebApi/` | analyzer (folder) | | `Application/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` | `Domain/`, its own use case folder, `Ports/`, `Application/ReadModels/`, the identifiers in other modules' Contracts projects, the facts its reactions answer, another module's public queries and query results with a declared `queries` edge, Platform abstractions; never another use case folder, never `Infrastructure/` or `WebApi/`, never another module's public command | analyzer (folder) | | `Infrastructure/` | `Domain/`, `Ports/` (to implement them), Platform, libraries | analyzer (folder) | | `WebApi/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` | its own `Application/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` (message and result), Kernel values, typed identifiers, Platform `Http/` and `Access/`; never `Ports/`, `Domain/` types, repositories, `Infrastructure/`, another module's public query, public command or result, or another use case | analyzer (folder) | | Hosts | Platform, each module's entry type, and the knowledge sets it registers | project references |
provisions.example: Domain references no Application, Infrastructure, or WebApi type, and none of the persistence, web, mediator, logging, and injection namespaces. Ports references no Application, Infrastructure, or WebApi type. Application references no Infrastructure or WebApi type, no ASP.NET Core type, and no other module's public command. A handler, reaction, or job names another module's public query or query result only with a declared `queries` edge, and only a reaction or job names another module's public command or command result. WebApi references no Domain type outside typed identifiers and Kernel values, and no repository. An adapter in `Infrastructure/{Port}/` names no Domain type outside typed identifiers, shared-kernel values and the types the interfaces of the ports it implements name in their member signatures, and no WebApi type. A knowledge set references its model and the Kernel, and a module references the model of each knowledge area it reads.

provisions.heading: Hold Each Layer in Its Own Folder
provisions.evidence: Does every module hold its Domain, Application, Ports, Infrastructure, and WebApi code in those folders, with one plural aggregate folder holding one folder per use case inside each layer that serves it, one folder per module-level read directly in each layer that serves it, every port in its own `Ports/{Port}/` folder, and every adapter in its `Infrastructure/{Port}/` folder? Look at the module folders.
provisions.statement: Each module MUST hold its Domain, Application, Ports, Infrastructure, and WebApi code in those folders, with one plural aggregate folder holding one folder per use case inside each layer that serves the use case, and one folder per module-level read directly in each layer that serves it.
provisions.rationale: The folders make each layer visible at a glance: a reader opening a module sees its domain, its use cases, its ports, its adapters, and its endpoints in the shape every .NET backend uses. A use case spreads over one folder per layer that serves it, inside the plural folder of its aggregate, and every port of the module lives in its own `Ports/{Port}/` folder with its adapter in `Infrastructure/{Port}/`. The code mirrors the records, so a reader moves between a record folder and its code folder by the same names, and the plural keeps the aggregate type visible to every handler instead of hiding it behind a singular namespace that fails with CS0118. Settled by [decision/0107-kernel-platform-and-one-project-per-module](decision/0107-kernel-platform-and-one-project-per-module).
provisions.example:
| Folder | Holds | Present when |
|---|---|---|
| `Domain/{Aggregates}/` | the aggregate with its act, part, fact, event, and refusal groupings | the module declares an aggregate |
| `Application/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` | the message, handler, validator, one definition class per concern, the result, the reaction or job that runs the use case | always |
| `Application/Settings/` | the module options class | the module binds a setting |
| `Ports/{Port}/` | the interface `I{Port}` with its signature types in `Models/` | the module declares a port |
| `WebApi/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` | the endpoint, its request and response models | the use case is reached over HTTP |
| `Infrastructure/Messaging/` | the module's message pipeline pieces | the module registers message pipeline pieces |
| `Infrastructure/Pipeline/` | the module's HTTP pipeline pieces serving no single use case | the module holds HTTP pipeline pieces |
| `Infrastructure/{Port}/` | the adapter implementing the module's port, with its options class, its wire types in `Models/`, and the collaborators it needs in `Parts/` | the module declares a port |

A module-level read drops the aggregate segment: `Application/{UseCase}/` and `WebApi/{UseCase}/`.

provisions.heading: Keep Application Types in Their Layer Folders
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for a port folder holding no interface or more than one, for a port folder whose name is not its interface name without the `I`, for a type in a port folder outside `Models/` that the interface signatures do not name, for a type beside the adapter class outside `Models/` and `Parts/`, and for a `Models/` or `Parts/` type no adapter file names, and `dotnet build` reports `LS2018` for a `Ports/` file naming an `Application/`, `Infrastructure/` or `WebApi/` type.
provisions.statement: An application MUST place each use case's messages, results, handlers, validators, definitions, and triggers in the use case's folder inside `Application/`, every port of the module in its own `Ports/{Port}/` folder holding the interface `I{Port}` with its signature types in `Models/` and no files directly in `Ports/`, each port's adapter in its `Infrastructure/{Port}/` folder with the same folder name, holding the adapter class with its options class `{Adapter}Options.cs`, its wire types in `Models/`, and the collaborators it needs in `Parts/`, and cross-module contracts grouped by aggregate in its Contracts project.
provisions.rationale: One use case keeps its command, query, result, handler, validator, definitions, and triggers in its `Application/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` folder, and its endpoint and transport models in its `WebApi/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` folder; a module-level read drops the aggregate segment in each. A use case's own models never move up: two use cases with one shape each declare it, under `litespec/core/backend-architecture#give-each-use-case-its-own-models`. Rules used by two or more use cases of one aggregate sit in the aggregate `Domain/{Aggregates}/` folder.
