Every port of the module sits in its own `Ports/{Port}/` folder, whether one use case or many call it, so `Ports/` is the complete list of what the module needs from outside: `Ports/{Port}/` holds the interface `I{Port}` with the types its member signatures name in `Models/`, with no files directly in `Ports/`, and each port's adapter sits in its `Infrastructure/{Port}/` folder with the same folder name, holding the adapter class with its options class, its wire types in `Models/`, and the collaborators it needs in `Parts/`; several adapters of one port sit side by side. Whether an interface is a port at all is a judgment the reviewer answers under `litespec/core/backend-application#declare-a-port-only-for-what-the-module-does-not-compute`. A module publishes data only in its Contracts project, grouped by aggregate: each `Contracts/{Aggregates}/` folder holds the identifier another module carries, one `On{Fact}/` folder per fact another module consumes, and one folder per public query or public command with its message and result, so the public surface of a module stays visible in its Contracts project. It publishes no refusal and no interface.

provisions.heading: Keep Business Values in the Kernel
provisions.evidence: Does the Kernel project hold only shared business values and the refusal exceptions of product rules, with no package reference and no project reference? Look at the Kernel project file and its files.
provisions.statement: The Kernel project MUST hold only the business values and the refusal exceptions every module uses, with no reference outside the base class library, grouped into `Domain/`, `Values/`, and `Auditing/` with no files at its root.
provisions.rationale: Only the values every module speaks live here: money, typed identifiers, dates, the aggregate root, the domain exception, the refusal exceptions of product rules, and closed sets every module uses. The Kernel takes no package reference and no project reference, so a type a domain model may use is separated from a type only a host touches by the project boundary itself. A technical capability in the Kernel would drag its libraries into every module. `Domain/` holds the aggregate base, the domain event marker, and the domain exceptions; `Values/` holds money and the typed id marker; `Auditing/` holds the audit vocabulary.
provisions.example:
```text
{Product}.Kernel/
  Domain/      AggregateRoot.cs  IDomainEvent.cs  DomainException.cs
  Values/      Money.cs  TypedId.cs
  Auditing/    the audit vocabulary
```

provisions.heading: Keep Closed Folder Sets at Every Level
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for a folder outside its closed set or naming no declared record, for a file directly at the Kernel or Platform root, for a file in the wrong layer folder of its use case, for a reaction or job outside the folder of what it runs, for an `{Aggregates}/` folder naming no declared aggregate, for a use case folder naming no use case of that aggregate, for a file directly in an `{Aggregates}/` folder, for a singular `Domain/{Aggregate}/` folder, for a Domain type directly in `Domain/` or a use case directly in `Application/` or `WebApi/` that belongs to an aggregate, for an exception file outside `Exceptions/` and a domain event file outside `Events/`, for a state file beside its aggregate root, for a second store interface of one aggregate, for a file directly in `Ports/`, for a port folder with no adapter folder in `Infrastructure/`, for an adapter folder with no port folder, for a type beside the adapter class outside `Models/` and `Parts/`, for a `Models/` or `Parts/` type no adapter file names, for a port or adapter folder naming a declared module, for a repository implementation outside its aggregate's `Persistence/` folder, for a use-case model or adapter file in `Persistence/`, for any other file directly in `Persistence/` outside the module store contribution, for an interface in a Contracts project, for a fact in a Contracts project outside its `{Aggregates}/On{Fact}/` folder, for an event file in an `On{Fact}/` folder that names no declared event or another fact, for a fact in an `On{Fact}/` folder outside the aggregate of the domain event it translates, for a command in a Contracts project outside the `{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` folder of a public command, for a public use case message or result outside its `Contracts/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` path, for a test folder naming no declared record, and for a type whose namespace does not match its folder path through its layer segment, for a folder under `Knowledge/` that is neither a model nor a set of a model the folder holds, for a file directly in the Knowledge root, `folder-ungrouped` for a folder past 20 files that holds none of its allowed groupings, and `mark-folder-drift` for a marked element outside the folder its mark names.
provisions.statement: Each level of the Kernel, Platform, and module projects MUST hold only the folders the closed set table in this section allows.
provisions.rationale: Only the folders the table lists are allowed, so a catch-all folder has no home and review refuses it. Product-wide values sit in the Kernel, product-wide technical capabilities sit in the Platform, and cross-module contracts sit in each module's Contracts project. `litespec/core/backend-architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers` decides between a use case folder and the module and product folders. Module folders mirror record homes: each layer folder holds one plural aggregate folder with one folder per use case inside it, plus one folder per module-level read, each reaction and job sits with the use case, notification, or external system it runs, sends, or calls, and each read model sits in the `Application/ReadModels/` folder. Settled by [decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs](decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs). A use case record at `modules/{module}/aggregates/{aggregates}/use-cases/{use-case}` maps to code at `Application/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` and, when reached over HTTP, `WebApi/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/`, and an aggregate record at `modules/{module}/aggregates/{aggregates}` maps to code at `Modules/{Product}.{Module}/Domain/{Aggregates}/`. A module-level read record at `modules/{module}/use-cases/{use-case}` drops the aggregate segment in every layer. Code drops the typed container folders of the record tree (`aggregates/`, `use-cases/`, `rules/`, `domain-events/`, `module-events/`, `integration-events/`) and keeps the module, aggregate, and record names in PascalCase, plural for aggregate folders. `Domain/{Aggregates}/Events/` is the stated exception: it groups the domain event types of one aggregate, which stay inside the module. A project that keeps one modules project holding every module maps each module to one folder of that project instead.

| Level | Allowed folders |

provisions.heading: Keep Composition in Hosts
provisions.evidence: Does every host compose its process in `Program.cs` and host registration modules through `AddPlatform` and `AddModules`? Check each `Program.cs`.
provisions.statement: Compose each host in `Program.cs` and host registration modules: register transport services there and call `AddPlatform` and `AddModules`.
provisions.rationale: Domain and Application declare abstractions for the hosts to implement. A registration call inside either layer makes the abstraction depend on the thing it abstracts, which inverts the dependency direction and drags Infrastructure into layers that must not name it. Each module registers its own types through its entry type, and `Program.cs` calls `AddPlatform()` and `AddModules(...)` in one visible order, so two hosts share wiring through the platform instead of through a folder beside the modules. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-architecture#keep-service-registration-in-hosts` and `litespec/core/backend-architecture#compose-each-process-explicitly` for .NET.
provisions.example:
The platform call, the modules call, and the endpoint map, in order:

```text
AddPlatform(...)     persistence, messaging, access, auditing, HTTP, country packs
AddModules(...)      one entry type per module that runs in this host
MapEndpoints(...)    the endpoints the platform discovered
```

`Program.cs` keeps their call order visible. The platform owns endpoint discovery, Problem Details, refusal mapping, and JSON; the host owns transport security, authentication, authorization, and OpenAPI.

provisions.heading: Keep Each Identifier with Its Owner
provisions.evidence: Does every business identifier live in the Contracts or Domain folder of the module owning its aggregate, and does every Kernel identifier have a decision record naming the Contracts cycle it breaks? Look at each identifier beside its aggregate record and the decision records.
provisions.statement: A business identifier MUST live in the project of the module that owns its aggregate, in `Contracts/{Aggregates}/` when another module carries it and in `Domain/{Aggregates}/` otherwise, except in the Kernel with a decision record naming the Contracts cycle it breaks.
provisions.rationale: The identifier names its aggregate, so it lives where its aggregate lives: in the owner's Contracts project when another module carries it, beside the `On{Fact}/` folders and the public queries and public commands of its aggregate, and in the aggregate's `Domain/{Aggregates}/` folder when no other module carries it. An identifier placed by convenience instead drifts: a copy in the consumer, a shared copy in the Kernel, and the owner holding a third. The Kernel holds an identifier only to break a cycle between Contracts projects, and only with a decision record naming that cycle, because a shared identifier hides which module owns the aggregate it names. The marker generic technical code uses for converters lives in the Kernel. Settled by [decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data](decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data).
provisions.example: `ExpenseId` belongs to `aggregate/spending.expense`. The reporting module carries it, so it lives in `Claimwick.Spending.Contracts/Expenses/ExpenseId.cs`. An identifier no other module carries stays in `Claimwick.Spending/Domain/Expenses/`.

provisions.heading: Keep Host Endpoints in Hosts
provisions.evidence: Does every host endpoint without a handler live in its host project and carry its mark? Check the host endpoints beside the use case folders.
provisions.statement: Each host endpoint without a handler MUST live in its host project.
provisions.rationale: Protocol endpoints, static assets, and development-only tooling belong to no use case folder, so the host keeps them. Each still carries its mark, and the placement check accepts a host endpoint in the host.

provisions.heading: Keep Implementation Types Internal
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2001` for an implementation type that is not `internal sealed`.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, repository, endpoint
provisions.statement: A handler, validator, definition, persistence implementation, or endpoint implementation MUST be declared `internal sealed`.
provisions.rationale: A public type is visible to every assembly, so an implementation left public can be referenced by callers it was never written for. Messages, results, and ports turn public only inside the Contracts project, while handlers, validators, and implementations stay `internal sealed`. Assembly scanning reads internal types through the module entry type, so scanning never justifies widening visibility. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-architecture#keep-implementations-hidden-and-closed` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Technical Capabilities in the Platform
provisions.evidence: Does any Platform file name a module, its aggregates, or its use cases, or does the Platform project reference a module project? Look at the Platform sources and its project references.
provisions.statement: The Platform project MUST hold only technical capabilities that name no module, referencing only the Kernel, its libraries, and the base class library.
provisions.rationale: Persistence setup, messaging, authorization, HTTP conventions, country pack loading, and module composition are built once and stay generic. A module plugs in by contributing data, never by copying platform code. A business word in the Platform names a module the Platform never knows, and a module reference fails the build because the Platform project references no module project. Inside a capability past 20 files, one folder per sub-area groups it further, with each pack file beside the facts it reads.
provisions.example:
```text
{Product}.Platform/
  Persistence/    store setup, serializer, Money and typed id converters, discriminator registry
  Messaging/      mediators, outbox, in-process dispatch, recurring jobs
  Access/         sessions, authorization guards, composable policies
                  (Permission, RecentSignIn, Self, System)
  Http/           endpoint discovery, problem details, refusal mapping, JSON
  CountryPacks/   pack loader and dated lookups
  Modules/        IModule contract and AddModules(...)
```

provisions.heading: Keep Use Case Folders Isolated
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2019` for a use case folder naming a type in another use case folder.
provisions.artifact: use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, endpoint, reaction
provisions.statement: The folders of one use case MUST reference no type in the folders of another use case.
provisions.rationale: The folders of one use case hold that use case, so a reference between the folders of two use cases couples two behaviors that change for different reasons. A reaction or job that runs a use case sits in that use case's own `Application/` folder, so it references the message from inside, and no handler sends a command: another module's public query is the one message a handler sends, with a declared `queries` edge. A shape two use cases need is declared in each, under `litespec/core/backend-architecture#give-each-use-case-its-own-models`. Behavior they share belongs in the module or product folder that holds every consumer, under `litespec/core/backend-architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`. The rule applies to files and to global usings alike. Kernel values are referenced directly, never copied: money, typed identifiers, dates, and closed sets the Kernel owns are referenced from any layer the layer table allows, and WebApi models carry them on the wire. Copying a Kernel value into a use case folder breaks the rule. The module's shared `Application/` folders, `Notifications/`, `ExternalSystems/`, `ReadModels/`, and `Settings/`, belong to no use case: a use case folder names the types there freely, and the rule reports neither a name from a use case folder to one of them nor a name from one of them to a use case folder.

provisions.heading: Mirror Modules, Aggregates, and Use Cases in One Namespace Tree
provisions.evidence: Does every type in the Kernel, Platform, and module projects carry the namespace its folder path implies? Compare the namespaces with the folders.
provisions.statement: Every type in the Kernel, Platform, and module projects MUST live in the namespace tree that starts with the product name and follows the folders below the project root.
provisions.rationale: When the namespace matches the folder path, `Claimwick.Spending.Application.Expenses.SubmitExpense` states the product, module, layer, aggregate, and use case without a map. A reader moves from a Domain aggregate to its handler, its repository, and its endpoint by name alone, following folders under `litespec/workspace/naming#keep-namespaces-aligned-with-folders`. Each project takes its own name as its root namespace, so every namespace still starts with the product name. The aggregate folder is plural, so the namespace never hides the aggregate type the way `...Application.Expense.SubmitExpense` hides `Expense`. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case` for .NET.
provisions.example:
The Expense aggregate of Claimwick's Spending module fills one branch:

```text
Modules/Claimwick.Spending/Domain/Expenses/Expense.cs
Modules/Claimwick.Spending/Application/Expenses/SubmitExpense/SubmitExpenseCommandHandler.cs
```

The handler in the tree above has namespace `Claimwick.Spending.Application.Expenses.SubmitExpense`.

provisions.heading: Name No Business Identifier in the Platform
provisions.evidence: Does any Platform file name a module identifier? Look at the Platform sources beside the module Contracts projects.
provisions.statement: The Platform MUST name no business identifier.
provisions.rationale: The Platform speaks the tenant and the actor: the execution identity tenant and the principal subject. A business identifier in the Platform names an aggregate of a module the Platform never knows, and every module then converts through the Platform's copy instead of the owner's. The owner of each identifier converts at the module edge, from the tenant or subject into its identifier and back, so the Platform stays free of business words. Settled by [decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data](decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data).
provisions.example: The workspace module converts the tenant string into `WorkspaceId` at its edge and back when it answers; the Platform names only the tenant.

provisions.heading: Place Each Read Model in Its Application Read Models Folder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for a class carrying a read-model mark outside its read-model folder, and for a folder under `ReadModels/` that names no declared read model.
provisions.statement: Each read model MUST live in a folder named for the read model in the plural inside its `Application/ReadModels/` folder, holding the read-model document, one projection per source event named `{ReadModel}On{Fact}Projection`, the reader interface `I{ReadModel}ReadModel` and its implementation, each carrying the read model's mark.
provisions.rationale: A read model's projections answer module events and integration events like reactions, but they write only their read model and run no use case. Placed with a use case, they would look like reactions; placed with the read model, one folder shows every event that fills it and the one reader its module's use cases call. The mark links each class to the record that names its sources. A projection that wrote anything but its read model would be an unrecorded reaction. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-application#read-another-modules-state-through-a-read-model` for .NET.
provisions.example:
```text
Modules/Claimwick.Reporting/Application/ReadModels/ReimbursedExpenses/
  ReimbursedExpense.cs                                        the read-model document, keyed by ExpenseId
  ReimbursedExpenseOnExpenseReimbursedProjection.cs           one projection per source event
  ReimbursedExpenseOnExpensePersonalDataErasedProjection.cs
  IReimbursedExpenseReadModel.cs                              what Reporting use cases read
  ReimbursedExpenseReadModel.cs                               its store implementation
```

provisions.heading: Plug Modules into the Platform Through Contributions
provisions.evidence: Does any module hold serializer, store, guard, converter, or endpoint-discovery code the platform provides? Look at the module projects beside the platform registries.
provisions.statement: A module MUST plug into a platform capability by contributing data to the platform registry instead of copying platform code.
provisions.rationale: Each module entry type contributes its stored types and closed-set discriminators to the persistence registry, its policies to access, and its routes to HTTP discovery; the platform builds the one serializer, the one guard evaluation, the one converter set, and the one endpoint map. No module writes serializer, store, guard, or converter code, and the platform never names a module type. A copy drifts with the next platform change, while a contribution composes.
provisions.example: The spending module contributes its stored types and closed-set discriminators, and the platform builds the one serializer from every module's contribution.

provisions.heading: Publish Only Data from Each Contracts Project
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for an interface in a Contracts project, for a fact in a Contracts project outside its `{Aggregates}/On{Fact}/` folder, for an event file in an `On{Fact}/` folder that names no declared event or another fact, for a fact in an `On{Fact}/` folder outside the aggregate of the domain event it translates, for a command in a Contracts project outside the `{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` folder of a public command, for a public use case message or result outside its `Contracts/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` path, for a module event or integration event record with no `On{Fact}/` folder, and for a fact type naming no declared module or integration event.
provisions.statement: Each Contracts project MUST publish only data grouped by aggregate, with no interface anywhere in the project.
provisions.rationale: The project is the module boundary: what sits in it is what other modules may name. Data states what crosses; an interface states a call shape the provider owns and every consumer couples to. The root holds one folder per aggregate with anything public, in the plural, and one folder per public module-level query, with no files. Each `Contracts/{Aggregates}/` folder holds the aggregate identifier when another module carries it, the types facts or messages of more than one aggregate carry when the aggregate owns the concept, one `On{Fact}/` folder per fact about the aggregate another module consumes, and one folder per public query or public command of that aggregate with its message and result at the same path the use case has in the provider's `Application/` folder. Each fact sits in its own `On{Fact}/` folder in the aggregate whose domain event it translates, beside the aggregate's public query and command folders, as its module or integration event record's `translates` names, with namespace `{Product}.{Module}.Contracts.{Aggregates}.On{Fact}`. `{Fact}` is the record name in PascalCase, so `module-event/spending.expense-reimbursed` gives `OnExpenseReimbursed`, and the record tree maps one to one: `aggregates/expenses/module-events/expense-reimbursed/` gives `Expenses/OnExpenseReimbursed/`. The folder holds the event type and the types only it carries. A module-level public query sits in its own folder directly in `Contracts/`. Names are business names: `ReadBusinessQuery` and `BusinessResult`, `CloseBusinessCommand` and its result, never request or response models, routes, or HTTP methods. Settled by [decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data](decision/0109-module-contracts-publish-data).
provisions.example:
```text
Modules/Claimwick.Spending.Contracts/
  Expenses/
    ExpenseId.cs
    OnExpenseReimbursed/
      ExpenseReimbursedModuleEvent.cs
    ReadExpense/
      ReadExpenseQuery.cs
      ReadExpenseResult.cs
    CloseExpenses/
      CloseExpensesCommand.cs
      CloseExpensesResult.cs
  ReadExpenseDirectory/
    ReadExpenseDirectoryQuery.cs
    ReadExpenseDirectoryResult.cs
```

provisions.heading: Reach Another Module Only Through Contracts
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2020` for a module reference naming another module type outside its Contracts.
provisions.statement: A module MUST reach another module only through types its Contracts project publishes.
provisions.rationale: The Contracts project is the public surface of a module, grouped by aggregate: each `Contracts/{Aggregates}/` folder holds the identifier another module carries, the types facts or messages of more than one aggregate carry when the aggregate owns the concept, one `On{Fact}/` folder per fact another module consumes, and one folder per public query or public command with its message and result. Each layer names only what it needs from another module's Contracts: identifiers in `Domain/`, `Ports/`, `Application/`, and `WebApi/`; facts an `Application/` reaction answers; a handler, reaction, or job names the provider's public queries and query results with a declared `queries` edge, and only a reaction or job names the provider's public commands and command results with a declared `commands` edge. With one project per module, project references and visibility enforce the boundary: only the Contracts project and the entry type are public, so a module cannot name another module's internals and the compiler refuses the reference. A project that keeps one modules project holding every module enforces the same boundary through `LS2020`. A module publishes no refusal and no interface: another module triggers its acts by sending its public commands upstream from its reactions and jobs, and each module refuses with its own refusals. A module that needs another module's current value asks the provider's public query from its handler, reaction, or job with a declared `queries` edge; a module that needs another module's data reshaped and kept locally keeps its own read model built from the owner's module events. It loads no foreign aggregate or repository. A reaction to another module's fact subscribes to the published module event, never to the domain event, and answers upstream facts only.

provisions.heading: Reference Knowledge Models from Modules and Sets from Hosts
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `knowledge-reference-invalid` for a module project referencing a knowledge set project, for a knowledge set project referencing anything but its model and the Kernel, and for a knowledge model project referencing a module.
provisions.artifact: knowledge-model, knowledge-set, command-handler, query-handler, reaction, job
provisions.statement: Project references MUST run from modules to knowledge models, from knowledge sets to their model and the Kernel only, and from hosts to the sets they register.
provisions.rationale: A module that references a set binds itself to one country or branch, so a module references the model and leaves each set to the hosts that register it: the model gives modules one stable surface across every variant. A set that references anything but its model and the Kernel pulls operational or technical code into values that ship per variant. A host references the sets it runs because registration is composition, which lives in hosts. This provision binds `litespec/core/knowledge#read-knowledge-through-its-model` for .NET.
provisions.example: Claimwick's spending module references `Claimwick.Travel` and names no country project. `Claimwick.Travel.Germany` references `Claimwick.Travel` and `Claimwick.Kernel`. The API host references both country sets to register them.

provisions.heading: Register Each Module Through Its Entry Point
provisions.evidence: Does every module expose one public entry type implementing `IModule`, and does every host add its modules through `AddModules`? Look at each module project and each `Program.cs`.
provisions.statement: Each module MUST expose one public entry type implementing `IModule` that registers everything the module holds.
provisions.rationale: The entry type is the module's only public surface beside its Contracts project: it registers the module's adapters, contributes its stored types, discriminators, policies, and routes, and gives hosts and scanners the assembly reference. Each host adds the modules that run in it through `AddModules`, so two hosts share wiring through the platform instead of through a folder beside the modules that reaches into module internals. Settled by [decision/0107-kernel-platform-and-one-project-per-module](decision/0107-kernel-platform-and-one-project-per-module).
provisions.example: `SpendingModule` implements `IModule`, and each host program calls `AddPlatform()` and then `AddModules(...)` with the modules that run in that host.

provisions.heading: Separate the Kernel, the Platform, and the Modules
provisions.evidence: Does the solution hold only the Kernel, the Platform, one project per module, the knowledge models with their sets, and their hosts, with the reference direction the dependency rules state? Check the solution file and the project references.
provisions.statement: Use a `{Product}.Kernel` project for the business values every module speaks, a `{Product}.Platform` project for the technical capabilities, one `{Product}.{Module}` project per module grouped under `Modules/`, one `{Product}.{Area}` knowledge model project per knowledge area with one `{Product}.{Area}.{Variant}` set project per variant grouped under `Knowledge/`, and WebApi and optional Worker hosts grouped under `Hosts/`, at every size.
provisions.rationale: Each module project then holds one complete business capability: a reader opening it sees the module's domain, use cases, ports, adapters, and endpoints in the module's layer folders. The compiler enforces the boundaries: the Kernel references only the base class library, the Platform references no module, and each module exposes only its Contracts project and its entry type. Each knowledge model exposes its lookups to the modules that read it, and each set is referenced only by the hosts that register it. Hosts stay separate projects, because two hosts can run the same modules. The names come from the Shared Kernel pattern of domain-driven design and the microservice chassis pattern, as "Why the Names Kernel and Platform" above explains. A project that keeps one modules project holding every module is an allowed deviation; `LS2020` then enforces the Contracts boundary that project references otherwise enforce. Settled by [decision/0107-kernel-platform-and-one-project-per-module](decision/0107-kernel-platform-and-one-project-per-module).
provisions.example:
```text
apps/api/src/{Product}.Kernel/
apps/api/src/{Product}.Platform/
apps/api/src/Modules/{Product}.{Module}/              one project per module
apps/api/src/Modules/{Product}.{Module}.Contracts/    its sibling Contracts project
apps/api/src/Knowledge/{Product}.{Area}/              one model project per knowledge area
apps/api/src/Knowledge/{Product}.{Area}.{Variant}/    one set project per variant
apps/api/src/Hosts/{Product}.WebApi/
apps/api/src/Hosts/{Product}.Worker/     only when background work needs its own process
```

provisions.heading: Bind Every Keyed Setting in One Options Class
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `setting-unimplemented` (level S) for a keyed setting no options class marks, and `setting-key-drift` (level S) for a marked options class whose `SectionName` constant and property do not spell the setting's `configurationPath`.
provisions.statement: An options class that binds a setting with a `configurationPath` MUST carry an `implements` mark naming the setting, with a `SectionName` constant and property that spell the setting's `configurationPath`.
provisions.rationale: The options class is where configuration becomes a typed value the code reads. It is the code element that implements the setting, so marking it names the promise the class holds. Comparing its section name and property with the record's path finds a renamed section or a typo before the product starts with a default. This provision binds `litespec/core/use-cases#bind-every-keyed-setting-in-one-marked-element` for .NET.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `SpendingOptions` class declares `SectionName = "Spending"`, an `ApprovalReminderDelay` property, and `/// <implements>setting/spending.approval-reminder-delay</implements>`.

provisions.heading: Centralize .NET Build Settings
provisions.evidence: Does `apps/api/Directory.Build.props` set the manifest target framework with nullable types, implicit usings, and warnings as errors? Look at that file.
provisions.statement: `apps/api/Directory.Build.props` MUST set the target framework of the manifest .NET stack release, and enable nullable types, implicit usings, and warnings as errors.
provisions.rationale: Build settings drift project by project when each project owns its own: one project targets an older framework, another drops nullable types, and warnings pile up where nobody reads them. One file owns the framework, nullability, usings, and warnings-as-errors, so a change applies to every project and review sees it in one diff.

provisions.heading: Centralize NuGet Versions
provisions.evidence: Does `apps/api/Directory.Packages.props` enable central management with the manifest pins, with versions in no project file? Look at the central file beside the project files.
provisions.statement: `apps/api/Directory.Packages.props` MUST enable central package management and carry an exact version within each manifest pin.
provisions.rationale: A version written in a project file is invisible to the manifest that owns it, and two projects drift to two versions of one package. Central management leaves project files naming packages only, while one file carries the exact version within each manifest pin, so an upgrade changes one file.

provisions.heading: Commit the Tool Manifest
provisions.evidence: Does the root `.config/dotnet-tools.json` pin every local tool a documented command invokes, including the Stryker.NET runner? Look at the tool manifest.
provisions.statement: The root `.config/dotnet-tools.json` MUST pin every local .NET tool that a documented command invokes.
provisions.rationale: A tool installed by version range resolves differently on two machines, and a build that passes locally fails in CI. Pinning every tool a documented command invokes keeps local and CI runs on one version; when a tool ships in the manifest's .NET release, its pin matches that release. The manifest pins the Stryker.NET runner that `litespec/quality/testing#refuse-surviving-mutants-on-changed-lines` names.

provisions.heading: Set the SDK Floor at the Workspace Root
provisions.evidence: Does the root `global.json` set the manifest major release's first feature band with `latestFeature` roll-forward? Look at the root `global.json`.
provisions.statement: The root `global.json` MUST set the first feature band of the manifest .NET major release as its SDK version and roll forward with `latestFeature`.
provisions.rationale: The first feature band of the manifest's major release is the lowest SDK that builds the workspace, and `latestFeature` roll-forward lets a later feature band of the same major release build it too. A newer major release needs a workspace change, so a local machine and CI stay on one major line. The compiler and its analyzers ship with the SDK, so a different SDK can still build different output within that line; the floor sets the minimum, not identical output. The manifest names the major release; `Directory.Build.props` sets its target framework.

provisions.heading: Construct Aggregate Parts Only Inside the Root
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1014` for a file outside an aggregate's `Domain/` folder that constructs a type from that folder other than the root's input records and typed identifiers.
provisions.statement: A file outside an aggregate's `Domain/` folder MUST NOT construct a type from that folder other than the root's input records, typed identifiers, and the types the interfaces its class implements name in their member signatures (a repository building the query result its Domain interface returns, an adapter building the result its port returns).
provisions.rationale: The root's factories and methods are the one entry point to the aggregate, under `litespec/core/backend-domain#reach-an-aggregate-only-through-its-root`. A caller that constructs an entity or value object of the aggregate builds a part the root never validated, and a caller that constructs a part to pass it in takes over behavior the root should own. Callers pass plain inputs instead. Input records and typed identifiers carry no aggregate behavior, so constructing them stays outside this rule. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#reach-an-aggregate-only-through-its-root` for .NET. Settled by [decision/0104-reach-each-aggregate-only-through-its-root](decision/0104-reach-each-aggregate-only-through-its-root).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, the submit-expense handler constructs no expense line and no allocation. It passes the identifiers, the line inputs, and the submitted time to `Expense.Submit`, and the root builds its lines and its allocation inside the factory.

provisions.heading: Define the Shared Domain Contracts Once
provisions.evidence: Is every shared Domain contract declared once, with `DomainException` and `AggregateRoot<TId>` in their declared shapes? Check the shared contracts; `dotnet build` reports `LS5013` for a base that declares a non-virtual `Code`.
provisions.statement: Declare the shared Domain contracts once in the shared kernel Domain folder and reuse them across every module.
provisions.rationale: Every module raises events, throws domain exceptions, and identifies aggregates. A shared contract declared twice becomes two contracts that drift. Declaring `IDomainEvent`, `DomainException`, `IStronglyTypedId`, `Entity<TId>`, `IAggregateRoot`, and `AggregateRoot<TId>` once in the shared kernel Domain folder gives every module the same mechanics. `DomainException` takes only the message in its constructor and declares `Code` abstract, so the generator writes each refusal code as an override in the partial exception; a base that declares a non-virtual `Code` is reported instead of overridden. Generic handling constrains its parameters with `IAggregateRoot`, as in `IRepository<T> where T : IAggregateRoot`. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#reuse-the-shared-domain-contracts-across-modules` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Hold Every Monetary Amount in the Shared Money Object
provisions.evidence: Does every monetary amount live in the shared `Money` object as a `decimal` with amount and currency? Check each monetary amount.
provisions.statement: A monetary amount MUST use `decimal` inside one shared `Money` value object carrying an ISO 4217 currency code and serializing as `{ "amount": "12.50", "currency": "EUR" }`.
provisions.rationale: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal amounts exactly, so money computed in `double` drifts by cents. The shared `Money` object keeps a `decimal` amount with an ISO 4217 currency code. The owning module record defines supported currencies, scale, rounding, sign rules, and cross-currency arithmetic. Infrastructure maps that precision explicitly. A use case fixed to one currency accepts an amount alone while stating that currency in its record. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#model-money-with-exact-decimal-values` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Implement Domain Services as Stateless Classes
provisions.evidence: Does every domain service stay stateless, take only Domain values, and avoid provider calls? Check each domain service.
provisions.statement: A domain service MUST be a stateless sealed class holding only a calculation that spans aggregates with no owning aggregate, accepting and returning Domain values.
provisions.rationale: Some calculations span concepts with no natural aggregate owner, such as pricing an order from its lines. A stateless service holds that calculation with no persistence, messaging, logging, clock, authorization, or provider call. A calculation one aggregate owns stays in that aggregate's root. The root calls the service inside its own method, or Application passes the service's plain result into a root method as an input. The service carries a mark naming its rule. The builder links it to the rule it computes. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#use-stateless-domain-services-for-ownerless-rules` for .NET. Settled by [decision/0104-reach-each-aggregate-only-through-its-root](decision/0104-reach-each-aggregate-only-through-its-root).

provisions.heading: Keep Clock Reads and Random Values Out of Domain
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1009` for a clock, randomness, or identifier read in Domain.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST NOT read a clock, a random source, or a new `Guid`, so every such value arrives as an argument.
provisions.rationale: Each of `DateTime`, `DateTimeOffset`, `TimeProvider`, `Random`, `RandomNumberGenerator`, `Guid.NewGuid`, and `Guid.CreateVersion7` returns a different value on every call. A Domain method that reads one cannot run twice with the same result and cannot be tested with a fixed value. Receiving each value as an argument keeps every Domain call a pure function of its inputs. The Application layer obtains each value through the port it owns and passes it in. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#pass-nondeterministic-values-into-domain` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Domain Free of Outer-Layer Concerns
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1001` for Domain code naming an outer-layer type.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST reference only the .NET base class library and product-owned Domain types.
provisions.rationale: Once Domain names a persistence or web type, business rules depend on the framework instead of the framework depending on them. Keeping Domain to the base class library and product-owned types means a provider change cannot reach business behavior. Infrastructure registers persisted discriminators and mappings, so Domain carries no serialization attribute. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#keep-domain-independent-of-outer-layers` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Double and Float Out of Exact Quantities
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1008` for a `double` or `float` type in Domain.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST NOT declare a `double` or `float` for a monetary amount, a rate applied to one, or a quantity compared for exact equality.
provisions.rationale: `double` and `float` represent most decimal fractions only approximately, so two amounts that read as equal compare as different. The shared `Money` object holds a `decimal`. A rate applied to a `Money` amount is a `decimal` too. The analyzer reports the Domain declaration that breaks this form. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#keep-binary-floating-point-out-of-exact-quantities` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep ID Representations Aligned at Every Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does every identifier keep the same UUID text form across Domain, persistence, transport, and client boundaries? Trace one identifier through each boundary form.
provisions.statement: Represent an identifier the same way in Domain, persistence, transport, and generated clients.
provisions.rationale: An identifier crosses every boundary in the table below. Each boundary that invents its own text form forces converters at both ends. One UUID text form everywhere means a value copied from a log, a route, or a JSON payload parses at the next boundary without translation. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#align-id-representations-at-every-boundary` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Repository Interfaces in Domain
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1010` for a repository interface exposing a query surface.
provisions.statement: A repository interface MUST expose only aggregate and Domain types for exactly one aggregate root, without `IQueryable`, a session, or a generic CRUD surface.
provisions.rationale: One repository per aggregate keeps the write boundary aligned with the consistency boundary: the interface loads and stages complete aggregates of its own type, and nothing else. `GetByIdAsync` throws `{Aggregate}NotFoundException` for a required load, which frees handlers from repeating null checks. A nullable `FindBy...Async` stays reserved for lookups where absence is normal. A flow that finds a record or creates it is two use cases, and the boundary owning the flow chooses between them, following `litespec/core/backend-application#implement-one-outcome-path-per-command`. `IQueryable`, sessions, and generic CRUD surfaces would leak query shaping and provider behavior into Domain, so the interface exposes none of them. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#limit-each-repository-to-one-aggregate` for .NET. The repository is the write side only. A query reads through a read model owned by Application and shaped by Infrastructure. That path declares no Domain interface. A repository that gained a projection method would put query shapes in Domain, which is the coupling this layer exists to prevent.

provisions.heading: Mark Each State-Changing Root Method with Its Use Case
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS5003` for a root method carrying other than one use-case mark, and `LS5002` for a mark on a reading or private method.
provisions.statement: A root method that changes state MUST carry exactly one `<implements>` mark naming its use case.
provisions.rationale: The `<implements>` mark is the XML documentation tag that ties a method to the use case whose act it performs. The builder and the analyzer read the same link from it. A reading or private method performs no act and carries no use-case mark. `LS5002` reports one that does. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#give-each-use-case-its-own-act` for .NET. The model check for the same rule stays on that generic provision.

provisions.heading: Model Child Entities as Sealed Classes
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1015` for a public setter, constructor, or mutable public collection on a non-root type of an aggregate.
provisions.statement: A child entity MUST be a sealed class deriving from the project-owned `Entity<TId>`, with no public setter, mutating method, or constructor.
provisions.rationale: Deriving from the project-owned `Entity<TId>` gives the child typed identity and identity equality, so it declares only its own data and behavior. The root creates, finds, and changes its children through business methods. A child exposes no mutable state outside the root. Construction and mutation stay internal or private, so only the root reaches them. A child is a design choice inside its aggregate: it appears in code and the glossary, never as a record. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#keep-child-entities-inside-the-aggregate-boundary` for .NET. Settled by [decision/0104-reach-each-aggregate-only-through-its-root](decision/0104-reach-each-aggregate-only-through-its-root).

provisions.heading: Model Every Aggregate Lifecycle with State Records
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1003` for an aggregate with no `State` property, `LS1004` for a state case left unsealed, and `LS1013` for a switch that leaves a sealed state case to its discard arm.
provisions.statement: An aggregate MUST expose its lifecycle only through one `State` property backed by an abstract `{Aggregate}State` record with sealed per-state records.
provisions.rationale: An enum, a status string, a boolean flag, a parallel nullable field, or a computed state cannot carry state-specific data such as a publication time. State records hold each state's data where it belongs. Aggregate methods own the transitions between them. Even a one-state aggregate defines its hierarchy, so later states have a home. The C# compiler does not check that a switch over the hierarchy covers every sealed case: a switch expression needs a discard arm to compile without warning CS8509, and a sealed case with no arm of its own reaches that discard arm at run time. `LS1013` reports a switch that leaves a sealed case to its discard arm. Tests cover the discard path for a case added later. The sealed set matches the aggregate's declared `states`, which is the link the builder follows. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#model-every-aggregate-lifecycle-with-state-types` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Model Every Closed Set of Domain Values Without Enums
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1002` for an enum declared in Domain and `LS1013` for a switch that leaves a sealed case to its discard arm.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST model every closed set as an abstract record base with sealed cases exposing one stable `Code`, converting labels through `FromCode`.
provisions.rationale: An enum is a named integer, so it carries no case data and admits undefined values through a cast. When a case later gains data, the enum grows parallel fields. A record hierarchy carries each case's data in its own sealed record. A boundary converts a label through `FromCode` instead of `ToString`, which turns an unrecognized label into a validation failure rather than a silent default. The C# compiler does not check that a switch over the hierarchy covers every sealed case: a switch expression needs a discard arm to compile without warning CS8509, and a sealed case with no arm of its own reaches that discard arm at run time. `LS1013` reports a switch that leaves a sealed case to its discard arm. Tests cover the discard path for a case added later. A static class of string constants, such as a set of reason codes, is the same closed set without its cases. The compiler cannot tell a valid code from a typo, so it becomes a record hierarchy too. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#model-every-closed-set-as-a-type-hierarchy` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Model Value Objects as Records
provisions.evidence: Is every value object an immutable record with static creation and no base type? Check each value object.
provisions.statement: A value object MUST be an immutable C# record with no base type.
provisions.rationale: Comparison by complete value lets two instances with the same data stand in for each other. The type exposes no setter and no implicit conversion. Creation through a named static method keeps every construction path under the validation the type declares. A value object that holds a collection implements content equality and a matching hash for its declared ordering rule. It copies incoming collections and returns read-only views. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#use-immutable-value-objects-for-domain-concepts` and `litespec/core/backend-domain#compare-collection-values-by-their-content` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Offer a Non-Throwing Parse on Validated Value Types
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1017` for a Domain struct whose constructor throws and which declares no non-throwing parse.
provisions.statement: A typed identifier or value type whose constructor throws on invalid input MUST offer a static `TryParse` that returns false instead of throwing.
provisions.rationale: A serializer and an API boundary meet invalid input as a normal case: a malformed identifier in a route, an empty value in a stored payload. When the only way in is a constructor that throws, the boundary answers a server fault for a caller's mistake, and a serializer that cannot call the constructor rebuilds the value empty without saying so. A `TryParse` lets the boundary refuse with 400 and lets a converter fail loudly on a value it cannot read.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `ExpenseId` throws on an empty `Guid` and offers `ExpenseId.TryParse(string? text, out ExpenseId id)`. The route binding calls `TryParse` and answers 400 for `/expenses/not-an-id`; the JSON converter calls it and fails the read for a stored empty value.

provisions.heading: Raise Immutable Domain Facts
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1007` for a domain event that is not an immutable record.
provisions.statement: A domain event MUST be a public immutable record named `{Aggregate}{PastFact}DomainEvent` implementing `IDomainEvent`, carrying business data only and one mark naming its domain-event record.
provisions.rationale: The `{Aggregate}{PastFact}DomainEvent` name tells a reader which aggregate raised the fact without opening the file. The event carries business data only: the typed identifiers and the values its reactions need. It carries no aggregate, session, service, mutable collection, or exception, because a mutable payload lets a reaction observe state that changed after the fact. Envelope identity, such as message and causation identity, lives on the published integration event that carries the fact outside the process. Its `Classification` comes from the domain-event record its mark names, under `litespec/packs/dotnet/stack#generate-runtime-values-from-the-records`. Only the aggregate root raises events, through `RaiseDomainEvent` on the shared base. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#raise-immutable-facts-as-domain-events` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Reference Other Aggregates by Typed Identifier
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1016` for a property of one aggregate whose type is another aggregate's root or entity.
provisions.statement: An aggregate MUST reference another aggregate only through a property typed as its typed identifier, never through a property typed as its root or entity.
provisions.rationale: An object reference between aggregates loads one aggregate's data through another, which couples their consistency boundaries and their storage. A property typed as the other aggregate's typed identifier keeps each aggregate loadable on its own. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#reference-other-aggregates-by-id` for .NET. Settled by [decision/0104-reach-each-aggregate-only-through-its-root](decision/0104-reach-each-aggregate-only-through-its-root).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, an expense holds the submitting employee as `EmployeeId`, never as an `Employee` object. Application loads the employee through its own repository when a command needs both sides.

provisions.heading: Reject Business Violations with Domain Exceptions
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1005` for a throw outside a `DomainException` subclass and `LS1006` for a domain exception that is misnamed or open.
provisions.statement: A rejected business rule MUST throw a `DomainException` subclass named `{DomainType}{Reason}Exception`, carrying the refusal `code` and one mark naming its rule.
provisions.rationale: One exception type per rule puts the stable code and the message in the type. The call site passes only domain values. Two rules never share a type by accident. A shared rule exception with caller-supplied codes lets any caller invent a code and lets unrelated rules merge silently. Its `Code` comes from the refusal result its rule names, under `litespec/packs/dotnet/stack#generate-runtime-values-from-the-records`. Each exception's code equals the refusal `code` on the result record it answers. The root's factory and methods check an invariant rule. The use-case validator or the root's method checks a precondition rule. Names lead with the aggregate root and follow `litespec/workspace/naming#name-exceptions-by-failed-rule`. This provision owns the one-type-per-rule shape and the code each type carries. Domain throws no `InvalidOperationException`, `ArgumentException`, validation, HTTP, or provider exception for a business rejection. It carries no transport status. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#reject-business-violations-with-dedicated-refusals` for .NET. One type per rule still holds when every module refuses with one code: the product holds one product rule with the product name as its home, and the Kernel holds the one exception that marks it.

provisions.heading: Split a Large Root into One File per Action
provisions.evidence: Does any root file hold more than one business action or run past 500 lines without following this layout? Look at each root file beside its actions.
provisions.statement: Declare a root whose file passes 500 lines as a partial class with one folder per business action named `{Act}/`, holding the partial file `{Root}.{Act}.cs` with the action's inputs and its private rules.
provisions.rationale: A root grows with every business action it owns, and one file holding every action reads as one long listing. Splitting the root into one folder per action keeps each action readable on its own while the root stays the one entry point to its aggregate. The name is the use case's act, so `Domain/Entries/PostInvoice/` mirrors `Application/Entries/PostInvoiceEntry/`. The action's rules stay private to the root, as private members or private nested types, so no caller reaches them past the root's methods. Settled by [decision/0104-reach-each-aggregate-only-through-its-root](decision/0104-reach-each-aggregate-only-through-its-root).

provisions.heading: Throw Only Refusal Codes the Module Owns
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `refusal-module-foreign` (level S) for a refusal code carried from another module's code, `refusal-code-duplicate` (level S) for a refusal code two exception types carry, and `code-placement-drift` or `record-placement-invalid` for a refusal and its exception declared under different homes.
provisions.statement: Each refusal code a module declares MUST be carried by at most one exception type, in the module that declares it, under the aggregate whose set declares the refusal.
provisions.rationale: A refusal code tells the caller which module refused and why. An exception in one module that carries another module's code blames the wrong owner. Two exception types carrying one code leave the caller unable to tell which rule failed, so the code stops meaning anything once it travels. Each aggregate declares the refusals its rules raise once in its own set, with the module's set keeping only the refusals no aggregate raises, under `litespec/core/use-cases#declare-each-aggregates-refusals-once` and `litespec/core/use-cases#declare-each-modules-refusals-once`. Each exception type carries its rule's code from that set in `Domain/{Aggregates}/Exceptions/`, under `litespec/packs/dotnet/domain#reject-business-violations-with-domain-exceptions`. One carrying type per code in the declaring module keeps the blame and the rule behind each code fixed. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#reject-business-violations-with-dedicated-refusals` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Use Strongly Typed Version 7 Identifiers
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1012` for an `Id` struct outside the strongly typed form, or a raw `Guid` as an aggregate identity.
provisions.statement: An aggregate identity MUST be a `readonly record struct` wrapping one version 7 `Guid`, declaring no implicit conversion, primitive alias, or public parameterless creation path.
provisions.rationale: A bare `Guid` parameter accepts any identifier, including an empty one and one meant for another aggregate. The typed struct rejects `Guid.Empty` and the struct default in every factory, implements `IStronglyTypedId` and `IParsable<TId>`, and declares no implicit conversion or parameterless creation. A wrong identifier therefore fails at the boundary. New values arrive from the caller. A factory takes its identifier as an argument. A method that needs several takes a generator. Domain reads no clock and calls no static source of time or randomness, which keeps business behavior deterministic and testable. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#identify-each-aggregate-with-a-typed-version-7-identifier` for .NET. When two callers generate the same value, persistence rejects the duplicate key. The operation fails on the same path as any other write conflict, with the violation mapped to the use case conflict refusal under `litespec/core/backend-persistence#map-a-constraint-violation-to-its-refusal`.

provisions.heading: Use the Project Aggregate Root Contract
provisions.evidence: Does every aggregate root stay a sealed class derived from the project-owned `AggregateRoot<TId>`? Check each root declaration.
provisions.statement: An aggregate root MUST be a sealed class deriving from the project-owned `AggregateRoot<TId>`, taking identity and event mechanics from that base.
provisions.rationale: One project-owned base gives every aggregate the same mechanics: typed identity, a pending event collection with protected recording, and clearing. The shared base supplies exactly those mechanics and nothing else: no timestamps, audit, tenancy, lifecycle, or persistence that would force every aggregate to carry behavior most never need. It carries the aggregate version only as persistence metadata, which Domain never reads or sets. The root stays a sealed class, so no behavior extends an aggregate by inheritance. It carries a mark naming its aggregate record for the builder to link. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-domain#take-identity-and-events-from-the-shared-root-contract` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Implementation Style Consistent
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS3004` for a concrete class with no derived type that is not sealed.
provisions.statement: Production C# MUST use file-scoped namespaces, braces on every body, explicit access modifiers, and sealed concrete classes.
provisions.rationale: File-scoped namespaces, braces on every body, explicit access modifiers, and sealed concrete classes change diff readability rather than behavior. One shared setting removes the debate from every review and keeps generated and hand-written code consistent.

provisions.heading: Match C# Files and Primary Types
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS3003` for a C# file whose name differs from its primary type.
provisions.statement: A C# file MUST contain one primary top-level type and take that type's exact name.
provisions.rationale: A file named for its type lets a reader and a tool find the type by the path. Two top-level types in one file break that lookup and merge their histories in review. Only a small private or file-scoped nested type stays with its owner.

provisions.heading: Name Every Event Type by Its Kind
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2031` for an event type whose name does not end in the suffix of its kind.
provisions.statement: An event type MUST end in the suffix of its kind: `DomainEvent` for a domain event, `ModuleEvent` for a module event, and `IntegrationEvent` for an integration event.
provisions.rationale: A codebase holds all three kinds at once: the domain event an aggregate raises for its own module, the module event other modules consume, and the integration event that leaves the product. A bare `Event` suffix, or no suffix, never says which contract the type carries: whether the fact stays inside its module, is versioned for other modules, or has external consumers. The kind suffix puts that answer in the name, beside the `Command`, `Query`, `Result`, and `Id` suffixes the Role Suffixes table assigns. eShopOnContainers names its events `DomainEvent` and `IntegrationEvent` the same way.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, the expense aggregate raises `ExpenseApprovedDomainEvent` from `Domain/Expenses/Events/`, and the spending Contracts project publishes `ExpenseReimbursedModuleEvent` from `Contracts/Expenses/OnExpenseReimbursed/` for the reporting module. A reaction keeps the fact without the suffix: `SubmitPayoutOnExpenseApprovedHandler` answers the approval.

provisions.heading: Name Every Folder and Type for Its Reason
provisions.evidence: `litespec model review` reports `name-reason-missing` (level R) for a folder or type named for the absence of a reason outside the declared shared kernel.
provisions.statement: No folder is named `Shared`, `Common`, `Util`, `Utils`, `Helpers`, or `Misc`, and no type carries one of those names or ends in `Helper`, `Manager`, `Util`, or `Utils`, outside the declared shared kernel.
provisions.rationale: A folder named `Shared` or a type ending in `Manager` states no reason in its name, and each such name collects unrelated code. The shared kernel project is the one declared exception, named in one place, so the exception stays visible instead of spreading.
provisions.example: The declared shared kernel project passes; `Billing/Helpers/` and `OrderManager` outside it are reported.

provisions.heading: Put the Cancellation Token Last
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS3002` for a cancellation token that is misplaced or misnamed.
provisions.statement: In the dotnet stack, a method that takes a `CancellationToken` MUST place it last, or second to last before a `params` array, and name it `cancellationToken`.
provisions.rationale: A token in a fixed trailing position lets every caller pass cancellation without reading the signature, and one name lets every reader tell the token from the data beside it. A token in the middle of a signature is passed in the wrong position, and a renamed token hides what it is at the call site.
provisions.example: `SubmitExpenseCommandHandler.HandleAsync` takes `SubmitExpenseCommand command` and then `CancellationToken cancellationToken`, so a caller passes the data first and cancellation last.

provisions.heading: Raise the LiteBus Handler Analyzers to Errors
provisions.evidence: Does `.editorconfig` set `litebus_forbid_nested_commands` to `true`, `LB1023` and `LB1024` to error, and list `litebus.LB1024.forbidden_types`? Look at `.editorconfig`.
provisions.statement: A project using LiteBus sets `litebus_forbid_nested_commands = true` in `.editorconfig`, sets `LB1023` and `LB1024` to `error`, and lists its outside-world client types in `litebus.LB1024.forbidden_types`.
provisions.rationale: Both LiteBus rules are off by default, so a command handler can send a second message or call an outside system with no report. `LB1023` reports nested mediation in a command handler and reports nothing until `litebus_forbid_nested_commands` is `true`. The runtime counterpart is `ForbidNestedCommands()` on the command module builder, which throws `NestedMediationException` before the inner pipeline starts, so the option pairs the build check with that guarantee. `LB1024` reports an outside-world client in a command handler. Consequences then leave through event handlers after the commit, under `litespec/core/backend-application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage`. The client list replaces the defaults, so it names every port that leaves the process. The same file lists the project pipeline-owned collaborators under the key the [Configuration section of the LS2016 rule page](../../analyzers/rules/ls2016.md#configuration) names, such as its uniqueness claim service.
provisions.example:
```text
litebus_forbid_nested_commands = true
dotnet_diagnostic.LB1023.severity = error
dotnet_diagnostic.LB1024.severity = error
litebus.LB1024.forbidden_types = Claimwick.Payouts.PayoutBankClient
litespec.LS2016.pipeline_owned_types = Claimwick.Spending.ExpenseKeyClaims
```

provisions.heading: Reference Only the LiteBus Module Required
provisions.evidence: Does every project file reference only the LiteBus modules its code dispatches? Look at each project file.
provisions.statement: Reference the LiteBus command, query, or event module that the code actually uses.
provisions.rationale: A unified bus package pulls contracts for commands, queries, and events into a layer that dispatches only some of them. Referencing only the module the code uses keeps each dispatch surface exact.

provisions.heading: Run LiteSpec Analyzers in the Business Projects and Hosts
provisions.evidence: Does every Kernel, Platform, module, and host project file reference `LiteSpec.Analyzers` at the manifest pin with `PrivateAssets="all"`? Look at each business and host project file.
provisions.statement: Reference `LiteSpec.Analyzers` at the manifest pin, with `PrivateAssets="all"`, from the Kernel, Platform, and module projects and each host project.
provisions.rationale: The analyzers report a breach of a .NET provision in the editor and the build, at the line that breaks it, with a link to the provision. Without them, a breach surfaces only in review, if at all. The analyzer package is a development dependency: it adds nothing to the built assemblies, so Domain stays package-free at run time. `LS2016` reports a pipeline-owned collaborator in a handler constructor. Its default list covers the LiteBus unit of work, idempotency store, and outbox, and a project adds its uniqueness claim service. [Check .NET code with the analyzers](../../analyzers/check-dotnet-code-with-the-analyzers.md) sets it up, and [Analyzer rules](../../analyzers/README.md) lists what each rule reports. Settled by [decision/0103-dotnet-stack-binding](decision/0103-dotnet-stack-binding).
provisions.example:
```xml
<ItemGroup>
  <PackageReference Include="LiteSpec.Analyzers" PrivateAssets="all" />
</ItemGroup>
```

An unreleased build is consumed the same way, through a local feed. Pack the analyzers from the LiteSpec checkout, so the package carries the analyzer, rule library, and mark reader assemblies in its analyzer folder:

```sh
dotnet pack apps/analyzers/src/LiteSpec.Analyzers
```

Then point a local source at the packages folder, with source mapping for `LiteSpec.*`:

```xml
<packageSources>
  <add key="litespec-local" value="../LiteSpec/artifacts/packages" />
</packageSources>
<packageSourceMapping>
  <packageSource key="litespec-local">
    <package pattern="LiteSpec.*" />
  </packageSource>
</packageSourceMapping>
```

A project reference to the analyzer project does not carry its dependency assemblies with it, so the analyzers fail to load. Use the local feed instead.

provisions.heading: Apply Optimistic Concurrency to Every Aggregate Document
provisions.evidence: Does every Marten aggregate document type enable optimistic concurrency? Look at each document type and the document policy.
provisions.statement: Each Marten aggregate document type MUST enable optimistic concurrency.
provisions.rationale: The store compares the version each command loaded with the version it commits against, so a stale write fails the commit instead of silently overwriting newer work. Each aggregate document type enables it with `UseOptimisticConcurrency(true)`, or one `Policies.ForAllDocuments` policy covers every aggregate document type at once. No aggregate document type is left without it. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-persistence#version-every-aggregate` for .NET.
provisions.example:
The expense document enables the check on its own type:

```csharp
options.Schema.For<Expense>().UseOptimisticConcurrency(true);
```

provisions.heading: Apply Schema Changes in a Migration Step
provisions.evidence: Does any hosted schema change run from application startup or through `AutoCreate.All`, or does any host open its store with a schema-changing `AutoCreate` value? Look at the migration step and the host store configuration.
provisions.statement: Outside development, schema objects MUST change only in a migration step that runs before the hosts start and applies the difference with `CreateOrUpdate`, never `AutoCreate.All`, while the hosts run with `AutoCreate.None`.
provisions.rationale: A schema change that runs from a starting replica races every other replica, and `AutoCreate.All` drops and recreates tables that do not match the model, so it would destroy the data in a database that holds it. A migration step applies the difference once with `ApplyAllConfiguredChangesToDatabaseAsync(AutoCreate.CreateOrUpdate)` before any host starts, and each host opens its store with `AutoCreate.None` so startup never alters the schema. Development and disposable integration databases may still create schema automatically, as the shared rule allows. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-persistence#control-production-schema-changes` for .NET.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, a release adds an index over submitted expenses. A deployment step applies the difference with `AutoCreate.CreateOrUpdate` before the Claimwick WebApi and Worker hosts start, and both hosts configure the store with `AutoCreate.None`, so neither changes the schema at startup. No host carries `AutoCreate.All`.

provisions.heading: Claim Cross-Record Keys with a Claims Document
provisions.evidence: Is every cross-record key claimed through a claims document written with `session.Insert`, never with `Store`? Look at each key claim.
provisions.statement: Each cross-record uniqueness key MUST be claimed through a claims document keyed by the key text and written with `session.Insert`, never with `Store`.
provisions.rationale: Some keys admit no index: Marten cannot index elements of a list inside a document, cannot enforce uniqueness across document types, and computed indexes do not work on `DateTime` or `DateTimeOffset` members. Those keys are claimed through a small document whose id is the key text, so the store still arbitrates the race. The write uses `Insert`, which fails when the key document already exists. `Store` upserts, so it would overwrite a competing claim instead of colliding with it. The repository compares the aggregate keys at load with the keys at commit, and inserts the added key documents and deletes the removed ones in the same transaction. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-persistence#claim-a-cross-record-key-at-commit` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Commit Once in the Command Pipeline
provisions.evidence: Does exactly one post-handler file call `SaveChangesAsync` in each pipeline? Look at the `SaveChangesAsync` calls in each pipeline.
provisions.statement: Exactly one global command post-handler MUST call `SaveChangesAsync` for a command pipeline.
provisions.rationale: When exactly one post-handler commits, a failed command leaves the scoped session uncommitted and no partial work persists. A second commit, in a handler, repository, validator, reaction, job, or endpoint, would store work the pipeline later refuses. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-persistence#commit-each-command-pipeline-once` for .NET. The obligation is one commit per pipeline, not one named method. Under the baseline provider that commit is `IDocumentSession.SaveChangesAsync`. Under `consistency: atomic` it covers everything the handler staged. Other modes split work across commands. Each command still commits once, and the job resumes from its cursor or runs the declared compensation.

provisions.heading: Compare Typed Identifiers by Their Underlying Values in Queries
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2032` for a query passing a list of typed identifiers as a database parameter. It reports `LS2037` for a query reading the document's own identity value inside a queryable expression.
provisions.statement: A query MUST compare typed identifiers by their underlying values instead of passing a list of typed identifiers as a query parameter.
provisions.rationale: The database driver binds a list parameter by the element type it knows. A list of typed identifiers reaches the driver as a list of an unknown structured type, and the comparison then fails or matches nothing at the database. Comparing the underlying values keeps the parameter a list of values the driver binds. Each identifier still travels as its typed form in code and crosses into its underlying value only at the query.
provisions.example:
In the library product, the list-loans query takes a list of reader identifiers and compares `reader_id` against the underlying values:

```csharp
var ids = query.ReaderIds.Select(id => id.Value).ToList();
```

The query passes `ids` as its parameter, so the database compares values it binds.

provisions.heading: Enforce Uniqueness with Marten Unique Indexes
provisions.evidence: Does every Marten aggregate document with a uniqueness rule carry a unique index or an owner-derived identity? Look at the store configuration.
provisions.statement: Each Marten aggregate document MUST enforce its uniqueness rules through a unique index over the stored value or an identity derived from its owner.
provisions.rationale: A unique index makes the store arbitrate the race at commit, where every concurrent write is visible. The index is declared with `options.Schema.For<T>().UniqueIndex`, or as a computed index carrying `IsUnique`. The index name follows `litespec/core/backend-persistence#use-database-naming-conventions`. A record that exists at most once per owner takes a document id equal to the owner id instead, so a second record for the same owner collides on identity. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-persistence#enforce-uniqueness-in-the-store` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Evolve Stored Documents When They Are Read
provisions.evidence: Is any stored document missing a contract version, any contract change missing a registered upgrade step, any stored form rewritten outside the next save without an approved deploy rewrite for a query or index, or any broken upgrade chain accepted at composition? Look at the document contract versions, the registered upgrade steps, and the store configuration.
provisions.statement: Each stored document carries its contract version, a registered upgrade step for each version runs on the JSON before deserializing, the stored form is rewritten only when the aggregate is saved again, composition refuses a broken chain of steps, and a rewrite at deploy is reserved for documents that may change and only when a query or index needs the new shape.
provisions.rationale: Marten upcasts only events, never documents, so a stored document keeps the JSON an earlier version wrote. Chaining one step per version and refusing a broken chain keeps a document at any old version readable. Because the upgrade runs on read and rewrites only on the next save, an append-only record or a hash-chained audit record keeps its stored form: the upgrade shapes the in-memory object without changing the bytes on disk. A deploy-time rewrite would touch those records, so it stays limited to documents whose form may change and only when a query or index cannot work with the old shape. This is how a .NET consumer meets `litespec/core/backend-persistence#evolve-stored-document-contracts-explicitly`.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, version 1 of an expense document stores the submitter under `submittedBy`. Version 2 renames that member to `employeeId`. A registered step from version 1 to version 2 rewrites the JSON on read before deserializing, so both old and new documents load as the current aggregate, and the old document's stored form changes only the next time that expense is saved. For an append-only approval record, the same read step produces the current in-memory shape but never rewrites the stored document.

provisions.heading: Implement the Unit of Work Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does the project's unit of work implement `IUnitOfWorkBoundary` with `BeginAsync` and `RollbackAsync`? Look at the unit-of-work type beside the pipeline composition.
provisions.statement: The project's unit of work MUST implement `IUnitOfWorkBoundary`.
provisions.rationale: LiteBus calls `BeginAsync` after guards, validators, and shortcuts and before the first pre-handler, commits on success, and rolls back otherwise. The one commit per command pipeline under `litespec/packs/dotnet/persistence#commit-once-in-the-command-pipeline` and the guard read lock under `litespec/packs/dotnet/persistence#read-each-guarding-aggregate-under-a-shared-lock` then run inside one transaction that LiteBus opens.

provisions.heading: Keep Pipeline-Owned Collaborators Out of Handlers
