provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2016` for a command or query handler whose constructor takes a pipeline-owned type.
provisions.statement: A command or query handler MUST NOT take a pipeline-owned collaborator, such as `IUnitOfWork`, `IIdempotencyStore`, or `ITransactionalOutbox`, through its constructor.
provisions.rationale: The pipeline owns the unit of work, the idempotency store, the outbox, and the uniqueness claim service. A handler that takes one of them commits or reserves work outside the post-handler that owns the commit. The analyzer's default list names the LiteBus types, and a project adds its own claim service to the `litespec.LS2016.pipeline_owned_types` key. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-persistence#keep-uniqueness-out-of-handlers` for .NET.
provisions.example: The submit-expense handler takes its Domain repository and no unit of work, so the commit stays in the one post-handler. A handler constructor that adds `IUnitOfWork` is reported at the parameter.

provisions.heading: Load Documents Keyed by Typed Identifiers One at a Time
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2033` for a batch document load keyed by typed identifiers.
provisions.statement: A repository MUST load documents keyed by a typed identifier one at a time instead of batching them in one load call.
provisions.rationale: A batch load call keys its lookup by the identifier form the store understands. A batch of typed identifiers reaches the store in a form its key comparison does not match, so the call returns nothing or the wrong documents. Loading each document by its typed identifier through the single-document load keeps every lookup on the path the typed-identifier mapping defines.

provisions.heading: Map Constraint Violations with the PostgreSQL Refusal Classifier
provisions.evidence: Does every unique index name map to its conflict refusal code in the PostgreSQL refusal classifier? Look at the service registration.
provisions.statement: Each Marten unique index MUST map by name to its conflict refusal code in `PostgreSqlConstraintRefusalClassifier`.
provisions.rationale: The `LiteBus.Storage.PostgreSql.PostgreSqlConstraintRefusalClassifier` carries the map from index name to refusal code and is registered through `UseFaultRefusalClassifierInstance`. The pipeline fault classification then turns a unique violation into the use case named conflict refusal under `litespec/core/backend-application#refuse-a-lost-race-as-a-conflict`. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-persistence#map-a-constraint-violation-to-its-refusal` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Map Marten Concurrency Faults to Conflict Refusals
provisions.evidence: Does every `ConcurrencyException` path at commit reach the use case conflict refusal? Look at the registered classifier.
provisions.statement: A classifier MUST translate Marten's `ConcurrencyException` into the use case conflict refusal.
provisions.rationale: A `ConcurrencyException` names a provider type that Application does not expose. The registered classifier translates it into the use case named conflict refusal, following `litespec/core/backend-application#refuse-a-lost-race-as-a-conflict`. A version race and a uniqueness race then reach the caller through the same refusal path. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-application#refuse-a-lost-race-as-a-conflict` for .NET.
provisions.example: Two approvers race on one submitted expense; the loser throws `ConcurrencyException` at commit, and the classifier returns the approve conflict refusal so the caller re-reads the expense before deciding again.

provisions.heading: Plan Each Schema Change Before Applying It
provisions.evidence: Does any migration step apply SQL it has not printed, pass a destructive statement without an explicit allowance, or leave the ledger without this build's schema fingerprint at readiness? Look at the migration step output, the allowance, and the ledger.
provisions.statement: The migration step prints the SQL that `CreateMigrationAsync()` plans, marks every destructive statement, refuses those statements without an explicit allowance, records each applied run in a ledger with the build's schema fingerprint, and requires the ledger to hold this build's fingerprint before the release is ready.
provisions.rationale: `CreateMigrationAsync()` computes the difference without applying it and `ToDatabaseScript()` gives the full creation script, so the step can show what it will run and stop on a drop no one approved. `AssertDatabaseMatchesConfigurationAsync()` and Weasel's `db-assert` report drift on demand. A ledger keyed by schema fingerprint tells the readiness check which schema a database already holds, so a build is not applied twice or applied to a database at a different schema.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, the migration step prints the planned SQL for a new index over expenses and flags a statement that would drop an old column; the release stops until an owner allows that drop. After the step applies, it writes the build's schema fingerprint to the migration ledger, and the readiness job checks that ledger entry before opening traffic to the Claimwick hosts.

provisions.heading: Query Through IQuerySession
provisions.evidence: Does every query handler project through `IQuerySession`, with filter, scope, ordering, and limit applied before materialization? Look at each query handler file.
provisions.statement: A query handler MUST project through `IQuerySession`, applying filter, scope, ordering, and limit before materialization.
provisions.rationale: The read session already filters, orders, pages, and projects. A read-store interface per aggregate, a generic read repository, or a callback wrapper adds a layer that repeats it. Ordering and paging follow `litespec/core/backend-api#bound-collection-queries`. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-persistence#query-through-the-read-session` for .NET. Under the Marten baseline the query surface is `IQuerySession`, and the obligation to project with filter, scope, ordering, and limit holds. A table the project keeps beside its documents, such as a counter or an append-only ledger written through plain SQL, is read through the same session. Under Marten, `AdvancedSql.QueryAsync<TRow>` returns any JSON-serializable type. The SQL selects one JSON object per row, keyed in the casing the store's serializer uses, with the filter, ordering, and limit in its `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, and `LIMIT`. The handler keeps no repository for such a table, and the project adds no read interface for it.
provisions.example:
In the Claimwick product, each spending owner's running totals live in a `spending_totals` table that a command updates in place. The read-spending-totals query reads it through the session:

```csharp
internal sealed record SpendingTotalRow(Guid OwnerId, string Currency, decimal Submitted, decimal Approved);

var rows = await session.AdvancedSql.QueryAsync<SpendingTotalRow>(
    """
    select jsonb_build_object(
        'ownerId', owner_id, 'currency', currency, 'submitted', submitted, 'approved', approved)
    from spending_totals
    where owner_id = ?
    order by currency
    limit 100
    """,
    cancellationToken,
    query.OwnerId.Value);
```

provisions.heading: Read Each Guarding Aggregate Under a Shared Lock
provisions.evidence: Does every guarding-aggregate read go through `GetForGuardAsync` with a shared row lock in the command's transaction? Look at each repository guard read.
provisions.statement: A repository MUST read a guarding aggregate through `GetForGuardAsync`, which runs a `FOR SHARE` query through the Marten session in the command's transaction.
provisions.rationale: A read followed by a write does not keep the guard true: a competing command can change the guarding row between the two. The guard read runs `SELECT ... FOR SHARE` on PostgreSQL through the Marten session, with `session.QueryAsync<T>` carrying the SQL or with `AdvancedSql.QueryAsync`, inside the transaction LiteBus opens through `IUnitOfWorkBoundary`, so a competing command that changes the guarding row waits until the guarded command commits, and a guarded command that starts after the change reads the new state and refuses. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-persistence#honor-the-declared-consistency-mode` for .NET.
provisions.example: Claimwick's submit-expense command guards on the expense report staying open. Its repository reads the report through `GetForGuardAsync`, so a close-report command that lands first makes submit-expense read the closed report and refuse, while a close-report that lands during the submit waits on its lock until the submit commits.

provisions.heading: Register One Scoped Session
provisions.evidence: Does the service registration wire `IDocumentSession` once per WebApi request or Worker operation scope? Look at the service registration.
provisions.statement: Register `IDocumentSession` with the WebApi request or Worker operation scope.
provisions.rationale: One session per WebApi request or Worker operation means the repositories and the commit handler in one command resolve the same instance. Two sessions would stage and commit separately, splitting one command across two units of work. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-persistence#use-one-session-per-command` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Share One Serializer Configuration Across Marten and the Outbox
provisions.evidence: Does every store build its serializer options from the one factory method, with no store carrying its own converters? Look at the Marten, outbox, and job store registrations beside the factory method.
provisions.statement: Marten, the outbox store, and any scheduled-job store MUST share one serializer configuration built by one factory method.
provisions.rationale: This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-persistence#serialize-every-persisted-payload-with-one-configuration` for .NET: one factory method builds the `JsonSerializerOptions` with the converters and discriminator registrations, and each store takes its options from that method. A converter added in one place then reaches every store, and a typed identifier with a validating constructor and a get-only value round-trips identically through each one.

provisions.heading: Stage Aggregate Writes Through Repositories
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2004` for a command handler writing through a document session or database context.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST reach persistence only through a Domain repository, never through `IDocumentSession`.
provisions.rationale: Infrastructure implements each Domain repository with the scoped session, so the handler stages work without naming a provider type. A repository that exposed the session, a generic query, or a save operation would hand the handler the provider surface the layer exists to hide. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-persistence#stage-aggregate-writes-through-domain-repositories` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Store Each Aggregate Root as Its Own Document
provisions.evidence: Is any aggregate stored through a parallel document type instead of as its own document? Look at the stored document types beside the aggregates.
provisions.statement: Marten MUST store each aggregate root as its own document, with no parallel document type for an aggregate.
provisions.rationale: A parallel document type duplicates the aggregate shape in Infrastructure, forces mapping code between the two, and splits reads between two models of one thing. Storing the root keeps one shape from the handler to the disk. Infrastructure owns the JSON contract that makes it work: the store serializer handles non-public members and constructors, one registered discriminator per closed-set case, and converters for values such as `Money` and typed identifiers, while Domain carries no serialization attribute. Query handlers query the aggregate type through `IQuerySession`. This provision covers the stored aggregate; a query-shaped read document under `litespec/core/backend-persistence#add-read-documents-for-query-shaped-data` serves queries and is no parallel aggregate document. This provision binds `litespec/core/backend-persistence#keep-serialization-behavior-out-of-domain` for .NET. Settled by [decision/0105-store-each-aggregate-root-as-its-own-document](decision/0105-store-each-aggregate-root-as-its-own-document).

provisions.heading: Declare `dotnet` as the Backend Stack
provisions.evidence: Does `.litespec/project.yaml` list `dotnet` in `stacks` when the backend runs on .NET? Check `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A project whose backend runs on .NET MUST name `dotnet` in the `stacks` of `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: The `stacks` entry applies every page in this folder with its checks and analyzers. An undeclared backend follows no .NET rule, and the model builder selects no readers for its C# handlers, events, refusal codes, and scenarios.

provisions.heading: Declare Marked Events and Exceptions as Partial Types
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS5006` for a marked domain event or rule exception that is not `partial`, in every project that references the analyzer package.
provisions.statement: A project that references the analyzer package MUST declare every marked domain event and rule exception as a `partial` type.
provisions.rationale: The source generator adds the runtime value as a second part of the type. A type that is not `partial` cannot take one. The generator writes a value only where no member of that name is declared in source, so a hand-written value is compared with the record rather than duplicated. A code fix adds `partial` and deletes a hand-written value that equals the record.
provisions.example: The declaration `public sealed partial record ExpenseSubmittedDomainEvent(...)` takes its generated `Classification`, while the same record without `partial` is reported.

provisions.heading: Generate Runtime Values from the Records
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `runtime-value-drift` (level S) for a hand-written value that differs from its record, and `dotnet build` reports `LS5005` for the same value.
provisions.statement: A domain event `Classification` and a domain exception `Code` MUST equal the values their records state.
provisions.rationale: The record states each identifier and refusal code once. A second hand-written copy in code is a second source that drifts. With the analyzer package installed, its source generator writes the value into the `partial` type from the mark and the record. The event `Classification` is the event identifier, and the exception `Code` is the `code` of the refusal result its rule names. Without the analyzer package, the value stays hand-written, and the check compares it with the record.

provisions.heading: Generate the Registry, Permissions, and Roles from the Records
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS5009` for two records generating one constant name, `LS5011` for a message two marked handlers serve with different use cases, and `LS5012` for a role allowing a permission no record declares.
provisions.statement: Code MUST read a use case's identity, its grant, a permission's facts, and a role's permission set from the classes the analyzer package generates from the marks and the records, never from a hand-written copy.
provisions.rationale: Each of these facts is written once, on a record or in a mark. A hand-written table of them is a second source that drifts the first time a record changes. The generator writes them per project. `LiteSpecRegistry` answers a message type's use case (`UseCaseOf`), a marked type's use case (`UseCaseOfType`), a message type's grant (`GrantOf`), and in an API project an operation name's use case (`UseCaseOfOperation`). `LiteSpecPermissions` holds one constant and one entry per `permission/` record, and `LiteSpecRoles` holds each role's scope and the permissions its record allows. In the module layout the modules project generates all three, and the host beside it reads them from there. The shared kernel project generates none, and the host generates only `LiteSpecHostOperations`, which answers `UseCaseOfOperation` for the endpoints the host itself holds. A role that names a permission no record declares, and two records that generate one name, stop at build time.
provisions.example: When Claimwick's `role/finance` record gains a permission, `LiteSpecRoles.Of("role/finance").Permissions` carries it at the next build with no hand-written table to update, and `LiteSpecRegistry.GrantOf(typeof(ReimburseExpenseCommand))` answers the reimbursement grant.

provisions.heading: Identify an Aggregate Root by Its Mark and State Record
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `aggregate-unimplemented` (level S) for an aggregate record that no type with its mark and its state record, and no type deriving the aggregate root base, implements.
provisions.statement: The .NET stack reader MUST recognize a type that carries an `aggregate` mark and a `State` property backed by an abstract state record as an aggregate root.
provisions.rationale: A project that claims Implementation with `own` keeps its own code layout and its own aggregate base, so a root that follows the LiteSpec base type is not the only root the code holds. The aggregate mark names the record the type implements, and the state record states its lifecycle. Together they identify the root without the base type. A type with only the mark, or only the state record, does not state both facts, so it stays unrecognized. This provision states the `trace: yes` reading of the aggregate root beside `litespec/packs/dotnet/domain#use-the-project-aggregate-root-contract`, which governs the full contract.
provisions.example: The library loan type carries `/// <implements>aggregate/lending.loan</implements>` with a `LoanState State` property backed by the abstract `LoanState` record, so the reader treats it as the loan aggregate root and reads its public methods as aggregate methods.

provisions.heading: Pin the Test Packages in the Manifest
provisions.evidence: Does every test project reference each test package at its manifest-pinned version? Check each test project file beside the package pins in `litespec.manifest.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A .NET test project MUST reference each test package at the version `litespec.manifest.yaml` pins.
provisions.rationale: A test package that moves to a newer version changes what the tests prove without any change to the code under test. The manifest is the one place the release names its pins, so the test SDK, the Microsoft.Testing.Platform extensions, the xUnit runner, the property-test and mock libraries, and the PostgreSQL container each resolve to the version the release reviewed.

provisions.heading: Read Every Declared Web and Worker Host
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reader-missing` (level S) for a named host folder that does not exist, and reads the handlers, endpoints and jobs of each named host that does.
provisions.statement: The .NET stack reader MUST read every project that `stackConfig.dotnet.webapi` and `stackConfig.dotnet.worker` name, whether each field holds one glob string or a list of glob strings.
provisions.rationale: A backend can serve its use cases from more than one web host and run more than one worker host. Each host holds endpoints or jobs the others do not. Reading only the first host leaves the use cases that only the other hosts serve looking unimplemented. Each named host is therefore a source root of the read. A host that is not a WebApi or worker project, such as a command-line host, is not a stack root.
provisions.example: Claimwick serves member requests from one web host and partner requests from a second, so `webapi` lists both host projects and the reader reads the endpoints of each.

provisions.heading: Read .NET Code Through the Stack Reader
provisions.evidence: Does the .NET reader read every shape the statement names? Check the stack reader source for marks, injected repositories, returned codes, dispatch calls, aggregate method calls, raised events, and test results.
provisions.statement: The .NET stack reader MUST read marks in both styles, injected repositories, returned codes, dispatch calls, aggregate method calls, raised events, and test results.
provisions.rationale: Each level S check reads one of those shapes. The mark links a code element to its record: a handler, an event handler, an endpoint, an aggregate root and its methods, a domain event, a refusal type, and a test each name what they serve. The reader reads a mark in either style and reports the style the project did not declare. Injected repositories prove `writes`: a repository serves the aggregate its implementing class names in an `implements` mark, or, with no such mark, the aggregate its interface names. Returned codes prove declared results and refusals, and dispatch calls prove declared effects. The reader reports `behavior-unrecorded`, `use-case-unimplemented`, `write-undeclared`, `result-undeclared`, `effect-undeclared`, and `refusal-unimplemented` from code. Test marks with the latest test run prove each scenario. The reader reports `proves-unreached` and `use-case-scenario-missing` from tests. The reader also reads the options classes that bind keyed settings, through each class's `SectionName` constant and properties, under `litespec/packs/dotnet/config#bind-every-keyed-setting-in-one-options-class`. It also reads the template store `stackConfig.dotnet.templateStore` names: one C# file whose top-level dictionary initializer keys are the template keys and whose texts write each parameter as `{{PascalCaseName}}`. Level S checks block where this reader is qualified and report elsewhere.
provisions.example: Claimwick's reimburse-expense handler carries `/// <implements>use-case/spending.reimburse-expense</implements>`, and its approver-reminder event handler carries `/// <implements>reaction/spending.send-approver-reminder-on-expense-submitted</implements>`.

provisions.heading: Report a Stack Root That Matches No Folder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reader-missing` (level S) naming the field, the written pattern and the resolved folder that does not exist.
provisions.statement: The model builder MUST report `reader-missing` for a configured .NET stack root that matches no folder, and for the default modules root, when that default matches no folder in a project that selects the .NET reader.
provisions.rationale: A root that matches no folder reads no source, so the records that source would implement are not gaps in the product. The tool read nothing where it expected code. Reporting the missing root beside the unimplemented findings lets a reader tell a reader gap from a product gap. The WebApi, worker, and shared kernel defaults name hosts and a kernel that a valid project may omit, so a missing default for those roots stays silent. Only a configured host or kernel path reports.
provisions.example: A library project that keeps its code under a product folder and names no stack root reports `reader-missing` for the default modules root instead of reporting every aggregate and use case as unimplemented.

provisions.heading: Run Mutation Testing with Stryker.NET
provisions.evidence: Does the mutation gate run Stryker.NET at the version the root tool manifest pins? Check `.config/dotnet-tools.json` and the mutation job's command.
provisions.statement: Run the mutation gate with the Stryker.NET runner that the root tool manifest pins.
provisions.rationale: Stryker.NET is the .NET runner for the mutation gate that `litespec/quality/testing#refuse-surviving-mutants-on-changed-lines` names, and the root tool manifest pins its version, so a developer and CI run the same mutants against the same tool.

provisions.heading: Start the Integration Database in a Container
provisions.evidence: Does the integration test project start the pinned PostgreSQL in a Testcontainers container for every run? Check the integration fixture and the Testcontainers package reference.
provisions.statement: The .NET integration test project MUST start the pinned PostgreSQL in a Testcontainers container.
provisions.rationale: A container from the pinned image gives every test run the database version the release runs. It starts and stops with the test run, so no shared server carries state from one run to the next. The fixture that owns the container is the one `litespec/core/testing#share-one-production-faithful-integration-harness` names.

provisions.heading: Test with xUnit v3 on Microsoft.Testing.Platform
provisions.evidence: Does every test project reference xUnit v3 and run on Microsoft.Testing.Platform, with `global.json` naming that runner? Check each test project file and `global.json`.
provisions.statement: A .NET test project MUST reference xUnit v3 and run on Microsoft.Testing.Platform, with `global.json` naming that runner.
provisions.rationale: The .NET 10 `dotnet test` command refuses the VSTest mode for xUnit v3 projects. Each test project therefore runs on the platform runner. The root `global.json` states that choice once for every project beneath it. A project that runs on another runner reports its results in a shape the model builder does not read, so its passing tests prove nothing.

provisions.heading: Write Each Mark in the Declared Style
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-style-invalid` (level S), and `dotnet build` reports `LS5004`, for a mark written in the style the project did not declare.
provisions.statement: A .NET mark MUST be an `implements`, `proves`, or `follows` documentation tag when `marks` is `xml`, and an `Implements`, `Proves`, or `Follows` attribute when `marks` is `attribute`.
provisions.rationale: The `xml` style keeps business code free of attributes that are not of the business. The mark is a documentation tag read by the stack reader and the analyzers, which need the documentation file every LiteSpec project already generates. The `attribute` style carries the mark into metadata, so it survives compilation and reflection can read it. Its attribute types are generated into each project as internal types by the analyzer package, so no runtime package is referenced. Domain stays free of outer-layer dependencies. A code element takes one mark per record, and a code fix converts a mark between the styles. This provision states the .NET form of `litespec/core/model#declare-one-mark-style`.
provisions.example:
In the `xml` style, Claimwick's reimbursement handler carries its marks as documentation tags:

```csharp
/// <summary>Reimburses an approved expense.</summary>
/// <implements>use-case/spending.reimburse-expense</implements>
/// <follows>litespec/core/backend-application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage</follows>
internal sealed class ReimburseExpenseCommandHandler
```

In the `attribute` style, the same handler carries them as attributes:

```csharp
[Implements("use-case/spending.reimburse-expense")]
[Follows("litespec/core/backend-application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage")]
internal sealed class ReimburseExpenseCommandHandler
```

provisions.heading: Write Test Results the Model Builder Reads
provisions.evidence: Does every test run write TRX or JUnit XML under `paths.testResults`? Check the test run output beside `paths.testResults` in `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A .NET test run MUST write its results as TRX or JUnit XML under `paths.testResults`.
provisions.rationale: The model builder computes verified status from TRX and JUnit XML only. A run written in another format, or outside `paths.testResults`, proves no scenario even when every test passes, so passing tests would show as unproven. A JUnit `testcase` proves a Behavior scenario without a `proves` mark by carrying the scenario id in a `litespec.proves` property, one property per scenario or several ids separated by commas in one value. The case proves each id it names with the same rules as a `proves` mark on a test method.

provisions.heading: Assert Observable Outcomes
provisions.evidence: Does every BDD scenario assert a response, read, event, record, or other observable outcome? Look at each BDD scenario in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD scenario MUST assert a response, later read, durable event, audit record, or other observable outcome.
provisions.rationale: A scenario that runs requests without asserting proves only that nothing threw. Asserting a response, a later read, a durable event, an audit record, or another observable outcome shows the public boundary achieved the expected behavior.

provisions.heading: Avoid Routine Scenario Duplication
provisions.evidence: Does any unit or validation test repeat as a duplicate BDD scenario? Look at the narrower suites beside the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A test author MUST NOT duplicate every unit or validation test as a BDD scenario.
provisions.rationale: A unit test fails at the exact rule and runs in milliseconds. The same test duplicated as a BDD scenario fails at a public boundary after a full setup. Duplication slows the suite and moves the failure away from its cause, so routine behavior stays in its narrower tests.

provisions.heading: Call Public Boundaries from BDD Steps
provisions.evidence: Does every step definition stay within the HTTP API and the declared public boundaries? Look at each step definition in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD step MUST call the HTTP API or another declared public system boundary.
provisions.rationale: A step that calls the HTTP API or another declared public boundary proves what a caller can observe. A step that reaches past the boundary depends on implementation details, so a refactoring breaks the scenario without breaking the behavior.

provisions.heading: Drain the Outbox in Acceptance Tests
provisions.evidence: Does every acceptance test that asserts a reaction's effect drain the outbox before asserting it? Look at each acceptance test beside the outbox test package.
provisions.statement: An acceptance test that asserts a reaction's effect MUST drain the outbox through the durable-messaging test package before asserting it.
provisions.rationale: The test hosts a transactional outbox through `AddTestTransactionalOutbox` and drains it through `ProcessorPassHelpers.DrainOutboxAsync`, both from `LiteBus.Testing.DurableMessaging` at its manifest pin. Draining runs each subscribed handler in process, so the scenario observes the reaction's effect without the processor's polling delay. The suite still runs through the real application host under `litespec/core/testing#share-one-production-faithful-integration-harness`.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, the expense-approval acceptance test sends the approve command, drains the outbox, and then asserts the payout the schedule-payout reaction wrote. Without the drain, the test would assert before the processor delivers the approval.

provisions.heading: Exclude Production Internals
provisions.evidence: Does any step definition resolve a repository, handler, session, or the production service provider? Look at each step definition in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD step definition MUST NOT resolve repositories, handlers, sessions, or the production service provider.
provisions.rationale: Resolving a repository, handler, session, or the production service provider runs the behavior without the boundary the scenario claims to verify. The scenario then passes while the public path stays untested, so step definitions resolve none of them.

provisions.heading: Group Feature Classes by Module
provisions.evidence: Does every feature class sit under its `{Module}/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` folder, or under a documented grouping? Look at `Acceptance.Tests` beside the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Group feature classes under `{Module}/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` folders in `Acceptance.Tests`, with a module-level read dropping the aggregate segment.
provisions.rationale: A scenario filed by business module and aggregate sits beside the vocabulary it exercises, so a reader finds every example of one aggregate in one folder. A flat or technically grouped suite scatters those examples.

provisions.heading: Isolate Scenario Execution
provisions.evidence: Does every scenario pass alone and in any order, with state reset between runs? Look at the acceptance suite runs.
provisions.statement: The acceptance suite MUST reset database state between scenarios and avoid scenario-order dependencies.
provisions.rationale: State left by one scenario becomes a hidden precondition of the next. The suite then passes only in one order. Resetting database state between scenarios removes that coupling, so any scenario runs alone or in any order.

provisions.heading: Keep Steps Vocabulary-Scoped
provisions.evidence: Does every reusable step set serve one business vocabulary, or a documented scope? Look at each reusable step set beside the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Keep step definitions narrow and reusable only within one business vocabulary.
provisions.rationale: A step reused across vocabularies, such as a generic success step, means something subtly different in each place. It also couples unrelated modules to one definition. Steps narrow to one business vocabulary keep their meaning exact.

provisions.heading: Limit Database Assertions
provisions.evidence: Does every direct database assertion name a documented durable boundary? Look at each direct database assertion in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD scenario MUST use direct database assertions only for a documented durable boundary.
provisions.rationale: The database is an implementation detail, so asserting its rows couples the scenario to storage shapes. A direct assertion is allowed only for a documented durable boundary, such as an outbox record, where the stored row is itself the promised evidence.

provisions.heading: Limit Scenario Context
provisions.evidence: Does every scenario context object hold only scenario state, or a documented use? Look at the scenario context beside the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Store values for one scenario in a scenario context object.
provisions.rationale: One context object holding the scenario's own values keeps shared state visible and small. Resolving services from it turns it into a service locator that hides what the scenario depends on.

provisions.heading: Mark Pull-Request Scenarios
provisions.evidence: Does the marked pull-request subset stay within its stated bound with its owner named? Look at the marked subset beside the proves claims.
provisions.statement: Mark the small pull-request subset separately from the proves claim, with a critical test trait on the LightBDD scenario.
provisions.rationale: The critical trait selects the small subset whose failure stops a release, for fast pull-request feedback. The marking stays separate from the proves claim, which records scenario proof rather than release gating. A marking that every scenario carries selects nothing, so the subset keeps a stated size bound and an owner who keeps it within that bound.

provisions.heading: Own Scenario Data
provisions.evidence: Does every BDD scenario own its identifiers, actor context, requests, responses, and expected state? Look at each BDD scenario in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: Each BDD scenario MUST own its identifiers, actor context, requests, responses, and expected state.
provisions.rationale: A scenario that borrows identifiers or state prepared elsewhere breaks when that other setup changes. Owning its identifiers, actor context, requests, responses, and expected state keeps each scenario self-contained and runnable alone.

provisions.heading: Preserve Scenario Failures
provisions.evidence: Does every hook await setup and cleanup without replacing the original scenario failure? Look at each hook in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD hook MUST await asynchronous setup and cleanup without replacing the original scenario failure.
provisions.rationale: Setup and cleanup are asynchronous. An unawaited hook leaves the next scenario running against a half-reset database. A hook that throws during cleanup can also replace the scenario's own failure, hiding the real cause. Awaiting both without replacing the original failure keeps the evidence trustworthy.

provisions.heading: Select Shared Critical Examples
provisions.evidence: Does every BDD scenario trace to a cross-layer example the team discusses in business language? Look at each BDD scenario in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A test author MUST create a BDD scenario only when business-language form improves shared understanding of cross-layer behavior.
provisions.rationale: A scenario costs maintenance on every behavior change, so the suite earns that cost only where business-language form improves shared understanding of cross-layer behavior. Each selected scenario gives product, domain, engineering, and testing discussions one executable example instead of four retellings.

provisions.heading: Trace Every BDD Scenario to Its Scenario
provisions.evidence: Does every BDD scenario carry one `proves` claim naming its scenario? Look at each BDD scenario in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: Every BDD scenario MUST carry one `proves` claim naming the scenario it proves.
provisions.rationale: A scenario pairs one `given` situation and `when` action with the `then` result they lead to. The proves claim ties the BDD scenario to that record. The claim names it, the steps call the proved use case, and the assertion checks its result. Without the claim, the model builder cannot tell which scenario the BDD scenario proves. A LightBDD scenario carries the claim as a proves mark on the scenario method, in the style the project declares.
provisions.example: `/// <proves>scenario/cancel-order.canceling-twice-is-refused</proves>` traces a cancellation BDD scenario to its scenario record.

provisions.heading: Translate Business Phrases into Test-Driver Calls
provisions.evidence: Does every step definition translate its phrase through a typed test-driver call? Look at each step definition in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD step definition MUST translate a business phrase into a typed test-driver call.
provisions.rationale: HTTP calls, JSON shapes, and assertion mechanics in a step definition hide the business phrase the scenario promises. Translating each phrase into a typed test-driver call keeps the scenario readable while the driver owns the boundary mechanics.

provisions.heading: Exclude Development Shortcuts from Release Builds
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS5014` for a tagged type that a compilation without `DEBUG` declares, in every project that holds a shortcut. Review the host project file for the Debug-only `ProjectReference`, and `Program.cs` for the `#if DEBUG` registration, since no rule reads the project file.
provisions.statement: A .NET project that holds a development shortcut MUST stay out of release builds: referenced only in Debug builds, registered only behind `#if DEBUG`, with each shortcut type carrying its `development-shortcut` tag and refusing to start outside the Development environment.
provisions.rationale: A project referenced in every build puts its shortcut into the release artifact, where no deployment setting can remove it. A `ProjectReference` with `Condition="'$(Configuration)' == 'Debug'"` keeps the project out of release builds, and the `#if DEBUG` registration keeps the host from naming a type that a release build does not have. The types themselves stay outside the directive. The compiler drops a disabled region from the compilation, so `LS5014` could not report a shortcut that a release build compiles. The tag gives `LS5014` one way to find each shortcut, and the environment check stops a Debug build on a shared host from running the shortcut. This provision binds `litespec/quality/development#keep-development-shortcuts-out-of-release-builds` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep the AppHost in the Deploy Folder
provisions.evidence: Does every AppHost sit at `deploy/{Product}.AppHost/`, with none under `apps/`? Look at each AppHost project path from the workspace root.
provisions.statement: An AppHost MUST live at `deploy/{Product}.AppHost/` at the workspace root, never under `apps/`.
provisions.rationale: `apps/` holds the applications that ship, and an AppHost ships nowhere: it models how those applications run together, locally and in the deployment files it publishes. Under `apps/api/src/` it reads as one of the API's layers while it reaches out of that tree for every frontend it starts, and anywhere else under `apps/` it reads as one more application. In `deploy/`, beside the rest of the deployment description, its path says what it is. `ServiceDefaults` stays under `apps/api/src/`, because the API references it and the AppHost does not.
provisions.example:
A workspace with an API, a Worker and a frontend carries:

```text
apps/
  api/
    src/
      Hosts/{Product}.WebApi/
      Hosts/{Product}.Worker/
    tests/
      {Product}.Architecture.Tests/   references the AppHost for its model tests
  {frontend}/
deploy/
  {Product}.AppHost/
    {Product}.AppHost.csproj
    Program.cs
```

A root solution, where `litespec/packs/dotnet/workspace#list-every-deployable-unit-in-the-root-solution` asks for one, lists the AppHost, and the API solution lists it too when a test project references it.

provisions.heading: List Every Deployable Unit in the Root Solution
provisions.evidence: Does the root solution list more than one deployable unit, with builds, test runs, and configuration still naming the API solution? Look at the solution files beside the build configuration.
provisions.statement: A root solution MUST list the .NET projects of more than one deployable unit, with builds, test runs, and configuration still naming the API solution.
provisions.rationale: A workspace with a second .NET deployable, such as a command-line tool, otherwise has no single file an editor can open across both. The root solution gives editors that view. The API solution stays at `apps/api/` and remains the one builds and test runs name. Two solution files listing overlapping projects are a supported MSBuild arrangement, and the projects stay where `litespec/workspace/structure#keep-production-and-test-code-separate` puts them.
provisions.example: A workspace with an API and a command-line tool carries `apps/api/{Product}.slnx`, `apps/cli/{Product}.Cli.slnx` where one exists, and a root `{Product}.slnx` listing both sets.

provisions.heading: Enforce Trusted Types on Raw Markup
provisions.evidence: Does every raw markup sink run inside the named policy, with the frontend sending the Trusted Types directive? Check the Content Security Policy header and the violation reports.
provisions.statement: A web frontend SHOULD send `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` in its Content Security Policy and pass every raw markup string through one named policy that calls the recorded sanitizer.
provisions.rationale: A recorded sanitizer protects only the calls that remember to use it. Trusted Types makes the browser refuse any raw string written into `innerHTML` or a similar sink, so a component that forgets the sanitizer fails in testing instead of in a staff member's browser. A team first sends the policy as `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`, reads the reports, and enforces it once every reported sink passes through the named policy.

provisions.heading: Keep Component Boundaries Typed
provisions.evidence: `svelte-check` fails on an untyped Svelte prop, event, or snippet.
provisions.statement: A component MUST type its props, its events, and its snippets under strict mode.
provisions.rationale: An untyped prop fails at the call site the next author writes, after writing the code that uses it. Strict mode turns that failure into a build error at the author's own call. Typed events and snippets do the same for what the component reports and what it lets callers fill in.

provisions.heading: Name Visual Files with the Stack Suffix
provisions.evidence: Does every file holding a custom drawing end with the stated suffix? Check the component folders.
provisions.statement: A file that holds a drawing no composite makes MUST end with `.visual.svelte`.
provisions.rationale: The suffix identifies the one place outside the composites, so a search finds every custom drawing in one pass.
provisions.example: The Claimwick receipt sparkline lives in `ExpenseSparkline.visual.svelte`.

provisions.heading: Refuse Page Code Violations with ESLint
provisions.evidence: Does any refused element, binding, or layout utility show in the consumer's lint output outside visual files in route and module code? Check the lint output the consumer's configuration produces in CI.
provisions.statement: Route and module code MUST pass the ESLint rules that refuse raw layout and interactive elements, class and style bindings, and layout utilities outside visual files, with each refusal naming the composite to use.
provisions.rationale: A lint gate that only refuses leaves the author searching the shared package for the replacement. A refusal that names the composite tells the author the replacement in the error itself. Visual files stay allowlisted, because a drawing no composite makes has no composite to name. This gates the refusals the table above states: no raw elements, no class names, and no layout utilities outside visual files.

provisions.heading: Render Raw HTML Through the Stack Sink
provisions.evidence: Does every raw HTML write go through the stated sink? Check for raw markup in the component files.
provisions.statement: A component MUST pass raw HTML to the page only through `{@html}`.
provisions.rationale: One named sink gives every raw HTML write a name a search finds, so a review can check each use. Stored rich content renders only under its recorded sanitization decision.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense note passes its sanitized HTML through `{@html}`, matching its recorded sanitization decision.

provisions.heading: Use the Stack Class and Style Bindings
provisions.evidence: Does every class or style binding use the stated form? Check the component markup.
provisions.statement: A class or style binding MUST use `class`, `class:`, `style`, or `style:`.
provisions.rationale: Fixed forms keep styling in one vocabulary that the lint and a reviewer can read.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense status chip toggles its overdue tone with `class:overdue`.

provisions.heading: Add the Stack Query Plugin to the Client Generator
provisions.evidence: Does the client generator configuration add the stated query plugin? Check the generator configuration of the Svelte frontend.
provisions.statement: The client generator MUST add `@tanstack/svelte-query`.
provisions.rationale: The plugin gives every generated read a query key, so the cache entries of every route share one shape.
provisions.example: The Claimwick client generator adds `@tanstack/svelte-query`, giving each generated read a query key.

provisions.heading: Build a Web Form on the Shared Form Entry Point
provisions.evidence: Does every web form build on the stated form entry point? Check the form files under `src`.
provisions.statement: A web form MUST build on the shared form creator.
provisions.rationale: One entry point gives every form the same field setup and the same display for a refusal on its field.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense form builds on the shared form creator, with no form library of its own.

provisions.heading: Resolve Copy Through the Stack Dictionary Library
provisions.evidence: Does every copy call site use the dictionary library with fill, plural, typed keys, and a declared fallback? Check the copy call sites under `src`.
provisions.statement: The dictionary library MUST meet the locale-dictionary contract that the frontend data page states.
provisions.rationale: One contract keeps every sentence in one dictionary per language, with the same fill, plural, and fallback behavior.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console renders its receipt-required sentence through `svelte-i18n`, in every language it ships.

provisions.heading: Declare Titles and Indexing Policy on Every Route
provisions.evidence: Does every public route define its title, description, canonical address, and indexing policy, with every private route carrying a `noindex` marker? Check the route metadata.
provisions.statement: A public route MUST define its title, its description, its canonical address, and its indexing policy, while a private route refuses indexing.
provisions.rationale: A public route's title, description, canonical address, and indexing policy are what a search result and a shared link show. Without them, the result shows only a bare address. A private route refuses indexing, because an indexed console address exposes to search what a signed-in user believes is private.
provisions.example: A channel route states `og:*` tags and one alternate per language. A console route carries a `noindex` meta tag in its document.

provisions.heading: Show Route Failure on the Error Surface
provisions.evidence: Does every route failure render on the stated error surface? Check the error handling of each route.
provisions.statement: A route failure MUST render on `+error.svelte`, which draws the shared problem state.
provisions.rationale: One error surface gives every route failure the same problem state and the same recovery.
provisions.example: When the Claimwick expense list fails, `+error.svelte` shows the shared problem state with its trace identifier.

provisions.heading: Keep Route Group Names in Router Syntax
provisions.evidence: Does every folder under `src/routes` that shares a layout use a parenthesized name? Check the folder names under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route group MUST keep its parenthesized folder name.
provisions.rationale: The parentheses are router syntax: a group folder without them becomes an address the router serves.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console groups its expense pages under `(console)`, sharing one layout with no extra address.

provisions.heading: Resolve Imports Through the Lib Alias
provisions.evidence: Does every import into `src/lib` use the `#lib` alias? Check the import lines of each Svelte frontend.
provisions.statement: Imports MUST resolve through the `#lib` alias that `package.json` declares in its `imports` field as `"#lib/*": "./src/lib/*"`.
provisions.rationale: One declared alias lets a reader and a tool see every import of frame and module code without counting relative steps.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console imports frame code through `#lib/app/words.ts`.

provisions.heading: Write Components in Runes Mode
provisions.evidence: `svelte-check` fails on a legacy reactive statement or an untyped `$props` call.
provisions.statement: A component MUST hold its local state in runes, with props from `$props` and derived values from `$derived`.
provisions.rationale: Runes are the reactivity model the compiler understands: `$state` for local state, `$props` for inputs, and `$derived` for computed values. Legacy reactive statements and untyped prop access bypass that model and behave differently under the compiler. An effect covers what derivation cannot express, so nothing needs the legacy forms.

provisions.heading: Write the File Extension in Each Import
provisions.evidence: Does every import name its module file extension? Check the import lines in the `src` tree of each Svelte frontend.
provisions.statement: Each import MUST name its module file extension.
provisions.rationale: SvelteKit 3 requires the extension, because it resolves each import to its exact file.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console imports `#lib/app/words.ts`, extension included.

provisions.heading: Generate the Records File into the Frame
provisions.evidence: `litespec model render` writes each frontend's file into its frame from its own entry points, and `litespec model check` reports `mark-unknown` (level S) for a mark naming a use case or screen outside its frontend's entry points.
provisions.statement: A frontend's generated `litespec-records.ts` MUST sit in its frame folder and hold only the use cases and screens of that frontend's own entry points.
provisions.rationale: The records file is a cross-route value every module and route imports, which is what the frame holds. It lives in the frame folder at `src/lib/app/`. A union holding every browser use case of the project would let one frontend mark a use case only another frontend reaches, and the type check would pass; a union per frontend makes that mistake a type error. The file exports the `UseCaseId` and `ScreenId` unions, the `LiteSpecMark` type, and the `proves` helper that browser tests annotate with. The render reads the screens and use cases of the frontend's entry points, not the code marks, so it writes the file before any screen exists: run `litespec model render` once when the web app is created. A frontend holding no marked route yet reads every browser entry point.
provisions.example: `litespec model render` writes `apps/web/src/lib/app/litespec-records.ts` for the Claimwick web frontend, whose `UseCaseId` holds the use cases its entry point reaches and nothing else.

provisions.heading: Group the Web Frame by Capability
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `folder-ungrouped` for a frame folder past 20 files that holds none of its allowed groupings.
provisions.statement: A web frontend MUST group its frame folder into `session/`, `i18n/`, `api/`, and `ui/`, with no other folder.
provisions.rationale: One flat frame folder reads as one long listing: a reader finds a value only by search, and review misses what the frame holds. Each grouping names the capability its values serve, so a reader finds a value by what it is for. An agent never invents another grouping: a folder outside the allowed set is refused, and a folder past 20 files that holds none of its allowed groupings is a finding.
provisions.example: The Claimwick web frontend holds its session read and permissions in `session/`, its language dictionaries in `i18n/`, its API client setup in `api/`, and its formatting and shell data in `ui/`.

provisions.heading: Keep Web Layouts, Error Surfaces, and Route Groups Unmarked
provisions.evidence: Do any layouts, error surfaces, or route groups carry a screen mark? Check the non-entry files under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A layout, an error surface, or a route group MUST NOT carry a screen mark.
provisions.rationale: A layout, an error surface, or a group draws no screen of its own, so a mark on it ties an address to a screen it does not show.
provisions.example: The Claimwick `+layout.svelte` carries no screen mark.

provisions.heading: Locate the Frame in the App Folder
provisions.evidence: Do all cross-route values and browser uses sit in the frame folder their stack page names? Check the frame folder and the route and module sources.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST place cross-route values in the frame folder its stack page states: client configuration, session read, language choice, permissions, formatting, and shell data.
provisions.rationale: Client configuration, session read, language choice, permissions, formatting, and shell data cross every route. Placed in the frame folder, each has one home; placed in a route, each would exist once per route, with copies to keep equal. A browser API reached from a use-case module belongs here too, because a module renders and reads data rather than calling such APIs directly.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Use-Case Module with Its Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` (level S) for a use-case folder exporting no `litespec` constant, `mark-unknown` (level S) for one naming no written use case, and `code-placement-drift` (level S) for a folder whose path does not mirror its marked use case.
provisions.statement: A frontend use-case folder MUST export one `litespec` constant whose `implements` names its use case, typed against the generated union of use-case identifiers.
provisions.rationale: The folder path mirrors the backend use case, which shows a reader where to look, but a path alone gives a tool nothing to check. A typed constant is the frontend mark in both mark styles: a mistyped identifier fails the consumer's type check against the generated union, and `litespec model check` reports it as `mark-unknown` where no type check ran. The route files import the module instead of restating the identifier. The calls a screen makes through the generated client remain the computed `calls` link; the mark adds the written link from the screen to the use case it serves.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Web Route Entry with Its Screen
provisions.evidence: Does every route entry export its screen mark from the stated place? Check each route entry.
provisions.statement: A route entry MUST export its screen mark as the same typed constant a use-case module exports, from the `<script module>` of `+page.svelte`.
provisions.rationale: A mark where the address is declared ties the address to its use case in one link, so the builder and the check read one place. A wrong identifier fails the consumer type check against the generated union.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list exports its mark from the `<script module>` of its `+page.svelte`.

provisions.heading: Refuse Stack-Specific Folder Names
provisions.evidence: Does any Svelte folder under `src/lib` take the name `stores`? Check the frontend tree.
provisions.statement: A Svelte folder under `src/lib` MUST NOT be named `stores`.
provisions.rationale: A `stores` folder would gather shared state in one place, while the rules put shared state in the frame or beside its readers. Refusing the name keeps each value in the one place the rules give it.

provisions.heading: Use the Frontend Application Tree
provisions.evidence: Does every frontend tree follow the frame, routes, and modules layout its stack page states? Check the frontend tree.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST use the frame, routes, and modules layout its stack page states.
provisions.rationale: The frame, routes, and modules layout gives every file one predictable home: cross-route values in the frame, one address per route file or folder, and use-case code under the module that owns it. A reader moves from a use case to its code by path alone.
provisions.example:
```text
apps/{frontend}/
  src/
    routes/    one folder per address, with a page per folder
    lib/
      app/       the frame: client configuration, session, language, permissions, formatting, shell data
      modules/   one folder per backend module and use case
  tests/
    unit/      logic tests
    routes/    the route contract suite
    e2e/       evidence specifications
  vite.config.ts
  package.json
```

The generated route artifacts, build output, and dependency folders stay untracked. SvelteKit configuration lives in `vite.config.ts`: SvelteKit 3 reads no `svelte.config.js`.

provisions.heading: Use the Generated Route Tree
provisions.evidence: Does every build and type-check script run the router's generate command, with no generated artifact staying tracked? Check the package scripts and the version control status.
provisions.statement: Generate the typed route artifacts from the files under `src/routes` with the router's own command, and keep them untracked.
provisions.rationale: The typed route artifacts derive from the files under `src/routes`. Generating them with the router's own command and leaving them untracked keeps one source of truth. Committed artifacts add a second copy that goes stale when a route file is renamed.

provisions.heading: Use the Stack File Extension
provisions.evidence: Does every shared file use the stated extension? Check the `src` tree of the web frontend.
provisions.statement: A shared file MUST use the file extension `.svelte`.
provisions.rationale: One extension lets the compiler, the lint, and a search treat every shared file the same way. No file needs a second guess.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console holds its expense total as `ExpenseTotal.svelte`.

provisions.heading: Keep Web Test Mocks to the Stack Libraries
provisions.evidence: Does any test replace a library the stack keeps? Check the mocks in each test file.
provisions.statement: A test MUST NOT replace Svelte, SvelteKit, the query library, or the form library.
provisions.rationale: Those libraries are the stack's own behavior, and a stand-in for any of them tests the stand-in instead of the screen.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense page test runs against the real query library, replacing only the network call.

provisions.heading: Refuse a Test Without an Assertion
provisions.evidence: `pnpm eslint` reports `vitest/expect-expect` for each test that contains no assertion.
provisions.statement: Lint MUST fail a Vitest or Playwright test that contains no `expect` assertion, through the `expect-expect` rule.
provisions.rationale: A test that calls code and asserts nothing passes unless something throws: it raises coverage while proving nothing. The `expect-expect` rule of the Vitest ESLint plugin reports each such test before it runs, at no measurable cost. The rule is free and maintained under MIT.

provisions.heading: Align Property Columns in PropertyList
provisions.evidence: Do all property columns align with tabular numerals for amounts? Check each property list.
provisions.statement: Key and value columns MUST use `PropertyList` with aligned columns and tabular numerals for amounts.
provisions.rationale: Aligned columns let values scan down: the reader compares down a column instead of hunting across rows. Proportional numerals shift totals by digit width, so tabular numerals hold every amount in place.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense summary aligns payer, date, and total in `PropertyList` columns with tabular totals.

provisions.heading: Build Pages from Locked Primitives
provisions.evidence: Does any route or feature component build grid, bar, property, or metric geometry outside the four primitives? Check the route and module sources.
provisions.statement: Page geometry MUST come from `FieldGrid`, `ActionBar`, `PropertyList`, and `MetricGrid`, each used for its single job.
provisions.rationale: One primitive per job keeps geometry consistent without per-route tuning. A hand-built grid beside `FieldGrid` reimplements its alignment and drifts on the next edit.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense form lays its fields on `FieldGrid`, and its submit row uses `ActionBar` with primary and cancel in order.

provisions.heading: Compose One Archetype per Route
provisions.evidence: Does every route compose one archetype with only declared slots filled? Check each route entry.
provisions.statement: A route MUST compose exactly one page archetype and fill only its declared slots with primitives and feature components.
provisions.rationale: One archetype per route gives each address a single job and a fixed shape. A route that mixes two archetypes serves two jobs, and a slot filled with raw elements bypasses the primitives that keep geometry steady.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list composes the list archetype: header, filter bar, table, and pagination slots, each filled with primitives.

provisions.heading: Declare One Visual Reference
provisions.evidence: Does the product record name exactly one visual reference? Check the product record.
provisions.statement: A product MUST declare exactly one visual reference in its product record.
provisions.rationale: One reference gives every route the same density, navigation, tables, and hierarchy. Two references split the product into two looks, and no check can tell which route follows which.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console declares one calm business reference, and every list and settings route follows it.

provisions.heading: Group Form Fields in FieldGrid Sections
provisions.evidence: Does every form group hold at most 6 fields on aligned 12-column rows? Check each form.
provisions.statement: Form fields MUST sit in `FieldGrid` groups of at most 6 fields on 12 aligned columns.
provisions.rationale: Small aligned groups scan as one task: the reader finishes a group before meeting the next. Long ungrouped forms blur tasks together, and unaligned columns make labels jump. Twelve columns divide evenly for halves, thirds, and quarters, so related fields share rows without custom widths.
provisions.example: The Claimwick entry form groups payer, date, and amount in one `FieldGrid` group, and lines in the next.

provisions.heading: Keep Focus Visible on Every Control
provisions.evidence: Does every control show visible focus at 3:1 contrast? Check each route with keyboard navigation.
provisions.statement: Every interactive control MUST show a visible focus indicator with at least 3:1 contrast against its background.
provisions.rationale: Keyboard readers tab through controls without a pointer, so a control that hides focus strands them: they act without knowing where they are. A visible indicator at 3:1 contrast shows position on every theme.
provisions.example: The Claimwick entry form outlines the focused input with the focus ring from the shared package.

provisions.heading: Keep Form Content Narrow
provisions.evidence: Does any form stretch inputs across the full desktop width? Check each form container width.
provisions.statement: Cap form content at the narrow width with full-width inputs never stretching across the desktop.
provisions.rationale: Narrow forms scan in one column: labels, inputs, and errors stay in one vertical rhythm. Full-width inputs stretch across the desktop and break that rhythm, so the eye travels instead of reading down.
provisions.example: The Claimwick entry form caps its sections narrow with inputs at full section width, never at full desktop width.

provisions.heading: Keep Metric Grids Symmetric
provisions.evidence: Does every metric grid show balanced rows with no orphan tile? Check each metric grid at desktop width.
provisions.statement: Lay metric tiles in balanced desktop rows with no orphan trailing tile.
provisions.rationale: An orphan tile stretches or shrinks against empty space and draws the eye for no reason. Balanced rows keep every metric equal weight. A set that never divides evenly needs one recorded rule, not per-route improvisation.
provisions.example: The Claimwick period summary shows four KPI tiles in one symmetric row, never three plus one.

provisions.heading: Keep One H1 per Route
provisions.evidence: Does every route render exactly one `h1`? Check each route entry.
provisions.statement: A route MUST render exactly one `h1` naming its job, with section titles as lower-level headings.
provisions.rationale: One `h1` names the route for readers and assistive tools. Two `h1` headings split the page into two subjects, and none leaves the route unnamed. Lower-level headings structure the sections beneath it.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list renders one `h1` with the list name, and its filter groups use lower headings.

provisions.heading: Keep `shadcn-svelte` Close to Upstream
provisions.evidence: Does any shared component rebuild an upstream primitive with different padding or height? Check the shared package beside the registry output.
provisions.statement: The shared package MUST build on shadcn-svelte near its upstream defaults, at the manifest pin, with no rebuilt wrapper that drifts in padding or height.
provisions.rationale: Near-upstream code merges cleanly on each release. Rebuilt wrappers with drifting padding and heights multiply upgrade cost and hide intent: review cannot tell drift from design. Settled by [decision/0024-keep-the-ui-source-lock](decision/0024-keep-the-ui-source-lock), which keeps `litespec model render` writing each copied component's digest into the source lock. Settled by [decision/0102-draw-platform-composites-with-native-elements](decision/0102-draw-platform-composites-with-native-elements), which draws dialog, popover, and details composites from native elements and takes the rest from the baseline.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console uses the registry output as built, pinning `shadcn-svelte` from the manifest.

provisions.heading: Keep Spacing on the 4px and 8px Scale
provisions.evidence: Does every gap and padding value sit on the stated scale? Check the shared primitives and the route sources.
provisions.statement: Gaps and padding MUST use the scale: 8px inside button and control groups, 16px inside sections and between fields, 20px or 24px card padding, and 24px between major regions.
provisions.rationale: One scale keeps rhythm steady: cards from different authors still line up. Ad-hoc values break alignment one route at a time.
provisions.example: The Claimwick record card pads 24px, its inner sections gap 16px, and its action row gaps 8px.

provisions.heading: Keep Uniform Control Height
provisions.evidence: Does every control stand at its stated height? Check the shared field and button components.
provisions.statement: Text inputs, selects, date pickers, money inputs, and standard buttons MUST stand 36px tall, with compact table and inline actions at 32px.
provisions.rationale: Uniform height lines up every row and bar. Mixed heights force per-case tuning and show as ragged edges on every form.
provisions.example: The Claimwick entry form holds every input at 36px, and its table row actions at 32px.

provisions.heading: Order ActionBar Buttons Primary First
provisions.evidence: Does every action bar carry one primary first with matching sizes? Check each action bar.
provisions.statement: An `ActionBar` MUST order its buttons primary, then secondary, then danger, with one primary per bar and matching sizes.
provisions.rationale: One order puts the safe forward action where every reader looks first. Two primaries, or danger beside primary, force the reader to weigh buttons instead of reading them. Matching sizes keep the order visible instead of size-led.
provisions.example: The Claimwick approval bar shows Approve, then Cancel, with Approve as the single primary.

provisions.heading: Refuse Nested Surfaces
provisions.evidence: Does any card, panel, drawer, or dialog render inside another card, panel, drawer, or dialog? Check the component markup.
provisions.statement: A component MUST NOT render a card, panel, drawer, or dialog inside another card, panel, drawer, or dialog.
provisions.rationale: Nested surfaces stack shadows and borders until hierarchy flattens: everything looks equally raised, so nothing reads as primary. One level of surface per region keeps the primary action obvious. Settled by [decision/0118-layer-surfaces-by-role](decision/0118-layer-surfaces-by-role), which layers surfaces by role so a card inside a card reads as two levels instead of one.
provisions.example: The Claimwick record page holds one card per region instead of a card inside a card.

provisions.heading: Refuse Raw Layout Utilities in Routes
provisions.evidence: The route layout-class ESLint rule fails on any banned utility inside `apps/web/src/routes/**/+page.svelte`.
provisions.statement: Route files MUST NOT use raw layout or spacing utilities directly: `m-*`, `mt-*`, `mb-*`, `mx-*`, `my-*`, `p-*`, `px-*`, `py-*`, `gap-*`, `space-*`, `flex`, `flex-*`, `grid`, `grid-*`, `w-*`, and `h-*`.
provisions.rationale: Raw utilities in routes rebuild geometry per address, so two routes drift apart one class at a time. Primitives and feature components already carry the approved spacing and sizes. The ban forces authors to compose instead of styling.
provisions.example: A Claimwick route lays its filters through the list archetype filter slot, not through `flex` and `gap-4` classes in `+page.svelte`.

provisions.heading: Use One Icon Set
provisions.evidence: Does any icon come from outside the pinned set or at an ad-hoc size? Check the icon uses in each route.
provisions.statement: Icons MUST come from the single icon set the manifest pins, at consistent sizes per use.
provisions.rationale: One set keeps stroke weight and style steady: mixed sets show thick icons beside thin ones. Consistent sizes per use keep actions aligned in bars and rows.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console draws every action icon from the pinned set at the bar and row sizes the shared package states.

provisions.heading: Use Subsection for Grouped Content
provisions.evidence: Does every grouped card divide its groups with `Subsection`, with no nested surface? Check the card components.
provisions.statement: A card that truly holds two labeled sub-groups MUST divide them with the lightweight `Subsection` divider, never with a nested surface.
provisions.rationale: Two labeled groups inside one card need a visual break without a second elevation. `Subsection` draws that break: a label and a rule, no shadow. A nested card would add elevation where none is earned.
provisions.example: The Claimwick settings panel divides its notification groups with `Subsection` dividers inside one card.

provisions.heading: Assert Loading, Stability, and Blocking Time per Route
provisions.evidence: Does every route in the Lighthouse CI run assert largest contentful paint, cumulative layout shift, and total blocking time? Look in the Lighthouse CI configuration.
provisions.statement: Assert, for each route the Lighthouse CI run visits, a largest contentful paint of at most 2.5 seconds, a cumulative layout shift of at most 0.1, and a total blocking time of at most 200 milliseconds, as the median of three runs.
provisions.rationale: A Lighthouse CI assert that names no metric passes every build. Largest contentful paint says when the page shows its main content, cumulative layout shift says whether the page jumps while the staff member reads it, and total blocking time stands in for interaction to next paint, which a lab run cannot measure because nobody clicks. The defaults are the values the web community treats as good, and the median of three runs keeps one slow run from failing a build. Field interaction to next paint is measured in production, where the [Operations](operations.md) page places its signals.

provisions.heading: Check Documentation on Every Pull Request
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` (level G) for a page or configuration that breaks its contract, and `litespec model review` reports `page-section-missing`, `page-heading-invalid`, and `prose-missing` (level R) for a page missing a section or heading, or a record that lacks its prose field.
provisions.statement: The docs job MUST run on every pull request and fail on a page that breaks the page contract or configuration.
provisions.rationale: Documentation breaks come in small forms: a record with a missing field, a rejected term, a misconfigured path, a page outside its [page contract](../core/authoring.md). Each one is trivial to fix in the pull request that introduced it and hard to trace once later pages build on it. Running the docs job on every pull request catches each break where it started, and `litespec model review` reports the prose rules beside it.

provisions.heading: Keep Generated Contracts Fresh
provisions.evidence: Does regenerating OpenAPI and API types from source produce no diff? Regenerate them on the pull request and read the diff.
provisions.statement: CI MUST regenerate committed OpenAPI and API types from source deterministically and fail on any difference.
provisions.rationale: A committed contract that no longer matches its source sends consumers a stale API, and a frontend builds against operations the backend no longer serves. Regenerating from source in CI and failing on any difference proves the committed files match the code. Generation stays deterministic, with no timestamps, machine paths, or unstable ordering, so identical source always yields identical files.

provisions.heading: Refuse Backend Calls Outside the Generated Client
provisions.evidence: Does the contract job show a clean regeneration with no backend call outside the generated client? Read the contract job report and its lint report.
provisions.statement: The contract job MUST fail a pull request whose frontend code calls the backend outside the generated client.
provisions.rationale: Regenerating the contract proves the committed client matches the API, but a hand-written fetch beside it still compiles and drifts on the next contract change. Failing the pull request keeps every backend call inside the generated client. A contract change then breaks the build at the call sites that need to move.

provisions.heading: Run Applicable Gates on Every Pull Request
provisions.evidence: Does the pull request show every selected job passing, with each skipped job recorded with its reason? Look at the pull request checks list.
provisions.statement: Every pull request MUST run the jobs the jobs table selects for its changed areas.
provisions.rationale: Each job guards one surface. A pull request that skips the job for a surface it changed merges work nobody checked. A skipped job is recorded on the pull request with the reason its surface did not change, so the reviewer sees which surfaces stayed unchecked and why. A project that selects the Delivery extension adds its supply-chain gate as one of these jobs under `litespec/ext/delivery#enforce-the-supply-chain-gate`.

provisions.heading: Run Measured Checks on Every Pull Request
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `requirement-measure-missing` for a measured requirement with no check or no passing run.
provisions.statement: The measure job MUST run the check each measured requirement names for its kind.
provisions.rationale: Each kind of measure has one tool, as the measured-checks table above maps: k6 thresholds for API latency and errors, Lighthouse CI assert for frontend performance and weight, axe in the route suite for accessibility, OpenTelemetry signals for availability and latency objectives, and an ASVS 5.0 level with the ZAP baseline, free static analysis, OSV-Scanner, and Gitleaks for security. The tools write their result files under `TestResults/`, the builder reads them the way it reads test runs, and `litespec model check` reports `requirement-measure-missing` for a measured requirement with no check or no passing run. Every tool the table names is free and maintained; CodeQL runs only on public repositories, as `litespec/quality/security#scan-every-pull-request-with-a-free-static-analyzer` states.

provisions.heading: Add a Missing Example Fact to the Cast, Not to the Seed
provisions.evidence: Does every name, amount, and date in the seed resolve to a cast entry, with no value invented in the seed? Look at the seed code against `.litespec/cast.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A seed step that needs a value the cast lacks adds the fact to the cast and reads it from there; the seed invents no name, amount, or date.
provisions.rationale: A value invented in the seed answers no example the specification states, so the seeded product shows a figure no reader can trace. Adding the fact to the cast keeps the seed on the one source that `litespec/core/writing#take-each-example-detail-from-the-cast-or-a-cited-record` requires of examples.
