provisions.example: Claimwick's seed needs a hotel night for the client visit that the cast lacks, so the night joins the cast as a figure and the seed reads it. The seed holds no amount of its own.

provisions.heading: Authenticate as a Cast Person
provisions.evidence: Does the development sign-in call the product's sign-in use case as a cast person, with no other way to gain a session? Look at the development sign-in and the sign-in use case.
provisions.statement: A development sign-in replaces only the identity provider and completes sign-in through the product's own sign-in use case as a cast person, so sessions, tenancy, permissions and audit run as in production.
provisions.rationale: A sign-in that mints a session on its own skips the checks the sign-in use case runs. Going through that use case as a cast person exercises the same session, tenancy, permission and audit path as a production sign-in, so the shortcut hides no difference between local and released behavior.

provisions.heading: Check Seeded Figures Against the Cast
provisions.evidence: Does each seed scenario read back what it seeded, compare totals, counts and states with the cast figures, and report every difference? Look at the seed scenarios and the cast figures they cite.
provisions.statement: A seed scenario reads back the state it seeded and compares the totals, counts and states with those the cast states, reporting each difference; a project whose proofs do not run yet checks its calculated results this way.
provisions.rationale: A seed that writes commands and stops cannot show that the commands produced the figures the examples state. A calculated total or an approval state can be wrong while every command succeeds, and a project without running proofs learns that only at runtime. Reading the seeded state back and comparing it with the cast holds the results to the decided examples, and reporting each difference says which figure is wrong.
provisions.example: Claimwick's approval scenario reads the seeded expense list back and checks Ava's 48.90 EUR train fare for the approved state and the count of expenses in the open month against the cast. When a calculation writes 48.91 EUR, the seed reports the total difference instead of passing silently.

provisions.heading: Generate Volume Data Apart from the Cast
provisions.evidence: Does generated volume data come from a fixed random seed in its own scenario with a generated mark? Look at the volume scenario and its rows.
provisions.statement: Data generated for paging, search, and speed comes from a fixed random seed so a run repeats, lives in its own scenario, and is marked as generated, so it reads as load data rather than as an example the specification states.
provisions.rationale: A list under test needs more rows than the cast holds, but rows that look like examples teach the wrong specification: a reader takes a random amount for the policy figure. A fixed random seed repeats the run, its own scenario keeps the rows out of the occasion data, and the generated mark tells each reader what they are.
provisions.example: Claimwick's volume scenario generates 200 expenses from a fixed seed for the paging tests. Each row carries the generated mark, so no reader takes a random amount for the 48.90 EUR fare.

provisions.heading: Give Each External System a Stand-In That Answers Its Declared Operations
provisions.evidence: Does each stand-in answer every operation its external-system record declares, with no others? Compare each stand-in with its external-system record.
provisions.statement: A development stand-in for an external system answers the operations its external-system record declares, as the [External Integrations extension](../core/integrations.md) defines them.
provisions.rationale: A stand-in that answers operations the record does not declare teaches the local build a behavior the product never agreed to. Answering the declared operations keeps local runs honest to the external-system record.

provisions.heading: Keep Development Shortcuts Out of Release Builds
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS5014` for a type carrying `<development-shortcut>` in a compilation without `DEBUG`; reviewers check the same exclusion on other stacks by reading the build configuration each stack page states. A project with no shortcuts has nothing to satisfy, and each stack page states how its builds exclude a shortcut.
provisions.statement: A development shortcut MUST be excluded from release builds at compile time, refuse to run outside the development environment, and carry the development-shortcut mark.
provisions.rationale: A runtime setting leaves the choice to whatever the deployment passes. A missing setting fails open, so the shortcut that makes local sign-in fast becomes the sign-in bypass in a release: a sign-in shortcut that issues a session without the real identity provider lets anyone in. Compile-time exclusion removes the shortcut from the release artifact, so no deployment setting can bring it back. The development-shortcut mark gives a tool one way to find every shortcut and report the one that reached a release compilation. Proposed by [decision/0113-shortcuts-stay-out-of-release-builds](../intent/decisions/0113-shortcuts-stay-out-of-release-builds/0113-shortcuts-stay-out-of-release-builds.md).
provisions.example: Claimwick's development sign-in lives in a project the solution references only when `$(Configuration)` is `Debug`, its registration sits behind `#if DEBUG`, and its type carries `/// <development-shortcut>Sign in as Ava locally</development-shortcut>`. A `Release` build has no sign-in shortcut in its output: Ava signs in through Claimwick's own sign-in use case only in a development run.

provisions.heading: Keep the Real Identity Provider One Launch Profile Away
provisions.evidence: Is there a launch profile that runs the real identity provider, and does the release evidence record running it before a release? Look at the launch profiles and the release evidence.
provisions.statement: A second launch profile runs the real identity provider, and the project runs it before each release.
provisions.rationale: A shortcut that replaces the identity provider proves nothing about the real sign-in. A second profile keeps the real provider one launch away, so a release can be checked against the sign-in users will actually run.

provisions.heading: Provide Seed and Reset from the Local Orchestrator
provisions.evidence: Does the orchestrator offer seed and reset commands, as AppHost resource commands where .NET is selected? Look at the orchestrator project and `AGENTS.md`.
provisions.statement: The local orchestrator offers a seed command that fills the local state from the cast and a reset command that clears it; on .NET these are AppHost resource commands.
provisions.rationale: A seed that each developer runs from memory leaves a different local state on every machine. Putting seed and reset on the orchestrator gives one place that brings a clean stack to a known state.

provisions.heading: Review Screens with Seeded Data
provisions.evidence: Did the screen review and the rendered-page audit run on a stack seeded with every scenario, with each screen reached with data? Look at the review evidence and the scenario coverage.
provisions.statement: The screen review and the rendered-page audit run on a stack seeded with every scenario, and every screen in the model is reached with data by at least one scenario.
provisions.rationale: A review on an empty stack passes screens that break on content: lists with no rows, tables with no overflow, states with no badge. Seeding every scenario before the review shows each screen as users meet it, and reaching every screen with data leaves no screen reviewed empty.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense list is reviewed at phone, laptop, and wide widths with the seeded expenses in place, so the review sees the waiting rows and the 48.90 EUR fare instead of an empty state.

provisions.heading: Run the API Walker After API Boundary Changes
provisions.evidence: Does the change report show `litespec api explore` run from a fixed seed against the seeded local stack after the last API boundary change? Look at the completion report and the walker output.
provisions.statement: When a change touches an API boundary, a workspace MUST run the [`litespec api explore` command](../tools/api-explore.md) from a fixed seed against the seeded local stack.
provisions.rationale: A walker reaches endpoints and payloads that hand-picked calls miss. A change to an API boundary can add an endpoint, alter a payload or leave an event without a handler, and a build or one test does not walk the whole surface. A fixed seed repeats the same route on every run, and running against the seeded local stack puts each call on real data, so a handler that needs an id no read returns shows up before release.
provisions.example: After Claimwick changes its submit-expense endpoint, the team runs `litespec api explore` from the fixed seed against the seeded local stack. The walker reaches the endpoint with Ava's cast data and reports the response, so a payload the approval screen cannot read shows up in that run.

provisions.heading: Run the Local Stack on the Cast Day
provisions.evidence: Does the orchestrator set the development clock from the cast's `today`, do all hosts read the scoped clock, and does the frontend mark the date as a development date? Look at the orchestrator, the clock reads, and the frontend shell.
provisions.statement: The orchestrator sets a development clock to the cast's `today` that every host reads through the scoped clock, a seed scenario may move it to the day the cast dates an event and back, and the frontend marks the displayed date as a development date; with no `today` in the cast, the real clock runs.
provisions.rationale: Cast occasions carry dates, and rules compare them against the day the code runs. A stack on the real clock puts Ava's expense in the wrong month, so the open month under test holds nothing. Setting the development clock from the cast's `today` lines every host up on the date the examples share, under `litespec/core/backend-application#read-time-from-the-scoped-clock`, and marking the date keeps a reader from taking a development date for the real one. A use case that records the current day, such as submitting an expense, can only be seeded on its cast date by moving the clock there first.
provisions.example: Claimwick's orchestrator sets the development clock to the cast's `today`, so Ava's expense falls in the open month on every host. The frontend shows the date with a development mark, so Ben reads the approval list as a development copy.

provisions.heading: Seed from the Cast Through Public Use Cases
provisions.evidence: Does the seed call commands with values from the cast, with no direct writes to storage? Look at the seed code and its cast marks.
provisions.statement: Development seed data comes from the cast and goes through public use cases, never through direct writes to storage.
provisions.rationale: A direct write to storage bypasses the guards and side effects a command runs, so seeded state can be a state no user could create. Commands from cast values put the seed through the same path a production request takes.

provisions.heading: Seed Only Development and Test Environments
provisions.evidence: Do the seed and reset commands refuse to run in production, and does production reference data arrive only through migrations or startup data in the release? Look at the seed and reset commands and the migration and startup data.
provisions.statement: Seed and reset commands MUST refuse to run in production, with production reference data (charts, rates, country data) arriving only through migrations or startup data that is part of the release.
provisions.rationale: A seed that runs in production overwrites real data with example values, and a reset that runs there deletes it. Refusing outside development and test keeps example data where it belongs, while migrations and release startup data carry the reference rows production needs in a form the release controls and reviews.
provisions.example: Claimwick's seed and reset commands check the environment first and stop with an error in production. The country rows and rates production needs arrive in a migration that ships with the release, so the cast values the development seed writes stay out of production.

provisions.heading: Show Failure Causes in Development
provisions.evidence: Does a development server failure name its exception type and message in the problem detail, and can every host's logs be read from a terminal without a browser dashboard? Look at the development problem-detail writer and the host log output.
provisions.statement: In development, a server failure names its cause in the problem detail with the exception type and message, and every host's logs are readable from a terminal without a browser dashboard.
provisions.rationale: A generic problem detail hides which handler or rule failed, so a developer cannot tell a missing record from a bad payload. Naming the exception type and message in the development problem detail shows the cause, and terminal-readable logs keep failures in the WebApi, the Worker and the frontends diagnosable without opening a browser dashboard.
provisions.example: Claimwick's development WebApi returns a problem detail naming the exception type and message when an expense rule refuses a submit, and the WebApi, Worker and frontend logs print to the terminal that runs the AppHost, so Ben sees the cause without a browser dashboard.

provisions.heading: Split the Seed into Repeatable Scenarios
provisions.evidence: Is the seed split into named scenarios that each name their occasion, dependencies, and rerun check, and does the orchestrator offer each scenario and all of them? Look at the seed scenarios and the orchestrator commands.
provisions.statement: The seed is split into named scenarios after a baseline that sets up the parties, each naming the cast occasion it brings about, the scenarios it depends on and how it tells it already ran, skipping when it has, and the orchestrator offers each scenario and all of them.
provisions.rationale: One seed that always builds everything forces each developer to take all of it or none of it. Named scenarios bring about one occasion at a time, dependencies order them, and skipping a scenario that already ran makes a second run safe.
provisions.example: Claimwick's baseline scenario adds the consultancies Harbor and Pine, and the approval occasion scenario runs after it to bring about Ben's approval of Ava's 48.90 EUR train fare. Running the seed twice adds nothing the second time, because each scenario tells it already ran.

provisions.heading: Start the Stack with One Local Command
provisions.evidence: Does one command named in the consumer `AGENTS.md` start WebApi, PostgreSQL, the frontends, and the Worker? Look at `AGENTS.md` and the AppHost project.
provisions.statement: A workspace MUST start WebApi, PostgreSQL, configured frontends, and its Worker where one exists, with one local command named in the consumer `AGENTS.md`.
provisions.rationale: A stack that needs several terminals and a wiki page starts differently for every developer, and the differences become bug reports nobody can reproduce. One named command brings WebApi, PostgreSQL, the frontends, and the background Worker up together, so every developer and every agent starts from the same running system. The baseline command is the Aspire `AppHost`, with `ServiceDefaults` supplying the shared discovery, health, resilience, and telemetry defaults its resources rely on. A workspace that orchestrates the same set another way satisfies this rule with its own command: the obligation is one command that brings the stack up, not one tool that does it.

provisions.heading: Bound External Calls
provisions.evidence: Does each network call declare a timeout, a cancellation path, and bounded retries for idempotent operations only? Look at each HTTP client registration and its resilience policy.
provisions.statement: Every network call MUST declare an explicit timeout and cancellation path, with retries only for idempotent operations named by a bounded retry policy.
provisions.rationale: Every network call waits on a system the product does not control. Without an explicit timeout and cancellation path, one slow provider holds a request thread until that unrelated system recovers, and each held thread is one less thread for healthy requests. Retries stay bounded and idempotent-only, because retrying a call that already acted repeats the act.

provisions.heading: Emit Correlated Diagnostics
provisions.evidence: Do logs and traces carry correlation identifiers, and do metrics carry service labels? Look at one request's logs, traces, and metrics in the telemetry backend.
provisions.statement: A host MUST emit structured logs, traces, and metrics, with correlation identifiers on logs and traces and service labels on metrics.
provisions.rationale: One request often crosses several hosts, and each running service is a host. Logs and traces carry timestamp, level, service, environment, trace identifier, and span identifier, while metrics carry service and environment labels. The correlation identifiers let one request be followed across every host it touched: the only trail a cross-host failure leaves. Stable event names keep dashboards working across releases instead of breaking each time a message is reworded.

provisions.heading: Keep Production Secrets Out of the Repository
provisions.evidence: Do production values live on the host, with only placeholders in the repository example file? Search the tree for production values and read the example file.
provisions.statement: Production environment values MUST live on the host, never in the repository, under `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data`.
provisions.rationale: A secret committed once lives in history after deletion, readable to everyone the repository ever reaches, as `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data` states. Production values live on the host, and the repository example file holds only placeholders, so the values stay with the deployment that needs them and out of every clone.

provisions.heading: List Every Sub-Processor
provisions.evidence: Does each provider the release calls appear on the generated sub-processor list? Compare the release's provider clients with `.litespec/implementation/operations/sub-processors.md`.
provisions.statement: A release MUST call only providers the generated sub-processor list names from the project's provider actors.
provisions.rationale: Customers ask which providers touch their data, and the sub-processor list is the answer. The model builder renders it from the provider actor records, so a provider added in code but missing from the list answers that question wrong. Generating the list from records keeps the answer and the code in step.

provisions.heading: Operate Background Work Independently
provisions.evidence: Does the Worker publish its own health, processing rate, failure count, retry count, oldest pending age, and shutdown behavior? Look at the Worker's health endpoints and metrics.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST publish its own liveness, readiness, processing rate, failure count, retry count, oldest pending age, and shutdown behavior.
provisions.rationale: A Worker fails on its own schedule: its queue grows, its retries climb, and its oldest item ages, while WebApi keeps answering health checks. Without its own liveness, readiness, processing rate, failure count, retry count, oldest pending age, and shutdown behavior, the failure stays invisible until the backlog is the incident.

provisions.heading: Pass Trace Context in the W3C Format
provisions.evidence: Does one configured propagator read and write W3C trace context on every host? Look at the telemetry setup of each host.
provisions.statement: A host MUST read and write trace context as the [W3C Trace Context](https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/) `traceparent` and `tracestate` headers, using one configured propagator.
provisions.rationale: An identifier that each host formats its own way correlates nothing across the boundary between hosts. The `traceparent` format is what OpenTelemetry implements and every managed backend accepts, so a trace crosses a frontend, an API, a background host, and a provider without translation. One propagator, the component that reads and writes the headers, is the part that matters: two configured propagators produce two identifiers for one request, and the trace splits at whichever hop reads the other one.
provisions.example: The trace identifier in a Problem Details response is the `trace-id` field of the current `traceparent`, which is what `litespec/core/backend-api#return-stable-problem-details` returns.

provisions.heading: Place Each Runbook at Its Scope
provisions.evidence: Does each runbook sit under `.litespec/implementation/runbooks/` or its module's runbooks folder with its fields, or does the convention name another arrangement? Look at the runbook folders and their headings.
provisions.statement: Place a runbook under `.litespec/implementation/runbooks/` when it answers product-wide failures, or under `.litespec/implementation/modules/<module>/runbooks/` when every record naming it sits in one module, stating trigger, impact, prerequisites, procedure, verification, recovery, and escalation, covering restore, rollback, schema failure, leaked secrets, dependency outages, and extension recovery.
provisions.rationale: An alert names its runbook, and the reader follows the pointer under pressure. A runbook sits at product level when it answers product-wide failures, and under its module when every caller sits in one module, so each pointer resolves to a procedure with the same fields: trigger, impact, prerequisites, procedure, verification, recovery, and escalation. A runbook kept anywhere else breaks the pointer the alert gave.

provisions.heading: Point Every Runtime Record at Its Use Case
provisions.evidence: Does a pipeline stage stamp `litespec.use_case` on the span, log scope, and error report of each mediated message? Look at the mediator pipeline and one error report per host.
provisions.statement: A host MUST carry the use-case identity of every mediated message, resolved from the generated registry, as `litespec.use_case` on its span, its log scope, and its error report.
provisions.rationale: A trace identifier joins the runtime records of one request to each other, but not to the specification. A person holding a slow span, a log line, or an error report still has to guess which use case it was. The identity is already a generated value, so a pipeline stage reads it from the registry once per message and stamps it on every surface under one name. Reactions, jobs, and outbox consumers carry it as well as requests. A metric carries it only as a label on an instrument whose series stay bounded: a duration histogram labeled by every use case multiplies its series by hundreds, so request instruments label by module instead.
provisions.example: When Claimwick receives a request to submit an expense, the span and the log scope carry `litespec.use_case = use-case/spending.submit-expense`, and an unhandled failure inside it reaches the error tracker with the same tag.

provisions.heading: Separate Liveness and Readiness
provisions.evidence: Does `/health/live` answer without dependency checks while `/health/ready` includes the critical dependencies? Look at the health check registrations of each host.
provisions.statement: A host MUST expose `/health/live` without dependency checks and `/health/ready` including its critical dependencies.
provisions.rationale: Liveness answers whether the process is alive, and readiness answers whether it can safely serve traffic. When a dependency fails, readiness fails so the orchestrator stops sending traffic, while liveness stays true so the orchestrator does not restart a healthy process. One endpoint for both forces a choice between serving traffic the application cannot handle and restarting a process that only needs its dependency back.

provisions.heading: Apply Erasure and Export to Every Store
provisions.evidence: Do erasure and export reach every store on the inventory, with backups expiring inside their retention bound? Look at the erasure and export jobs and the backup retention setting.
provisions.statement: Erasure and export MUST reach every store holding personal data, with backups expiring inside the retention bound the retention schedule states.
provisions.rationale: The database is only one of the stores that hold personal data; logs, search indexes, and outboxes hold their own copies. Honoring a request in the database while leaving a log export untouched answers half the duty and breaks the promise to the person. A backup cannot erase field by field, so it carries a retention bound instead, and the data ages out when the backup expires.

provisions.heading: Authorize Each Target Resource
provisions.evidence: Does each protected operation pass the application guard from its use case's declared permissions? Look at the guard decision for each protected operation in the authorization tests and the pipeline.
provisions.statement: The application guard MUST authorize every protected operation from its use case's declared permissions, as `litespec/core/backend-application#enforce-target-authorization-in-the-pipeline` states, with endpoints adding only coarse policies.
provisions.rationale: Two operations about the same record ask the same authorization question. The use case declares the permissions it needs, the guard resolves the actor roles at the scope of the target, and the decision follows from that declaration. A message whose target is always the caller carries no target (`litespec/core/access#remove-a-target-that-must-be-the-caller`). A handler never compares the caller with a target and never throws the forbidden refusal itself: the guard decides. Endpoints add only coarse policies, because a policy that cannot see business data cannot decide about an aggregate.

provisions.heading: Bound Abuse at Exposed Endpoints
provisions.evidence: Does each public, authentication, webhook, search, and upload endpoint declare its setting with key and rejection response? Look at the setting records beside each endpoint.
provisions.statement: A public, authentication, webhook, search, or upload endpoint MUST declare its limit as a setting record with key and rejection response.
provisions.rationale: Public, authentication, webhook, search, and upload endpoints invite abuse: credential stuffing, scraping, flooding. Declaring the bound as a setting record names the key that isolates one caller from another and the rejection response the caller sees. The rejection is `429` with a stable code, so legitimate callers can back off and retry.

provisions.heading: Derive the Actor from Claims
provisions.evidence: Does WebApi map verified claims through the one current-actor accessor, with no request data supplying the actor? Look at the actor resolution in WebApi.
provisions.statement: Actor resolution MUST follow `litespec/quality/security#use-one-current-actor-abstraction`.
provisions.rationale: The actor comes from verified claims, not from the request. The WebApi boundary maps those claims to identity, roles, and scopes through the one current-actor accessor, and every operation reads the actor from there. Anything the caller sends can name anyone, so request data never supplies the current actor. With one resolution path, every operation answers who acts from the same verified source.

provisions.heading: Keep a Personal-Data Inventory per Store
provisions.evidence: Does the inventory name the fields, purposes, and retention of each store that holds personal data? Look at the inventory document beside the stores it lists.
provisions.statement: A platform holding personal data MUST keep a personal-data inventory per store naming the fields, purposes, and retention of each store.
provisions.rationale: Export, erasure, and breach answers each open with the same question: which stores hold this person's data, which fields, for which purposes, and for how long. An inventory the team can read answers it in one place. Without it, each request starts with a search across logs, indexes, and outboxes, and the store nobody remembers stays out of the answer.

provisions.heading: Keep Backend Authentication Provider-Neutral
provisions.evidence: Does the backend validate issuer, audience, signature, lifetime, and required claims, with no identity header accepted? Look at the authentication configuration in WebApi.
provisions.statement: A backend MUST validate issuer, audience, signature, lifetime, and required claims through OIDC and JWT Bearer.
provisions.rationale: The backend accepts one thing: a token whose issuer, audience, signature, lifetime, and required claims validate through OIDC and JWT Bearer. Provider-specific login and session behavior belongs to a frontend or an extension, because the API cannot recheck a login flow it cannot see. An unsigned token, an unvalidated decode, or a client-supplied identity header lets a caller mint its own identity, so none is ever accepted.

provisions.heading: Keep One Limit Store Across Replicas
provisions.evidence: Do all replicas read their rate and concurrency counters from one store? Look at the counter configuration of each deployment that runs more than one replica.
provisions.statement: A deployment running more than one replica MUST hold its rate and concurrency counters in one store that every replica reads.
provisions.rationale: With a counter in each process, the declared limit multiplies by the replica count: the specification states one limit while the system applies another. The multiplier shifts with every scale event, so the effective limit is never stated and never reviewed. One store that every replica reads keeps the applied limit equal to the declared one.

provisions.heading: Keep Personal Data Out of Logs
provisions.evidence: Do logs, traces, and diagnostic records carry personal data in clear? Search the log sinks and a sample of recent log output for personal fields.
provisions.statement: A log, trace, or diagnostic record MUST NOT carry personal data in clear.
provisions.rationale: Once a log line leaves the process, it flows through collectors, dashboards, and long-term archives the product does not control. Redaction at the sink is one pipeline stage that fails once, and by then the cleartext is already downstream. A field that is never emitted cannot leak from the pipeline.

provisions.heading: Keep Secrets Out of Tracked and Observable Data
provisions.evidence: Does any source, log, trace, exception message, generated file, URL, snapshot, container layer, or browser storage hold a secret? Search the tree and a sample of log and trace output for key and token values.
provisions.statement: A secret MUST NOT appear in source, logs, traces, exception messages, generated files, URLs, snapshots, container layers, or browser storage.
provisions.rationale: Every place a secret lands is a place it leaks from: source reaches every clone, logs and traces reach every dashboard reader, URLs reach every proxy log, snapshots and container layers outlive the process, and browser storage reaches the user. Platform secret stores hold the values instead, and diagnostics redact sensitive configuration before emitting it, so the value never enters the observable stream.

provisions.heading: Keep Secure Headers in Host Configuration
provisions.evidence: Do the secure headers sit in one host location, or does the convention name another arrangement? Look at the host configuration.
provisions.statement: Define Content Security Policy, frame restrictions, content-type protection, referrer policy, and transport security in one host location.
provisions.rationale: The browser reads the secure headers together: Content Security Policy, frame restrictions, content-type protection, referrer policy, and transport security form one set. Spread across middleware registrations, one of them is always the header nobody remembers. One host location keeps the set reviewable as a whole.

provisions.heading: Limit Each Use Case to Its Declared Fields
provisions.evidence: Does each use case collect, return, log, export, and retain only the fields its input and results declare? Look at each use case's input and result types and its log calls.
provisions.statement: A use case MUST collect, return, log, export, and retain only the fields its input and results declare.
provisions.rationale: A use case that collects only what it declares has nothing extra to leak. Collecting, returning, logging, exporting, and retaining only the declared fields keeps the exposure of each use case exactly what its page promises. A use case handling sensitive data states its classification, access, retention, deletion, and audit behavior on its page, so the promise sits beside the fields it covers.

provisions.heading: Limit Public Error Detail
provisions.evidence: Does each public error carry the HTTP API error contract shape, with no stack trace, SQL, or provider body? Look at the error responses the endpoint tests assert.
provisions.statement: A public error MUST use the error contract `litespec/core/backend-api#return-stable-problem-details` defines.
provisions.rationale: The HTTP API rules own the error contract, so every public error carries the same stable shape with nothing extra. A stack trace, SQL, connection detail, provider body, uncontracted internal identifier, or authorization reason that reveals resource existence hands an attacker the structure of the system with every error.

provisions.heading: Parameterize Database Input
provisions.evidence: Does each external value reach the database through a query API call or a SQL parameter? Look at the repository code and each raw SQL file.
provisions.statement: An external value reaching the database MUST travel through a provider query API or a parameterized SQL parameter.
provisions.rationale: String concatenation or interpolation into raw command text makes the value part of the statement, so a crafted value rewrites the query. A provider query API or a parameterized SQL parameter keeps the value as data. Under the baseline, the provider query API is the Marten API, and it parameterizes. The reporting extension owns the reviewed raw SQL patterns.

provisions.heading: Protect Browser Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does each frontend ship framework escaping, a Content Security Policy, secure headers, redirect validation, forgery protection, and rich-content sanitization? Look at the frontend host configuration and the response headers it sends.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST apply framework escaping, a documented Content Security Policy, secure headers, redirect validation, forgery protection, and sanitization of allowed rich content.
provisions.rationale: The browser renders every response as page content, so injected scripts, forged requests, malicious redirects, and hostile markup arrive as ordinary content. Each listed defense blocks one of those attacks. A route guard or hidden control only changes what the user sees, so it never replaces API authorization.

provisions.heading: Protect Live Data at Rest
provisions.evidence: Does each live store carry encryption, or does a waiver cover this provision? Look at each store's encryption setting and the waiver records.
provisions.statement: Live data at rest MUST carry encryption or a waiver covering this provision.
provisions.rationale: Live data at rest outlives the process: disks, snapshots, and replicas each hold a copy outside the application's control. Encryption keeps each copy unreadable without its key. Where encryption does not apply yet, a gap waiver covering this provision keeps the gap visible with its reason, exit, closing records, and expiry date instead of silent.

provisions.heading: Record Security Audit Events
provisions.evidence: Does each security audit event record actor, action, target, outcome, timestamp, trace identifier, and reason? Look at the audit writes and a sample of audit records.
provisions.statement: A security audit event MUST record actor, action, target, outcome, timestamp, trace identifier, and available reason.
provisions.rationale: After an incident, the review reconstructs who did what to which target, with what outcome and why. That reconstruction is guesswork unless each security event records actor, action, target, outcome, timestamp, trace identifier, and reason. Audit records follow a documented retention and access policy, exclude secrets, and stay available for incident review. A consumer that activates the audit extension records the event through that extension instead, which states a wider field set, a classification rule, and a tamper-evidence rule.

provisions.heading: Report a Breach Within Its Deadline
provisions.evidence: Does the breach procedure name the person who acts, a backup person, and the deadline the constraint record states? Look at the breach runbook and the constraint record it cites.
provisions.statement: A breach-notification procedure MUST name the person who acts and a backup person and meet the deadline the applicable constraint record states.
provisions.rationale: A breach deadline starts running at discovery, and the applicable constraint record states the deadline the outside rule sets. A deadline with nobody named to meet it slips past the team, and one named person fails on the first absence. Naming the person who acts and a backup before anything happens keeps the procedure starting on time.

provisions.heading: Restrict a Protected Collection in the Database
provisions.evidence: Does each protected collection query apply its authorization scope as a database predicate before paging? Look at each query handler that returns a collection.
provisions.statement: A protected collection query MUST apply its authorization scope as a database predicate, before paging, rather than filter a materialized result.
provisions.rationale: A collection has no single target, so the check that `litespec/quality/security#authorize-each-target-resource` states has nothing to resolve against. The scope becomes part of the database query itself. Reading the unrestricted set already exposes the rows to the process, and a page assembled from them leaks the total count even when every row is dropped. Filtering after the load is the shape [OWASP lists as broken object level authorization](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/2021/A01_2021-Broken_Access_Control/).
provisions.example: A Claimwick query for the expenses of an organization adds the organization predicate to the database query. It does not load every expense and drop the ones the caller may not read.

provisions.heading: Restrict Cross-Origin Access
provisions.evidence: Does the cross-origin policy list its origins, methods, headers, and credential mode, with no wildcard origin? Look at the cross-origin configuration in each host.
provisions.statement: A cross-origin policy MUST list its allowed origins, methods, headers, and credential mode without using a wildcard origin.
provisions.rationale: A wildcard origin lets any site call the API with the user's credentials and turns every malicious page into an API client. Listing the allowed origins, methods, headers, and credential mode keeps each cross-origin caller explicit. Validated configuration owns the allowlist so an unlisted origin cannot arrive by mistake, and deployment-owned origins are allowed when the allowlist shape is validated at startup.

provisions.heading: Rotate Production Secrets
provisions.evidence: Does each production secret carry an inventory entry with its location and next rotation date, beside its revocation runbook? Look at `.litespec/implementation/operations/secrets.json` and the runbooks.
provisions.statement: A production secret MUST have a secret-inventory entry naming its storage location and next rotation date, with revocation and recovery in a runbook.
provisions.rationale: Every secret leaks eventually, through a departing teammate, a copied file, or an old backup. A secret-inventory entry naming the storage location and next rotation date keeps the lifetime of each secret bounded, and rotation allows overlap while clients switch. Procedures, logs, artifacts, and audit records carry no secret value, as `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data` states, while revocation and recovery live in a runbook.

provisions.heading: Scan Every Pull Request with a Free Static Analyzer
provisions.evidence: Does the static analysis report for the pull request show a waiver for each accepted finding? Look at the analyzer report and the waiver records.
provisions.statement: CI MUST scan every pull request for security findings with a free static analyzer.
provisions.rationale: CodeQL needs no paid plan on public repositories, so it is free there. On a private repository the project uses a free alternative and records the choice in its CI documentation. An accepted finding lives as a gap waiver covering the finding, with its reason, exit, closing records, and expiry date, so each acceptance stays visible and dated.

provisions.heading: Scan Every Release with the ZAP Baseline
provisions.evidence: Does the ZAP result file under `TestResults/` show no medium or high alert for the pull request? Look at the ZAP report.
provisions.statement: CI MUST scan the running API with the ZAP baseline on every pull request.
provisions.rationale: The ZAP baseline runs the spider with passive scanning and no active attacks, so it is safe on every pull request. A WARN, FAIL, and IGNORE config file tunes it, its JSON report feeds the model with the other measured results, and the scan passes with no medium or high alert. ZAP is free and maintained under Apache-2.0.

provisions.heading: Set an ASVS Level as the Security Target
provisions.evidence: Does the security quality requirement name its ASVS 5.0 level, with a passing measure? Look at the requirement record and its measure.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST set an ASVS 5.0 level as its security target.
provisions.rationale: ASVS 5.0 defines three levels, L1, L2, and L3, with each requirement verifiable to pass or fail. The organization picks one by risk and records it on a quality requirement with its measure, as `litespec/core/intent#state-the-measure-on-a-counted-requirement` states, so the target is checked rather than declared. The level choice and each accepted finding are decided once by a person.

provisions.heading: Test the Resource Authorization Matrix
provisions.evidence: Does each protected operation pass every caller in the matrix, or does the convention name another set? Look at the authorization tests beside each protected operation.
provisions.statement: Cover anonymous, invalid-token, unrelated-actor, owner, and each privileged grant for every protected operation.
provisions.rationale: Authorization fails one caller at a time: the anonymous caller who gets in, or the unrelated actor who reads another tenant's row. Covering anonymous, invalid-token, unrelated-actor, owner, and each privileged grant for every protected operation proves each caller separately. The matrix also covers disclosure behavior and the collection query predicate, and a UI redirect or hidden control counts as no evidence.

provisions.heading: Treat an Unsalted Digest as Personal Data
provisions.evidence: Does each unsalted digest of personal data receive the handling its source data receives? Look at each hashing call on a personal field and the storage class of its result.
provisions.statement: An unsalted digest of personal data MUST receive the same handling as the data itself.
provisions.rationale: A digest without a salt reverses by table lookup: anyone holding a table of common values recovers the original. It hides nothing, so it gets none of the relaxed handling a truly one-way value gets. Handling it the same as the data itself keeps the digest from leaking what the data would.

provisions.heading: Use Deny-by-Default Policies
provisions.evidence: Does each new endpoint require authentication unless it carries `AllowAnonymous` on purpose? Look at the fallback policy and each endpoint marked `AllowAnonymous`.
provisions.statement: Set a fallback policy requiring an authenticated user, and mark each public endpoint with `AllowAnonymous` intentionally.
provisions.rationale: Without a fallback, a new endpoint nobody secured is public by accident. A fallback policy requiring an authenticated user keeps each new endpoint protected until somebody marks it public on purpose with `AllowAnonymous`. Named role or scope policies add coarse checks while the guard retains resource authorization.

provisions.heading: Use One Current Actor Abstraction
provisions.evidence: Does WebApi expose one current-actor accessor, or does the convention name another arrangement? Look at WebApi's identity code and the convention.
provisions.statement: Expose one narrow current-actor accessor in WebApi that maps verified claims to typed identity, roles, and scopes.
provisions.rationale: Claims mapping has one home: a narrow accessor in WebApi that maps verified claims once to typed identity, roles, and scopes. Application receives the actor through input that WebApi creates, or through a narrow trusted port when behavior needs to stay host-independent. A second accessor invites a second interpretation of the same claims.

provisions.heading: Validate at Trust Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does each trust boundary validate transport shape and file metadata before use? Look at the endpoints, the upload handlers, and the provider response readers.
provisions.statement: A trust boundary MUST validate transport shape and file metadata before use, leaving message checks to application validators as `litespec/core/backend-application#separate-input-validation-from-invariants` states.
provisions.rationale: Each layer validates what it can see: the boundary checks transport shape and file metadata, the application validators from `litespec/core/backend-application#separate-input-validation-from-invariants` check message shape, required values, length, range, format, and pagination bounds, and Domain checks business invariants. Database content, provider responses, file contents, and generated text stay untrusted when they cross into a new output context, because validation for one context proves nothing about the next.

provisions.heading: Derive Expected Values from the Scenario
provisions.evidence: Does any test assertion repeat values from outside the Then of its scenario? Look at each assertion beside its scenario text.
provisions.statement: A test MUST take its expected values only from the Then of the scenario it proves.
provisions.rationale: Expected values copied from the code under test restate what the code does, so the test passes with the code whatever the specification says. The Then of the scenario holds the expected ending, and the test asserts exactly that ending. The agent obligation behind this rule lives in `litespec/core/agent#take-expected-values-from-the-scenario`, with held-back example rows checked after implementation under `litespec/core/agent#verify-money-calculations-and-refusals-against-held-back-examples`.
provisions.example: When the Then says the expense is submitted, the test asserts the submitted state and the returned identifier from the scenario text. Its author reads no handler code to learn the expected values.

provisions.heading: Keep the Test Projects the Size Requires
provisions.evidence: Is any required test project missing for the declared size, or does any test project lack a page that names it? Look at the test folders beside `size` in `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A project MUST hold each test project its declared size requires, as the testing page of each selected stack names them.
provisions.rationale: The declared size decides which test projects prove the records. A project short of one has records that no boundary proves, and a project with an unnamed extra project collects tests that no page placed. Each stack names its projects on its testing page, so the required set reads in one place per stack.
provisions.example: A large backend holds the architecture, integration, and acceptance projects its backend testing page names, while a small backend holds the first two.

provisions.heading: Prove Each Rule Through Its Scenarios
provisions.evidence: Does any rule claim stand without a proved scenario claim on the same test? Look at each rule claim.
provisions.statement: A rule claim MUST confirm only through a scenario the same test proves.
provisions.rationale: Every rule holds at the point its kind names: an invariant inside the aggregate, a precondition at the guard, a calculation in its pure evaluation, and a rule whose `binds` names the aggregates it spans, at the state guard or the atomic use case. A scenario that walks through that point exercises the rule, so the rule claim rides on the scenario proof instead of carrying its own enforcement-point mark. A calculation rule earns its proof from a scenario carrying the examples table that `litespec/core/domain-model#tabulate-every-calculation-with-examples` requires.
provisions.example: A test proves the scenario for an expense above the threshold with no receipt, and claims the receipt rule alongside it. The scenario sends the command and asserts the `spending.receipt-missing` refusal, and the rule claim confirms because the same test proves the scenario. No separate mark names the validator or the store.

provisions.heading: Prove Each Scenario Through the Public Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does every scenario have a proving test with its mark, boundary call, and passing run? Look at the book beside the test bodies.
provisions.statement: Each scenario MUST be proved by a test carrying its proves mark, calling its use case through the public boundary, and asserting the result the scenario names.
provisions.rationale: A scenario states one behavior the product shows, and the proves mark is the test claim that it shows it. A test that drives the use case through its steps, its message, or its endpoint exercises the public boundary, while a test that constructs a handler, an aggregate, or a repository reaches past it and proves nothing. The assertion names the result: the success fields for a success, the refusal code inside an assertion for a refusal. A reaction or job scenario is proved the same way: its test fires the trigger and asserts what the effects declare, the use case result, the sent notification, or the outside call. A scenario no test proves is recorded as a gap waiver with its reason, exit, closing records, and expiry date. The latest test run marks each confirmed claim passing or failing.
provisions.example: An acceptance test for submitting an expense carries the mark for `scenario/submit-expense.submitting-with-a-receipt-succeeds`, drives the submit-expense steps, and asserts the submitted expense. An integration test for the same scenario builds the submit-expense message, sends it through the host, and asserts the same result. In both, the mark names the scenario, the call crosses the public boundary, and the model builder confirms the claim from the test body.

provisions.heading: Refuse One Coverage Percentage as Sufficient Testing
provisions.evidence: Does any build gate name a coverage percentage as sufficient? Look at the build gates beside the coverage numbers.
provisions.statement: A repository MUST NOT treat one coverage percentage as the definition of sufficient testing.
provisions.rationale: One coverage percentage rewards tests that execute lines without asserting behavior, so a suite reaches the target while proving no scenario. Coverage stays useful as review input: the project collects line and branch numbers without treating any value as sufficient. The evidence is scenario proof, domain edge cases, integration boundaries, security behavior, and architecture rules, with mutation results on changed lines under `litespec/quality/testing#refuse-surviving-mutants-on-changed-lines`.

provisions.heading: Refuse Surviving Mutants on Changed Lines
provisions.evidence: Did any change land with survivors above the recorded threshold and no covering waiver? Look at the mutation report beside the waiver records.
provisions.statement: Gate each change on the project's recorded mutation threshold over its changed lines, starting at zero surviving mutants; each equivalent mutant is recorded as a lasting waiver covering the mutation finding.
provisions.rationale: Mutation testing seeds small faults into the changed lines and runs the suite against them. Each killed mutant is a fault the tests catch, and each survivor is a fault they miss. The gate counts survivors on changed lines only, so every change arrives proven. A project-wide percentage confounds suite size with strength, and a full nightly run serves as a trend rather than a gate. An equivalent mutant preserves behavior by construction, so no test can kill it, and the waiver records that judgment with its reason and consequences instead of blocking the change forever.
provisions.example: A change touching the receipt check runs mutation over those lines with the scenario suite. Survivors at or below the recorded threshold let the change land, and the rest send the change back for a stronger assertion, or into a waiver when the mutant is equivalent.

provisions.heading: Use One Mock Rule for Every Stack
provisions.evidence: Does any test double replace the project's own repositories, handlers, modules, or generated contract types instead of an outside provider or a non-deterministic value? Look at each test double and the mocks each test file imports.
provisions.statement: A test MUST substitute only what the code under test does not own and what is not deterministic, and never the code's own repositories, handlers, or modules.
provisions.rationale: Every substitute replaces behavior the test does not run with its author's guess. A test that stubs its own repositories, handlers, or modules proves the guess instead of the code. A substitute belongs only where the code under test cannot reach the real thing: an outside provider it does not control, another deployable it calls over the network such as the API a frontend calls, or a value that changes between runs such as the clock or randomness. Settled by [decision/0032-one-mock-rule-for-every-stack](decision/0032-one-mock-rule-for-every-stack).
provisions.example: To test payment, the test substitutes the card provider and a fixed clock, and runs the expense handler against the real expense repository. A Claimwick web component test answers its API calls with network mocks generated from the published API document.

provisions.heading: Keep Documentation Directories Out of Build-Artifact Ignore Rules
provisions.evidence: Does each documentation directory stay tracked, with `git check-ignore` reporting no match for the record paths under `docs/`? Run the check on the record paths.
provisions.statement: Exclude a documentation directory from a build-artifact ignore rule that matches it by accident.
provisions.rationale: Platform `.gitignore` templates match broad names, so a documentation directory with such a name silently stops being tracked. Excluding the documentation directory from the rule keeps records tracked, and `git check-ignore` confirms each record stays visible.
provisions.example:
```gitignore
[Oo]utput/
!docs/<directory>/
!docs/<directory>/*.yaml
!docs/<directory>/*.md
```

Confirm with `git check-ignore docs/<directory>/<file>.yaml` that no record is ignored.

provisions.heading: Keep Environment Examples Beside Applications
provisions.evidence: Does each frontend and deployable host directory hold a `.env.example` with required names and safe values, or does the project documentation name a central example location? Look beside each frontend and host.
provisions.statement: Keep a `.env.example` beside each frontend and deployable host listing required names and safe values.
provisions.rationale: A new developer copies the example to start, and a reviewer reads it to learn which names the application needs. Kept beside the frontend or host it documents, next to the options module that reads those names, the example changes in the same edit as the names. Kept anywhere else, it goes stale without anyone noticing.

provisions.heading: Keep Local Overrides Untracked
provisions.evidence: Do developer overrides live in ignored local files or a platform secret store, with no second tracked environment-specific source? Look at the ignore rules and the tracked configuration files.
provisions.statement: Keep developer overrides in ignored local files or a platform secret store.
provisions.rationale: Developer overrides differ per machine by nature: ports, paths, and local endpoints. Committing them turns one developer's setup into everyone's default. Ignored local files or a platform secret store keep overrides personal, so no second committed source competes with the deployment platform for the same value.

provisions.heading: Keep Logging Configuration Provider-Neutral
provisions.evidence: Does application source log through standard abstractions with exporter configuration in hosts, or does the host configuration name the project's own logging setup? Look at the logging calls and the host configuration.
provisions.statement: Emit structured logs through standard logging abstractions and keep exporter configuration in hosts.
provisions.rationale: Application code writes through standard logging abstractions while each host configures its exporter, so application code carries no provider choice. Switching a log backend stays inside deployment settings instead of touching every call site.

provisions.heading: Keep Secrets Outside Source Control
provisions.evidence: Does each tracked configuration file carry only safe defaults and placeholders, with real values in user secrets or the deployment platform? Read the tracked configuration files.
provisions.statement: A tracked configuration file MUST keep secrets out of tracked and observable data, as `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data` states, and contain only safe defaults and placeholders.
provisions.rationale: A tracked file reaches every clone and stays in history after deletion. No real value needs to be tracked: local development uses user secrets and hosted environments use the deployment platform. Safe defaults and placeholders keep the tracked file working as documentation.

provisions.heading: Pin the JavaScript Toolchain
provisions.evidence: Does the root `package.json` declare `packageManager` and a Node.js engine matching the manifest releases, with CI provisioning the same releases? Read the root `package.json` and the CI setup.
provisions.statement: Root `package.json` MUST declare the manifest pnpm stack release in `packageManager` and a Node.js engine matching the manifest node stack release.
provisions.rationale: Different Node.js or pnpm releases resolve, build, and lint differently. Declaring the manifest pnpm release in `packageManager` and a matching Node.js engine keeps every developer and CI on the same toolchain. CI provisions that Node.js release and invokes the declared pnpm release, so local and CI resolve identically.

provisions.heading: Pin the React Version in the ESLint Flat Config
provisions.evidence: Does each React ESLint flat config set a concrete `settings.react.version`? Look at the flat config of each React frontend.
provisions.statement: When the workspace holds a React frontend, its ESLint flat config MUST set a concrete `settings.react.version` rather than leave it at `detect`.
provisions.rationale: The `detect` setting calls context APIs that the pinned ESLint release removed, so it fails under the pinned toolchain. A concrete `settings.react.version` skips detection entirely and lints against the version the workspace ships.

provisions.heading: Use One Frontend Dependency Graph
provisions.evidence: Does the workspace hold one root `package.json`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, and `pnpm-lock.yaml`, with no nested lockfile tracked? Look at the workspace root and each application folder.
provisions.statement: A TypeScript workspace MUST use one root `package.json`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, and `pnpm-lock.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: One root manifest and one lockfile resolve one version of each package for the whole workspace. A nested lockfile lets one application resolve a different version than the one workspace CI installs, so local builds and CI builds disagree about the same code. One graph keeps every install identical.

provisions.heading: Validate Backend Configuration at Startup
provisions.evidence: Does each backend section bind a settings type that fails startup on a missing field, a bad range, or a bad format? Read the settings types beside the backend host.
provisions.statement: A backend configuration section MUST bind to a named settings type validated for required fields, ranges, and formats at startup.
provisions.rationale: A missing or malformed setting fails somewhere. Bound to a validated settings type, it fails at startup with a named field, while the deployment can still stop. Read through a raw configuration lookup, it fails at the first request that needs it.

provisions.heading: Validate Frontend Environment Access
provisions.evidence: Does each frontend read environment values only through `src/lib/env.ts`, with server-only values apart from browser-visible ones? Look at the environment imports in each frontend.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST read environment variables through one validated module separating server-only from browser-visible values, at `src/lib/env.ts` through the framework alias.
provisions.rationale: A frontend bundle ships to the browser, so every value it reads becomes public. One validated module at `src/lib/env.ts` separates server-only values from browser-visible ones in a single place a reviewer can read. Browser-visible names use the framework prefix, so an unprefixed value stays out of the bundle.

provisions.heading: Approve New Packages Explicitly
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `dependency-undeclared` (level S) for a direct package in the bill of materials that the manifest does not pin and no decision admits, and `admission-invalid` (level G) for an `admits` entry missing any of its six facts.
provisions.statement: A package absent from the manifest MUST be admitted by a technical decision whose `admits` entry names the package with its owning layer, license, processing location, account owner, failure behavior, and operating cost.
provisions.rationale: Every package carries a cost nobody revisits: updates, advisories, license review, and migration work. A hosted one adds a place personal data can travel and an account someone must own. The decision answers those costs while the alternatives are still fresh: its options and choice give the use case and the alternatives, its `reopenedWhen` gives the removal condition, and its `admits` entry gives the facts a dependency gate asks per package. A baseline package is added to the manifest in the same change as its decision, while a consumer-owned package is added to the consumer central file instead, because the manifest belongs to the LiteSpec release rather than to the consumer.
provisions.example: The Claimwick `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` decision chooses a PDF library over an HTML-to-PDF browser and admits `nuget:PdfSharp` with layer `Infrastructure`, license `MIT`, location `in-process`, account owner `none`, failure behavior "the receipt download fails and the expense stays readable", and operating cost `none`.

provisions.heading: Assign Each Baseline Package to Its Owning Layer
provisions.evidence: Does each baseline package sit in the owning layer the table in this section assigns, or does the admitting decision name the project's own owning layer? Read the layer manifests beside the table.
provisions.statement: Assign each baseline package to the owning layer named in the table in this section.
provisions.example:
| Layer | Direct package groups |
|:---|:---|
| Domain | None |
| Application | Required abstractions only, plus the declared read boundary |
| Infrastructure | Providers and adapters required by implemented ports |
| WebApi | Host, authentication, and documentation packages |
| Test code | Test-only packages |

A new package belongs in the narrowest layer that needs it. A central version entry does not authorize every layer to reference that package; the table decides which layer takes each package. A consumer references conditional packages only after their extension activates.

provisions.heading: Follow the Declared Dependency Graph
provisions.evidence: Does each layer and module dependency follow the declared graph? Read the references between layer folders under `apps/api/src` and the imports in `apps/`.
provisions.statement: A dependency between layers or modules MUST follow the declared graph and add no other edge.
provisions.rationale: The declared graph names the crossings between layers and modules that review checks. An undeclared edge lets a layer reach past its boundary while review has no graph that forbids it. Each new edge then needs an explicit decision instead of arriving silently with an import.

provisions.heading: Keep Application Free of Provider Packages
provisions.evidence: Does the Application layer reference only messaging abstractions, read abstractions, and the declared read boundary? Read those folders and the manifests that serve them.
provisions.statement: Application MUST depend only on messaging abstractions, required read abstractions, and the one declared read boundary.
provisions.rationale: Application coordinates use cases through abstractions, while Infrastructure hides the technology behind them. A provider package in Application makes the coordination layer depend on the technology Infrastructure exists to hide, so a provider change reaches two layers. Only messaging abstractions, required read abstractions, and the one declared read boundary stay.

provisions.heading: Keep Domain Dependency-Free
provisions.evidence: Does any Domain layer folder need an external package or framework? Read the Domain layer folders and the manifests that serve them.
provisions.statement: The Domain layer MUST depend on no external package or framework.
provisions.rationale: Business rules outlive frameworks, and Domain holds the business rules. Depending on no external package or framework keeps the rules testable and portable on their own. Persistence, messaging, web, injection, serialization, and logging libraries all stay outside.

provisions.heading: Keep Frontend Applications Isolated
provisions.evidence: Does any import in one frontend name another application's source or another module's internal feature files? Search the frontend imports.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST NOT import another application's source or another module's internal feature files.
provisions.rationale: When one frontend imports the source of another, neither can change its internals without checking the other, so the two release as one. The same holds for the internal feature files of another module. Sharing goes through a shared package with a documented public entry point that depends on no application.

provisions.heading: Keep Generated Packages Dependency-Light
provisions.evidence: Does the generated API types package carry no dependencies, with the shared client limited to the generator runtime, its query plugin, and those types, or does the client package manifest name the project's own client dependency set? Read the generated package manifests.
provisions.statement: Keep generated API types free of dependencies and limit the shared client to the pinned generator's runtime, its query plugin, and those types.
provisions.rationale: Generated types mirror the API contract, and the shared client only passes them to queries. Keeping the types free of dependencies and the client limited to the generator runtime, its query plugin, and those types keeps regeneration dependent on the contract alone. A generated package that owns state, UI behavior, or authentication policy is no longer regenerable.

provisions.heading: Keep Providers in Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Do database providers, external SDKs, and resilience, discovery, and serialization adapters appear only in the Infrastructure layer folders? Read those folders and the manifests that serve them.
provisions.statement: A database provider, external SDK, resilience, discovery, or serialization adapter MUST live in Infrastructure.
provisions.rationale: Database providers, external SDKs, and resilience, discovery, and serialization adapters all change with their technology. Keeping them in Infrastructure keeps each provider change inside one layer, apart from the read boundary the ownership table assigns to Application.

provisions.heading: Keep Test Dependencies in Test Projects
provisions.evidence: Does any production project manifest reference an assertion, substitution, host, container, or architecture-test package, or does the project documentation name the shipped helper and its reason? Read the production project manifests.
provisions.statement: Keep assertion, substitution, host, container, and architecture-test packages inside test projects.
provisions.rationale: Assertion, substitution, host, container, and architecture-test packages exist to verify code, not to run it. Once a production project references one, it ships to production with its own dependencies and advisories. Keeping them inside test projects keeps test packages out of the shipped graph.

provisions.heading: Pin Every Dependency Version Centrally
provisions.evidence: Does every version resolve through central management or the committed lockfile within the manifest major where one exists, with no version inline in a module file? Read the central version files and the module files.
provisions.statement: Every dependency version MUST resolve through central management or the committed lockfile, within the major `litespec.manifest.yaml` pins where it pins one.
provisions.rationale: An inline version in one module file is invisible to the file that should own it, so two modules drift to two versions of the same package. Central management or the committed lockfile resolves every version in one owned place. The manifest pins the major of each baseline package, so a consumer takes a patch without waiting for a LiteSpec release, and it pins an exact version only where a check depends on exact output. The manifest belongs to the LiteSpec release rather than to the consumer, so the exact versions of a consumer live beside its code, admitted by `litespec/workspace/dependencies#approve-new-packages-explicitly`. Settled by [decision/0036-pin-third-party-packages-to-their-major](decision/0036-pin-third-party-packages-to-their-major).
provisions.example: The Claimwick central version file holds Marten at 9.50.2 while the manifest pins `9.x`, so the project takes a patch without waiting for a LiteSpec release. Its receipt PDF library is pinned exact in the same file with a decision record, because the manifest names only the baseline stack.

provisions.heading: Take Web UI Packages from the Approved Baseline
provisions.evidence: Does each React frontend take UI packages only from `uiBaseline`, and each Svelte one only from `uiBaselineSvelte`? Read each frontend manifest beside `litespec.manifest.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A React web frontend MUST take its UI packages from the `uiBaseline` in `litespec.manifest.yaml`, and a Svelte web frontend from `uiBaselineSvelte`.
provisions.rationale: A fixed UI baseline keeps every screen on the same design system, styling, base components, icons, and utilities. Taking UI packages only from `uiBaseline` for React and `uiBaselineSvelte` for Svelte keeps that set reviewed and versioned in one place. Each baseline pins the design system, styling, base components, icons, and the utility packages the installed source imports directly.

provisions.heading: Declare Each Pipeline Concern in Its Own Class
provisions.evidence: Does any class declare two pipeline concerns? Read each pipeline declaration beside its message.
provisions.statement: Each pipeline declaration MUST sit in its own class, implementing exactly one pipeline contract.
provisions.rationale: Who may send a message and how the audit trail records it change for different reasons, and are read by different people: an access review reads the authorization declaration, and an audit review reads the audit declaration. One class per concern keeps each review to its own file. Settled by [decision/0106-state-class-design-rules](decision/0106-state-class-design-rules).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, the submit-expense authorization and audit declarations sit in two classes: `SubmitExpenseCommandAuthorizationDefinition` and `SubmitExpenseCommandAuditDefinition`. Each implements its own pipeline contract, and neither names the other concern.

provisions.heading: Give Each Class One Responsibility
provisions.evidence: Does every class have one responsibility, readable in one sentence without "and"? Read each class beside its callers.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: A class MUST have one responsibility.
provisions.rationale: A class with one responsibility has one reason to change, so a reader reviews one job and a change risks one job. Without this rule, an author optimizes for fewer files and merges unrelated concerns wherever an interface allows it. The test stays plain: the class's job reads in one sentence without "and". Settled by [decision/0106-state-class-design-rules](decision/0106-state-class-design-rules).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, an expense repository that also renders the spending report splits into the repository and a report renderer. Each is read by different people and changes for different reasons.

provisions.heading: Implement One Capability per Class
provisions.evidence: Does any class implement interfaces for more than one capability? Read the interface list of each class.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: A class MUST implement more than one interface only when the interfaces describe one capability.
provisions.rationale: Interfaces that describe one capability offer callers one thing, so they belong together. Interfaces for unrelated concerns, such as authorization, audit, idempotency, persistence, and rendering, change for different reasons and are read by different people. One class implementing two of them merges those concerns into one file, and a later reader cannot review one without the other. Settled by [decision/0106-state-class-design-rules](decision/0106-state-class-design-rules).
provisions.example: A class implementing `IReadOnlyList<T>` with `IEnumerable<T>` offers one capability. A class implementing an authorization contract with an audit contract merges two concerns, and splits into two classes.

provisions.heading: Name Each Definition After Its Message and Concern
provisions.evidence: Does every pipeline declaration class carry its message and concern in `{Message}{Concern}Definition` form? Read each declaration beside its message.
provisions.statement: Name each pipeline declaration class `{Message}{Concern}Definition`, such as `SubmitExpenseCommandAuthorizationDefinition`.
provisions.rationale: The message leads, so every declaration for one message lists beside it, and the concern trails, so each review finds its own file. One naming shape lets a reader move from the message to each of its declarations without searching. Settled by [decision/0106-state-class-design-rules](decision/0106-state-class-design-rules).

provisions.heading: Take Shared Behavior Through Composition
provisions.evidence: Does any class derive from a base that collects unrelated helpers? Read each base class beside its derived classes.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: A class MUST take shared behavior through composition rather than through a base class that collects unrelated helpers.
provisions.rationale: A base class that collects unrelated helpers gives every derived class behavior most of them never use, and each addition to the base reaches every derived class. Taking the behavior through a constructor parameter keeps each class beside only the behavior it uses. A base that defines one shared contract, such as the aggregate root base, is no helper collection. Settled by [decision/0106-state-class-design-rules](decision/0106-state-class-design-rules).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, an expense validator takes its receipt checker as a constructor parameter instead of deriving from a validation base that also formats currencies.

provisions.heading: Align Business Names Across Layers
provisions.evidence: Does one business name for each module span Domain, Application, endpoints, features, and documentation, or does the project documentation name the project's own per-layer names? Read the module names in each layer.
provisions.statement: Use one business name for a module across Domain, Application, endpoints, features, and documentation.
provisions.rationale: One business name per module keeps every layer using the same word: the Posts module maps to `Shop/Posts`, `features/posts`, and `.litespec/behavior/modules/posts` without translation. A second name in any layer reads as a second concept that does not exist.

provisions.heading: Anchor Aggregate-Owned Types on the Aggregate Root
provisions.evidence: Does each aggregate-owned type name in `apps/api/src` begin with its aggregate root name, through nesting or prefix? Read the type names beside their aggregates.
provisions.statement: An aggregate-owned type's qualified name MUST start with its aggregate root's full name.
provisions.rationale: Leading with the root name reveals the owner without folder context. The rule covers events, states, child entities, values, and discriminated unions. A type nested inside a declaring type inherits the prefix of that type through its qualified name, so `PostState.Published` satisfies the rule, while a flat `PostStatePublishedState` repeats the anchor twice.
provisions.example: `PostPublishedDomainEvent` and `PostState.Published` both lead with `Post`. `PublishedState` declared at namespace level does not.

provisions.heading: Avoid Generic Type Names
provisions.evidence: Does each type name in `apps/api/src` avoid the listed generic names where a narrower name exists, or does the project documentation name the kept name and its reason? Read the type names.
